I'm thoroughly impressed with this Bluetooth speaker. It's very well built, dust proof and waterproof. It's an excellent choice to use around the pool, beach, in a shower and all water environments. It has an IP67 dust and waterproof rating. It can be submersed in 3 feet of water, for 30 minutes, without issue. It has a rugged rubber exterior, that will protect against shocks. It's an excellent choice for rough and tumble environments as well.

You can literally see and feel the quality in this little gem of a speaker.

Please note ::: I have not submersed it in water, but a video review on Amazon actually demonstrates that it can be fully submersed. It easily passed the test in that video. We aren't going to intentionally dunk our speaker in 3 feet of water. But if it should happen, it would survive and function. The IP67 waterproof rating is piece of mind and perfect for a near water lifestyle.

100% waterproof with the power/aux/micro SD cover securely closed.

What's included in box:

1x Waterproof/Dustproof Bluetooth Speaker
1x Velcro Carrying Strap
1x Custom Storage Bag
1x USB Charging Cable
1x AUX Cable
1x Power Adapter
1x User Manual

You can most certainly tell SHARKK took pride and no shortcuts with its packaging and included accessories. There's definitely pride here in the way they present this speaker to it's customers. Very well done! I really appreciate that SHARKK included the AC wall adapter in it's package of accessories. I've purchased Bluetooth speakers that did not include the adapter and ask you to use your smartphone adapter. Nice touch by SHARKK! The Velour carrying bag and Velcro strap are excellent additions and really give the entire package an upgraded feel and look. Everything you need is included and then some. I posted a few pictures.

Now to the meat and potatoes of this powerful waterproof speaker.

I'm not an audiophile, but I enjoy a quality speaker. This is a great sounding speaker, with crystal clear treble and the bass does not disappoint. There's a generous thump on tracks that have bass. It almost defies belief that it sounds so clear, rich and full. This little guy literally moves around when playing songs with bass. Wow! Make sure it's not on a slick surface. I've put a very small towel under it, to insure it wouldn't move and fall off a table. Volume was set two clicks from the max setting, in iOS. Speaker set to max setting. I played and tested music using Spotify.

There's no sound distortion, that I can hear, even at the max setting.

You can use it as a speakerphone and use Siri through the speaker as well. It handles these two functions perfectly. You can hear the person on the other end of the line perfectly and vice versa. Great feature and very well implemented by SHARKK. There's a micro SD slot as well. You can copy gigs of music to your micro SD card and play tons of music without the Bluetooth feature. You can use up to a 32 gig micro SD. Another excellent feature.

The 2200 mAh lithium ion battery gives you up 10 hours of playing time when fully charged. Since my speaker is relatively new, I will provide updated results on battery life later and edit this review. When connected to Bluetooth, a battery status symbol shows up in your iPhone/iPad/iPod. (Update: 4-5 hours higher volumes. 9-10 hours lower volumes.)

Two minor quibbles that I have with this speaker. As previously mentioned, the bass is impressive and this makes the speaker move around. Secondly, you have to hold the power button down for 4 seconds to power up the speaker and 2 seconds to power it off. Those instructions are reversed in the owner's manual.

If you need a speaker that is rugged, dust and waterproof, plays music beautifully and has useful features, then you can not go wrong with the SHARKK 2o. It's like SHARKK took the best of their Boombox,wrapped it in the SHARKK 2o and made it waterproof. There's plenty of thought and design that went into creating this speaker.

This waterproof Bluetooth speaker is a real winner in my book! This is an excellent product. I can highly recommend the SHARKK 2o without reservation.

1. Inteset has just a handful of codes for audio equipment; that's a far cry from being "programmed with the device codes for every TV, computer and A/V device known." None of the codes worked with my receiver; I had to learn them all from the remote that came with it.

You have to move the functions to the correct buttons yourself. The Inteset support forum has a post about how to do that; search for "roamio".

3. The remote has a glossy finish around the upper buttons that really shows fingerprints.

4. Four devices is pretty limiting.

With all that said -- it does in fact work with everything that I programmed it for, but it took a couple of trips to the support forums and some learn-mode programming to get it all to work.

PRO TIP: Many TVs have codes to directly select a specific input like HDMI 1, HDMI 2, etc. This is great for programming a device macro. Problem is, the factory remotes usually can't send those codes. HOWEVER -- if you have an Android phone with an IR blaster, set up the Peel Smart Remote app to switch your TV directly to a specific inputs (using the Activity feature). Then use the learning mode on the remote to teach it the direct-input codes from Peel. Works like a charm.

Both were very simple to do, but I found myself relying on the indicator light to know if pairing occurred when using NFC because I was holding the phone and the headphones together to pair in front of me and could not hear the audio prompts occurring in the headphones (NFC pairs by touching the devices together).

Regarding sound quality, I am not an audiophile, so if it sounds good to me, it sounds good. The sound that comes out of these headphones is super crisp in my opinion. To me, these seem to be lacking in the bass department, but mids and highs are good. I listened to some rock, rap, and movie soundtracks during my initial testing.

There is one big (at least to me) problem with these that I need to point out. The sound, at my normal listening level...which may be a bit high, leaks out of these headphones and the people surrounding you can hear what you are listening to. My wife pointed this out to me as I was testing (listening) to various kinds of music. She could tell me what song I was listening to. I am usually an earbuds kind of person, and this is not a problem with my earbuds. This may be a problem with headphones of this shape in general and I will have to go back and test other headphones to be sure if other products have this issue.

Overall, these are very nice. Just be sure not to listen too loud.

I have several Bluetooth speakers for various specific applications (one at work, one for yard work/ on the go etc...) This one I bought for personal listening around the house, on the back deck for music while bbq'ing or just hanging out etc...

I am absolutely impressed by its full range musical abilities. Clear highs, smooth mids & vocals that are rich & vibrant. It even has VERY respectable low end. The bass is punchy & very audible considering its size. it can even hit well below 100hz which is impressive all by its self.

It's covered with a nice hemp/cotton material that I've read is also made of recycled plastic bottles. It has a Real bamboo wood strip across the back with the company's branding (Marley). The plastic casing under the material is also made of recycled plastic. The overall feel of the unit is solid & sturdy. It "feels" like you're getting your money worth & isn't cheap.

The front grill is metal with the company logo on the bottom right. The logo lights up blue when the unit is on. Flashes blue when in pairing mode & flashes between red & blue when battery is low. Also, The indicator light isn't overly bright & annoying in dimly lit areas..but can be slightly seen even in brighter lighting.

The controls are EASY to use & understand even for a first time user of Bluetooth speakers. The Bluetooth button also acts as a call button & pause button for music as well as pairing although I'm not sure why it's called the bluetooth pairing button due to the fact the speaker goes into pairing mode as soon as you turn it on.

The micro USB port for charging is under a silicone flap on the right back/side & an Aux 3.5mm input is on the left side, also under a silicone flap. It has 2 silcone "feet" on the bottom so the unit isn't directly on the surface its placed on & they absorb much of the vibration from the bass of the music which could be an issue if there are other items on the table such as coins etc...that would rattle around if they weren't there.

I believe this speaker comes in 2 versions. I have read that this speaker is also available with 4, 1" drivers however which is either an earlier version of this device or what is being bought overseas, I'm not sure. I say that becuz my unit has 2, 1.65" drivers on the left & right for stereo sound & a large bass radiator in the middle which I suspect is why it sounds so amazing for bassy music considering small foot print.

As for battery life. I played it for just over 6hrs at work just to break in the speakers & it still had charge for about another hour-ish at home after work before it needed charging & that was JUST its charge straight out of the box. (Indicated by the blue Marley logo on the front flashing red & then back to blue)

In closing; if you have the money to purchase a "higher end" Bluetooth speaker, give this one serious consideration. In my opinion this is a very good buy for its purpose, for playing music. I had to create an adapter from a Tip-Ring-Ring-Sleeve 3.5mm jack, to a 1/4 inch stereo plug in order to test this way, but it allowed me to plug into a better signal than a phone or MP3 player for testing purposes.

What you'll be buying is just another good looking set of in ear 'phones, they appear to be what you should expect in this price range. You'll see the flat cable because that stands out right away. I'm not going to push flat or round on you, you decide, but this cable is not going to tangle as much and it's as close to perfectly quiet as they come. For you tall guys, this is a longer style cable and they've also included a removable clip on it. You'll also receive a hard shell case for them.

What's going into your ears is a small, lightweight earpiece. I think that this is important, because all of the 'phones that fall out of my ears, are the heavier models. These stay in my ears much better than most BlueTooth sports models do, and I think it's simply because of gravity, those are heavier due to batteries and circuitry. These are 100% perfectly comfortable in my own ears.

I haven't had a lot of phone conversations while wearing these, but my testing proved them to be adequate for it. I'm a bit of a dinosaur and feel like I'm tech support or something while talking on a headset.

So what Mr. Noontec sends me, is a set of good, high quality in ear 'phones that my associates and I agree sound extremely accurate at reproducing audio for their price. These are one of the best sounding in ear 'phones that I've ever heard. But I'm not talking about what is “liked”, you're free to like whatever you want, I said accurate.

What I'm talking about is when monitoring a drummer, miked up in the drum room through a console for instance. No EQ, just a good drum kit, with 14 microphones on it and ready to be recorded, with this headset connected to the headphone amp from the console along with the typical studio headsets to make comparisons. These sound like you're in the room with the drummer, I checked them extensively and they brought a smile to the faces in the two other facilities also, thumbs up, and at this price, two thumbs up.

Perspective, what this means to most users is that from any device that you plug these into you will be hearing very close to the true sound from it. If the recording or your device is poor quality, you'll hear that, and the converse is true also. I think that this is always a good thing, but opinions vary. Just remember that facts and opinions are not the same thing.

I can't rate the long term durability as I've only had these about ten days now, but nothing about the quality of this headset worries me either. I ran them up to painful listening levels and also let them run overnight twice.

If you want to hear what the actual recording sounds like from your in ear headphones, I recommend these. If you want to hear that and then tailor the sound to what you yourself like to listen to, I can recommend these. I don't recommend these for animals outside of the human species though, I cannot universally endorse this product after all and this is what I was afraid would happen. I don't stamp 5 stars onto products and yet, what Mr. Noontec has sent me, leaves me no choice.

I do believe that about 97% of the population will be happy with these 'phones and will agree that you don't need to spend any more than this on a set of in ear headphones. The other 3% of the population likely have some malady and are just unhappy about everything. If you don't like the music that you hear from this headset you should blame us, because you don't like how we did it in the studio.

I will start by saying that this Bluetooth receiver works well and is very compact. There are some specific details that I was concerned about for my application and I will clarify some of the functionality of the device.

The audio quality from the device is surprisingly decent (the paired device is in very close proximity during operation). There is an album that was particularly affected by lossy audio codecs even when ripped from Vinyl in 320Kbps MP3, and when playing a lossless format from my paired phone, there wasn't much of a perceivable difference in quality versus plugging directly into the headphone jack on the phone at the same volume.

The blue light behind the multi-function (Play/Pause) button is not particularly bright meaning that it doesn't consume much energy during operation. That also means that when I am attempting to turn it on/off in direct sunlight in my car, I am connecting via trial and error and I cant tell what stage the device is in by just looking at it.

The battery lasts a sufficiently long amount of time.

The +/- arrows on the edge of the device are handy. This is one of the features I was looking for most in a BT receiver device, and it was not expressly detailed in the description of this device. The buttons act as forward/back for tracks with short presses. They then act as volume up/down with long presses. This works well for me because when I am using my phone in my vehicle for longer trips, it is being used with a GPS app that is up on the screen constantly and to change tracks, I must use the interface on the phone. This device allows me to change tracks without even looking at the screen because I can feel for the device and then change the track with the physical buttons.

The device will wait in a standby mode for a few minutes if turned on and not connected to any paired device or if the paired device is disconnected. It will automatically attempt to connect to the paireddevice when powered on. The battery level of the receiver is relayed to the paired device if the paired device supports it.

The mic on the device itself works well enough but I have not tried it with excessive exhaust/road noise.

A cheap addition that would add value in my opinion would be a simple mounting solution other than the double sided headphone jack like a square of double-sided foam tape or velcro pad to allow mounting on to a certain part of the dash.

The reason for 4 stars instead of 5 is solely based in that I can't quickly turn it on when I get into my car, the button has to be held for 5 seconds. Even if I could wire it to turn on when it receives USB power and then wire a USB charger to be activated with my ignition when I start the car so that I do not need to hold the button to use it, that would be great as well.

Here are the pros of these headphones:
1. They are extremely comfortable. Pads are very soft and put little to no pressure on your head. Plus they look nice.

There were only two things that didn't work for me with these.
1. The delay in audio when watching a video was way too substantial to be used effectively.
2. I don't know if this was just a Sony thing, but the ear pads rotate which I found weird and a little concerning in regards to the price of these. Not sure if they are replaceable.
3. This was a personal issue I had with it, but I didn't like the pouch it came with. It was too difficult to slide the headphones in and out of.

I wish I could've kept them. I have, however, since bought a pair of Bluetooth Bose headphones. Those of which don't have any of the problems these had, but I will admit, the sound quality is not as good (but it's close). The Bose headphones can have two connections simultaneously which means you can have your phone and laptop (or tablet) connected at the same time. So if you're watching a video on a tablet and get a call, you can automatically take it with the headphones without having to re-pair it. Everything else is comparable though.

The last and only Walkman I owned was back in the mid-80s. That was a cassette tape player with headphones. Things have surely come a long way!

I was drawn to this because of its hi-res quality. So far I've not been disappointed on that score. The sound is excellent, probably better than my other equipment can reflect. The unit is light but not flimsy--extremely portable. While a touch screen would have been nice, things are easily navigable, much after the fashion of a digital camera. I'm a Mac user, and while some Mackies have complained that they can't export to this device from iTunes, I don't find that to be a hindrance. Unlike the iPod, the Walkman shows up on your desktop as an external disk. You can double click on the Music folder on the device, and simply drag files from your iTunes music folder without the mediation of iTunes itself. The Walkman's software makes good sense and organization out of the iTunes folders. In short, you can bypass iTunes altogether. While some may not like this, I find it gives me better control in loading just what I want onto the device. Using the Walkman disk this way, you can even rename folders and files on your Walkman when it is connected to your computer. I'm not even going to bother with the special Mac software for loading music files.

What else? No issues with Bluetooth connection. High-quality sound. Ample storage for such a portable device--although I'll be glad when I can fit my whole AIFF music library on a tiny player. Much as I've enjoyed my iPods in the past, I think this is better for those interested in one thing: listening to their music in high-quality format.

I want to start this review by saying that Monoprice sent me these headphones free of charge for review.
With that in mind the price point for these headphones is spot on. If one was looking for a set of headphones that were as functional as they were aesthetically pleasing, these would be the ones to look for, especially for $99.

The box these headphones come in is very clean, minimal and well built. The important information is written on the back of the box with listings such as 32 ohm impedance in passive mode, 100 ohms in Active Noise Cancelling and Bass modes. With up to 15dB of active noise cancellation on a 20Hz-20KHz frequency response these headphones are great for those long flights with screaming kids and noisy neighbors.

These come with a very nice semi-hard carrying case for ease of travel. Inside are the headphones with a nice 1.4m(4.5ft) cable with inline microphone and controls. In my particular case there were 2 AAA batteries, necessary for the active noise cancellation and bass modes. You can listen to music, videos, etc without the need of the batteries, passive only mode, but you will mist on the 15dB noise cancellation. These do a great job of eliminating outside noise on their own being close-backed headphones but that ANC mode is all the more better with 4 mics working to cancel outside noise.

Some cons are they are a little tight on the head, even though they are around the ear style headphones. The volume control does not work on Android, but the play/pause does. If not using the included case, which is a little bulky, the headphones do fold up for easy travel inside a smaller bag. Although the headband and ear cups are leather padded, they are a little uncomfortable after extended use.

All in all I really like these headphones, they are not as good as my Big Brand Name headphones, which were half the price but that’s a different matter entirely. If I was in the market for a great pair of close-backed, Active Noise Cancelling headphones for a decent price, these are the ones that I would look for and eventually purchase. The pros outweigh the cons with this pair and I would gladly recommend them to anyone else looking for a decent pair of noise cancelling headphones.

The Momentum 2.0 is absolutely the best portable headphone I've ever listened to. Period. Sennheiser has managed to accomplish a rare feat by producing a seat of headphones that are both aesthetically appealing as well as sonically impressive all for under $400.  I upgraded from my Shure SE-215's after finding that I wanted something that could deliver more in terms of soundstage. I tried the Bowers and Wilkins P7, Master and Dynamic MH40, and V-Moda Crossfade 100. Then came the Momentum 2.0.  The sound signature on these is downright impressive for a closed back headphone. The bass is punchy and tight (albeit marginally loose in the sub-bass area) and carries some serious heft in songs like Massive Attack's "Angel".  The mid range is equally impressive and isn't overpowered or muddied by the bass response - they are remarkably clear. Snare drums are crisp and snappy, pianos are seductively warm, and picked guitars are a joy. Fleetwood Mac's "Dreams" produced a serious "Wow!" Moment for me in this department.  The highs are a bit rolled off at the very top, but I can't complain too much, as I don't find it taking much away from the headphones. They still have plenty of sparkle to them. I still hear a decent amount of decay in cymbal strikes and plenty of detail, which allows these headphones to be light and airy when needed. This is extremely apparent in Tycho's track "Awake". In my opinion, the roll off on he high end prevents these cans from being too sibilant and fatiguing and lends a bit of a warmer sound. Not a bad thing - but it will bother those who want a less "fun" headphone and desire something more clinically accurate.  Oh, and these headphones look great. I bought the ivory ones because I just couldn't resist the white contrasted with the brown leather headband. Style is subjective so I won't go further here.  As far as comfort goes, Sennheiser deserves a serious pat on the back. I found the P7 and Crossfade to beway too clampy and had to take them off, as they were giving me a headache after 45 minutes or so. The MH40's, although built impressively well and absolutely gorgeous, were simply WAY too heavy. No go. The Momentums are incredibly light and not at all too tight. I have worn them while studying for multiple hours at a time and not once have I found them uncomfortable or too hot. It's easy to forget they're on your head.  Bottom line: these headphones sound wonderful. They are not the most accurate headphones on the market, but Sennheiser has found a very pleasing balance between clinical accuracy and a lush, welcoming sound that is difficult to accomplish without sacrificing much of anything in regards to clarity and performance. And they're gorgeous and comfortable, to boot.

Energy's RC (Reference Connoisseur) series of speakers are truly impressive in terms of both audio performance and value. I have been an audiophile for over 4 decades and never came across anything more sensible to own, i.e., one can spend a lot more and not get much more, and there is no match at the same price point.  They were probably introduced about 10 years ago. Reviews I found online date back to 2006 and the RC10 was chosen by Soundstage! as an award winner in the "Budget Leader" category. That was when they were sold for around $500/pr. In more recent years, Klipsch acquired Energy and the RC speakers are poorly marketed. Once in a while, one can find them at deep discount, making them an incredible bargain.  I own a total of 7 RC speakers, including a pair each of RC70, RC-R and RC-10, and an RC-LCR. My long post about them can be found under the RC-70 listing on Amazon.  The big sound coming out of the tiny box is simply hard to believe. I put them above the RC70 in my 500 sq.ft. listening room and they sound just as pleasant, just not as deep in bass. The clarity and overall tonal quality are very close. Most people would find them better than a lot of floor standing speakers.

Full disclosure- the company is offering me a free one year extended warranty in exchange for my review. Overall, we're very pleased with this clock. I work with headphones all the time and I particularly like active noise canceling (ANC) phones. The gold standard is Bose but you pay a premium if you want those phones. One of the issues I have seen with headphones is that many manufacturers claim to have noise canceling phones when they really are just noise isolating phones. These phones by AGPtEK are true ANC phones and while they are a far cry from Bose they are actually good headphones.

These are very lightweight and reasonably comfortable phones. The padding on the ears is a little stiff but they are not hard. I can wear them for a while and they do not get too warm and they do not pinch my ears. These are over-the-ear phones and they fit properly. I do not like the headband, though - there is no padding on the headband and if you have thin hair (or no hair) on the top of your head these have no cushion at all and they feel like they’re scraping when you put them on though they are fine once fitted.

I have noticed that these phones are not the very best when it comes to the sound profile, but they are certainly acceptable. The best way to describe the sound is “subdued”, though these phones are really strange in how they present sound. There are tracks I have loaded up and listened to that sound slightly muffled and quiet and at the same time I can hear details I never before noticed with any other headphones. I am not sure what to make of the sound profile as these sound different than any other headset I have used but they still sound good. An audiophile will not like these phones very much, but most will find these to be acceptable. I think the sound profile could use a boost in the midrange?

These headphones have the electronics in them to actively cancel low-frequency noise. So, when you have these on and you are on an plane or you are in a noisy car, turning on the ANC function drastically cuts down on engine and road noise so that you can hear the music better or you can enjoy a quieter ride. I have a fan I use to generate white noise, and I tried these phones’ ANC function with the fan on. The ANC circuit did cut a good portion of the noise, though nowhere near as much as my Bose set does. That said, these do a good-enough job of cutting sound to make them effective.

I like the fact that the phones continue to work even when there are no batteries. The only thing the batteries affect is the ANC function.

This headset does one thing correctly that many other phones I have tried has gotten wrong. Over and over, I have seen headphones that boost the volume of the music when the ANC function is engaged, and the tendency is to overcompensate. So, the ANC function means a substantial volume boost to music, and the claim is that the overall volume level remains the same. That might be true but it is deceptive. This headset does it right - the volume of the music is boost just enough to sound exactly the same whether the ANC is on or off.

Probably the most interesting point about these phones is the price. These are ANC phones and as I write this they sell for under $30 (price may change later, of course). To have ANC phones that cost so little and actually work is just amazing to me. I used one other similarly priced ANC-capable set some time ago and it was just awful. This set is actually decent. It is not up to the same capabilities as a set that costs three times as much, but it doesn’t need to be. The most important function with this set is the ANC and it does work, and it works better than some other sets I have seen and used.

I could name several sets of headphones that sound better or have better ANC, but all of them would cost at least double and it’s debatable if the cost difference is worth the difference. I use a lot of ANC phones and this set is probably the best value of those I have seen and used. It is not perfect but the flaws are small when you consider that these cost so little. If you specifically want ANC phones, and you want to keep the cost down, consider this set.

I live in the UK where this amplifier comes from . I have been using the Caspian Series M2 Integrated amplifier, initially as a stop gap measure until I could afford to have my high end system overhauled . That was three years ago. I am still using it with the Caspian cd player used in a balanced mode and a pair of Triangle Signature Delta speakers and I feel no urgent need whatsoever to have my Naim amps and Mark Levinson cd player overhauled. Why ? May you ask . Simply because the sound I am getting is as good as my so called high end super expensive system!
The Roksan amp is so good that it will make you think it's an amp costing several thousands $ more. The soundstage it produces is as good as my Naim 250s and 135s. It will drive difficult loads without any problem but more importantly, it can be happily partnered with a wide range of speakers. The funny thing is that the cables I am using cost more than the amp and cd player combined! You would think that the Kimber bifocal XL speaker cables would show up the Caspian M2 shortcomings. Well, they don't. As a matter of fact, the combination seems to be a perfect match with the internal Kimber wiring of the French speakers being used as well. The conservative 85 watts power per channel quoted by the maufacturer do not necessarily reflect on the loudness level this amp can subjectively produce. You can have Lady Gaga full blast at high levels if you wish and if you are prepared for a lawsuit with your neighbours. Your speakers might go first, and your wife next but not the amp which I believe has a very sophisticated protection circuit, unllike the Naims of earlier years.
What makes this amp so special is its versatility and ability to reproduce any music regardless of the genre. Whether you listen to Grace Jones, Count Basie or WA Mozart, it will invariably communicate the message and emotions contained in the music. The preamp section is so good that you can play older recordings without having to worryabout the potentially obstrusive background noise. Alfred Cortot playing Schumann Carnaval recorded in 1928 sounds amazingly fresh and exciting and Maria Callas singing Abigail in that impossible Verdi aria from Nabucco is simply out of this world. Mind you, using the Kimber Kable all round helps as well.
I hope that by now I have convinced you about makes this British amplifier so special. By the way, it is the top recommended amplifier in the UK What Hi Fi magazine for amps costing £ 1500 and above. So, even if you buy it in the US, it will not cost you that much more at $ 3000 a piece. It retails for £ 2000 in the UK.
I think anyone looking for a top performer at an affordable price should put this amplifier on their list for auditioning. I wonder if any dealer would dare use it with a pair of Wilson Audio speakers ! That would be an interesting alternative to the overpriced Naim Statement !
So, to sum up my review, the Caspian M2 series 2 amplifier is probably the best kept secret in the hifi world .
PS: I am not a member of the British Audio Indusrty trying to promote British equipment ! I am simply an ordinary guy who takes a genuine interest in high quality hifi products at a realistic price.

Every time someone calls, I have to deal with hearing, "what? What? I can't hear you. I'll try calling you back." I have to disconnect the mic and plug in wired headphones with a mic, defeating the purpose of the Bluetooth headphones. It's a shame because I would love to be able to be a bit more mobile while on these calls.

So, as noted, while the audio deserves a 4, the mic doesn't even deserve a star, balancing out the score at a substandard 2.

The QUALITY of the HDMI cable you use in your setup matters. To verify the quality of a HDMI cable, one test that is performed is called the "eye" test. I bought the Fusion4K cable because they proved their quality by showing their eye test results.
Doing a fair amount of research on this topic I learned the following:
As the length of the cable increases, the signal interference also increases. Think of this like the "resistance" of the signal in the cable increases the farther it has to go. Also, the more data you pass through the cable (bandwidth) the more interference you'll see as distance increases until the cable fails like cheap cables will.
The Fusion4K eye test shows a clear area around the "mask" (the middle shape in the eye) in their results. This means that there is no signal loss in the cable and that tells me that the materials used to make the cable are top notch. I found this information with simple internet searches and you can too.
My point is that better cable materials make a better cable and I want the best to future proof my setup. That's why I went with this cable. Also, the cables look great and "feel" well made when I held them next to my old cables. I'm very happy with my purchase.

I use this in my lab to power things like Arduino boards and my Raspberry Pi 2, and charge my phone and iPad when they get low without having to take them back downstairs to charge them.
I recently was powering my Rasberry Pi 2 with my 60W, 6 port and accidentally shorted the 5V pin out with the ground pin and the Pi turned off. I couldn't get it to come back on and thought I fried it. If you don't know about the Pi it's a small development computer with open pins for running and controlling other things and it's easy to short something by mistake. I saw that my iPhone and iPad were still charging so I didn't think it was the USB power block. Then I remembered reading something about a short cut off protection built into the IQ system on the these, so I unplugged it from the one USB port and plugged it into another and the computer came back one. So the one port was still off and then I remembered reading about how to reset it. You just unplug it from the wall for 10 seconds and plug back in. So I did just that and all the ports came back to life. That's when I realized that the IQ short protection probably saved my little computer from permanent damage, and also maybe saved my other things plugged in charging also. Most shorts will back feed and could damage other things charging also plugged into the other USB ports. If it didn't have the IQ protection I could have damaged 3 iPhones and a iPad I had charging, and I just got done fixing them also.

I know, in most cases you won't be shorting out anything because you won't be charging or powering something with open pins like a Rasberry Pi, but sometimes electronics them self will fail and short out and could backfeed into the circuit damaging other devices charging. This could save the other things also plugged in and charging if it was to happen.

This was a nice feature to have and probably saved me from having to repair or buy new things. It's not the kind of protection I expect from something that costs as low as this, but I'm glad it had it and has the 18 month warranty. Anker has not disappointed me and I own 2 USB power blocks, a Bluetooth keyboard, a multi size pack of micro USB cables, and a 10,000 mAh USB portable power battery pack.

I was original afraid that the IQ system would power down the port when charging things that don't take much power, I think it said something about turning off port to be energy efficient. These in-ear headphones come in three sizes, as do most others, but the fit is totally different. I tried these and so did my husband, and we were both able to get a perfect fit. When I say perfect fit I mean a fit that can withstand jumping, bending, and shaking your head. These headphones aren't going anywhere, but you can, because the fit doesn't block out so much of the outside world that you could easily be smashed flat by a semi. Using a bench power supply I am able to test this device on input voltages between 0-30 volts. At first everything seemed great, when input voltage was above 6 volts the output was always rock stable at 5v. But that's where the good news stops. After about 4 minutes with no load the TO-92 package device (probably a transistor) next to the input header started getting hot. The higher the input voltage, the hotter it got. The output voltage did stay at 5v. After 10 minutes of sweeping around between 6 volts and 30 volts the TO-92 was way too hot for my liking, and I stopped the testing. I suspect if you stay under 12-14 input voltage you'd be ok, but at this point I'm not risking my downstream USB devices on it.

If your input voltage is below 5volts, it will gladly pass that onto the output voltage (- about 0.7v), which can be bad. Some devices, if they are expecting 5V, and you give them say 3V, they won't be happy, and may damage the downstream device.

[USABILITY]: It's a little hard to actually use. It's got two buttons, Top button is main power, bottom button is output power switch. They are both "soft switches", meaning they are controlled by some form of logic, IE a microprocessor. I suspect the microprocessor is underneath the LED display. In order to get it to start outputting power, first you have to press the top button to turn on the main unit, then it starts displaying input voltage only on the LED, I wasn't able to get it to show anything other then the input voltage. After it's displaying voltage then you press the bottom button and it turns on the output voltage. Not sure why/what they intended that usage for.

Later I'll do a actual destructive test on it and see if it'll fail on me, and if it does fail, what output voltage it'll put out when it does fail.

Pros:

Small Size

Cons:

* Gets way too hot to handle/touch.
* Output voltage can dip below 5V ifinput voltage dips below 6ish volts.
* Have to manipulate buttons to get it to output any voltage.
* LED display only displays incoming voltage, no amperage, no wattage.
* No way to turn off the display, and provide output voltage.

The Geek Out 1000 (or GO1K as it has come to be called by many) is a fabulous little DAC + Headphone Amplifier combo device, but it's not alone.

Since the time of its introduction it has been hailed as one of the best sounding DAC+Amp combos for its size or in its price bracket by numerous hi-fi and audiophile reviewers. It "awesomifies" (a term coined by Gavin Fish, LHLabs' Chief Innovation Officer) virtually every 2-channel digital sound format out there from regular CDs and MP3s to Studio Masters at crazy high resolutions like 32-bit 384kHz. It even plays the exotic-but-beautiful Direct Stream Digital (aka DSD64, aka SACD), a 1-bit 2.8MHz audio format favored by many audiophiles.

I backed the project that gave birth to the Geek Out on Kickstarter years ago coincidentally for $199. Since receiving mine in April of 2014 my Kickstarter Green (or as I like to call it, "Pononite") GO1K has been my "Pride and Joy." I listen to it daily and use a variety of headphones with it. The full watt of Class A power can drive most of the headphones on the planet with aplomb and makes for a nice hand warmer in the winter months as well (this by design -- if you're not familiar with Class A amplifiers, they run hot because unlike the more common Class A/B designs, they never 'switch off' or take a break when the music stops or gets quiet). You can rest assured that the extra warmth isn't a problem: I've run my Geek Out non-stop for months at a time as part of my home audio system with nary a problem.

By way of comparison, I own (or have spent significant time with) several similar combos from other manufacturers, each of which has their relative charms: the Audioquest Dragonfly (1.2), the Meridian Explorer, and the ifi Nano iDSD. The Geek Out stands up proudly in this company. It is more capable than the Dragonfly (both in terms of the range of headphones it can drive and the range of music formats it can play back without prior down-sampling). I also think it sounds better, but it should be noted that the Dragonfly ($149) costs half as much as the GO1K's $299 MSRP, so all of this should come as no surprise. I'm only listing it here because at the time of the Geek Out's introduction, there were very few "truly audiophile" thumb-drive and super-portable options, and the Dragonfly was one of them and worth all of its accolades.

Compared to the similarly priced Meridian Explorer ($349), it is a toss-up at lower playback resolutions. The Explorer excels at 24/96 and below (CD, DVD Audio, etc.). It has a very natural, very musical quality to its presentation that really draws you in. Meridian has a very deep well of experience to draw from here, and it really comes through in the Explorer. The Geek Out also sounds excellent with the same sources, but the presentation is slightly different. I would describe the Geek Out's sound as favoring precision over musicality. The Meridian favors the opposite way, but in most cases, we're talking about subtle shades of difference. It may well be that the electrical characteristics of a given set of headphones and how they relate to each of these amplifiers may well have more tonal impact than anything the DACs are doing. That said, when you step up into the rarefied air of DSD, DXD, and high-res PCM playback, the Geek Out really shines. It may cost less than the Explorer (even at MSRP), but like the Explorer, it "punches far above its pay grade" in terms of quality and capability. At $199, the Geek Out 1000 is a steal!

The similarly priced iFi Nano iDSD DAC ($199) is a great device that actually sports more "native sound format" compatibility than the highly-capable Geek Out in that the Nano can not just "single" rate DSD, but also "double" and "quad" rate DSD (DSD128, DSD256), and all via ASIO without any prior format or source-rate conversion. It also features the sexiest volume control of the bunch, a brilliant silver knob with nearly perfect "feel" to it. It turns smoothly and near the start of its range there is a satisfying spike in resistance followed by a "click" which tells you the device is now On and ready to rock. This kind of sex appeal is only available because of its substantially larger chassis and beautiful industrial design. The Nano *will* fit in your pocket and it can even be affixed to your phone (via provided rubber bands), *and* it even has a built-in rechargeable battery (for jamming with said phone on-the-go or for isolating the DAC from the noisy power that is found in PCs).

All of the little "extras" the Nano has make audiophiles rejoice, but at the end of the day what matters most to us is "how does it sound?" On its own, the Nano sounds great. Like the Geek Out and the rest, it is *vastly* better than the $2 sound chip on your motherboard and even the one in your iPhone or Android... and far more capable; however, when compared side-by-side to the Geek Out (and even the Meridian), its sound comes up a little wanting. The Geek Out 1000 has an "it" quality to its presentation that the Nano lacks. There is a mix of immediacy, musicality, punch, drive, and fullness that embodies the Geek Out's sound which the Nano can't quite manage (at least with my headphones -- I used a pair of Sony's flagship, the MDR Z7, to compare with).

Therefore, I find that the Geek Out is a superior performer to the Nano even though it lacks some of the "creature comforts" of its larger rival. While the volume knob is nice, the delineating factor here truly is the integrated battery -- all things considered, I'd rather spend the same money on a Geek Out 1000 because it sounds better to my ears. As long as you buy those noise isolating pieces like Westone W4 or Shure SE215, I think the problem will still be there. So do NOT use them in quite libraries or offices. I don't see the problem of having this while working out.

I'm actually quite surprised at the other reviews. I've been using this power strip for awhile and I've never had any issues with it. The setup can be a bit confusing I guess, but you catch on quick after using it. Basically, there are three different settings that you can plug into. There's your standard "always on" outlet, which is exactly as it says. It's always on. It's just like a regular outlet. Then you have the two others, which are coupled. Plugging anything into the master controlled outlets will not get power unless whatever is plugged into the master outlet is on. I always thought this was a great way to save a bit of electricity. I used it by having my TV plugged into the master outlet, and then having external things that I only use for my TV plugged into the master controlled outlets (like my xbox, blue ray player, controller charger, basically anything that the TV needs to be on to use). This product worked just fine for me. If you don't like the setup of the master controlled outlets, however, then I would recommend just buying a standard power strip.

[[VIDEOID:36cb8f168cf666f0f37d28296599131a]]When compared head-to-head with the Turcom HR-903, I have to say the Voombox Party does come out the subjectively lesser... but not necessarily in terms of what you are looking for - far smaller sizing being the biggest positive for the Voombox.

Turcom's HR-903 has a stated IP waterproofing rating of 5 (Water jets from all angles) - and I can attest to it's durability as it has been sitting on my pool deck for the past months.

The Voombox doesn't have any IP rating I can find either on the box, the manual, or online - other than \\"Water Resistant\\". Without knowing what kind of internal proofing it has, I would say IPx4 (typical shower speaker level, spray and splashes) based off the grill and the cover flap on the side.

The HR-903 is about 2 and 1/2 times the mass of the Voombox and certainly heavier, and that very well may be a big point for you. Yet, I do frown at the complete lack of any kind of carrying case or such for the Voombox. At this price range, I would expect some sort of case or bag. Or for the HR-903's, an in-built handle.

The controls on the HR-903 are touch sensitive, and can be a problem if water collects inside the little divots. The controls on the Voombox are push buttons under a rugged silicone band - and uses the \\"+\\",\\"-\\" for both Volume and Track (Short Press Volume), whereas it is all separated on the HR-903.

Now for the meat-and-potatoes, audio.

The Voombox certainly holds its own, the 20W volume being pretty much the same level as the 30W put out by the HR-903. Mellow yet clear spectrum with a balance between punchy and rumbly bass response. However, the HR-903 has a more rumbly, more expansive bass response. So it boils down to how much overdriven bass rumble you like. I do like a gritty BEWM. :)

One thing to note about the Voombox, be sure the back or top isn't up against anything - the bass it pushes out will cause rattling buzz within the casing. Also, I found the AUX In to be somewhat disappointing. The volume basically halved, though still sounded great, and will not work with a 4 pole jack (i.e. \\"wired\\" microphone input), just a standard 3 pole.

I spent a lot of time researching receivers and thought the Pioneer VSX-1130 would be perfect for my needs.  Unfortunately, I will never know because it would not connect to the internet, which is the first step in setting up the receiver.  The Set Up app on my Android said that the Wi-Fi configuration was complete, but then when I chose the next step of connecting peripherals, the app said that the receiver could not be found.  I verified using the status screen on the receiver that it was not connecting to the internet.  There is nothing wrong with my network.  A Wi-Fi Dish DVR was installed just two weeks ago using the same network and it works like a charm.  If only the Pioneer were designed so well.  Also, I should mention that the Android Navi app crashed a couple of times as well.  It does not get very good reviews overall in the Play store.  Edit 8/27/15:  So I spent many hours trying to get the receiver to connect to the internet.  After setting up the Wi-Fi with no luck, I moved it over to my router and used an Ethernet connection and went through the Pioneer setup app over and over.  No difference.  I went back to the Wi-Fi connection.  After tearing my hair out, I started connecting my A\V components to the receiver without the help of the app.  I was sure I was going to have to ship the receiver back, and then, all of a sudden, it connected.  I did not make any changes to my router settings.  My other internet-connected products have had no problems at all with my network, so I don't know what the problem was with the receiver. However, once connected, I took the opportunity to immediately update to the latest firmware.  The Pioneer has had no trouble keeping the internet connection so far, so I have raised my review rating from one to three stars.  I do want to like this receiver, because it has the specs I want.  My new speakers are still on the way from Amazon, so I will be doing a lot more work with setting up the receiver and will probably have another update to my review.  Edit 9/13/15: Alright, so I got my brand new speakers connected and it sounds great.  I found out that whenever the power supply is interrupted, I have to power cycle my router to get the Pioneer to connect again to the internet.  I don't have this issue with any of my other Wi-Fi devices.  So far, the biggest disappointment is that the Bluetooth music streaming from my less than a year old Motorola phone is marred by constant stuttering.  An old Samsung phone works fine with it.  I should mention that the Motorola Bluetooth has no problems with my other Bluetooth devices.  With all the different brands of phones out there, and different flavors of Android, I probably shouldn't expect everything to work well together.  Edit 10/06/15:  After the annoyances I experienced, I decided to keep the receiver.  I got it on sale for $499.99, and the only other receiver I found with similar features was an Onkyo that was priced $85 higher.  Also, I should mention that the latest firmware upgrade included the addition of HDMI 2.0a support, which means that the Pioneer should now be able to work with the latest HDTV's that have HDR technology.

The high-amp Andersons (also called “Sermos”) are by far the best electrical connectors for countless applications. I have been using them for a long time to connect high-powered Nickel- Cadmium (NiCd or NiCad) batteries and Lithium- Ion Polymer (LIPO) batteries to various devices and they have never failed me. They have the unique ability to be connected either vertically or horizontally to insure that the correct connection for the correct application is made at all times.

Aside from the highly efficient transfer of current between the connectors that their clever design provides, while they solidly and positively lock together and have never accidentally disconnected in all the time I have been using them, they are easy to connect and disconnect within the circuit, a claim that many of their competitors cannot honestly boast of. In addition, many different gauges of wire can be attached to the Andersons using a crimp tool; no soldering is required. Not only does this make a perfectly secure physical connection but it also promotes a very efficient transfer of energy from the wire to the connector as the very tight crimp offers both low resistance and capacitance which are problems engendered by even perfectly executed soldered connections.

There are other similar connectors out there and I have tried them all, but I always go right back to the Andersons. They are the best.

In addition to the surge/spike protection, it has digital filter outlets that EMI/RFI interference from certain home appliances like vacuums, microwaves, washers, or high draw filter current to provide additional protection for sensitive items like Televisions and other AV gear. It won’t improve the performance of your AV equipment under normal use but will make it less susceptible to interference from other power drawing items. I’m not a big fan of power regulating surge suppressors for computing equipment but feel they work well with AV equipment however. I have teens and they love leaving televisions, game consoles and other AV equipment on long after they’re done with it. This helps alleviate that issue. The number of outlets is just right for a typical home theater. Mine accommodates a 55” LED TV, Blu-Ray surround sound system, cable DVR, Apple TV, PS4, Wii-U. The remaining plugs are used for charging and accessories. Like I said, it’s heavy. So it’s not the type of protector that can be moved from room to room frequently, such as I do when I want to use several computer items in a different part of the house where there are no electronics and thus no protectors. The metal and gloss finish along with the LEDs do make it an attractive accessory when compared to the typical top outlet utilitarian looking protectors. It has a reset/power button and also offers coax and single-line two-wire phone/modem protection.

One of the most valuable yet overlooked features is wiring fault indicators, such as the one found on this APC C25B.
I love protectors with wiring fault indicators because they reveal problems that you may not otherwise know exist. I once had a surge protector wiring fault LED illuminate and subsequently discovered that the outlet was wired incorrectly with the neutral going to the hot side. I’ve had a few other faulty outlets trigger warning LED’s. One was caused by a loose wire and another was caused by a metal housing surrounding the outlet. That was a frightening light show when the “too cool to turn of the circuit power first” electrician tried to troubleshoot the outlet while it was still hot and found out about the metal housing via a very scary show of sparks and pops. My mother had a similar incident when she was vacuuming in her home in a faulty outlet. Her outlet sparked, burned, melted, fried her vacuum and ruined her carpet from the hot sparks landing and singing holes. Thankfully, she wasn’t injured. Wiring faults are more common than people think. Sometimes it takes a while for a long existing problem to finally reveal itself, as it did with my mother. The speaker is quite large and operates on AC power only (no internal batteries.) It's about 20 1/2\\" wide, 7 3/8\\" tall and 5 3/4\\" deep. Concerning the depth, considering the power cord sticking ouf of the back, it's actually going to require a minimum of 7 1/4\\" of depth to accommodate the plug. The power supply/adapter has two cords... an AC power cord that is 6' in length which goes from the wall into the power supply and then a thinner 6' cord that connects the power supply to the speaker.

On the top of the speaker are a number of touch controls. Update – I have had to stop using this clock after several months of operation. The clock just stops momentarily, resetting to 12:00 midnight on Jan 1. I initially thought that the AC power was being stopped because the input from the transformer might have come loose, so I arranged to it to be attached more securely, but the same thing still happened, even though there was no one near the connection when the interruption occurred. I then went to battery power, but the projection system does not work on battery power, so I used both the battery and AC in hopes that if there was an interruption in the AC then the battery backup would prevent the clock from resetting, but it does not. Even a broken clock is right twice a day, but when this clock resets it is never right, and gives an erroneous time. I have therefore had to downgrade from two to only one star.

Original review
I do not recommend this clock for the reasons described below. The clock worked and I purchased it on a half price closeout, so as a clock it was OK, but overpriced if you just operate it as a simple digital clock, hence two stars instead of the minimum one.

Why do I call this a “brain dead” - described below in order of the most annoying features first:
· The projector feature is poorly designed. When you face the clock, it projects the time on the wall behind or above the clock upside down and backwards. The time is projected correctly on the wall facing the clock and can therefore be read when you are facing this wall and have your back towards the clock. However, this most likely requires projecting the time more than the six foot focusing distance, as it did in my case. The result is a large somewhat blurry image. The correct orientation is also displayed when you turn the clock with its back facing you, so you can only read the projected time on the wall facing the clock. BETTER PROJECTOR CLOCKS HAVE THE ABILITY TO FLIP THE IMAGE IN ORDER TO CORRECT FOR THIS, and give you the ability to view the correct image with the clock in a different orientation relative to the way that you are facing. Also, while the projector can be rotated about one axis, that is all. Therefore, I found it impossible to orient both the clock and the projected image to optimum orientations.

· The clock face is tilted backwards at a fixed angle, which cannot be adjusted. This made it difficult to read the clock while lying in bed, and required me to make a jury-rigged system to keep the face at an orientation where I could read the clock. Unfortunately, the clock was less stable in this position, requiring still further modifications. Even a moderately thoughtful deign would have eliminated this problem without adding to the coat of the clock.

· The temperature readings were three degrees high (compared to two other digital thermometers in the room). This may seem petty, but if you are interested on knowing the temperature and its changes over a period of days you should at least see the correct value. This incorrect value may be due to the heat given off by the projecting LED and there is no way to turn off the projector, except to run completely on batteries. (The clock can be run completely on battery power, or with the batteries as a backup for a power failure but unused when the clock is running on AC.)

· The clock is very bright, perhaps too bright when you are trying to sleep and there is no way to reduce the brightness. The numbers are 1/2 an inch high as opposed to ¾ of an inch on other clocks. Instead of a larger image this clock has color bands that go up and down and cycle, illustrating the temperature changes over the last five days. The bands take up most of the lower half of the clock face and I found them to be distracting, so I had to cover over this feature, as there is no way to turn it off.

· Setting the clock up was a pain – not at all intuitive and probably almost impossible without the instructions, so if you lose them the clock might become useless.

All in all this is a prime example of a poor (brain dead) design. The clock would have been more useful as more than a simple clock if the clock face could be tilted and more useful as a projector clock if the projected image could be rotated about more than one axis and flipped so that it could be read when one was facing the clock, instead of only when the clock face is not also visible. OK, I've reviewed a similar player and hated it, but I like this one, for this price, and here is why.

For $20, you get a decent FM radio (with recording capability), 16GB of storage for music, and a nice voice recorder, as well as a few other features. You also get a nice lanyard and decent (not great, but surprisingly adequate) headphones. Are there limitations? Sure, of course - this is a 16GB $20 device with a color LCD screen... you need to manage your expectations.

What is the target demographic for these? Likely small kids (cheap device that they likely won't break), people who want a cheap FM radio, and/or people who want a cheap voice recorder. Yes, you can play movies on it, but odds are you won't be able to properly format them for this, so don't count on that capability - at all.

Here's what you can expect:

First of all, hardware wise, this is the size of an old school iPod nano but without the click wheel - yes, there's a "wheel", but it's really just four click locations and a center button - no scrolling capability. You also get a decent lanyard and really pretty nice headphones - I mean, you'd likely pay $8-$12 for these, so they're quite good when included in a $20 purchase. You also get a mini (not micro!) USB charging cable, which is unfortunate, because almost everything is micro USB these days. The LCD screen is nice enough - certainly for a device at this price range, and, honestly, you're not going to be watching movies on it, so it's more than adequate for the other features. There is either no micro SD card, or it's internal. Similar devices have them as removable, but, actually, I prefer this way - nothing to lose, nothing for kids to pull out and toss.

"Apps":

(1) "Music"

It comes with a couple of songs, and you can add more by connecting it to essentially any computer. Yes, this means you need a computer to add music - there's no WiFi, no iTunes, no Google Play, no Amazon Prime, etc - you need MP3s or the like to add to this manually, but that's OK. If you're getting this for kids, it means you have absolute control over what they listen to, music-wise. And you can add almost 16GB of music, because the device uses essentially none of the available space. BE AWARE: there is a menu option to delete files, or to delete *all* files, so, if you have small children, you know as well as I do that they will do exactly that, at least once. Anyway, music quality is quite good, both through the included headphones and via nicer ones of mine I tried.

(2) "Movie"

This comes with one movie, and it's a video some woman in a bikini singing on a beach. You've never heard of her, and you likely never will - after all, she's allowed her video to be on a $20 player. You can delete it, or you can keep it on. Video quality is surprisingly decent for such a cheap device. However... while I've not tested this device *yet* (will do soon when I post the video review of this), other devices with *very* similar firmware suggest that you'll never be able to encode movies for this, so you can probably forget ever putting other videos on this.

(3) "Record"

Shockingly useful. Using the menu, you can change the recording quality - it is actually really decent at the higher bit rates, and there's an option for automatic voice recognition, so it can record only when people are talking.

(4) "Voice"

This seems redundant - recordings show up here as well as in Music, although *only* recordings show up here, so it's a way to filter out music. Same options for deleting files as elsewhere.

(5) "FM Radio"

AWESOME. OK, it's not HD radio, but the quality is adequate. Noticeably worse than MP3s stored locally, but fine. Also: you *CAN* RECORD FM RADIO using the menu. Up to 16GB of it, which is an eternity. I'm not saying you want to record it, but you can. Bring it while travelling. Record local stations. Listen while flying home. Fun. You can auto-search stations, set it to use Japan radio bands, etc. Once programmed, press the center button to go through stations. This is very nice in this price range.

(6) "Photo"

Lets you look at photos you've added, in the same way you'd add music. They look fine, as long as you're 5. This is not a high-res display, nor would you expect it to be. Note: if you've putting pictures on this, *reduce the resolution*!! Hi-res photos will take extra space and, most importantly, will take forever to render, and they won't look any better. You can, as with music, delete one or all photos, and, yes, your kids will do this.

(7) "Setup"

Basics, like time, LCD mode, language, firmware upgrades, etc. Odds are you'll never need to use any of these.

(8) "E-book"

Ships empty, and while I suspect you can find file formats it'll accept, I can't imagine reading an e-book on this. Maybe I just have a poor imagination.

(9) "Game"

- Boxman: You move boxes around to clear up space. Not a terrible time consumer, especially for kids

- Tetrix: Shockingly, a Tetris clone. I bet you couldn't have guessed that!

- Snake: Brings back fond memories of my Nokia. Yours too, perhaps.

- Road: I Have *no idea* how to play this. Some sort of tile game.

OVERALL:

Look, this costs $20 or so. It is NOT an iPod nano. It is not, really, a movie player (unless you can find the proper obscure format), It isn't, really, an e-book reader. But: it's a good FM radio (with recording!), it is a good voice recorder, and it stores a ton of music (and/or pictures). I think it is *easily* worth what they are asking, and I think it'd be great for kids or as a cheap radio/recorder for adults.

Cons:

The menu system is... non-intuitive, to say the least. The device is aggressive about power savings and will power down if not used very quickly - much less than 30 seconds. However, when in use (music, radio, recording, etc), it works fine, and battery life is good. I wish it used micro USB, but thems the breaks. Still, overall, a 5 star device for this cost.

This review will concentrate on using these on airplanes. I have seen folks for years with headsets on airplanes, but I have always just used either the ones supplied by the flight, or sometimes my own earbud style. The earbuds however are just too uncomfortable to wear for long periods. Recently, I had to travel to Australia from the US, and that involves some very long flights. Upon arrival in Sydney, my ears hurt and I was pretty tired from lack of sleep. While waiting for a connection, I saw some TKD brand noise canceling headphones on sale for $99 in the airport. I also tried on the Bose QC25, but I just couldn't bring myself to spend $300, so I took a chance and bought the TDK NC 400.

The TDK NC400 were OK. The ear muffs were round, so I guess they are knows as "on the ear" style, not "over the ear". The noise canceling worked, but I wasn't overwhelmed by it, and in part that is probably due to the ear muff not really covering my ears, so a little sound gets past the muffs. They also weren't super comfortable. Again, this is the ear muff style, not a brand thing. After a few hours more flying, I realized that a really good noise canceling headset could make a difference. Three weeks later, heading back through Sydney, I purchased these Bose QC25 and wore them all the way back to JFK; about 20 hours of flying. I will never fly without them again.

They were the most comfortable way to listen to music or watch the in-flight movies I have ever worn. The noise canceling is outstanding, and I really didn't hear the background noise at all. At one point, I turned off the music and just left the noise canceling on, and I slept for about 6 hours without disturbance. I felt much more rested when we arrived in LA than I ever had after 15 hours of flying.

When they are on my head, I can barely even feel them as they are so light and the cushioning is so soft and well made. They are very easy to adjust and don't pinch on your head.

I can only compare these to the TDK NC400 that I also had. In my opinion, there is no comparison - the Bose are in a completely different league. Yes, they are 3 times the price, but I have to admit that they are 3 times better.

PROS:
- super comfortable
- amazing noise canceling
- really nice carry case.

CONS:
- not wireless (would be a nice feature)
- not even discrete.
- large muffs may interfere with your ability to rest your head on a pillow when compared to earbuds

If you are thinking about noise canceling headsets, I would urge you to consider these. Using them for a 15 hour flight made me a believer.

I just bought my second set of these. I'm shocked they are still selling this model as i got my first set back in the early 2000's when they were 80 dollars in stores. they lasted me 9 years of uber brutal heavy, "dear god how could you do that to them" use. yeah i broke them. i broke them alot.. super glue to the rescue every time. let me explain the extent of my abuse. I work at home with my hands, i do all chores in this household too. I get bored of music all the time, so instead i get my computer to read me novels, audio book, or by text to speech. i am not picky. over those 9 years i probably have funneled about 2000 novels thru these babies. Day in, day out use... i've probably fallen asleep wearing them 500 or 600 times... other times i took them off and left them on my bed next to me while i slept.. and then they would fall 2.5 feet to the concrete floor, and i may or may not step on them in the morning while rolling out of bed.. there is no such thing as a pair of headphones i can't break. thankfully i am also good at fixing things too... the old ones have been broken in about 5 different places. first thing to brake was the swivel to get the angle right on your head.. lots of super glue fixed that. a tip though is to figure out the correct angle for your head so you can have them turned back at a comfortable angle. then the second angle on the other side broke. then the bar that holds onto the ribbon thingy that holds the head strap in place broke it's mount.. but if you took the screws out there are internal bits inside the grey part that you can just loop the ribbon onto and screw closed.. i think i had to fix the other side a year later.. then i broke one of the parts that holds onto the ear muff... honestly i can't remember what i did to fix that.. i probably splinted a wire on it to make a new pivot though. i'm sure, with normal use and people won't have to deal with as many breakages as i did. because wearing headphones for 16 hours a day for 9 years straight i am sure is not normal use. their final death 9 years later happened while on vacation... i don't think the antenna base likes being packed away into a suitcase and driven 400 miles yearly.. on the 9th year the base died.. on inspection because i opened it.. the circuit board was cracked in half... which i soldered back together and got 3 or 4 months more out of it before well.. i dunno.. i am not the greatest solderer... R.I.P. RCA WHP141.. Hello Sennheiser TR 140. the rest of the review will be a comparison between the rca vs. sennheiser.
lets talk performance. Snap Crackle POP! rca has no features to protect your ears from the crackling noises that happen when you are way too far away from the base. sennheiser does... sennheiser will mute your feed to save you from a loud pop and replace it with a very annoying beeping noise... grrrrr i hate you beeping... but you get uset to it after a few months.. i don't even get annoyed anymore truthfully.
So yeah, that last
statement makes you go oh hell yeah i like no painful crackles right? well it's at a cost.. which brings us to our next topic.. range.... honestly.. rca says 150, back then sennheiser said 350.. i was super excited about the extra range as my 70' by 25' ranch style house didn't get full coverage as the 150 foot range does not include walls.. so, 3 of my walls = 25 foot range with some interference on rca, and sennheiser, the liars... well, the antenna strength is identical... there was absolutely no difference in signal strength.. range would be identical if it wasn't for the snap crackle pop interference feature.. so, if you go 3 walls away, and you held your head juuuuuust right, you could hold an ok signal for maybe 20 seconds before it cuts out and beeps at you.. so listening without beeps is more like 2 walls away instead of 3 walls with rca... so yeah... range is better on the rca then those super expensive sennheisers...
but wait... that sounds too good tobe true right? cheaper rca being better then sennheiser? yeah.. it is.. this brings us to ergonomics... this is where sennheiser blows rca out of the water and reigns supreme.. i can't say enough good things about sennheiser's ergonomics.. the comfort levels of just wearing the 2 different headphones... rca are like wearing 4 inch high heels, vs, sennheiser feeling like super comfy sneakers that are perfectly molded to your feet just for you.. now.. lets get this straight.. if your wearing rca for 4 hours of tv use... no problem.. 16 hours and then falling asleep wearing them multiple times a week... let me explain what doing that will do to you... before i ever wore wireless headphones my ears stuck out... if they stuck out any bit more then they did, i know i would of been ruthlessly teased for them.. having constant pressure on your ears to be folded back for years on end.. yeah.. my ears are the perfect distance required by beauty now.. about a 10 degree angle difference... beauty is painful.. including unintentional beauty.. i wore the rca headphones too much... they occasionally gave me bed sores in the cartilage of my ears and i'd have to take a week off of wearing them for my ears to heal. I've been using my sennheisers for... oh... 5 or 6 years now? not totally sure.. but i've never once had sore ears from them..
audio performance.. i'm not an audiophile rca sounds like any old wired pair of headphones i've ever used... it works and works less good the further from the base. if your very far it is reminiscent of walkie talkies.. sennheiser audio performance? thats a hard one.. the sound is very very different from rca.. i remember when i first switched over i absolutely HATED it.. it sounds muffled and super clear at the same time.. really hard to explain.. i'm years into using them so.. i no longer care what it sounds like anymore... besides, i am trying to listen to an audio book, or a computer generated voice... i just want to understand words... both work for that perfectly..
Why am i switching back to rca whp141 from sennheiser the top of the line wireless headphones world wide you ask? well.. i am not totally switching back.. see.. my sennheisers have a problem.. one which involves me soldering.. and we know how well that worked out... and the problem with the sennheisers are my own fault... extremely my fault.. so, by the time i got my sennheisers i figured out how to abuse headphones for as long as i wanted to.. 24 hours if i wanted.. just have a second set of batteries charging at the same time.. switch out the batteries.. see, on both rca and sennheiser... they do a trickle charge to recharge my rechargeable batteries... and that's just not fast enough.. they do that because it extends the life of the batteries.. and under normal use this is great... but no, i gotta wear them 16+ hours. so i would be changing the batteries at least daily and sometimes twice a day when the batteries where towards the end of their life... sennheiser doesn't make the ear covers or the battery bay strong enough to have that many battery changes.... we are talking in the hundreds... (i repaired my ear covers from falling off with magnets) so, when i lean forward the batteries no longer are in contact with the contacts.. and they turn off.. i lean back and they are fine.. this is driving me batty... because when i do chores or make jewelry i lean forward... soooooooo.. eventually i will mount an outer battery case and solder the leads onto the battery posts on my sennheiser.. but.. well.. i'm not the greatest solderer.. so i keep on putting it off.... and..... i want my range back so i can work in my garden again.. sooo... rca whp141, welcome back... rca, i won't be using to as my mains... you hurt my ears too much, but when i want the range.. you will be there for me.. and sennheiser will be there for me long before my ears begin to hurt.. best of both worlds! yay!..
as for my advice of which to get. if your a normal user and won't wear them a ridiculous amount of time like me.. get rca whp141 and save that extra 100-ish bucks for something else, if your ridiculous like me listening to now somewhere over 3400 books... you might want to go with sennheiser.. your ears will thank you.
p.s. durability on sennheiser is alot better then rca.. if i wasn't doing any battery changes then i suspect i would have almost no damage to my sennheisers (excluding the missing head pad, and weird warping shape falling asleep in them has created (pad got loose because i kept on trying to straighten the warping) soo, both issues.. my fault)
