OK, I've reviewed a similar player and hated it, but I like this one, for this price, and here is why.

For $20, you get a decent FM radio (with recording capability), 16GB of storage for music, and a nice voice recorder, as well as a few other features. You also get a nice lanyard and decent (not great, but surprisingly adequate) headphones. Are there limitations? Sure, of course - this is a 16GB $20 device with a color LCD screen... you need to manage your expectations.

What is the target demographic for these? Likely small kids (cheap device that they likely won't break), people who want a cheap FM radio, and/or people who want a cheap voice recorder. Yes, you can play movies on it, but odds are you won't be able to properly format them for this, so don't count on that capability - at all.

Here's what you can expect:

First of all, hardware wise, this is the size of an old school iPod nano but without the click wheel - yes, there's a "wheel", but it's really just four click locations and a center button - no scrolling capability. You also get a decent lanyard and really pretty nice headphones - I mean, you'd likely pay $8-$12 for these, so they're quite good when included in a $20 purchase. You also get a mini (not micro!) USB charging cable, which is unfortunate, because almost everything is micro USB these days. The LCD screen is nice enough - certainly for a device at this price range, and, honestly, you're not going to be watching movies on it, so it's more than adequate for the other features. There is either no micro SD card, or it's internal. Similar devices have them as removable, but, actually, I prefer this way - nothing to lose, nothing for kids to pull out and toss.

"Apps":

(1) "Music"

It comes with a couple of songs, and you can add more by connecting it to essentially any computer. Yes, this means you need a computer to add music - there's no WiFi, no iTunes, no Google Play, no Amazon Prime, etc - you need MP3s or the like to add to this manually, but that's OK. If you're getting this for kids, it means you have absolute control over what they listen to, music-wise. And you can add almost 16GB of music, because the device uses essentially none of the available space. BE AWARE: there is a menu option to delete files, or to delete *all* files, so, if you have small children, you know as well as I do that they will do exactly that, at least once. Anyway, music quality is quite good, both through the included headphones and via nicer ones of mine I tried.

(2) "Movie"

This comes with one movie, and it's a video some woman in a bikini singing on a beach. You've never heard of her, and you likely never will - after all, she's allowed her video to be on a $20 player. You can delete it, or you can keep it on. Video quality is surprisingly decent for such a cheap device. However... while I've not tested this device *yet* (will do soon when I post the video review of this), other devices with *very* similar firmware suggest that you'll never be able to encode movies for this, so you can probably forget ever putting other videos on this.

(3) "Record"

Shockingly useful. Using the menu, you can change the recording quality - it is actually really decent at the higher bit rates, and there's an option for automatic voice recognition, so it can record only when people are talking.

(4) "Voice"

This seems redundant - recordings show up here as well as in Music, although *only* recordings show up here, so it's a way to filter out music. Same options for deleting files as elsewhere.

(5) "FM Radio"

AWESOME. OK, it's not HD radio, but the quality is adequate. Noticeably worse than MP3s stored locally, but fine. Also: you *CAN* RECORD FM RADIO using the menu. Up to 16GB of it, which is an eternity. I'm not saying you want to record it, but you can. Bring it while travelling. Record local stations. Listen while flying home. Fun. You can auto-search stations, set it to use Japan radio bands, etc. Once programmed, press the center button to go through stations. This is very nice in this price range.

(6) "Photo"

Lets you look at photos you've added, in the same way you'd add music. They look fine, as long as you're 5. This is not a high-res display, nor would you expect it to be. Note: if you've putting pictures on this, *reduce the resolution*!! Hi-res photos will take extra space and, most importantly, will take forever to render, and they won't look any better. You can, as with music, delete one or all photos, and, yes, your kids will do this.

(7) "Setup"

Basics, like time, LCD mode, language, firmware upgrades, etc. Odds are you'll never need to use any of these.

(8) "E-book"

Ships empty, and while I suspect you can find file formats it'll accept, I can't imagine reading an e-book on this. Maybe I just have a poor imagination.

(9) "Game"

- Boxman: You move boxes around to clear up space. Not a terrible time consumer, especially for kids

- Tetrix: Shockingly, a Tetris clone. I bet you couldn't have guessed that!

- Snake: Brings back fond memories of my Nokia. Yours too, perhaps.

- Road: I Have *no idea* how to play this. Some sort of tile game.

OVERALL:

Look, this costs $20 or so. It is NOT an iPod nano. It is not, really, a movie player (unless you can find the proper obscure format), It isn't, really, an e-book reader. But: it's a good FM radio (with recording!), it is a good voice recorder, and it stores a ton of music (and/or pictures). I think it is *easily* worth what they are asking, and I think it'd be great for kids or as a cheap radio/recorder for adults.

Cons:

The menu system is... non-intuitive, to say the least. The device is aggressive about power savings and will power down if not used very quickly - much less than 30 seconds. However, when in use (music, radio, recording, etc), it works fine, and battery life is good. I wish it used micro USB, but thems the breaks. Still, overall, a 5 star device for this cost.

This product would be a great investment for giving you a Bluetooth option to a device that did not originally have that capability.

I receive many many bluetooth speakers to review so I have gotten fairly well acquainted with the nuanced differences between them. The speaker manufacturers are always looking for a way to set their speaker apart because with the ubiquity of these speakers they need to find a niche that would have buyers spending on their product over they're competition's product.

Enter the BV350.... This is a true rugged outdoor speaker. The company has supplied it with a bicycle mount (similar to the water bottle mount) so that you can easily affix it to your bike or pull it off of your bike and tote it with you. It comes with a karabiner for attaching to your belt loop or backback as you partake in outdoor activity.

ONE OF THE BEST FEATURES OF THIS SPEAKER.... is the easy to manipulate dedicated physical volume dial located at the top of the unit. If bluetooth speakers have volume buttons, all too often those buttons are shared with the "previous song/next song" button. If you are riding your bike at a good clip and you want to turn up the volume, you don't want to be fumbling with a shared button.... half the time when I hit those shared buttons to turn up the volume because I like a particular song, I hit it the wrong way and end up skipping to the next song. Trust me, this volume dial is a real pleasure.

But a volume dial alone isn't' enough to make a speaker into a five star wonder. Sound is probably the most critical, no? The sound on this is very good. Not the best I've heard in the portable speaker lineup but definitely very respectable. The sound favors the mid ranges and high notes but it is not tinny and there is some discernible bass. If you are a bass junkie this probably wont satisfy you but for the rest of us it gives enough hint of bass to make it pleasurable to listen to. I tried assorted music genres and all sounded good.

[[VIDEOID:650269cb170c560d01c58b48656739f3]]What's better than a single Bluetooth speaker? Two! And even better than that? Throw in one of those new Bluetooth transmitters than can pair TWO Bluetooth speakers at once, and get... FOUR!

:)

Paired with Samsung Galaxy S6; paired with a DBPower Bluetooth Transmitter/Receiver in conjunction with Artchros Bluetooth Dual (Wired) Speakers and AUX sourced from my S6. Also later added in the Creative Sound Blaster Roar 2 as a third \\"Buddy\\".

Audio Characteristics:
As a single speaker, rich, full spectrum with bumping bass, especially when you put on that little casing on the bottom - yet just not that loud. Good, comfortable volume when right-near-by... it does open up quite a bit, though, when you put two together.

The AUX Out, e.g. the \\"Buddy Stereo\\" seems to work best with I assume shadow powered speakers, like another UB+ that is turned off, so I am guessing the main unit (whichever one is turned on and actively paired) supplies power to the \\"Buddy\\". The AUX Out cord goes from Buddy Stereo to Buddy Stereo port, and not in the other AUX In port on the speaker, which also leads me to believe there is some special wiring going on inside.

**Update: These use four pole AUX cables (e.g. three rings around the jack) - will NOT work with typical three pole jacks (two rings around the jack). This may explain why the crackling I got on the Roar 2. Something to take note of if you are wanting to use a much longer cable (and there isn't much on Amazon in four pole, long audio cables, but I did buy a ten footer male to female extension from KableDirect).**

Still I did try out the Y-splitter that comes with each UB+ Eupho on a Creative Sound Blaster Roar 2, and it resulted in some crackly, crackly power interference until I gently fiddled with the cord. And yes, it seems older reviews took the Y-splitter as merely a way to connect two sources into one speaker. I immediately saw it the other way around. Three UB+ Euphos! But that also probably leads to a much shorter battery life (if I am right about the shadow powering).

**Update: I did get direct confirmation about daisy chaining UB+ Euphos - you can chain as many as you like with the splitter (apparently the biggest test was with FIFTY of them at once). No word about actual battery impact, but I can say its really good even with two.**

BATTERY LONGEVITY & COMPARATIVE MARKET PRICING:
20 Hours is when you have a single speaker playing at a moderate level; that is an outstanding battery for a speaker this size. On average, the play time is more like 4-5 hours for similar sized speakers in the budge range. Once you get around $25 +, the play time tends to improve to 8 to 10 hours. Here, twenty hours! The only other Bluetooth speaker I have that matched the play time is an Anker speaker I bought last year, specifically because of the incredible play time, and also priced at around $40. So that is the comparative market range this speaker, as a single, truly belongs in. However, if you have shopped about like I have for dual wired speakers that are Bluetooth enabled, 80 bucks for a set that has great audio response AND tiny footprint is also quite favorably comparative. That Artchros set I have cost me $50, and it does have far less bass sustainability than these put together.

As another example, iDeaUSA is selling a pair of dual synched Bluetooth speakers (no intervening wire) for $80 - yet those require a particularly strong, stable Bluetooth connection (like a Personal Computer) and didn't work with my DBPower transmitter... and are the much larger standard-sized speakers.

The UB+ Eupho does actively play while being concurrently powered by a USB source - just be aware that for most 5V rechargeable battery powered devices, this can have a negative impact on the battery capacity.

SUMMARY:
Gong back to the similarly priced, similarly rich sounding, similarly long life Anker Bluetooth speaker, the UB+ is a huge step forward with the \\"Buddy\\" connection. If Anker had the foresight last year to allow the same capability, I would have long purchased a second. Now, I am pondering purchasing a third one to try connecting via the Y-splitter. Would love to run one more behind me.... mmmm, Android gaming immersion. >Insert Homer Simpson Drooling Here<

OK, I've reviewed a similar player and hated it, but I like this one, for this price, and here is why.

For $20, you get a decent FM radio (with recording capability), 16GB of storage for music, and a nice voice recorder, as well as a few other features. You also get a nice lanyard and decent (not great, but surprisingly adequate) headphones. Are there limitations? Sure, of course - this is a 16GB $20 device with a color LCD screen... you need to manage your expectations.

What is the target demographic for these? Likely small kids (cheap device that they likely won't break), people who want a cheap FM radio, and/or people who want a cheap voice recorder. Yes, you can play movies on it, but odds are you won't be able to properly format them for this, so don't count on that capability - at all.

Here's what you can expect:

First of all, hardware wise, this is the size of an old school iPod nano but without the click wheel - yes, there's a "wheel", but it's really just four click locations and a center button - no scrolling capability. You also get a decent lanyard and really pretty nice headphones - I mean, you'd likely pay $8-$12 for these, so they're quite good when included in a $20 purchase. You also get a mini (not micro!) USB charging cable, which is unfortunate, because almost everything is micro USB these days. The LCD screen is nice enough - certainly for a device at this price range, and, honestly, you're not going to be watching movies on it, so it's more than adequate for the other features. There is either no micro SD card, or it's internal. Similar devices have them as removable, but, actually, I prefer this way - nothing to lose, nothing for kids to pull out and toss.

"Apps":

(1) "Music"

It comes with a couple of songs, and you can add more by connecting it to essentially any computer. Yes, this means you need a computer to add music - there's no WiFi, no iTunes, no Google Play, no Amazon Prime, etc - you need MP3s or the like to add to this manually, but that's OK. If you're getting this for kids, it means you have absolute control over what they listen to, music-wise. And you can add almost 16GB of music, because the device uses essentially none of the available space. BE AWARE: there is a menu option to delete files, or to delete *all* files, so, if you have small children, you know as well as I do that they will do exactly that, at least once. Anyway, music quality is quite good, both through the included headphones and via nicer ones of mine I tried.

(2) "Movie"

This comes with one movie, and it's a video some woman in a bikini singing on a beach. You've never heard of her, and you likely never will - after all, she's allowed her video to be on a $20 player. You can delete it, or you can keep it on. Video quality is surprisingly decent for such a cheap device. However... while I've not tested this device *yet* (will do soon when I post the video review of this), other devices with *very* similar firmware suggest that you'll never be able to encode movies for this, so you can probably forget ever putting other videos on this.

(3) "Record"

Shockingly useful. Using the menu, you can change the recording quality - it is actually really decent at the higher bit rates, and there's an option for automatic voice recognition, so it can record only when people are talking.

(4) "Voice"

This seems redundant - recordings show up here as well as in Music, although *only* recordings show up here, so it's a way to filter out music. Same options for deleting files as elsewhere.

(5) "FM Radio"

AWESOME. OK, it's not HD radio, but the quality is adequate. Noticeably worse than MP3s stored locally, but fine. Also: you *CAN* RECORD FM RADIO using the menu. Up to 16GB of it, which is an eternity. I'm not saying you want to record it, but you can. Bring it while travelling. Record local stations. Listen while flying home. Fun. You can auto-search stations, set it to use Japan radio bands, etc. Once programmed, press the center button to go through stations. This is very nice in this price range.

(6) "Photo"

Lets you look at photos you've added, in the same way you'd add music. They look fine, as long as you're 5. This is not a high-res display, nor would you expect it to be. Note: if you've putting pictures on this, *reduce the resolution*!! Hi-res photos will take extra space and, most importantly, will take forever to render, and they won't look any better. You can, as with music, delete one or all photos, and, yes, your kids will do this.

(7) "Setup"

Basics, like time, LCD mode, language, firmware upgrades, etc. Odds are you'll never need to use any of these.

(8) "E-book"

Ships empty, and while I suspect you can find file formats it'll accept, I can't imagine reading an e-book on this. Maybe I just have a poor imagination.

(9) "Game"

- Boxman: You move boxes around to clear up space. Not a terrible time consumer, especially for kids

- Tetrix: Shockingly, a Tetris clone. I bet you couldn't have guessed that!

- Snake: Brings back fond memories of my Nokia. Yours too, perhaps.

- Road: I Have *no idea* how to play this. Some sort of tile game.

OVERALL:

Look, this costs $20 or so. It is NOT an iPod nano. It is not, really, a movie player (unless you can find the proper obscure format), It isn't, really, an e-book reader. But: it's a good FM radio (with recording!), it is a good voice recorder, and it stores a ton of music (and/or pictures). I think it is *easily* worth what they are asking, and I think it'd be great for kids or as a cheap radio/recorder for adults.

Cons:

The menu system is... non-intuitive, to say the least. The device is aggressive about power savings and will power down if not used very quickly - much less than 30 seconds. However, when in use (music, radio, recording, etc), it works fine, and battery life is good. I wish it used micro USB, but thems the breaks. Still, overall, a 5 star device for this cost.

I have been an audiophile for about 4 decades. Over the years, I have used the finer speakers made by AR, JBL, Ohm...eventually settled on Carver ALS-3+ more than 15 years ago and have been very happy with it, no thought of ever replacing them. Since the early days of surround sound, I have also had a home theater system as well. The speakers in that system included Advent, Boston Acoustic, Jamo, Mirage, Polk Audio and Yamaha. I never paid attention to Energy speakers because it's not a highly recognized name in the US and I have never had a chance to see or hear them in the showrooms of hi-fi stores before they pretty much became extinct. About 5 years ago, I came across the RC50 on clearance sale for a modest sum, thought I would take a chance to order a pair. It was immediately obvious that it was better than any of the front speakers I ever had in my HT system. That prompted me to get 5 more RC speakers to revamp all my HT speakers except for the subwoofer: 2 RC-R for the rear, LCR for front center, and RC10 for front surround. They were all on some kind of clearance discount, probably because the company was sold to Klipsch and had some new models coming out. I later came across the Veritas V5.2c center that was supposed to be the reincarnation of the LCR. I bought one to see how it compared. The Veritas' wood finish was superb, but the old LCR is the clear winner in sound quality. After playing the Veritas long enough to be sure that it's not an issue with break-in, I returned it for a refund, something that I rarely do. I was aware that RC70 was the flagship model in the product line, but it was unavailable at the time. Some months later, an authorized dealer's web site showed that there would be a forthcoming stock. I pre-ordered a pair with no hesitation, got them a few months later to replace the RC50. That completed the upgrade.

What distinguishes the RC speakers is the lack of coloration and distortion, i.e., the tonal balance is very neutral, voices and instruments sound smooth, natural and clear. The sound quality is consistent across the product line, matched much better than other company's. The tiny RC10 sounds very much like the big RC70, except a little shy in the bass, but there is enough that many marveled at how big its bass sounded. Putting on the grilles softens the treble a bit. They're magnetically attached, could be easily removed or reattached as one feels like, no worry about breaking some mechanical clips. The appearance also changes with the grille off. The silver/black drivers set in real wood veneer gives an aggressive "robocop" kind of look. This is very practical if a driver ever needs to be replaced. All that's need is to take out a few screws and the driver can be pulled off from the front. I actually had to do that once. Energy sent me a 6.5" driver and it took just a few minutes to make the swap. Were it not covered by the 5-yr warranty, the cost would have been about $60, minimal sum in hi-fi repair. So as long as the company lives, one doesn't need to worry about the RC speaker ever dying. I don't think I'll ever have to think about "upgrading" this 7 speaker HT system.

The tonal quality of the RC70 is actually not that different from the Carver. Both are smooth and neutral. I've found myself using the RC system more and more for listening to music as there are growing numbers of concert DVDs and multichannel music recordings available (SACD, BluRay Audio, DVD Audio, etc.) For most music, the RC70 has a bass that's good enough. The spec goes down to 31 Hz, but that's at -10db level. It could benefit from a subwoofer. I use a Mirage BPS-150i, which is my first and last sub. It works with the RC70 nicely both for music and movies. It doesn't cause an earthquake in the house, but more than my spouse can stand.

Many owners of RC speakers commented that they're incredible value. They seem to have a small random supply that would suddenly appear and then quickly sold out. In recent years, they're offered at a fraction of their original MSRP, and so nothing else could approach that quality/price ratio. Klipsch bought the company but didn't really market the orphaned products to meet the demand. RC70, RC-10 and RC-LCR are still shown on the company web site as current products. I think they actually taken off for a few years and brought back from the grave. This is very rare except for special products that have a real following. I suspect if Klipsch markets the RCs properly, make them widely available, they may take a lot of sales away from other more profitable speakers.y sold out. Worth a look if you need good capacity and not too much else.

I have owned many headphones. Last year I was on a mission to find the best for the buck.... from $9 ear buds to over the ear headphones for $200. These Sony MDRV6's are without doubt the best by a loooooooong way! Amazon had a 12 hour sale on these bad boys, sale price $55! I couldn't say no! I had already reviewed these and the Sony 7506 (same headphones) a long time ago, when I saw the $55 price I jumped on it.

They arrived within the week. Well packaged, nice box with red velvet cloth, carry bag and the actual coiled cord has the 3.5mm connector but you get the 6.5mm adapter as well. (not gold). They fit 'my' head very comfortably. So enough about the headphones......you know it's a Sony product and you'll get quality! Now for the sound !!!!

I like all types of music except rap and maybe hip-hop. My fav is more along the lines of Depeche Mode, Fusion, Coffee Shop Music...with a little Pink Floyd, Yes, ACDC, and many many others. Anyway....the sound!

First the loudness. I've read many reviews about these headphones and people made comments that they used an amplifier.... I honestly don't see the need (yet). They are plenty loud! I use an iPod (6th Gen) and have the volume at 3/4 or 75% and it's loud!!! Yes, you could use an amp and ramp up the volume but right now, for me, I don't see the point. The actual quality of sound blew me away from the very first song. OMG!!!! I can't begin to explain the quality of sound!!!!!!!!! People have reviewed that these headphones do not bloat the bass or put shine on the treble and I believe they are right. The sound seems very true, very sure, very REAL !!! and VERY PERFECT !!! and you really do hear things you've never heard before. As I've said, I've used Beats, Sennheisers, JVC, Bose.... but for whatever technical reasons, Sony have done something magical here....it's insane at how clear and crisp the sound is! This is great for audio systems where turning on the receiver can automatically turn on other components like a blu-ray player or subwoofer. This compact USB device works well for receiving GPS. The main 'brain' of this unit is a chipset called U-blox7 which is a modern GPS device designed by (and made for) UBlox, a Swiss fabless semi-conductor company which specializes in high quality communications and positioning components.

This receiver receives the USA medium-earth orbiting GPS satellites as well as the Russian GLONASS positioning satellites system plus several other supplementary satellites that are in certain parts of the world to supplement reception.

When the device is 'locked' onto several satellites, the yellow LED flashes once a second to show that it has a constant lock on the GPS satellites.

Full technical specifications are available in a comprehensive document from u-blox.com which detail full features of the device and cover commands that it accepts if you wish to program the devices many options youself. (document "u-Blox7 Receiver Description including Protocol Specification" - a 209 page document in English for geeks).

The receiver is compatible with the Industry Standard NMEA (National Marine Electronics Association) command language which ensures that it is compatible with a wide variety of standard software.

Drivers are available also from Ublox which work well with this device. I installed for Windows 7 Professional Edition without issues. It also works on Windows XP, Windows 8, Linux. I do not know if it is compatible with Windows 10 yet.

It has been demonstrated that hi res audio files, like the one PonoMusic store sells, may or may not offer sonic differences over CD audio. When they do, it's because it's a different master of the CD.

However, the PonoPlayer is designed to make your CD audio sound worse than a higher sampled version of the same exact song (not a re-master). Stereophile measured the PonoPlayer's output and found that when using 44.1 sampling rate (that of standard CD audio quality), the treble is slightly rolled off within the range of human hearing from what it should be. In other words, if you take the same CD audio file and resample it to a higher sampling rate--like the hi res audio on PonoMusic--it will sound better with the high res file because the original is not being played accurately, but with slightly less highs, which tends to affect how one perceives detail in music.

So definitely not a good player for CD audio. Get yourself a FiiO X3 or X5 for that. And then if you buy a hi res song from Pono Music and compare it to your CD quality version, how will you ever know if its actually better?

Is this design flaw intentional? Impossible to know. But it certainly does deceptively work to encourage people to buy Pono Music.

OK, I've reviewed a similar player and hated it, but I like this one, for this price, and here is why.

For $20, you get a decent FM radio (with recording capability), 16GB of storage for music, and a nice voice recorder, as well as a few other features. You also get a nice lanyard and decent (not great, but surprisingly adequate) headphones. Are there limitations? Sure, of course - this is a 16GB $20 device with a color LCD screen... you need to manage your expectations.

What is the target demographic for these? Likely small kids (cheap device that they likely won't break), people who want a cheap FM radio, and/or people who want a cheap voice recorder. Yes, you can play movies on it, but odds are you won't be able to properly format them for this, so don't count on that capability - at all.

Here's what you can expect:

First of all, hardware wise, this is the size of an old school iPod nano but without the click wheel - yes, there's a "wheel", but it's really just four click locations and a center button - no scrolling capability. You also get a decent lanyard and really pretty nice headphones - I mean, you'd likely pay $8-$12 for these, so they're quite good when included in a $20 purchase. You also get a mini (not micro!) USB charging cable, which is unfortunate, because almost everything is micro USB these days. The LCD screen is nice enough - certainly for a device at this price range, and, honestly, you're not going to be watching movies on it, so it's more than adequate for the other features. There is either no micro SD card, or it's internal. Similar devices have them as removable, but, actually, I prefer this way - nothing to lose, nothing for kids to pull out and toss.

"Apps":

(1) "Music"

It comes with a couple of songs, and you can add more by connecting it to essentially any computer. Yes, this means you need a computer to add music - there's no WiFi, no iTunes, no Google Play, no Amazon Prime, etc - you need MP3s or the like to add to this manually, but that's OK. If you're getting this for kids, it means you have absolute control over what they listen to, music-wise. And you can add almost 16GB of music, because the device uses essentially none of the available space. BE AWARE: there is a menu option to delete files, or to delete *all* files, so, if you have small children, you know as well as I do that they will do exactly that, at least once. Anyway, music quality is quite good, both through the included headphones and via nicer ones of mine I tried.

(2) "Movie"

This comes with one movie, and it's a video some woman in a bikini singing on a beach. You've never heard of her, and you likely never will - after all, she's allowed her video to be on a $20 player. You can delete it, or you can keep it on. Video quality is surprisingly decent for such a cheap device. However... while I've not tested this device *yet* (will do soon when I post the video review of this), other devices with *very* similar firmware suggest that you'll never be able to encode movies for this, so you can probably forget ever putting other videos on this.

(3) "Record"

Shockingly useful. Using the menu, you can change the recording quality - it is actually really decent at the higher bit rates, and there's an option for automatic voice recognition, so it can record only when people are talking.

(4) "Voice"

This seems redundant - recordings show up here as well as in Music, although *only* recordings show up here, so it's a way to filter out music. Same options for deleting files as elsewhere.

(5) "FM Radio"

AWESOME. OK, it's not HD radio, but the quality is adequate. Noticeably worse than MP3s stored locally, but fine. Also: you *CAN* RECORD FM RADIO using the menu. Up to 16GB of it, which is an eternity. I'm not saying you want to record it, but you can. Bring it while travelling. Record local stations. Listen while flying home. Fun. You can auto-search stations, set it to use Japan radio bands, etc. Once programmed, press the center button to go through stations. This is very nice in this price range.

(6) "Photo"

Lets you look at photos you've added, in the same way you'd add music. They look fine, as long as you're 5. This is not a high-res display, nor would you expect it to be. Note: if you've putting pictures on this, *reduce the resolution*!! Hi-res photos will take extra space and, most importantly, will take forever to render, and they won't look any better. You can, as with music, delete one or all photos, and, yes, your kids will do this.

(7) "Setup"

Basics, like time, LCD mode, language, firmware upgrades, etc. Odds are you'll never need to use any of these.

(8) "E-book"

Ships empty, and while I suspect you can find file formats it'll accept, I can't imagine reading an e-book on this. Maybe I just have a poor imagination.

(9) "Game"

- Boxman: You move boxes around to clear up space. Not a terrible time consumer, especially for kids

- Tetrix: Shockingly, a Tetris clone. I bet you couldn't have guessed that!

- Snake: Brings back fond memories of my Nokia. Yours too, perhaps.

- Road: I Have *no idea* how to play this. Some sort of tile game.

OVERALL:

Look, this costs $20 or so. It is NOT an iPod nano. It is not, really, a movie player (unless you can find the proper obscure format), It isn't, really, an e-book reader. But: it's a good FM radio (with recording!), it is a good voice recorder, and it stores a ton of music (and/or pictures). I think it is *easily* worth what they are asking, and I think it'd be great for kids or as a cheap radio/recorder for adults.

Cons:

The menu system is... non-intuitive, to say the least. The device is aggressive about power savings and will power down if not used very quickly - much less than 30 seconds. However, when in use (music, radio, recording, etc), it works fine, and battery life is good. I wish it used micro USB, but thems the breaks. Still, overall, a 5 star device for this cost.

Update – I have had to stop using this clock after several months of operation. The clock just stops momentarily, resetting to 12:00 midnight on Jan 1. I initially thought that the AC power was being stopped because the input from the transformer might have come loose, so I arranged to it to be attached more securely, but the same thing still happened, even though there was no one near the connection when the interruption occurred. I then went to battery power, but the projection system does not work on battery power, so I used both the battery and AC in hopes that if there was an interruption in the AC then the battery backup would prevent the clock from resetting, but it does not. Even a broken clock is right twice a day, but when this clock resets it is never right, and gives an erroneous time. I have therefore had to downgrade from two to only one star.

Original review -
I do not recommend this clock for the reasons described below. The clock worked and I purchased it on a half price closeout, so as a clock it was OK, but overpriced if you just operate it as a simple digital clock, hence two stars instead of the minimum one. Note that this clock is sold by numerous vendors at varying prices. While not noted here, this is model 2200.

Why do I call this a “brain dead” - described below in order of the most annoying features first:
· The projector feature is poorly designed. When you face the clock, it projects the time on the wall behind or above the clock upside down and backwards. The time is projected correctly on the wall facing the clock and can therefore be read when you are facing this wall and have your back towards the clock. However, this most likely requires projecting the time more than the six foot focusing distance, as it did in my case. The result is a large somewhat blurry image. The correct orientation is also displayed when you turn the clock with its back facing you, so you can only read the projected time on the wall facing the clock. BETTER PROJECTOR CLOCKS HAVE THE ABILITY TO FLIP THE IMAGE IN ORDER TO CORRECT FOR THIS, and give you the ability to view the correct image with the clock in a different orientation relative to the way that you are facing. Also, while the projector can be rotated about one axis, that is all. Therefore, I found it impossible to orient both the clock and the projected image to optimum orientations.

· The clock face is tilted backwards at a fixed angle, which cannot be adjusted. This made it difficult to read the clock while lying in bed, and required me to make a jury-rigged system to keep the face at an orientation where I could read the clock. Unfortunately, the clock was less stable in this position, requiring still further modifications. Even a moderately thoughtful deign would have eliminated this problem without adding to the cost of the clock.

· The temperature readings were three degrees high (compared to two other digital thermometers in the room). This may seem petty, but if you are interested on knowing the temperature and its changes over a period of days you should at least see the correct value. This incorrect value may be due to the heat given off by the projecting LED and there is no way to turn off the projector, except to run completely on batteries. (The clock can be run completely on battery power, or with the batteries as a backup for a power failure but unused when the clock is running on AC.)

· The clock is very bright, perhaps too bright when you are trying to sleep and there is no way to reduce the brightness. The numbers are 1/2 an inch high as opposed to ¾ of an inch on other clocks. Instead of a larger image this clock has color bands that go up and down and cycle, illustrating the temperature changes over the last five days. The bands take up most of the lower half of the clock face and I found them to be distracting, so I had to cover over this feature, as there is no way to turn it off.

· Setting the clock up was a pain – not at all intuitive and probably almost impossible without the instructions, so if you lose them the clock might become useless.

All in all this is a prime example of a poor (brain dead) design. The clock would have been more useful as more than a simple clock if the clock face could be tilted and more useful as a projector clock if the projected image could be rotated about more than one axis and flipped so that it could be read when one was facing the clock, instead of only when the clock face is not also visible. Sewell seems to be savvy at filling a niche market with cabling products for discerning "cine-mediaphiles" and audiophiles. The wires sound good however, you'll want to do an inspection of connection points, like the jacket and composite connector to ensure they are not separating, exposing the shielding underneath.

Try a gentle test bend at each end. In this case, the wire remains functional and electrically sound however the jacket separated from the connector plug. The 12 gauge speaker wires are sound transparent, claiming high strand counts and upscale connectors. Unfortunately troubleshooting intermittent signaling to one channel was required leading to a discovery that the set screws located under the milled barrel covers, which hold the actual wire in place were all loose to varying degrees. The barrels themselves were also an issue because of loose thread tolerances. Loctite resolved this issue. Tightening these screws resolved the continuity issue and now the sound output is great.

Good - the performance claims seem valid
Bad - Quality Control is spotty requiring inspection to avoid electrical issues.

Troubleshoot the product to resolve issues. Or, find some other cabling product.

Over the past couple of years, Amazon has been increasing the number and types of products offered on the site that are made for them and bear their own brand as Amazon Basics. I have heard these items criticized as being somehow ‘generic’ and, therefore, not in the same league with the name brands – especially in electronics. These Premium Over-Ear Headphones prove that aspersion without foundation.

Like many of the other Amazon Basic items I have used, these headphones do a better than ‘adequate’ job of what they do. At this price point, one must accept that they are not trying to compete with Dr. Dre or BOSE – these are straight-forward plug-in headphones, well-padded and comfortable to wear that deliver good sound from good sound sources.

Although their frequency range is markedly limited compared to more expensive equipment (15 Hz to 22 Hz), only the most discriminating audiophile would notice the difference. The bulk of musically audible sound falls within that range and headphones with broader range have it, primarily, for show.

I found these to be more than adequate for most listening purposes. I get tired of recharging Bluetooth devices and actually enjoy a plug-in listening device from time to time. Today, I have been using them to review some old tracks on my iPhone – the plug works perfectly with my Apple phone and Pad. The sound is good. The bass is solid but not overpowering. The trebles are clear and true and the mid-range sounds play through as they were intended – right in the middle. No complaints.

I have more expensive and more highly developed listening equipment but I believe that these Premium Over-Ear Headphones from Amazon Basics can fill a real need for better than average, well-engineered, comfortable plug-in headphones.

They are somewhat less than ‘great’, but a great deal better than ‘adequate!’

Give ‘em a try.

OK, I've reviewed a similar player and hated it, but I like this one, for this price, and here is why.

For $20, you get a decent FM radio (with recording capability), 16GB of storage for music, and a nice voice recorder, as well as a few other features. You also get a nice lanyard and decent (not great, but surprisingly adequate) headphones. Are there limitations? Sure, of course - this is a 16GB $20 device with a color LCD screen... you need to manage your expectations.

What is the target demographic for these? Likely small kids (cheap device that they likely won't break), people who want a cheap FM radio, and/or people who want a cheap voice recorder. Yes, you can play movies on it, but odds are you won't be able to properly format them for this, so don't count on that capability - at all.

Here's what you can expect:

First of all, hardware wise, this is the size of an old school iPod nano but without the click wheel - yes, there's a "wheel", but it's really just four click locations and a center button - no scrolling capability. You also get a decent lanyard and really pretty nice headphones - I mean, you'd likely pay $8-$12 for these, so they're quite good when included in a $20 purchase. You also get a mini (not micro!) USB charging cable, which is unfortunate, because almost everything is micro USB these days. The LCD screen is nice enough - certainly for a device at this price range, and, honestly, you're not going to be watching movies on it, so it's more than adequate for the other features. There is either no micro SD card, or it's internal. Similar devices have them as removable, but, actually, I prefer this way - nothing to lose, nothing for kids to pull out and toss.

"Apps":

(1) "Music"

It comes with a couple of songs, and you can add more by connecting it to essentially any computer. Yes, this means you need a computer to add music - there's no WiFi, no iTunes, no Google Play, no Amazon Prime, etc - you need MP3s or the like to add to this manually, but that's OK. If you're getting this for kids, it means you have absolute control over what they listen to, music-wise. And you can add almost 16GB of music, because the device uses essentially none of the available space. BE AWARE: there is a menu option to delete files, or to delete *all* files, so, if you have small children, you know as well as I do that they will do exactly that, at least once. Anyway, music quality is quite good, both through the included headphones and via nicer ones of mine I tried.

(2) "Movie"

This comes with one movie, and it's a video some woman in a bikini singing on a beach. You've never heard of her, and you likely never will - after all, she's allowed her video to be on a $20 player. You can delete it, or you can keep it on. Video quality is surprisingly decent for such a cheap device. However... while I've not tested this device *yet* (will do soon when I post the video review of this), other devices with *very* similar firmware suggest that you'll never be able to encode movies for this, so you can probably forget ever putting other videos on this.

(3) "Record"

Shockingly useful. Using the menu, you can change the recording quality - it is actually really decent at the higher bit rates, and there's an option for automatic voice recognition, so it can record only when people are talking.

(4) "Voice"

This seems redundant - recordings show up here as well as in Music, although *only* recordings show up here, so it's a way to filter out music. Same options for deleting files as elsewhere.

(5) "FM Radio"

AWESOME. OK, it's not HD radio, but the quality is adequate. Noticeably worse than MP3s stored locally, but fine. Also: you *CAN* RECORD FM RADIO using the menu. Up to 16GB of it, which is an eternity. I'm not saying you want to record it, but you can. Bring it while travelling. Record local stations. Listen while flying home. Fun. You can auto-search stations, set it to use Japan radio bands, etc. Once programmed, press the center button to go through stations. This is very nice in this price range.

(6) "Photo"

Lets you look at photos you've added, in the same way you'd add music. They look fine, as long as you're 5. This is not a high-res display, nor would you expect it to be. Note: if you've putting pictures on this, *reduce the resolution*!! Hi-res photos will take extra space and, most importantly, will take forever to render, and they won't look any better. You can, as with music, delete one or all photos, and, yes, your kids will do this.

(7) "Setup"

Basics, like time, LCD mode, language, firmware upgrades, etc. Odds are you'll never need to use any of these.

(8) "E-book"

Ships empty, and while I suspect you can find file formats it'll accept, I can't imagine reading an e-book on this. Maybe I just have a poor imagination.

(9) "Game"

- Boxman: You move boxes around to clear up space. Not a terrible time consumer, especially for kids

- Tetrix: Shockingly, a Tetris clone. I bet you couldn't have guessed that!

- Snake: Brings back fond memories of my Nokia. Yours too, perhaps.

- Road: I Have *no idea* how to play this. Some sort of tile game.

OVERALL:

Look, this costs $20 or so. It is NOT an iPod nano. It is not, really, a movie player (unless you can find the proper obscure format), It isn't, really, an e-book reader. But: it's a good FM radio (with recording!), it is a good voice recorder, and it stores a ton of music (and/or pictures). I think it is *easily* worth what they are asking, and I think it'd be great for kids or as a cheap radio/recorder for adults.

Cons:

The menu system is... non-intuitive, to say the least. The device is aggressive about power savings and will power down if not used very quickly - much less than 30 seconds. However, when in use (music, radio, recording, etc), it works fine, and battery life is good. I wish it used micro USB, but thems the breaks. Still, overall, a 5 star device for this cost.

BT speakers are dime-a-dozen these days; many are cheaply made; some are expensive but feels cheaply made. The Crystal Base BT Spear is the polar opposite; it commands respectable performance and solid construction feel for a great price!

The package is compact and no-nonsense. Inside you will find the speaker itself, instruction manual, and a USB/3.5mm axillary audio cable combo.

The speaker itself has a nice pink exterior, with shiny pink rhinestones to further increase its aesthetic value. Volume is adjusted by the black ribbed plastic band, which I thought was very interesting. On the side you will find a SD card insert (a feature not found on most speakers, sure can come in handy), charging/BT light indicator, and a mini-USB port for charging and audio input. The speaker, despite it's relatively small size (a hair over 2-inches tall and wide) actually feels quite hefty in your hands, which I love.

On the bottom are the mode selector (to go between BT and 3.5mm), +/- buttons to select song/volume (depending on how long you press it for), on/off switch, and pause/play button. I actually kind of wish they would incorporate these buttons on the side of the speaker, but for something so compact it really isn't a hassle to simply flip it, set what you want, and keep playing.

Now here is something I have never seen done on a speaker: it SPEAKS TO YOU! When you turn it on, it announce itself to be in Bluetooth mode in a rather pleasant female voice and let you know if it is waiting for a connection/is connected. It will let you know when it has switched over to line-in mode as well. Now I wish there was a way to select whether to have this function on or not, but the instruction manual did not say how/if it is possible.

Also a feature to note: the speaker automatically detects your audio input method. If you were streaming via BT but wanted to plug your phone in via 3.5mm, simply connect the devices with the included combi-cable; the speaker will automatically announce it has switched over to line-in mode and resume streaming.

Finally, the combi-cable was a very clever concept. With some of my other BT speakers I have to carry 2 cable: 1 USB for charging, 1 3.5mm in case I want/need a hardwire connection. With the Crystal Base speaker, the cables are one! On one end is the mini-USB plug that goes into the speaker; on the other are a USB plug for your normal charging, and a 3.5mm plug for music! The upside would be you'll very likely to have this cable with you to charge it whenever you need to; the downside would be you'd be SOL if you want the hardwire connection but doesn't have this combi cable with you as the speaker itself does NOT have a 3.5mm jack on it.

This is a very well thought-out BT speaker and quite nicely implemented. It will be sitting pretty on my nightstand!

It’s a little hard to say how well the APC Home Theater Power Filter works, since for comparison I’d need something like, say, an electrical storm that damaged electronics on another surge protector but not on this one, and even then there are so many variables that a side-by-side comparison wouldn’t be all that meaningful. The unit certainly makes me feel confident, though.

For starters, it’s heavy. Okay, “heavy” isn’t a feature, but it’s likely indicative of sturdy, heavy-duty construction. The equipment protection guarantee is valued at $350,000, and while even very low-end surge protectors that are really little more than extension cords often claim cash-value equipment protection, $350,000 is pretty substantial.

This unit is designed and arranged very thoughtfully. The glossy black exterior works well with all of the other components in my home theater system, and the plugs can be rotated to the most convenient orientation. I will admit I laughed a little at the box’s suggestion that it could be placed on top of other components, like it was so good looking that one wouldn’t even notice the spaghetti farm growing out of it, but still, it is attractive as these things go. It also uses master outlets that can stop the power flow when an outlet senses that a device is not in use, and claims to save up to $40 on your electricity bill with this feature; not sure how they arrive at that figure, but it is an eco-friendly option nevertheless.

I work at home and depend on my company’s tech support to keep my equipment working well, and the APC brand is suggested every time power protection is discussed. I’m not paid if I’m not working, so I sometimes push my luck a little during thunderstorms. I own two other APC surge protectors and an APC uninterruptable power supply, and they have worked flawlessly. I expect to be just as satisfied with the Home Theater Power Filter.

If I discover the answer I will post that.

**** Update on DVD 2d-3d conversion jitter ****
I found the answer to the problem. under Screen Settings on the Sony player, Go to Output Video Resolution. By default it is set to Auto, change it to either 720P or if your TV is capable 1080P. The problem is that the DVD is not natively 1080P and so when converted to 3d, it goes to 1080i. If you force the 1080p or 720p it will stay that way. though I did have a few times on some previews or menus that it changed to 1080i but the movie itself stayed in 1080p and so no jitter. I had to make no setting changes to my TV. I have a Vizio 42" Passive 3D TV.

[[VIDEOID:81a195ab62552d5461d8932449079a2e]]Let me start off by saying I am a big fan of this speaker. The title says it all. I have had a number of different bluetooth speakers that were acceptable. While they all can connect wirelessly and produce sound, this product is simply at another level, it is exceptional.

I first noticed the heft of the speaker. Although compact (about the size of a hardback book) the weight and feel gave it a solid and quality presence. Included in the packaging was a power cord and a micro usb cord. Pairing was a snap and the Bluetooth range is what is typical for all bluetooth devices (about 30 feet in open air). What blew me away was the thought that went into the design and of course the sound.

This is a full feature speaker with some nice perks that are available. First the sound though. The speaker easily fills a normal sized room on its own. If you want a bit more punch the tera bass button functions like a built in eq to produce more bass and lows. When outside or when you really need the speaker to preform you can also use the roar function. This is an eq balance intended to be used at louder volumes to help carry the lows and highs.

I appreciated that the speaker can be laid flat with the main speakers facing up to fill a room with sound or placed upright with a more directional orientation of the speakers so you can point them where you want. As for the speakers the literature says there are two amps and 5 drivers on board. What does that mean?? One amp drives specifically the higher tones while the other dedicated driver drives lower and midrange notes. 5 Drivers refers to the speakers. They are hard to see behind the mesh but there is a 2.5-3 inch sub in the center with 2 seperate speakers on either side for higher frequencies. On either side are diaphragms that you can see and feel move with the bass. I am not sure if they are independently powered or just function secondary to the speakers on top but they work and are impressive.

Now for the extra features. The Mic works great and when used the folks I was speaking with had no idea I had them on speaker. There is also a recording feature which is interesting. You can use this to take memos or even record phone conversations which is interesting. To use the recording feature you need to have an SD card inserted which can also play back MP3 files (I couldnt test this feature because I dont have any files stored in MP3 format. You can also use the onboard battery to charge your USB device. The speaker can be hooked up to your computer and used as a powered speaker. There is software you can download to use together that gives you more EQ settings to further fine tune the speaker.

All in all, a feature packed speaker that preforms a lot better than I have come to expect bluetooth speakers to preform. Full disclosure this was provided to me to review by the seller but I would not hesitate to recommend. If you have any questions please leave a comment.

OK, I've reviewed a similar player and hated it, but I like this one, for this price, and here is why.

For $20, you get a decent FM radio (with recording capability), 16GB of storage for music, and a nice voice recorder, as well as a few other features. You also get a nice lanyard and decent (not great, but surprisingly adequate) headphones. Are there limitations? Sure, of course - this is a 16GB $20 device with a color LCD screen... you need to manage your expectations.

What is the target demographic for these? Likely small kids (cheap device that they likely won't break), people who want a cheap FM radio, and/or people who want a cheap voice recorder. Yes, you can play movies on it, but odds are you won't be able to properly format them for this, so don't count on that capability - at all.

Here's what you can expect:

First of all, hardware wise, this is the size of an old school iPod nano but without the click wheel - yes, there's a "wheel", but it's really just four click locations and a center button - no scrolling capability. You also get a decent lanyard and really pretty nice headphones - I mean, you'd likely pay $8-$12 for these, so they're quite good when included in a $20 purchase. You also get a mini (not micro!) USB charging cable, which is unfortunate, because almost everything is micro USB these days. The LCD screen is nice enough - certainly for a device at this price range, and, honestly, you're not going to be watching movies on it, so it's more than adequate for the other features. There is either no micro SD card, or it's internal. Similar devices have them as removable, but, actually, I prefer this way - nothing to lose, nothing for kids to pull out and toss.

"Apps":

(1) "Music"

It comes with a couple of songs, and you can add more by connecting it to essentially any computer. Yes, this means you need a computer to add music - there's no WiFi, no iTunes, no Google Play, no Amazon Prime, etc - you need MP3s or the like to add to this manually, but that's OK. If you're getting this for kids, it means you have absolute control over what they listen to, music-wise. And you can add almost 16GB of music, because the device uses essentially none of the available space. BE AWARE: there is a menu option to delete files, or to delete *all* files, so, if you have small children, you know as well as I do that they will do exactly that, at least once. Anyway, music quality is quite good, both through the included headphones and via nicer ones of mine I tried.

(2) "Movie"

This comes with one movie, and it's a video some woman in a bikini singing on a beach. You've never heard of her, and you likely never will - after all, she's allowed her video to be on a $20 player. You can delete it, or you can keep it on. Video quality is surprisingly decent for such a cheap device. However... while I've not tested this device *yet* (will do soon when I post the video review of this), other devices with *very* similar firmware suggest that you'll never be able to encode movies for this, so you can probably forget ever putting other videos on this.

(3) "Record"

Shockingly useful. Using the menu, you can change the recording quality - it is actually really decent at the higher bit rates, and there's an option for automatic voice recognition, so it can record only when people are talking.

(4) "Voice"

This seems redundant - recordings show up here as well as in Music, although *only* recordings show up here, so it's a way to filter out music. Same options for deleting files as elsewhere.

(5) "FM Radio"

AWESOME. OK, it's not HD radio, but the quality is adequate. Noticeably worse than MP3s stored locally, but fine. Also: you *CAN* RECORD FM RADIO using the menu. Up to 16GB of it, which is an eternity. I'm not saying you want to record it, but you can. Bring it while travelling. Record local stations. Listen while flying home. Fun. You can auto-search stations, set it to use Japan radio bands, etc. Once programmed, press the center button to go through stations. This is very nice in this price range.

(6) "Photo"

Lets you look at photos you've added, in the same way you'd add music. They look fine, as long as you're 5. This is not a high-res display, nor would you expect it to be. Note: if you've putting pictures on this, *reduce the resolution*!! Hi-res photos will take extra space and, most importantly, will take forever to render, and they won't look any better. You can, as with music, delete one or all photos, and, yes, your kids will do this.

(7) "Setup"

Basics, like time, LCD mode, language, firmware upgrades, etc. Odds are you'll never need to use any of these.

(8) "E-book"

Ships empty, and while I suspect you can find file formats it'll accept, I can't imagine reading an e-book on this. Maybe I just have a poor imagination.

(9) "Game"

- Boxman: You move boxes around to clear up space. Not a terrible time consumer, especially for kids

- Tetrix: Shockingly, a Tetris clone. I bet you couldn't have guessed that!

- Snake: Brings back fond memories of my Nokia. Yours too, perhaps.

- Road: I Have *no idea* how to play this. Some sort of tile game.

OVERALL:

Look, this costs $20 or so. It is NOT an iPod nano. It is not, really, a movie player (unless you can find the proper obscure format), It isn't, really, an e-book reader. But: it's a good FM radio (with recording!), it is a good voice recorder, and it stores a ton of music (and/or pictures). I think it is *easily* worth what they are asking, and I think it'd be great for kids or as a cheap radio/recorder for adults.

Cons:

The menu system is... non-intuitive, to say the least. The device is aggressive about power savings and will power down if not used very quickly - much less than 30 seconds. However, when in use (music, radio, recording, etc), it works fine, and battery life is good. I wish it used micro USB, but thems the breaks. Still, overall, a 5 star device for this cost.

I purchased this mounting bracket to hang a 54" Samsung LED TV on my living room wall. The bracket arrived in a box that was so small I questioned whether it was the correct item. Upon opening the box and reading the instructions I discovered that the wall mount is shipped in 2 pieces that have to be assembled as well as the two vertical brackets that attach to the rear of the TV also have to be assembled from 2 parts. This process was easy and once assembled the wall bracket and TV mounting brackets feel well made and solid.

The process of mounting the wall plate was the most difficult part as I wanted to make sure I hit vertical 2x4 studs to support the TV. I had already cut a small hole in the wall to run cables back into a closet, so I was able to measure from that hole laterally to find the 1st stud. By using an electronic stud finder and ruler I was able to locate the 2nd stud. My house is a 1950s era home, so I have a plaster coating over some type of very hard, thick drywall so I used a mortar bit to begin drilling. Once I hit wood, I switched to a standard bit in the size recommended in the instructions. I used an adjustable wrench to cinch down the lag bolts holding the wall bracket to the wall without any incident. I'd read other reviews about people using too much force on the bolts and actually snapping the head off. I did not have that problem, but I was extremely careful when I was cinching them down. I will note that I used the level that was included with the bracket and that is the only reason the bracket doesn't get 5 stars. The included level was inaccurate and left me with a bracket that was maybe 1/8 of an inch off of level. I corrected this problem later in the process by sliding a thin shim between the wall mount and the bracket on the back of the TV, but I wish I had used a different level to make my drill marks.

With the wall bracket mounted to the wall and the vertical brackets attached to the back to the TV, I got some help lifting the TV up and hooking it onto the wall mount. The process (with the exception of the inaccurate level) was fairly easy straight forward.

The bracket allows the TV to be tilted easily and holds the angle of tilt well. It allows some lateral movement once attached (before you cinch down the locking screws) in case you need to fine-tune the horizontal placement of the TV.

I'd recommend this bracket to mount your TV, but as I said earlier I'd use my own level or buy a better quality level to use for this installation. I purchased these to help me clean up the wiring behind my receiver more easily. Before these plugs, I had to "screw in" each bare wire of my surround sound speaker system individually into the posts on the back of my receiver. With 5 speakers for a surround sound setup, that's 10 wires total which made it very difficult to make the wires look neat, (which requires being able to cut each wire to the same length and route them in a way that they are not tangled) because disconnecting and reconnecting each wire was a real pain. But with these plugs, it made it enjoyable (and very quick) to clean up my wiring because it is so easy to terminate the wires and fix any tangled cables by plugging and unplugging until everything was untangled.

These plugs are so easy to use. To terminate them you just need to strip off about a half inch of your speaker wire, push it into the back of the plugs, and then fold it over onto the ridged edges of the plug (I like to split the wire strands in half and fold half of the strands to one side, and the other half to the other side of the plug). Then you just screw the back on and you're done. Once assembled, the plugs feel rock solid and like they have just the right amount of tension when plugging and unplugging them.

Like I said, I love these plugs and they are now an essential part of my setup. I highly recommend these.

Without wasting a square inch of the space, SoundMagic packed the box very efficiently with a foam cutout piece holding E80 IEMs and a spacious hard case holding all the eartips. Though nothing can beat Brainwavz IEM cases, I found SoundMagic square IEM case with pockets on each side to be my 2nd favorite. As a matter of fact, it’s spacious enough to hold comfortably both E10 and E80 where I have both of them now, and red zipper accent makes it stand out with red design of E-series IEMs. Keep in mind, other finish colors might be available soon, but hasn’t been released yet.

In addition to a cable clip, which you may or may not use and I do appreciate it being included separately rather than attached, there is also a plethora of included eartips. You have 3 pairs of silicone S/M/L with narrow bore opening, 3 pairs of silicone S/M/L with wide bore opening, a pair of large double-flange tip, and 3 pairs of genuine Comply Foam eartips in S/M/L. Though other silicone tips are generic, 3 pairs of Comply Foam tips have a $15 value you are getting along with a quality hard shell zippered cases.

As you can see, I already mentioned a few times the value E80 brings to the table in terms of its pricing, accessories, and also a build quality with all metal construction. Everything from slim metal housing of gold plated 270deg headphone plug with a nice rubbery strain relief, to a slim cylindrical metal y-splitter with a great strain relief and a tight rubber chin-slider, and going up to metal barrel shells with a molded cap piece on the back flowing into a strain relief – all this speaks highly of a durable build quality.

I like 270deg angled headphone connectors since they are perfect when used with a phone or a DAP in your pocket. Cable is very similar to E10 with a twisted wire which is shrink-wrapped in a tight rubbery shielding. Cable has some microphonics effect, also a little springy, and yet still soft enough for an easy storage management. I have seen a lot worse stiff wires, so this one is not that bad in comparison.

Earpieces are relatively small with a smooth rounded short barrel shape and rather unique wire attachment on the back. Though I’m more used to a traditional wire connection from the bottom of the shell, SoundMagic wire attachment felt confident. There is a vent at the base of the nozzle, and L/R marking at the bottom of the shell. A small font in white color with a circle around it makes it a bit hard to read which is important considering symmetrical design, so I would like to see a better ID, perhaps making a Left side dot-bump on a strain relief a little bit bigger.

Considering this E80 model is part of a new SoundMagic Reference Series, I’m sure a lot of you are curious to find out how they sound. E80 has a neutral revealing bright sound with a touch of mid-forward signature. I found it to have an excellent low end and treble extension, where it's all about quality rather than quantity, and a nice airy soundstage with a good level of depth. Imaging is not exactly 3D, but it still has a good positioning of instruments thanks to an excellent separation of sounds with a decent layering effect between instruments and vocals.

I find their low end to be a touch north of neutral, but it's not boosted or exaggerated. Very natural balance between intelligent sub-bass rumble (only comes out to play when called upon) and a tight mid-bass punch. There is no spillage into lower mids, bass is under control, and in perfect harmony with the rest of the spectrum.

Lower mids are not too thin or too thick, with a bit of warmth that gives sound a convincing natural body. Upper mids are a bit forward, bright and detailed, and never crossing analytical threshold or becoming harsh. Vocals sound bright and clear, a bit less organic in comparison to a slew of warm multi-BA driver IEMs I have been listening to lately, but it still smooth, never becoming harsh or grainy.

Treble has an excellent extension with a bright crisp sound. I'm very cautious using “bright” in describing treble because it always leads to sibilance, but in here SoundMagic managed to tune their treble without crossing that sibilance threshold, while still remaining bright, crisp, and airy.

Conclusion.

I typically stir away from neutral sound that is tuned toward bright signature because I’m “allergic” to analytical harsh sound. Here I believe SoundMagic hit a sweet spot with E80 that "magically" draws you right into its "sound" filled with revealing details without any exaggerated peaks. Sound is neutral, but it’s not flat-neutral, and actually very engaging. To be honest, I was a big worried when I read “reference” series name, thinking it will have a bright analytical signature. Instead, I was pleasantly surprised with a sound that is easy on your ears, gives you plenty of revealing details, even has a touch of a fun bass, and still great for an extended listening period without causing ear fatigue. Definitely recommend this one!of the spectrum.

The set-up problem:
I purchased the Nuforce MCP-18 to solve a very specific problem I had with my set up. I wanted to be able to use the balanced stereo outputs and the 7.1 surround outputs from my BDP-105D Blu-ray into a single set of power amps. Part of the issue I have is my front L/R speakers are Goldenear Triton 2 which have a built in sub, including amp and crossover. The Goldenear speakers will accept full range signals over the standard 5 way binding posts (low frequencies are crossed over internally and directed to the sub section) or they can accept an LFE signal direct to the sub section. I wanted to be able to direct a full range signal when listening to stereo music (using the Oppo as a source) to the speakers, whereas when listening to a 7.1 (or in my case 5.1) surround signal I wanted the output to the front L/R outputs to be rolled off and use the .1 RCA output to provide the bass to the speakers. This allowed me to get the full fidelity of the stereo music signal as well as allowing me to tune the bass output when watching a movie. As a final bonus, the pre-amp allowed me to connect a fully balanced signal path from the Oppo to the balanced mono block amplifiers powering the front channels.

The resultant solution:
While originally looking for the Nuforce pre-amp to give me some functionality to basically make my life a bit simpler, I actually ended up with a very good component that provides a really good level of functionality with seemingly very good quality components. Just for the volume control function alone the Nuforce is a worthwhile investment to pair with the Oppo. The only other components I have seen that will provide the functionality I am looking for without doing massive amounts of processing to the signals, are high end home theater pre-pro's that retail in the thousands. I think the key for me is the Nuforce does everything I need it to, without doing anything I don't need it to, and that is difficult to find ina world of single box home theater solutions.

Overall I have been living with the Nuforce for around 6 months now and don't think there is a better solution for my scenario. Some of the functionality is a bit clunky (it can take a long time to ramp the volume up and down via the remote) but in general I don't think there is anything in the price range that can come close to the same solution. Unfortunately it looks like the product has been discontinued, I'm just glad I got one while they were available.

I still recommend it despite having the USB port fritz out last year.  If you have a large iTunes or mp3 library and love streaming stuff, this is worth it at the price point. These are the best speakers I've had (besides the speakers in my car) for my music collection, including CD's.    As for the sound Volume, for my mp3 players or streaming Bluetooth, I have the speakers set to level 31, which provides more than enough loudness necessary for my space (I then control the volume up or down on the connected digital player or computer). If playing a CD, my stereo CD player has much more  "sound power" going out of it, so the volume level on the speaker only needs to be set to 10 (to start with) and then control the volume on the speaker as needed. Some CD's need more volume than others. The speaker goes up to 40, which is overkill in my apartment setting.     Lately I've been using the Auxilary plugin more for my Sansa Clip+ players (hooked up to a C-moy) to play my songs from my iTunes library, or to play CD's.  The bluetooth still works and sounds great, but I still like listening to music without computers sometimes. Streaming is nice, but I often  get indecisive about what the hell to listen to next because there are so many options on the computer or tablet.   I usually turn it off each day when I leave, or if gone on a trip, and it has always powered up. I also forget to turn it off sometimes and it stays on.  ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Update 06/30/2016: I bumped the rating up to four stars. Despite the USB port issue I had, I still use the speaker everyday and appreciate the great sound quality. I'm still surprised it's a bluetooth speaker when I listen to stuff. Also the aux port still works great, I have it hooked up to a stereo-five-cd changer for playing CDs.  I have the speaker up on top of a shelf above my desk (above my head when sitting down), and it connects well to all my bluetooth devices. The apple laptop can have interference issues if moved around, or blocked,  but my samsung tablet and LG phone don't have issues. If I am downloading stuff on wifi in the background on the tablet it can cause skipping, but that's a device issue.  I highly recommend it, a great value overall!  UPDATE: 12/10/2015   USB port Problem!  It fritzed out yesterday and ruined two SMALL devices I plugged into it to charge! It had been working fine to charge for months, either my Nexus smartphone or my Samsung tablet. But yesterday I plugged in a Chromecast Audio device, and the speaker clicked on and off repeatedly and the Chromecast thing died totally. The speaker still worked fine after this, however. Then today I just  plugged in a Sandisk mp3 player, to see if the charger worked, but no. There was nothing happening and then I smelled burning plastic from the mp3 player! Now it too is dead, but I think the damage was done after plugging in the Chromecast device. I have not yet contacted customer service, it just happened, but I will be. I am not sure I want to ship it back for repair because the speakers still work and sound great, but I am not pleased with the USB charge port fritzing out and killing two devices. It may not even be covered by the warranty, since it was a usb power thing. This has never happened with any  of my electronics!  I am changing the rating to three stars because the speakers, bluetooth and aux in port still work fine. Still, it is dissapointing because the speakers sound great! The company really needs to work on this aspect of the design of the speaker. Granted, it could very well be my fault for not checking the power requirements of a particular device, but still, there should be some kind of built in protection to prevent this type of thing from occurring. Further UPDATE: 12/10/2015   I did talk to customer service, and indeed the usb issue is not covered under the warranty for repair (I figured it would not be). The first thing you'll notice with Braven's 805 wireless speaker is its clean and streamlined physical design. In the hands the product has a solid, hefty feel weighing in at over 3 pounds and remains well balanced and stable whether you position it horizontal or vertically. The 805's are available in 9 different color sets (I have the red/gray) all of which are extremely attractive and have just the right balance of style pop without stepping into the realm of 'garish.' The external housing is comprised of durable plastic and rubber but nothing about it feels or looks cheap - this is a stylish and elegant speaker from head to toe.

Functionality is fairly basic but everything seamlessly and intuitively works as intended. The product is very easy to pair (I used iOs devices), maintains an extremely stable bluetooth connection over the course of hours and comes packed with a chunky 4400mAh battery that is good for 18 hours of playback. The speaker itself can also be used as a power bank to charge other devices (via USB) which is a feature I find myself using more than I thought I would.

Sound quality is where this product gets docked a point. The unit is plenty loud enough but acoustics are tuned for bass at the sacrifice of overall clarity across the spectrum. Don't get me wrong - the 805 sounds good, great at times even - but I would've much preferred the muddiness of the bass dialed back some to enhance articulation. Still, a well performing bluetooth speaker that looks great, is easy to use, with monster battery life and decent sonics.

After being without vinyl for more than 20 years I started building a new record collection in 2014 and now have more than 200 albums. Of these, about 2/3 are new and 1/3 used. Some of the used ones looked pretty bad and I thought a good cleaning system would help. I received this cleaning system 5 days ago and have since cleaned about 180 albums. Here is my 2 cents:
Pros:
1. Relatively easy to setup and use
2. About 5 minutes to take an album off the shelf, clean and dry it, and return to the shelf
3. Records look visibly cleaner
4. After one cleaning with this system I don't think my collection will need to be cleaned again.

Cons:
1. The ad says the directions are printed on the lid; mine were not. Still pretty simple
2. Other reviewers have stated they had a lot of dirt and debris in the reservoir after cleaning. I saw very little dirt in the solution. I did change the solution after every 30 albums. Maybe that was why or maybe my records were not as dirty as some.
3. The roller on the leading edge of the record (depends on which way you're spinning the record) continually pops out of the slot. This is very annoying and could easily be remedied with a simple design change.
4. My used albums are all thin vinyl while my new ones are thicker (180 grams). It seemed to me that after cleaning a number of the 180G albums that the brushes no longer made good contact when I cleaned an old record. In hind-sight I probably should have cleaned the thin records first.
