I wanted to upgrade from a cheap pair of Denon in-ears I bought for $30 in a bind. The headset I was looking for had to be in-ear, have bluetooth connectivity, active noise cancellation, and cost less than a hundred dollars. The Phiaton fit all those requirements. The set comes with a wired connection, mini usb charging cables, and various sized ear pieces. I found the medium sized rubber ear pieces to be the most comfortable, I can usually shove a large foam ear piece in my ears like with the Shure IEMs I use when I'm playing music, but these foam pieces (only comes with one size) were down right uncomfortable for my ear size. Setup was relatively easy once I realized there was an on/off for the bluetooth, on/off for the ANC, and a phone button (I intuitively thought holding down on the phone button would turn on the device and could've save some time if I just looked at the manual).
1. The Active Noise Cancellation- Pretty mediocre. This is not a "suck the air out of your ear" noise canceller. Rather it mutes a small spectrum of droning hum, that when you listen to music at a comfortable volume, you can't even tell if it's on or off. I think the headset would perform better if it isolated sound as well as cancelled, but I was not able to get isolation even with a nice tight seal. Because of this, the Phiaton with ANC on was no better than my sound isolating Denons. So it's a wash with my Denons and in fact a step down if I turn ANC off.
1a. If you are wanting noise cancelling for the airplane you may want to consider something else. Like I said regarding noise isolation, this headset does a poor job. I could hear the conversations behind me, the flight attend and pilot on the intercom, my Denons can block all those noises out. It did cancel out the engine noise okay, but no better than the Denons.
1b. I wore these at a busy restaurant and at a Starbucks and the ANC seemed to work much better in these type of situations than on an airplane, but once again, not much better than my Denons. I can say though, the benefit of ANC over a noise isolator is you don't hear your feet when you walk or the cords when they bump up against your shirt.
2. Sound quality- Highs are crisp, mids are present, lows are not punchy enough. I only wear in-ears and come to expect bass to be less than over the ear headphones, but this is weak even for in-ears. It's a clean sound and it is acceptable, but don't expect to be wowed with audio fidelity. One note, I was thinking how weak the volume was when I was trying to control the volume on my iPad. I forgot that there is a volume control on your dongle, you can crank that up all the way if you like to control the volume on your device or vice versa.
3. Bluetooth connection- Pretty standard setup. Turn on headset, hold the phone button down, look for the headset on your bluetooth menu, and connect. Simple, no issues. You get a tiny buzzing sound once you connect to the bluetooth, but it seems to disappear when the audio is playing.
4. Build Quality- As the other reviewers state, the dongle is made of plastic, but I like it this way as it keeps the dongle lightweight. I clip it on my shirt and forget it's there. The clip is plastic, but it seems solid. The access panel on the bottom is easy to access for wired connection and charging. Overall I think it's a nice design and I have no issues with it except perhaps they can make it smaller.
5. Telephone- People on the receiving end say they have trouble hearing me when I'm in a noisy location, so I don't know if the mic is noise cancelling or not. No issues with calls using the headset in a quiet area.
Overall, I think it's slightly overpriced at it's current price of $67 and I know it used to retail for twice as much as it is currently. The bottom line is, this headset isn't for everyone, in fact you might be better off paying for a cheaper bluetooth in-ear sound isolater without the ANC as it would get you the same results. Also, I would test these out if you can before you buy. PROS: Wireless, portable, solid wireless Bluetooth connection, quite comfortable once you pick the right ear pieces. Cons: Mediocre ANC, mediocre sound

Full review (Used these on an LG G3 phone):
I've had a chance to try out several ear buds recently so I was excited to try out this set of SoundPeats.
The packaging is awesome & shipping was lightning fast.
Cord length is a little on the shorter side of other ear buds, but still adequate.
I can still stick my phone in my pocket and walk around with the earbuds on (I'm 5' 9").

Build Quality:
They appear to be plastic all the way through, but still have a nice feel.
There's no metal on the mic or the plug, but it still doesn't look bad.
I'd call it an understated look & feel.
The ribbon cord is reinforced at the earbuds and at the plug, but not at the mic or the splitter
The cord also looks a little narrow than others I've tried, but still feels robust
They also come with 2 other sets of rubber ear inserts.
The set that came on mine were very comfortable and I didn't have to switch them out.

Sound Quality:
The clarity of sound that comes out of these is great! Nice, crisp highs, good mids, and good bass.
They're not particularly loud, so you don't get a LOT of bass, but it's a good, crisp sound with minimal distortion
The drivers themselves are somewhat on the smaller end so that contributes to the lower sound output
I've definitely had louder earbuds, but the clarity and sound quality is really clean coming out of these.
You can turn them up all the way and they won't overpower your ears, so that's nice.
If you're looking for a loud set (ie. outside use or in a noisy environment) these probably aren't what you want
But if you want a nice, crisp set of headphones, these are really nice.
I'd call the sound somewhat understated, but crisp and clean
It's a nice, lightweight set of headphones.

Mic/Button:
I really like the position of the mic button these
It's nice and close to my mouth which means it's easy to find without "hunting" for it.
It's also very responsive. Push it once, the song pauses. Push it again and it starts back up
Push it twice and it advances to the next song.
I also like that it's square shaped. It makes it much easier to grab the button vs. round mics that leave you hunting for the button.
I didn't test out the mic on it though, so can't comment on how well it works.

Cord Length:
I actually really like this length. It's a little on the shorter end but it keeps from getting tangled in things like longer ones can do.
The thinness of the ribbon is also nice too. Definitely on the "lightweight" end of things.

Overall:
I really liked this set of headphones. While they're on the "lightweight" end of things and not as loud as others out there, they make up for it in their crispness of sound and overall sound quality. They're also extremely comfortable and easy to put in my ears. Love the position on the mic and how short the cord is. Solid 4 out of 5 stars. I wish they were slightly louder and had a little more bass to them, but still a great set of compact headphones.

This item isn't compatible with the Raspberry Pi 2 Model B. Other reviews have stated that you're able to make it work by simply switching certain colors of the different plugs. Maybe this worked for older versions of the Raspberry Pi, I don't know. But none of that worked for me.

If you're planning on using this with the Raspberry Pi 2 Model B, don't. the pinout of this plug simply won't work. It's important to know what pinout the Raspberry Pi 2 Model B expects. I was able to find this information on a website after doing a little research. The pinout is key since these types of plugs follow different standards, but they all essentially look the same. When searching for a plug that will work for the Raspberry Pi 2 Model B, please make sure that you get a plug that follows the given pinout diagram, which I've included. I was able to get this plug to work, only after cutting it, and rewiring it to fit the pinout shown in the attached picture.

This item assigns the ground plug to the "sleeve" ring, and the video plug to the "Tip". Because of this, the only way I was able to get it to work with my Raspberry Pi was to cut it, and rewire it. Had ground been assigned to "ring2", then swapping colors would have worked. However, because all three plugs share the same ground, the only way it could work for me was to cut and rewire.

I'm giving this item three stars because, although it didn't work for me, it may work for a different device that requires a different pinout.

Pros: Lightweight, Comfortable, Great Build, Big Bass, Detachable cable, Fun Sound Signature

Cons: Non-Bass Lovers Need Not Apply, Small Carrying Bag, Detachable Cable is a Tad Thin

--

The back of the box reads "Mega Surround + Deep Bass". I'm going to admit, after reading that, I had my doubts. I'm not a basshead and I was scared to ask what Mega Surround is.

Within minutes of my first use, my fears quickly dissipated. These are just a tamed lion, scary at first, but oh so cuddly.

Let me break down the I-MEGO MAZE.

*Packaging*
Box is pretty and packed well. These look even better in real life than printed.

*Accessories*
- Detachable 4ft (1.2m) audio cable with microphone controller
- Compatible audio adaptor (apply to Samsung, Nokia and Song-Ericsson smartphone)
- 1/4” (6.3mm) Hi-Fi adaptor
- Soft Travel Pouch

The travel pouch is a tad small and flat, takes some getting used to when putting in the headphones.
The detachable cable is also a little on the thin side, though seems to be tough enough.
Nice that you substitute the stock cable for any high end version you might desire.

*Build*
The I-MEGO MAZE is well built, using high quality materials that feel premium in the hand.
Design is classic, sophisticated and smart. You can tell a lot of thought went into the making of the MAZE.
The headband is flexible, yet tough enough to take a beating. All around great build.

*Functions*
The MAZE is a portable headphone that easily folds up to provide a smaller footprint, for on the go.
It also comes with a microphone that works well, callers can hear you loud and clear.

*Fit*
For an on-ear headphone, the MAZE is surprisingly comfortable. The pads are lush with soft leather.
The headband is light and does not apply much pressure to the ears. This makes the MAZE easy to wear for extended periods.
The pads also provide a decent amount of noise isolation. You don't have to worry about others around you hearing your music, nor do you have to hear them if you don't want to.

*Sound*
"Deep Bass", it says right on the box. Yes, these have deep bass. Deep, Controlled Bass. That said, I would not classify these as Basehead headphones. The MAZE does a wonderful job of keeping the bass down low, where it belongs. If you crank the volume up, the lows can creep slightly into the mids, but never takes away from any vocals. Nor does it ever become muddy.

Speaking of the mids, they are shockingly not recessed. These also do not have a V shaped sound signature. I-MEGO did a spectacular job tuning the MAZE. Vocals, while not the most crystal clear I have ever heard, are very much present and accounted for. This is where the MAZE really impressed me, in the middle. Keeping frequencies neat and tidy, this is why this headphone is so fun to use. A lot of big bass headphones loose mids, completely ignoring them. Not the MAZE.

The upper range might not sparkle, it might not impress, but it goes far enough to give you what you need. I would use the words, rolled off. This is also what gives the MAZE the power of extended use as they never become harsh or fatiguing.

"Mega Surround", more words written right on the back of the box. These words both confused and intrigued me. Though once in use, it is easy to understand what it means, space. Often, most closed headphones suffer from a condensed Soundstage, but with some kind of trick up their sleeve, I-MEGO managed to eek out some distance. Not open-headphone distance, but enough to make the MAZE a very playful breath that stretches farther than it should. I would not go as far as to say it is a Big Soundstage, no, but it is very flirtatious and fun.

*Overall Thoughts*
The MAZE is not quite on an Audiophile level and is not quite a true Basshead Headphone either. The MAZE is a headphone that just sounds deliciously fun. Big bass, controlled mids and a decent soundstage all lead to a decisively good all around sound. It is easy to like the MAZE, it does a lot well. Even those not prone to big bass might still want to give these a chance. Great for on the go and blocking the world around you. Sound signature is cheery and easy going, but does have enough detail to keep you interested. I think I-MEGO has a great little headphone on their hands. My wife also seems to think so, as I now have to pry them away from her. Note to self, never leave the MAZE laying around, someone else might like it.

This radio is, quite simply, one of the best AM-FM radios I have ever owned (and I own many!). No, it does not have digital readout. It has first-class analog tuning which is extremely easy to adjust. The sensitivity and selectivity of the radio is excellent on both AM and FM. Many manufacturers have been giving AM radio reception the short-shrift, but not Crane. They have a big ferrite antenna inside, with an external antenna trimmer that you can adjust if necessary. AM reception is a pleasure to behold - the audio quality is almost as good as those big console radios that were perfected in the 1930s! FM fidelity is fantastic with the radio's 5-inch speaker.

The radio has separate bass and treble controls as well as a "wide-narrow" selectivity control which comes in handy when receiving distant AM stations that are close in frequency to nearby stronger stations. And, magnificently, there are connections for an external AM radio antenna. I've hooked up one of those Kaito tunable loops and was astounded at how well it works. You probably would not need an external antenna for most AM listening, because the internal ferrite antenna is so good. But for AM DX-ing the external connections are very helpful.

If you want to store favorite stations in digital memories this radio is not for you. If you appreciate just how good an analog radio can perform, this AM-FM unit from Crane will definitely meet and even exceed your expectations.

Black with stainless steel accents, these Bluetooth 4.0 passive noise cancelling headphones have a handsome appearance – sleek and modern. Most important factors are how do they sound and are they comfortable to wear. Yes and yes. Oh, and is the battery life really 19 hours, as stated? Actually my headphones played for over 21 hours before they required recharging. A louder volume may reduce that number but I checked the time to confirm the 19 hours was a realistic claim.

Given the low price point I was pleasantly surprised by the quality of the sound. The headphones are definitely bass heavy, which I prefer, but that does not mean it muddies up the mid and upper ranges. I listened to a wide range of music to test the headphones and am impressed. Rich deep booming bass, and clear mid and upper range. I handed them off to the other adult in residence and we do not always agree, but comments mirrored mine. I have more expensive headphones that do not sound this good.

The build quality is good – no rough or sharp edges – all nicely finished. The fold up mechanism and the adjustable headband both operate smoothly. And, although full-size, the set is very compact to store and transport. The controls are easy to access and I they require a definitive press so I did not accidentally switch songs, etc. The passive noise suppression does not completely block out surrounding noise – it is certainly muffled but can be heard.

The headband and ear pieces are well-padded with materials that I found to be non-irritating and do not create that hot sweaty feeling that occurs with some brands. I have a medium sized adult head and the other adult in residence has a large to extra-large head and we both found the set adjusts comfortable to wear.

To test the operating distance between the music player and the headphones I placed the music player in the house and from there walked into the garage and followed it to the furthest point, a distance I measured to be 64 feet. The manual says 33 feet which may be affected depending on obstructions in the path – and I did not have many – primarily a door and a wall but that is almost twice the distance claimed and I experienced no drop-outs or interruptions.

In the box are a fabric drawstring dust bag, a clearly written User Manual and a 48 inch 3.5mm to 3.5 mm audio cable which creates a wired set. On arrival I began charging by connecting the included 26 inch micro USB to USB cable to the headphones and to a port in my laptop. A red light glows steady during charging which turns blue when charging is complete. It blinks red every two seconds when the battery is low and needs charging. Charging took 2 ½ hours our-of the box.

Controls are straightforward -- use the button featuring a telephone receiver icon to power on, off and pair the device. To power on press and hold the button for two seconds until the blue LED light flashes. To power off hold the button for three seconds until the LED flashes red.

To pair the headphones first turn on the Bluetooth function on whatever device is being used, MP3, smartphone, iPod, PC, etc. then hold the button on the headphones until the LED alternately flashes red and blue. Search on the list of devices and select Audiomax. I did not need the pairing code, but if requested it is 0000. The volume on the set is loud so I played them at about 1/3 of their volume without loss of detail.

When the connection is made the LED will flash only blue. It should automatically connect with the same Bluetooth device the next time it is turned on, but if connecting to another device is desired it may be necessary to disconnect, remove, them from to pair with another.

The controls are standard – use the arrow keys to increase or decrease volume, and hold them down to advance to the next track or return to the previous one. Press the phone receiver icon button to pause and press again to proceed. Phone answering worked well and on both ends, and microphone picked up my voice clearly, and I also clearly heard the person on the other end of the call.

Given the freedom Bluetooth headphones offer it is hard to consider returning to a tethered set, and this pair permitted movement all through the residence so I didn’t have to think about staying put. The sound and comfort are excellent. Operation is simple. They exceeded my expectations, and for the price this is a terrific pair of headphones.

Having owned these for several months now, I feel that I can post a fairly decent review. These headphones are very versatile, and you can really tailor the sound to your user preference with the included (passive) filters. The cord feels very sturdy, and well built. Everything feels like it will last for a long time. However The ear tips do not fit my ears will, and as a result the sound isolation can tend to be fairly poor. While I do appreciate the durability of the flexible over ear piece, I do not find it very comfortable. The sound is good, not great, and I find them to be relatively uncomfortable. I have owned Bose, Klipsch, RHA, and now B&W, and these are by far the biggest disappointment of the bunch. The sound quality rivaled the S4i form Klipsch, while priced in the X11/X10 range. I came to these from the X10 from Klipsch and was very sad with the lack of bass (though the filter does definitely help), comfort, and noise isolation. I have bought a pair of B&W P5 S2's to replace the RHA T10's, and I am much happier with the P5. I would definitely recommend going with Klipsch, or B&W over RHA. However you if you do decide to get these I will say that the durability, and filter options will provide you a really good listening experience.

Update*** After 5 days of use: The Bluetooth range has a very small radius which feels constricting at home. If you are ~10 feet and there are some obstacles between device and speaker you get static.  Hasn't really been that much of a problem for me but I have noticed it.  Outdoor use is still fine. I mostly use it in my bedroom watching shows on my ipad.    This thing is great. It's heavy in the hand and looks great with the aluminum finish and brushed black sides. Little pads on the bottom keep it stable and transmit some bass. Comes with a travel slip case. I love how thin and portable this speaker is. I can take it anywhere and with the quality I'm not worried about breaking it. If it did it wasn't a 200 dollar speaker so no stress.  It is quite loud. I have a 2700 square foot house and I can hear it from all rooms. The speaker sounds really good, but the bass isn't that great but it's a tiny speaker not my home theatre system.   The best part is the internal battery charging capability.  I love the fact that I can charge my phone right from the speaker. It really adds a whole new level of function.  Overall I'm happy with this purchase and product.

When the built-in amplification is turned on, you may well hear intermittent crackling noises if you are indoors near a wifi connection. And if you plug directly into the headphone jack of a power amplifier or receiver, you may hear hum or other noises.
I called PSB and was told this is a known problem arising from the high gain of the built-in electronics. The suggested work-around: When you use these headphones with a home theater amplifier or receiver, turn off the built-in amplification. And when you are connected to a portable media source (I listen to mp3s saved to my cell phone), put the device in airplane mode, so it will not pick up RF noise.
Both of these workarounds work -- not ideal, but this is one price you must pay for the really excellent sound of this headset.

I received one of these from the manufacturer for reviewing purposes.

My entertainment system is located in the kitchen, But the TV and speakers are in the family room. I did this because we had a cabinet that was not being used in the kitchen and did not want components visible in the family room. I have used many HDMI cables, My personal preference has been towards Blue Rigger Brand for years. I've also never purchased one that is flat before and that drew me to taking a closer look at this one.

I'm going to break this down to 3 categories 1. Build quality 2. signal transfer and 3. Overall usefulness.

So

1. Build quality

The cable is 35 feet long it has industry standard gold plated connectors on each end. The cable itself measures only 1/8" thick by 1/2" wide. so compared to the standard cable that is 3/8" round it is very easy to conceal. Just as you would expect from any good quality cable the ends are properly attached and they feature strain relief fittings to prevent damage when the cable is flexed.

2. Signal transfer

This one is hard to test without proper equipment as you would expect it easily transferred a 1080P signal from my Denon AVR4520ci with no issues. However, I did test the cable for signal interference and results were mixed results. I laid the cable out (on the floor) from the kitchen to the family room connected it to the receiver and my Sharp Aquos television. I ran a Bluray through it to an as expected excellent picture. However when I played with a 110v extension cord or the DC adapter to my children's Xbox 360 charger the cable picked up some interference which showed up as distortion on the TV. Now in all fairness when I ran 4 HDMI cables from my media cabinet to the family room I did not test them in the same way. Secondly I don't have an unused one to test either so it may be something that happens with all HDMI cables.

3. Overall Usefulness

So as far as cables go it is a well built unit. What was a major turn off for me is two fold. First is labeling. Here is what I mean by that. I pick up a competitors cable and on the cord it says the following " High Speed HDMI tm Cable with Ethernet E329703 (UL)TYPE CL3 75*C 26 CSA250674 CMG 26AWG FT4"

So what does this cable say? "High Speed Cable"

So which one would you pick? Well here are two things that the labeling tells me. 1. UL Underwriters Laboratory, now do ALL electrical devices need to be UL listed? No. But, it tells me they took that extra step. 2. CL3, What does that mean? well it means that the cable is suitable for running through a wall. Remember I said that my media cabinet was in the Kitchen? Well I used 50' CL3 cables to run down into the basement ran them to the family room and then back up to provide a clean installation. This particular cable is not suitable for that purpose.

Conclusion

If you just need to run between point A and point B and NOT go into a wall this is a great cable. Personally I don't see a huge demand for such a long cable that is not CL rated but I may be wrong. Quality construction is there the lack of labeling is a huge turn off for me.ess

These are a great pair of headphones that deliver strong sound for a low price. Much to my surprise they come packaged in a stylish metal storage box, tucked neatly into protective foam with two additional sets of ear tips, so you get a set of small, medium (which are installed already), and large all marked for left or right ear, plus a helpful instruction booklet.

I like the fact that the cord is the sort that won’t tangle up. It comes with a has a standard audio port plug that fits most devices, and has an in-line microphone that lets you take calls, change songs, and access Siri. Although there’s no built-in volume control, these features are certainly very handy. I wore these out to Costco to shop while testing them and had a call come in, and the sound quality was excellent as was the external noise isolation.

Years of hastily snapping stethoscopes on while running busy emergency rooms has resulted in having a very sensitive left outer ear, so I normally find it difficult to wear ear buds for long without them being uncomfortable. The ear buds that come with this set are ergonomically shaped for each ear, and comfortable enough that I was able to use the medium size ones that came already installed and wear them for four hours straight without the slightest bit of irritation.

I’m definitely not a music expert by any means, and how one perceives sound is subjective, but that being said, I thought that this headset delivers strong, clear base when listening to music - definitely enhanced, but not overpowering. Some may think the sound seems muffled because of it, but it's nothing that fiddling around with the equalizer won't fix. Overall the sounds are very clear and without distortion or crackling. They’re not Bose but these do deliver a way above-average music-listening experience at a very reasonable price.

I have an audiophile set up in doors including a very expensive "reference amp". Outdoors I only have a pair of Cambridge mini-speakers, a poor man's Bose.

Pros:
1. I needed a way to split output for indoors (A) and outdoors (B) that also protected from impedance mismatches. It worked well for this, including the ability to have different sound levels indoors and outdoors. I did no notice a significant degradation of audio quality.

2. I bought this for impedance protection because I was worried that my expensive system could be damaged by accidentally over driving with impedance mismatch. It works. My $2400 amp is fine.

Cons:
3. I agree with one disgruntled reviewer; it is extremely difficult to insert even 14 gauge wires in the back. This is a nonstarter for audiophiles who almost use the thickest, low impedance speaker wires they can afford. I only had to attach 4 pairs. The ones going outside were 16 gauge, so no problem. The indoor speaker wires were 12 gauge and I had to solder a workaround. The 12 gauge are short runs and I don't drive the system much, so it's working for now.

I replaced this with a different zone splitter that accepts larger speaker wires. But my sister thinks it's great. If you only have 14 gauge wires or thinner, then this product works quite well. It's a 4/5 stars for non-audiophile users with thin speaker wires. It's a 2/5 for audiophile users. The connectors alone tell you that this was not designed for them.

For experienced Harmony Users, its OK, but just barely. If you are a new user I sure it is the beez kneez compared to what ever you used before. If you are looking for a replacement for your Harmony One+, though, LOOK ELSEWHERE. Logitech has completely destroyed the ONE THING that made them far and away the best remotes on the market. We are talking serious competitive advantage here folks.

What the heck am I rambling about, you ask? Its this: the ACTIVITY BASED PARADIGM. The Ultimate still has activities, sure, but it concept has been crippled beyond recognition. Specifically, on the Harmony One+ you could define 'favorite channels' which would appear on the screen so you didn't have to remember the channel number for every thing - FOR EACH ACTIVITY. If you had two 'Watch TV' activities, you would have two sets of favorites. Example: you might have a 'Watch Cable TV' activity and a 'Watch Free-to-Air' Activity - each with its own channel changing mechanism (Cable box or TV) and each with its own channel numbers of course.

The Ultimate does not allow this, there is one set of 50 favorites that you can associate with one 'Watch TV' activity. If you are in some other activity and accidently press one of your favorites, it will terminate your current activity and switch to that 'Watch TV' activity. This is NOT the behaviour we have come to expect from our Harmony remote where the programming hides the complexity and the buttons, all the buttons whether software or hardware, apply properly in the context of the activity we are using.

The disastrous effect of this designed functionality transforms the Harmony range from head and shoulders above all the rest of the 'Universal Remote' into an expensive, beautiful, well made but 'Ultimately' flawed run of the mill remote.

It seems that I have been reviewing a great many blue tooth speakers and earbuds lately and I basically knew what to expect these earbuds came in. Let me make it clear that these were sent to me by the company in exchange for a review but, if you are familiar with any of my reviews, I do not hesitate to point out any negatives I find as well as praise the positive. I have lived with this speaker for over a week and don't buy into the hyperbole of using a product for an hour and thinking it is absolutely great just because it was free.

Not everyone has a blue tooth connection so these buds are connected to your device via the supplied cable. The connector is quite small so even if you have a tight fitting cell phone or iPod case, you should have no problems with the connection.
Extras ear pieces are supplied should you have larger or smaller ear canals but I found that the ones on them were already pretty comfortable.

Audio quality is the most important thing and the Mengo Bumps stand out in a few categories and fall short in one as well. The transparency of the music reproduction is quite excellent. There is no veil over the audio you are hearing, no muffling and excellent transient response throughout the entire frequency range. Though VOIX says that these ear bumps have Ultra Bass, I did not find that to be the case. The bass, while very decent in its response when I was listening to an audiophile jazz recording of Charlie Byrd as well as some ZZ Top tunes, does not go any lower in bass reproduction than the great majority of ear buds, bluetooth or cable connected, than any others I have listened to and reviewed.

This does not mean that these aren't quite good, they are good but do not expect audiophile type earpieces for this very inexpensive cost. For yourself or as gifts, they are some of the better looking buds I have seen, if not the best. They certainly do not appear cheap and plastic-like as most of the others on the market. They look far more expensive than they are.

Personally, I do prefer the convenience of blue tooth ear pieces so I do not have cables hanging down to be caught on an exercise machine or something, but if this is your choice than you shouldn't be unhappy with them at all. They sound fine, just do not expect an explosive bass and deep bottom end.
I do hope that this review has been of some help to you in deciding upon your purchase.

The iPod came early in the morning which almost never happens when I shop online and I was super excited. I opened the box and even though I bought a used one, it looked almost brand new. I plugged it in to my Windows 10 computer and had it reset completely to factory settings. I then proceeded to sync the iPod and all my songs downloaded without a problem.  Everything seemed great until later that evening when I noticed some of my songs weren't playing at all and would just skip them altogether. I've had two iPods before and this had never happened so I knew it wasn't the song files' fault. I looked up solutions online and it said that maybe the song files' bit sizes were too small or too big or whatever. So I did what any logical person would do and plugged it back in to my computer.  But unlike last time, iTunes didn't come up. Instead, I had to click on it where it reluctantly opened. iTunes failed to recognize that the iPod was plugged in so I had my computer safely eject it and then plugged it in again. This time, my computer said it had detected corrupted files so I scanned it. Computer said iPod was okay but then iTunes suddenly shut down, taking down Google Chrome and all my work I had open. Then the blue screen of death appeared (something the particular computer I was using had never experienced).  After my computer rebooted, a few things wouldn't work properly. The brightness setting was all over the place and I couldn't change it using the buttons, I was logged out of my Google Chrome, Bing became my default browser and I couldn't reset it back to Google, and none of my work was saved (I found them to be in the same condition as the day before I plugged in the iPod). I decided to plug the iPod back just to make sure if it was the iPod or possibly something associated with it that caused it. iTunes wouldn't boot so I had to click that manually. And sure enough, my computer found corrupted files and iTunes closed. Fortunately everything else was still fine. I took out the iPod, I clicked on iTunes again, and it along with Chrome shut down again. So now I was getting really suspicious that it was probably iTunes that was messing things up and, since it wasn't like that before the iPod, I suspected that the iPod must have caused this somehow.  It was only after I uninstalled iTunes completely that things suddenly functioned normally again. However when I scanned for any malware, my computer detected none. I looked online to see if this was even possible, that my iPod had some sort of corrupted file that attacked iTunes and my computer. And sure enough, it is possible that stuff like that could attach itself to the device, even if it is an iPod, when you download music from shady places. That's why I have reason to believe that the previous owner of this iPod may have gotten something nasty on it that just wouldn't go away even when it had been reset.  Okay, I know that this may not have been the seller's fault but this experience has made me think twice about buying used electronics. I wanted to give this a one star but I'm giving this product an extra one because of the speedy shipping, the good physical condition of the product, and the no hassle return and refund. So by all means, if you buy a used one just be careful and scan it like crazy when you first plug it in to your computer (especially if you have Windows).

I received a sample antenna to use and then wrote an honest review.

I like the Onh Amplified 50 mile indoor HDTV antenna. It works very well for me. It is the very thin antenna like the similar "Leaf" or [[ASIN:B00DIFIP06 AmazonBasics]] models. I have the AmazonBasics model and this is my standard for comparison in this review.

When setting up any HDTV antenna the results will vary depending on exact orientation, distance to the transmitter, topography and what might be in front of the antenna (brick wall, light wood frame wall, window, etc.). There are several good web sites to help you find what stations are likely in range providing general guidance. Just remember your results may vary.

IN THE BOX:
The Onh antenna comes in a very plain and easily accessible box. No frills and I like that. Besides the black on both sides antenna with a amply long attached cable there is an AC to USB adapter able to put out 1A with a USB A to round power connector plug for the amplifier. The amplifier with a short pigtail to connect to your TV antenna input. There are several pieces of adhesive backed Velcro which I did not use (don't like to stick things to the wall!) and finally a small but pretty good instruction booklet. Pretty standard for this kind of antenna.

My only complaints about this antenna are with the power cable. What were they thinking? Why not just use a standard USB A to Micro B like the similar AmazonBasics model? Which brings me to my second concern: the power cable is way too short. It will just barely reach my power strip and that's after I moved it as close as possible! Onh: please switch to a common USB cable for power and make it 50% to 100% longer. I have dozens of USB A to Micro B cables hanging around I could have used.

To be fair I could use a USB A male to female extension or plug it into a TV USB (but those are only rated at 500ma) but I bet few people have those extensions hanging around. I don't.

SETUP:
Assembly is well covered in the manual. Just screw the end of the antenna cable into the amplifier F connector and screw that into your ATSC tuner F connector. Then plug in the power cable to the supplied adapter or an available USB charging port. Assembly done!

The next step is to place the antenna. A window where the flat side is facing the general direction of the broadcast antennas is best. Be sure it's not behind an aluminum screen! :-) Some UV blocking window glass has a metallic coating that will block signals. I placed mine on the back of a wall unit next an exterior wall in the same place as my AmazonBasics 50 mile antenna (not at the same time).

When the antenna was placed I scanned for channels. With the Onh antenna I got 32 channels and every one came in well. With my AmazonBasics my scan got 38 but none of those extra channels were reliable - pixelation and dropouts. The effective results with the Onh showed me it was as good at bringing in a signal as my AmazonBasics model. Well done Onh.

CONCLUSIONS:
The Onh 50 mile flat and thin amplified antenna is solid performer. In my use it performs as well as my AmazonBasics 50 flat antenna with 32 clear channels. I like it very much in use.

My only concerns are around the non-standard and short power cable. All things considered it's a pretty minor beef and not even worth half a star to me.

This charger sold by Aibcn does the job at a great price. Yes, it's cheaply made but what do you expect for just $7? Charging a battery should be a non frivolous task and this charger does exactly that. There are 2 placeholders for batteries and there are green/red LEDs inside the body of the charger that light up and show through the translucent white plastic body. When you first plug it in, it's green with no batteries in the charger. Then when you put a battery in to charge, the LED inside the unit will turn red to show that it's charging. It turns to green when the battery is fully charged. The great thing about this charger is that it will charge just one battery so that you don't need to do them in pairs. The LED lights are independent as well so that you can see the red/green only on the side that you're doing the charging.

What I don't like so much are the metal spring prongs that you have to pull down in order to insert the battery. First of all, it's very stiff so you can't really use one hand. Also, the prong themselves are flattish which you can see from the photos. That makes it more difficult to align the battery when you're inserting it as it slips around, again, needing a two hand operation. The other thing that's annoying is that it makes a buzzing noise. I've heard it in other cheaply made power supplies so this is not too huge of a deal. Lastly, the design of the charger seems upside-down. The label EBL looks like the top of the unit but is actually the bottom in relation to how the unit works. The charger has a retractible wall jack like many other travel chargers and it's directly behind the EBL badge label. However, you insert the battery with the + sign towards the other end of the charger where the half-circles are. Those half-circles are also where the LED lights are. So, you have to pull the charger metal prongs towards the EBL badge which seems backwards when you're actually using it. It always takes me a few seconds to try to figure out the orientation when I use it.

OK, I've reviewed a similar player and hated it, but I like this one, for this price, and here is why.

For $20, you get a decent FM radio (with recording capability), 16GB of storage for music, and a nice voice recorder, as well as a few other features. You also get a nice lanyard and decent (not great, but surprisingly adequate) headphones. Are there limitations? Sure, of course - this is a 16GB $20 device with a color LCD screen... you need to manage your expectations.

What is the target demographic for these? Likely small kids (cheap device that they likely won't break), people who want a cheap FM radio, and/or people who want a cheap voice recorder. Yes, you can play movies on it, but odds are you won't be able to properly format them for this, so don't count on that capability - at all.

Here's what you can expect:

First of all, hardware wise, this is the size of an old school iPod nano but without the click wheel - yes, there's a "wheel", but it's really just four click locations and a center button - no scrolling capability. You also get a decent lanyard and really pretty nice headphones - I mean, you'd likely pay $8-$12 for these, so they're quite good when included in a $20 purchase. You also get a mini (not micro!) USB charging cable, which is unfortunate, because almost everything is micro USB these days. The LCD screen is nice enough - certainly for a device at this price range, and, honestly, you're not going to be watching movies on it, so it's more than adequate for the other features. There is either no micro SD card, or it's internal. Similar devices have them as removable, but, actually, I prefer this way - nothing to lose, nothing for kids to pull out and toss.

"Apps":

(1) "Music"

It comes with a couple of songs, and you can add more by connecting it to essentially any computer. Yes, this means you need a computer to add music - there's no WiFi, no iTunes, no Google Play, no Amazon Prime, etc - you need MP3s or the like to add to this manually, but that's OK. If you're getting this for kids, it means you have absolute control over what they listen to, music-wise. And you can add almost 16GB of music, because the device uses essentially none of the available space. BE AWARE: there is a menu option to delete files, or to delete *all* files, so, if you have small children, you know as well as I do that they will do exactly that, at least once. Anyway, music quality is quite good, both through the included headphones and via nicer ones of mine I tried.

(2) "Movie"

This comes with one movie, and it's a video some woman in a bikini singing on a beach. You've never heard of her, and you likely never will - after all, she's allowed her video to be on a $20 player. You can delete it, or you can keep it on. Video quality is surprisingly decent for such a cheap device. However... while I've not tested this device *yet* (will do soon when I post the video review of this), other devices with *very* similar firmware suggest that you'll never be able to encode movies for this, so you can probably forget ever putting other videos on this.

(3) "Record"

Shockingly useful. Using the menu, you can change the recording quality - it is actually really decent at the higher bit rates, and there's an option for automatic voice recognition, so it can record only when people are talking.

(4) "Voice"

This seems redundant - recordings show up here as well as in Music, although *only* recordings show up here, so it's a way to filter out music. Same options for deleting files as elsewhere.

(5) "FM Radio"

AWESOME. OK, it's not HD radio, but the quality is adequate. Noticeably worse than MP3s stored locally, but fine. Also: you *CAN* RECORD FM RADIO using the menu. Up to 16GB of it, which is an eternity. I'm not saying you want to record it, but you can. Bring it while travelling. Record local stations. Listen while flying home. Fun. You can auto-search stations, set it to use Japan radio bands, etc. Once programmed, press the center button to go through stations. This is very nice in this price range.

(6) "Photo"

Lets you look at photos you've added, in the same way you'd add music. They look fine, as long as you're 5. This is not a high-res display, nor would you expect it to be. Note: if you've putting pictures on this, *reduce the resolution*!! Hi-res photos will take extra space and, most importantly, will take forever to render, and they won't look any better. You can, as with music, delete one or all photos, and, yes, your kids will do this.

(7) "Setup"

Basics, like time, LCD mode, language, firmware upgrades, etc. Odds are you'll never need to use any of these.

(8) "E-book"

Ships empty, and while I suspect you can find file formats it'll accept, I can't imagine reading an e-book on this. Maybe I just have a poor imagination.

(9) "Game"

- Boxman: You move boxes around to clear up space. Not a terrible time consumer, especially for kids

- Tetrix: Shockingly, a Tetris clone. I bet you couldn't have guessed that!

- Snake: Brings back fond memories of my Nokia. Yours too, perhaps.

- Road: I Have *no idea* how to play this. Some sort of tile game.

OVERALL:

Look, this costs $20 or so. It is NOT an iPod nano. It is not, really, a movie player (unless you can find the proper obscure format), It isn't, really, an e-book reader. But: it's a good FM radio (with recording!), it is a good voice recorder, and it stores a ton of music (and/or pictures). I think it is *easily* worth what they are asking, and I think it'd be great for kids or as a cheap radio/recorder for adults.

Cons:

The menu system is... non-intuitive, to say the least. The device is aggressive about power savings and will power down if not used very quickly - much less than 30 seconds. However, when in use (music, radio, recording, etc), it works fine, and battery life is good. I wish it used micro USB, but thems the breaks. Still, overall, a 5 star device for this cost.

This is a review for the Bose SoundTrue Ultra in-ear headphones (charcoal color) designed for Samsung Android devices.

These in-ear buds offer great, well balanced sound for any stereo music device, but they are designed to offer in-line controls and microphone support with Android phones, and surprisingly, they work with some Windows Phone devices as well.

The buds come with small, medium, and large soft silicone tips that are easy to snap onto the in-ear speakers. The tips also have a silicone flare that helps wedge the buds in your ear and keep them in place. The flare is comfortable for extended use and it kept my buds in position while walking and jogging. Given the flexibility of the silicone, I think they will fit in almost anyone’s ear. The entire length of the cord is a little over 3 feet, from the input jack all the way to the end of a bud. The thin leads from each bud eventually join at a hard plastic Y-piece before continuing to the jack. That hard plastic Y seems durable and helps to maintain spacing as the thin left and right wires go up to your ears. On the right lead, between the bud and the Y-piece, is a small plastic button panel. It houses three buttons on the front side, and a mic input on the back. The 1/8” jack has 3 standard connections for Left and Right stereo music, as well as the mic. Altogether, the hardware is well designed, comfortable, durable, and sweat-proof. The icing on the cake is the included stylish, convenient storage case that zips close. The case isn’t exactly a hard shell, but it has some thick cardboard-like toughness to it that will protect your buds from any dangers they might encounter while buried in a backpack.

The sound from these buds is well-balanced. The lows and highs do not dominate, which results in a nice, dynamic blend of sound at soft and loud volume levels. They don’t sound as good as my over-the-ear $250 Monster headphones, obviously, but for earbuds, they are at the top of the quality list. These buds will work well for reproducing most types of music. There is no active noise canceling, but the silicone does an acceptable job of insulating your ears from outside noise. The microphone performance is better than I expected, to be honest. The normal resting position for the mic is down against your chest, but somehow the people on the other end of the phone call could still hear me. The mic performance was very good in quiet, indoor rooms. While outside jogging or in the car, the people on the other end of the call could still hear me, but they also heard quite a bit of background noise. Still, the mic performance was as good as could be expected for this type of hardware.

The inline controls worked great on my Samsung Galaxy S6. The up and down buttons shift the volume. Hitting the center button pauses the music, and a quick double hit skips to the next track. Hitting the center button once also switches over and answers an incoming call.

As an unexpected bonus, the buds/mic worked flawlessly on my Windows Phone Lumia 830 as well. I could adjust the volume, pause and skip, and answer calls. I can’t test all Windows Phones, but I suspect any Windows 8.1 or later device that supports incoming mic sounds through the headphone jack will work with these buds.

Honestly, I don’t really have any complaints about these buds. With the convenient storage case, they are going to become my primary travel headphones. It’s possible to complain a little about the price point, but given the sound quality and expected durability, they are very competitive with the other similar options out there. Additionally, if you’re a Windows Phone user and want something that will work with your phone, there is a good chance these Bose earbuds will have you covered. The other thing is that the digital display and the frequency the device is getting is not accurate. Example, for FM the display will say 88.9 but the channel is actually 96.5, same issue with AM. If anyone has knowledge of this, please enlighten me. My parents love listening to a few AM stations in my city and I was going to buy an extra one of this item for them if it had worked properly.

Secondly, it's the temperature. I am not sure if it's faulty but I noticed that I get different reads when I put the outdoor reader next to the clock itself. In addition to being more powerful, they changed the inputs so there is a port for charging and a separate port for an audio connector. It looks like the older version in the pictures has just one input for both the audio and the charger so you were limited to using their proprietary cable if you wanted to connect a non bluetooth source. Now you can use any 'male to male' audio cable to connect to a non bluetooth compatible source.

I first learned about this speaker in a CNET article that listed the best affordable bluetooth speakers available. CNET (and most other reviewers) loved it when it was 4 watts, and now it is even better as the power has been increased by 25% to 5 watts.

1. Sound Quality - This is really what you care about and I am VERY impressed with the sound quality for something so portable. Given that some reviewers complained that the speaker wasn't loud enough, I can only assume that the increase from 4W to 5W has improved the volume as well as the quality of the sound at higher volumes. I have never actually heard the older 4W version, but I have listened to a lot of other bluetooth speakers like the JBL Clip Portable, the Bose Soundlink, Bose Soundlink Mini 2, the Harman Kardon Esquire Mini, the Jawbone Jambox Mini, and several others I can't remember off the top of my head. I'll revisit some of these speakers as a point of reference in this review. I won't be referencing the Jawbone Jambox Mini because I hated everything about it and believe that almost any bluetooth speaker is better.

A. Volume: I can't imagine anyone being unhappy with the volume at this small size. You need to be realistic with your expectations here. If you want to host a dance party in an empty warehouse, then look for something bigger.
B. Clarity and Distortion: Just like any small speaker, there can be distortion at maximum volume - there are zero distortion-free alternatives at this size no matter how much money you spend. HOWEVER, after reading some reviews, I was expecting (and would totally accept) more distortion at maximum volume. I am actually surprised by how little distortion there is at high volumes. Of course some songs (usually with mucho bass) distort more than others, but really not that bad - I suspect that the 5W version has improved quite a bit from the 4W. Below maximum volume (about 80% and below) the clarity is very good. You will notice that certain genres play better than others, but nothing is bad. Mids and Highs are likely a bit better with the Bose Soundlink ($129) and Harman Kardon ($150), but not by much. And those speakers have a MUCH higher price tag and pathetic bass.
C. Bass: When properly placed, this little thing seems to have better bass than most anything I have heard for this size and wattage - in fact the bass is much better (louder and clearer) than many bluetooth speakers that are bigger and more expensive. The bass blows away the Harman Kardon Esquire Mini, the Bose soundlink, and the JBL clip. More expensive speakers like the Bose Soundlink Mini 2 and the UE Mini Boomhave better bass, but they are MUCH more expensive ($199) and usually bigger/less portable.
The "good bass in a small package" comes from the Voombox-travel's well-thought-out design with an active speaker on top of a passive speaker that faces down. So keep in mind that the best bass comes when you have it sitting on a solid surface so the bass from the passive woofer can be reflected (it sounds really good on the hood of a car). When the speaker isn't on a solid surface the bass goes down by a significant amount (like 50% or more in my opinion).

2. Size/Weight/Design. This is a very convenient size and shape and I love the versatility the top clip gives you. If you're looking for super slim/thin - like to carry in a pants pocked or slide into an over-stuffed backpack or purse, then you would do much better with the Harman Cardon Esquire Mini. That thing is crazy thin and probably would be the most convenient to carry around. Of course the thicker design is 100% the reason the Voombox has good bass and the Harman Kardon has none. The Harman Kardon has great sound with no bass if you are into that - It seems better as a speaker-phone than music-player.
The Voombox is heavier than it looks, but it's not inconvenient. If anything the weight speaks to the quality of the unit. For me, the Voombox is 'Just Right' size/shape/weight for the sound quality. I actually think that this is the best bluetooth in this size category, regardless of price.

3. Durability: I have only had it for a few weeks, so I can't comment on long-term use. I will say that it feels very durable and I love the water/shock resistant design. It opens up MANY more applications than most bluetooth speakers (shower, outdoors, whatever). If anything is going to break, it will probably be the top clip. That said, it doesn't seem cheap, it's just more vulnerable than the rest of the unit. I would guess that to top clip will be perfectly fine for 90% of users.

4. Features: Bluetooth works great - easy to pair and good range. The speaker-phone feature was something I didn't care about at all... but I was PLEASANTLY surprised how well it works. It's such a great feature I never knew I wanted. If you're within about 8 feet it works great. Haven't tried it beyond that. I also haven't tried it with massive amounts of ambient noise, but my spouse could hear me fine even with kids playing in the background.

5. Battery life: I haven't done specific tests on this, but at 50% volume I would guess it'll go beyond the stated 6 hours. It will go several hours on full volumes. The nice thing is it will display how much battery is left on your phone next to the bluetooth icon. So convenient. I don't know if they updated the battery in the newer version, but I listen to it for an hour or two here and there and it will last for days.

6. Price: Really this is an incredible value for such a high quality piece of equipment that performs all-around better than most speakers three to four times the price. Yes there are better bluetooth speakers (like the UE Boom and Bose Soundlink Mini 2), but nothing near this price point and portability.

You will not be disappointed with the updated 5 Watt version of this product. If you think there is a better or equivalent speaker within this size/price range, please comment on my review with the info. I'd love to know.

I was looking for a way to get more OTA stations without putting an antenna on the roof. This did the trick - suddenly we're getting twice as many stations, using the same attic antenna setup as before!

I installed an indoor/outdoor UHF/VHF antenna in our attic about 6 months ago, using a 100 foot coaxial cable to connect it to a TV on the first floor of our home. It took a while to find the best position for it, and the best I could do was get 4, sometimes 5, of the stations that are located in Boston and Providence, RI - each about 25 miles away. Adding this preamplifier made a huge difference. We're now getting all 11 stations that antennaweb.org says we should get from both cities, covering all the major networks.

Installation was easy, though you'll need two short coax cables that were not included. I used one three foot cable to connect the antenna to the pre-amplifier, and a second to connect the preamplifier to the power inserter. The original coax to the TV then connects to the other end of the power inserter. (See diagram http://www.winegard.com/help/images/0/09/2452296.pdf) The only challenge for me was getting an electrical extension cord into the attic so that I could plug in the USB power adapter for the power inserter. (UPDATE: Later learned that the power inserter does NOT need to be near the pre-amplifier, so I moved it to the TV end of the long cable run, downstairs. No more extension cord in the attic, which is very good. Reception was not affected by this change. Thanks to G. Morris and Ron Musgrave for this tip.)

Then it was just a matter of running the channel auto-scan on the TV again, and watching all the new stations show up!

I plugged it into my car's audio input and then also plugged the charging cord in because it didn't have any juice the first time. It connected to the phone via Bluetooth seamlessly and I could instantly play music or podcasts through my speaker with minimal effort. You use the controls on the phone to pause/play/etc. and the received does the rest. There is a blinking blue light to let you know its ready and it does have microphone capabilities as well, so you can probably use it to handle calls. I found the sound quality to be good and was overjoyed to be able to hear whatever I wanted coming out of my car's speakers (compared to the normal radio/cd only). I love fitness and I love music. Finding the right headphones for exercising can be really irritating because of comfort and fit issues. I initially purchased the famous jaybirds x but for their price they were really disappointing. They never fit really well, water resistant wasn't good (broke from rain) and most importantly their battery life were terrible, not even close to the advertised time. After that disappointment I decided to look for another product at a much more affordable price since I didn't want to deal with warranty issues and something that wouldn't break the bank if it were to break. Considering I had positive experiences with Brainwavz products before, I decided to give these a shot and I am glad that I did. The headphones aren't the most secure fit when it comes to exercising but the sound is incredible. For such an affordable product, it has great bass, clarity and most importantly a balanced sound. Even at max volume the bass is solid and the highs does not distort. Battery life is also superb compared to it's competitors. On one full charge, I can get around 4-5 hours of continuous playtime, which is almost double of what I received on the Jaybirds. Now the aspect that impressed me the most about these were the build quality. The wire is not too long and the headphones themselves are cased with a aluminum body which not only looks premium, but feels premium also. I would not feel worried if I were to drop them or put them under rough usage, they feel very solid. Overall a wonderful product that I am glad that I have tried, If you are in the market for an affordable Bluetooth headphone which not only looks good but performs well, these are a great choice!

Overall, this is a good value for the price you are paying. This MP4 player has SO many options! I got the cute blue one. This would be great for a beginner’s MP4 player for a small child. We live in 2015 so the kids have to be introduced to it somehow, and this player is going to my friend’s child for a birthday gift.

The player has a bright title screen with many options. You can: listen to music, watch a movie, record stuff, recording voice lectures, listen to the radio, look at photographs, read an eBook, and play games. It is really easy to scroll through and I love how the MP4 player uses larger font for easy reading. I don’t like how you have to hit “UP ARROW” to select items. I wish it were more intuitive and you could hit the center button like the Apple products this is emulating.

The top has an easy slide switch, and this holds a charge for a LONG time. It also has auto shut off on the screen. So if you select something and throw the unit down it will turn off within I think 10 seconds. This saves the battery. It also plays music great and the FM radio surprisingly works well in my large metropolitan area. The unit is very light which is perfect for pockets and purses, and there is a handy O ring at the bottom to attach the included lanyard for convenience.

Overall, a good beginner’s MP4/3 player. 4/5 stars for design, value and functionality.

For example, we got Tornado and Flash flooding alerts at 4 PM on my smartphone and nothing at all came through from the radio. Then at 9PM we got the all clear from the same smartphone apps. Then at 2AM that night, this radio started screaming about the warnings we had received 10 hours earlier. I checked online to see if there was another storm coming through and it was nothing. It appeared as if my radio was reporting alerts 10 hours behind what was actually going on.

This unit doesn't always report things late and sometimes it seems to work as intended, but the inconsistency of reporting and alerting combined with the difficulty in getting this unit configured has made it pretty much worthless for us. Bose is a name best known for its high-fidelity sound, which the SoundLink Mini II delivers just as well as its predecessor, the original SoundLink Mini. The SoundLink Mini 2 is the new GOLDEN STANDARD for audio quality in portable speakers, as its compact audio drivers deliver a surprisingly full range of sound. It has the same iconic look with the same sturdy metal enclosure as its predecessor, albeit a new micro-perforated steel grille. It is a hefty 1.5 pounds, which gives it a nice weight to resist vibration.

As for sound, it carries an incredible frequency response, offering rich bass tones and crisp high ends that must truly be experienced in person. You might not believe the quality and volume that these speakers otherwise pack, especially when it comes to delivering booming lows. While Bose has obviously chosen to maintain its proprietary audio technology from the previous model, it does offer some much-needed improvements to general usability.

For instance, the speaker now supports speakerphone calling, where it previously did not. It now charges with a much-preferred Micro USB charger, plus you still have the option to use the included charging cradle. And though the battery life has been improved from 7 to 10 hours of play time, it could still be better on this speaker. Voice prompts are also now available on the speaker to walk you through the pairing process, but this was a questionable addition because instructions weren’t necessarily needed for pairing to begin with. So while some improvements can be distracting, the SoundLink Mini 2 only further cements Bose as the #1 name for portable speakers. If you’re looking for a less portable model with higher volume and almost double the battery life, you might also consider the Bose SoundLink Bluetooth Speaker III.

I used this speaker as a comparison point for a number of other top speakers in my review here:
http://heavy.com/tech/2015/01/best-bluetooth-wireless-portable-speaker-reviews/

For the most part, the SoundLink Mini II stacks up excellently with other brands, but there are lots of speakers that deliver near-equivalent sound quality without the hefty price tag. Still, if you are willing to drop the $200, this is probably the best Bluetooth speaker out there.

PROS:
+Durable aluminum enclosure
+Amazing frequency response
+Reaches high volume

CONS:
-Fairly expensive
-Voice prompts for pairing seem unnecessary
-10 hour battery life could still be better

Other than the time it takes to charge "dead" batteries (approx. 5 hours) this is a GREAT charger. And, while I complain about the charge time, the low 500mA charge current is what makes this charger so safe for use with Lithium Ion batteries. I had about 15 cells freshly pulled from old laptop batteries and it only took about 2.5 days to charge them all. All 15 were charged to the perfect 4.2v regardless of their starting voltage. Lightly used batteries, just needing to be topped off, only took about an hour on average to reach the 4.2v.

One of the questions I had prior to this purchase was whether this charger could "wake" 0v cells. Three of the cells I pulled from laptop batteries were 0v and all three were recovered to full charge (albeit was minor mAh reductions) on this charger. So for those people asking, yes, this charger is capable of 0v recovery.

I bought two of these to complement a pair of B&G Radia 520 speakers: I've held off on the whole surround sound thing but having picked up two surround speakers and a crown amp at a garage sale, of all places, I might go 4.2 in the near future (the Radias image so well that a center speaker would make things worse, and my processor can output a phantom center -- like I said I'm more into music than movies).  The Radias really don't like to be driven below 80 Hz, stereo subs have advantages, my processor has dual sub outputs, and at $299 a pop, I figured "Why not?"  These are not musical subs: they have HUGE ports in the rear which prevents any decent low bass tightness (we're talking 18 Hz and lower, and these are spec'd 3 dB down at 24 Hz). Above 80 Hz, they are very boomy. That said, it's not fair to compare a $299 sub to a $1500 sub (which would be four times the volume and four to five times the weight), and ANYTHING to keep signals below 80 Hz out of the Radias is a good thing: with the addition of the subs, they tightened up nicely.  However, if you feed them what they like: signals in the 24 to 80 Hz range, they perform surprisingly well, at significant volume (the benefit of a ported design: volume, some extension, for a relatively small cabinet). (I had to turn down the gain to maybe 25% of full to match my mains: the room is 16x24 with an opening into a large kitchen/dining area of about 16x30 (L-shaped off the living room)).  The ironic thing is that while these are mid-range (quality-wise) subs, they best complement speakers that can already go quite low (80 Hz, 70 Hz would be even better), and those tend to be spendy (The Radias retail for around $5k). I would NOT recommend pairing them with small satellite speakers that want everything under 120 or 160 Hz sent to a sub: you will NOT be happy.  Dial them in right, and don't drive them too high or too low (I have some music with very very low organ notes that very few systems can reproduce faithfully -- most movies don't do this), and they'll serve you very well while you save up for decent ones at five times the price (if you want).  On edit: This DOES struggle a bit with interlaced video. 1080i30 will deinterlace with VAAPI Bob in real time but at the expense of around 70% CPU on both cores. Forget using the yadif filter to do this: you will lose frames. Still, not a bad little box.

PU Leather is not "Leather". I knew this was vinyl when ordered (what did I expect for eight bucks?), but it seems the product name is deceptive.

That said, it's of fairly decent quality and fits the Bose Mini like a glove, to protect the corners and edges from dings and scratches. It even looks pretty decent for a "pleather" product. The stitching seems well done and I don't expect it to fall apart.

The major problem is that the case is advertised thusly:

"• Speaker can be charged when the case is on."
"• Speaker is not included. (Not for Charge Cradle)"

Given that the advertiser is not a native speaker of English, I probably should have taken that "Not for Charge Cradle" as just meaning that the cover wasn't designed to hold the charge cradle as well as the speaker. And I shouldn't have taken the "Speaker can be charged when the case is on." as meaning it could be charged on the charge cradle. To be sure, there is a large opening on the bottom of the case (shown in the accompanying photos) that provides a gap where the charging station contact bad protrudes from the bottom of the speaker. However the material is too thick to allow the speaker to charge on the cradle when it's in the case; you can only charge it with the direct pin adapter (for which a convenient opening is provided).

So it's not a bad product or deal for the low price - just don't expect it to be made of anything once associated with a cow and don't expect it to allow for charging on the docking cradle (even though it looks like it's intended to) while the case is installed.

This bracket is heavy duty. It's installed, working and I have no intentions of returning it, or purchasing a different bracket. Here's my take of what I liked (a lot) and didn't like (a little):

Pros
- This thing is Heavy Duty, there is nothing cheap about the metal (or the finish) that makes up the bracket and arm.
- There are four serious lag screws to anchor in masonry or wood studs.
- There is a LOT of hardware that comes with the bracket, and it is clearly labeled. There are extra bolts, washers and spacers of various sizes - it's hard to imagine a TV that could not be installed with the various hardware provided.
- The instructions are much better than average for a "low tech" product like this. They are thorough and written clearly. There are instructions for small, large and odd shaped TV installations, and I had no problem understanding the directions.
- I thought the self-adhesive bubble level would be gimmicky, but it's easy to use and worked well. The mounting template was useful and thick enough to tape to the wall without tearing.

Cons:
- Once the bracket/arm is installed on the wall, and the adjustable bracket is installed on the back of the TV, the instructions indicate it might take two people to put the two together for the final installation. Well, it took three of us for our wall mounted application about 4 feet off the ground. The TV has to be held still for the left and right, top and bottom bolts/washers to be installed. Even with the arm extended, it's tight behind the TV, and I cannot imagine trying to do this installation with only two people.
- The bracket allows for a -5 to 15 degree vertical plane adjustment. We wanted ours at 0 (parallel to the wall) - to keep it at 0, we had to tighten the spring loaded adjustment arm/bolt and the corresponding top installation bolt VERY TIGHT. Otherwise, the weight of the TV (nothing unusual - normal Wal-Mart Samsung) kept tilting the bracket forward.

All in all, we are completely satisfied.

If your old device has only one audio output, buy a stereo "Y" connector for the red and white receptacles so that you get sound in both left and right channels. I almost thought I would have to send it in for warranty repair. I would have given it 5 stars if it were not for the two things I mentioned.

I'm not sure what people are expecting from this amplifier or am I sure if people understand how wattage works when it pertains to amplifiers. This Amp is rated at 8000 watts peak (meaning it could probably play that wattage for nano seconds not continuously) Clearly this is an exaggeration as an 8000 watt amp would certainly need it's own separate power source etc.

Now that is out the way, my suggestion is people to evaluate what they need this amp for. For high end home theater? Certainly NOT. However to power multiple speakers in a home or business for 'Fill' music. Not a problem.

All 8 channels in my amp are being used to power my whole home music. Channel 1/2 power the bathroom speakers (6.5inches), 3/4 power both the speakers in the foyer and kitchen[6.5 inches] (I used piggy back banana plugs), 5/6 power speakers in the Great room (8inches) and 7/8 each power a 10inch in ceiling subwoofer (one in the kitchen and the other in the great room). It does it effortlessly and without problems.

I purchased my amp used from Amazon warehouse deals for $171, which is a steal. Still came with the warranty but did have a few scratches on the rack mount system. Since I was installing this in a dedicated music cabinet, the scratches weren't a problem. Unit works well.

Cons
Trigger does not work as it should. I have never been able to get the input trigger to receive signal from my Denon x4000. Checked the settings etc. The denon can signal other devices, just not this one. Since my amp is out of reach, I used a WEMO wifi outlet. That way I can use my phone to power on/off the amp. (I can be lazy).

This is not an amplifier for Audiophiles. It will not provide clean, tight power but it will give you adequate sound and be reliable.

The lights in the front are quite bright but as mine is out of sight, it doesn't bother me. Plus I prefer to see the Spectrum lights to determine if I'm clipping or not.

The Denon x4000 has 3 zone capability therefore I can listen to one source in the bathroom, another source throughout the house and watch a movie in 7.1 in the Man cave. The 8 channel amp handles everything outside the Man Cave and the Denon handles the Man Cave speakers.

I ran all the wires through the attic and connected in-wall volume control components so I can adjust the volume independently for each room even though I can just use my phone to adjust the volume also. (This is more a feature of the Denon rather than the Pyle.)

The Amp does come with a fan but it's best to put it in a well ventilated area and/or install a a/v fan.

I've ran this playing music throughout the day and night and it runs without problems. Pair it will pyle in-wall speakers and it will give you decent whole home music. Nothing spectacular but definitely adequate.

Highly recommend it. Any questions, feel free to ask away.

I was torn between a four and a five for this one, but decided that since I use it everyday I'd give it the nod for a five. This is my new favorite tiny portable speaker. It has a number of features that have pushed it past numerous others that I've evaluated.

Pros:

1. Sound: It's single channel (no stereo), but it projects a nice, clean sound that is loud enough for casual listening while cleaning dishes, doing chores, etc. It is not "party" level, but it's not wimpy. Compared to other small speakers in the class (Philips, Creative) this comes through loud and clear without gross distortion. Is it like listening to my 5+2 NHT home theatre system fed from the 175W/Ch receiver in my family room - of course not, but this one packs a punch for what it is. I can carry it to the garage, out back while painting, etc. and it sounds good when fed from my iPhone.

2. Bluetooth connection: This unit passed my "easy pairing" test. That is, if I can pair it to my phone in less than a minute without referring to the instructions, then it passes the test. I was able to do the work in more like 90 seconds because there are two power switches on this device. One is hidden by the rubber flap that covers the analog audio jack, USB charging port, and the battery switch. This switch connects the battery circuit. Of course, this does not have a lot to do with BT, except that the unit does not work at all if this switch is not on. It won't change, won't play, etc. If this were not the case I would have had it paired in 30 seconds. There is an on/off, BT button on the outside of the speaker. You just have to press and hold it until the LED light for the BT blinks red and blue. I'm giving this a passing grade because I was able to do this without instructions, even if it took a bit longer to do. YMMV

3. Smallness: It is not very big. Smaller than a small ("tall") cup of coffee at Starbucks.

4. Nice ergonomics. It has rubber portions where it is supposed to grip the surface it is set on so it won't slide or roll inadvertently.

5.. Appearance: It doesn't look "cheap". Looks nice and has enough weight to it that it feels like it has quality (yes, I know weight is not the best indicator).

6. Analog 3.5mm jack as well as BT. If you want to save battery power and/or just don't have BT, this is still a great way to connect a speaker.

7. Can be easily positioned sideways or vertically.

8. You can hear some bass - not common with these smaller speakers.

9. attractively priced.

Cons

1. See the discussion in section 2 under pros above. I think the main slider switch should still allow charging when the switch is off. As it is, nothing can happen with the switch off. This is different enough from other devices that I suspect many will think their battery is charging when it isn't.

Conclusion.

On with the review: I'm no audiophile and I don't want to spend hours fine tuning a sound system since neither I nor the others in my family would likely be able to tell the difference in subtle settings.
