That said, there are no complaints with any of these components. (We spent just about $500 for all 4 components. I kept the center speaker and the two surrounds from our previous system and there has been no issue with that set up.) The settings available on the Onkyo AVR make it possible to listen to true stereo music when we want (that was not possible with the old AVR, which was really designed just for surround), and then get the full theater experience for movies and TV shows. It works great with our LG TV and DVD player and our Roku. I have not set up second region yet, but I plan to put some speakers in our back yard. Bottom line: after about a month we are very happy with this purchase, for now, at least.

I purchased the SEK-3500U for my 2014 75" Samsung UN75HU8550 TV.  While there are positive things about this upgrade kit my review is going to focus on input lag which should be of significance to anyone who is using their TV for gaming.  Input lag is the delay between the display receiving a signal and actually displaying it on screen.  When you have high input lag you will notice a delay between button presses on a gamepad and some sort of action (firing, jumping, etc.) on the screen.  My test setup consisted of two different computers (one a laptop and one a desktop with secondary external monitor).  I also have a friend who has the same TV as me and I performed the testing on his TV as well to ensure the results were consistent.  I initially tested WITHOUT the SEK-3500U hooked up.  I tested with default settings (game mode off) then enabled game mode and retested.  I then hooked up the SEK-3500U and repeated both tests.  The results were disappointing (see my attached image).  With the SEK-3500U attached to my TV input lag increased by ~85ms.  Even with game mode enabled on the SEK-3500U my input lag was noticeably higher than my TV before with game mode disabled!  What does this mean?  If your primary use of the TV is for gaming stay away.  The lag is too high and noticeable.  If you use the TV for occassional gaming and primarily movies / 4K content then you should enable game mode when gaming and disable when viewing other content (a hassle but doable).  If you don't play games at all then the lag should not affect you.  After spending several hours testing the SEK-3500U I ended up returning it.  Even if it were free I would be reluctant to use it due to the input lag.  It's possible Samsung could release newer firmware to address the issue in the future.  If that happens I will retest and update my review.  Otherwise, i'll wait for the 2016 evolution kit and try again.

Pros:
- big, handsome set of phones

Cons:
- Somewhere between 150-300k is a miserable bass/low-mid hump. It is utter mud.
- treble (after a quick and easy mod - removing some felt behind the plastic lense cap) is somewhat clear but eventually you'll interpret it as noisy.
- mids are fairly warm for a $60 set but are all but ruined by that aforementioned bass hump
- the iTunes EQ doesn't offer enough control to set these cans up for any happy use, at least for me.

From what I've read, the folks that are happy with this set have some nice upstream equipment. If you've got an analog receiver or a headphone amp (ideally w/ some EQ carving) then maybe you'll be able to drive these cans to sound nice, but otherwise they're muddy and boring. I wanted them for work - I've been plugging them into my macbook and have been really unsatisfied. I'll likely hang onto them because they were affordable enough and I do think they're comfortable. Otherwise, I don't recommend unless you want to mod them or something.

Number one reason to get these is if you lose your keys all the time. Also great for finding purses/wallets and tv remotes – BUT that’s only if you can keep track of the Click ‘n Dig’s remote!  Oh, the irony.  The remote is fairly small: 3 inches long x 1 ½ inches wide x ½ inch deep.  There is a ¾ inch x ¼ inch molded plastic loop on the end with a ½ inch key ring attached to it so you can hang it on a hook or attach a lanyard if you’d like.  The buttons on the remote are color coded and it’s up to you to remember which color goes with what.  Maybe you could use a sharpie marker to label each key, or put a sticky label on the back listing what each color corresponds to ( such as green for checkbook, blue for briefcase, yellow for gym bag, purple for dayplanner, etc.).  The receivers are small but not tiny (so no good for glasses). This particular set comes with 6 receivers - 3 with key rings and the other 3 designed to be afixed flat with included adhesive pads. Flat receivers are 3 ¼ inches long, 1 ¾ inches at the widest, and about ¼ inch deep. Key ring version is almost ½ inch thick, 2 inches long (not counting ring) and 1 ½ inches wide. The ring is ½ inch diameter. The receivers all have rounded/tapered edges, except for the backs of the flat ones.  Before using these I suggest reading the directions, which despite not being entirely intuitive, are very simple. I foolishly didn’t and got frustrated because the receivers didn’t beep every time I clicked the remote. “What’s up with that?” I thought. Well, turns out you need to HOLD down the button for a few seconds.  When I did that they worked every time.  The reason for needing to hold the button down is that the remote sends out signals in pulses, and the receivers might not pick up every pulse.  On the plus side, the batteries are already inside everything, you just need to pull out the plastic tabs before each unit will work. Comes with a full set of extra batteries too - verynice! Not sure about the lifespan of the batteries if you use these frequently.  On the downside, to open the battery compartment on the remote and flat recievers you need a very tiny philips head screwdriver.  A design flaw with the flat receivers is that the battery panel is on the back where the double sided adhesive goes, which will make changing the battery difficult.  Since I’ve gotten these I haven’t lost anything (what luck!), but someone I gave these as gifts to last Christmas has told me how useful they’ve been in finding lost keys and books (there’s a flat reciever on the bookmark she uses).  Depending on where your stuff is hiding you may need to get rather close to it before hearing the beeps.  The receivers are more muffled if they land upside down or are enclosed in something. Since these flash as well as beep, you might try turning out the lights if you can’t exactly track down the sound.  Overall, for what these can do, they do it pretty well.  They can’t solve every problem, such as if your keys get dropped outside and the receiver is ruined in the rain or the toddler has pulled off the receiver to play with it, but I think the Click ‘n Dig can be very useful and may on occasion save your sanity.

The best kind of general purpose shortwave antenna is, of course, a long-wire wire antenna (50 - 100 feet long) mounted up high in the outdoors. If that solution is impossible or impractical for you, an active loop antenna is an outstanding substitute. It is well known that resonant loop antennas can perform nearly as well as long-wire antennas in the outdoors, even when the loop is only a few feet off the ground.  The trade-off is that the tuned-resonant loop antenna is narrow-band and must be adjusted as you change frequency.  If you use the loop indoors, as is intended with this product, you will get surprisingly good performance that represents the best compromise in a small space.  This loop includes an amplifier as well that enhances the performance.  You simply select the band of interest on the controller and you are set to go. You can mount the antenna on a window using the enclosed suction cup and/or clip.  This loop will perform better than any other indoor antenna solution for shortwave listening.

I currently have a couple of pairs of headphones for different purposes: Sony MDR-V6 for keyboard/piano and other studio purposes, and Sennheiser HD598's for comfortable listening at home. I was looking to round out this collection with something that met the following criteria:

- Closed (for use in an office environment and when traveling)
- Made for pleasurable listening, so could be a little colored as long as it was still detailed and clear
- Not overly analytical or sibilant (harsh treble that can cause fatigue over long periods)
- Very comfortable
- At least decent build quality (I'v seen some pretty creaky, crappy plastic sets out there)

Basically, I'm looking for the perfect pair of closed headphones, lol. But chief among these for me has to be comfort and clarity, because I would be using these for long periods of time and don't appreciate muddy music. Here's how the B&W P7s did:

Build Quality:
Among the best I've ever seen with a pair of headphones, and better than anything else I got to compare it with in brick & mortar stores. The metal is solid and polished, the leather (whether or not it is real) feels very plush, smooth, and remains cool. Almost everything is wrapped in that leather. The ear pads can be easily removed because they are magnetic -- an awesome feature, I think -- and even underneath that you will find a good looking metal shield covering the driver.

Sound Quality:
This set is very close to what I was looking for. It provided pretty clear and detailed sound without sounding too harsh or analytical on the top end. That means the top is rolled off in an almost ideal manner and does not cause fatigue, to my ears at least. They also meet the need of being geared toward pleasurable listening, with a slightly colored, pleasing sound signature. However, I will say that I found the mids to be just slightly left behind, which was a bit of a disappointment coming from the more balanced sounding Sennheiser HD 598. For a close pair of headphones, the P7s also do an admirable job of creating a decent soundstage, though again it won't be on par with good open headphones.

Comfort:
This turned out to be the deal breaker for me with these headphones. Let me say that I do wear glasses, but usually it's not a major problem with over the ear headphones, and wasn't the issue with the B&W P7s either. Yes, the materials are very nice and do help with the comfort, but I just could not get over the clamping force these apply. In addition to the ear cups being slightly on the small side, the clamping force left my ears, my head, and even my jaw slightly hurting if I went more than 30 minutes at a time. I did use these over a week and tried stretching the headphones out overnight on most nights, but there is still quite a bit of clamping force left and I just can't use these comfortably for extended periods at work.

So there you have it. These headphones were almost exactly what I wanted, and there are very few things wrong with them. Slightly recessed mids would not really be an issue as I'm not using these for critical listening, but comfort is a compromise I simply can't make. It could also be a factor that I'm used to a set like the Sennheiser HD598, which has large, deep ear cups and light clamping force. Those I've listened to for literally 4 hours at a time with no problem. Plus those velour pads are heavenly on your head.

On to find a more comfortable version of these headphones, or a closed version of the HD598s.

There were two things that I did before ordering Echogear's TV wall mount bracket. The first thing was to checking the weight of my 42" Vizio TV set; and the second was making sure that the wall I was mounting it to had a stud in approximately the place I was going to mount it on. It's very important that it's mounted to a stud in the wall. When it arrived I immediately noted how easy the directions were to follow, and it had lots of illustrations. And don't be confused about all the hardware that you see in the sorted plastic packets. Most of them you won't even use. They give you options depending upon your brand of TV set. Most of the bracket is assembled. You'll have to configure the part that attaches to the TV set. The easiest way to attach the bracket is to lay your set face down on a bed. Next, find the stud, level the bracket, mark the holes, drill the holes to the appropriate size, attach the lag screws with a socket and ratchet, and then mount to the TV and secure it with a couple of small screws. They do provide a hex wrench, but you'll need some basic tools. I was strong enough to lift the TV set myself, but it's best you get someone to help you. You won't regret the purchase of this product.

This product has two flaws - each is individually puzzling as a design choice, and the combination of the two makes the device defective.

(1) The shape of this dock suggests that it has a recessed slot that the iPad or iPhone sits in, and that holds the device in place while docked. However, this gap is practically cavernous - it is so oversized that it doesn't hold the device at all. It is also so shallow that even if you lean an iPad way back to make contact with it, the contact point is way at the bottom, so it will fall over. As a result, the device is only supported by standing on the Lightning connector.

Besides being disappointing, this flaw is problematic for several reasons. First, frankly, any device that's not gigantically sized will look ridiculous, standing in the middle of this huge hole. It's probably intentional that none of the photos for this product at Amazon show the dock with a device attached - see the one that I attached to this review to understand how pathetic it looks. Second, any dock that supports the device only by standing on the dock connector will put strain on the Lightning port *and* the connector: over time, one or both will be damaged. Third, because the Lightning connector is fairly short, the device is really unstable - perhaps not bad for an iPhone, but an iPad will not be secure at all.

So that's bad, but it gets worse, because:

(2) The socket that holds the Lightning connector has some wiggle room, so it can pivot forward and backward. So the dock doesn't feature a fixed prong upon which you can stand the device; rather, you have fuss with the connector to get it into the port on the bottom of the device. This is just a very strange choice for a dock connector; I can't even imagine a reason for this design.

When you put these flaws together, what you get is a port that's not only frustrating to connect, but also provides little support for the device.

Try this:Take an ordinary Lightning cable; bend the connector part upward and set it on a table; then take your device with both hands, and try to mount it on the totally unsupported Lightning cable. Nearly impossible, right? That's what this device does, only it costs $60.

I've never been the type who particularly cares about synthetic chemicals. They make our lives better, they are reasonably priced, and they tend to be very effective.

However, I was cleaning my kitchen a few months ago, and it occurred to me that I was essentially eating the antibacterial cleaner I was spraying on every exposed surface. Now that gave me pause.

I set out to find good cleaning products that I could use in the kitchen, and ended up ordering quite a few of them. They tend to be hard to find locally, hiding out in overpriced "organic" grocery stores, and cost about three times what you would normally expect to pay.

Some of them worked, and very well. I had particularly good luck with the liquid soaps and the general "all-purpose" spray cleaners. The ones the didn't work as well were the ones for glass. They don't use alchohol, so not only is that not there as a solvent, it also takes forever for the stuff to dry. It saturates the cloth and makes it ineffective for drying off the surfaces. And, when it does finally dry, it leaves streaks. I hate streaks.

I tried this new one to see if it would work better than the others. It isn't actually new, just new over here, as it has apparently been around for a while in the UK, and the company has had such great success there, that they are trying their hand at international distribution.

The microfiber cloth that comes with it is uncommonly thick. Not fluffy - dense. I wasn't sure if this would be good or bad, but in general I have experienced poor results from thin ones, which quickly become over-saturated with fluid, and fluffy ones, which lack the flat surface required to wipe without the dreaded streaking.

First, I sprayed it on my very expensive laptop screen. A quick wipe with the heavy towel, and it was mostly clean. A few quick spritzes on the trouble spots, another wipe, and it was like new. For good measure, I also wiped down the keyboard using the residual left in the towel (don't spray your keyboard!), and it came out cleaner than I've seen it in years. Heck, the rubber trackpoint was actually grippy after the quick wipe-down. And, no streaks! This was very promising, so I decided to give it the ultimate test.

I have a new AV rack with black chrome accents and large pieces of darkly-tinted glass. I had just finished assembling it, so of course there were fingerprints and handprints everywhere. There may have even been a face print or two. (I love the stand, but it wasn't the easiest thing to put together by myself!)

Spritz, spritz, spritz, then wipe. The first thing I noticed is that this stuff dries insanely fast. Too fast for the way I was trying to use it, which was to cover an entire glass shelf with mist, then wipe the entire thing down with the cloth. Halfway through, the mist was dry, and I was only using the towel. Doing half at a time instead, however, worked wonders. That dark glass shows everything, and the fluid with the towel took it all off and made everything shiny and clean again. It wasn't just the towel, either, because when I tried the towel on the areas that had dried, it just pushed the smears around instead of lifting them.

This comes in different sizes, so be sure to get the one that is right for your purposes. The 50 Ml bottle is large enough to hold enough product, but small enough for travel. It would tuck nicely into a dopp kit. If you just want to give it a shot before ordering a bigger one, that's the way to go. I'll probably take that one to work, and get the bigger size to use at home.

Highly recommended.

The unit is very lightweight, easily sliding into just about any type of pocket - jacket, shirt or pants. All in all, this Martinsen player is not the absolute best I have used, but it only has a couple of drawbacks and it has a pretty fair price point to boot. The wires were able to be run behind the storage cabinet and then through the floor by removing a drain plug underneath the carpet. Must use extreme caution to protect the wire from rubbing bare against any metal or plastic to prevent a short/fire. I used zip ties and plenty of electrical tape. I'm not sure why Amazon indicates 2 wire install kits are required for the 2500 watt inverter, I used 1 wire kit and it works just fine. Just be sure to use a 250 amp fuse within a short distance of your power wire connection. I was able to get power near my A\C filter in the engine compartment

UPDATE June 2016:
Apparently using just one set of wires wasn't a good idea after all. The unit worked fine for awhile until one day when I apparently had 1 too many appliances running at the same time. The power consumption was too large for one set of wires to handle and they burnt to a crisp. While looking for a budget bluetooth headset for working out or running, I encountered multiple positive reviews from reviews and blogs for the 66 Audio BTS. Seeing the price and not expecting much, the BTS generally surprised me. This stems from the quality of the BTS and most importantly the service from 66 Audio tech technical support. In a little over a week from receiving my first set, I was able to reported a defective pair, talk with technical support regarding the precise issues, and have them replaced with no hassle.

As a person that relies on Voice Over and Talk Back as the screen readers on iOS and Android, bluetooth headsets must meet a stringent series of requirements for me to provide a high rating. First, the audio sound must be clear, especially when listening to text to speech voices talking at rates between 500 to 700 words per minute. The BTS preforms very well. Male and female voices do not come out either too much bass or having too much pitch.

Since I rely on swiping and listening for a vocal response, there cannot be too much latency between gesture and feedback. The first pair of BTS failed at this, but the second pair possesses nearly no lag, responding promptly. Yes, this actually is an issue with other bluetooth headsets, where half a second does mean the difference between accurately preforming the right gesture or hitting the right key on a keyboard or not.

Finally, the battery life must be able to last a day. Six hours of playback for a person with a screen reader means you have less than six hours of time with the headset. Everytime I touch my device, swipe, read an article, or conduct any action, the headset is technically playing back audio. The BTS delivers on its ability to not only last one day on a charge, but multiple. I have not been able to test if the claim of 30 hours is accurate, I can say that I can use my devices for two days without any fear of battery life cutting me off in the middle ofan action.

There seems to be some confusion of what the actual ohm rating on these speakers are. There is conflicting information if they are 8ohm or 4ohm. But from my measurements and direct comparisons with the Pioneer BS22 and Infinity Primus p153, the Supernova S didn't measure as though it was drawing more power from the amp. So I'm going to guess, that these are 8ohm nominal.

In my time listening to them, I immediately noticed midrange output that was giving every voice a tunnel like quality to it. There is also some major elevated tweeter output (+10db from ~7khz to ~15khz at close mic measurements, ~+6db at 1m measurements) causing some pretty extreme sibilance with just about any hard S sound. This has been the first time it was some obvious to me. Snares/high hats are all just in your face and distracting. I don't think the midrange in playing full range, but it had obvious audible output till about 9khz. Maybe as an attempt to help combat the huge peak in tweeter output. Regardless, it’s doesn’t seem to be helping. And if it actually is, then there are some other design choices that should have been rectified before extending the output that far was the chosen solution. In addition to the elevated and harsh tweeter, there is a major lack of bass.

Now, I do my listening with the speakers pretty far away from any rear walls, so that may contribute to that slightly. But speakers like the Pioneer BS22 or TEAC LS-H265 have no problem making plenty of bass in the same room. I have reviewed and enjoyed speakers that were weak in the bass department (Insignia NS-SP213), but did a lot of other things well enough instead. The combination of the way too loud tweeter and the extreme lack of bass make for a combo that is pretty hard to listen to. In some of the less measurable areas, I found the sound stage to be pretty narrow smeary mess. The audio is very contained to the edges of the speaker cabinet. There isn't anything going on that helps envelopeyou in sound or make the audio feel bigger than the speaker locations.

If you are looking to speakers in the $120 range there is no reason to put these on your short list. Skip right past these and look to the Pioneer BS22 or the Infinity Primus p153 .

First up, the caveats. I did receive one of these free in return for writing this review. However, I had purchased one of these for my wife for Christmas previous to this. She is frequently misplacing her keys so this product seemed like just the ticket for her. Between the two of us, I can confidently say that for the money this product is worth every penny plus for anyone who has a need for something like this. In the month+ I've had this set, I have only had occasion to use it once. However, my wife makes use of hers on a weekly basis since last Christmas when she received it, and it has never failed to help her. She keeps the main unit in the kitchen with all her phone chargers and other stuff. I keep mine on my dresser in the bedroom. She has one of the beeper thingies on each of her key rings, her personal keys and her work keys. I have one on my key ring, and do not yet use the other. There are only two issues with this product from my perspective, and they are both very minor in comparison to how useful and effective this product is. The first is that the beepers are fairly bulky, about the size of an automotive key fob. Combined with the actual automotive key fob in one's pocket this just adds a bit of bulk. Second, with two units in the house, we have noticed that both units use the same frequency, so when she pushes the blue button to find her keys, it also sets off my blue beeper, and vice versa. A switch, perhaps, to tune each set to a different frequency would be useful for folks like us who have more than one set. Still, neither of these issues alter the usefulness and bang for the buck of this product, so five stars from me.

All in all, this was a good buy so far. I will update this review if need be if I run into any other issues with this. But for a $22 device, its doing pretty good. My cons with the device makes me rate it a 4/5 for right now. These are velcro straps that work just a bit differently from others I've seen - the loop is used to wrap around whatever is being tied together, and the one end then wraps around and attaches to the other in order to hold the bundle at whatever size is needed, within the capability of the strap.

The effective 'usable' length of the straps is therefore less than the 16\\" total length. The straps can usefully wrap something that is about 4\\" in diameter, at most, which is still pretty sizable. When used at that maximum 'capacity', the velcro attachment or 'holding' area (overlap where the two velcro pieces attach) is minimal, however, so the strength of the strap will be at it's lowest. They will be best used to wrap things that are probably 3\\" or less in diameter, I think. I consider that to be very good and useful.

This is not necessarily the heaviest 'weight' velcro material I've seen, and each 16\\" strap consists of two pieces that are glued together in the middle, each piece being the two sides of the velcro fastener. That attachment point is probably the weak spot and if they fail, I expect that is where they might pull apart, if they're used for something too heavy or demanding. I don't consider that a negative for what these are, although at just over a dollar per strap they're not that inexpensive, really.

If I find any points worth mentioning here after I've used this for a longer period of time then I will return to this review and update it accordingly.

With a BRP, Cable Box, Streaming player, and soon to be game console, it looks like an insect when all the slots are in use. Customers would be better served if they had given up some of the compact design to make a bigger box that had all the inputs and outputs on the back.

The only other glaring issue is that, as is the case with most of those credit card remotes, the responsiveness of the remote/IR receiver connection is dubious. It can sometimes take several attempts to make it switch. It's not a deal breaker, but for $50+, I'd rather have a stronger connection, than a tiny remote that is just begging to get lost or broken.

Conclusion: It's a handy thing to have in your media setup if you don't have a receiver with HDMI capability, and you need all your playback units to reach more than one Monitor/TV/PJ. You just have to accept that it's not going to be perfect

I've never been the type who particularly cares about synthetic chemicals. They make our lives better, they are reasonably priced, and they tend to be very effective.

However, I was cleaning my kitchen a few months ago, and it occurred to me that I was essentially eating the antibacterial cleaner I was spraying on every exposed surface. Now that gave me pause.

I set out to find good cleaning products that I could use in the kitchen, and ended up ordering quite a few of them. They tend to be hard to find locally, hiding out in overpriced "organic" grocery stores, and cost about three times what you would normally expect to pay.

Some of them worked, and very well. I had particularly good luck with the liquid soaps and the general "all-purpose" spray cleaners. The ones the didn't work as well were the ones for glass. They don't use alchohol, so not only is that not there as a solvent, it also takes forever for the stuff to dry. It saturates the cloth and makes it ineffective for drying off the surfaces. And, when it does finally dry, it leaves streaks. I hate streaks.

I tried this new one to see if it would work better than the others. It isn't actually new, just new over here, as it has apparently been around for a while in the UK, and the company has had such great success there, that they are trying their hand at international distribution.

The microfiber cloth that comes with it is uncommonly thick. Not fluffy - dense. I wasn't sure if this would be good or bad, but in general I have experienced poor results from thin ones, which quickly become over-saturated with fluid, and fluffy ones, which lack the flat surface required to wipe without the dreaded streaking.

First, I sprayed it on my very expensive laptop screen. A quick wipe with the heavy towel, and it was mostly clean. A few quick spritzes on the trouble spots, another wipe, and it was like new. For good measure, I also wiped down the keyboard using the residual left in the towel (don't spray your keyboard!), and it came out cleaner than I've seen it in years. Heck, the rubber trackpoint was actually grippy after the quick wipe-down. And, no streaks! This was very promising, so I decided to give it the ultimate test.

I have a new AV rack with black chrome accents and large pieces of darkly-tinted glass. I had just finished assembling it, so of course there were fingerprints and handprints everywhere. There may have even been a face print or two. (I love the stand, but it wasn't the easiest thing to put together by myself!)

Spritz, spritz, spritz, then wipe. The first thing I noticed is that this stuff dries insanely fast. Too fast for the way I was trying to use it, which was to cover an entire glass shelf with mist, then wipe the entire thing down with the cloth. Halfway through, the mist was dry, and I was only using the towel. Doing half at a time instead, however, worked wonders. That dark glass shows everything, and the fluid with the towel took it all off and made everything shiny and clean again. It wasn't just the towel, either, because when I tried the towel on the areas that had dried, it just pushed the smears around instead of lifting them.

This comes in different sizes, so be sure to get the one that is right for your purposes. The 50 Ml bottle is large enough to hold enough product, but small enough for travel. It would tuck nicely into a dopp kit. If you just want to give it a shot before ordering a bigger one, that's the way to go. I'll probably take that one to work, and get the bigger size to use at home.

Pros:

* No microphone or controls, which are always the first thing to fail in my experience.
* 90 degree plug, these seem to last much longer than straight plug, particularly if you put your phone/iPod in a front pocket and sit down.
* Low profile, they don't stick out.

Cons:
* Cheap construction. The cables are extremely thin and tangle very easily.
* Somewhat muddy mids and upper-mids. Has a little bit of that "listening underwater" sound.
* Plug pops out more easily than my other headphones, a minor annoyance.
* Really needs a clip to hold it in place on your shirt, especially if you run the cable under your shirt, since the spot where the wires meet will get caught on your shirt neckband and pull them downward.

To be clear, these are EXCELLENT for the price. I've tried a variety of cheap earbuds active use (gym, bicycling, working in the garage) and these are by far the best. The sound is a bit muddy in the upper-mids, but they're so much better than most other low-end headphones I've tried.

Regarding the missing headphone controls and microphones, they always cause me problems, so I'm glad they're gone. Sweat will get in there or they'll rub on my shirt, and suddenly Google Now is talking to me, or the phone is redialing, or the songs are skipping. They're just an annoyance and a point of failure. In my opinion, either unplug the headphones and take the call directly or get a proper headset. Obviously this is subjective.

Their low profile makes them great for bicycling. They're almost entirely covered from the front by the tragus (the bit of your ear that sticks out in front). This means very little wind noise. Many other headphones I've used stick out far enough that you'll end up hearing the wind whistling past them and have to significantly increase the volume.

My point of comparison for sound quality are Etymotic ER4 and Sony MDR-V6 headphones which are vastly more expensive than these Panasonics.

To program as a duplicate remote:

1. Turn your receiver and TV on, and press SYSTEM INFO on the front of the receiver.
2. Confirm that you see the System Info screen.
3. Note the remote address shown in the UHF remote address box. It will be a number from 1-16.
4. Press and hold the SAT mode button on your new remote until all of the mode buttons light up.
5. All four mode buttons should light up.
6. Use the number pad on your remote to enter the remote address from Step 3.
7. The SAT button should light up.
8. Press the POUND (#) button.
9. The SAT button should flash 3 times.
10. Press the RECORD button.
11. If the steps are successful, the number entered in Step 3 should display on the "System Info" screen.
12. Select "Done" to close the "System Info" screen

The instructions that come with the remote tell you how to program as a replacement remote:

1. Turn your receiver and TV on, and press SYSTEM INFO on the front of the receiver.
2. Confirm that you see the System Info screen.
3. Press RECORD on your remote. The receiver updates to match the remote’s address.
4. Confirm that your remote operates your receiver by pressing remote buttons. If this is not working, go back to step 3.

This is my first "smart" charger, so i really can not compare it to any other brand or model, as all of my previous models, were all "dumb" chargers, ones that you usually need 2 batteries in the thing to charge them. but here is what i can say.

While I do like the charger, and have had fairly good luck with it, I have found a few problems that I have had with it. I have found that multiple times, it has stopped charging the battery, and said full, for absolutely no reason. For example, I will have the charger unplugged (I unplug it when not using it), plug it in, put in some batteries that are just about fully drained, and say, my 2000 mah AA ones, will charge, say 500 mah, then say full. I will take the battery out, and push it back in immediately, and then it will charge for an additional say 1400 mah. So basically, as of the time that it said it was full, it was only charged about 25%. I have had this happen with Energizer, Juice, and Eneloop brands, and with anywhere from 2 to 4 batteries in it, and anything from AAA, AA, and D sized batteries. Funny thing is, take it out, put it straight back in, and they charge the rest of the way with no problem, so i am not sure why it does this. Also, I only charge my batteries on the 400ma setting, so it is not because of them overheating due to fast charging, or anything else. I dont have to let it sit any time to cool down either, so I doubt it is a heat thing. Glitch??

The other thing I have noticed is, a few times, the device did not kick off when the battery is full, When you have a 2500 mah battery, the charger says that the battery has charged to 3000 mah, and is still charging, I would say it is over charging it. If i take the battery out, and immediately put it back in, it will say full though, so for some reason, it does not always kick off. I have only had this happen a few times, so it is not a big deal. Just another glitch.

These 2 problems, I have found happen in all slots and sizes and brands of batteries that I have charged. Also, having it plugged in and charging for a while, or just plugged in, or even the number of batteries I put in, has no relevance as to when, or which slot glitches out, and which way. I would say that about 95% of the time (maybe a little more), they charge all batteries fine with no problems, but there are those few times that it does glitch.

As for the good parts, most of the times it works flawlessly. I like the idea of knowing when it is fully charged, so I do not damage the batteries due to overcharging. It is also good to be able to see just how much the batteries can hold too. and the fact that I can charge just one battery at a time. I have flashlights that use AA and AAA batteries, that use 3 of them, and there is nothing more annoying then going to charge the batteries, and not being able to because it is not in a set of 2. The display is fairly simple to understand.. "Charge" for charging, "discharge" for discharging, "charge test" to charge, then discharge, then fully charge, "discharge refresh" to do 3 full charge, discharge cycles, etc. The batteries are fairly easy to put in and take out. I have seen some chargers that almost seem like you need to use a screwdriver to pry them out. This one is not like that.

I have the v2.1 2nd generation firmware in the one I got. While I can not say that it is cheap, I feel that in the long run, vs paying for extra batteries from them getting damaged due to being overcharged, I say that this thing will pay for itself. Also, the added bonus of knowing when the battery is full, you dont have to wait for the battery to go through a certain amount of time to know that it is fully charged, which means that if the batteries are only half drained, you can charge twice as many batteries in the same amount of time, as you are not waiting for it to kick off by a timer, and you will know that they are fully charged. Knowing if a battery is bad, or has low mah values is nice too, because you know which battery is going bad, or just how good they all are. Overall, I am happy with my purchase and hope that it lasts for years to come. I think I have had this for about 6 months now too, so I have had plenty of time to test it out. Along with that, I have charged probably about 150-200 batteries in it, if not more. With the glut of earphones, headphones, buds, etc. on the market it's tempting to imagine them all made from the same base components at some Chinese factory and simply customized per casing and brand.

But listening experience suggests otherwise and, for anyone seriously interested in audio, I would recommend direct A-B comparisons using the same set of music – ideally each piece featuring various instruments, textures, ambience, and frequency span.

It’s really enlightening and just plain fun to uncover real and often dramatic differences in relative signal strength, frequency response as well as the overall 'voicing' of the devices that can drastically alter the clarity and warmth of what you hear.

I compared the Bose earphones to two sets of Brainwavz earphones and a no-name import brand that impressed me with its bass response.
The Bose phones have neither the richest bass response nor the shimmering top end, but what they have hands-down over the other phones is amazing clarity and superior gain - even compared to some full over the ear headphone phones I own.

Clarity in this case means the instrumental separation and detail is at the forefront and not obscured by excessive bass (don’t get me wrong, I love bass, but not overall muddiness). The other phones sounded either more-distance, with excessive high-end, or unbalanced compared to the Bose.

Just for kicks I tried the Bose phones in a non-musical context (an online class) and they performed great – although I wish the cable were a couple of feet longer for plugging into a desktop computer rather than a portable phone or player.

While sound is job one a very close second is comfort and the Bose phones really shine here for me. For some reason a lot of ‘deep ear’ phones are flat out uncomfortable for me to wear - with or without the surrounding hook. If you wear these things in public whether at work or while commuting you goingto have to take them out occasionally and doing that comfortably makes a real difference.

As someone famously described talking about music, talking about sound is like dancing about architecture so I can only repeat my earlier suggestion: gather together a bunch of phones, choose some music you enjoy listening to and know well, and go round-robin. You’ll learn things I promise - and you just may decide to hang onto multiple pairs of phones for different kinds of listening.

If you understand how Ikea products are make and how they’re used, you will “get” this TV stand. The number one reason Ikea products exist is functionality, followed by design. They are rarely what would be called “fine furniture” … they are made to serve a practical purpose and be sold at a reasonable price. Like most Ikea furniture this is made of recycled wood fibers with a hard, semi-gloss painted coating. It is available in white or black.

This product is intended to be used with a small, lightweight LED TV. Unfortunately the product description isn’t as clear as it could be in that regard but from my first-hand experience I would say it is intended for TV’s that are 40” or smaller. It is a lowboy stand that works best for people who prefer their TV to have a low profile, so in other words it is not your best choice for watching TV in bed or laying back in a reclining chair.

Like virtually every Ikea product, this is RTA (ready to assemble) furniture. It ships knocked down and comes with a pictures-only assembly manual. If you have experience assembling Ikea furniture you will probably consider this one of the simplest thing you’re assembled … 10 minutes maximum. Tools required are a Phillips screwdriver and a hammer. There are only 3 major parts … the top, the middle shelf, and four legs. You hand-screw each of the four legs into the top with double-ended screws that are included. Then you attach the shelf using 90° angle brackets. That’s it.

But, as is so often true with Ikea furniture, the pictorial diagrams are very vague, so here are a few helpful hints:

1. The illustrations show you screwing the double-ended studs in with your fingers. DON’T. You will end up with sore, bloody fingers if you do. To attach the top, insert the screw and twist slightly until it just stays in place without falling out. Then match the other end with the predrilled hole in the leg and with BOTH hands screw the two pieces together. When you meet resistance, only continue tightening until the leg is squarely aligned with the top … do NOT force it any further.

2. The middle shelf is very non-Ikea-like in that the holes in the legs are not predrilled. Instead they include a little plastic template that you must use to punch screw holes at the appropriate height. The following is very important: following the pictorial drawings align where the hole should be punched and tap one of the longer screws GENTLY with a hammer, just enough to make a small indentation where the screw should go. Do NOT hit the screw so hard that it completely punctures the leg or you won’t be able to screw it down tightly.

3. While Ikea’s instructions only show the middle shelf being able to be installed at the fixed location that they’ve determined, you can actually attach the shelf slightly higher or lower. If you look at my attached photos you will see that I bought two of these stands … one is used to held DVD’s and the other is used in another room to hold a speaker. The location that Ikea wants you to mount the shelf is not tall enough for anything except the old CD jewel cases. So here’s what you do. Measure where you want the shelf and hold one of the angle brackets under it. Mark where the hole should be with a pencil. Then align the plastic guide with that hole and make another pencil mark on the guide at the bottom of the leg. Then use the guide to punch the holes, aligning the pencil mark you made on it with the bottom of each leg.

4. The instructions are also unclear about how to screw the middle shelf in. They show inverting the table upside-down and mounting the shelf. That is very difficult to do because you have to hold the shelf with one hand, align the brackets with your other hand and screw the screw in with your third hand. So here’s the trick I discovered … after you punch the holes lay the table on its LONG end. When you insert the middle shelf it will be supported by the two legs on the bottom and gravity will assure the shelf is mounted to the leg with no gaps (see photo).

5. The stand is capable of supporting most 40” or smaller TV’s, however the middle shelf is NOT capable of holding much weight. The DVD cases as shown in my photo or a lightweight speaker is about all you should put on that shelf.

Finally, Ikea does not give you an option about screwing the entire stand to the wall behind it. Their lawyers want to make that very clear to you. I suggest you follow their instructions if you will be using this as a TV stand. My photos show that neither of my two stands are being used as a TV stand and I chose not to use the wall bracket for that reason.

Bottom line: This is an attractive stand to look at and is functional. It is not fine furniture and is not very big or substantial. Read the measurements, as the actual stand may be much smaller than you expect. But for what it is, I am 100% satisfied with both of them for the way I am using them. Pro's, this works as advertised - you can actually locate something that you have misplaced.  It includes 6 receivers:  Three (3) that work as a key chain (or attach to a key chain with the split ring included), and three (3) that can be attached to an item with sticky backed tape that is included.  The item also comes with additional replacement batteries so unless you are constantly losing and finding your 'lost' items you are probably good to go for a year or more.  Now, this is what I've observed through normal use and testing.  The receivers are small, and thus, do not produce a 'super' loud alarm. I would compare it to a small kitchen timer in terms of sound. I find the sound level adequate to locating my items, even if stuffed under a couch cushion.  Remember that it is possible you misplaced those keys 'far away' and it might be well advised to walk a larger area if you are not having any luck locating your item.  I've seen people's car keys on top of the community mail boxes.  I wish that this product included a way to label the colors for what you attached the receiver to.  A simple attached key ring that would allow the user to write notes on which colors go to which items would be helpful.  This sounds 'lazy' in a way, but when you attach these, you will quickly forget which color is on which set of keys or other item, especially if you are not looking for the item regularly.  As far as I can tell, there is no way to trigger all receivers at once, so you must press the corresponding color code to the key receiver you are looking for.  As an example, which color did I attach to my post box key that I never misplaced until today!  Clearly you can find a way to keep a list of colors, it would just be nice if the item included a way to label the buttons.  So overall, if you 'think' you have a need for something like this, and you are not really hard of hearing and understand you may still need to walk through the area where the item is misplaced, this will work and remove a lengthy search and probably help you keep your hair a little longer.  On a personal note, this saved me when it turned out I had picked up trash in my car and thrown it in the trash cart along with my car keys.  I probably would not have looked inside the trash container (who could be so stupid as to throw their keys in the trash), but I heard it beeping from the trash cart while I was pressing the button and looking around inside my car.

If you are already happy with the apparent volume and sound quality of your current listening experience, a headphone amp (with built-in DAC) such as the PHA-3 is not likely to benefit you. The basic reason for purchasing a headphone amplifier is that most portable devices have trouble driving expensive headphones. There are two effects: the volume is too low, and the sound quality suffers. For most listeners, the soundstage isn't as clear and the music seems "dull." When a headphone amplifier is used, the headphones seem to "wake up" and volume is normal.

However, if you have high quality headphones or in-ear-monitors and value portability (convenient use on travel, or at home around the house), then you should strongly consider the PHA3. There are many fine headphone amplifiers with an integrated DAC, but the PHA-3 is surely one of the best and likely unmatched in flexibility and user features.

I am extremely happy with the PHA-3 and highly recommend it for single ended use with the Etymotic ER-4S In-Ear-Monitor (IEM) and I especially recommend pairing it in the balanced mode with the Sennheiser HD-800 headphones - which sound absolutely fantastic on this amp in this configuration. I still use the ER-4S IEM for exercise, airplane flights, and business travel, but I mostly live with the HD-800's connected in balanced mode with the PHA-3 when I'm relaxing to music or writing.

PHA-3 Critical Feature Summary:
1) Single ended output for regular devices (100mW per channel into 32 Ohms) and balanced (differential) output (320 mW/per channel into 32 Ohms) for specially cabled headphones. I found that for 100 Ohm devices the single ended power sounds wonderful and has plenty of volume.

For the HD-800 (300-600 Ohms), single ended power sounded very good and volume was fine for my tastes, but after listening to the higher power balanced output, I strongly prefer it, even if I do not listen at anywhere near maximum volume which I would find painful.

Balanced output provides a theoretical 4x (6dB) - Sony shows a 3.2x or 5 dB - increase in the power per channel versus single ended and provides more than enough volume and slew rate performance for high impedance (300-600 Ohm) headphones like the HD800. The HD-800 sound absolutely fantastic when driven in this configuration. This critical feature takes quite a bit of explanation. The key point is that you need the right cable to access this feature. More detail on balanced operation is provided at the end of this review.

2) Internal battery - sufficient but you will often operate with the device plugged in and charging while you are listening
-- this is direct experience. At the power levels I use while listening, the unit does in fact charge while I am listening.
-- note: in balanced mode, (which I recommend), the power available is 4x the power from single ended mode, so sizing an internal battery for extended playback is difficult, no matter how "efficient" the amplifier is... Given that limitation, Sony's compromise between battery size and convenience seems perfect to me. (Note: balanced mode doubles the voltage going to the headphones. Doubling voltage, yields a 4x power increase at "high volumes" over single-ended mode, or in this case battery consumption, because power scales with the square of the voltage).

3) small size (about twice as thick as a smart phone and similar in length and width) in a very convenient and attractive form factor. The design of the unit provides audio cord connection protection because the cord jacks are "recessed" behind the volume knob and a projecting metal flange. Supplied silicone bands are perfect for attaching phone devices or mp3 players.

4) accepts digital inputs from all Apple devices, Windows, Android, Linux, etc.
-- Sony licensed from Apple the iOS direct digital interface, so the PHA-3 supports any combination of digital inputs from all Apple iOS devices and the older iPods. I frequently use the PHA-3 with a 160GB iPod Classic when I'm outside.
-- Sony uses a standard micro-USB connector for all Android phones, tablets, Windows, Linux, MacOS, laptops, desktops, and music servers.

5) very high standard of digital data format flexibility and analog sound reproduction ... read detailed reviews online if these items are a critical factor in selecting the PHA-3 over other competitors. The sound quality and dynamic range (no-hiss) is stunningly beautiful on the HD-800 and the PHA-3 easily accepts all the most common music data formats. In my case I use Apple products (MacBook Pro Retina, iPod, iPhone, Apple TV Music Server) to manage my music files and all of the various file formats, encoding bit rates, and sample rates in my collection have worked perfectly for me. If you are a DSD or FLAC music format enthusiast, Sony provides a music player that runs on your laptop for DSD files, and there are many laptop players for FLAC. Also, although it takes extra disk space, you can use a lossless converter to store a FLAC file into an iTunes/Apple format.

6) Sony has a feature called DSEE HX to improve the sound quality of many digital formats... other reviewers have found this helpful but I find it hard to discern the benefit, so this is not a critical feature to me.

7) Cables: The PHA-3 needs at least two micro USB plug to USB Type A cables (one is provided): one for charging while listening, and the other for connecting to your laptop for digital output. I found that a 6 inch 30 pin Apple iPod to USB Type A "synch" cable (not just charging cable) was perfect to connect an iPod Classic. Over time, I purchased another 2 micro USB to USB Type A cables to leave around some fixed charging locations. 4 foot flat cables pack nicely into a carry bag.

Additional Notes:
AN1) headphone impedance:
The higher the impedance of a headphone, the harder it is to drive (it takes more voltage to send the same amount of current). Typical earbuds are about 16 Ohms, high quality in-ear-monitors are often 30 to 100 Ohms, and many high quality headphones are 100 to 600 Ohms. There are interesting engineering reasons for this, but basically it is easier to make a better motor with a higher impedance. There is a very nice discussion of this on http://nwavguy.blogspot.com/2011/02/headphone-impedance-explained.html

AN2) Drive strength and Pairing:
The PHA-3 was designed to pair with the Sony MDR-Z7 headphones. Those headphones are 70 Ohms at 1 KHz (mid range). The PHA-3 pairs extremely well with the Etymotic ER-4S (100 Ohm) and also pairs extremely well with the Sennheiser HD-800 (300-600 Ohms) using a balanced cable. It also pairs acceptably well with the HD-800 (lower maximum volume) using single-ended operation, but most audiophiles will want to purchase or make a balanced cable. It is always hard to know, but to my ears, the balanced cable and differential drive of the PHA-3 make the Sennheiser HD-800 really sing. I purchased my balanced cable from customcans.co.uk. I normally listen to the PHA-3 from a MacBook Pro or an iPod Classic so customcans "default" 1.5 meter size was perfect for me.

AN3) More discussion on balanced outputs and balanced cables for the PHA-3
A balanced cable using the Sennheiser connectors and the 3.5mm TRS jacks the PHA-3 requires is easy to make or purchase. I bought a very high quality one from customcans.co.uk. They will also make a balanced cable for any headphone to your specifications. It takes about 1 week for them to ship your order. Note: although I personally do not use a Pono player, the Pono player also uses two 3.5mm TRS jacks for balanced (or differential) output, so any cable that will connect your headphones to a Pono player will also connect to the PHA-3.

Balanced output is an incredibly nice feature for this price range and yet Sony has also managed to make this conveniently portable. If you are using the Sony MDR-Z7 headphones, Sony provides the appropriate cable with their headphones and there is nothing else to do. If you want to pair the PHA-3 with the Sennheiser HD-800's or another high quality headphone it will take only a little extra effort, but it is well worth it. This feature really influenced me when I made the decision to purchase the PHA-3.

All high quality headphones can be cabled for balanced (or differential) output, however the reason it takes a little extra effort - or an additional cable purchase - is because balanced drive is not a headphone industry standard and companies offer various solutions. For example, Sony (and apparently Pono) chose standard 3.5mm jack cables to keep their product small over the large XLR cables in common use in microphones, audio mixing equipment, and some keyboards (my old Roland RD700 has XLR). A good discussion of balanced cabling and some of the advantages is located at http://www.headphone.com/pages/balanced-headphones-guide. If your headphones use connectors on each driver (like the Sennheiser HD800, HD600, HD650, all Audeze, and HiFiMAN planar-magnetic headphones) it is very simple to make or have made a balanced cable (see the end of this review for basic advice).

AN4) Why is balanced operation important?
To achieve the same sound quality, a differential amplifier system is substantially easier and less costly for a manufacturer to design and package into a tiny, 5 volt or less (4.7V Lithium-ion) USB style battery subsystem, than one single amplifier. The net result is that the PHA-3 has 4 amplifiers ( 2 for each channel), each running on 5 volts or less, instead of 2 "bigger" amplifiers running at 10 volts or less.

In balanced mode, the signals swing differentially, effectively doubling the voltage delivered to the headphone. Hence, from the same USB style battery subsystem, the power available to drive the headphones is nominally 4x (6dB) the power from single ended mode. This results in more than sufficient volume and slew rate for high impedance headphones like the HD-800. In differential mode, two amplifiers are used instead of one to "split the effort" to drive each of the headphone channels (left or right). The positive and negative leads from each (left or right channel) headphone driver coil are independently driven by a separate amplifier. Using two amplifiers per channel doubles the amount of voltage that can be delivered to the headphone driver using the same battery power system. Doubling voltage, yields a 4x power increase because power scales with the square of the voltage.

AN5) Note on modifying your own headphones:
If your headphones are hard wired, you can modify the cable directly and solder it to your own connectors (like 3.5mm sockets) to make it simple to build a replacement cables for single ended or balanced use. In a 3.5mm TRS jack, the Tip is the "+" terminal, the Ring is the "-" terminal, and the Sleeve is connected to the electrical shield (often a "braid") around the two wires inside the cable. Headset coils or transducers are symmetric devices, so labeling one side "+" and the other "-" is only important to keep the phases correct. If you make your own cable or connector, it's easy to use an ohm-meter to find out which wire is "+" and which wire is "-." If the wires are color coded, it's very simple. If not, then as you cut each wire, carefully label each end (4 labels) with a piece of tape. Now use the ohm meter to find which wires are connected to the Sleeve of the TRS jack (probably 1/4 inch) on the cable you just cut. These wires are the "-" leads and need to be ultimately connected to a 3.5mm "Ring" when you are done with your cable. The other wires are the "+" wires and will ultimately connect to the "Tip" of the 3.5mm jack.r balanced (or differential) output, so any cable that will connect your headphones to a Pono player will also connect to the PHA-3.

NOT RELATED TO THE PRODUCT BUT READ ON IF YOU NEED HELP WITH BAD COLORS/ BRIGHTNESS ON HDTVs CONNECTED TO A PC VIA HDMI-
OK, so just trying to help some folks who might be having the same problem as I did.
I connected a 32inch 1080p HDTV as a computer monitor via HDMI to my PC. The colors and brightness looked weird and washed off especially on desktop and while playing games etc. Movies seemed to be unaffected, in my opinion. To fix this you either Plug in a good old DVI cable from the PC to TV (if your TV supports it) , or buy this cable (DVI to HDMI, DVI end in PC and HDMI to the TV)- however, some people (like myself) will still have the problem despite his cable. To circumvent this, use a small software program "CRU" (Custom resolution utility", which is free ...install it, and run CRU.exe from the folder. It is pretty simple, just select the desired refresh rate, resolution etc of the HDTV (highest supported e.g. 1920 x 1080 @ 60hz)...after that what worked for me is that if you have an AMD/ ATI Radeon card use "no extension block" , hit OK to save it. Your are NOT done yet. Now run "restart.exe." or "restart64.exe" (depending on your windows version 32 vs 64bit). these files will also be in the same folder as CRU installation. Running them will restart the video drivers and force the PC to think it is connected to a PC MONITOR in DVI mode rather than a HDTV, since the color profiles (RGB/ YCbCr444 etc) are changed based on the detected display; causing the color/ brightness anomaly. You have to do this just once and not every time you restart your PC. However I have noticed at times waking up from sleep mode, I have run it again, as the PC again goes to the weired color/ hdmi mode.

ALERT- just remember if you do use CRU to fix the colors/ brightness you are basically tricking the drivers to think it is a pure DVI connection to PC/ TV and you will loose the ability to stream audio on this cable. Since I use headphones, I didn't miss it, but if needed just reset the CRU (run reset-all.exe) and restart the pc to get audio back for movies, directly from the hdtv speakers.

The original house wiring (built in 1994) used three splitters, and my cable modem was hanging on to life by a thread, and would frequently lose sync. The phone adapter (my landline runs through the cable company, but connects to coax for its signal) wouldn't work at all. TVs were pixelating at random.

My downstream signal strength on the cable modem, at its worst, would often be -9dBmV or lower. -5dBmV is typically the lowest you can go and keep a solid connection. Upstream would be around +60dBmV, while you want low 50s at the highest. I now see upstream power around +45dBmV, which is exactly where you want it, and downstream power around +2dBmV (you want it as close to 0 as possible). The modem hasn't lost sync once since I got the amp.

Thankfully, there's an outlet in the attic right by where the original splitters were, so I was able to use a spare cable for power and place it where all of the original house cabling could reach it. Just make sure to use terminators on unused ports.

As the title suggests, this energy monitor works similarly to the "Kill-A-Watt" type of energy monitors. For those unfamiliar with energy monitors, the idea is fairly simple: you plug the monitor into a wall outlet and then plug whatever device you want to track into the monitor. Depending on the sophistication, you can track all sorts of metrics. And while the Kill-A-Watt offer far more monitoring options, Belkin's "Conserve Insight" gives the user convenience. Specifically, the readout of energy usage is not part of the wall plug assembly, so you don't have to get under your desk with a flashlight to see your usage.

Belkin keeps things fairly simple with the information it provides. You get either instantaneous or average (monthly or yearly) readouts of carbon footprint (you can set the conversion factor), cost (you have to enter the cost manually), or raw energy usage in kWh. Because the readout is attached with a fairly long cord, you're able to set it up somewhere that it's easier to read (e.g. your outlet is below a desk or behind furniture). That's it! Basically, plug it in, choose the readout you want, decide on instant or average and then let it do its business.

The device itself is well built. Though the wall plug is a bit large, in my experience, it did not obscure the second plug.

All told, I'm glad to have an easier-to-read alternative to my Kill-A-Watt (though I still love all the information my KAW can give me).

First of all, the SurgePlus is a lot bigger than I expected - for some reason the unit looks nice and compact whenever I saw a photo of it, but when it arrived i was slightly surprised at the larger size. I do however like a lot of the features - starting with the 360 degree rotating plug. There's a small lock button you push to free up the prongs so that you can rotate them in 90-degree increments, then once you have the right position you want the push button locks the prongs in place. This is super helpful when plugging in the SurgePlus in either the top or bottom wall socket because it allows you access to all of its ports. The lock button is nice in that if you have the unit set to 90-degrees horizontal, it will stay that way and not interfere with the other wall outlet. The three AC power outlets are grounded, so you don't have to worry about not having the ground pin available when you plug in a device. Back to the size - sure, i said it was bigger than I expected, but the upside to this is that inside the unit there's a built-in surge protection circuit to help protect your gear. Belkin also attaches a $75,000 "Connected Equipment Warranty" just in case something bad happens, and the unit itself comes with a limited lifetime warranty as well.

There are a couple little things that I wasn't so happy about feature-wise, but I didn't mind mainly because of how I personally was going to use it. For one, the two USB ports can do 5-volts at each port, but only 2.1-amps total. Some devices need at least 2.1-amps to charge as intended, so if you use both USB ports at the same time and your two devices need more than 2.1-amps total, they will still charge - but at a much slower rate. To some people this might be a problem, but for me I intended to use it as an overnight charger, so charge time wasn't an issue. The second thing is that it's only rated for 125V. I found this odd since it's called a "travel charger" and all of the travel charges I've seen are autovolt 110/220v, but then again I rarely travel outside the US so this doesn't affect my travels much.

All in all it's a nice unit for me to take along on road trips, since I no longer need to try to find outlets in different areas of a hotel room to charge/power my gear. I don't even have to bring the individual devices USB chargers anymore thanks to the two built-in USB ports. The Soundpeats M20 are a great set of cheap in-ear buds, with sound quality far exceeding their price. The

The M20s are packaged in a clear plastic box, reasonable but not great in appearance or quality -- mine arrived somewhat banged-up and dented. Inside, you'll find the earphones along with a baggie of extra tips in various sizes. I found the initial fit good enough that I didn't need to experiment too much with the others, though they're nice to have. The earphones themselves are well-made, light enough to stay in the ear without much fuss. The cable is flat and soft-feeling; the one major problem with it -- and the set as a whole -- is the amount of noise it transmits. Handling the cable or brushing against it at all results in quite a bit of in-ear noise.

The sound, though, is impressive for earphones this inexpensive, rivalling sets that cost two or three times as much. I found it satisfyingly bassy and also sharp at the top end, with perhaps a bit of a hole in the lower midrange, though not too bothersome or steep. Everything from vocal and guitar-heavy music to jazz ensembles to hip-hop sounds well defined and surprisingly clear, considering the price.

The M20s' sound is really impressive for earphones this inexpensive, and I'd recommend them for any use except exercise, given the slight problem of cord-handling noise.

Due to shipping issues that I will not go into, I ended up buying my APC units in person at a retail supply store.

I have some important feedback regarding these units for anyone considering purchasing one.

I bought a new desktop computer with a PSU that requires pure sine wave input and all of my existing APC units (CS, BK, etc.) output an approximated step wave when running on battery. The SMC series is the cheapest APC product line that I could actually find in stock anywhere that outputs pure sine wave when running on battery. (Note: there are other manufacturers that make backups that output pure sine wave when on battery and these units are cheaper than APC ones but I did not test any of them.) I notified a dealer that's about a 2 hour drive for me to let me know when they received new units. That way, I could come and test it out in the store. I did this because I had read a lot of negative feedback about both the SMC and SMT series of backups.

The two SMC units I tried (SMC1000 and SMC1500) were very loud compared to all of my other old units. All other APC backups that I've purchased in stores (probably 20+ units over the years) are virtually 100% silent when operating normally (fan does not run at all and there is NO noise) and when on battery, you hear only a little bit of noise from the fan. You have to literally put your ear 1 inch away from these units to hear anything when they're running on AC. However, for the SMC units, the fan runs constantly and you can hear the units across the room. More importantly, the SMC units emit some kind of constant hum or whine. It is very annoying and I could not stand it. It also drove my dog crazy. I brought the SMC1500 home for a few days and the whine was very noticeable at the base of my stairs, with the unit installed upstairs between the wall and a cabinet. When the battery kicks on, the fan really speeds up and the whine also gets a louder. This whine noise is emitted as soon as you power the unit on--not a single device plugged into it, so it has nothing to do with what's plugged into the unit. Due to this annoying whine, I took the unit back.

In several places, I read that the pricier SMT series were quieter so I decided to try one of those--SMT1500. The constant whine/buzz is still present but it is not as loud as on the SMC units I examined. Also, the fan ran much slower when not on battery. I decided that this was acceptable so I purchased and APC 9630 network management card for it (more on that in a moment). This SMT was manufactured in May 2015. When I decided to pick up a second SMT1500, I was disappointed because its fan was much louder when operating on AC power. This unit was manufactured in March of 2015 so I wondered if it was a hardware change. The fan was so much louder that I took the unit back. Later I purchased another SMT1500 and this one was manufactured in July of 2015 and it exhibited behavior like my first (the May 2015) one. So right out of the box, new from the manufacturer, some of these units exhibit different hardware characteristics. I should mention that on all three of the SMT1500 units, the factory firmware version was the same--9.2 ID 18.

So then I ordred another 9630 card for this second unit. Meanwhile, I installed a 9630 in my first SMT1500 unit. It is very straight forward and I did not have any problems. If you search on YouTube, APC has a video with a step by step guide on installing and configuring the network card. I will provide my details below, for reference:
-Power down unit and disconnect battery
-Remove rear Smart card cover
-Insert card and tighten screws
-Connect battery and plug in unit (no need to power on)
-Connect one end of the serial cable supplied with the card to the Console port on the card and connect the other to your computer. The other end is a standard DB9 serial connector and I did not have any puters old enough to have a serial port so I used a serial to USB adapter.
-The APC instructional video that I mentioned uses the old HyperTerminal application (that got removed in Win7) to configure the card. To get HyperTerminal on my Win8 machine, I copied the Hyper* files from the I386 folder on an old WinXP CD that I had lying around. Those files end with .XY_ and all you have to do is use the EXPAND command to uncompress them. Then just run the .exe. This gets you HyperTerminal. The video explains step by step how to do the rest.

Next, I hit the IP I specified for the unit in my browser and I was able to login to the web interface with no problems. I had downloaded the 9.3 ID 18 ENC firmware file from APC's site. I selected the Update firmware option, uploaded the file, and let the process run. About 8 minutes later, it finished and the firmware update was successful--VERY EASY.

So later when my second network card arrived, I repeated the install process in my other SMT1500--that went fine. But when I hit the web interface and tried to upgrade the firmware using the same file I had used for my other unit, it failed--it said something like XMODEM disconnected. This left my unit running but not turned on and the fan was running at full speed. I could toggle through the menu options but the power button did not respond. I had to pull the power cord and disconnect the battery and turn it back on. I tried two more times, thinking it was just a fluke, but I got the same results. Then I started asking myself what was different about this time compared to the first? Then I remembered that I had used Chrome the first time and this time, kind of by accident, I had used IE 11. So I opened Chrome, logged into the web UI, uploaded the file, and let it go. It finished successfully, without any problems. So keep this in mind--the upgrade process can be quirky. However, I was very happy to see that upgrading the firmware did not affect the idle fan speed because I was hoping that it wouldn't cause the fan to run faster. My fans barely turn when the unit is on AC power--if you put your hand beside the fan vents, you can feel a very, very small amount of air flow coming out.

So overall, I would like to stress that if you have always been used to store-bought APC backups, like the CS, BK, ES, etc., models, and you think that you will just plop one of these SMC or SMT models in the floor beside your desk or wherever and everything will be same, THING AGAIN. This was a real wake up call for me. I had always taken for granted the fact that APC battery backups are totally silent except for when running on battery. Keep in mind that the SMC and SMT units will emit a hum/whine and the fan will run constantly (the speed, it seems, will vary depending on the hardware configuration). And I'm not just being picky. I promise you that you will notice this hum/whine/squeal noise even when standing across the room away from the unit. I guess that consumers must rarely purchase either one of these product lines because otherwise, I can't imagine APC not doing something about the annoying whine noise. But when these things are sitting in server rooms in the mix of a lot of other noisy fans and equipment, you would never hear them.

I highly recommend getting a 9630 card. It is very nice being able to sit down at your computer and login to the web interface for the backup because you can see and managed all of the settings without having to fiddle around with the buttons and menu system on the front of the unit. You can also configure settings via the web interface that you cannot get access to via the control panel on the front of the unit.ers old enough to have a serial port so I used a serial to USB adapter.

The Bose SoundSport are the most comfortable earbuds I have worn yet. As an overall package, the Bose headphones deliver.

The standout feature of the SoundSport is the in ear comfort. The silicone inserts distribute the weight and friction over a larger part of your ear and do not rely solely on insertion into the ear canal to hold the earbuds in place. I found it easy to wear these for 3-4 hours a time.

The construction of the Bose is largely plastic. After a month of use, they have held up well. The overall design seems focused on minimizing weight which makes them light and comfortable to wear. This choice also means they lack robustness. I would not want to keep these in my pocket the way I do cheaper buds. As shown in other reviews, the 3.5mm headjack appears prone to breaking. I would use the supplied carrying pouch at all times.

Performance wise, I had no issues using these buds w/ my Nexus 5. The inline controls and mic worked flawlessly. The sound is clear and detailed with a focus on treble and mid range and a de-emphasis on base. The lack of bass may bother some users since many products on the market focus heavily on base reproduction. I find the de-tuned base refreshing and makes the buds easier to wear for longer periods of time w/o fatiguing my ears.

The SoundSport are expensive but not excessively so in a crowded market. For once, Bose has a nice product at a reasonable price when compared to Beat's product line. I gave the Bose SoundSport four stars instead of five as I am not sure if they will hold up over time, especially to sweat. Overall, I am super pleased w/ the Bose SoundSport and they are best pair of earbuds I have used in recent memory.
