The BS3 is more than loud enough for any room in my house. The sound is not as tight and crisp as I prefer,  but at only 5 watts per each speaker (10w total) ,  this is understandable.  I don't notice a difference in sound with the 3D on or off, but I need to test it by remaining stationary while someone else changes the setting before  I can honestly review this feature. I compared this Bluedio speaker with my neighbor's UE Mini Boom ($99),  with both speakers sitting on the picnic table in the back yard.  The BS3 was louder overall than the UE mini,  but the UE Mini seemed to have a little more punch and bass.  This is likely due to being outside,  and the fact that the BS3 has passive bass porting in the rear of the housing,  which directs the bass out and away into empty space.  Inside, with the speaker sitting on my wood stove in the corner of my great room,  I was impressed with the sound output. I actually mumbled "Wow" to myself. While there is no comparing this small portable speaker to my home stereo or my cars Bose system,  it does impress for the price,  and suits it's intended purpose as a small portable speaker.  I found that the fidelity of this speaker can be much improved and very impressive at mid volume by using an equalizer. I imagine this may be because that the more expensive speakers from high end manufacturers such as Bose have more advanced audio amplifiers and circuitry inside. Talk radio sounds great on it. I give it 5 stars for it's price category,  but for  a portable bluetooth speaker only 4 stars,  as there are many 5 star (but much more expensive ) speakers available.  Keep an eye out for sale prices.  I've only had it a week,  so I can't speak to its long term durability or quality.  FYI,  on my unit,  the stenciled BLUEDIO emblem on the front is barely visible. I should stencil BOSE right over it just for the fun of it. For those looking for great stationary indoor bluetooth speakers for your home,  consider buying a $10 usbpowered bluetooth stereo receiver dongle and connect it to your home stereo's long unused cassette or phono input.  Or maybe even dig out those 90's amplified computer stereo speakers you have stashed away in a closet and hook them up to a dongle for the kids to use in their room. Bluetooth technology remains “all the rage” in the consumer marketplace, and kudos to the folks at ZealSound for supplying consumers with yet another cost-effective alternative in the shape of their Magic Cube Portable Wireless Speaker. It comes in a tight little black box perfectly shaped to hold the ‘magic’ trapped inside; and the collection comes with both the required USB power cable and an old-style RCA cable for the cube’s aux input.

Naturally, what really matters when considering an effective wireless speaker remains the user interface and the sound quality. ZealSound’s interface is great, both with flashing light promts and voice queues from the speaker itself, giving the user the assurance that he (or she) are using it properly when setting it all up. The Bluetooth functionality is solid, as I had absolutely zero issues connecting this little thing with my iPhone right away. If there’s any real drawback to this fancy little gadget, then it would probably be the quality of the tunes coming out of the speaker: it’s definitely what I’d rate “above average,” but it properly comes in a bit lower the louder it plays. (I’ve seen this phenomenon with some of the wireless models I’ve tinkered with over the years, but I honestly expected a bit better from this one only due to its new birth in the market.) Crank this up about halfway, and it’s still performing admirably; when you get it louder than that, the speaker suddenly sounds a bit tinnier than it did just a click before, and that’s definitely noticeable.

As for the telephone interface, the Magic Cube is good. I noticed absolutely no echo (a drawback common to some of the cheaper marketplace knockoffs in the Bluetooth category), and the receiver of my call also noticed so significant issues. That’s good – especially if you’re going to make some frequent use of this for that purpose – but I honestly don’t use any of my speakers for such connectivity.

Still, because it works as advertised, I’m inclined to give this one five stars. There’s arguably a great audience for this product, and so long as you know its limitations and respect them you’ll likely not be disappointed with the purchase.

Recommended. So far as Bluetooth speakers go, this one from ZealSound is pretty nice. Basically, I’d recommended it for desktop-style usage and listening; the quality gets a bit tinny the louder one goes with it, but it still surprises as it puts out a fairly respectable volume all of its own accord. Phone functions are good, probably at least on par with anything else comparable I’ve tried in the marketplace these days. Kudos to ZealSound for “keeping the faith” and provided a traditional RCA-style plug-and-play cable for those of us who still like old-school connectivity (believe it or not, I still have two functioning MP3 players with no wireless capability which I love).

It looks super cool - just like a big dynamic microphone. It is incredibly well made and heavy. The aluminum body is rugged and feels fantastic. Yeah, this thing is way awesome looking. If only it sounded as awesome as it looks. The sound isn't bad, it is just closed and the bass is restricted. iGadgitz has a similar design speaker, the Volcano, that rocks big time - huge nice bass. So I was a little disappointed with this speaker.

Now cool looks are really good. This is worth the low price just for the cool looks. The grills are wire mesh and will take a huge beating. And the speaker sounds pretty good at medium to low volume. It is when you pump up the sound or the bass, things get a little strained.

There is another thing I'm not a huge fan of - the controls. On the Volcano, they did something remarkable - made the controls part of the speaker body - twist to change volume, press down to stop play, or press down long to power off. That's intuitive and awesome. iGadgitz used the same old nasty buttons so many other companies use. There are three buttons - center is power, play, pause, answer phone. The right and left buttons are volume up / down; and track change. I hate the track change function with these speakers. The track changes if you short press the button. To change volume you long press the button. I frequently want to change the volume a little bit, so I short press, and end up with a new song.

There is a difference with other companies and these buttons - iGadgitz used really good buttons - they are firm and feel good. They're just too multifunctional for my taste.

I have a feeling the Volcano and Mic Idol both use exactly the same electronics, speaker, and speaker placement inside. The difference here is the metal speaker grill - I think that is dampening some of the sound.

I live in Decatur IL. and I've been playing around with TV antennas for a few years. I used to build the coat hanger style 2/4 wood antennas from you tube videos that actually pulled in some stations, I ordered a powerful lava antenna from antenna deals that would not pull any stations in at all looked impressive but it was junk. If you play around with these antennas enough you will find some sweet spots for good reception. Now to the Mohu Leaf 50 indoor antenna, it is amplified and it does actually works pretty well my recommendation would be to power the amplifier to the wall. Thats because i found that the wall outlet works better than the usb on my tv. Now checking reception for channels on my tv i first used supplied velcro supplies to mount the antenna to either of my windows in my bedroom reception was poor. i have a tree outside of my north window so i layed the antenna down on a wooden stool just in front of the window approx. 3ft off the floor then i pulled in 19 digital stations 2 of them that were 60 miles + from my house fox bloomington and others now i have my antenna mounted to a coat hanger using small plastic zip ties to hang it on my curtain rod on my west window because i get all of my stations on that side with the best signals. The antenna has 2 small pin size holes in it for mounting it on a wall but i choose to use zip ties and a coat hanger to move from place to place to receive different and extra channels that a roof top antenna would normally get. Let me say ladies and gentlemen normally the best option for over the air tv would be a roof top antenna but this indoor antenna really good for indoors if you don't want to deal with grounding a antenna outside running cable lines and all the stuff this is the right antenna for you. But this isn't so bad, since the labels have nothing to do with what the buttons do. * To move up or down through menus, you click left or right. * To play or pause music, you push down (play) * To back up to the previous menu, you push down (play), unless you're at a music track, when you push up (menu) * To select a menu item, you push up (menu) * To adjust volume you first push center (select), then press left or right  UPDATE: I've discovered further drawbacks, and docked a star: * Most of the display is taken up with an EQ animation, leaving little room for track, album, and artist information. I'm listening to an audiobook, "The Queen of the Tearling," which displays as "The Queen of the." * Fast-forward and Rewind are at a fixed, rather slow rate. It takes a long time to advance 5 minutes, and if you have a one hour audio file, and you need to find your place 45 minutes in, you would probably have to hold "Fast" Forward for about nine minutes. Well, to start off, let me say this headphone was designed to work with apple products. What this actually translates to is that you won't be able to use the volume buttons for the headphone while using android or windows. For me personally, this wasn't a deal breaker. However, there is an option to buy a cable from Sol Republic that allows for the use of the mic button if you want that feature, but I don't really need that either. What made me interested in this was that fact that it was under $100 (on sale for ~$60 at my time of purchase) and the unique design of the product. I've never gotten used to ear-plugs since they keep falling out of my ear when I used them, so I gave these on-ear headphones a try and they are surprisingly good for the price. Now there are some people who say these are uncomfortable to wear with glasses for a long period of time, and I slightly agree with this, as I wear glasses and use them for 4+hrs sometimes, but if you adjust the position of the cups (you can slide them higher or lower on the band since they are removable), you can make it comfortable enough that it won't hurt your ears with the pressure it has. Speaking of the pressure, it is able to isolate a fair amount of surrounding noise from the outside. It's not the most noise cancelling headphone ever, but it does a good enough job for my needs. The sound doesn't leak out either unless you put the noise really high up (I use it with 50% or lower on windows laptop). Something did bother me though, and that was the initial sound quality not being clear out of the box and sounded muffled. I went into the Windows audio settings and enabled the equalizer, set it to the Shooter option, and viola it now sounded amazing, at least for my own taste. If you want you can leave the headphone with the default sound quality with everything flat on the equalizer, or even customize it to whatever you prefer, but I honestly have to say after that preset change I made it sounds so much better. This is a good buy for a budget headphone under $100 and I would recommend it to someone with Android/windows (I have both of those lol) even though it was made more for apple users. This is a review of the Sony SRSX77 portable speaker. I received it at no cost as an evaluation unit for review. These are my honest comments written from the POV I take when I've paid for an item.

This is a pretty substantial item, comparable in size and weight to a house brick. There are smaller and lighter competitors out there (see photo showing it next to a Bose Soundlink Mini). It belts out the tunes with plenty of volume for a bedroom, study or office and yes, it's portable, but its size and weight really suggest a mostly stationary role. I'm hearing punchy bass, nice mids and sparkly highs. Heavy bass will rattle stuff on the table with the speaker. You don't feel it like you would with a subwoofer but you can clearly hear low frequency notes, not just a bit of percussive noise that wants to be that low note if you know what I mean.

Sony offers a free app called Song Pal that you can use as a remote control for the speaker on an Android or iOS device. You use it to select a preset equalization or set your own, control how long the speaker idles before automatically powering down, Google Cast settings and other general operational-type stuff. Song Pal can also be used as a music player. I have to admit that I found Song Pal a little tedious in that role and I found it most useful to tweak settings on the speaker. I used other apps that I'm already familiar with (e.g. Amazon Music, RadioTunes) to play tunes.

I told a friend that I was going to review this and he loaned me his Bose Soundlink Mini to compare. The two don't compete directly (this Sony costs ~64% more than the Bose at this writing). The Sony is louder, more interface-able, has crazy longer battery life and sounds a lot better to me. But the Bose is much more portable and would suit me better for use in a product demo or a hotel room, and it sounds awfully good. This isn't a review of the Bose; I bring it up to make the point that whether the Sony isright for your application depends on how you want to use a device like this. I'm liking it for ambient tunes in my kitchen/dining area. It turns my phone or tablet into an exceptional table radio, and it could serve as a complete audio system for a guest or kids room TV (you can plug it into a 3.5" jack too). I'm giving it 5 stars because even at this price point, I think it succeeds at what it's trying to be.

I'll open this review stating that I was looking for a low cost, decent sounding bluetooth speaker. The SoundBot SB571, is just that, a DECENT sounding cheap little speaker. I am a bit of an audio snob, so when I say decent, that might mean superb to you. While the unit itself does supply quite a bit of volume for such a tiny little package, I would hardly call the sounds that come from it "crystal clear" "crispy" or "dynamic deep bass" There is hope yet, though, as it performs better than expected for a sub ~$50 unit. I suppose if I had to highlight an aspect of the speaker playback, I would highlight its ability to to almost isolate and amplify the vocals. The bass is fair, actually. No, it isn't room shaking, but it is present and far from muffled. Volume control on the unit itself is a huge plus, as well as the ability to take calls from the device directly. In addition, the ability to pause or skip tracks forward and backward on bluetooth from the device itself is life changing. It blows my mind other units don't think to include this feature. Those are features I didn't think would even be an option on such a low priced product, so hats off to SoundBot there. The 3.5mm jack is also a nice little touch, as my ipod, though it doesn't have bluetooth, does have over 10,000 songs on it some of which aren't available on music streaming apps. Including a 3.5mm cord was also a good call by the manufacturer. I tried to find bluetooth connection issues on my Samsung Note, but couldn't. It connected fast, and I found the range to be as advertised. I still have yet to have it drop connection, but there is a possibility it will never as my phone is a feature packed beast. One major con for me, however, has to be how loud it starts its volume, and the sheer blaring sound it makes when it announces that is connecting, or dyeing. Perhaps the manufacturer will produce a firmware update correcting that "feature" as I've seen a few negative comments regarding the issue.  Overall, would purchase again. Build quality is proficient, its a big sound for such a small device (far from a bose soundlink mini, however) and it offers many handy features. This product leaves me questioning what kind of quality SoundBot offers with their higher price range products, as this product delivers for its price. Will leave a follow up when I manage to kill it, as I am pretty rough with my electronics.  EDIT: It would also be nice to add a feature to view battery life of the device on an Android device. Android Lollipop does have support for such a feature, but the way its formatted on this product is not compatible with its settings.

The Bose Solo 15 Series II is a single unit sound bar that is designed to sit underneath your TV like a front speaker/shelf.

The unit comes with a universal remote control that feels very sturdy, and two connection types, an optical cable, that is VERY short (and likely won’t work for you), as well as a 3.5mm audio cable.

As far as I can tell the difference between the original and the series II is the addition of a Bluetooth connection and only the remote allows you to adjust the bass.

Installation
* One cable goes to the electric outlet, one cable goes into your TV, or you can pair with a Bluetooth device. No receiver or HDMI connections. This is really meant for your TV (or other connected device) to be in control of the sound distribution.
* Things you can configure: Bluetooth devices (up to two), the bass level, volume and auto start when music plays or not.
* The universal remote has all the buttons you expect for controlling your smart TV, and it does feel nice in the hand. An instruction book comes with the remote if you need to program specific codes.
* Size is 24” wide x 14” deep, but keep in mind you need to attach your cables, so that adds roughly another inch on the back. The height is ~3 inches.

The good
* The sound is great coming out of these speakers. It is clear, full and rich. High and mid-range is great. With other words, standard Bose quality (I have headphones and an entertainment system by them). It does sound much better than the Sony I have with my TV which was twice the price (and has satellite speakers). The bass can be adjusted but will not fill up a room with those deep vibrations you sometimes may want.
* The optical input for sound is good since the quality is better than analogue (blue/red connector).
* Bluetooth connection works very well. It immediately finds my phone and tablet (both Samsung Android) and gives a beep when paired.
* The unit has clean lines and doesn’t draw attention to itself. Only two dim LED lights indicate what is going on. That is good, but can also be bad if you happen to want some settings displayed, like the volume level for example.
*When connected to a TV or other hardwired sound device, the unit can be set to auto-wakeup. This is great if you turn on your TV, and don’t want to use a second remote for the sound bar.

The detractors
* It only allows two devices to be paired at one time. In a modern world of one tablet, one laptop and one cellphone, that is really not enough.
* The max volume is not very loud, but I think this is intentional because the units profile is meant for a TV max weight of 75 Lbs. (most TVs up to 50 inches), which are smaller entertainment systems.
* The Bluetooth connection does not work with the auto-wake feature.
* Connecting a pair of headphones can only be done through the back. This is just because they re-use the stereo connectors, so you will need a custom wire for that. Not sure why you would do this, since this unit is meant to be used with your TV or through a Bluetooth connection and be as unobtrusive as possible.
* Because I am a techie, I like to know what the wattage is of the speakers, but there is nothing mentioned in the manuals.
* No controls on the device, if the remote stops working the device won’t be usable.

The manufacturer could provide more tech specs in my opinion. There is more technical information about the batteries, voltage, milliamp hours, etc on Amazon than is included in the manual. I regularly backpack and camp so having data on how much charge the batteries hold, how long it takes to charge with solar, etc, would be nice.

On the bottom of the unit the battery is rated 7.4V 2600mAh. Since Amazon indicates there are two lithium batteries I assume that means there are two batteries with this voltage and capacity. The unit holds a total of 5200mAh. This would make sense, given the charge time indicated in the manual indicates 2 - 2.5 hour charge times on the DC adapter. The DC adapter power supply is rated 9V output at 3A.

If my math is right, given the 15 hour solar charge time in the instruction manual, the solar charge should produce 416 mAh at peak capacity. This concerns me since I typically take my iPhone 5 and my Tikka RXP headlamp when I'm outdoors. Both devices have battery capacities of around 1,900mAh.

Why does this concern me? I need to know how much solar charge time is needed to fully charge the battery of a device. Basically I will need to allow the unit to charge in direct sunlight for 4.5 - 5 hours to fully charge one of these devices. This does not include any electricity needed for music. Based on the battery capacity and the play time of 8 hours it seems the unit consumes 700 mAh while playing music (if not more).

All-in-all I love this product but would like to have more information from the manufacturer for my needs.

I've been using these for only seven months so I haven't been through many charging cycles, but I must say that my initial impression is 100% positive. We have a small digital Panasonic Lumix camera that would burn though my 2500 mAh Rayovacs fairly quickly. I was suspicious of this unknown "EBL" name claiming 2800 mAh capacity, and furthermore even if the claim were true, I didn't know whether the extra 12% capacity would be really that significant, Well it is. The EBLs seem to last noticeably longer in our camera. Part of this might be due simply to the newness of the EBLs, but I remember always having been slightly disappointed at the duration of the Rayovacs, and the EBLs give me the opposite impression. While I'm on the subject I just thought I'd pontificate on small rechargeable batteries in general. I have been a Rayovac fan for two decades and I still use their batteries heavily, but recently they seem to have lost the leadership position I felt they held. The EBLs are now clearly higher capacity and longer lasting in the AA and AAA categories. In D and C batteries there is a brand called Tenergy that makes real-live 10Ah and 5Ah batteries, respectively. These have incredible capacity, comparable to non-rechargeables. In contrast, the major brands (including Rayovac) package a AA (or slightly larger than AA) core in a mostly empty D or C size shell. So it seems that there is a new set of names taking over the rechargeable standard-size battery market, while the big names are riding on their name recognition to sell us older technology and downright deceptive stuff. I'm following the new leaders.

After reading the many positive reviews here, I bought a pair of AW 6500s in white as open-box specials for $190 each and they arrived in perfect working order. I mounted them horizontally about 12 feet apart a few inches beneath the eaves overhanging our back deck so they have some protection from the weather. It was simple to paint them according to the instructions provided and mounting them with the included brackets was also a snap, the biggest installation challenge was snaking shielded 14-gauge speaker cables through our attic to connect them to an amp inside the house. I'm using an old (pre-HDMI) Sony STR-DE615 receiver rated at 100 watts RMS per channel into 8 ohms to drive the speakers. The input source is a Logitech Squeezebox Touch audio streaming device, which is connected wirelessly to our home media server and controlled by apps on our phones.

I'm pretty fussy about sound, but I really couldn't be happier with the performance of these speakers given their price and weather resistance. In particular, the bass output is pretty phenomenal considering the bass/mid drivers are only 6 1/2" and I have the cabinets mounted 7 feet up (the drivers are slanted downward toward the deck with the passive radiators pointing up toward the eaves). All genres of music I've played so far sound great throughout our back yard at modest volume levels, and paired with this receiver I can crank them up much louder than my neighbors would appreciate before hearing noticeable distortion.

I haven't auditioned any other outdoor speakers so I don't have a basis to compare these to competitors' offerings, but they're definitely a huge step up from the portable Apple stereo I was lugging outside for music and it's hard for me to imagine anything in this price range sounding better!

I just bought a Raspberry Pi 2 Model B, which doesn't have a VGA output port.  Instead, the Raspberry Pi has HDMI and composite outputs.  I wanted to use this device to convert a composite signal to a VGA signal for my older computer monitor, which is VGA.  The result was complete failure.  After hooking it up, I was only able to see a continuously-scrolling, distorted picture.  The picture was far too distorted in order for me to make sense of anything that I was seeing.  Now I'm off to plan B.  I just bought an HDMI to VGA converter.  I haven't received it yet, but hopefully that'll work a lot better.  If you plan to use this device with a Raspberry Pi, I would advise against it.  For the price, I was hoping for a much better outcome.  Unfortunately, I was wrong.  %%%% Update %%%%%  I originally gave this item one star, but that was premature.  I have since learned that the reason this device didn't work with my Raspberry Pi is because my 3.5mm composite cable was wired inappropriately.  The cable wasn't designed/wired to work with the Raspberry Pi 2 Model B.  There's no way for anyone to know this since all of these cables look the same, but are sometimes wired differently.  So beware of this if you're looking for 3.5mm composite cables.  After rewiring my cable, this device did give me an adequate picture.  The picture was a bit shaky, but that may have been due to the fact that I had to cut, and rewire my cable.  Though the picture was shaky, it was certainly usable -- unlike before.

If you understand how Ikea products are make and how they’re used, you will “get” this TV stand. The number one reason Ikea products exist is functionality, followed by design. They are rarely what would be called “fine furniture” … they are made to serve a practical purpose and be sold at a reasonable price. Like most Ikea furniture this is made of recycled wood fibers with a hard, semi-gloss painted coating. It is available in white or black.

This product is intended to be used with a small, lightweight LED TV. Unfortunately the product description isn’t as clear as it could be in that regard but from my first-hand experience I would say it is intended for TV’s that are 40” or smaller. It is a lowboy stand that works best for people who prefer their TV to have a low profile, so in other words it is not your best choice for watching TV in bed or laying back in a reclining chair.

Like virtually every Ikea product, this is RTA (ready to assemble) furniture. It ships knocked down and comes with a pictures-only assembly manual. If you have experience assembling Ikea furniture you will probably consider this one of the simplest thing you’re assembled … 10 minutes maximum. Tools required are a Phillips screwdriver and a hammer. There are only 3 major parts … the top, the middle shelf, and four legs. You hand-screw each of the four legs into the top with double-ended screws that are included. Then you attach the shelf using 90° angle brackets. That’s it.

But, as is so often true with Ikea furniture, the pictorial diagrams are very vague, so here are a few helpful hints:

1. The illustrations show you screwing the double-ended studs in with your fingers. DON’T. You will end up with sore, bloody fingers if you do. To attach the top, insert the screw and twist slightly until it just stays in place without falling out. Then match the other end with the predrilled hole in the leg and with BOTH hands screw the two pieces together. When you meet resistance, only continue tightening until the leg is squarely aligned with the top … do NOT force it any further.

2. The middle shelf is very non-Ikea-like in that the holes in the legs are not predrilled. Instead they include a little plastic template that you must use to punch screw holes at the appropriate height. The following is very important: following the pictorial drawings align where the hole should be punched and tap one of the longer screws GENTLY with a hammer, just enough to make a small indentation where the screw should go. Do NOT hit the screw so hard that it completely punctures the leg or you won’t be able to screw it down tightly.

3. While Ikea’s instructions only show the middle shelf being able to be installed at the fixed location that they’ve determined, you can actually attach the shelf slightly higher or lower. If you look at my attached photos you will see that I bought two of these stands … one is used to held DVD’s and the other is used in another room to hold a speaker. The location that Ikea wants you to mount the shelf is not tall enough for anything except the old CD jewel cases. So here’s what you do. Measure where you want the shelf and hold one of the angle brackets under it. Mark where the hole should be with a pencil. Then align the plastic guide with that hole and make another pencil mark on the guide at the bottom of the leg. Then use the guide to punch the holes, aligning the pencil mark you made on it with the bottom of each leg.

4. The instructions are also unclear about how to screw the middle shelf in. They show inverting the table upside-down and mounting the shelf. That is very difficult to do because you have to hold the shelf with one hand, align the brackets with your other hand and screw the screw in with your third hand. So here’s the trick I discovered … after you punch the holes lay the table on its LONG end. When you insert the middle shelf it will be supported by the two legs on the bottom and gravity will assure the shelf is mounted to the leg with no gaps (see photo).

5. The stand is capable of supporting most 40” or smaller TV’s, however the middle shelf is NOT capable of holding much weight. The DVD cases as shown in my photo or a lightweight speaker is about all you should put on that shelf.

Finally, Ikea does not give you an option about screwing the entire stand to the wall behind it. Their lawyers want to make that very clear to you. I suggest you follow their instructions if you will be using this as a TV stand. My photos show that neither of my two stands are being used as a TV stand and I chose not to use the wall bracket for that reason.

Bottom line: This is an attractive stand to look at and is functional. It is not fine furniture and is not very big or substantial. Read the measurements, as the actual stand may be much smaller than you expect. But for what it is, I am 100% satisfied with both of them for the way I am using them. So initially I had a little difficulty exiting the music function but after playing around with it was able to figure it out.  The main thing to remember is if you want to exit any function you press and hold the M(menu) button for a second.  Once you get to the main function cycle screen, you use the left or right buttons to cycle through the main functions, once you get to the function you want you press the M button to enter that function and be presented with a list of options and use the left or right button to select the one youu want.  Once you are in any function a quick click of the M button will bring up a list of menu options and you use the left or right buttons to cycle through those.  Quick clicking the M button will cycle through additional menu options if available or eventually take you back to the function you are using.  To get to the main screen press and hold the M button for a second.  After figuring this out was able to access any function.  This player is a little more limited in available functions then another similar product but what it does have it does a little better than those other products.  I really like the size and the matte green color.  When you first get the player the easiest way to open the box is to take a knife and slice along the slots where the plastic case connects together.  I leave the top side connected which leaves me with a flip top case.  The player comes with earbuds and a charging cable.  It also comes with what appears to be a carrying strap but I have not been able to figure out where you are supposed to connect that.  It is all about figuring out the controls, once you do you will love the player.The screen is a little small to use the movie/video and photo functions but they are there and work well, the picture quality is pretty good. Even with that the reception could have been better but the stations I did get came in quite well and the sound quality was great.  The battery time was a big plus, I listened to the radio for over 12 hours on one charge and there was still a couple of bars of power left. This little speaker really does epitomize the old "bang for the buck" saying. When I was putting this speaker through the paces by playing different types of music at different volumes and seeing how the controls all work it really reminded me a lot of another speaker that I had tested from another company. When it all came down to it I thought this one fell a little short in the overall sound because the bass of the other unit was simply better. When I realized the cost on this speaker was about 1/4th of what the other one cost there was no way I could not rate it as a 5-star speaker.

This speaker puts out an exceptional amount of sound. I pulled out my trusty decibel meter and tested the volume of this speaker on a loud rock song with the volume all the way up and got a maximum reading of 104 decibels at a foot away from the speaker which is actually louder than your average home lawn mower. At the maximum volume the speaker was starting to strain a bit but I did not hear any major cracking or distortion.

The sound overall is nice and accurate with a very nice mid-range and high-end. As with a majority of small speakers the bass is a bit weak. This is because bass requires the movement of a lot of air and smaller speakers just cannot do that. That's why home systems like the Bose speakers all utilize subwoofers for the bass.

The volume on the speaker is not connected to the volume of your cell phone or tablet so you'll want to set your phone or tablet to the maximum volume then adjust the level on the speaker to your liking.

The controls here are nice and easy to use. There are only three buttons and a power switch. As with most speakers the volume and track skip buttons share the + and - buttons. Pressing quickly will move tracks backwards and forwards and holding the buttons down will control the volume up and down.

The speaker allows you to receive calls and use the device as a speakerphone. The quality of the incoming sound was great but the outgoing sounded a bit muffled but still very usable.

This speaker is splash proof, not water proof which was another different between it and the more expensive unit I talked about earlier. This means this speaker will hold up to being splashed at the side of the pool but should not be thrown in the pool.

Overall this is a really nice speaker that packs a lot of features and durability for the price point. Recommended.

For a $16 pair of earbuds, these things pack excellent sound and durability. Add to that the fact that these earbuds have "tangle proof" and flexible wires, customize-able earbud sizes, are compatible with making phone calls on my Galaxy s4, have a gold-coated plug, and have a diagonal connector, you could consider these earbuds to be a steal. It has been over a year since I've used my pair, yet the thing is still holding itself mostly intact! Both earbuds are still working, the bass is still good, and the sound has yet not become distorted (at any frequency, nor the bass in any case, as far as my young ears can tell). Flickering has begun to occur more frequently, however, since about two months before this review was written.

The only downside to these earbuds is that they can come off fairly easily, especially when wax gets on them. Because of this, I have not bothered wearing these headphones when I go for a sprint or when I work out. The earbud casing is also cheap (but there shouldn't be a complaint here, since these things only cost $16 and not, say, $150.) Moreover, making phone calls with these things on can get frustrating when you are in a loud environment, as the mic does not filter out background noises. That being said, the microphone picks up heavy breathing too.

Unfortunately, like all good things in life, I foresee that these earbuds shall last me no longer than 13 months, which puts them in 2nd place for the most durable pair of earbuds ever (on my list of purchased earbuds, that is), with the Klipsch s4 earbuds being the most durable earbuds I have ever used; those things lasted almost 2 years. Note that the Klipsch s4 also costs almost 5 times the price of these earbuds! Do be wary of the fact that I prevent my headphones from tangling up, that I have never dropped them in water, or that I have put them through a mechanical test course (which would probably involve having my 330 pound friend step on them to see if they would still be usable afterwards.)

On a scale of 1 to 10, I give these earbuds a rating of 8.8, and would definitely recommend them to anyone who is looking for a cheap, yet good pair of headphones. Keep in mind that these things will only last long when they are taken good care of. If you are one of those people that toss their headphones around the house after you've finished them, don't expect them to last more than several months (or weeks for that matter.) Also, if your ears tend to get sweaty (as mine do) or you are looking for earbuds for your workout, you may want to consider wearing a different pair of earbuds (preferably a type of earbud that has the little piece that digs into your earlobe, whatever that is called).

PROS:
BATTERY - rechargeable and good for several days (mfg says 15, my experience is about that).

LOCATION ACCURACY - use of GSM so can be wildly inaccurate, a quarter mile or more, the same as a phone with GPS turned off. Lugloc uses "traces" - you request a location from your smartphone and it tells you - MAYBE (see CONS). Its very slow - 2 minutes or much longer.

BLUETOOTH - if your luggage is nearby (30 feet more or less) - like delivered to the wrong room - you can locate it by walking the halls with your smartphone using the rangefinder. Then you only have to figure out how to get in the room. (See update in CONS below.

ONGOING COST - annual fee required. These may be dynamic so its hard to predict the cost.

CONS:
MAYBE - Lugloc seems to shut down (go into airplane mode) any time there is movement - like driving in a car or walking while in your pocket, or rolling your luggage at an airport. It can take a while to come out of airplane mode, and you can't get a trace if there is movement (see photo). This means if someone steals your luggage, throws it in a car and drives away, you can't get a location until after they stop moving the luggage. Since you don't control the movement, there is nothing you can do to help. I've had a trace take over 5 minutes with a perfectly still Lugloc. This feature is not well thought out, and its the primary purpose for the device.

BLUETOOTH UPDATE 10-11-15 - to use the Bluetooth feature, you have to login - which can be difficult (as I found out) if their web service is down, or if you don't have WiFi and don't have data service. There is no good reason (that I can think of) that the phone app shouldn't be able to do Bluetooth communication with the LugLoc device without logging in. Minus one more star for this poor feature.

SUMMARY:

Note that if your luggage doesn't get lost, it is not needed. If your luggage does get lost, I'm not sure - in a hotel/motel mis-delivery Bluetooth is a plus, for bus travel or very long flights long battery life is a plus.

SCORING: -3 for movement sensitivity (if I can't get a trace what good is it), +1 for Bluetooth rangefinding, UPDATE - minus 1 for poor Bluetooth (see above).

The most recent comparison was with Musical Fidelity V90 DAC. I liked the outlook of V90 DAC better. The build quality of the case of the V90 DAC looked higher. I liked two Toslinks and one coaxial on V90 DAC better than one Toslink and two coaxials on DacMagic 100.

V90 DAC sounds clearer; DacMagic 100 sounds less fatiguing.

Both processed de-emphasis.

Both showed low jitter in the spectrum of high frequency sinusoidal test tones when measured with Focusrite Scarlett 2i2. This is a popular USB audio interface (containing AD and DA) in musical instrument market, but the resolution and self jitter is nowhere near what Stereophile uses for jitter measurement.

FYI, the V90 DAC came with 110V only adapter which generates more heat than usual switching power adapter. The DacMagic 100 came with free voltage adapter and three interchangeable blades.

FYI, the DacMagic 100 does not handle 176.4kHz sample rate.

FYI, the V90 DAC had date of manufacture sticker, and was made in EU (not Taiwan). The DacMagic 100 was manufactured in China.

FYI, both had feet that seem to absorb little vibration. The feet of V90 DAC felt like a hard plastic. The DacMagic 100 had rubber feet, but the rubber feels too hard for the weight of the DAC.

Wow! "Bang for the Buck" would be my springboard, (literal), comment. I'm an A/V Tech and I have to say I'm VERY impressed. I auditioned it to a personal trainer who needs a solid audio speaker for a larger group and to a family member who has a beach cabana and entertains often on the sand for 30+ people. What I've found...all good because I understand the limits of audio power supply's, acoustic wave propagation and long throw drivers. What does that all mean, you ask. In the simplest of terms, if you jack the bass up to 10, as the volume is turned up...once the subwoofer has reached its "physical limit" of excursion, the additional volume dialed up only increases the four mid/treble speakers. A GOOD Thing...the built in electronics monitor an limit levels that would damage the bass driver. Not a problem...a blessing really. The Blue Tooth range is adequate, 33' Max., BUT...it performs very well within said...however, if you are on the cusp of that range, streaming is possible, but the volume up/down command is not always recognized.

Bottom line - this speaker kicks ass and takes names and I'm as pleased as punch with my purchase. A phone charging USB port would have been nice but no points off for not having it.

Just buy one if you'd like to have one of the best out there. I have a Bose, JBL, and a Braven in smaller footprints for portability. This speak is ALL Battery and Magnets in a Rugged Portable Frame - hence the sound quality. Not a good camping speaker for backpacking - 12+ lbs. The "fit and finish" is impressive...rubber in all the right places and chrome handle either a gun metal grill finish. The first thing I want to address is the charging problem some have and it has to do with one thing, it uses USB which requires it to be charged from a computer(trickle charge) and some outlet chargers. Some have mentioned that with this version and others they are only able to get about a half an hour to an hour worth of play time. A charging cable, earbuds and a 32 GB micro SD card.  Most will not need more than 32 GB but because of the Micro SD card slot you can have a card for each one of your media, one for music, one for books, one for movies,...etc.  Let's start with the packaging and honestly this might be my biggest negative but really didn't effect my rating. It comes in a two part clear plastic case wrapped in glued on cellophane. Don't try to remove the cellophane, take a knife and slice along the sides where the two pieces of plastic come together, slice along the two long sides and the bottom short side, you will feel your knife slightly enter the slot along the sides. By leaving the top side connected you will have a flip open case.  The player itself fits my needs perfectly, mostly for walking and listening to music and audio books. I got over 4 hours of playing time using it for that and probably had more but decided to charge the player, I don't like to let the battery get to low. The player does so much more than play audio files, there are even 4 games included but watching video and playing games might not be the best things to use the player for because of the small screen size but you can, pictures and video quality were very good. You can also record what you are listening to onthe radio to or use it as a voice recorder. The radio worked great and the reception was surprisingly good. My only real negative was the bass with the supplied ear buds was not very good even at the rock setting on the equalizer but I rarely get good bass out of ear buds, the bass was a lot better with an over the ear pair of headphones.  The player was very intuitive, I never did look at the instructions and only encountered a few minor bumps in the road that I eventually figured out. The interface has a quaint old school pixelated look but really was a non issue for me. For my needs it was perfect and is very highly recommended for those with similar needs to mine.

The material of the wire casing, however, was this sticky, rubbery type of sheath that would just kinda stick to my hands whenever I would accidentally brush them, often causing the earbuds to fly out of my ear and slam onto the floor. Like all other earbuds that I have gone through, these ones would fall off my ears whenever they picked up sweat, which became (somewhat annoying, but bearable, since this happens to be almost all the time, anyway.)

The primary reason I gave this pair a 2 star rating out of 5 was because of the fact that in addition to all of the aforementioned things, these buds were ready for the electronic scrapyard after 3 months of use. When put into abusive hands, these earbuds probably would last a month, and that would be it. Overall, if you are looking for a pair of buds that are durable, have good sound quality, rugged wiring, and don't have to be worn in a PERFECT POSITION ALL THE TIME TO GET THE RIGHT SOUND, get another pair.

I have a pretty revealing set of speakers, so both compressed audio and non-compressed always had sounded a little harsher in my system, but this unit does an amazing job with smoothing out the sound and delivering a huge, clear, performance regardless of what I throw at it. Whether it's the Beatles, Taylor Swift, Billy Joel, Lagwagon, AC/DC, Dropkick Murphys, or Bruno Mars, this absolutely delivers. Again, this is on the pricer side, but in my system, I think it delivers a smoother and wider soundstage than the Stream Magic 6 V2, but that streamer is a great alternative if your speakers don't tend to be fussy. I inherited a pair of Energy Veritas 6.3 floorstanders and they are light on bass and accentuated highs, but this machine offsets that and is a great match for a brighter speaker in my opinion. Haven't hear it with a more neutral sounding speaker, but I wouldn't imagine this to be dull sounding within any system. I am primarily using this as a network streamer via DLNA, but Pandora sounds fantastic through this even with all the compression. Cannot comment on the USB DAC, but given the performance over streaming, I would say this is definitely worth a listen if you are in the market for a streamer and a DAC all in one.

This is a great cover considering the price.  I was really shocked at the price of TV covers when shopping on Amazon.  I stumbled across this one and ordered it immediately.  It arrived in 3 days, super-fast considering it's not a Prime item.  In my situation, my TV is installed on the wall in my garage.  Certainly away from rain and excess moisture but not away from lots of dust and dirt.  This will work perfectly for that, it covers front and back (with minor modifications in my situation) to prevent dust from getting in the vents and all over the TV.  If your TV is out closer to the elements, I would be hesitant to use this cover for full protection.  That is clearly the difference here and the seller calls it a dust cover so they are describing the item properly.  The item is made of a thin slightly stretchy material so it fits nicely around the TV, it is black and slightly see-through but good enough to do its job.  Make sure you follow the directions on how to order the correct size.  I have a 32" TV and ordered the 29" cover.  Measure the TV's width (side to side) for the correct measurements.  TV screen sizes are measured diagonally by the manufacturer so my 32" TV was actually 28.5" wide.  I was very pleased with the fit.  Now back to the minor modification.  This cover is solid material all the way around which works perfectly for a TV that is on a stand but not so much for one mounted to the wall.  The back of the cover had to bunch up around the mount and wasn't really able to cover much of the back.  I was a little hesitant to just hack it with scissors as I was fearing the material would fray.  Well, I cut it anyway because I figured if it was ruined I would just order another one.  I like it that much.  So far, so good....no fraying of the material and it hangs perfectly around the TV.  Now, don't compare this $7 cover to a $35-$50 vinyl cover and you won't be disappointed.  It will keep dust away, it will keep your TV covered and it will look great.  That's what this is designed for and it does it extremely well.

This is where the wheels fall off. Right off the bat the rubber tips come off very easily. After two months the volume buttons stopped working...mildly annoying and can learn to live without. After 4 months the sound in the left ear bud starts flickering. Wiggling the wire around the area where the flat cord inserts into the rubber sleeve just before the male plug would make the sound come back however, the flickering became progressively worse every day. After day three of flickering sound it was not possible to hear one complete song with both headphones working. I take care of my electronics. I never wrap cords tightly and do not subject them to various forms of teenage type abuse.

Rubber tips: As of this review, it is not possible to buy replacement tips. You will eventually lose them over time because they pull off too easily. I called JBL's customer service line from their website to inquire about buying replacement tips. Just getting a customer service rep was challenging. I would sit on hold for a couple minutes only to hear a clicking noise (the type of noise that suggests someone is answering) only to be put back on hold again. A few minutes later same clicking noise as if someone was about to answer and the call would get dropped. On my third try I finally got a rep that said the replacement tips are on backorder and they have no idea when they will become available. The rep referred me to a third party independent electronics website and was assured I would be able to find there. When I scoured the third party website I did not find them so I called their toll free tel #. They said not only do they NOT carry the replacement tips they also do not carry ANY JBL products. They went on to say they would never sell replacement parts to products they do not carry so they were very surprised JBL would even refer someone to them. So even if you have luck with the sound not flickering, you will not be able to buy replacement tips when you lose them.

These earbuds lasted less than six months and i'm not interested in looking into any warranties for replacement since they fell apart so quickly. JBL customer service was very disturbing which hit home since I have always stood by their home speakers for many years. I have always had a pair of their studio monitors. I would rather continue my search for earbuds that last longer than a couple months. I have used 4 different earbud manufacturers in 6 years and this model takes first prize for quickest to fall apart to the point of unusable.

One important take away from this experience: always check to see if replacement tips are avail online BEFORE you buy your next pair of earbuds. If you cannot find replacement tips easily then you are taking a huge risk. It sounds so simple that it feels embarrassing saying this but i've never owned a pair of earbuds where the tips would come off this easily. Matter of fact I don't remember ever losing one of the ear tips on previous earbuds i've owned. The fit was always firm/super stable until I ran into these.

I have been wanting some wireless headphones for a long time but I was finding the prices too high. I jumped at the chance to review these wireless headphones when they became available. Here is what I like about these earphones so far:

- They are very comfortable to wear. Though I am a fully grown female, I have to wear therm on the smallest sized so I don't think these would work for smaller kids unless they have big heads. They will extend quite a lot so even my big-headed husband can comfortably wear them.
- The material around the ears is extremely soft and supple. I don't think it's leather (might be) but it's very easy to wear these for hours at a time. And I am very picky about what's on my head.
- The sound coming through is incredibly good. I was watching a movie and actually got startled when a helicopter in the movie flew right over my house but it was actually the stereo in the headphones. Very realistically clear. Listening to classical guitar music through these is almost as good as being at the concert in person....maybe better except you can't watch the guitarist play in person. I teach classical guitar and am very particular about the sound quality of the instrument through any speaker. I have no complaints whatsoever in the sound quality of these headphones.
- The distance I can get from the source is everywhere in my house. I can go down into the basement or upstairs and still maintain a strong bluetooth connection. I went outside (we have a solid brick house) and was able to get approximately 20-30 feet away before the connection started to break up.
- These headphones are lightweight and the earphones are slim with the contours of your face. I like the narrow profile.
- Very clear audio when using the phone. People I spoke with said they could hear me loud and clear including leaving voice mail messages.
- Connected via bluetooth to all of my devices easily except my chromebook. These devices were: phone, laptop, tablet and iPod 4 so far.
- Relatively quick recharge. My earphones came with some charge in the battery, but I exhausted it and they shut off. I connected them to a wall outlet using the enclosed USB cord and an adapter and in about an hour they were fully charged.
- What's included: a soft, zippered pouch case (no strap or handle), USB and a cord to hardwire the earphones to a device. I used that wire to watch and listen to Youtube videos on my chromebook.
- The instructions come in a LOT of different languages.
- Online registration was easy.
- Every time they are turned on the automated voice tells you how much battery you have left.
- It's very easy to answer phone calls, and adjust the volume on the right side earphone.
- These can get very loud.
- It's really freeing to be able to wear these headphones to listen to my favorite podcasts or music and not be tethered to the computer by a cord. I can move about the entire house freely doing what it is I need/want to do. That's the biggest perk!

What I don't like:
- I can't figure out how to get these to connect via bluetooth to my chromebook. Other bluetooth devices will connect but the earphones won't. I will keep trying and update if I get it to connect.
- They don't filter out outside ambient noise very well so don't expect them to exclude a lot of external sounds much while using them. I can still hear everything my husband and kids are saying unless I turn them up louder.

UPDATE: 3.30.17 - These are still working flawlessly and I use them for hours every evening listening to my favorite Youtube videos. Soft and comfortable, they hold a charge for a L-O-N-G time too and recharge extremely fast.

Overall: I find these to be very good having crisp, clear, bright and exceptional sound quality. Easy to wear for long periods of time, and the battery life seems long. I don't know how much they cost since as of this review the product page has not been posted.

From the reviews of the Tomameri portable players (they sell this same player in 8, 16, and 32GB versions), this seems to be a love it or hate it type of product - which might come down to your expectations before you get it. Let me try to help with that - this is not a super-high-quality piece of hardware. The plastic pieces seem kind of cheap, and the ear buds aren't very nice. However, the aluminum case is actually pretty decent, the Micro SD card seems about as well made as others that I've bought, and the mini USB cable (yes, it charges with mini USB versus the more prevalent micro USB) is surprisingly nice. Audio performance is pretty decent, but don't expect much from the video. I gave the 16GB version four stars but am giving this one three stars because I don't think it's as good of a value at the current $36 price (more on that below).

If I were looking for something like this for myself or anyone that didn't destroy electronics quickly (like a young child), I'd heavily consider just using an older (or even new) smart phone - because most of those will do everything that this does but do it MUCH better. Bigger screen, probably as much memory (but maybe requiring a micro SD card)...and so on. If you wanted to get a young child their first music player and didn't want to risk having something more expensive get busted, this might not be a bad choice...because odds are you won't mind if this gets broken. I don't mean that in a mean way to this player - I'm just saying that I think it falls squarely into the niche of disposable products. This is exactly the kind of product that I wouldn't mind taking on a plane trip because it sounds pretty good and because I wouldn't be upset if I lost it or broke it...inexpensive hardware like this definitely has a place.

I do want to point out that the lower memory size Tomameri players are currently a better deal, with the 8GB version being only $14 right now ($22 cheaper at current prices). When you do your shopping, if you decide that you want one of these players - I highly recommend that you check the other models. The ONLY difference (that I can tell, and I have the 16GB and 32GB models) is the memory card. Even the sample files that come on them are the same. You can buy 32GB micro SD cards faster than the one that comes with this product for under $15, so it might pay off to get the cheapest version out there and then get a separate card for it. I gave the 16GB model four stars because it was a pretty good value even with its flaws, but this 32GB version is currently $36 - and you can buy pay-as-you-go smart phones for similar or even less money that will beat this player (just don't activate the phone service and use the \\"phone\\" as a media player). For example, the Moto G for Verizon prepaid seems to often be under $40.

Although not the best value, I still think it's worthy of three stars even at the current $36 price tag because:
(*) First, you get some individual pieces that are useful with or without the player, most notably the 32 GB Micro SD card that would cost you around $10 by itself
(*) Speaking of the memory card, I love that this player uses one instead of needing to sync up with a computer to load files onto it. That is more convenient to me than my iPods that sync up with iTunes
(*) Next, it actually works pretty darn well for audio - the internal amp isn't half bad and powered my larger headphones just fine, and the voice recorder worked quite well once I went into the menu and changed the recording quality. I was surprised by how well the audio sounded on this
(*) Charges pretty fast, and battery life isn't too bad, either
(*) Small and lightweight

Now, for some of the detractors:
(*) Although it has the look of an older iPod Nano, which I happen to own and have used for years, it doesn't operate like one. The wheel on the front doesn't respond to you sliding your finger along it like a Nano does, but rather just mimics the look of it while requiring you to click on it. The four labeled areas on the wheel are essentially four separate buttons, with a fifth button under the circle in the center of the wheel. If you've never owned a Nano with the scroll wheel, likely none of that will matter to you
(*) The \\"MP4\\" player part is a little misleading, as this will not play regular .MP4 files. It plays .AMV files, which I'd never heard of until I got this and tried to load video files onto it
(*) The screen is okay quality, but it's tiny - you shouldn't expect to ever use this as an E-Book reader like mentioned in the product title. Watching a video might work okay if you decide to convert your files into AMV files
(*) The menu system can be a little tedious. Okay, make that a lot tedious
(*) Charges with a mini USB cable, which might be less common in your house/car/luggage than a micro USB cable used by pretty much every other piece of electronics these days

In summary, this is a disposable piece of hardware that has surprisingly good audio quality, probably useless video capability to most people, a slightly aggravating menu system, and a Micro SD card that you can use for something else if you decide to chuck the player into the garbage. If it was $10, I'd be recommending it for the spare parts alone because the 32GB card is pretty decent if not the fastest out there. At $36, it's not a horrible deal...but it's not a great deal, either. Seriously, check out inexpensive smart phones and see if they'll be a better fit for you.

This is a slim good looking surge protector. This power strip surge protector does two things, it has digital filters to prevent low or high frequency signals from passing, and protects against an over voltage like when your house is struck by lightning. It does nothing to help with brown outs or low voltage, or to condition the voltage to a constant value.

In a roundabout way the quality of the surge protection equipment can be gauged by the warranty APC offers, the higher the warranty value, the more they believe in their product. APC is willing to replace or repair up to $350,000 worth of equipment plugged into this device - in the event the equipment is damaged by a surge. I can't imagine anybody with $350,000 worth of electronics plugging those things into this protector - they would use things that cost thousands more, and do mysterious audio improving things. However, any average person could easily use this to protect a television and audio system - and might get near a $5,000 price tag.

APC tries to differentiate the plugs on this device - there are a set for digital protection and two for high current. Not sure why in the world they did that - receivers and amplifiers (the most common high current device you'd plug into those outlets) all have digital equipment in them and probably need the digital protection more than the other devices. Not sure what APC is thinking with those outlets.

The device has a bar of outlets that can be rotated. Two are fixed facing to the side. The rotation is nice, but not a major important thing. Rotation doesn't really help with wall warts, or the big AC adapters. That would have been better treated with outlets scattered wider around the box.

The front and back of the unit are glossy black plastic. The top is matte black plastic. The unit is handsome. On the other hand, you'll never put this out in a show place - the good looking part will have a ton of electrical plugs in it - all ugly things.

They add the standard not very useful coaxial cable and phone jacks (who uses land line phone jacks anymore - or have expensive equipment connected to them).

As a power strip, this thing is nice. As a surge protector it works. As a product to provide the cleanest best power to audio equipment, well you really need a line conditioner and much more expensive gear for that. The power strip looks nice.ugly things.

From the reviews of the Tomameri portable players (they sell this same player in 8, 16, and 32GB versions), this seems to be a love it or hate it type of product - which might come down to your expectations before you get it. Let me try to help with that - this is not a super-high-quality piece of hardware. The plastic pieces seem kind of cheap, and the ear buds aren't very nice. However, the aluminum case is actually pretty decent, the Micro SD card seems about as well made as others that I've bought, and the mini USB cable (yes, it charges with mini USB versus the more prevalent micro USB) is surprisingly nice. Audio performance is pretty decent, but don't expect much from the video. I gave the 16GB version four stars but am giving this one three stars because I don't think it's as good of a value at the current $36 price (more on that below).

If I were looking for something like this for myself or anyone that didn't destroy electronics quickly (like a young child), I'd heavily consider just using an older (or even new) smart phone - because most of those will do everything that this does but do it MUCH better. Bigger screen, probably as much memory (but maybe requiring a micro SD card)...and so on. If you wanted to get a young child their first music player and didn't want to risk having something more expensive get busted, this might not be a bad choice...because odds are you won't mind if this gets broken. I don't mean that in a mean way to this player - I'm just saying that I think it falls squarely into the niche of disposable products. This is exactly the kind of product that I wouldn't mind taking on a plane trip because it sounds pretty good and because I wouldn't be upset if I lost it or broke it...inexpensive hardware like this definitely has a place.

I do want to point out that the lower memory size Tomameri players are currently a better deal, with the 8GB version being only $14 right now ($22 cheaper at current prices). When you do your shopping, if you decide that you want one of these players - I highly recommend that you check the other models. The ONLY difference (that I can tell, and I have the 16GB and 32GB models) is the memory card. Even the sample files that come on them are the same. You can buy 32GB micro SD cards faster than the one that comes with this product for under $15, so it might pay off to get the cheapest version out there and then get a separate card for it. I gave the 16GB model four stars because it was a pretty good value even with its flaws, but this 32GB version is currently $36 - and you can buy pay-as-you-go smart phones for similar or even less money that will beat this player (just don't activate the phone service and use the \\"phone\\" as a media player). For example, the Moto G for Verizon prepaid seems to often be under $40.

Although not the best value, I still think it's worthy of three stars even at the current $36 price tag because:
(*) First, you get some individual pieces that are useful with or without the player, most notably the 32 GB Micro SD card that would cost you around $10 by itself
(*) Speaking of the memory card, I love that this player uses one instead of needing to sync up with a computer to load files onto it. That is more convenient to me than my iPods that sync up with iTunes
(*) Next, it actually works pretty darn well for audio - the internal amp isn't half bad and powered my larger headphones just fine, and the voice recorder worked quite well once I went into the menu and changed the recording quality. I was surprised by how well the audio sounded on this
(*) Charges pretty fast, and battery life isn't too bad, either
(*) Small and lightweight

Now, for some of the detractors:
(*) Although it has the look of an older iPod Nano, which I happen to own and have used for years, it doesn't operate like one. The wheel on the front doesn't respond to you sliding your finger along it like a Nano does, but rather just mimics the look of it while requiring you to click on it. The four labeled areas on the wheel are essentially four separate buttons, with a fifth button under the circle in the center of the wheel. If you've never owned a Nano with the scroll wheel, likely none of that will matter to you
(*) The \\"MP4\\" player part is a little misleading, as this will not play regular .MP4 files. It plays .AMV files, which I'd never heard of until I got this and tried to load video files onto it
(*) The screen is okay quality, but it's tiny - you shouldn't expect to ever use this as an E-Book reader like mentioned in the product title. Watching a video might work okay if you decide to convert your files into AMV files
(*) The menu system can be a little tedious. Okay, make that a lot tedious
(*) Charges with a mini USB cable, which might be less common in your house/car/luggage than a micro USB cable used by pretty much every other piece of electronics these days

In summary, this is a disposable piece of hardware that has surprisingly good audio quality, probably useless video capability to most people, a slightly aggravating menu system, and a Micro SD card that you can use for something else if you decide to chuck the player into the garbage. If it was $10, I'd be recommending it for the spare parts alone because the 32GB card is pretty decent if not the fastest out there. I was not really expecting too much from this headset but in fact I was pleasantly surprised by them.

The headset arrived nicely presented in an attractive windowed display box with the information on it largely in Chinese. Inside was the headset itself, a red USB to micro-USB charging cable, a white 3.5mm jack to 3.5mm jack audio cable, a warranty card (in Chinese) and a dual language User Guide which although poorly translated was large, easy to read and simple enough to make sense of. There was also, and this is not something I have encountered before in a Bluetooth headset in this price range, a user replaceable rechargeable battery.

The build quality seems pretty good throughout. The body of the unit is made from a tough plastic with what feel to be durable hinges where the earcups swivel and revolve, the mechanism to extend the arms seems positive and firm too. The rather small on-ear cups are reasonably well padded as it the headband, the earcups are marked as L or R, which is nice. The left earcup has an input for the jack cable which allows the device to be used when the battery is dead or with non Bluetooth audio devices. On the side of this earcup at the top there is groove you can get your nail into to gain access to the battery compartment where the replaceable reusable battery is housed. I mention this because the User Guide illustration is unclear which earcup the battery is housed in and I spent ages trying to open the wrong one! The battery compartment cover is secured by a magnet and once the trick is known can be easily removed. Another nice touch is the inclusion of a small ribbon to prevent the battery cover getting lost. The right earpiece has a micro-USB slot for charging the battery as well as the controls for the unit. There is a large and easy to feel central MUltifunction button with the volume and track controls housed along the four sides of the earpiece panel. The buttons are large and well positioned but are not easy easy as they could be to find touch alone. Perhaps it's just me but instinctively I went to press the top button for volume UP, the lower for volume Down and the front and rear for track controls. No, here it is the other way around. There is a single quite large blue/red status LED on the right earcup which flashes when the device is in use.

Setting the device up was quick and easy by holding the MF button to initiate pairing. It is a pity that there are no voice status prompts as only the old style bleeps are available with red/blue LEDs.

Sound quality is excellent and places this device amongst the best Bluetooth headsets I have used for music reproduction. There is plenty of bass, but not too much as the Dr Dre ones are. The mid tones and treble are good but good be a little punchier - but better that than being to sharp or abrasive. No, the sound here really is very good indeed.

Phone calls are easily made and received with the voice easy to make out both ends. Calls have to be initiated and responded to by pressing the headset MF button -there is no option to make or answer calls by voice alone.

This is an excellent set of Bluetooth headphones and has to be one of the best I have used, perhaps the best in this budget price range.

After going through about one pair per year of Skullcandy Ink'd earbuds for the past five or so years I decided to change things up. The price of Skullcandy Ink'd's keep increasing and the quality seems to be decreasing. I stumbled across these "Sentey" Earbuds and I saw the amount of good reviews and thought I'd give them a try. I'm currently listening to music through these earbuds and after 30 minutes of listening I'm just as disappointed as when I opened the Amazon package.

First, I opened Amazon's padded envelope and found the Sentey box smashed on one end with none of the other items in the envelope damaged (Strike 1). After I opened the damaged box I immediately saw that the earbud cable was not wrapped neatly but rather smashed into the opening where the cable belonged (Strike 2). I decided to try out the earbuds anyhow. I switched out the stock rubber tips for the larger set that came in a small, opened ziploc-style bag. I plugged them into my phone's earbud port (I noticed that the earbud plug seemed to fit a bit too tightly) and gave them a listen. This is where they failed to impress yet again (STRIKE 3).

When it comes to sound quality I consider myself to be an audiophile in training. I'm currently a college student and can't afford to be buying and using top-end audio components all of the time but I do happen to have a USB DAC and a pair of Sony MDR V6's for my everyday listening pleasure. I even tested the earbuds with the DAC to make sure that it wasn't just my phone's headphone port that wasn't cooperating. These earbuds seem to be designed as in-ear subwoofers rather than in-ear speakers. The amount of bass that these earbuds put out is overwhelming in a completely negative way (and this is coming from a guy who absolutely loves bass-heavy music). The sound produced by these earbuds is completely muddy and muffled. I understand that these are only $15 earbuds but I am completely disappointed.

I will be copying this review and sending it to the seller promptly. Please heed my warning and DO NOT buy these earbuds. I've heard that Panasonic RPHJE120K earbuds are fairly worthy of a $15 price-tag but sell for about $6. I intend to try them out with my refund money.

I bought a used yamaha a-s500 off ebay for about half the original retail price.  Initially I had a problem with turning it on but I turned off the power management switch on the back and have had no further issues.  It also has a subtle transformer hum that's not really noticeable unless you put your ear up to the amp, but is still not totally silent like my other amps.  It is not coming from the speakers but from the amp itself.  I was underwhelmed at first.  It had great imaging and soundstage, but sounded washed out and weak, with no guts, compared to my old yamaha rx-397 receiver, the lowest of the line.  Admittedly my range of reference is limited but I was contemplating selling it and going back to the receiver.  Months passed and I was still not really satisfied.  Then I read about how critical it is to plug a Rega-Brio-R amp directly into the wall rather than a surge protector.  It was said to be more dynamic.  So I thought maybe that's my problem with the Yamaha.  I plugged it into its own outlet and what a transformation!  The silences are black, the sound sharp and powerful.  Now I see how people can be satisfied with it.  I had so much plugged into the old cheap surge protector (an amp for the subwoofer, cd players, lamp, etc.) that the amplifier was being throttled.  I hear things on my old CDs I've never heard before.  Perhaps it isn't the most powerful, dynamic amp with real slam, but instrument separation, imaging, and soundstage are fabulous.  Resolution, imaging, and detail are its strengths.
It broke within few months,  had to buy another kind of headphones for my daughter to replace this.
