This thing sounds amazing. Like really really good. I can compare it to the Anker Premium Stereo Speaker that has recently been released at $60, which sounds flat next to this beast. The Anker really let me down since its pretty well rated, but the bass recedes at higher volumes and doesn't respond well to EQ. And at the $60 Price Point I purchased it at through Best Buy, this is a 5-star product; that isn't to say it doesn't have it's cons.

Order of Importance (This is what I was looking for when making this purchase. Starts from most important.)
°°°° Sound Quality. Bar None. I need good sound. I cannot have flat sound. If it could spend 90% less than I did, and have 75% of the same quality, I would probably return the product. Which I have done. This is not somewhere I am willing to settle.
°°° Battery Life. It better have good battery or a replaceable one. If it's easily recharged using a portable battery, that is OKAY too.
°°° Durability. Needs to be able to withstand a beating. Water Resistance is awesome too.
°°° Warranty/Customer Service. This can be make or break for me, but CS I don't have to contact is the best CS.
°° Bluetooth Strength. Inherently part of the product group. It needs to work. AUX cable is secondary to this.
°° Product Material. If it looks and feels good, I most likely will like it more. Not necessary, but welcome.
° Portability. Also part of the product group.
° Additional Features: NFC, Bass/Treble, Ability to change music from device, Daisy-Chaining, Multiple Device connections, etc. etc.

Pros
+ Built Like a Tank! I'm pretty sure I can whack someone in the head with it and it may leave them with a concussion.
+ LOUD. No loss of Fidelity at maximum volumes! That means no receding bass, no high frequency sibilance, just really amazing sound!
+ Dedicated sub woofer!
+ Bass and Treble adjustments? GET OUT.
+ Pretty LED lights around volume knob to indicate volume level.
+ A much welcome handle!
+ Can be played while charging.
+ Has a USB-out to charge other devices at .5A.
+ Replaceable battery! Wow! Not all glory here though...
+ No annoying voice or connecting sound! This is big because companies seem to believe that a loud tinny voice or sound is the ideal way to let people know it's connected to Bluetooth or it's been disconnected!
+ Bluetooth has pretty great range. At least 30 ft! AT LEAST! Connects fast too!
+ IPX3 Water Resistant Rating. Not good for submersion, but at least you can have it safely at pool side!

Cons
- Built Like a Tank! Yes this is also a pro, but this thing is not nearly as portable as other devices. It's unorthodox cube shape is excellent and sturdy, but it's going to be harder to throw in a bag and carry it around.
- Battery Life. I am not looking forward to it. In fact, I would implore purchasers to buy extra batteries and carry a screw driver because, well it's short. It's rated at about 6-8 hours at 75% volume which is pretty unacceptable for a device this size. Which leads me to the next con.
- AC Adapter REQUIRED to charge. This is a con mostly because most speakers are conveniently charged with USB cables, and portable batteries are easy to find nowadays, but this one can't be charged with USB. So you better keep a spare battery at hand because you'll be stuck trying to find an outlet and carrying this bulky AC Adapter. Don't forget the screwdriver! Blah.
- This is just nitpicking, but you have to wait about 5 secs after you press bass/treble if you want to change the volume. I would have preferred a quicker way to change the Master Volume, maybe by pressing the Bass/Treble button a third time?

Room for Improvement!
* NFC! Easy to implement and makes pairing an easy task.
* A remote? Maybe an IR port so I can use an APP? This thing gets loud and you can get very far from it.
* I don't know why they do not have dedicated Pause/Play Next/Previous Song Buttons! This is a serious omission!
* Bigger Battery! I've also read somewhere that they use older battery tech in this device, which makes no sense! Lithium Polymer all day!
* A Standard USB port to charge. AC Adapters should be reserved for battery-less devices. This is 2015 TDK!
* SD/Micro SD port for adding your own music, but this isn't necessary, just a welcome addition.
* Ability to Daisy Chain would be cool, also unnecessary.
* AM/FM Station, also unnecessary.
* An LED Display that can show the time, date, radio station, etc. Unnecessary but it would really give some extra functionality.

Conclusion
I purchased the Anker Premium Stereo hoping that it would end my hunt for the best portable speaker, but this went on sale literally 5 days after. I have never seen this product, nor have I known that TDK made speakers! This is especially strange because I have been hunting for speakers for about 2 months now, and have seen a fair number of brands, styles, and prices, but this caught me off guard through a well-known deal website. The sound coming out of this is phenomenal. Unfortunately, I cannot compare it to other portable devices due to my lack of experience with others, but I can say that it's better than the Anker Premium in Sound Quality. I do not mind the price I paid for this, but I would be hesitant if it was over $80 simply because that are more feature filled products above that price point. I'd be hard pressed to say that the sound can get better though; it can get to 85% of the quality of my Computer speakers (Logitech z-2300), and that is saying A-LOT. GOOD WORK TDK!

°°° Warranty/Customer Service. This can be make or break for me, but CS I don't have to contact is the best CS.

To start off, my headphone credentials are not that of an "audiophile" but I listen to music almost every day on multiple sets of headphones. In the past I have owned the Beats studio HD (1st edition), Beats in-ear headphones, Skullcandy Skull Crushers, Beats Mixrs, Bose QC15, Powerbeats wireless, and the Beats Studio Wireless. Of that list of headphones, I was never satisfied with a pair of headphones until the Bose. Both pairs of Beats had just "eh" sound and terrible build quality. Both pairs were broken, replaced, and returned at least once until I bought the Bose close to 6 years ago. Unfortunately, the headphones finally showed they were made of earthly materials as the speakers began to crackle and fade. After a couple weeks of research, I finally decided to take a leap of faith and go with another pair of Beats. I recently purchased the Powerbeats wireless and they really made me re-evaluate my opinion of Beats. Whether it was the buyout by Apple or years of negative reviews, it seems as if the company finally decided to make a change. Now that I've had the Studios for a few days, I figured I'd share my first opinions:

Build:
Much better than the 1st edition of the headphones, as they feel much more solid and a lot less plastic feel. The outer layer feels like a metal substance while all clasps/enclosures feel like metal as well. The ear cushions are made of a comfortable and soft leather. The headband is a simple rubber band with a little air pocket/pad inside. This is the main area for concern for me as this was the big problem I had in Beats past, but only time will tell.

Comfort:
One of, if not the main reason I gave the product 4 stars. The materials used are solid as listed above, but the total weight of the product is definitely felt after a little while of usage. The headband is the biggest problem so far, as it feels like someone is pressing their thumb to the top of your skull while you wear them. I've found a few different areas on the top of my head that are a little more comfortable, but regardless I find myself adjusting them every 20 minutes or so. The ear cushions are a nicer feeling leather but aren't big or deep enough to completely encase your ears. It isn't noticeable until a half hour or so, but the combination of the small ear holes and how the speakers stick out to the point they touch your ears, leaves your ears hot and hurting. While this may not be as big as a problem for some people, I'm used to the extreme comfort of the Bose QC 15's which aren't noticeable after 6 hours of use.

Sound:
Like I said, I'm not the most qualified to give a review on sound, but I know enough and have heard enough headphones to understand the difference in sound and quality. This is where Beats truly surprised me. The first generation headphones were nothing more than mediocre which caused waves of negative reviews. In the second outing by Beats, they really stepped up their game and put out a pair of headphones that are well balanced through the lows, mids, and highs. With the Bose, I always felt like there was something missing with the lows, and Beats really did a good job bringing down the low levels and balancing them out. Overall they do sound a little heavy, but the mids and highs are still crisp and evident whether listening to classic music or watching movies.

Wireless:
The main reason I went with the Beats Wireless. The Powerbeats wireless made me realize how annoying wires can be especially moving around or doing something as simple as laying in bed. The bluetooth works well and smoothly with minimal problems so far. The headphones quickly recognize the last device you were using with them and transition to another device quickly. Definitely puts the product above the competition.

Noise Canceling:
Nothing special here. The noise canceling isn't very noticeable compared to the QC15's which are still the best noise canceling for the price out there. I really do wish there was an option to use the headphones without noise canceling to save battery but then the sound quality would probably go down as well. The noise canceling in these headphones is by no means something to brag about, but a nice feature as it most likely improves audio quality etc.

Overall:
I've had the headphones for only a few days, but I really enjoy them. The big thing to me is the price. I was able to score these for 225 new on a prime deal. For 380, I wouldn't buy them. I put them at the 300 price range like the Bose or non-wireless Studios, but for 225, it was definitely a steal. The sound of the headphone, to me, was and upgrade from the Bose, but the comfort and lack of noise canceling was definitely a let down for sure. I didn't expect the noise canceling to be anything near Bose (which make those the great headphones they are), but the comfort was a big turn off for the headphones. The overall build of the headphones was a nice surprise, but the big win in these headphones was the wireless feature. I loved my Bose and would buy another pair if the price were the same as these, but the lack of wireless really was annoying at times especially when I have a life proof case which means you have to use an adapter to even use the headphones. The wireless means no adapter and no wires. All in all, the headphones were an amazing buy for the price, and if you can buy them for anything near (I saw the blue pair was around 260) they're definitely worth it, but unfortunately I had to give them 4 stars solely for the discomfort I have when wearing them.

This product does exactly what I wanted to do, and at a great $39.99 price as of the time I paid for it. There are a total of 5 HDMI input ports that you can hook into it, + one HDMI output port that you would most likely be connecting to your HDTV. Personally, I'm only using 4 of the 5 as of now because I only have 4 devices that need HDMI: my Wii U, PS3, PS4, and AT&T U-Verse TV box. All of them work great with no glitches, quirkiness, reduced quality, or any of that.

Each of the 5 inputs are labeled 'Input 1', 'Input 2', 'Input 3', and so on up to 5. There's a button on the device itself called "Switch" that you can press to sequentially switch through all of your available connected devices. However, this product also comes with a very cool and small remote that lets you control the switches from it via Infrared signals. The remote has up/down arrow buttons that respectively increment and decrement the current HDMI input device you're on. However, it gets a little bit better as there are also 5 other buttons on the remote (numbered 1-5) which map to your 5 HDMI input devices. This lets you freely control which HDMI device you want to display without having to use the linear up/down arrows or the 'Switch' button itself on the device. There's also 1 more button on the remote called "Memory". When you press the Memory button, Kinivo remembers the current HDMI device that is being displayed, such that whenever you turn your HDTV on, Kinivo will automatically switch to the remembered HDMI device. I haven't tried this feature yet so I can't comment on how good it works but it sounds promising.

Last thing I want to touch on is what I mentioned in my review title. This device has two interesting auto-switch features that can be either handy or annoying depending on the context of your usage. Firstly, when you turn on a device that is connected to your Kinivo, Kinivo will recognize this and automatically switch the currently displayed HDMI device to the new one that was just turned on. i.e. You're currently watching TV, and you turn on your game system that's connected to your Kinivo. Kinivo will automatically switch to displaying the game system. As I said above, depending on the context of your usage, this feature can either be very useful or very annoying because maybe you didn't want to play your game system at that point in time. Maybe you were just turning it on now in order to play it later. Secondly, if you turn off the device that is currently being displayed on your HDTV, Kinivo will recognize this and automatically switch to the next available sequential HDMI input. Using the above example, let's say your TV box was Input 2, and your game system was Input 3. If you're currently watching TV, and you decide to turn your TV box off, Kinivo will automatically switch to the next available sequential HDMI input, which in this case would be Input 3, the game system. Again, it largely depends on the context of your usage, but this can also be either very useful or annoying.

All in all, I'm still giving this 5 stars because the auto-switch features aren't that big of a deal. Even if Kinivo auto switches to an HDMI device that you do not want displayed, you can always just whip out your remote and change it back. I am not a snob about sound quality, and I purchased this record player because I wanted something portable. This thing is as portable and compact (10lbs) and the speakers are loud. But this product is flawed and will leave many dissatisfied.

First, let's focus on the main features offered by this player, as it would be very unfair to judge this product based on qualities that it cannot promise or provide:

The trouble starts when you turn the thing on. The turntable is extremely loud as it spins. It isn't one of those free spinning tables that generates it's own momentum and rotates silently. Every rotation sounds like an incredible undertaking for the meager motor inside the turntable. The sound it produces is like grinding, and there is a repetitive clicking noise as it goes around. These are mechanical sounds I'm talking about. You can hear them across the room even when there is no record on the turntable. In the audio output, this sound manifests as rumbling, so the record player is not only generating loud mechanical noise but also distorting the audio. I also noticed some minor pitch and speed distortion as the arm gets closer to the center of the record.

Many have commented that the player has no lift arm, meaning that you must manually drop and remove the needle each time you listen to a record. If you haven't owned a record player before, you should know that this is a hassle, and will basically guarantee that those who do not know how to use record players will scratch and damage your albums if they try to operate this thing. I bought it thinking it has an automatic stop function, but THE AUTOMATIC STOP DOES NOT WORK PROPERLY. It will reliably stop your record about 10-20 seconds before it has finished, meaning the end of the song will be cut off. This is especially annoying with 45s. So forget about the automatic functions on this one. There are many cheaper record players that have such automatic functions, so I can't understand why they don't exist/work on this Crosley.

If not for these mechanical flaws, I might be willing to give this product as high as four stars based on what it sets out to accomplish.

Now for the sound:

The speakers are loud, but they also sound muffled. There is no way to adjust the treble or bass. As it is, these speakers will make it sound like your favorite old songs are being suffocated under a pillow.

If you hook it up to the phono output or headphones, the sound quality is actually pretty good, but if you are going to use such external output, you might well invest in something higher quality or not even buy something with built-in speakers.

The USB output is, when compared with comparable products, not bad. Many low-end USB turntables fail to generate output that is loud enough to make a good recording. This one certainly produces a loud output. However, like most other USB turntables, the output is not good enough that you would ever listen to it if there is a professionally produced digital version or CD available. If you have any piece of vinyl rare enough to not have a digital copy extant, then it is probably your duty to humanity and music history to find a better way to digitize it.

This brings me to a larger point about the low quality of this turntable, which may be shared by others in its class.

The main reason to buy vinyl is that it offers a special tone and quality that you can't get from digital recordings. I was born in the 80s, so I grew up around my father's records but had been essentially raised by cassettes and digital recordings. I fell in love with listening to vinyl after buying a high-end German-made Dual turntable from the 1970s. It is able to produce a very bright and rich sound. It never skips. It brings old music to life in a way that I had never heard it. It fills the room and changes the entire atmosphere.

This Crosley, by contrast, makes your records sound old and dead. They won't sound like those classics of the 70s that were once played on large sound systems with wooden speakers. When played through the portable speakers, this Crosley turntable sounds more like a beat up phonograph from the 1930s or a cassette boombox than anything we expect from vinyl today.

If you are buying newly-pressed vinyl, THIS PLAYER will not make it sound as good as whatever you can get off iTunes.

This leads to another issue. The records play if they are in mint condition, but the arm is pretty cheap, and records with scratches that might play fine on other turntables will skip on this model. If you're out gathering vinyl of the more obscure, old, and discarded variety, this turntable may not meet your needs, as it will not handle scratches and other issues very well.

I bought this turntable for its portability. I knew that would entail sacrifices. I know that some of the shortcomings of this player are sacrifices made to lower costs and increase portability. However, given what I have said above about its mechanisms and features, I feel that this player is sloppily designed or inadequately tested. It is hard for me to give Crosley the benefit of the doubt given those unnecessary flaws.

Here are the problems you will most likely come across within the first year or two of ownership:  1. The black (vinyl?) insulation will start splitting and distorting/stretching exposing the internal wires to the outside.This will happen near the earbuds themselves but also any where along the cord. If you have a large external acoustic meatus (opening to the ear canal) then the tips supplied will not give you the bass you are expecting to hear. Etymotic's only solution is a bright yellow foam plug that needs to be replaced often. Buy many beforehand. Once they were out of stock for a month and I was without portable music for that time period.  3. The slider that pulls the left and right cord closer together will bind because, as described in part one, the insulation distorts preventing the slider from sliding. If you don't use this feature, then it's not a problem. Just don't pull it up as you may have some difficulty getting it to slide down and end up tearing the insulation around the cord.  On the whole these headphones just don't hold up for long. It's a pity as they do sound very good. Extremely neutral sounding but do have some breakup with only the deepest bass notes. However, due to their short longevity, I would not recommend buying them. There are many other choices that are more robust and sound as good for the same price.

I was provided with a free copy of this item for testing and my fair and honest evaluation.  Of course receiving something for free may impact any review, but I can honestly say this is a solid product and worth the cost listed here. I have used it in my office both as a charger and speaker.  Packaging -  shipped in solid packaging that was padded well, there is no way this should be damaged in shipping.  Comes with the charging cable and a cloth bag for carrying and keeping from dust.  Ease of setup - Charged it for the recommended time of two hours and easily got 8-10 hours of use before recharging.  Powered up and started the pairing process, which connected without a hitch on the first try.  Have not had any issues connecting via bluetooth at any point.  I have not figured out the NFC option, but I am confident that is user error, and not really necessary.  Buttons/Features - Has power, phone, play/pause, and volume or track buttons.  I will say that everything works as advertised, but remembering the button combination to make things work takes a little bit of a learning curve.  It is as simple as pressing or long pressing combinations, but if I had a complaint, I wish that I didnt have to think before pressing, but not a deal breaker.  I like the ability to answer my phone while listening to music.  This comes in handy when at the office and having hands free talking that seems to be clear enough.  The sound through the speaker for calls is plenty clear, and nobody has complained when I have used this method to talk with them.  Sound Quality - This is not a surround sound experience, and sound at maximum volumes isn't as rich as a high dollar audio system.  (I have edited this portion of the review)  The speaker is surprisingly loud, and I have yet to have a need to turn the sound all the way upother than for testing.  All of my testing has been done with an LG G3 phone connected to the speaker, and a Asus Chromebook.  I would rate the sound quality a 4 of 5 considering the size and a 3 - 5 if I was just rating pure sound quality regardless of price.  I think it is important to consider what you are using.  If I wanted a high dollar sound system, I would not be buying this device.  For the market of portable bluetooth speakers I would say the sound quality is very good.  Use as a Power Bank - I think this is probably the feature that has me most interested in buying a second unit.  When at my office, my desk is small and the compact speaker size is great, add the sound from that compact space and the device is solid.  Add to it that I can give my phone a fast charge when needed is a nice bonus.  The manual also claims that you can connect more than one speaker together.  I have a feeling I will be buying a second speaker to keep at home so this one can stay at my office.  I will test this out and edit the review if I do end up buying a second one.  I also will get a video review posted as time allows and after using it for a little longer.  Overall, this is a quality device.  I have bought a few other Sharkk products and so far I have not had any issues with their products. Bose's VideoWave line of systems truly show how surprising it is that all the immersive sound is coming from just the screen.

Speakers on the back of the display bounce the sound to the sides creating the illusion that there is a surround sound system installed even though there isn't any speakers mounted at the walls.

While this technology sounds very pleasing and definitely deserves some attention, the VideoWave product line never survives for long (They barely last a year on the shelves) since it fails commercially every time due the ever-changing smart TV market. I find that very strange due to the fact the VideoWave was never meant to critically compete in the general TV market anyway, rather it is only marketed as a surround sound system embedded in a display if your home theater architecture doesn't let you mount speakers in easily.

I would really love it if Bose continued selling the VideoWave products (They probably have a surplus of them left, anyway) or even start making a newer model as these are very hard to find now due to their heavily limited shelf life. If you find one up for sale, consider yourself lucky.

Just trying to bring a balanced review here. I have multiple bluetooth speakers and Sonos speakers, so in terms of the bluetooth speakers I'll compare this to the original Jambox and the JBL flip. There is no way anyone could honestly compare the sound quality of the Oontz Curve to the JBL flip which is much louder, has more bass and much better sound quality or the Jambox which although not louder has more bass and better sound quality. Also keep in mind that the Oontz is a single mono speaker (not a big deal since in speakers this small placing separate drivers a couple of inches apart doesn't give much separation either. By itself I would give the Oontz the following pluses and minuses:

Pros:

Seems to be well built and pleasantly styled.
Sound quality isn't horrible considering how small it is, it beats any cellphone or ipad speaker and probably all but a few laptops.
I was surprised at how long the battery lasts, the manual claims 2.5-3 hours at full volume, at a bit above medium I've had it playing for over 5 hours
It's nice to have the pause and track controls along with the volume control
A real plus to have a speakerphone built in so if your phone rings you can just answer it at the speaker.

Cons:

You must repair every time you connect it to a new product. Not a big deal, but a bit of a pain.
Would have been nice to have included a small pouch for travel
Not the quietest, there is some hiss that is normally covered by the music playing.

So why am I giving it a 5? Because it's tiny, sounds pretty good and it only costs a few dollars. It's the perfect size for travel as opposed to the Jambox and Flip, and unlike the Flip it recharges with a standard microUSB so you can charge it with most cellphone chargers or your laptop's usb ports when you travel so that you don't have to carry yet another charger. All in all this does exactly what it claims to do at an extremely reasonable price. This is my first review on Amazon, although i have been their customer for 10 years. just to show you how i love this product!

My goal
wanted earphones better than the ones that came with my iPhone 6 for the office, they need to be light and have good sound isolation to not bother people next to me, also going to use them several times a year as i travel a lot. and yeah i love bass! i listen to rock only. On the other hand i wanted something for 100$ or less.

Design and weight
they look really nice, specially compared to typical looking earphones or the ones that come bundled with your mobile. the glossy finish with silver details are amazing, i wouldn't say they are heavy, compared to my iPhone 6 (white) earphones they are a bit heavier putting on mind the size of the 16mm drivers it's expected, but nothing to worry about! amazing for the office and travel as they are so practical .

Included stuff
even the empty box looks nice lol! they have a really nice light black case to keep them safe, has two little mesh pockets for all the extra earbuds, as it comes included with 6! 3 are the regular ones in small,medium and large, the other 3 look identical but have the grey foam-like material for isolation which is inside the earbud and not visible to anyone, they also come in 3 sizes small, medium and large. On the other hand comes with a Japanese manual which for most is useless, but what would u need a manual for? and a nice little black plastic clip for your shirt.

Sound
Okay just so you know i am an audiophile, been like that for at least as long as i remember (20+ years) i have tried at least 10 different types and sizes of headphones/earphones, and i will simply tell you for their size and price nothing matches them, am sure up to at least double the price you can't find something better, the bass is solid, punchy, articulate and if i could say detailed, the mid frequencies are a bit calm and neutral nothing in your face or too harsh, the treble is a bit harsh (but i like them! remind me of Klipsch (horn) speakers!) specially for metal and rock. not too harsh that are tiring after a while. I have the 1st gen studio beats and the marshall monitor headphones and i can tell you they are much cleaner sounding and have more accurate bass (not boomy) than the beats! which are like 3 times the price. one more thing which might be important, they do sound louder than my iPhone earphones by at least 25%(i don't use an amp just connected directly to my phone) i now listen to most of my music like 4 clicks from max, while i used to listen 1 click near max volume. not only that but the louder you go the better they sound (it's like having an amp = very low distortion nearly inaudible)

Fit
they look tricky to wear but they are really easy, just stick them in your earholes! simple as that, they go right in which is great so it also isolates the sound even without wearing the isolated earbuds, and are really comfy, my size was medium (the ones that come fitted on it out of the box)

Cons?
I would only say no mic, nothing else really, but not a big deal if your going to use them for your tab,ipad,laptop or ipod. Also they were released by Sony Japan so they come usually shipped from Japan to the US which might take at least a week.

I definitely recommend them, come on they are only 85$ and for what they do it's really a good deal.

From the reviews of the Tomameri portable players (they sell this same player in 8, 16, and 32GB versions), this seems to be a love it or hate it type of product - which might come down to your expectations before you get it. Let me try to help with that - this is not a super-high-quality piece of hardware. The plastic pieces seem kind of cheap, and the ear buds aren't very nice. However, the aluminum case is actually pretty decent, the Micro SD card seems about as well made as others that I've bought, and the mini USB cable (yes, it charges with mini USB versus the more prevalent micro USB) is surprisingly nice. Audio performance is pretty decent, but don't expect much from the video. I gave the 16GB version four stars but am giving this one three stars because I don't think it's as good of a value at the current $36 price (more on that below).

If I were looking for something like this for myself or anyone that didn't destroy electronics quickly (like a young child), I'd heavily consider just using an older (or even new) smart phone - because most of those will do everything that this does but do it MUCH better. Bigger screen, probably as much memory (but maybe requiring a micro SD card)...and so on. If you wanted to get a young child their first music player and didn't want to risk having something more expensive get busted, this might not be a bad choice...because odds are you won't mind if this gets broken. I don't mean that in a mean way to this player - I'm just saying that I think it falls squarely into the niche of disposable products. This is exactly the kind of product that I wouldn't mind taking on a plane trip because it sounds pretty good and because I wouldn't be upset if I lost it or broke it...inexpensive hardware like this definitely has a place.

I do want to point out that the lower memory size Tomameri players are currently a better deal, with the 8GB version being only $14 right now ($22 cheaper at current prices). When you do your shopping, if you decide that you want one of these players - I highly recommend that you check the other models. The ONLY difference (that I can tell, and I have the 16GB and 32GB models) is the memory card. Even the sample files that come on them are the same. You can buy 32GB micro SD cards faster than the one that comes with this product for under $15, so it might pay off to get the cheapest version out there and then get a separate card for it. I gave the 16GB model four stars because it was a pretty good value even with its flaws, but this 32GB version is currently $36 - and you can buy pay-as-you-go smart phones for similar or even less money that will beat this player (just don't activate the phone service and use the \\"phone\\" as a media player). For example, the Moto G for Verizon prepaid seems to often be under $40.

Although not the best value, I still think it's worthy of three stars even at the current $36 price tag because:
(*) First, you get some individual pieces that are useful with or without the player, most notably the 32 GB Micro SD card that would cost you around $10 by itself
(*) Speaking of the memory card, I love that this player uses one instead of needing to sync up with a computer to load files onto it. That is more convenient to me than my iPods that sync up with iTunes
(*) Next, it actually works pretty darn well for audio - the internal amp isn't half bad and powered my larger headphones just fine, and the voice recorder worked quite well once I went into the menu and changed the recording quality. I was surprised by how well the audio sounded on this
(*) Charges pretty fast, and battery life isn't too bad, either
(*) Small and lightweight

Now, for some of the detractors:
(*) Although it has the look of an older iPod Nano, which I happen to own and have used for years, it doesn't operate like one. The wheel on the front doesn't respond to you sliding your finger along it like a Nano does, but rather just mimics the look of it while requiring you to click on it. The four labeled areas on the wheel are essentially four separate buttons, with a fifth button under the circle in the center of the wheel. If you've never owned a Nano with the scroll wheel, likely none of that will matter to you
(*) The \\"MP4\\" player part is a little misleading, as this will not play regular .MP4 files. It plays .AMV files, which I'd never heard of until I got this and tried to load video files onto it
(*) The screen is okay quality, but it's tiny - you shouldn't expect to ever use this as an E-Book reader like mentioned in the product title. Watching a video might work okay if you decide to convert your files into AMV files
(*) The menu system can be a little tedious. Okay, make that a lot tedious
(*) Charges with a mini USB cable, which might be less common in your house/car/luggage than a micro USB cable used by pretty much every other piece of electronics these days

In summary, this is a disposable piece of hardware that has surprisingly good audio quality, probably useless video capability to most people, a slightly aggravating menu system, and a Micro SD card that you can use for something else if you decide to chuck the player into the garbage. If it was $10, I'd be recommending it for the spare parts alone because the 32GB card is pretty decent if not the fastest out there. At $36, it's not a horrible deal...but it's not a great deal, either. Seriously, check out inexpensive smart phones and see if they'll be a better fit for you.

The Disc ID on these discs is MEI-T01-001.  That means Panasonic made them and not CMC.  Unlike the last MEI BD-RE's I had, some branded by Maxell, that were rated 2x, these actually wrote at 2x!  The Maxell's only wrote at 1x max.  The fact that CMC did not make these is the biggest reason I have these 4 stars.  Verbatim, TDK, and JVC Victor BD-RE were all made by CMC.  CMC is CMC Magnetics, the worst manufacturer of optical media out there.  Their DVD recordable products are notorious for their high failure rates.  CMC makes things cheap so most manufacturers farm out their optical products to CMC.  Even Verbatim, which used to make their own high quality BD-RE, now farms out to CMC for their BD-RE.  Verbatim still makes quality products but most of them are only under the DataLife Plus series.  Their Life series CD-R and DVD-R are, yes, you guessed it, CMC made.  I've not had a chance to see the quality of playback on these media.  I've only burned a DVD-5 DVD-Video image to one as a test.  I was mostly concerned it wouldn't write at 2x, but it did.  It wrote and verified in ImgBurn in my Pioneer Blu-Ray drive fine.  I don't have an inkjet label capable printer so I can't test the quality of printing to the inkjet label surface on these media.  If I were to get more BD-RE's, I'd definitely go to these first over the CMC junk from Verbatim, TDK, and JVC Victor.   EDIT 02-01-2016: I wrote this review August 22, 2015.  It's been less than a year and I've already gotten my first failure.  After only 1 write, the 2nd write failed to Verify towards the end of the disc in ImgBurn.  This does not bode well for the quality of these discs.  I'm not ready to call these junk just yet, though.  Could be just 1 failure out of the bunch.  If I get more, I'll have to reserve the right to deduct stars from my review.

First dive into premium, more expensive headphones.  At first I considered Beats, and only Beats, because many audiophiles describe other-than-Beats-and-VModa headphones are bass-empty, sort of. After reading many negative reviews about the Beats, I took my excitement elsewhere: V-Moda; but then there was a lot mentioned about it being uncomfortable and needing an amp to deliver so I took (my excitement) to the first gen' of Sennheiser Momentums; those too, had comfort issues, in fact their ear-cups were too small for over-ear headphones.   So I decided to settle for the M2's. 240-something for a pair of headphones which I don't particularly like, or didn't at first. Did my homework and was disappointed to find a lack of in depth reviewing about these. Still, decided I'd be better off ordering them based off the few reviews I watched/read about them.  Only Lord knows how excited I was about this purchase. Did I expect heaven from a mere technological device?  Straight out of the box, I plugged them into my iPod–no time for "burn-in", and listened to the few songs which musical arrangement I was already very familiar with, to see how well these will perform.   The first thing that stood out to me  was the mid-bass. Very subwoofer like, in fact I read somewhere that there's a subwoofer in these cans. Very pleasing, especially since it was the first time I experienced that quality sub-bass through headphones.   The upper-bass was also quite astounding. I like to think of it as a bubble: Thinly layered; only that  this layer is thin, yet very strong in that it handles impact well, paradoxically. That's how intriguing the bass was to me. And for the first time I finally understood what people meant by clean, crisp, non muddy,non overpowering bass. It wasn't Beats-bass heavy, or your-average-headphones-bass heavy, but it was really pleasing to listen to, so pleasing I never listened to music past 50% the first days of listening.   The mids were good but not particularly fantastic; same for the lows. Often time the instruments in the "far back" would "mesh" into each other.  Unfortunately the infatuation was cut short.   I started getting extremely annoyed at the mid-bass, which would often time ruin my enjoyment of songs I was listening to. See, midbass is one of those things which appeals because it's novel to the ear, but as you get used to it, it becomes quite boring; not to mention midbass doesn't have a rich texture, it's not complex–therefore not very engaging So you can see how annoying it would be having it pumped in your ears in an obvious, overpowered, manner.    Also, the upper bass could hardly keep up with the midbass, felt delayed, slow, softer-than-should-be at times.    The vocals also felt a little bright and "accelerated" at times. A slow upper-bass, a "loud"–but loose mid-bass and bright, accelerated vocals, made my music sound badly arranged.    I searched everywhere to see if others had the same opinions, but while some other people don't like these headpones, they dislike it for reasons different than mine. For that reason I returned these as defective. Will keep looking around to make sense of my experience with these.  I will give these 3 stars because they're ok, for casual use, instead of casual-critical listening or (full blown) critical listening. Again maybe it was just mine.  Edit: Now I remember exactly why I started hating these headphones after a short while: In addition to everything I mentioned above, the strong emphasis on the mid-bass (and percussion) revealed the "baseline" of the genres I listened to. After listening to 4 songs who have the same drums patterns, and same mid-bass patterns–and after having that sameness all up in your ears in such a blatant manner disgusted me; And that bored me to death, almost making me regret the very idea of making playlists. In a way it was eye-opening though; I love patterns (that's why I create playlists which have the same overall vibe), but at the same time I grow tired of said pattern if it's presented to me in a blatant way. I just realized this by listening to music with my ATH 900X; I picked a few songs which I'd listen to by only focusing on the mid-bass, then, upon realizing I wouldn't have to pick more than one song as they all have the same mid-bass, told myself it wasn't so bad afterall that the ATH had a subtler mid-bass. Then these just came back to my mind straight away.

This does technically work, but has a few flaws that led to it being my first Amazon return after well over a decade.

The two biggest offenders:

1. There's no output power switch.
2. The same input is used to adjust magnitude and value in current and voltage.

It's really easy for a simple adjustment to accidentally supply tremendous power surges. e.g. I wanted to check to see how low I could take voltage on a LED on my desk. I reached up to adjust the voltage magnitude (press voltage dial). It jumped to the tens place *and* interpreted my press as a rotation and increased the voltage by 10V. This kills the component. Because you can't cut output while making these adjustments, you just have to be incredibly careful to not have anything that can be detected as rotation in your button presses, especially in the higher magnitudes.

I replaced mine with [[ASIN:B0085QLNFM KORAD KA3005P - Programmable Precision Variable Adjustable 30V, 5A DC Linear Power Supply Digital Regulated Lab Grade]] which is just barely more expensive but much safer to operate (and has a lot more features).

I purchased 5 of these to power hobby projects.  I was using three constantly for about a month and two of them failed and one would have failed within a very short time had I not unplugged it.  When I opened the case on the one that had not failed I could see the electrolytic capacitor bulging.  The problem is a small surface mount resistor on the back of the circuit board, marked 680, which means it's 68 ohms.  It across the 9V output of the power adapter.  It's a 1/8 watt device that's dissipating more than a watt.  It gets extremely hot and kills the power adapter.  I've modified all 5 of the ones that I bought by removing this 68 ohm resistor and replacing it with a through hole 1/8 watt 2.2K ohm resistor as well as the damaged electrolytic capacitors.  They all work just fine now.  The adapter is easy to open and work on but won't last the way it's delivered.  I fixed them because they were past the 30 day return period but they work just fine now.  I figured the 680 marking on the part may have been mistaken for a 680 ohm resistor which would have just made it under the 1/8 watt power handling capability of the resistor.  Maybe it would have worked OK at 680 ohms.

(Updated Note: Been putting this through its paces the past few weeks: my summation on its performance/battery life is, it's fantastic, sound-wise, well, it's quite good, if not earth-shatteringly great. If you're not expecting some mind-blowingly loud system, or wall-shaking bass, this will do fine, if you are, I suggest you look elsewhere. This Altec delivers good sound but I wouldn't say it's anything audiophile, obviously, and I notice if you push it a bit too hard, the cabinet tends to vibrate or distort a bit, but generally, you really have to push it pretty hard and pretty loud. Mainly I'm digging it, it just sits on my bookcase and lets me stream music for hours  while the PC is freed up for other things, you know, like ranting and raving on Amazon.)  I notice Marshall is putting out beefier Bluetooth systems and if you really want something 100-200  watts or more, I might check those out first. The LJackets are  better for portable use, or for where you don't need a high-power high-output system that still sounds good and listenable. And who wants a mono speaker system? Not I.  I had nearly zero plans to buy a bluetooth speaker, given I have 3 systems in my apt. already, including Alesis monitors for the PC and other things, but, I had credit suddenly at a certain retail store, and saw these and demo'd a few, and I liked the idea of being able to truly put the Iphone/Spotify into heavier use, at home anyway, given if you use it on the go you eat the battery and run down your data plan for the month, which is absurd.  I also don't like tying up the laptop with apps. (unless I'm using it on the day for a specific media reason--I do have a Kindle Fire but don't use that often, but I suppose I could use that with these, also) it just slows it all down, so this seemed like a good solution, theory being, let the Altec handle the music duties, dedicated, most of the time. Plus I needed something where it wouldn't necessarily blast the walls with bass all the time,or late nights.  I've got great headphones too, but sometimes you wanna hear it live and let it rip!  I've only had it a few hours, but unpacking it, it worked fine right out o' the box, I have had no recognition pairing issues, thus far, sounds fine, paired immediately, plugged it in, and was instantly playing music from the phone. It seems pretty rugged, it's a simple device to get up and going, I just hope I don't encounter the issues that others have complained about on here.  So far, so good, I think it's well worth the money.  There are a myriad of Bluetooth audio systems and alarm clocks and all sorts of nonsense out now, from something in this price range upwards of $5-600 for a Marshall or top of the line Bose or whatever. I dunno, if you aren't expecting a full-size system, 5.1 sound, or really just want good sound and total portability and waterproof, etc., this seems like the type of thing to go for.  The female pairing chick bot voice (! Ms. Lansing?) was a bit overpowering, but hey, at least it's audible and I was just glad it worked first time out. "It's 5 o'clock and time for your penguin/AL device to pair up and explode."  Not.  I had a pair of Altec Lansing PC speakers a number of years ago, that were fantastic, got them used and the bass on them was just phenomenal even without any subwoofer! I gave them away later, but they were outstanding. The only thing better were some later 5.1 Altec Dolby home theater with sub. (sadly the sub. cable input eventually fried), and my current Alesis monitors which also have tons of bass with no sub. at all.  But in an apt., sometimes this is overkill. If you really want an audiophile pair of PC speakers then go for something like AudioEngine or Yamaha monitors, but there's no need unless you need them for pro. use, or you're really that much of an audiophile nut.  Well, I sort of am, but not that much so.  The Altec is fine for every day listening, and the Alesis are a bargain for the money for more critical listening applications. So far, these don't sound tinny to me at all, but playing through the phone which often sound "flat", as Apple devices often do, and at a moderate volume thus far. The store demo machine set to drum/bass dance music, and the bass was impressive for such a small speaker set.  I also noticed the smaller Lifejacket mini and H20 versions, which seem more for kids, shower, or for bicycling use, or the beach, or whatever. Those won't pump out much power but they should sound ok for outdoor usage, or work. Still, this Life Jacket 2 seems just muscular enough for any of these purposes.  The only thing that might've been nice is a radio function, but who cares, given you can play all that via your phone or tablet or PC these days. I haven't even looked at the instructions, that's how low-learning curve these are!  Packaging is pretty attractive and sturdy itself. It makes you just want to take a look at it on the store shelf out of sheer curiosity. Red or blue, take yer choice. It comes with full mounting bracket kit, instruction booklet, minijack 1/8" connector, USB and AC adapter.  Add your device or audio source of choice, and you are good to go.  If I have any issues I'll come back and update, but thus far, the Life Jacket 2 is a winner for me. They had other sort of boombox systems as well in-store, but the brand was unfamiliar, and I don't like that at all. I know Altec makes a solid product, so I rolled the dice. Or rather, hoped I wasn't!  I'm giving it four stars for now.

From the reviews of the Tomameri portable players (they sell this same player in 8, 16, and 32GB versions), this seems to be a love it or hate it type of product - which might come down to your expectations before you get it. Let me try to help with that - this is not a super-high-quality piece of hardware. The plastic pieces seem kind of cheap, and the ear buds aren't very nice. However, the aluminum case is actually pretty decent, the Micro SD card seems about as well made as others that I've bought, and the mini USB cable (yes, it charges with mini USB versus the more prevalent micro USB) is surprisingly nice. Audio performance is pretty decent, but don't expect much from the video. I gave the 16GB version four stars but am giving this one three stars because I don't think it's as good of a value at the current $36 price (more on that below).

If I were looking for something like this for myself or anyone that didn't destroy electronics quickly (like a young child), I'd heavily consider just using an older (or even new) smart phone - because most of those will do everything that this does but do it MUCH better. Bigger screen, probably as much memory (but maybe requiring a micro SD card)...and so on. If you wanted to get a young child their first music player and didn't want to risk having something more expensive get busted, this might not be a bad choice...because odds are you won't mind if this gets broken. I don't mean that in a mean way to this player - I'm just saying that I think it falls squarely into the niche of disposable products. This is exactly the kind of product that I wouldn't mind taking on a plane trip because it sounds pretty good and because I wouldn't be upset if I lost it or broke it...inexpensive hardware like this definitely has a place.

I do want to point out that the lower memory size Tomameri players are currently a better deal, with the 8GB version being only $14 right now ($22 cheaper at current prices). When you do your shopping, if you decide that you want one of these players - I highly recommend that you check the other models. The ONLY difference (that I can tell, and I have the 16GB and 32GB models) is the memory card. Even the sample files that come on them are the same. You can buy 32GB micro SD cards faster than the one that comes with this product for under $15, so it might pay off to get the cheapest version out there and then get a separate card for it. I gave the 16GB model four stars because it was a pretty good value even with its flaws, but this 32GB version is currently $36 - and you can buy pay-as-you-go smart phones for similar or even less money that will beat this player (just don't activate the phone service and use the \\"phone\\" as a media player). For example, the Moto G for Verizon prepaid seems to often be under $40.

Although not the best value, I still think it's worthy of three stars even at the current $36 price tag because:
(*) First, you get some individual pieces that are useful with or without the player, most notably the 32 GB Micro SD card that would cost you around $10 by itself
(*) Speaking of the memory card, I love that this player uses one instead of needing to sync up with a computer to load files onto it. That is more convenient to me than my iPods that sync up with iTunes
(*) Next, it actually works pretty darn well for audio - the internal amp isn't half bad and powered my larger headphones just fine, and the voice recorder worked quite well once I went into the menu and changed the recording quality. I was surprised by how well the audio sounded on this
(*) Charges pretty fast, and battery life isn't too bad, either
(*) Small and lightweight

Now, for some of the detractors:
(*) Although it has the look of an older iPod Nano, which I happen to own and have used for years, it doesn't operate like one. The wheel on the front doesn't respond to you sliding your finger along it like a Nano does, but rather just mimics the look of it while requiring you to click on it. The four labeled areas on the wheel are essentially four separate buttons, with a fifth button under the circle in the center of the wheel. If you've never owned a Nano with the scroll wheel, likely none of that will matter to you
(*) The \\"MP4\\" player part is a little misleading, as this will not play regular .MP4 files. It plays .AMV files, which I'd never heard of until I got this and tried to load video files onto it
(*) The screen is okay quality, but it's tiny - you shouldn't expect to ever use this as an E-Book reader like mentioned in the product title. Watching a video might work okay if you decide to convert your files into AMV files
(*) The menu system can be a little tedious. Okay, make that a lot tedious
(*) Charges with a mini USB cable, which might be less common in your house/car/luggage than a micro USB cable used by pretty much every other piece of electronics these days

In summary, this is a disposable piece of hardware that has surprisingly good audio quality, probably useless video capability to most people, a slightly aggravating menu system, and a Micro SD card that you can use for something else if you decide to chuck the player into the garbage. If it was $10, I'd be recommending it for the spare parts alone because the 32GB card is pretty decent if not the fastest out there. At $36, it's not a horrible deal...but it's not a great deal, either. Seriously, check out inexpensive smart phones and see if they'll be a better fit for you.

Basically it is lacking in the intuitiveness aspect.

At the price point it both offers more than expected and works better as well.

All of these worked exactly as expected and was playable through the device without any issue. All were also transferred over via drag and drop using a Windows 7 x64 based PC.

If the navigation were more intuitive and the headphones a little better quality 5 stars may be the rating but as is 3.5 stars...except Amazon doesn't allow half star ratings unfortunately so round up to a 4.

From the reviews of the Tomameri portable players (they sell this same player in 8, 16, and 32GB versions), this seems to be a love it or hate it type of product - which might come down to your expectations before you get it. Let me try to help with that - this is not a super-high-quality piece of hardware. The plastic pieces seem kind of cheap, and the ear buds aren't very nice. However, the aluminum case is actually pretty decent, the Micro SD card seems about as well made as others that I've bought, and the mini USB cable (yes, it charges with mini USB versus the more prevalent micro USB) is surprisingly nice. Audio performance is pretty decent, but don't expect much from the video. I gave the 16GB version four stars but am giving this one three stars because I don't think it's as good of a value at the current $36 price (more on that below).

If I were looking for something like this for myself or anyone that didn't destroy electronics quickly (like a young child), I'd heavily consider just using an older (or even new) smart phone - because most of those will do everything that this does but do it MUCH better. Bigger screen, probably as much memory (but maybe requiring a micro SD card)...and so on. If you wanted to get a young child their first music player and didn't want to risk having something more expensive get busted, this might not be a bad choice...because odds are you won't mind if this gets broken. I don't mean that in a mean way to this player - I'm just saying that I think it falls squarely into the niche of disposable products. This is exactly the kind of product that I wouldn't mind taking on a plane trip because it sounds pretty good and because I wouldn't be upset if I lost it or broke it...inexpensive hardware like this definitely has a place.

I do want to point out that the lower memory size Tomameri players are currently a better deal, with the 8GB version being only $14 right now ($22 cheaper at current prices). When you do your shopping, if you decide that you want one of these players - I highly recommend that you check the other models. The ONLY difference (that I can tell, and I have the 16GB and 32GB models) is the memory card. Even the sample files that come on them are the same. You can buy 32GB micro SD cards faster than the one that comes with this product for under $15, so it might pay off to get the cheapest version out there and then get a separate card for it. I gave the 16GB model four stars because it was a pretty good value even with its flaws, but this 32GB version is currently $36 - and you can buy pay-as-you-go smart phones for similar or even less money that will beat this player (just don't activate the phone service and use the \\"phone\\" as a media player). For example, the Moto G for Verizon prepaid seems to often be under $40.

Although not the best value, I still think it's worthy of three stars even at the current $36 price tag because:
(*) First, you get some individual pieces that are useful with or without the player, most notably the 32 GB Micro SD card that would cost you around $10 by itself
(*) Speaking of the memory card, I love that this player uses one instead of needing to sync up with a computer to load files onto it. That is more convenient to me than my iPods that sync up with iTunes
(*) Next, it actually works pretty darn well for audio - the internal amp isn't half bad and powered my larger headphones just fine, and the voice recorder worked quite well once I went into the menu and changed the recording quality. I was surprised by how well the audio sounded on this
(*) Charges pretty fast, and battery life isn't too bad, either
(*) Small and lightweight

Now, for some of the detractors:
(*) Although it has the look of an older iPod Nano, which I happen to own and have used for years, it doesn't operate like one. The wheel on the front doesn't respond to you sliding your finger along it like a Nano does, but rather just mimics the look of it while requiring you to click on it. The four labeled areas on the wheel are essentially four separate buttons, with a fifth button under the circle in the center of the wheel. If you've never owned a Nano with the scroll wheel, likely none of that will matter to you
(*) The \\"MP4\\" player part is a little misleading, as this will not play regular .MP4 files. It plays .AMV files, which I'd never heard of until I got this and tried to load video files onto it
(*) The screen is okay quality, but it's tiny - you shouldn't expect to ever use this as an E-Book reader like mentioned in the product title. Watching a video might work okay if you decide to convert your files into AMV files
(*) The menu system can be a little tedious. Okay, make that a lot tedious
(*) Charges with a mini USB cable, which might be less common in your house/car/luggage than a micro USB cable used by pretty much every other piece of electronics these days

In summary, this is a disposable piece of hardware that has surprisingly good audio quality, probably useless video capability to most people, a slightly aggravating menu system, and a Micro SD card that you can use for something else if you decide to chuck the player into the garbage. If it was $10, I'd be recommending it for the spare parts alone because the 32GB card is pretty decent if not the fastest out there. At $36, it's not a horrible deal...but it's not a great deal, either. Seriously, check out inexpensive smart phones and see if they'll be a better fit for you.

I use it the most in my car, however.  When used in conjunction with my FM Transmitter (also by Avantek,) I can listen to my mp3 player, tablet, or phone via my car stereo.  This is excellent, since my car lacks an auxilliary port.  I plug this into my FM Transmitter to give it Bluetooth connectivity and pair my phone or other device. I like this better than the former way of using my device in a car (through a tape deck "transmitter.)  My device remains free of wires and is easily accessable while I tuck my little Avantek Bluetooth transmitter out of the way.  I love it and highly recommend it. I have used one UPC or another for years, and swear by them. (Sell no computer without a UPS!) As I replace one with another possessing more outlets (that seems to be the direction of the world...), I migrate the older one downstream so that I now have all my electronics on battery, or at least surge protection. Only makes sense whenever you live in lightning country, or work with variable electrical supply (e.g., generators). I have never had a power or reliability problem with an APC unit. The price is very good.

I bought this Back-UPS 750G for its green features, as well as 10 clean outlets--look around your computer and count the surprising number of devices that require power (not overlooking modems and routers). I dare say the power supply side of this Back-UPS really is more efficient, but the Master/Controlled outlet business was a big disappointment. It ought to be the biggest contributor to saving electrical costs, but does not work for me. When my iMac computer is the Master and is put to sleep, it will turn off up to three Controlled peripherals, but as they are shutting off a few seconds later, some of them (external hard drive or printer) seem to send a signal to the computer that wakes it up again, which then turns the peripherals back on. This cycle defeats the whole purpose, doesn't it. Customer service had me change the wattage sensitivity controls, since some Macs seem to consume lots of watts in sleep, but that did not solve my problem. If anybody has a workaround, let me know.

I have also tried a Master/Slave surge arrest with a television, and ran into a similar problem: if the TV was master, the slaved receiver did not turn on soon enough to supply a signal in time to the TV, or if the receiver was master, there was not enough delay before the TV lit up to have a signal available. I had then to power cycle one or the other to get the signal in the right sequence. These problems cannot be general, or no one would produce these controlled power regulators, so I may be unlucky with my particular combinations of equipment.

If this could be you, I suggest you try this Back-UPS, or similar, only if you have return privileges. The Master outlet can also be turned into an ordinary one, with battery backup. At this point the Brainwavz earpads are well known and well regarded in terms of comfort, quality, and sound. There are many reviews for the pleather and velour versions of these pads, which you can find here:

[[ASIN:B00MFDX4YO Brainwavz HM5 Velor Memory Foam Replacements Earpads - Suitable For Many Other Branded Large Over The Ear Headphones - AKG, HifiMan, ATH, Philips, Fostex]]

[[ASIN:B00MFDT894 Brainwavz Replacement Memory Foam Earpads - Suitable For Many Other Large Over The Ear Headphones - AKG, HifiMan, ATH, Philips, Fostex]]

There was also a post about those earpads on Cnet's Audiophiliac blog. I was looking into these to use with a newly purchased pair of Audio Technica ATH-M50x, which you can see here:

[[ASIN:B00HVLUR86 Audio-Technica ATH-M50x Professional Studio Monitor Headphones]]

Basically, I was having an extremely hard time deciding between the velour and pleather options. On the one hand, pleather makes my ears sweat a lot, which is extremely uncomfortable. On the other hand, velour provides less noise isolation, and I intended to use these headphones almost exclusively on the go. Velour also reduced bass response compared to pleather. For me this was a concern, but a secondary one to comfort. I went back and fourth for a while, but eventually found this hybrid pair on Brainwavz website. They have velour where they touch your ears, and pleather on the inside (perforated) and outside. These are very similar to the earpads that Hifiman is using on their newer high end models, and they are called focus pads. In any case, these seemed like they would offer the best of both worlds for my needs, and were only slightly more expensive than the non-hybrid versions, so I bought a pair.

I have to say, I am extremely happy I made this choice. As many others have noted, the difference in comfort is day and night. I found the stock pads on the ATH-M50x to be okay, but not very comfortable. They didn't fit completely around my ears, and they were relatively shallow, putting pressure on my head. The small pleather pads also made my ears sweat quickly. After only one day with the stock pads my Brainwavz already arrived so I switched immediately. The process of swapping the pads is not super easy, but pretty much anyone can do it with a little fiddling. With the Brainwavz on, my Audio Technica's easily became the most comfortable headphone's I own. Before the pads, they were only slightly (though still noticeably) more comfortable than my Monoprice headphones which cost less than $20.

The Brainwavz earpads are nice and thick, and extremely soft. They really do feel like pillows on your head. The velour feels great against my skin, and the noise isolation is completely adequate for my needs. You still hear everything around you, but it's muted enough to enjoy the music. As for sound, I think most people make a slightly bigger deal about it than they need too. Yes, the sound is slightly different, but the difference is not huge. It is definitely not better or worse though, so whether you like it more or less is really up to your personal preference. As others have noted, the bass is slightly less strong. There is more room between your ears and the drivers with this pad, and the perforated pleather probably also softens it a bit. The drop in bass is only slight, and it isn't any less accurate. For me the Brainwavz pads also made the mids a little more smooth. Ultimately, YMMV. But the most important thing I can say about the sound is that you shouldn't worry too much about it (for what it's worth I don't know if the same can be said about the velour pads, I haven't tried them myself). Get these if you want to exponentially increase the comfort of your headphones.

A short anecdote. I recently took these on a flight with me. The flight was delayed for 5 hours so we got on the plane tired from sitting in an airport. Then we found out the air conditioning on the plane wasn't working so it was extremely hot. The plane took off and I put on my Audio Technica's. (For those curious I was listening through a Fiio E17 connected to my iPhone digitally using Apple's Camera Connection Kit). After a few minutes, I was completely into my music. The pads blocked out just enough of the engine noise to let me hear my songs, and they felt great on my head. From the reviews of the Tomameri portable players (they sell this same player in 8, 16, and 32GB versions), this seems to be a love it or hate it type of product - which might come down to your expectations before you get it. Let me try to help with that - this is not a super-high-quality piece of hardware. The plastic pieces seem kind of cheap, and the ear buds aren't very nice. However, the aluminum case is actually pretty decent, the Micro SD card seems about as well made as others that I've bought, and the mini USB cable (yes, it charges with mini USB versus the more prevalent micro USB) is surprisingly nice. Audio performance is pretty decent, but don't expect much from the video. I gave the 16GB version four stars but am giving this one three stars because I don't think it's as good of a value at the current $36 price (more on that below). I will say, though, that the purple color is quite attractive.

If I were looking for something like this for myself or anyone that didn't destroy electronics quickly (like a young child), I'd heavily consider just using an older (or even new) smart phone - because most of those will do everything that this does but do it MUCH better. Bigger screen, probably as much memory (but maybe requiring a micro SD card)...and so on. If you wanted to get a young child their first music player and didn't want to risk having something more expensive get busted, this might not be a bad choice...because odds are you won't mind if this gets broken. I don't mean that in a mean way to this player - I'm just saying that I think it falls squarely into the niche of disposable products. This is exactly the kind of product that I wouldn't mind taking on a plane trip because it sounds pretty good and because I wouldn't be upset if I lost it or broke it...inexpensive hardware like this definitely has a place.

I do want to point out that the lower memory size Tomameri players are currently a better deal, with the 8GB version being only $14 right now ($22 cheaper at current prices). When you do your shopping, if you decide that you want one of these players - I highly recommend that you check the other models. The ONLY difference (that I can tell, and I have the 16GB and 32GB models) is the memory card. Even the sample files that come on them are the same. You can buy 32GB micro SD cards faster than the one that comes with this product for under $15, so it might pay off to get the cheapest version out there and then get a separate card for it. I gave the 16GB model four stars because it was a pretty good value even with its flaws, but this 32GB version is currently $36 - and you can buy pay-as-you-go smart phones for similar or even less money that will beat this player (just don't activate the phone service and use the \\"phone\\" as a media player). For example, the Moto G for Verizon prepaid seems to often be under $40.

Although not the best value, I still think it's worthy of three stars even at the current $36 price tag because:
(*) First, you get some individual pieces that are useful with or without the player, most notably the 32 GB Micro SD card that would cost you around $10 by itself
(*) Speaking of the memory card, I love that this player uses one instead of needing to sync up with a computer to load files onto it. That is more convenient to me than my iPods that sync up with iTunes
(*) Next, it actually works pretty darn well for audio - the internal amp isn't half bad and powered my larger headphones just fine, and the voice recorder worked quite well once I went into the menu and changed the recording quality. I was surprised by how well the audio sounded on this
(*) Charges pretty fast, and battery life isn't too bad, either
(*) Small and lightweight

Now, for some of the detractors:
(*) Although it has the look of an older iPod Nano, which I happen to own and have used for years, it doesn't operate like one. The wheel on the front doesn't respond to you sliding your finger along it like a Nano does, but rather just mimics the look of it while requiring you to click on it. The four labeled areas on the wheel are essentially four separate buttons, with a fifth button under the circle in the center of the wheel. If you've never owned a Nano with the scroll wheel, likely none of that will matter to you
(*) The \\"MP4\\" player part is a little misleading, as this will not play regular .MP4 files. It plays .AMV files, which I'd never heard of until I got this and tried to load video files onto it
(*) The screen is okay quality, but it's tiny - you shouldn't expect to ever use this as an E-Book reader like mentioned in the product title. Watching a video might work okay if you decide to convert your files into AMV files
(*) The menu system can be a little tedious. Okay, make that a lot tedious
(*) Charges with a mini USB cable, which might be less common in your house/car/luggage than a micro USB cable used by pretty much every other piece of electronics these days

Now to the performance of the product. It's not very good. Here are my complaints:

- Noise. It's not as noticeable at higher volumes because of the signal-to-noise ratio increase, but at low volumes and with "quieter" music, you can hear a weird high-frequency noise. I don't know what it is (maybe interference from poor shielding?), but it wouldn't go away. Try listening to some Nick Drake or Vashti Bunyan at 25% volume. No good.
- Bluetooth pairing. Wow. Terrible. My iPhone 5S would pair and then if I stop the music for a few minutes, it was unpaired and pairing it back up again sometimes would take 60+ seconds. Periodically the speaker would produce a loud *beep* (different from the sound it makes when turned on or when pairing). I don't know if that's an indication that it's trying to pair but failing. In any case...the whole reason I want a bluetooth speaker is for the bluetooth connectivity. If that feature is weak, I'm not keeping the product.

I bought a JBL Flip 2. More money, yes, but for the improved sound and connectivity, I'm happy to spend a little extra.

Bottom line: this is a $25 bluetooth speaker. IF you think you're getting a $100 speaker at a great price, think again.

I own several Bluetooth speakers and paid well over $200 for our JBL speaker at the time of it's first release- I am very critical of design and execution in portable sound technology but I have to say, right up front, I was blown away with the amount of speaker you get for such a low price here. I do not write glowing reviews, and always have notes of improvement but it's literally hard to pick apart a speaker that does everything it promises to such great execution. I would buy these for gifts in a heartbeat and am looking to invest in a second to test the possibility of surround sound or continuous syncing. Here are my thoughts:

Appearance: Very well built, heavy in the hand but very modest in size for the amount of sound it can output. I love the 360 speaker design but find the speaker is a little tall can can be wobbly unless on a very flat surface, since it is slender and tall. We usually place this face down on the buttons/front when we take it out and about to avoid mishaps with falling when at the pier or park.

Waterproof: This speaker offers a level of IPX4 protection- this means you shouldn't swim with it or submerge it underwater, but having it out while camping, or in areas where weather may be tentative is acceptable. Minor splashes and water encounters should be fine. The bottom charge ports and on/off switch are protected by a silicone fitted flap. I've had no issue removing the flap (which is securely attached by a small tab at one end,) though it does fit flush with the speaker for waterproofing purposes.

Streaming Options: While this is a Bluetooth speaker there is a TF/Micro SD port for you to introduce your own media- I've found that this seems to add extra life to the playback time (about an hour more when directly reading media.) Bluetooth connects and pairs quickly and intuitively. There is a voice acknowledgement system that sounds like an Asian woman with a French accent- it's a little robotic and really livens up our listening experience- we are constantly trying to place her accent.

Connectivity + Life: We get about 5 3/4 hours continuous playback via Bluetooth on a full charge (full charge takes about 2.5 hours.) The Bluetooth range is about 30 feet before interference/cutting out. Note: even a human body can disrupt the clarity of the feed, resulting in a crackling/breaking up effect. The field between the Bluetooth device and speaker should be kept directly clear at all times for functionality. This is where the price level of the speaker shows itself- it's truly a minor inconvenience, as I rarely am using my phone while streaming. Like so many people I play music while cleaning up the house, hosting a party, or relaxing in the backyard.

The 'Clip': In an effort to market this as more of an active lifestyle speaker a pull out tab and complimentary caribiner style clip has been included with this speaker. The tab doesn't seem like something I'd quite trust clipped to my belt while biking (as in one of the stock images) but is convenient to fasten in a backpack, or to one's belongings while out and about. In my opinion the aluminum clip is by far the cheapest looking element of that is otherwise a very slick speaker package.

There is not carry pouch or sleeve like many other speakers on the market have. I suppose that's another thing that refers to the price point, but it's such a gorgeous speaker that I'm sad to note this. We store ours in the original box when not in use....which is pretty much never, since it's usually on display in the living room when not being charged.

The Sound: I wanted to dislike this speaker but it's hard to argue with the sheer power of this tiny unit. I am amazed by the amount of sound being pumped out of it and the clarity from all angles. In our 2 bedroom condo I can hear music clearly and comfortably with the volume at about 80 percent! Even more impressive, there is minimal muffling and distortion when up so loud. BASS highs and lows come in fairly clear with decent depth- the only issue with sound quality would be interference when handling the bluetooth streaming device, or when the device gets out of range.

We also thought it was worth noting that the device can actively be charged while in use- and will power off the included cable endlessly if used as a power source. Clarity for calling modes seems okay but is not the highlight of this unit. In all, I am blown away at the quality and performance of this speaker, with the added benefit of waterproof protection, for it's price.
