These BÖHM wireless bluetooth headphones come in a sleek, minimalistic design that is deceptively high-end and luxe. The box, zippered case it comes in and the headphones itself look impressive upon unboxing. However, at $79, don't expect the build and quality to compare to name brand high end headphones. While these are not for audiophiles, they suited my needs perfectly and I like them a lot!

While my boyfriend, an audiophile, pointed out the cheaper aluminum casing and faux leather build, to me, these features actually increase their portability. The aluminum casing on the headphones make them lightweight, which is great for wearing for long periods or taking around. The faux leather is soft and plush enough for me. The wireless bluetooth & noise canceling capability of these headphones make them perfect for traveling, and at this price point, I don't have to worry about damaging them or losing them on my trip!

Comfort: The headphones were a little tight at first, but you can just open them up and they became very comfortable. They are easily adjustable to fit different sized heads and stay snugly in place without slipping. These are on-ear headphones, which means that the ear cups rest on your outer ear rather than encircling them, which may be more uncomfortable than over-ear headphones. For me, the ear cups and band are soft and comfortable.

Bluetooth: The bluetooth was very simple to pair to my phone and computer. It works great and worked up to a range of a little over 30 feet. Calls were crisp and clear.

Noise Cancellation: The noise cancellation works great. There is a switch on the right side of the headphones that allows you to turn the noise cancellation on or off.

Sound Quality: Again, I am not an audiophile but I was pleased with the sound quality. I thought they sounded great: clear with great mids, until my boyfriend let me try his Shure SE215 earphones. His Shures were so crisp I was able to hear sounds that I didn't even hear on the BÖHMs while listening to the same song. However, those are $100 wired earphones and these are $80 wireless headphones, so I don't think it's fair to compare the two. Also, the BÖHM headphones come with a cable, which do actually increase the sound quality. So if you want better audio or your battery is running low, you have the option to plug them in. A few of the reviews mentioned that the sound quality is better when the noise cancellation feature is off. While the bass does become significantly stronger, the sound becomes kind of distorted. My resident audiophile mentioned that the lows and the highs become overemphasized and the sound becomes muffled. When the noise cancellation feature is on, the bass is weaker but the sound is more balanced overall. So for a better listening experience, I would keep the noise cancellation feature on and plug in the headphones if I don't need the wireless capability at the time.

There will always be products with better sound or of higher quality, but these BÖHM wirelesss headphones are a well rounded package at an attractive price!

I just purchased these for an absurdly low price below $500 band new (Retail $1,000).  I currently have these paired with the Audioquest Dragonfly v1.2 DAC/Amp.  While this is far from high end, it gets the job done with these headphones.  I listen to a mix of classical, jazz, show music, pop, soundracks and some rock.  Everything I have thrown at these headphones so far has sounded great!  I primarily stream losses music utilizing Tidal streaming service.  At first listening, the sound is highly accurate and detailed.  Every nuance in the voice picked up during recording is instantly obvious (good or bad).  These headphones are amazing on live recordings (Judy Garland at Carnegie Hall is phenomenal!).  However, if you listen primarily heavily produced pop/rock/R&B, these will not be your best fit.  You may want to try something else as these will show every evidence of poor recordings intended for radio/cell phone playback.  These headphones also lack a bit of bass impact.  While it is definitely there, it will not be the same if you are used to having an independent subwoofer in your system.  Bass has good extension to low frequencies and what is produced is highly clean and very accurate and separated.  Definitely worth a try.  I'm considering pairing with the Marantz HD-Dac 1 in the near future.  I have also considered upgrading to a tube amp for the warmer sound and additional harmonics (i.e., tube sound).  However, not sure I am ready to take the leap to tubes just yet.  I upgraded to the HD 700 headphones after listening to the HD 558s for a period and the HD 598s.  The HD 558s were just too laid back.  Great to relax with but really can sound boring after a while (still very clear/clean sound).  The 598s were also great, however lacked bass.  The 700s add significant bass, much more detail (i.e., enhanced treble and instrument separation).  In general, they produce a fun sound that is very enjoyable, which I have not heard on other headphones at this clarity.

You’ve been there before, your iPod earbuds break and all of a sudden you’re on the prowl for a new pair of headphones. Maybe earbuds have wronged you in the past. Suddenly you realize you want to be the kind of person that owns an actual pair of headphones rather than those tiny opaque white orbs that barely fit into a normal person’s ear comfortably. In walks these Hi-Fi Lightweight Headphones and for $14.99, how can you say no?

For the casual, non audiophile listener, these headphones are really top-notch, they have really good frequency response, particularly in the mids and highs. The low-end leaves something to be desired, but for the price of 2 Chipotle burritos, I’d be lying if I said I wasn’t impressed. The mids come in clearly and that’s where the 36mm driver really shines; the highs are nice and bright as well, very pleasant to listen to. Overall, I came away very impressed with a selection of music listening and some podcast listening on these headphones using my iPhone as an audio source.

As a reference, my favorite pair of headphones are the Audio-Technica ATH-M50Xs. Those headphones are amazing, so the price of these headphones is extraordinarily competitive for something that achieves maybe a half of the quality of sound for a tenth of the price. If you are looking for something to hook up to listen to your lossless Flac files or direct input your DTS-MA tracks onto, these will still perform admirably, but you’ll be leaving sound on the table unless you upgrade to a signficantly more expensive pair of headphones.

With regards to comfort and fit, this pair sits snugly on your head and ears for a long period of time with no problem. The earcups are made of polyurethane which has a leather-like feel to them and fit incredibly snugly against your ear (they don’t actually envelop the entire ear, but rather sit on the ear). The fit of the ear cups is good enough that you get some decent sound cancellation. It’s enough that in a quiet office you no longer hear your noisy coworkers typing away on mechanical keyboards. My only complaint with the fit of the headband is that if you have a larger head (like I do) the furthest reach of the headband only barely manages to fit on my head and it won’t extend further, even so, the fit is still pretty comfortable regardless.

Hands down though, if you’re looking for something that’s a great pair of headphones at the cost of budget earbuds from your local retailer, definitely get these, they’re well worth the money!

If you have a pretty basic home theater or computer system this little 40" fabric sleeve can do wonders at cleaning up the wire clutter. It is a simple design but it is quite effective. You have 40" of a stretchy fabric that you lay your cables in then connect the Velcro strips that run down both sides to seal them together.

I love the fact that there are slits about every 2 inches that you can slip the cables through so that lower items in your home theater rack don't have to come out the top and then come back down. Again, it is a simple design but it really works well.

The black fabric looks nice and it stays together nicely. If you have a more advanced theater system you might need a few of these. If you're using 12 gauge speaker wire and are running 5 or more speakers those wires alone could fill the diameter of one of these.

The Velro is a great choice here over the zipper design that some use as you can open and close just small sections of the length as needed, hopefully not having to re-wrap all of the wires every time you need to add, remove or move a wire.

Overall this is a nice wire management system that is easy to use and won't bust the bank. Recommended.

You get what you pay for. This dock is junk. And the cables it comes with are junk. The only purpose of this dock is that it offers the ability to charge your iPod while playing it through your stereo unit. And offers a remote I guess. But you can play the music through your stereo receiver without a dock. Here's how: Get yourself a "Y" cable. One end has a headphone connection, and the other end has the red and white sound connections. Plug the red/white connectors into the back of your stereo receiver, plug the headphone connector into the headphone jack of your iPod, and you're in business. Connect your iPod to a charger cable at the same time to keep it charged while it plays.

I bought this dock thinking it'd be nice to be able to throw my iPod on it and keep it charged and hey, a remote, so bonus. However, I hooked the dock up to my stereo receiver and there was a pretty significant hum right off the bat. The hum seemed to go away when I put the iPod on the dock, but I had trouble even getting the music on my iPod to play through my stereo -- it needed to be in the exact perfect position on the dock or you just get noise that will make your ears bleed. And even when I got music coming through my speakers, I couldn't get the sound to be any sort of quality I'd actually be able to listen to. Also note that this dock would not fit my iPod Classic 5th Gen with a case on it. So I tried hooking it up just using the Y cable it came with and bypassing the dock altogether. The sound quality was still awful.

So I unhooked everything and I'm returning this dock. I now have my iPod hooked up to my stereo receiver using the method I first mentioned, with a new Y cable that is clearly much better quality than the cable this dock comes with (and Y cables are inexpensive to begin with). I lose the remote ability, but that's not really that important to me. Definitely read the bad reviews for this product. Don't waste your money on this dock.

I was just about to place an order when I got hit with a power outage to remind me that I hadn't yet reviewed this UPS. I originally bought two of these; one for work and one for home. The work UPS was to be used on a boat with dirty unreliable power. We had some sensitive laboratory equipment that needed stable power to get stable readings. This UPS logged an average of about eighty events per day, and it never once let me down. The readings on the lab equipment remained stable and held their calibrations all day long, without needing to recalibrate. The home unit is, as of right now, on its tenth event. That one has never failed me, either. With my desktop computer active it provided enough power to finish watching online videos in two instances. It promises more than an hour and a half of run time with the desktop computer running, though I still haven't had a power outage long enough to test that. If I power down the computer and let it run only the cable modem and the router, then use the netbook instead, it adds about another hour to its predicted run time. I never installed the packaged software, as Windows has its own native power options and was able to recognize and install the UPS when I connected the USB cable. It shows up in the system tray as a battery icon with a plug (or without one in a power outage) the same as though it were a laptop. Hence, I can set my power options to put the computer to sleep earlier during a power outage. If the computer is already in sleep mode and the UPS runs out of power, then it doesn't matter so much, because the computer protects itself by writing its memory to disk, and it picks up back where it left off the next time the computer is powered-up.

The alarm can be permanently silenced, but it will always beep if the UPS is powered on or off. The display is set to only illuminate if something happens, though it can be set to remain permanently on. USB ports on the front are for charging and donot act as a USB hub, even with the UPS connected to the computer by USB cable. That having been said, all those things are negligible because the charge isn't built properly.. The unit ran for just over a month before failing, emitting a rancid odor.. I do run the unit just about continuously.. However it was situated in a cool room with a fan drafting over it.. Without the fan, it was quite hot to the touch.. I've worked with the older version of this charge before.. There is one at my church which has been running for over a year continuously without problems.. The unit has crisper, clearer sound than the Roar 2 and Bose Soundlink Mini or III, Sonos Play 1, Amazon Echo and is in the same ballpark with the Big Jambox in terms of sound signature with the X55 having more bloated bass.

I'd give it a 4* if it wasn't for the bluetooth delay using Netflix, HBO GO, SlingTV, Youtube, etc on my iPad Air. The voices were mismatched in videos to the point of it being a total deal breaker and a slap in the face to this poor unit b/c it IS so competitive/superior in other areas relative to the competition. In comparison, the units above never had this same issue with bluetooth delay. I suspect it's Sony's LDAC bluetooth tech that's responsible, wheareas the other units use different bluetooth tech such as Aptx, etc......IF you never plan to watch video on it, then this doesn't apply to you and thusly this unit is easily in the 4 star range for sound versus the competition in this category. Also know, that I haven't given any of these units 5 stars as they all sound VERY mediocre, at best.

Other things to know....The bass is good and strong at lower volumes (its true design) but as you increase the volume the bass quantity stops at a point and the whole sound signature just gets louder, where it just gets to blaring/shouty. This is typical of many such bluetooth units, btw. These units are all gimped so that the little woofers don't blow or distort. If you're planning to jam, then all the little units will fail to please you. Mid or low volume/small rooms is exactly where they'll shine--their sweet spot. No more, no less.

Another note, the bass on bassy songs deviates in a weird way as if one bass note is strong then, all of a sudden....a different bass note volume goes down substantially in volume/presence as if the unit ran out of power...up/down, up /down..wobbly....wow! WTH?! You have to closely listen to this after extended listening on more COMPLEX bass note rhythms. I strongly suspect it's the DSP. The DSP is tweaked to give "false" big sound with the tiny woofers and on heavy bass complexity, the unit tries to "compensate" throughout the song. If you don't listen to bassy/dynamic songs, then you'll probably not notice this phenomenon/speaker limitation.

Overall, if you asked me to recommend a solid product in this category that provides a clean sound versus the competition at a decent price for its market, I'd recommend the <$200 Big Jambox (or , if you have the money, the best-in-class JBL Xtreme). If it wasn't for the bluetooth/video voice delay issue and bass/dynamics issue of this Sony unit, it'd be a closer toss-up with the Big Jambox in CLEAN sound dept.. As it stands, the Big Jambox is clear throughout and doesn't hide the bass on the upper end of the dial with complex bass notes like the Sony does.

Despite all this. One has to be realistic. NONE of these units from the muddy sounding $300 Bose Soundlink III on down are impressive. These are all beach toys (boomy bass, muddled sound, not really loud, shouty at the top 1/4 of the volume dial) and you will be sacrificing serious good sound versus using headphones or a wired sound system. If you understand this expectation to use them really at lower volumes and mainly as background music, you'll do OK with these "sound toys".

Keep in mind that I audtioned the best-of-the-best rated units, side by side, in my house with many music genres and I'm more critical than most people when it comes to decent/acceptable sound in this toy category.

I have two main concerns with these headphones to start out with, but those issues will be mentioned later. This review will be divided into different sections, going from most important to least important.  - Sound Quality  The headphones are quite consumer friendly, meaning they are bass and treble accentuated. There are 3 EQ presets, that apparently people don't really know about, people really need to start reading manuals when they are provided to them. Not one of the presets are flat (which is what I like) so lets just go through them, preset one (it goes in an order but I don't know which preset you, the reader, started out on so...), bass heavy slightly more so of upper bass, lower mid accentuated, high end is good, a bit crisp. Preset two, mid accentuated, not too bassy, but no high end (crispness to the sound). Preset three, bass and treble accentuated, barely any mids whatsoever, voices sound far away, it's fun, just not accurate. You might be asking, "then why the 4 stars wise one?". Well, confused, I went to a forum where all of the audiophiles dwell and saw them mention a mod similar to a lot of cheaper Sennheiser headphones, where you remove a foam padding covering the drivers. I did it.... and it greatly improved the quantity and quality of the mids and highs greatly (mids and highs are an area of audible frequencies that people call vocals and treble). The headphones improve 10x over if any one of you have the guts to do this mod, just pull off the ear pads carefully and the piece of plastic that the ear pads were held onto, rub off the foam covering the drivers, then put the ear pads back onto the plastic then snap the plastic back into place in the headphones, piece of cake. The sound still isn't as accurate as my Sennheiser Momentum over ear, but I enjoy this more for certain types of music. - Build Quality  Not great..  Simply, it creaks like a rocking chair when stretching the headband to place the headphones on your head. Not simply, from what I've read there is no metal support whatsoever in the headband, just plastic (metallic plastic too) and padding, plus the metal hinges use plastic in certain areas. They cheaped out to make their product cheap, I don't think it was necessary though. I'm guessing it costs $30-$40 to mass produce a pair of Bluedio R+ headphones maybe another $10 on steel support/durable plastic and these headphones would have been the biggest headphone deal on the internet, at least to non audiophile bass lovers. RANT OVER  anyways, they probably will last a while if you (like me) baby them, don't use them for physical activity, and don't stretch then more than necessary to place them on your head. If you want durable go to their flagship headphones, the Bluedio UFO (I'm waiting for their next release of the Vinnyl LP and V headphones, they are the sexiest headphones I've ever seen).  - Design  Although not durable, these are one of the coolest looking headphones I've ever seen, the stories of them breaking a few months after purchase kept on pushing me away but I kept on imagining me wearing such sexy headphones and my common sense couldn't fight anymore. Titanium isn't really the color I wanted, but I bought it anyways because it was being sold at great discount. It looks so much cooler in person than it does in video or picture honestly. Bluedio knows how to design cool looking headphones. I can't even tell you how I like it's design so much it just looks gorgeous.  - Comfort  The unusual cubed head padding is so comfortable, it's weird that no other headphones I've seen really do this. Oh and the over ear ear pads are so comfy and perfectly shaped that I forget I'm wearing these headphones, even with the 282 grams of weight it's so well padded and divided among my head that I forget I'm wearing it sometimes  - Battery  I've found them to last me between a week and 2 weeks, but I also listen to music probably 5 times the average person so that long is really amazing.  Overall: Best bass heavy, treble heavy, mid accurate pair of bluetooth headphones under $300. The only issue is that they won't last long if they aren't taken care of.   I've owned many Bluedio products now and have loved every one of them, and occasionally when one was detective, Bluedio or the seller replaced it with minimal fees. I love Bluedio! (I think I've owned 15 Bluedio products now) Bluedio is an amazing company with great customer support, be positive and they'll gladly help you out.  Please check out my review of the Bluedio UFO, they are worth the extra $80 for the quality and craftsmanship of them.

I am an electrical contractor. this Is my second one of this particular model. The only reason I bought another one is because the other is in another truck. The last was moved between three different trucks, purchased in 2010 and still going strong.
I bought this one to install in my new work truck. The instructions call for (2) #4 awg wires for positive terminals and same for negative terminals and they should not be more than 4feet long. I ran (1) single piece of flexible DLO type cable, 1/0 awg directly from the battery, through a 200amp manual reset circuit breaker to the inverter. I only connected it to one of the positive terminals. Ground wire is same size and bolted directly to frame of truck. I also only used one of these instead of two cables.
I am not crazy about the remote switch that cobra offers since it is so big. I figured out that all you need is a momentary type switch to turn the inverter on and off. The plug on the inverter for the remote is just an RJ-11 (phone jack) connector. One of the pins is putting out +12volts DC (pin #2 in attached photo). Pin #4 is the switch leg of the circuit. I made a connector with an RJ-11 male end, used pin #2 and pin #4. I used CAT5 wiring to run up to the front of my truck dash. The on / off switch I used is just a lighted single pole momentary push button. when I push the button, the 12 volt signal from the inverter goes through the switch, out the other pole of the switch back to the inverter and turning it on.
I have never had any trouble with these inverters in five years. I have used this to power Bandsaws, Hammer drills, even a pipe threader machine. I have found that it will not Operate my 5gallon Rigid air compressor. I think the startup is just too much for it. Again, this is a great inverter, it is modified sine wave, so I never charge batteries or power anything like a laptop with it. it may be fine but its not recommended and im not going to ruin my batteries.
My install is my own design and plan. It may not be exactly correct or the best way but it works for me and I have no troubles with this. Hope this is Helpful!

I just received this item today, and here are my initial impressions:

[the good]
-This device has no problem powering headphones. It can drive them with a respectable amount of power. The sound quality through headphones is way better than expected. I had different model of one of these bluetooth to audio devices, and the headphone output is really bad, both in sound quality and volume. This item is way better. The volume buttons on device work nicely for this.
-This device also has no problem providing input to powered speakers. The sound quality is good. There are no problems with frequency response or volume output.
-This device draws very little current from a charger. I measured about 0.2 watts with a USB power measuring stick.
-This device is stable. I have maintained a connection for about three hours with no issues
-You can UNplug your charging cable with no issues. (see below)
-The unit does NOT shut off if there is no sound for a little while. This is good because I don't want to re-pair just because I paused music for a while. I think it will eventually time out and shut off, but it takes a while. I may update my review if I figure out how it stays on with no sound.

[the bad, although i may be nitpicking a little]
-Someone posted that you can't charge the unit while it's playing. That's wrong. You can. I would put this under the good, but this is something I'd expect from any device like this. THE BAD part is that if you plug in the USB cord while it's playing music, the unit will hiccup and reboot itself. I don't know if this problem is electrical, or software based. (Would a better filter cap fix it? Perhaps a firmware update?)

Other observations:
-This item takes a little longer to pair (or show up for pairing/connecting) than other devices after it's turned on. It takes around 5-10 seconds instead of 3-4. Not a big deal, but it was long enough to cause me to end up playing with settings to see if something was wrong.
-This is a very small device. It's about the size of an ipod shuffle.

What I have not tested:
-Range. I may play with this and update the review.
-Play time (batteries). I plan to have this unit plugged in most of the time, since I'm just using this so I don't have to run a wire from my laptop to my speakers.

Overall, I'm glad I bought this thing. It's good in general, but very good for the price. It saves me from stringing a wire across the floor. Yes! :)

I bought this stereo about a year ago. It's maiden voyage was a small rafting trip down a river with a bunch of friends. It worked really well for that. It was nice to have my phone with me, in a waterproof compartment, and even had room for about two large car key/fobs. My friends were impressed with the fact that this was waterproof. I threw it in the river and it kept playing music, all while everyone around had a look of udder shock on their faces. The sound quality is good. It doesn't suck, like most small bluetooth speakers, but it doesn't have that big sound like larger name brand stereos do. And the volume it puts out is pretty good as well. I can fill my two car garage with a good amount of sound with this. I also used it on a few camping trips. It played music for about 2 days straight with high quality batteries in it. We were all surprised at how long it lasted.

Another reviewer on amazon said that they would like to see a slightly larger version of this powered by D cell batteries (instead of the 8 AA batteries this one takes) and I would have to agree 100% with that. Also have some slightly larger speakers, maybe a pair of tweeters, and have it put out some more sub-bass. I would buy this in a heart beat.

After that trip, I used it in my garage as a small stereo. It works pretty well for that, but if you try to turn it all the way up, the sound will start to distort.

I noticed about 8 months after the purchase, that the stereo would start to distort at any volume after about 30-50 mins of playing time. Then finally one day the left speaker completely quit on me. It was about 2 weeks shy of having it for a full year. I looked on ECOXGEAR's website and found that they just increased the product's warrantee to three full years on most of their products. I printed and filled out their return policy (you don't even have to email them) then shipped it away, and about 3 weeks later I had a brand new replacement at my door. I have yet to operate this one. Hopefully I won't have the same problem again and have to get them replaced every year.

All in all, I think this is a good unit. I'm hoping that my defect was just a fluke and others won't have the same problem I did. But it was nice to have a replacement shipped to my door with no hassle at all. I would recommend this to others and I would LOVE to see a larger unit with more frequency response (sub bass) and larger batteries or even an internal battery.

I'm only giving this thing 3 stars because I feel it is missing some basic functionality and the way the buttons operate is counter intuitive. It is made to look like another very nice player...BUT IT'S NOT THE SAME! The instructions it came with did not match the device. Had to read through the reviews to find out how to operate it and there are multiple items on Amazon depending on the color you want. I have a Sony Walkman which has nice navigation and I thought it would have this same kind of interface but it doesn't. However, the Walkman costs a lot more than this device. If might be worth it! Or not, depending on what you can live with.

You get an amazing amount of space for the price of this player. I don't use iTunes but I do use Windows Media Player to synch to my devices. The navigation is terribly unfriendly but once I figured it out it does work.

My major complaint is that it does not support play lists that you create in Windows Media Player. It will download all of the songs in all of the playlists you select but not the playlist. This player acts more like a USB storage stick. If you connect to your computer you will see a "Music" folder. After Windows Media Player synched with it I could see that it had created a folder for every artist and under every artist was one folder for each album and under each album were all the mp3s for that album. The problem is that when you go to play music you have to select a folder (which equates to an album)--NOT a playlist. You can set it to play random but it will only be playing random songs from the folder/album you selected.

Music is arranged like this after synching with Windows Media Player:
Music\Artist Name1\Album1\song1.mp3....song2.mp3....song3.mp3
Music\Artist Name2\Album2\song1.mp3....song2.mp3....song3.mp3
Music\Artist Name3\Album1\song1.mp3....song2.mpe....song3.mp3

Using Windows Explorer...I went back and copied all the mp3 files to the root of the Music folder then deleted all the folders. So now the structure looks like this:
Music\song1.mp3...song2.mp3...song3.mp3...song4.mp3....song5.mp3 etc.
Music\Christmas\song1.mp3...song2.mp3...song3.mp3...song4.mp3 etc.

Now I can at least select the Music folder and then random play selects from every song I have in there but you loose the ability to play by Artist or Album and the ability to make a playlist in the order you want. You can simulate a playlist by creating an additional folder such as "Christmas" under the Music folder and then I put all the Christmas songs in the root of that folder. But with this "folder" setup, you can't make multiple play list that have songs from all the folders or make them play in the order you want except by renaming them alphabetically in the order you want. You'd have to copy the mp3 file to each of those folders to have it play from each one.

Bottom line is that it does work, has an amazing amount of storage for the money but interface is terrible. They didn't promise anything more in the item description either so you get what it says.

Hi,

This is my review of the TT-SK08/ TaoTronics waterproof speaker. Amazon lists the product as:

Waterproof Bluetooth Speakers TaoTronics Wireless Portable Outdoor Bi-directional Sound Bluetooth 4.0 Speaker (Up to 15 Hours of Playtime, Rugged, Compact, IPX5 Waterproof)

I received this product last weekend and had time yesterday and today to evaluate it for a detailed review. I have also included a set of photos in case anyone is interested in taking a look at it in more detail.

UNBOXING AND OBSERVATIONS:

When I first got this product in the mail, I thought that the design of the product box looked very simple and classic.

The top side of the box has an image of the product getting splashed on with the name of the product and model number visible.

The right side has the serial and unit number for the product. Both the left and right side have a camouflage type of design that reminds me of a military pattern.

The bottom of the box has the e-mail and phone support for North America, as well as e-mail contact support for Europe and Asia Pacific.

This product has passed FCC, CE, and ROHS quality control checks among other things shown.

I like the layout of the design of the box because it’s a simple single flap that gets pulled out to open and is easy to insert back. There was no seal or sticker label that required a box cutter knife to cut across. Very simple.

Inside is a good arrangement of packaging. The User Manual is what you will first see followed by the Bluetooth speaker.

The Bluetooth speaker itself was wrapped in a plastic bag held with a little cushion of space in place. Above it is the soft rubber handle that’s bent over in a small cardboard cutout section inside the box.

When removing the speaker and handle, underneath the handle area is the Micro USB cable and an AUX cable.

Micro USB is a common standard for charging Bluetooth products and with or without this cable, it is cheap to get and they’re all relatively effective. I suggest that Taotronics move towards gold plated connectors or a nylon braided design for its micro USB cables.

The AUX cable is for situations where the phone or tablet you’re trying to use this speaker on doesn’t have Bluetooth. Then the AUX cable can allow you to still use the speaker with limited control settings. It does not take up or consume the battery on the speaker. This works out well in areas and locations where you may need to place your phone or tablet on airplane mode and still be able to listen to music. Having gold connectors for the AUX cable would also be desirable and I suggest Taotronics include that with these types of products in the future model releases.

But it’s nice that Taotronics offers this assembly into the product package.

I suggest all users read the User’s Manual prior to using this product to be aware of what it can and can’t do.

Some notables in the User’s Manual include the following:

Technical Specs:

Bluetooth Version: 4.0+EDR
Bluetooth Profile: A2DP, HFP, HSP, AVRCP
Waterproof: IPX5
Power: 3W
Sound Frequency: 100Hz-18KHz
Input: DC 5V / 500mA
Battery: 1500mAh Lithium Battery
Range: 33 feet (10m)
Working Time: Up to 15 hours
Charging Time: 3-4 hours
Dimension: 3.9 x 3.5 x 1.9 inches
Weight: 9.56 oz.

So let’s take a look at some of these in detail.

EDR is an optional design component in Bluetooth 4.0. Bluetooth 4.0 is the latest standard among Bluetooth devices. Although Bluetooth 4.1 is out there, 4.0 is pretty common standard and have had good improvement over its predecessors in terms of connection stability and improved battery management.

Waterproof IPX5 means that it should be able to handle water jet in any direction for a short duration of time. This is an upgrade to IPX4, which only tolerates splashes of water. With this IPX5, it should be good enough to handle taking out in mild rain. This is an outdoors speaker, and although it’s not raining where I am during this season of summer, I suggest users take this out during the winter and fall time to try it out to see if there’s any distortion of sound or music being played from the rainy weather. You get 12 months warranty on it, so feel free to test against the IPX5 rating to see if it holds up well in those common outdoor conditions of those seasons. If it damages from that, then notify Taotronics to ship your defective unit for an exchange. Taotronics is usually pretty good at this as long as you show proof and you’re not taking advantage of their customer satisfaction guidelines.

3 watts driver doesn’t sound a whole lot, and I wasn’t expecting for too much when I got this product, but I’ll do a test later on and see how it holds up in this later portion of the evaluation for the review. Many common Bluetooth speakers around this $29.99 price range that are waterproof grade IPX4 or IPX 5 offer 5 watts driver. I suggest for a design like this from Taotronics that they stay competitive and improve their driver output.

The 1500mAh Lithium battery and 15 hours working time is very impressive. This is the first outdoor Bluetooth speaker product that I’ve evaluated and used at this price range that offers over 10 hours of working time. A lithium battery of over 100mAh for these types of Bluetooth speakers is always a good idea, especially when this is meant to be used in the outdoors. This works well for a weekend outing for a camping or adventure trip to use for a few hours in the evening or nighttime and have room to spare for the second day out under one charge.

The charge time of 3-4 hours sounds reasonable for this type of battery capacity. Although not stated in the User’s Manual, it may be 3 hours charge if you use a wall charger, charging station, or power bank to charge this product. I would not advise to charge this product with a PC USB 3.0 port unless there is no other option available, or else it may charge slower than the mentioned range.

For Dimension and Weight, I will be taking a look at the speaker next.

The speaker itself is built really well. I had a feel of the speaker taking it out of the plastic bag and it felt really hard. It feels baby proof because I had this on a granite table top on my kitchen and I pretended to do light drops and knocking it around and it feels pretty durable to some light levels of impact. Actually, if it falls on the front or back side, it will create a lot of noise from the hard plastic frame that takes the impact. On these two sides, it seems like more of a weakness to absorbing impacts, although still tough in its own sense. But, if you have the speaker drop and land along its sides, then it has more hallow sound from the impact and absorbs better overall.

The speaker has a rubber handle that’s about 3 and ½ inches in length across the loop to fit through the 4 fingers of one person’s hand to clench into a fist and carry it around with you while you’re walking. This loop can be connected to a lanyard or a nylon braided rope and then wrapped onto your shoulder bag or equipment. The handle feels very soft, flexible and smooth. The weight of the speaker onto my fingers don’t feel much of any discomfort or fatigue thanks to how lightweight the speaker is, weighing less than one pound.

All 4 sides of the speaker has some rubberized bumpy treaded design that allows it to have some grip and take the absorption of impact first before the impact hits the core design of the product. The odd thing is that on the left and right sides, those bumps and grooves feel tougher and harder than the bottom. Because they’re tougher and harder, I was able to slide them around by swinging my arm against it, causing it to move a little. However on the bottom, the same treaded design look feels much more software and flexible. In fact, as a result of this, I tried to push or pull the speaker against my laminated wooden tabletop while the speaker stood on its bottom and while I was able to rock around the speaker trying to move it, it didn’t budge much. It had very good grip from the bottom of the speaker.

The left side of the speaker has the cover for where the AUX and Micro USB cable goes into to play or charge the speaker.

One of the front sides has the Taotronics brand logo on the top of the hard plastic square frame. I think this frame is the weakest part of the speaker in terms of handling drop impact. Although I haven’t tried, these hard plastics can tend to crack from drops depending on the angle and surface it lands on. I’d actually like to suggest to Taotronics to try a more shock absorbing material that would also allow it to continue to be IPX5 for that protective metal frame. Some examples would be a TPU material or silicon material.

The center on both sides of the speaker has a metal casing that has an engraved X mark pattern that overall, makes the product look more appealing.

The top of the speaker has the rubber padded push buttons for power, volume down, play pause answer, and volume up. The user’s manual calls the play pause answer a multifunction button. Pressing on each button has a soft quiet mechanical sound. Each button takes minimal effort to press down. The buttons are protected by the rubberized casing.

The disappointment that I had in which I’ll suggest is that the volume up and volume down buttons don’t have a second function of being able to skip back or skip forward. Up until now, every Bluetooth speaker that’s been portable that I’ve checked out has had these common 4 buttons that Taotronics has in this outdoor speaker, but they had the skip back and skip forward feature on their volume controllers. Why Taotronics didn’t include this when they entered into this market of Bluetooth speakers, I have no idea. But I add that as a suggestion to improve this model. There’s so many good things about this model from inspection so far, but to be missing common features like skipping forward or backward is a disappointment because while you’re able to operate this product away from your phone or tablet, you can adjust the volume and pause, but if you don’t like a song or video and want to move forward or backward, you’d have to walk back to get your phone to do it rather than do it off of this Bluetooth speaker.

Next step is to use the product and I will try the music quality first before the calling quality.

USAGE:

The first step to do before being able to use the product is to pair it with your phone or tablet. In my tests, I had an iPhone 5s that I tested this speaker with.

To pair the speaker to your phone, you hold down the power button for about 3 seconds until you hear the musical beeping sounds come up and the top left corner of the front metal casing of the speakers show the blue LED blinking, which means that it’s in discovery mode and ready to pair. Then on the iPhone, going to the Bluetooth settings will find the Taotronics TT-SK08 and you can connect from there, causing a beeping sound on the speaker and a solid blue light visible where the flashing blue light was before.

The thing with this LED light is that it’s very weak in terms of lighting strength. Even when I have the lights turned off in my area, I could barely see it. Part of the reason is that the metal casing causes a net of small holes and the LED light has to try to pass through that to be visibly seen. I suggest Taotronics improve this LED light location if it’s supposed to matter how visible it is to the eye.

The first thing I saw that I liked a lot about this Bluetooth outdoors speaker that many competitors don’t have is that Taotronics included in this model a Bluetooth battery level meter indicator on the iPhone, which can be seen next to the Bluetooth symbol on the top right hand corner of the screen. Linkin Park – What I’ve done
Puddle of Mudd – Famous

However, what my previous observation was that applied here was that when I walked towards the front of the speaker about 5 feet away, there’s an obvious sound level difference in how loud and clear it is when listening from the front side, and comparing to walking from the backside. The backside you can still hear the music playing, but it sounds shallower overall.

At about 50% volume, I could say that it sounds reasonably good in a quiet setting from about 5-10 feet away. When I walked about 20 feet away from the front side while testing the Bluetooth 4.0 connectivity, I had to raise the volume up to 75% to hear it fairly loud and clear in an open space setting.

This was tested while listening to one more song:

3 Doors Down – Here Without You

Which is mostly lyrical singing and calmer instrumentation to hear the clarity of the voice while walking around. It felt pretty good at 75% volume setting for about 20 feet away from the speaker on the front side.

The Bluetooth 4.0+EDR connectivity is great. Whereas Bluetooth 3.0 portable speaker devices crackled and had connection problems causing the music to jitter at a certain distance and location in my house, this Taotronics speaker with the Bluetooth 4.0 had no stability issues when I had placed the speaker in the center of my kitchen and walked around the first floor in semi open space, with occasional dry wood walls. I was able to hear the music smoothly the whole time, which is a good sign of value in this product. I was able to test an estimated 30 feet from a slanted angle towards one room and stood there for a while with a stable connection of music playing. Most of my test was within 20 feet, which is good. I don’t live in a huge house, but a distance like this all around serves well for the average household size in my area.

The important factor to consider in how loud or quiet the speaker is at a certain volume is based on the quality of your streaming radio station and also if you play files from your playlist, the bitrate quality they are. From my tests, one radio station, such as AOL Radio, had music that was quieter of the same volume on my iPhone as compared to my Amazon Prime Music radio stations. This is something to keep in mind.

The last test was to test the call quality.

For this, I had with me my landline phone that I placed on speaker to test the call quality and multifunctional buttons on the Bluetooth speaker.

First, I tested having an incoming call from my landline to my iPhone. I heard the ringtone play from a sudden spike of moderate through the speakers to a low level sound of my ringtone music that was not too quiet but it wasn’t painful to hear as well. It was more on the lighter side though. I suppose that’s fine because in the environment that I was in, I could tell when the music playing stopped and then hear a lower toned ringtone music playing to know I had an incoming call. Even in a noisy party scene, you’d know when someone was calling when the music is playing loud and then all of a sudden it changes tune to a quieter scale. I had previous Bluetooth speaker products that failed on the projected ringtone music play because they would all of a sudden spike up and play extremely loud beyond the volume I set on my iPhone’s ringtone and the volume of my music. So Taotronics does a good job here.

The great thing about this was sound quality. I talked into my landline phone and heard my voice pretty clearly through the Bluetooth speaker at a low volume setting. I tested saying random gibberish through my landline phone and I did not hear any crackling or muffling through the speaker. It didn’t sound crystal clear for an audiophile, but it sounded good enough to hear what I was saying in a raised projected tone of voice through the speakers.

When I tested putting my landline phone about 10 feet away in another part of the room with the volume of the speakerphone about halfway up, I talked through to the front of the Bluetooth speaker initially up close and heard myself very well. Then I talked further and further away from it by the feet while walking away, stopping, talking, and then moving back. The microphone sensitivity is very good. I was able to test hearing my voice pick up through the Bluetooth speaker and echo back through the landline speakerphone initially at a 5 feet level, then 10 feet, and at one point, I had been close to 15 feet away from the Bluetooth speaker while raising my voice just a little higher than a normal outspoken voice, and yet, I could hear my voice echo through the landline speakerphone. This is almost as good of a microphone as an iPhone’s built in microphone, which people use to record things as far away as a public speaker at a seminar, symposium, or public announcement event from the seats. I was happy to find out and test the quality of the microphone.

After that test, I tested simple multifunctional checks like redialing from the speaker by double tapping the play pause button, which would call the last number no my dialed list. Then I could press the play pause button again to hang up a call or cancel a call while it is dialing. Each time, I had music playing, which would automatically pause when dialing out or receiving an incoming call, and resume where it last played automatically when I hung up the call or rejected the incoming call. These are pretty standard and working features among other Bluetooth speakers.

Overall, I tested all the wireless features of this Bluetooth speaker from music listening to call quality.

IN SUMMARY:

PROS:

1) Supports a Bluetooth Battery Level Indicator on iPhone's to check how much of the battery has been drained (rough estimate) to know when it's going to be time to fully charge up the unit.

2) 15 hours battery life for a product in this price range of $29.99 is a noticeable advantage over other waterproof Bluetooth speakers, and will work great for camping or weekend long trips with casual use

3) Feels generally baby proof from getting the internal circuitry damaged due to its rugged exterior design

4) Comes with a soft rubber handle loop to hook onto your fingers lanyard, or carabineer to bags while traveling

5) Bluetooth 4.0 technology handles well with testing the limits of the Bluetooth connectivity in a semi open space without causing jittering or breaking the signal of the music being streamed

6) AVRCP 1.4 and above specs allow this product's volume to be controllable in sync with the smartphone volume controller

7) Great microphone sensitivity for talking from a distance

CONS:

1) Front and Back frames have a hard plastic which looks and feels like that would be the weakness in taking damage from drops of impact over the other parts and components of the rugged exterior design

2) No Skip Forward or Skip Backward integrated functionality with the volume buttons, which is pretty standard with other portable speaker products

3) Not a very bright or noticeable LED light indicator due to the metal frame enclosure and the original source of light not being that bright to begin with

4) Particular unit I had was defective with an intermittently functional Power Button, but Taotronics responded swiftly with processing a replacement

5) Sound quality from the front sounds more clear and loud than hearing the sound quality from the back side, which is inconsistent expectations from this product being labeled as bidirectional

SUGGESTIONS:

1) Use gold plated connectors for Micro USB cable

2) Use gold plated connectors for AUX cable

3) Consider upgrading this design from 3W to 5W to stay competitive with the current market standard within this price range among waterproof portable Bluetooth speakers

4) Replace the hard plastic square frame on the front and back sides of the Bluetooth speaker to use instead TPU or Silicon

5) Rather than have the current LED indicator hidden and partially covered by the metal frame, have a strip frame around one or both sides of the speaker to have an insulated LED glow or light up when powered on in use or in pairing mode

6) Include Skip Forward and Skip Backward functionality on this speaker

7) Reevaluate the consistency in the sound quality of the bidirectional speakers from the front and back of the speakers

USER SCENARIOS:

People who should use this product are those who:

1) Love to go wireless with this accessories for their smartphone or tablet

2) Love music

3) Like an integrated solution to listen to music and handle calls within reach

4) Want better sound quality projected through speakers than their speakerphone or internal speaker of their smartphone or tablet

5) Like to go outdoors and bring along something to listen to on a trip

6) Want to be able to take their music to listen to in mildly wet conditions without ruining the electronics

Overall, I think this is a pretty good outdoor speaker. It beat my expectations when hearing that it was only 3W. Although I would still like for this to potentially upgrade to 5W, the current model serves well for boosting up music in a mildly quiet environment or when there’s a small get together. I think you’ll need a stronger and more powerful Bluetooth speaker for more talkative and crowded events. But take this with you on your journey to keep you from getting bored, enjoy the quality of the music, share the crowd or group around you into a call with a personal friend or loved one.

I knock off a star for many reasons. Other portable speaker designs with PASSIVE radiators (more tightly constructed) didn't have this issue to this same disastrous(!) extent.  Manufacturers design passive radiators into small units to give the impression of "bigger" sound but when bass hits hard, as most of today's music is geared to do, the Roar2's bass flubbily wooooonks with an EQ...and without the EQ the bass sounds unimpressive relative to competition.  The recently released SonyX55, for instance, has better/tighter radiators for its bass AND also sounds more clear in comparison, from bass to highs (not to mention 1000x more aesthetic).  Another note, when the amp is activated and playing sound, there's white noise.  If you're listening to quiet passages of Opera or movie, the white noise hissssses will be noticeable when it's amplifier is working.  The Bose Soundlinks, in comparison, DO NOT have white noise....good BLACK background (astonishing difference actually).  To be fair, other units of this ilk have this problem, like the Big Jambox, etc, btw.  Most people will probably(?) not notice this as much depending on what you're streaming to it, but it's there, and eventually you WILL notice it.  Another dig is that this unit sounds best when it's on it's vertical (sound is properly directional in this placement, like its competition).  BUT, this leaves the AC wall plug cable sticking UP as it's vertical too (they should have added a flush plug, since MOST people will use it vertically).  The plug is aesthetically very unsightly if this unit's used vertically........In contrast, layingit on it's belly the sound isn't more "room filling" as it's advertised in its brochure, just more distant and less clear....inferior.....especially in head-to-head contrast to the Bose Soundlink Mini or III whose sound is purposely & successfully equalized/designed to sound "room filling", but at a compromise of clarity which the Roar2 has to a better degree.  All in all, there are units that add a sound that could be more to one's liking.  The value with the Roar2 is its feature set like the SD card, recorder, etc.  As far as sound goes, it doesn't distinguish itself in this category...or really offend too badly (aside of the radiators not behaving themselves well with any alteration to an EQ)  I've head-to-head compared this unit with other top-rated units in this category such as the:  Bose Mini 2, Bose Soundlink 3, Big Jambox, Sony SRX55, Sonos Play 1, and Amazon Echo, so I know what I'm talking about.  Nothing better than to sit these units down side by side and have them go at each other.  I'll break my results down: **  Best Overall Sound for Music (NO bluetooth):  No question. Sonos Play 1 (plays off WiFi technology which allows for much better/higher BITRATE sound than compromised bitrate bluetooth right off the bat....AND also is 'voiced" better from top to bottom overall. Not as crystal clear as Sony or Big Jambox up top, but overall, the least sonically compromised.  If this unit had both bluetooth and Wifi and a battery, then this would be in all ways THE no-brainer of this category. It all DEPENDS on your specific needs.)  **  Best Sound with bluetooth but WON'T use for movies:  Sony SRX55  (bluetooth with movies has serious voice sync issues, which other units don't have to such extent, but the sound is indeed very good from top to bottom.  IF you won't watch movies on such units, then this is a winner).  **  Best Sound with bluetooth AND will watch movies:  Big Jambox or Soundlink 3 (Jambox has lesser bass than some others, especially the boomier Bose, but its sound is CLEAR from top to bottom and it's bass is good enough.  An overall great unit in this product bracket...In comparison, the Soundlink 3 has big boomy room filling, home theaterish, sound that works OK with movies but sounds LESS clear/intelligible than the Jambox in dialogue which is why I'd definitely choose the Jambox for this application. BUT Bose gives more of that Home Theater car crash boom sound...so it all depends on what "type" of sound you want.  Remember, however, that neither is loud enough to be really immersing in watching a movie (after all, look how small these units are!).  Better whip out good headphones instead for this purpose....or you can alternatively, with the wife watch on an Ipad with bluetooth speaker, in the backyard, summer evening, drinking a whisky.  ;)  **  Most "Room-Filling" Sound:  Soundlink 3 or Sonos Play 1 (Sonos Play 1 is definitely punchier/meaty...but it unfortunately lacks bluetooth, which some people need. Sonos uses WiFi which gives *MUCH* higher bitrate sound than the gimped-up bluetooth technology.  Soundlink 3 is great to fill a small room.....what Bose have accomplished is good for this "fill effect", but you will give up on overall CLARITY....but it at least has bluetooth....which the Sonos unfortunately doesn't).  **  Most Utilitarian:  Roar2 or Amazon Echo  All in all, you have to take these units for what they are.....small, portable sound "TOYS" to take to the beach/patio/kitchen for background music.  You WON'T get musical fidelity from ANY of them, just "good enough" sound to not offend too badly.  The products I tested above are all top user/critic rated -- some of the best-of-the-best.  My advice to you is to test 2-3 that have the "sound" you're looking for and test them at HOME. Then choose the best one that fits your needs.  Testing in a big store won't accomplish this as the sound dynamics of a big open noisy floor won't give you the speaker's true personality! It's day and night difference when you test them in your reflective furniture surroundings.  For your serious consideration, other top rated portable units (that can fit in a standard backpack) are:  the Denon Evaya units, Damson Vulcan (top reviews on UK Amazon/critics), JBL Charge 2 (firmware 1.41) or Charge 2+.  These units won't give boombox sized sound but  portable size and thusly equivalent sound to its relative size/woofers.  I haven't tested these units out but I assume I tested enough of the very best universally top-rated ones to guesstimate they'll be in the same ballpark. BATTERY POWER may be even MUCH MORE important for your usage at this size (as sonics is "meh" on all of them, except the standout Sonos Play 1). ......The reality is that at this small-sized level, the sonics can't realistically really matter all that much, aside of just being good enough "BACKGROUND" sound relative to a legion of "me too" portables, as it will NEVER be toe-tapping "great" sound that you would get from a wired home system or a bigger/heavier sounding boombox that can deliver with bigger woofer sizing.  It is what it is!  Physics is physics after all!

The Lexmark MS610DN is a good mid level networked workgroup printer. It's comparable to the [[ASIN:B008CJ1N5M Brother HL6180DW Printer]]. It's a little faster but without built-in wireless networking and the toner is more expensive than the brother. Lexmark makes the [[ASIN:B009SM8F0I MarkNet N8352 802.11b/g/n Wireless ]] kit for the MS610DN at about $40 additional.

Setup was simple and mostly consisted of removing various pieces of tape, a couple pieces of plastic on the imaging unit, placing it on an appropriate flat surface, plugging in power and network (assuming you are going for a network install), and loading paper into the generous 650 page paper tray.

Drivers installed easily and found the MS610DN on the network. The printer also has a web interface which is pretty useful. I've only begun to explore the features of the MS610DN but one that is of interest is the ability to setup forms in the printer. I'm thinking about building my letterhead design for head and foot of the page. The instructions are on the Lexmark web site.

The printer comes with 256MB of RAM memory, but has a slot for a DDR3 SODIMM RAM module. Lexmark sells these for $80 but I tried a SODIM from an old netbook to max out the printer at 1.25GB. These 1GB DDR3 SODIMM modules can be found dirt cheap and more memory means more document information can be stored in the printer and more complex printing can be performed. Here is one on Amazon similar to the one I had on hand: [[ASIN:B009KH4596 1GB Memory DDR3]].

Duplexing seems like a pretty standard feature these days and the MS610DN seems to actually print close to half its one sided print speed when print two sided. Not many printers achieve this feat. Nice!

One thing caught my attention enough to look for more detail. The printer comes with a "Return Program" starter toner cartridge. When I read about the return program cartridges this caught my eye: "In addition, the cartridge is designed to automatically update the memory in your printer to protect against the introduction of counterfeit and/or unauthorized third-party cartridges."

The included starter cartridge is a return program cartridge. This seems to mean it will alter the printer so it will not longer work with third party toner cartridges. It seems at least Lexmark requires you to agree to this if you use the included return program cartridge. I can understand why they would want to lock-in customers to buying Lexmark branded toner...

Lexmark toner is more expensive than comparable toner from Brother. With heavy use the toner is much more costly than the printer itself over the lifetime of the printer. A 5K page [[ASIN:B009SM8HL0 Lexmark High Yield Return Program Toner]] is currently $129 here on Amazon. A [[ASIN:B0084JMCF0 Brother TN750 8K Page Toner]] is currently selling for $75 here on Amazon.

There are 3rd party cartridges available but I've not gone through my starter yet so I can't say if they will work after an official return program cartridge has been loaded. I'll update the review when I find out!

Print quality is very very nice monochrome printing. Time to first page is impressive.

Like with any laser printer it's not a good idea to plug it into your UPS unless it's really beefy - FYI. I've had some clients kill their smallish UPS battery backup by doing this.

Since it does not have wireless built-in but does have that return-program starter cartridge and high toner cost adds to the total cost of ownership the MS610 gets 4 stars. It would get 5 but the return program feels like a vendor lock-in to me, though I tend to purchase cartridges made by the manufacturer anyway. I don't like feeling coerced.

This is an exciting idea. A wifi IR blaster for 40 bucks... exciting. And it works. And no one should waste their money one it. Because:

1. Requires an Android or iPhone app - opps phone rang turn down the stereo - I can't because I use my phone as my remote and I can't get to the app because the phone is ringing. Brilliant. Convergence is great unless you need to use the same device for two purposes at the same time.

2. The only app choice is rampant with permission abuse.

3. Requires Android 4+ (regardless of what the play store says), really? Why, Android 2 had network communication. And you want this to be on an older device not the latest greatest device, by the time you use a current device you have blown any advantage to the price... no longer an iTach beater.

4. The only app for this device is portrait only.

5. The app is pretty and nice, if you are using a predefined device. If you are using a pre-defined device there are tons of easier to use remotes for less right here on Amazon. If you want to create a custom device, it's like using Pronto back in 2003 - except you get to do it on a 5 in diagonal screen.

6. Here is the worst of all. It doesn't communicate directly with the phone. It goes back to Broadlink servers then they send to the RM2. So if Broadlink decides they want to quit supporting this device, more land fill. If Broadlink goes out of business, more land fill.

7. It can be controlled when you are away from home because it goes from your home to Broadlink's server then to the device. Or that guy who hacked Broadlink's server can do it for you! That's cool stuff.

This could so quickly be 5 star device. Open the api so that users can communicate directly with the device with simple telnet commands then open source guys will be all over coding for this. Make the call home part of the device optional - same with the app.

So from ahardware point of view this is an easy 5 star device - abused to the point of negative stars by bad software and proprietary desire to steal personal information and control your use of what you paid for. Don't buy this.

There was the alternative of playing the music through the line in jack on the back of the amp. In January of 2015 I noticed that one of the ear cushions was torn nearly half of the way off on the outside, I took a closer look and realized that they were separating from the rubber insert. A light pull peeled the cushion the rest of the way off.

I contacted Monster Support the next day, and after some delays I received my RMA information. Please note that I had to speak to 3 representatives before I got someone that actually had a clue how to process the RMA. The next day I shipped the headphones back to Monster, at my cost (expected). It would be nearly 3 weeks before I received my replacement headphones.

Fast forward to today, 7 or so months later. I have literally babied my replacement pair for fear of having to go through the same process and wait time I experienced the first time. They have been assigned to home use only, no travel whatsoever, and have had even lighter use than before. AGAIN, the ear cushion has fallen apart. Exactly the same way it did first time.

I immediately stopped what I was doing and called Monster Support. After being left on hold for 20 minutes I had to call back in. The next representative that I spoke with took my SN info and informed me that my headphones were out of warranty. I initially thought that couldn't be right... but then he explained. If Monster has to process an RMA on your product and sends out a replacement you are still under the same warranty window as your first product, which in this case was 1 year. If I had waited to use my replacement pair until mid February or so, which in all likelihood could have happened, and found that they were dead on arrival, Monster would not have replaced them. They quite literally do not warranty the replacement products they ship out. Couple this with the fact that they DO NOT offer replacement ear cushions and you basically have a $150.00 pair of unserviceable headphones with mediocre sound and extremely low build quality.

Stay far away from this garbage. I'm so disgusted with this situation I'll no longer be using their cables, either.

I highly recommend if you are even glancing at these to go look at a pair of Sennheiser HD 280 Pro's. 2/3 of the price, much higher build quality and sound, and they sell replacement cushions as well.

I will admit I was not expecting a whole lot from a speaker of this size. At approximately 3"x2"x2" this is a tiny speaker but for the size it puts out a decent amount of sound and a pretty good quality sound. As for the total volume I used a decibel meter at about 1 foot away from the unit and it pegged out at 93.5 decibels. For comparison one decibel comparison guide listed things in the same range as a blow dryer or gas powered lawn mower.

Due to its small size the speaker is a bit limited on bass. You can place it near a wall or a corner to accentuate the bass a bit. Even with the low, booming bass I still found this to be a very pleasing speaker to listen to. There is a little area to attach a lanyard to the speaker and I could see using this while out taking a walk rather than listening through headphones.

The volume on the device is directly tied to that of your phone or tablet so if you adjust the volume on the device you will see a corresponding move on your phone. One thing that annoyed me about the unit is that the volume up / down buttons share the same buttons as the track forward / reverse. The problem, for me, was that the volume changes required you to hold the button down for it to work as a quick press changed the track. I think it would have made more sense to do it the opposite way to make it easier as since you have to hold the button down to get the volume to change it is easy to go too far in one direction.

The Bluetooth works well here and has a good 20 to 30 foot range as expected. The outer case has a rubberized coating which makes it easy to grip and I really like that the unit is weather resistant. It is NOT water proof so don't throw it in the pool or anything.

My mother wanted a small speaker to use outside that she wouldn't have to be worried about getting wet and she really enjoyed this unit for listening to music (Michael Buble, Sinatra) and listening to the ballgames through her iPhone or iPad.

Overall this is a nice little weatherproof speaker that offers nice sound and decent volume. It's a little short on bass and the volume controls take a bit of getting used to but still a quality speaker. Recommended.

This device enables Bluetooth 3.0 communication between two devices. One of them must have a 3.5 mm input or output connector, and the other must have complementary Bluetooth capability. It does not matter if the Bluetooth is a transmitter or receiver because this device conveniently switches to connect to either one.

For example, in transmitting mode a music player with a headphone output jack can be connected wirelessly to Bluetooth headphones up to thirty feet away. In receiving mode, a wired pair of headphones can be connected to this tiny device and can then be paired with a number of Bluetooth devices like a smartphone, music player or tablet. With this piece of equipment it doesn’t matter if the Bluetooth device used is a transmitter or receiver.

This one by two inch transmitter/receiver comes with a four inch cable that has male 3.5mm stereo plugs on both ends, a 31 inch USB to micro USB charging cable, and a brief, easy to understand User Manual.

The TX/transmit mode is used to attach the device to a sound source using the included 3.5 mm cable, which I tested with a laptop computer, iPod music player, television, and a smartphone. Once the source is connected and the transmitter is turned on, a receiving device, such as a Bluetooth speaker or earphones can be connected by putting them into pairing mode and keeping them in close proximity until the pairing is automatically completed.

Depending on the listening device, either a confirming beep or voice affirmation will indicate successful connection. Both the headphones and speakers tested, connected almost immediately. Once pairing is complete, the devices can be moved up to 30 feet apart, and the signal will travel through walls or outdoors without degradation.

In RX/receive mode, the listening component is connected using the cable, and then can be connected wirelessly to an audio source that transmits using Bluetooth. I tested this using Bluetooth transmissions from a music player, smartphone, laptop and tablet.

Basic operation information -- initial charging took just over two hours when plugged into a laptop. The LED surrounding the front-mounted power button glows red while the unit is charging and turns off when fully charged. Controls are simple and effective. While the unit is powered off, set the sliding switch to TX for transmit or RX for receive.

Then, hold the power button in for nine seconds or until the LED begins to blink – blue in TX mode, alternating blue and red in RX mode. To turn the device off, press and hold the power button until the LED is solid red, then release. During operation, the LED flashes twice every four seconds to show that it is connected. If it becomes disconnected, it flashes once per second.

Whether used in transmit or receive mode, the sound quality is excellent, and I found it undistinguishable from a direct connection to the source device. I encountered no static or interruptions in the sound, even at the maximum distance. Depending upon the needs of the user this device has tons of potential to solve problems. Stellar functionality..

The extensions require 2 bolts each with a flat rounded head so the mount will fit close to the back of the TV and each of them have a square on the underside of the head to keep from spinning when tightening.  HORRIBLE PAIN to hold them in with your fingers or vise grips (which scratch) to tighten!!!  Remember there are 2 each which makes 8 fun times till finished.  After this painstaking time you move to attaching it to the back of your TV and the wall.  The single mount bracket works like any other as far as attaching it to the wall with lag bolts but the arm IS one piece as others have mentioned. We even sent one back with the extension piece bent over as we couldn't get it off no matter how hard we tried.  It had the square headed bolts that I described above.My final assessment is that this mount could most definitely be improved to make it easier for the consumer to assemble but most importantly change the type of "swivel ball" that hold the TV adjustment. Apple's first .mp3 player, known initially as simply the iPod, was introduced on October 23, 2001. It marked the beginning of Apple's entry into the field of portable music devices, and it joined and eventually helped accelerate a revolution in the digital music world that is still continuing today. Apple was not the first company to produce a portable .mp3 player, but their product did become the leading music player for many years.

This '7th Generation' model is the final 'Classic' that the company produced. It is actually the same as the 6th generation model, with an increase in capacity from a maximum of 120 GB to a maximum of 160 GB. It was introduced in September, 2009, and continued without change until the company finally discontinued the iPod Classic entirely on September 9, 2014, just under a year ago.

I have both this 160 GB iPod Classic, and a slightly older 120 GB model. I paid $249 plus tax for that 160 GB model at the local Apple store in September, 2010. I think that the 120 GB model was the same price when I purchased it a year or two earlier. They've both been great music players, even as I've found myself using them less and less. The great advantage of these iPod models was always their capacity, and for a very long time it was not possible to get a .mp3 player with greater capacity. I keep all of my music as lossless files, so they are large in size, and the capacity was even more important to me for that reason.

Today, the iPod Classic has several significant disadvantages when compared to the most up-to-date devices. The display and controls are still a similar scroll wheel style that is quite recognizable to someone who owned one of the very first iPod's. It works fine but can't match the current touch-screen displays that everything has today. The other disadvantage is that these iPod models use traditional mechanical spinning hard drives, which will eventually fail. They can be replaced, but is it worth continuing to spend money on something that is now basically a decade old (or more) design?

For many users, it is worth continuing to keep these iPod Classic music players running, and I understand the appeal. I'll probably keep mine until they find a home in the display cabinet as a kind of historical curiosity! I doubt very much that I'll use a single-purpose music player again anyway - streaming, or storing music files on my iPhone, can satisfy my requirements these days.

EDIT - READ MY ADDENDUM FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL REVIEW.   1 star out of 5 - I buy A LOT of Monoprice stuff.  All the cabling in my HT, my "man cave" and my Honda Accord video system is Monoprice.  I have a Monoprice HDMI distribution box and two HDMI over Cat5 kits.  I just purchased the HDMI Matrix Switcher to add some coolness to my man cave before football season.  My main 75" display is flanked by four 32" LED sets each with their own dedicated Directv HD receiver.  The four sources into the switcher I have are bottom left HD Receiver, bottom right HD Receiver, PS3 and AppleTV.  The Apple TV is just temporary until I get the Wii U moved.  The outputs are going to the bottom left 32", bottom right 32" and the 75" via an HdMI input on the Onkyo AVR.  For some reason the switcher does not mind the 1080 signals from either directv box or the PS3 but the Apple TV will not display.  Actually it has displayed a couple of times by turning the switcher on and off but it is VERY sporadic.  I assumed it was a bad cable.  Nope.  Tried swapping the inputsand out outs around, bypassed the Onkyo to go straight to my 75".  Only get consistent picture from Apple TV when the Monoprice is not in the signal chain.  I'm going to try Monoprice customer support and will change my review to reflect the outcome.  At this time though I can't give it a recommendation. EDIT I revised my review to three starts because even though Monoprice customer support could not figure out what my issue is, it was not for lack of trying.  I am sure it is a handshake issue but of the five monitors NONE of them will display the signal from this particular device.  HOWEVER I can get the 32" sets to display by switching inputs ON THE TV and back to the original HDMI input and all is well.  Not ideal but this kind of confirms in my mind that something is getting lost in translation during the handshake.  Now I don't lay this all at the feet of Monoprice because it is my fervent opinion that HDCP sucks... BIG TIME.  At the same time, there is a standard to the specs and either the switcher or Apple is not 100%.  I tend to think the Apple is not at fault.  Not that Apple is infallible, but the only time that device displays correctly is when the switcher is out of the signal chain.  I am going to be replacing the Apple TV with a Wii U and if it does not present the same issue I am going to revise my review to five stars with the caveat that Apple TV owners may have issues.  Last update forthcoming.
