From the reviews of the Tomameri portable players (they sell this same player in 8, 16, and 32GB versions), this seems to be a love it or hate it type of product - which might come down to your expectations before you get it. Let me try to help with that - this is not a super-high-quality piece of hardware. The plastic pieces seem kind of cheap, and the ear buds aren't very nice. However, the aluminum case is actually pretty decent, the Micro SD card seems about as well made as others that I've bought, and the mini USB cable (yes, it charges with mini USB versus the more prevalent micro USB) is surprisingly nice. Audio performance is pretty decent, but don't expect much from the video. I gave the 16GB version four stars but am giving this one three stars because I don't think it's as good of a value at the current $36 price (more on that below).

If I were looking for something like this for myself or anyone that didn't destroy electronics quickly (like a young child), I'd heavily consider just using an older (or even new) smart phone - because most of those will do everything that this does but do it MUCH better. Bigger screen, probably as much memory (but maybe requiring a micro SD card)...and so on. If you wanted to get a young child their first music player and didn't want to risk having something more expensive get busted, this might not be a bad choice...because odds are you won't mind if this gets broken. I don't mean that in a mean way to this player - I'm just saying that I think it falls squarely into the niche of disposable products. This is exactly the kind of product that I wouldn't mind taking on a plane trip because it sounds pretty good and because I wouldn't be upset if I lost it or broke it...inexpensive hardware like this definitely has a place.

I do want to point out that the lower memory size Tomameri players are currently a better deal, with the 8GB version being only $14 right now ($22 cheaper at current prices). When you do your shopping, if you decide that you want one of these players - I highly recommend that you check the other models. The ONLY difference (that I can tell, and I have the 16GB and 32GB models) is the memory card. Even the sample files that come on them are the same. You can buy 32GB micro SD cards faster than the one that comes with this product for under $15, so it might pay off to get the cheapest version out there and then get a separate card for it. This is a superb amplifier and one I strongly recommend to anyone looking for a modern, good value valve alternative to a sub £500 integrated amplifier.

Before the detail here is some context.

I have a long history of choosing valve amplifiers over transistor and subsequent IC options, starting using ones my dad made when he was an apprentice in the 1950s through to more modern options from Fatman, Little Dot and GemTune. This is not to ignore great non tube amplifiers and my reference set up is Exposure with QAcoustic 3020, custom Wharfedale or Celestion F2 speakers depending on the room. This new amplifier will end up in one of two places and so it has been tested in both rooms, a smallish Northumbrian farm cottage with thick stone walls and a modern 1970s house with a concrete and plasterboard construction, and the speakers used have all been floor or low stand mounted.

So, I accept my own bias towards the valve sound but stack this amplifier against some good modern stuff including Cambridge Audio, Exposure as well as my every day Fatman Carbon.

This is my second amp from Grandview via Amazon UK and my experience is that they work hard to make sure all is well with your purchase. The amplifiers have been very professionally packed for shipping with the valves wrapped separately in foam moulds inside the larger foam amplifier carriage. Once again there were power leads for the UK and U.S. include in the box. All was labelled well and accurately for delivery with tracking information, and communication with Grandview is exceptional seeming most of the time to be almost by return of email.

Set up was straightforward using the supplied valves which were two Russian made EL34-Bs, two Shuguan 6N8P double triodes and a single Shuguan 5Z3P. The only slight glitch here is that there are no instructions about which valve goes where and so the obsessive in me double checked with the manufacturer images to confirm which way round the EL and 6Ns went.

After connecting the Wharfedale speakers and some input leads I switched on and let the valves warm and settle over a couple of hours before first use.

Over the last thirty years I have moved away from analogue sources and now use either a Cambridge Audio CD player or Apple lossless tracks via an iPod or laptop. The latter uses a standalone PCM2704 DAC converter from Squirrel Labs but this does mean I'm entirely digital and so can't comment on how this amplifier will pair with a turntable or quality tape setup.

My initial response was that this was a very good amplifier, solid low frequency response across classical and rock music with excellent higher frequency in the female vocal range. For the first outing I played through Elgar's Nimrod, Barber's Adagio for Stings, Barclay James Harvest's Child of the Universe, Led Zep's Going to California before moving to folk music and Show of Hands, Annemarie Quinn, Kate Walsh and Heidi Talbot. Sitting down and listening to several tracks from each artist, rather than jumping from one to another really started to show the warmth and depth of this amplifier with a clear soundstage and nothing 'muddy' or blurred.

The next day, having left the amplifier on to warm the cottage overnight and further burn in the tubes I switched speakers to the QAcoustic and moved on to listen to some different music. Armin van Buuren's album Intense was up first followed by A State of Trance 2014 and then Emma Hewitt with Burn the Sky Down and all the way through I was blown away by just how competent this amp sounded, never missing a beat or feeling lacking on the loud tracks. Then it was time to quieten things down a bit with some old favourites from Fleetwood Mac, Roxy Music, Judy Tzuke and Elkie Brooks, all handled really well and the years just falling away.

Later in the evening I switched speakers again to the Celestions and started playing though some softer favourites, Norah Jones, Simply Red, Tracy Chapman, Madeleine Peyroux, Joss Stone and Jack Johnson amongst others. Mellow stuff for a glass of red and a comfy sofa and all good with the floor standers responding well to just a few watts out of the available eight at peak power.

So a few days in and with a change of listening space coming up my initial impressions are being confirmed that this is a really, really good valve amplifier. Well able to shine with both classical and more modern music, handling deep lows from the strings and bass through to the higher range female vocals of electronic and progressive trance music with equal panache.

A couple of days on now with a change of space and speakers have confirmed what I thought, this amp is really, really good.

It's been switched on pretty much continually for about a week and then last couple of days have been spent switching between the QAcoustic and Celestion speakers. Is there a difference, yes but I don't really have a preference as both set sets sound good to me in this more modern room.

Music has been a real mixture, from soul through classical to trance favourites but across all genres the sound has remained warm and solid with no coloration or fuzziness. Running the GemTune alongside some modern integrated amplifiers shows again the differences you get with the 'valve sound'. There's a warmness, it's involving and yes, it's a little old fashioned but if you like valve amplifiers that's what you go for. As for my collection it's definitely moved up to the top spot and the Fatman, great amp that it is will have to take a break.

So, where is this amp going to end up, I think in the Northumbrian farmhouse paired with the QAcoustic 3020 speakers. There's plenty of power to fill the room, certainly sounding grander than the rated 8 watts, and the warmth of the sound matches the space we listen in, plus my wife really likes it as it matches our Edisonfilament lamps !

Overall this is an amplifier I'd strongly recommend if you're contemplating going over to valves or upgrading to a more powerful amp. It's a good price (currently around the £300 delivered to the UK) and will easily stand along side integrated offerings in the sub £500 bracket. Next to my older valve amplifiers, the Fatman and the Mini Watt and some good IC offerings this is our clear favourite and will be back in the Volvo with the speakers and heading 'up country' this week.

I got one of these kits for a Christmas present last year, but never had the chance to see the key finder in action. The company contacted me recently and provided me with the same key finder kit for free in order to provide my review for it. My mom was visiting at the time, so I had her use the product, given that she loses things quite often. The pros of this key finder kit are that you get plenty of receivers: 3 that stick on to things, and 3 that are keychain-based. We used the keychain receivers for keys and attached to the inside of a purse, while the stick-on receivers we placed on cell phones and remotes. The key finder and receivers have a good range, within my house we were able to always locate the items whenever they were lost. It also served as a good check before leaving the house to make sure my mom had everything she needed in her purse.

However, there are some limitations and issues, which is why I am giving this 4/5 stars. First, the receivers are bulky, so putting them on phones or remotes doesn't work so well. If you lose things like glasses, this won't work at all. If they were smaller or flatter, they would be a better fit for such use. Secondly, the ringer on the receivers could be louder. If an item is buried under a blanket or other things, it may be hard to find.

Overall, I'd recommend this for folks who lose their valuables throughout the house or car, it gets the job done and you won't lose things quite so much.

Comes packed in bubble wrap with no instructions or specs. There are two boards, both single sided.  One is pots and some resistors and caps.  There are 3 - 50k ohm potentiometers on the daughterboard, they have a smooth feel, but measure 24.4 , 47.4, 30.3 kohm.  I haven't hooked this up yet but assume it is one pot per channel..This is connected by a ribbon cable to a board with three chips marked TDA2030A, HLF1008.  Electrolytic capacitors are marked Chong CD11X -40-105F and 25V  The rest of the components appear to be tantalum or film caps and 1% resistors, along with an LED and an NE5532 op-amp and a +5V regulated output .  There is a discrete bridge made of diodes marked RL207  Input is achieved via 2 RCA jacks, or a three pin molex, or a TRS jack.  Output is via screw terminals.  There is no heat sink grease or isolators between amp chips and heatsink, so the heatsink should be enclosed in a ventilated case.

But at a recent funeral for a relative, I needed to send an HDMI video from my Canon camcorder (Canon VIXIA HF G20) to a nearby building, where overflow crowd was being put, since the main building would be over capacity. Audio was handled via wireless mics, no problem, but sending a 1080p video feed was another story.

I ran a 20' HDMI line from my camera to a projector, as a test, and everything worked perfectly. So I tried a quality manufactured Belkin CAT 5e 100' cable, using the extenders, and again, it worked perfectly. My concern, of course, was longer distances, since I would be operating near the maximum stated spec for the extenders... much more of a challenge than the best-case scenarios I had just tested. A couple of days later, when my box of cheap CAT 5e bulk cable arrived from Amazon, I dutifully measured out a 300' cable (the distance I needed the run to work) and crimped connectors on it. I coiled it all up, and plugged everything together, for a close-quarters test. Imagine my dismay when it did NOT work! But looking at the large coil of network cable, it occurred to me that "cable loops are bad" or so I've always been told. They just never seem to matter, to me ... at the short distances most normal people work with. But this was a relatively extreme setup, so perhaps one more test? I took the long cable on a long walk around my backyard, eliminating any loops in favor of a straight run, much like I would have in the final installation. Plugged it all in again, hey, it worked! There was much relief.

On the day of the event, we set up the camera, and ran that same 300' cable over to the next building (all connected through hallways), taping it down and cleaning it all up neatly dressed. Plugged the camcorder into the transmitter one side (via 6' HDMI cable), plugged the projector in the receiver side (via another 6' HDMI cable), fired it all up in sequence, and what do you know! The picture came up perfectly, just like with the shorter, easier tests.

History and preamble - you may skip to the review:

I bought this remote to replace my old Denon AVR-789 unit because the ON and OFF buttons had ceased working. I considered an "OEM" replacement because of the complex setup buttons that the original RC-1099 had inside a "trap door" on the back. My AVR-789 is still functional but so old that the remote control is no longer available from Denon and what was available, was obviously a look-alike universal control that had programming for my particular AVR and several others. It appears that the RC-1099 was a popular control configuration that Denon shipped with many of their AVR's and that it was programmed for whichever AVR it accompanied. Thus, I was faced with many "identical" choices but only one that was specified for my AVR-789 and a few other Denon units with dissimilar model #'s. None of these had reviews, they were marketed by various vendors and they all seemed to ship directly from somewhere on the Pacific Rim. Needless to say, this situation did not inspire confidence and I seriously considered replacing the entire A/V Receiver with a new one, just to have the assurance that the remote control and the AVR would function as a unit.

Actual experience:

Yes, I read reviews - exhaustively. I was struck by the number of positive reviews for the Inteset INT-422-1 and the apparent ineptitude of the few negative reviewers, one of whom was politely answered by the supplier who showed unusual pride in this product. The price was good, on a par with the fake RC-1099's, and much better that any of the Logitech units which I also considered. So, I bought it and 2 days later, it was in my hot little hands and ready to be programmed.

Now, right off the bat, the packaging is not impressive. The instructions, while adequate, are quite cryptic, and visiting the web site to obtain "codes" falls short of confidence inspiring. Never-the-less, Ipressed on and copied out a list of 5 AVR codes and 2 AMP codes for A/V Denon, and then, 16 possible codes for my 65" Panasonic Plasma TV (which BTW, will ONLY be replaced by a BIGGER 4K OLED when they become economical) because, why not?

Anyway, I read through the entire instruction sheet again, twice, and then, taking the simplest approach, started with the Denon. The technique of entering the codes, for a neophyte like myself, is to not look for too much handholding in the instructions. What they do NOT say and what I am telling you, is to enter the entire 5 digits all at once, and then, look for the affirmation blink from the red LED. If you get it, test the programming with the ON/OFF button and like the instruction sheet says, if your "device" turns off, the code is working.

Well, with the Denon, the first code was the charm. The AVR-789 turned off. So, I pushed the button again and voila! it came back on. Sucess! I searched for the mute button and it worked too. Then the volume buttons and they worked. OK, great, that was all I usually used the old, taped-together RC-1099 for anyway and if I needed to change inputs, well I could figure that out later.

Now, on to the Plasma TV. The Denon was now button "A" so the Panasonic would be button "B." This setup was not so easy. The first and second 5 digit codes got no response from the INT-422-1. The third did. OK, I was getting pretty good at punching these in and had 13 more to go so, mash the power button and Hey, the TV switched off. Neat, mash again and it turned on. No need to try the volume buttons, that was handled by the Denon so on to the UP/DOWN channel buttons and THEY worked! I tried out the channel numbers and THEY worked. This was looking good. Let's see what else this puppy will do. The "Menu" button brought up, of all things, the MENU. Wow! Now, what is this button down at the bottom, Input? Mash that and there's the Input screen. So I scroll down to my DVD setting, press OK and there I am. This baby is emulating my Panasonic remote perfectly. Better in fact, because I can just tap in the number of the input I desire and it dumps the selection screen switches directly to the input. Oh yeh, and I can see it in the dark.

Well, I'm delighted. The backlight is beautifully done, I have confidence in the remote and its coding, it feels good in my hand and I can hardly wait to explore those "macro" features. Best of all, If I foul things up, I can reset the whole thing or any part of it. This is a really neat toy and it is as useful as can be.

Conclusion:

Not only is the INT-422-1 a replacement remote control, it is an improvement!

This mount is NOT adjustable once it's set (without re-hanging). It also is not tiltable or turnable. The TV will be parallel to the wall on both pitch and yaw. There is no means of adjusting level, so be absolutely certain you get it level when mounting, or your TV will be crooked.

That said, it comes with a variety of mounting hardware to fit onto a studded or concrete mounting surface and is a super simple install. I used only two of the 4 included lag bolts to secure it into a stud and it hasn't budged a smidge, holding a 37" appx 24lb TV. This is after a lot of futzing with it to get cables run behind the wall. As I discovered you will want to pay careful mind to where you run a cable hiding bracket box, as this mount is extremely slim and holds the TV only about an inch from the wall. If the exit cable bracket box is too near the mounting brackets, you may have some issues getting the cables to run above or below the brackets. Behind the brackets is not an option (not enough distance from the wall for even a networking or RCA cable).

All of the above issues are just due to this mount being extraordinarily affordable. I've not found an adjustable, slim wall mount for less than $70. If you can hang a level bracket, and can position the wall cable bracket boxes correctly, this is an excellent mount.

It's true, but it doesn't tell you very much, because so many MANY headphones are superior to the stock iPhone earbuds. Phone calls sound good, and the other party says they can hear me well. I like the pause and volume buttons on the remote control thing. Audio that sounds SSSSSSSOOOOO SSSSSSSIBILIANT and pierces my eardrums with the iPhone earbuds will turn into just sssssssslightly tinny on these. I'm emphasising the s because they sound ear-splitting with anything less than good headphones.

If you're using these for anything except running, they're an utter waste. Why? The design of the wire that comes down one side makes it awkward for it to use when sitting down at a table (for example). The particular way that the band wraps around the back of your head makes it impossible to lie down with it. The reason I mention all this is because if I am spending this much on a pair of headphones, I'll want more than to be able to say that I can use them for one purpose alone: workouts.

For comfort, these are terrible. In any configuration I put them on, they don't feel comfortable in my ears. After a fairly short amount of time, they grow painful to wear. I managed the first day to wear them for about an hour, with no problems. I'm not working out for an hour, but I wanted to wear one pair of headphones for the commute and for the session. After about an hour, my ears started to hurt from how hard the headphones were pressing against them. THAT SAID, they did not budge or fall off. That was probably because they had my head in a vice-like grip, but there you go.

The package arrived as a box in a box. The outer shipping box with a small amount of paper as a buffer for the inner product box. The inner box arrived with the product undamaged but seriously - whoever packs this stuff at the Amazon warehouse is cutting corners.

Contents of the box
- speaker
- manual
- usb cable (no charging cube or transformer - supply your own)
- a short stereo mini cable (about 3')

The speaker
- looks nice
- nice handles
- average build quality
-- the outside flanges at each end of the cylinder attach with 4 (each) short tapping screws tapped into the plastic cylinder. Over time will work themselves loose.

The product pictures really don't show this so - the side with the knobs and controls have 2 small drivers and a small acoustic port of about an inch in diameter. I did not measure the drivers but they look to be between 2 and 3 inches in diameter. The other side is the 6" woofer. Speaker drivers are adequately protected by nice grills.

The knobs stick out a bit and could be damaged. They feel like cheap knobs that may not hold up to the test of time and use.

The tuner - seemed to work as designed with an auto tune feature whereby it set into presets any station it tuned to. The reception without an antenna was marginal and noisy, Who wants to listen to that? I live in the NYC metropolitan area so there is an abundance of strong stations here so take that for what it is.

The Bluetooth
Useable range for me was about 30', Pretty average
There is an audible electronic whizz/buzz when it is in bluetooth mode that is a dealbreaker for me. If you listen to nothing but loud or dynamic music, the music will drown this out. Its not something you have to put your ear next to to hear but it is audible, especially when you have the volume cranked at or near max.

Every piece of electronic gear makes background noise. The better ones have a better "signal to noise ratio" which in normal english translates into it is whisper quiet and you really have to be listening to it or you need sensitive instruments to measure it. I assure you, you need no instruments to appreciate this.

The bluetooth pairing was actually very easy. Also, if you power the speaker off it will almost immediately re-pair with the last device. You have to un-pair or turn off the blutooth of the last device before it will let you pair another device to it.

Now for the sound which is what everyone was waiting for.
Yes - it did play pretty loud but it would distort at or near maximum volume. With my portable at full volume and this at around 95% it just didn't seem loud enough though. I did not actually measure spl levels with my instruments, just sampled using various selections of music that i also use when testing audio systems

The tone control is a single knob whereby at one extreme it boosts the treble and cuts out the bass. At the other extreme it cuts the treble and because of that it will seem to the untrained ear that you are boosting the bass. I actually used my iphones and ran a little test whereby one iphone fed the speaker with white noise (fed at max volume) and the other phone using a real time audio analyzer verified what my ears were telling me.

The tone control actually boosts the sound in the 2 to 5 kilohertz range where we as human beings are most sensitive, This is why sirens and horns are tuned to these frequencies so that human ears can hear them. Unfortunately this is also what contributes to the poor sound quality of the speakers. To call it shrill is being generous. The only way I can listen to this is to have have tone control at almost the other extreme and then to back it off a little bit. The bass measured relative to everything else down to about 110 hz where it dropped precipitously. Switching my white noise app to play tones, I could play audible bass through the speaker down to about 40 hz but it does not translate to the listening experience because there is no way to boost this so you can actually hear it in your music. You should know that to hear the bass you had to really crank the speaker's volume where it quickly went into distortion because it did not like to play any bass below around 80 hz. I did not actually expect this speaker to sound like a decent full range bookshelf but 110 or 120hz is just not what I expected from a 6 inch "sub". Let's call it what it is. This is NOT a "SUBWOOFER". A subwoofer is a speaker capable of reproducing low bass tones with authority. This was barely a woofer but could work if the tone control was better. Don't get me wrong, there is better bass than my Oontz by virtue of the fact that there is a 6" driver but not what I was underwhelmed or maybe overwhelmed by the abundance of mids.

There is no separate bass control which is unfortunate because the bass is just not what I expected. I wanted the ability to boost it a little for some punch and fullness. Despite my audiophile and recording engineering background - I am not interested in listening to musically accurate renditions of my music when I am in my car or working on a job.Still, there is a fine line for me where too much bass is just not pleasant to listen to

If I were designing this I would include separate bass, treble and midrange tone controls. The bass to boost the bottom end a little, the midrange to cut entirely and the treble to add just a little bit of brightness that this speaker is also lacking.

I went so far as to disassemble this (carefully) to see if thee was a way to upgrade the parts or to improve upon the sound. I can probably stuf the cylinder with some insulation or use some polyester pillow fill found at crafts stores like Michaels - probably better than itchy fiberglass but what does this actually do for me? it will reduce the internal resonance of the speaker a little resulting in smoother sounding bass but less of it because I am reducing the internal volume of the cylinder a little by adding the fill. I came to the conclusion that i would be returning this so why bother.

Admittedly, this did not sound too bad listening to some EDM beats. It was punchy enough and the music genre is not reliant on midrange.

In conclusion:
I think my quest continues. This may be a good purchase for you because it is much fuller than the mainstream portable bluetooth speaker while still remaining a portable speaker. I am not sure I want to upgrade to a large blutooth PA speaker as a 30 lb speaker with wheels and extending luggage handles may not be for me either.

Price wise - It was a good deal to me. At $70 it is a very good bargain and there reallyisn't much that can compare to it in this range. I did not even consider the Pyle offerings because I know they are built like crap and did not like the bells and whistles from the cheap Asian imports either. I am almost tempted to keep this because the speakers are almost listenable if I place a thin piece of soft foam over them and may overlook the bluetooth noise or just use the Aux input.

So I'm trying to find the perfect VR Headset without spending tons of money and while shopping the only thing I could find was that each headset seemed to vary in features and so did the reviews. My solution... buy a few based on current top reviews and then pick what I feel to be the best. Below are the headsets purchase, used and now reviewed.

DESTEK® 3D VR Virtual Reality Headset ($39.99 version)
http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00S6EIIPQ?psc=1&redirect=true&ref_=oh_aui_detailpage_o01_s00

GOODO® VR Virtual Reality Helmet ($26.99 version)
http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00ZEUHR70?psc=1&redirect=true&ref_=oh_aui_detailpage_o03_s00

== DESTEK® 3D VR Virtual Reality Headset ==
Out of all of them this one was my least favorite which surprised me because it had the most reviews. I found it very difficult to insert my phone and ended up having to put the unit on it's side to be able to line up my phone. This make for switching apps very tedious as each time you remove the phone you have fiddle with getting it back in.

I'm not sure why a magnetic button is not just something standard, but on the DESTEK it is missing so basic VR apps that require simple selection inputs is not going to happen until you open the phone compartment to select what needs to be selected and well then you get to fiddle with lining the phone up again. This makes it necessary for a controller and I've had no luck getting one to work with my iPhone, but Android seems to be just fine.

I found this headset to also be very uncomfortable. The face padding seems very thin and I found myself compelled to remove it rather than sticking with it to see if I could get used to it. Mine did come with the nose pads and NFC tag.

It's not all bad though. The lens seems very clear and are big enough to display the iPhone 6 plus screen. For me, it was a little blurry and had they of included some lens adjustments and focus abilities I'm sure it could of been tweaked to be much better.

== SUNNYPEAK® Virtual Reality Headset ==
This one is my favorite and the one I'll be keeping, but still it isn't perfect and it's a shame because it would be such an easy fix. First off the unit feels solid, not heavy, but not flimsy either. Most importantly it feels really really good while wearing it and the head strap is snug and comfortable. The face padding feels good, but for whatever reason there is no nose padding. I'm not understanding this as the nose is supporting much of the weight so you would think it would be included. Also missing is a NFC tag although I'm not really sure of it's importance. I actually purchased the nose pads and NFC tag from DESTEK which should work well to solve these missing items.

This VR headset holds the phone in a much better way. Instead of opening a compartment and sticking your phone to suction cups or trying to line it up so a foam pad can hold it in place this has a removable trey that you put your phone in. Switching apps is a breeze as all you do is slide out the tray access your phone and slide it back in. Love it! The back right section also comes off to allow for camera access which is a nice addition.

I think the best part about this VR headset is the ability to adjust the lens width position and do some basic focusing. I was able to get the picture quality to look pretty darned good based on my eyes and preference. Also on this unit are vents where the phone resides to help keep it cooled.

Missing on this unit as well is the magnetic button. I'm not sure why, but again it means you must have a controller and if your on iOS you may be out of luck.

== GOODO® VR Virtual Reality Helmet ==
This is a solid VR headset as well and has just about everything you could want, but for me the picture is just a little blurry and since it lacks any type of focus it just won't get any better. The unit does allow for the adjustment of the lens distance so if you have wider or narrower eyes you can compensate a little.

The fit is good and comfortable, but again the absence of nose padding really is evident with just a short bit of use. This unit as well in my opinion has a rather thin face padding, but other than the nose it's not as noticeable.

Your phone fits into this VR headset by an outside compartment that snaps open. Inside is a row of suction cups which work well to hold the phone in place. Changing apps is not a big deal as you can just open the door, make your selections and then close it. There are cooling vents and surprise surprise this one has a magnet button. A controller is still very useful, but with the magnetic button simple apps can be used. NFC is missing from this unit as well and with the suction cups in the center placing a 3rd party NFC tag might not work.

Overall these units all do what they are supposed to do and at a cost that won't break the bank especially if you need more than one headset. I have used Bose in-ear modules (IEMs) in the past and the biggest problem for me was achieving a tight seal in my ear, to both improve the richness or bass response of the sound, and for keeping out external noise.

Bose seems to have solved that problem with the new Bose SoundTrue Ultra In-Ear headphones for Samsung and Android devices.
The StayHear Ultra tips fit tightly in my ear canals. The tips look similar to those provided in the past but these deliver a much tighter seal, improving the sound (especially the bass) and passively eliminating most external noise. I use IEMs when commuting on a noisy train, and these earphones do a remarkable job cutting out all external noise, including the noise of the train.

With the tight fit my music sounds much better and more detailed. The earphones are light and comfortable to wear for long periods. Bose provides three different sizes of tips, Large, Medium, and Small, and a nice soft carrying case.

From a sound perspective, the Bose SoundTrue Ultra headphones provide mostly balanced sound, with a slight prominence on bass. I listened to different genres of music (like I always do when I test headphones), listening to mostly FLAC or MP3 files ripped at 320 kbps. The headphones performed consistently well, with subtleties of the music more apparent since the tight seal eliminates external noise.

I used the headphones with a Samsung phone, and the inline microphone and remote worked fine, although the controls are a little too high on the wire of the headphone, making it hard (if not impossible) to see the controls.

Summing up, these are very good in-ear headphones, providing very consistent and clear sound. The big plus for me, however, is the improvement Bose made to the StayHear Ultra Tips. The super tight seal provides excellent isolation to outside noise. Remember to try each size to make sure you are getting the tightest seal possible. The correct fit and seal makes a huge difference with how these headphones sound.

The "European" (plug) side of the adapter fit perfectly in all of the sockets, and the plugs on our American electronics/devices all fit very snugly in the "American" (socket) side of the adapter -- not too tight, and definitely not too loose. I was skeptical before receiving the NRG (nylon cable) headphones after owning a few pairs of low priced headphones that where lacking in either the bass, mids, highs, or build quality, but after handling and listening to these, I am quite impressed. The only flaw I could find was in the pause/play button which requires moderate pressure or the click doesnt register.

- SOUND QUALITY -
The sound quality is very good. In my tests I loop a few seconds of different songs that encompass a range of instruments, and then listen to each pair of headphones one after the other. Compared to a few other pairs in this price range, these seem to be the most balanced. Bass is nice and deep, mids and vocals are clear and natural, and highs are fairly crisp but not painfully sharp. I do not feel the need to use an equalizer with these. There no "tin can / hallow tube" sound to them like in some low priced headphones. Compared to my stock galaxy S4 headphones, these have slightly more bass, and richer mids. Using a tone generator, at half volume I can hear from 20hz to 17000hz (may vary depending on person). Note: To get the best sound, make sure to try each size of silicone tips.

- BUILD QUALITY -
The physical construction is made of mildly polished wood, with metal accents (not chromed plastic). The ear buds are not cold when putting them in, and they push in without causing uncomfortable eardrum pressure. They are comfortable and stay in while running (if tucked under shirt) and while chewing.

The 51inch (measured) cable is nylon and is smooth and light weight. I personally don't have problems with tangled headphones, and these don't seem to tangle any more than other pairs. Being nylon, the cord should not break at stress points. Given the pros of nylon over rubber cables, there is one downside which is the noise transferred to your ear. Any kind of movement in the cord is audible. To stop this, you can loop them behind your ear, or tuck them under your shirt. I wish a clip was included.

The headphone jack is at a 45' angle, made out of a flexible rubber, and is easy to put in the device because it measures only 6mm in diameter. This works well with all my phone cases. There is no static feedback when rotating it.
Up on the left part of the cable is a microphone and pause/play button. It also has long press, and double press functions which I could configure in music player apps (android). I can feel the button click when pressing it, but I have to use moderate pressure or the click doesnt't register in my phone.
The microphone works fine and sounds almost the same as my phones built in mic, maybe a little less bass. It also seemed to pickup less background noise.
Also included is a cloth case, and 3 different sizes of ear tips.

- PROS -
Sound quality
Build quality
Classy style

- CONS -
More cable noise than rubber cables
Play/pause button requires moderate pressure
No shirt clip

- CONCLUSION -
I would recommend these to anyone who wants good sound, a classy design, or has problems with their cables breaking. Due to the nature of the nylon cable and it's noise, I would not recommend these if you move around a lot, and to opt for a pair with rubber cables. I've now had these a few days and I think I can now provide an in-depth review.  Several other reviewers have mentioned that these are not for active use. The collar bounces around a little bit, but its nothing compared to the annoyance of corded headphones getting caught on your hands or clothing and getting yanked out.  However, when I went to the gym, anything that had me lay even slightly back the collar would slide off, occasionally taking the earbuds with it.  I feel the same would happen if I were riding my motorcycle, though I haven't tried it yet.  I'm considering adding a small cord to attach the open ends of the collar and prevent it from sliding off in the wind.  Otherwise these are pretty good headphones.  I think they sound pretty good and they don't stick out very far when being worn.  I've been using these with my iPhone 6+ and my laptop.  The iPhone seems to be slightly strained by Bluetooth, as I get a small click or pop when I turn the screen off and sometimes when the phone plays system sounds, texts/alerts.  The phone seems to account for the delay from compressing and processing the audio though, so watching videos on my phone works just fine.  With the laptop, however, there is a noticeable delay which must be accounted for by whatever software you use to play videos, I use VLC and set the delay to 0.15 seconds.  Otherwise, they also worked perfectly with the laptop.  As far as comfort goes, I'll just say the first day I had them I fell asleep on the couch for about an hour and a half with them in and wore them for another 2 hours after I got up with minimal discomfort.

Based on reviews of other stands, these are one of the few that will work with the Vizio speakers...and they do mostly, with a little tweaking to the mounting bracket to accommodate the RCA connector as mentioned in other reviews.  That said, the overall quality of the speaker stands is mediocre at best. The bases are heavy but made out of "lumpy" metal and appeared to be painted with a spray can. The logos are splotchy and also poorly painted on. The metal is soft...one of the support columns easily cross-threaded. The support columns are adequate. They come in two pieces and adjust like a mic stand, but they are no where near mic stand quality.  The rest of the pieces were all there but are typical low-end Chinese manufacturing standard in that everything just barely fits. Chinese manufacturing can be exquisite of course...it all depends on the seller's specs, and in this case Pyle's were not very demanding.  The good news is that the inside of the columns and the holes in the mounts are large enough to accommodate the straight end of the RCA connectors when they're threaded through...something others had problems with on other stands.  So for holding a pair of really light, basic surround sound speakers where quality isn't top of mind they'll do. If you want to impress friends with your audio system in your living room or HT, these are not your best option.

The downloadable DirecTV app for my phone worked well until a necessary change-up of our wireless system put that very short-ranged solution out of business. You pretty much had to be in the same room with the wireless router for the DirecTV phone app to work, and now that option was gone.

I tried the radio frequency DirecTV remotes (claims are it goes through walls), but no soap. I tried wireless InfraRed repeaters, but the distance and the 2 exterior walls defeated that as well. It was looking like I had a very difficult wire-stringing job for a wired signal repeater and I just didn't want to do that.

So after spending some time on Amazon looking for one of those, I stumbled upon "Blumoo". Hmmmm...Bluetooth connection, would it work? Honestly I didn't have a lot of faith in it, and it cost about twice a standard IR repeater...but a signal repeater that does not work is not a bargain at any price.

Two days later Amazon Prime delivered it to my door, and 20 minutes later I was up and running. The Blutetooth handshake is almost immediate, and there is no noticeable lag from pressing the button on the phone remote to the change on the screen. Eureka ! perfect solution.

The option to customize the buttons on your new phone remote is added value and fun to fool with. One other reviewer suggested a snap-to grid would be great for button alignment and neat appearance, but since this customizing is all gravy I won't criticize.

The Blumoo gets my highest recommendation for anyone dealing with distance and too-solid walls.

I LOVE this iPod. LOVE isn't even a strong enough word for how I feel about it. I lap swim 6-7 days a week for 30-60 minutes per day. I have now used this product for the two days that I have owned it and I don't want to get out of the pool. It makes lap swimming enjoyable. I usually count my laps to keep myself entertained and to keep my mind occupied but with my music playing I haven't counted a lap yet. I honestly can't imagine going back to lap swimming without this awesome device.

As an FYI...on my first swim I used only the short cord and attached the iPod to the back of my goggles. This caused the earbuds to be pulled back a bit thus ruining the angel of the buds in my ears and ruining the waterproof seal. I was constantly messing with the earbuds as they were consistently losing their waterproof suction every time I took a breath. Last night I played around with the earbuds a bit while at home and found that the smallest earbuds were the most comfortable fit and that they had to be positioned correctly in my ear to keep the waterproof seal. I added the cord extension to the short cord and tied it up so it wasn't too long. Also, I pulled up and back on my outer ear as I inserted the earbuds into my ear canal. It really is the only way to get a waterproof seal that lasts. So, the iPod is still attached to the back of my goggles, the short cord comes forward around my swim cap and the long cord (which is fastened so it is not too long) goes under my swimsuit strap and then hangs under my chin. I swam for 60 minutes today and never lost earbud suction and the sound quality was awesome! I truly enjoyed every lap.

The Mpow Muze Touch Headset is a unique pair in that it features touch controls for volume level and track skipping. Sound quality is pretty good and bass lovers will be impressed. The build quality is good, and they are quite comfortable. The battery lasts 12 hours, and recharges in 2 hours, but don't worry because the supplied aux cable allows continuing the music even without power, but the controls do not work without a bluetooth connection. Bluetooth pairs fast, the range holds up to 80ft outside, and almost anywhere in my house except to the far corners.

▌ SOUND QUALITY
The sound quality is good but maybe a bit bass heavy. Compared to most headphones, bass is very deep, mids and vocals are a bit quiet and almost sound slightly further away, but overall still good. These are not APTX enabled. I also have Mpows Swift headphones, and hey have a more dynamic and clear sound which I kind of prefer. Using a tone generator, at half volume I can hear from 18hz to 17000hz (may vary depending on person). Sound isolation is moderate with these.

Audio quality is same with the cord as with bluetooth. The microphone quality is also fine, picks up my voice and other room noise clearly, but has some distortion.

▌ BUILD QUALITY / DESIGN
The headphones are mostly plastic with a matte rubber texture. They're very comfortable even with hours of use, but when taking them off they hurt a bit for a second. The ear pads pivot a little and are very sponge but not as big as gaming headphones so they dont go around the entire ear, but mostly rest on the earlobe, although my ears can fit inside fine them if I position them right. When running and moving around, they stay in place. They can be lengthened to accommodate difference head sizes, and can fold up for travel storage.
The included cable is flat and measure 47" long. It plugs into the left side of the headphones.

▌ FUNCTIONS
On the right side is the touch controls. Swiping up / down changes volume, which takes about 2 slow swipes to go from 0-100% volume. I found I had to have the BT volume at half or else the headphone volume had to much of a gap between low and high, and they're also very loud at max. Device volume must be about half, or there's a risk of turning the volume up to easily via the touch controls.
Swiping forward or backwards will skip or previous songs, but does not fast forward or rewind part of the song. It is responsive so swiping forward 3 times in a second will skip 3 songs, and I dont have to be perfect with my finger placement. Touch also works with those "touchscreen finger" gloves, but not regular gloves. Also, the controls only work when using bluetooth, not while using the cord which is to bad. When max/minimizing volume, there are beeps, but they are quiet.

Power on/off: Hold main button. Play/Pause: Press main button. Volume up/down: Swipe up/down. Skip or replay song: Swipe forward/backward. Answer/End calls: Press Main button. Reject Calls: Hold main. Redial: Doable press main. Mute calls: Double press main during call.

▌ CONCLUSION
PROS
- Comfortable.
- Long Battery.
- Lots of bass.
- Optional aux cable.

CONS
- Sound quality could be slightly clearer in the upper mids and treble.
- No touch controls when using aux cable.

Soundstage: The first thing immediately obvious to me upon using these earbuds was what soundstage actually is. I've heard this word thrown around before. Frequently when talking about the KC06As. The sheer "wideness" of the sound these put out is amazing, compared to my previous sets of earbuds (Thinksound ts02, Brainwavz S1). Actually got my jaw to drop upon using them the first time.  Warmth: These really are warm sounding earbuds. Strings, vocals, midrange are all emphasized and focused on. These earbuds accomplish this very well, but this better be what you want from them. My Brainwavz seem a lot flatter in comparison.  Comfort: Easily the most comfortable of the earbuds I've tried. This is a very important one to me, as I use earbuds exclusively for comfort reasons. Haven't found any Over-Ears or On-Ears that I can comfortably wear for 8+ hours. These feel very light in the ear, although they certainly aren't in the hand (full metal casing). I think it's from being flatter and keeping the cord close to the head. The shirt clip helps a lot here as it takes the weight of the cord off of the earbuds.  I really like the sound these put off. I feel comfortable turning the equalizers off on my devices (previously tended to have the EQ a bit bass focused). They're warm and punchy, and if you buy them you really ought to be seeking those attributes out. You can make them pretty damn bassy if you want (three of the tip pairs seem to be intended for this).  Onto the physical stuff: Surprisingly good. These are obviously Chinese. The website is in almost-Engrish, and so are the manuals. Lots of Chinese writing on the packaging. The kickass sound and shockingly solid construction (metal casings, metal plug grip, metal Y splitter) make that inconsequential. My set came with 7 pairs of silicone tips (one pair with mesh filters), a shirt clip, ear hangars, and a carrying pouch.  If these were priced at $120, I wouldn't bat an eye. Pleasantly surprised they aren't.  End of 2015 edit: So I actually wear these so much it makes my ears bleed. Literally. I think it's because the housing is metal and somewhat sharp, but I have these in so frequently that I have to stop myself from wearing them for a few days or I get abrasions in my outer ear canals that bleed.  So yeah, while they're comfortable for wearing for 8 hours at a time... doing so for weeks might not be sustainable. For casual use, these are pretty much flawless. As a lifestyle choice I'm not so sure anymore.

Pros: Crystal Clear Highs, Wonderful Retro Look, Microphone, Open Sound, Great Build
Cons: Earcups do not swivel or flex, Bass impact can depend on fit

The KZ LP3 is an interesting headphone. It is really like nothing out there right now.
Small, Retro, Well Built and Very fun to use.

Warning, because these are fully open headphones, they are not ideal for travel or public places.
Everyone around you is going to hear what you are listening to. Now this is not a con, but just
a result of the headphone design to get a big airy sound signature.

*Accessories*
No accessories come with the headphones, but for the price, the original design of the KZ LP3 is more than enough.

*Fit*
The earcups do not swivel and do not flex. However, with some simple and careful pressure, you can bend the headband to contour you head.

*Build*
These are tough headphones. Built to last and look great as well. The attention to detail in the design is amazing.

*Sound*
The open design leads to a big airy sound signature. Distance can be felt in the music. Vocals and highs come through loud and clear. Bass can feel a little recessed depending on your fit. The closer you can get the drivers to your ears, the bigger the bass will be. The drivers themselves are impressive, you can hear the quality in both instrument separation and speed.

*Overall Thoughts*
These are a VERY fun, VERY retro pair of headphones. These are a step apart from every other product out there with form and function. The price makes it a great value. An easy recommendation.

This is truly a very nice upgrade over the AQ Evergreen version of this type of cable.  I had used the Evergreen happily for the past nine months with the AQ Dragonfly DAC between my PC running JRiver and my Yamaha RX-A710 AVR connected to B&W 685 speakers (via AQ X-2 speaker wire) and a REL T5 subwoofer.  Most of my music files are ripped from CD in dBPoweramp to lossless and uncompressed FLAC files, along with some 24-bit downloads from HD Tracks and Acoustic Sounds (converted to uncompressed).  I have a huge Amazon MP3 library but strongly prefer the higher quality FLAC format available elsewhere.  When I got the Evergreen cable last year, I was very impressed with how much better it sounded than the six dollar cable I had from Radio Shack a few years back.  Well, now I'm thrilled to say the Big Sur just blows away the Evergreen.  Seriously, this was another one of those priceless "I never heard these details in my music" moments, which get increasingly difficult to achieve unless you've got a ton of cash lying around.  I didn't really consider the next level up for another hundred dollars, Sydney, because I'm not sure if my amp and speakers would really be revealing enough to justify the cable expense.  I did A/B testing between the two cables for my wife, as well, and she immediately noticed how much better the Big Sur cable performed.  She's not the audiophile I am, but she thought the money was well spent on such a clear improvement.  Until about a year ago, I was highly skeptical of just how much difference a pricey AQ cable would make over a decent Monster cable, but from direct personal experience, I can say that the ones I’ve tried so far do indeed.  I recently got some AQ Forest Ethernet cables to run between my NAS and my music server / HTPC to my main audio system (different room / setup), somewhat doubtful that they would do much, but they made such a noticeable difference that I now plan to replace them with higher quality Cinnamon Ethernetcables in the near future and re-use the cheaper Forest ones elsewhere.  FWIW - I also got two AQ Jitterbugs to try in my Dragonfly/Evergreen/Big Sur setup, and while they most certainly altered the sound, we mutually chose not to use them based on many A/B tests with both the Evergreen and Big Sur cables.  Unexpectedly, audio quality was like two steps forward and three steps back, so ultimately the cons outweighed the pros.  I'm quickly gathering from early reviews that the Jitterbug may be more or less useful in a given setup or application, so YMMV.  However, I have a couple other scenarios elsewhere in the house to try so I haven't given up completely in finding a use for the Jitterbugs.  As for Big Sur, it’s a major winner.  Give it a try and trust your ears!!!

This was delivered to my home theater only 10 days ago. I must say I will need to give some more time to give a truly fair feedback. Thus this review is only 'preliminary' in my opinion. Since this will be the first review on this product on Amazon, and since I assume there must be some people out there who are wondering how well this product performs, I have decided to put my short review here.

I had been using my 9 year old Dennon AV receiver until recently. Its HDMI outputs got killed by a thunderstorm we had in July, which forced me to obtain a new one. At its price point, this Pioneer receiver is one of the "entry" products of the Elite line, however it is not cheap by any means as it costs $1000 basically.

The built quality is excellent. Heavy, sturdy and solid. You can expect this level of quality as it costs as such. It is about an inch taller than my old Dennon and it would not fit in my cabinet if I make the Wi fi antennas stand vertically on the back. I have decided to keep them horizontal therefore. They still catch the Wi fi signals without any problem. I have my Wi Fi router in the same room coincidentally. Connecting it to Wi Fi was a breeze. It is Air Play ready and Blue Tooth ready by the way. You can also play Pandora, Spotify, Internet Radio.

I have a mix impression about the initial set up process. I downloaded the app as Pioneer recommends on my Android phone for the set up. This app works well for the most part as it navigates you through the process of the set up step by step. However it makes you go back to the very first step once you screw up something. It makes you run the MCACC, an automated audio calibration system developed by Pioneer, at the end of the set up. I wanted to re-run it because my kids were very noisy upstairs during the first run. I pressed the 'back' botton on my phone and I had to start the set up process all over again.

Also, please note that this receiver does not have any component video output. Modern receivers tend to omit analog ins/outs. If you use or plan to use analog connections in your system, you should make sure the reciever you are getting has them adequately.

The MCACC works very well. You can manually adjust the sound of each channel if you want to. I have decided to keep the setting made by MCACC because the sound is fantastic and I see no urgent reason to fiddle the setting further.

My theater system is only 5.1, thus it does not allow me to assess the quality of the sound in Dolby Atmos format. I liked the sound of my old Dennon but I always felt that it added "airy" and "smooth" texture to any sound source it was fed. It did not bother me as long as I played jazz and classical, however it was slightly annoying when I played hard rock. And I love hard rock! You would not like Eddy Van Halen's solo sounds airy and smooth, would you? The sound this Pioneer guy produces does not seem to have this kind of noticeable additional texture. Compared to the Dennon, this has more "vicseral", round, and midrange-focused sound overall, which makes the sound of drums stronger and more defined, which is a better match for hard rock. I would not say the sound is "warm". I say it is "fulfilling". Its higher tone sound production is also wonderful. The sounds of symbals, pianos, trumpets, etc. are very crisp and realistic. Its power is more than enough to drive my Definitive Technology towers in the 5.1 channel system. I am liking the audio quality of this receiver very much so far. I have tried many Blu Ray discs, DVD Audios and SACDs on it already and they all sound great. I have not yet tried 24 bit/192kHz AIFF, which is also supported on this receiver.

Regarding video queality: My Oppo Blu Ray player has excellent abilifty to decodes and sends out HD video signals. My JVC projector projects great video image as longas you feed good quality video to it. The only job I require my receiver to do is to basically pass through video signals without any unnecessary modification. I have no complaint on how the Pioneer handles video signals so far. I don't do 3D in my house by the way. I just don't. So, I have no idea how this receiver handles 3D video signals.

Required Supplies/Tools are included in the guide so you can pick up what you need at the hardware/home improvement store before heading home. The antenna took approximately one hour to set -up and install. In addition, my husband purchased the RCA Digital TV Converter and the RCA Indoor Digital Signal Antenna Amplifier to complete the set up. With the GE Attic Mount Antenna alone, we received 32 channels from the Milwaukee/Chicago metro areas which were crystal clear. With the addition of the RCA Indoor Digital Signal Antenna Amplifier, we obtained 10 additional channels from the Milwaukee/Chicago metro area which were crystal clear. As a previous reviewer mentioned, I would check this website http://transition.fcc.gov/mb/engineering/dtvmaps/ to check the DTV signals available for your local area. After all is said and done, we are thrilled with the outcome of our DIY project. The money spent on the antenna, digital converter and antenna amplifier was equal to one month’s cost of satellite television.

No occasionally copious anal retentive audiophile jargon to endure from me. Just an honest fairly detailed non-Estuary English assessment after 5 days of using my new 225e's. Each day there has been an slow but steady improvement and now the headphones are starting to sound superb - with a decent sound source. Apple lossless bleeding obviously sounds far better than the 256/320 kbps that most people are force-fed with downloads. Remastered cds similarly are well worth the effort of reloading into iTunes at the much improved lossless quality and then transferring onto one's android devices. However now, after ensuring several hours a day of prudently intermittent burn in on my Galaxy phone even 320kbps usually sounds better/pretty acceptable, as the sound quality 'opens' up. My smallish iTunes collection of around 20K songs, pretty much entirely sourced from PC loaded purchased cds not downloads, has never sounded better. I've found the 'treble booster' EQ setting on my devices seems to work best with most tunes.

Supposedly, the sound will only get better as one approaches the 100/200 hour mark of pop music piped through.

Bending back the headband somewhat has greatly relieved the usual Grado ear pressure. The 225e's sound much better than my old SR 60's. The bass, the mids and trebles are all greatly improved. These new 'e' headphones are effectively five steps up from the old 60's. The gist of the many, often flowery audiophile reviews about the 325e's suggests that the extra $100 is split between a better quality, heftier build and a slight sound improvement.

The 225e's drive my Samsung tablet/phone brilliantly. To the point of invariably keeping the volume down to the level below the warning about loud listening. They do leak sound, unlike my much cheaper Bose OE2's, which are nowhere near the same sound quality, but can be safely used on cruise ships and elsewhere in public with no whining from fellow travellers.

This review is for the 1500VA model, regardless, the negatives listed blow will apply to any model.One reason why I'm not a systems engineer, I would have never approved the release of the PC software which is included.

I purchased two of the 1500 watt units.

As others have commented, I doubt the system will run for the time indicated should there be a complete power outage, it seems a bit 'hopeful', but I have not tested it to see just how far it will go. Doing so can damage batteries, etc., so for now I'll give it the benefit of the doubt.

The LCD front panel is nice, you can step through a number of displayed monitoring options, power level in or out, expected run time, load percentage, and several others.

It would have been better to have several displayed items at once, rather than having to step-through one setting or another, one at a time.

The first thing I did was turn off that annoying beep... that's all I need is for something to beep at 2 o'clock in the morning.
Why engineers put beeps on nearly everything they make, by default, is beyond me....

The first few days, everything was great.

When I noticed I was losing power to the house, I checked the 'Events' counter on the LCD panel, and sure enough the number that stayed at zero for several days, was now at 2.

Over the next few weeks, the 'Events' continued to increment. The UPS part is working great, my routers, computers, switches, nothing was getting hung, reset, or locked up anymore! I should have done this long ago.

I finally installed the monitoring software on a PC to see what was going on with all of these 'events'.

First, installing the software completely wiped out all settings I had painstakingly entered using the front panel.
Gone... It completely reset all of the options back to the default settings. Very poor design.

More 'Events' kept incrementing on the front LCD panel, the software shows: Last Event: None
An email from support said, the unit only displays 'major events'. Huh? If you loose power for more than 3 seconds those are recorded, or noted, anything other than that, any 'monitoring' isn't monitored or recorded.

What a shame! I don't have any idea what the power problems are...still.

The 'monitoring software' seems geared toward complete loss of power, rather than the temporary bad transient events that we all seem to have.

There is no way to exit the software. Once it installs, it will run every time your computer starts, you have no option select 'load at start-up', or 'exit', etc. You have to either un-install the software, or the more complicated route to disable it.

Finally with some more back and forth, the disk that is included with the unit, of course is never the latest software, so as a last effort, I downloaded the latest version from the company's website.

This was problematic as well. The software didn't want to update some newer files, while the files were being used with the currently running monitoring software. Since there is no way to exit the software, you apparently cannot install a new software once you install any version. I had to look through the Windows Running Processes and find the software (not that easy), and 'End Process' in order to finish the installation of the latest version.

What you should probably do, is completely uninstall the old software, before installing the new version. Of course, it would have been nice to know this first. Besides, better written software would have simply disabled the old version while the new version was being installed, or stopped the process from running, etc. Of course, that requires systems programmers to have a smidgen of insight and common sense.

Overall, the unit itself is nice, has a nice LCD panel and performs well. If you're looking for a basic UPS system, and are not concerned about much else than to set your system to power down on a power failure, or just protect what you have from power 'glitches', then this is a nice system. It doesn't seem to switch over as quick as units I've had in the past, however nothing has hung, or locked up, so regardless of it seeming to be a bit slow, it seems to be fast enough and I guess that's all that matters.

If you want or need to do anything else, the software is painfully inadequate and doesn't merit being included with such a nice UPS.

This is by far the best dongles I've used to date. I have a bunch of R820T's along with a r820t2. I didn't notice much of a difference between those units. When I saw these units appear I was hesitant because I already own a t2 but when I noticed the higher accuracy TXCO I decided to go in for 2 of them w/ the antennas. At first I was not impressed at all with the reception due to not being able to pickup the noaa. My little Baofengs have no problem with stock whips. All my other R820t's are connected to roof antennas and I didn't have the proper adapter to test with that antenna. So after playing around for awhile positioning the antenna I decided to mount the antenna onto a metal object, I used an old side cover from a PC tower and prepped the surface - removed paint in a small area.. That improved the signal, I could actually hear something now. I still wasn't satisfied, so I removed the sticker off the bottom of the antenna mount and checked for continuity. I noticed the metal dish had a good ground but the magnet did not, it was glued in. I removed the magnet, cleaned off the old glue, set the magnet back in and glued around the sides of it allowing the back of the magnet cover to sit metal to metal. (Removing the glue and redoing it might be over kill since the metal dish would make contact also) I also pried out the dish that the magnet sits in and re-seated it, getting it started where the ground wire gets pinched and on a flat level surface, I press down. Being this is mass produced it was uneven. I left the sticker off the base and retested, OMG I was getting crystal clear reception. I was getting as good as a signal as my roof mounted antenna!!

As for the freq correction (ppm) both my units are ZERO and centered on the freq. I'm really satisfied with this purchase and I would highly recommend getting a pair of these for trunking.

edit I've added some photos, glue glob that made the metal dish to be recessed, and a pic after I reset it. On this antenna base I didn't re glue the magnet as the metal dish makes contact. This isn't a real big deal, any antenna base you get with these dongles are pretty much the same, just slapped together overseas. I've tested SO many BlueTooth speakers in this price range, that I have to be critical.

Here is the short version, Geega, you know that I love your name? But why only a 1000mAh battery? Many competitors use a 2000 and we hate having to charge! I need six multiple port chargers stationed throughout my home because I want charging to be as easy as possible, because I do it too often.

Okay, now that I yelled at Geega, you will otherwise like this speaker. It sounds as good as any other like it and better than many, because it includes a passive radiator. To explain myself, it seems that almost all the speakers in this price range use 3 watt per channel amps, and 40mm speakers. So what's up with the better sounding models, is that they are using a passive radiator also, and this works.

A passive radiator amplifies the sound from the cabinet, which is the lower frequencies, making the speaker sound deeper. It's called passive, because it's like a speaker that isn't connected to the amp. It moves from the pressure changes within the sealed cabinet caused by the connected speakers. So it will work more when the volume is turned up, or when the speakers are moving in and out more, changing the pressure within the cabinet.

You'll get cables and a bag, everything that most all of the speakers include. You'll get a good sounding little speaker in this price range and you'll get a battery that's half what some are. Many others are also 1000-1400mAh, so if this is important to you, you'll have to shop a little harder. This also does not have a micro SD slot or FM, like I've seen on two others recently. The Geega does sound better than any other that I've tested with a 1000mAh battery, so don't shy away from it.

But I'm an audio engineer testing an audio product and I have to be critical. It's a 5 star speaker with a 3 star battery.

Geega, sent me this product to test, and I hope that they learned from this review that we all want to charge our products less.

I purchased these record sleeves for one reason, and one reason only -- they were less expensive than the Mobile Fidelity Sound Lab (MFSL) inner sleeves I usually order. I like the MFLS sleeves -- $20, and free two-day shipping because I'm an Amazon Prime member. But this time when I was shopping they removed the free shipping, so I searched for others and found these.

There's not much to say other than that they seem to have the similar, but not exact, qualities as the MFSL sleeves. Perhaps a little thinner. Perhaps not. I can't tell. In some other reviews users complain about static electricity being drawn to these sleeves making them more difficult to use. I don't see it. Or feel it. Or sense it. I am a sick record nut -- I have about 10k LPs, and quite a few 45s. I always replace paper inserts with poly sleeves such as the MFSL (and these!). To make sure I don't mar an album's surface I face the opening of the inner sleeve toward the opening of the album cover, so I just have to hold the album cover and slide out the record -- and I only have to touch the label and outer edge of the record when removing it. Whether or not there is static electricity doesn't really come into play. Yes, during the winter sometimes albums do have some static charge when I place them on the turntable's platter. In those cases I use an old Zerostat gun (they do not "wear out") to disperse the charge Remember, I said I was I was a sick record nut. Those of my ilk own a Zerostat, various stylus cleaners, and often a vacuum/wet record cleaner. As I do. Don't hate me because I'm beautiful.

PS -- any old vinyl laying around gathering dust that you don't want? Bringing them to a brick and mortar record store is a waste of time, they'll just give you pennies on the dollar for your records. I, in turn, will give them a loving home where they will be cherished and LISTENED TO. Box them up. I'll pay postage. PM (private message) me! ;) .

I bought this product because I needed an earbud with a mic. This product had attractive colors, had an enhanced base, and was affordable. The product came quickly and packaged securely in an oversized box which was probably a little unnecessary. So far, I have used these earbuds for 1.5 months. Here's a quick list of my thoughts:  +bold, neon color +strong, clear base when listening to music - The bass is definitely enhanced. Some may think the sound seems muffled because of it, but it's nothing that fiddling around with the equalizer won't fix. I can get an above-average music-listening experience on budget. Note that quality is fine for the price; don't expect bose-quality sound. +mic - my family and friends have had no problem hearing me from the other end; in fact, the mic seems to work really well, capturing not just my voice but also some of the background noise with it (ie, cars passing by when I'm on the street). +No sound leakage - I have not received any complaints from my roommates or office mates yet of being able to hear my music while it's playing.  -bass when NOT listening to music - It took me a little bit of adjusting to use these earbuds when taking calls. These earbuds amplifies the bass in music (great!), but also everything else, including the voice on the other line which made whatever the other person is saying a little difficult to understand (esp if the other person had a deep voice). However, this was a minor problem and just takes some getting used to - I have no problem taking calls with these earbuds now. -Sensitive cord (in the beginning) - I would hear crackles through the music whenever I rotated the jack; other times, the sound was cut off if the cord close to the jack positioned in a certain way. No such problems after about a month of use.  One quality that I like to check for in earbuds is whether sound travels through the cord. The sound does NOT travel through the cord if it's from the part of the core before the split to the earpieces; the cord above the split carries sound. If you could somehow clip the split securely onto your shirt to keep the cord above the split from bouncing around too much, you could probably go running without too much of the cord noise interrupting your music with each step.  Overall, it's a good budget earbud with mic. It's not high-quality in sound or in the way it's made, but it works. Bass is enhanced as advertised. I probably would not pay more than $15 for the item.

The Polk Monitors are fantastic budget speakers, if paired with an amp that can provide a lot of clean power (> 100 watts per channel). These are attractive speakers that put out a nice, slightly warm sound without being fatiguing. They are not quite full-range speakers, so if you're a bass head, you will want a good subwoofer. Also, they get better sounding as you listen to them more over time.

In addition to powering these speakers with a good amp, they will take a while to break in. When I first got mine, I thought they seemed somewhat dull and muffled, and the tweeters exhibited some sibilance. But my patience was rewarded, as with use over a period of several months, the treble mellowed and the sound became very clear. After a couple of years, they sound even better now.

Finally, these speakers are somewhat laid back. If you're into forward, in your face sound, these probably aren't for you. But if you prefer a more natural, balanced and musical sound, then you will probably enjoy these speakers.

Comfort: I wear glasses and am very sensitive. If they are comfortable for me they will be comfortable for most people.

These are collapsible for travel. I loved them so much for their other attributes I spent the time to super glue them so they weren't collapseable and used a little black gorilla on the plastic parts where the band extends from and that minor tweak should work ok. I fixed the one that broke and prevented it in the other. Granted this is a lot of trouble and for people that spent 2-300 I wouldn't be too happy either. These for a long time were available for 80-120 dollars and in my opinion for office use they are a strong head phone, and for that price a little glue isn't the end of the world. I'll be the first one to say I'm not a big fan of Monster Cables. It's my opinion that they produce overpriced garbage most of the time, and it's for that very reason I prefer to roll my own cables for studio use (because I know exactly what type of wire, connectors, and solder was used, as well as the time, energy, and workmanship that went into their production). That said, I bought this "power conditioner" long before I found out about Monster's dubious cable manufacturing and pricing methods, and it's lasted me around a decade (10 years) with zero problems until just recently when I've begun to notice a high pitch sound coming from it in the 18000hz-20000hz range. At first I thought it may have been the ballast on my DLP TV (which is also 6 or 7 years old), but I managed to track it down to the power conditioner itself.
The only issues I have with this power conditioner are that I have an older model without the LED load indicator on it (like the version in this listing), I have absolutely no idea what the noise suppression rating (in dB) is for this unit, nor do I know what type of waveform it actually outputs (a true/pure sine wave, a simulated/modified square wave [aka: pulse width modulated / PWM], or a basic square wave).
Based on the price I paid a decade ago ($150) my guess is it uses a modified square wave (PWM) at best. It is extremely unlikely that it outputs a pure sine wave, as power conditioners which output a pure sine wave tend to be very expensive, costing between several hundred and several thousand US dollars (depending on the number of outlets and features they have).
I do know that this conditioner has fairly good isolation for typical home theater use, though I would never trust it with anything you can not afford to replace (as it is only a "mid-tier" CONSUMER level product).
