I started taking an interest in headphones ever since my Dad brought me the sony mdr zx 100 for my birthday. At that age I didn't really care about sound quality or the cheapness of a headphone, just something I can listen to. But a couple of years forward my interest in headphones began to peak. I was listening from headphones like Audiotechnica m50x, JVC S500's and even the Sennheiser Momentums. So when I browsed amazon one day and found this little upgraded version of my first headphone, I was a bit excited. I started having this interest in comparing the two headphones. I also had brought the SONY MDR ZX 110 for a little extra.

So is it really an upgrade? Unfortunately, the looks and comfort of the headphone can only defined as an "upgrade".

The sound of the headphones is a bit bland, as it losses a little of the bass that the previous SONY MDR ZX 100 and 110 had. And though this headphone, the SONY MDR ZX310, has a bit, and I mean a tiny bit, more clarity then the SONY MDR ZX 100, it losses it's exciting signature from the previous models. And yes I have burned these headphones in for a decent amount of time.

In terms of outward appearance, these are definitely a step up. Personally the white and the lime green version of the headphone are a deal breaker for me as they really stand out. The only problem with the white is that it's literally a cheap looking version of the white SONY MDR ZX 600. On this headphone the outer rim of it gives off this nice black metallic look, similar to the SONY XB 450. There is also the green cord that comes with it, ending the tip of the L- shaped audio jack with a gray finish.

Yes this is a gray headphone, with green earpads, not black.

Comfort though is a bit debatable. You see these headphones come with ear pads that are like the cheap version of the SONY MDR ZX 600's. The feeling is like the same plastic material of the original SONY MDR ZX 100 but stretched out and more "clean" looking. There really isn't much padding as it's very thin, but because of the lightweight, you really wouldn't worry about it. They block out more sound outside then the SONY MDR ZX 100 and 110, but it's nowhere near the XB 450.

Also the pads do make your ear's sweat a little after extended use, but honestly I would pair them up with the replacement ear pads they sell on amazon for an extra five bucks. That's just my personal preference.

So if your excited about the sound these headphones deliver, you'll be a bit dissapointed, as the recessed bass is the only significant difference between the older models. Set up: Connected to Galaxy S4 via micro USB. Also works with Galaxy S6. Use Beyerdynamics DT-770 250 ohms version for listening. Note: the 'suggested headphone impedance' listed on the Fiio website says upto 150 ohms...while the actual E18 PDF manual says upto 300 ohms. The E18 has no problem driving my 250 ohm DT-770, most of the time I max out at level 3 on the dial (high gain and bass boost).

Audio quality: In "airplane mode" + WI-FI with the E-18 set to ' PHONE IN' and connected via USB (so it be both a DAC & AMP) I get no interference whatsoever when listening to media from my SD card (on the S4) or to streaming audio apps like Pandora. The sound quality is excellent and the external PLAY/PAUSE, BACK and FWD buttons work great with onboard player and streaming apps.

Charging: The instructions need to be followed to the letter:

The Tesla One Sub Mod is an awesome device. It has a 510 connection and works great for 22mm RDAs. I enjoyed building dual micro coil builds for it with smaller gauge kanthal wire from lighteningvapes.com. The smaller wire tends to promote great flavor and a nice, cool vape. The manual for the mod is petite and useful. The battery lasts a long time -40 vapes and it still took under 3 minutes to fully recharge. The 'smoke' button has both a red and a blue led for certain indications like low voltage and re-charging connection. As there are many 22mm RDAs on the market, I found the 'Turbo RDA' from vapenaked.com to be the most enjoyable, so far. 22mm RDAs can be found on amazon.com and fasttech.com, where one can find a great many 22mm RDA's and even 29mm RDA's for other devices. Clearimizers will work fine with this device. A great recommendation for three different sub-ohm clearimizers is www.goodprophets.com, where one can also find a Hades mod clone for 26650 batts. Sub-ohm clearimizers do not require a coil build and can come with replaceable atomizers with ohm resistance as low as .2 ohms (Herakles). The Tesla One works great for coil builds of ohms above .3 ohms and up to 3 ohms. The Omega 22mm RDA from amazon.com is about the least expensive RDA I have found and works great with the Tesla One sub mod. The Omega RDA even comes with pre-built micro-coils with fiberglass 'wicking' -very nice. I chose to add some organic cotton to the small coils for a cooler vape.
The sub mod can come in other colors - I did like my choice of the carbon fiber style. One would have to hold it to appreciate how neat it looks and feels. The 'smoke' button will turn off after ten seconds, however you can activate it for seven seconds or so at a time repeatedly. Though the specifications say it works at up to 100 watts (not including voltage drop), it is comparable to a 25 watt vape. One feature it has is a safety cut-off to ensure that the battery won't short circuit from an improper coil build. All in all this is a great device, and I appreciated the communication with the company. They answered my questions and were courteous, too. I recommend this product for anyone who is searching for an alternative from carrying a box mod in their pocket during commute. Recently I was on the hunt for a bluetooth speaker that fulfills three basic requirements: one, that it is truly portable, meaning it has an internal battery and is not reliant on a power cord; two, that it has powerful and accurate sound without that cheap artificial speaker sound; and three, that it looks great and uses renewable materials like wood or bamboo. There are actually not many products on the market that meet these criteria; most are either too small and mono-sounding or too large and require a power supply. In the end I narrowed my search to this House of Marley speaker and the interesting [[ASIN:B010VWLR7Q REVEAL Portable Wireless Solar Powered Bluetooth Speaker]]. While the Reveal has the solar feature which makes it even more portable and usable on things like camping trips, the HoM speaker just looked higher quality and gave me the impression that it would have superior sound characteristics. I haven't heard the Reveal so I can't make a direct comparison, but I can say that I am extremely pleased with the HoM and think I made the right choice.  For starters it is just an absolutely beautiful thing to look at. The bamboo is stained a rich, reddish color, which looks great set against the black speaker cones. The strip of fabric that sits in between the front and rear bamboo surfaces is a really nice contrasting material and makes the speaker easier to grip. The top-mounted controls are simplistic and easy to access. I like how the LED light is red when the unit is on and not connected to anything, and blue when it has made a bluetooth connection to your device, so you always know what state it's in. It's also a sizable and hefty device, which speaks to the quality of the materials and components inside. The Get Together is simply a beautiful and functional device. Aesthetics: 5/5  The main reason most people buy speakers is because of sound quality, and the Get Together doesn't disappoint here either. Let me get this out of the way first: it lacks asignificant bass presence, which is to be expected in a speaker that lacks a dedicated internal subwoofer. Electronic music like house and techno sounds a little on the weak side because of the lack of punch. Yet it does represent the upper low frequencies cleanly and without distortion (about 120Hz and up). Where the speaker really shines is in the mids and highs. It is just clean sounding, and there's lot of detail in these frequency bands. The speaker layout is one important reason why. Many other speakers in this price range have only two speakers that handle everything; the Get Together has four, with two separate L/R tweeters and two L/R main cones. This allows the high frequencies to be separate from the rest of the music, powered by their own dedicated drivers. Your music is going to sound bright and sparkly as a result. Also, there is plenty of juice available - this thing can get incredibly loud through a combination of your bluetooth volume and its own internal amp, but it maintains its clarity throughout. Pretty impressive for a battery powered speaker. Sound: 4/5  Finally, the bluetooth and battery performance have so far been excellent. It has not dropped my iPhone connection once, even when I've been walking around my house or outside on the patio. I haven't tested it over a really long distance but for my purposes it is totally sufficient. And the claimed battery life is accurate, if not even a bit conservative, because I've gone over 8 hours on it already. What more could you want in a portable speaker? Internals: 5/5  For all these reasons I say your money is well spent on the House of Marley Get Together. It is beautiful, sounds great, and is truly portable. A win on all counts.

For years, we have used UPSes to protect our computers -- we currently have two models, a CyberPower CP1350PFCLCD for my three computers, ink-jet printer and scanner, and a CP850PFCLCD to protect my wife's computer and multifunction ink-jet device. However, when a momentary power blip (sub-second) took our network off the air, I realized that we needed to protect our cable modem and WiFi router. This is increasingly important as we use cloud-based software, like Google Docs, where losing network access could be more than an inconvenience - it might also lose your work.

In our house, our cable modem and WiFi router are situated next to our big TV and sound bar, In fact, they were all on the same surge protector -- gotta protect those valuable electronics, especially here in Phoenix, which gets a lot of lightning. We decided to replace the surge protector with those CyberPower CP600LCD. This is a lower-end unit than what we use with our computers; it doesn't put out the pure sine wave electricity, the way the big ones do, but for protecting televisions, routers and modems, that's totally fine.

I chose the "LCD" version because our house does get occasional brownouts, and it's nice to be able to see the screen and verify the input voltage.

There's one big thing that I don't like about this model: The on/off switch is VERY easy to press accidentally. If you do so, even for a moment, everything turns off instantly. That's bad news, and of course defeats the entire purpose of having a UPS! So what I did is tape a piece of cardboard over the power switch, so that it can't be pressed accidentally. It's a bit ugly, but then again the UPS isn't visible (it sits on top of our soundbar's subwoofer) so nobody will know. Still, I think that CyberPower should have designed this switch to be harder to press accidentally, perhaps with a flip-up cover.

By the way, we plugged the cable modem and WiFi router into the battery-protected ports, and the TV and soundbar into the surge-only ports. I'd rather save the battery for the network. You buy this to hold your TV on the wall, this does exactly that. I have a 50" RCA LCD TV hanging on mine right now. It's been up for about 3 months now so I guess you could make the assumption that it's not going anywhere. I bought this primarily for the same reason you're reading this right now; I liked the price. Don't worry about the rest of it, your TV isn't going to fall of the wall because you chose to save some money by picking this bracket over some of the others. What makes a TV fall is a poor installation. With that said here is why it gets 4 stars and not 5 and what you should do to make this inexpensive bracket perfect for your beautiful TV. 1) Throw away the level that comes with it and buy or borrow a level. Flipping my copy of this level gave me two different pitches; on level and one not. It's a cheap piece of plastic, not a real tool. 2) Throw away the hardware meant to hold the bracket to the wall and buy some 1/4" x 2 1/2" lag bolts, washers and split washers and install this into two studs behind the drywall. I felt like the metric screws which attach the brackets to the TV itself fit well enough to not replace those but the lag bolts for the wall felt chincy. I've spent my life in the trades and these lag bolts have the in-the-hand weight of the kind that like to twist below the head as you snug them up. What that potentially means later is bolt failure. Not good when your beautiful TV is hanging by them. I could be 100% wrong but for about $1.50 I'll never have to worry about it and I got a TV bracket at a great price. Aside from that, the space behind the bracket is sufficient for making connections unless your connections are right in the middle of the TV. If they are, you might already hate your TV and want a new one. If so, put this bracket in your cart and start picking out a sweet TV that's going to hang securely on this bracket for ever.

I replaced a very cheap switching box I had been using with J-techs 3 to 1 switching box with audio extracter. The original switching box cost about $4 and I was happy it worked at all but after about 4 months of use it was becoming a bit unreliable. I was already using a j-tech splitter as well as a j-tech audio extracter and have been very happy with their products and this little switching box seems to be a winner as well.

Though I have kodi on an old ouya console I have in the living room I also have a 50 foot hdmi cable run from my pc in my bedroom to the living room. I use the pc as a media center for kodi as well as the heart of my whole home audio system. With the cheap switching box I couldn't get a strong enough signal when trying to switch to the pc, the video had "sparkles" and the audio was weak sometimes loosing the signal all together.

I purchased this switching box along with a voltage injector and a signal booster figuring that between the three I'd solve the issue and not wanting to wait for more gizmos if only one didn't resolve the issue. As it turned out this switching box was all I needed. The "sparkles" vanished the picture is up to par with my cable box which is direct out. I use the rca out which delivers an audio signal which is indistinguishable from my blue ray .

The auto on feature seems to work well but is actually annoying because the box switches every time my playstation updates. I wish you had the option to disable auto on. I have used the remote and it works well but I'm not planning on keeping it around because I'm striving to remove remotes from my setup not increase them . I don't really mind getting up to switch inputs .

I've read in reviews of many switching boxes that they can run hot which was a concern because this hdmi runs so far and is off a splitter I thought it might stress the box . This box is running cool and doesn't seem to struggle at all.

Overall this box is solidly built with enough weight to hold steady with all the cables plugged in which many of the competitors don't seem to do. Everything functions as I hoped and the box surpassed my expectations in many areas. The audio extracter works flawlessly and is a sweet feature and real selling point. J-techs 3 to 1 switching box as well as their other fine products have helped complete my whole home audio video setup which has been a 6 month long journey and been a real exercise in trial and error. I am glad I discovered J-Tech and I'll be using more of their devices as I expand my current setup further.

I will update as time passes on the long term reliability of this and their other products but as of now I'm pleased.

Let's look at the AUSDOM M04:

Looks - I like the style of the headphones; I think they look good.
Sound - Good all-around sound; strong bass without muddying up the higher freqs. Good for all listening modes (music, gaming, movies, etc.)
Comfort - These are oblong, over-the-ear 'phones. They cover the entire ear. This allows for better sound isolation, but can mean your ears start getting a little warm after a while. I've worn these for several hours at a time and not felt uncomfortable at all. The pads are covered with a soft material that feels good. They are flexible, twists in the right places, and once set are always comfortable.
Connection - BT 3.0 works well; easy to connect to and stays connected.
Battery - so far, very pleased with battery life. Have used these for about 20 hours activity before recharging (recharging wasn't yet required). I've left them on over the weekend so have gotten 3 days standby without requiring a recharge. I tend to recharge on my own, so I've yet to hear the "charge required" tone.
Functionality - I have not used these other than for listening to music from my computer and iPad. Cannot attest to the other functionality.

Summary - very pleased with these headphones and would buy AUSDOM again. I've heard headphones that are 50% more expensive but don't sound any better. Yet these sound MUCH better than the $20 headphones I've purchased. Overall I think these hit the sweet spot for price/performance. Would definitely buy again.

Let me preface this review by saying, I was provided a free sample for testing and review. I explained to the manufacturer that I would provide an honest review of this product. All experiences with this product and all opinions are solely my own.

I purchased the prior generation of this speaker, the OontZ Angle Plus, so I'll be able to compare them. The Plus has crystal clear sound and good bass. I really enjoyed the Plus, but where the Plus needed some improvement was with its volume and bass.

The new OontZ Angle3 significantly increases the volume and bass, but more importantly it retains and improves upon the crisp and crystal clear sound of its predecessor, plus it adds an ingenious bass design. More on that later.

What's included in the package:

1 - OontZ Angle3 Speaker
1 - Micro USB Cable
1 - 3.5mm Audio Cable
1 - Quick Start Guide

The OontZ Angle3 is a great sounding Bluetooth speaker, in a small compact package. It weighs in at about 9 ounces. It is 5 1/4 inches long and about 2 1/2 inches high. It will basically fit in the palm of your hand. Please refer to the pictures I posted. It also retains the angular design of its predecessor, but now has a silicone rubber type finish on both ends of the speaker. It's still void of any sharp edges. It's a great looking speaker, with a unique design. I like this Angle3 design better than the Plus.

It's significantly louder than the Plus and has nice bass, for a unit that's this small. If you enjoy music that has some bass, this unit should meet your needs and be truthful, the sound that comes out of this speaker is mind boggling to me and the size of this speaker belies that fact!

The passive radiator, which produces the bass in the Angle3 and most Bluetooth speakers, is located on the bottom of the unit. If you place it bottom down, the bass effect is more pronounced. If you want a little less bass, you'll stand it on end. When it's bottom down, the bass has a nice little thump. I believe this was done by design and it's an ingenious feature.

Be careful where you place the speaker bottom down, because it does want to move when playing music with bass. The speaker has pads on the bottom, but they work better on very smooth and glass surfaces.

You can hear that Cambridge Soundworks spent the majority of its time improving and refining the sound of the Angle3. That focus on improving acoustics shows up big time in this tiny, but crystal clear and loud speaker.

There's no distortion at max volume. The speaker has 10+ watts of peak power. It's now loud enough to fill up your backyard party with clear, great sounding music. My wife heard me playing music upstairs and she was in the garage. It's plenty loud!

All my music testing was done using Spotify. Speaker was set to full volume and iOS volume was set two clicks from max, for most of my testing. I also tested both settings set to max.

Bluetooth connectivity is super easy. It connects from one device to another effortlessly. I found you don't have to press a button on the speaker to pair it with a different device. I like intuitive functions and this one fits the bill. It also has a speakerphone function. You can play and pause your tracks from the device as well.

The OontZ Angle3 doesn't have all the options others have. You don't get NFC support, a micro SD card slot or the ability to skip tracks using the speaker controls. There are other Bluetooth speakers that have these options, but if you value how well your music sounds over a myriad of options, this beautiful sounding speaker is for you.

The Angle3 has an IPX5 certification, which makes it splash proof and dust proof. Great for the shower and other wet environments. Don't be afraid to shower with it or have it out in the rain. It can't be submerged in water with this IPX rating.

Battery life isabout 7 hours, at 60% volume. It will be less at higher volumes. This is definitely less than the Plus unit, which does 12-15 hours of use. You have to take into account that the battery is driving much more sound and requires that extra battery power. I personally like the trade off and all that's required is to charge the unit a bit more frequently. A battery status symbol shows up in my iOS devices.

If you're like me and aren't interested in the all the above mentioned options, that you may never use and just want a beautiful sounding speaker that's main focus is perfecting and delivering crystal clear sound, than this speaker is an excellent option to consider.

To me, the OontZ Angle3 has no real negatives to mention. You could quibble about having more features, but I really don't consider that a negative. I'd rather have a great sounding speaker, over more features. In my opinion, this is a great Bluetooth speaker for the price.

The OontZ Angle3 is a very solid speaker, that now has outstanding volume and good bass. It retains and actually improves upon the crisp highs and strong mids of its predecessor. I like that Cambridge Soundworks is actually focusing on sound quality and not loading up on tons of features.

I can highly recommend the OontZ Angle3.

Cannot stress this enough - kinks in the cabling will be more detrimental to signal than will antenna placement.

I'm in pretty much downtown/west Houston, and the towers are 13 miles just about due south of me.
The windows range between 6 and 12 feet from my TV, and go up to 9 feet above ground.
If I stick the antenna anywhere in the window, the cabling is kinked up (comes that way from the box), and I get ~50 channels, most of which are gibberish, and I do *not* get CBS or ABC.

If I stretch the cabling across my living room and place it in the kitchen - yes, the kitchen - further from the window, surrounded by walls (townhome complex), with what should be infinitely greater obstructions, I get ~90 channels, and CBS/ABC reappear.

Product deficiency? Not sure. But it's certainly cheap cabling if kinks cause this much effect. Of note, the cabling is *not* the same thickness as traditional coaxial cable you might find elsewhere in your house. Trouble is, it comes pre-packaged with kinks in it.

I should not have issues picking up signal from 13 miles away with minimal obstruction downtown in the 4th largest city in the US.

I *can* make it work, if I want to clothesline any visitors coming in through my front door. I'm going to see if I can smooth out the kinks, and if I can, this will be more than adequately usable. If I can't, I envision drunken friends knocking out the antenna regularly during football season...

I sweat a lot on my treadmill, especially during the summer months, and I always listen to music while exercising. My headhones of choice have been cheap Sennheiser open backs hardwired to an 'ancient' Sony CD player - the sound of the phones is adequate but the main reason is it's easy and inexpensive to replace the ear cushions that deteriorate every year from the dousing they take.

The main appeal of the SoundPro buds is their 'waterproof' design and I have to say they do hold up well. The 'fins' have enough give in them to be quite comfortable yet support the individual phones enough that it's not neccessary to jam them tightly into the canal, which I find uncomfortable.

Even in constant motion, the buds sat tight and delivered quality sound. Good separation, mid-range, and high-end. The bass is defined clearly without being especially pronounced and boomy. My experience is it's very difficult to get quality bass with ear buds at comfortable listening levels and I'm fairly protective about my hearing. On the treadmill there's a fair amount of ambient/external noise competing with the music. The SoundPro buds aren't quite what I'd call 'isolating', but they provide about the same filtering as the Sennheisers and are fine for my purposes.

I keep a soft towel close by to give the buds a light rub over after I'm done. They air-dry easily. I would recommend giving the tips a 'serious' cleaning every month or so.

The only reason I deduct a star is the controls didn't work with my Samsung Galaxy Express phone that runs Android 4.1.2. I can pair fine with the phone and I find the reception to be solid while keeping it close by on the treadmill console. The volume and track advance controls would come in handy but I've had the same problem with other buds I've reviewed and I'm resigned to the Android limitation until I upgrade my phone and/or change carriers.

Bottom Line:Good sound and adequate protection against sweat. Be sure of your Android version if the controls are a deal-breaker.

I picked these up as my second pair of Bluetooth earbuds, after the experience with my first pair (SoundPeats Qy7) didn't go so well. Unlike the SoundPeats, these earbuds are pretty well-balanced, and feel comfortable in the ears. I think the biggest advantage is that some of the circuitry is located in the "remote" on the wire, rather than the earbuds, so you don't have the entire weight hanging off your ears all the time.
The sound is very clear, though it's nothing spectacular. The bass isn't particularly strong, but I've only found one song so far that actually clipped on the bass. Acoustic tracks, alt rock, and similar styles sound good, while genres like hard rock and metal suffer a little from the lack of heavy-hitting bass. However, as I'll talk about later in the review, you probably won't be taking these to the gym, so missing out on the heavy stuff shouldn't be a big deal.
Bluetooth range is fine, I can usually get around 20 feet away without any hitches in the sound. Even then, the hitches are minimal, as long as I don't put my hand in front of the remote.
When it comes to fitting the buds to your ears, you can choose from three pairs of tips, and three pairs of those rubber bits you see sticking up from the earbuds in the stock photos. I've been able to build a fairly snug fit, although it is not quite as snug as I'd like. This will likely require more time experimenting with different combinations of tips and bits.
The earbuds work fine for most daily tasks, as long as you're not making any vigorous movements. They're great for doing tasks where you want to listen to music without getting tangled in earbud cords. Folding laundry is a prime example. There are limits, though, as I mentioned before. While taking a walk with these in is fine, running is not. I tried to wear them for my morning jog, and found that the earbuds worked themselves loose from my ears pretty quickly. The right ear is far worse than the left, as the designers chose to place the remote close to the right ear. Having the remote on one side makes it more accessible, and the weight difference is generally not noticeable. But once you start moving quickly, the extra weight swinging and pulling the right bud is obvious.

I am a huge fan of Sennheiser headphones and have purchased this brand for a while, including a previous iteration of sport headphones.

This headphone is for sporting activities such as running, hiking, walking and the gym. The particular model I tested was for Iphone and IOS based systems.

1. What's in the box?: You receive the headphones, which are wrapped up and ready to go, plus instructions in multiple languages that are really graphics-based, plus a attachment clip and a really useful mesh bag.

2. Aesthetic?: Since there are designed to be for sport, these headphones are really designed to be sporty. Therefore, I received the jaunty grey, white and mint green version. As far as the design, there are really quite nice looking and feel like a quality construction. The cord is green, which in my mind helps with night identification along with rear headband which is white and is probably reflective (though I cannot confirm this at this moment).

These headphones look like what they were designed to do and look nice. I like the chrome touches inside the earbuds as well!

3. Use?: Well, my first impression was the flat cord which is a good length for putting the phone in the pocket while doing activities and it is long enough for even taller people (though not NBA types). The cord is tangle-free apparently, and it appears this is accurate.

Fit?: I suppose I have regular dimensions because I found the fit to be comfortable and fine in terms of placing the band around my head and putting the buds in my ears. There is a slight pinch, but I found this to be minimal and not the worst I have experienced ever. However, of you are very sensitive to having even the slightest pressure around your head, you may want to try a different approach.

Overall, I found the fit to be more than adequate and to my mind necessary to ensure the headphones don't just drop out during use. I haven't experienced the idea that this becomes painful, but perhaps others might.

Sound?: I consider myself sensitive and wanting good sound. On the other hand, I also consider the standard Apple headphones pretty adequate for sound so judge my opinions accordingly. Here, these are sport headphones, so I want good basic sound, but I do not want isolation because that could be dangerous. Moreover, these phones are not for an audiophile experience.
I tried the sound out using the music on my phone and Ipod. I found the overall music quality to be more than adequate. By that I mean I found the quality to be pretty excellent with most every form of music considering the purpose of the headphones. The music sounds live enough and on listening to music without activity, the quality is pretty excellent considering. I would expect that the phones require some burn-in period and I have not reached that yet (some hours of listening) but based on initial listening experiences, the music is well-distributed. There is not a excess of bass (hip-hoppers and metal-bangers should look elsewhere), but rather a pretty good balanced approach to the music without moving into the audiophile category.

IOS controls?: The controls here work well for the IOS system. I found no issues with manipulating the music and voice control in whatever method I wanted. The instructions were pretty clear in terms of the various button presses, but if you have used these controls before, the responses are pretty standard as here.

Overall?: My only concern about these headphones are given the price. Sennheiser is probably the best brand I have found for headphones (though Klipsch and others are very good as well) so the quality seems like it be present. However, these are might expensive. There is one cable point with the tangle-free cable to the left ear and everything seems like it is built robustly. So, this is a choice of price point. On the other hand, sincethe active headphones are typically a purchase needing some quality, this is not way out of line.

On the whole, these are an excellent pair of headphones. I will update this review as I continue to put the headphones through their paces with lots of exposure to tough conditions. I love these things!! I use them when I run five miles every morning so the ear padding gets a little damp, but I've not had any problems yet and they stay on just fine. The battery seems to last forever and connecting with my iphone is a snap (just turn it on and press play)  UPDATE:  Now that I've used these for about 7-8 months, hopefully I can say a few helpful things, both pro and con:  One issue began after about 6 months: about 5-10 minutes into my run, I usually hear a little static then then silence for 5-10 seconds after which they work just fine for the rest of my session. Yesterday, however, they failed completely. I suspect something is wrong with the bluetooth connection because my iphone wouldn't connect even though the headphones were on, charged, and in range. I'm wearing them now and they are working, so obviously this is an intermittent problem that is worsening. I've emailed the company about a warranty replacement/repair and I will update this this review based on their response and customer service. I checked the moisture issue and it's just the ear padding that gets damp and only from my ears sweating (I wear a headband so the working parts of the headphones never get wet, and since I run on a treadmill, there's never any rain to worry about.) This is the main reason I'm tentatively reducing the rating from 5 stars to 3 stars, as I expect better than this.  If this issue is resolved, I will be a very happy customer again based on my experience to date. After 7 months of regular use, here is what I've found:  Sound quality: really good. not audiophile quality but really good in all ranges from highs to lows. I listen to all kinds of music and I'm quite happy with the sound. And they sure beat ear buds and a stupid wired connection. Battery life: I can usually get about 2 weeks on one charge, so about 10-15 hours (about 2 hours per use) -- which is in line with the advertised charge length. The headphones usually tell me "device 1 connected,battery high" -- however if it ever says "battery medium", it really means "low", because it'll be dead within 30 minutes. I have to remind myself to charge them on a regular basis. Charging cable: proprietary -- I hate proprietary cords, we end up with drawers and boxes of cords for all the devices we own. Can't we all just be (the same) micro usb? However, I can deal with this.... it's a minor thing. Comfort: never had a problem, I find them very comfortable. yeah, your ears get warm because of less air circulation, but so what? Ears are supposed to vent body heat.... And they aren't so bulky that they block out voices and sounds in my immediate environment (although sometimes I wish they would...) Blue Tooth distance: The only time I've gone out of range was to test the distance. I left my iphone in one corner of my 2000 sq ft home, and walked to the opposite end of my home -- easily 35 feet and 6 walls -- I was 4 feet short of the other corner before the signal started to drop and I finally got an "out of range" prompt. I know I've walked a good 40 feet away at the gym, but that was uninterrupted line of sight. I can't count the number of times I've walked away and forgotten my phone somewhere while using these until I remember 5 minutes later. Microphone -- I bought these to listen to music and don't get many calls between 5-7am. The first few times I got a call, they didn't seem to work (other than alerting me to a call). However, once i figured out I had to switch the call to my bluetooth device with one touch (doh), the mic and sound quality proved just fine. It would be nice if they switched automatically, and then let me switch back manually --- especially when I'm running, but that's a minor annoyance I can live with.

Everything negative that has been said about this headphone regarding the 5 kHz treble spike... well I simply don't see it. I am running these headphones with a Fiio E10k amp with bass boost on most of the time, and they are an extremely accurate and enjoyable headphone to listen to, retaining an exciting treble, but it is not as sibilant as everyone tends to claim in their exaggerated reviews citing some objective charts. You have to listen at extremely high levels to even come close to a fatiguing experience for most genres of music. It's incredible how these headphones make even 70 year old recordings sound smooth and, in addition to their technical prowess resulting from great microdetailing, have superb timbral transparency and imaging, with an excellent sound stage that few headphones can rival. These are my first pair of high-end open headphones, and I really enjoy Sennheiser's sound signature, as this headphone truly is the perfect balance between the HD600 and the HD800. What I mean by this, simply, is that they have a warmer, more bass-rich sound than the HD800, and are more forgiving. Are they as accurate as the HD800 or as impressive technically? No; however, they work with a wider range of setups that doesn't require "perfect everything" (amps, source, etc) as the HD800s do, for they are a bit warmer and less of a weaponized face speaker. Bass lovers should definitely pair these with a Fiio E10k. You can sense the texture of the bass with these headphones: if you want very boomy and loud bass that rattles your skull, these headphones are not for you. But, if you love a tight, powerful, and very accurate bass that maintains crystal clarity throughout the rest of the track, then these are for you. I'm impressed with how loud I can listen to music with the HD700s and not experience harshness like most other headphones that are too forward. These have an aural airiness to them that continues to amaze even first time open back, over ear listeners like some of my family members. The only downside of this design is they leak a ton of sound as is expected. Definitely worth it if you are an audiophile of any kind.

As expected for an under-ten-dollar-radio, it feels cheap and flimsy, but I was prepared to give it a chance. The antenna does not telescope very far so it always remains very short. The sound quality from the speaker is also what you expect in this price range.

When I first tried every shortwave band, I couldn't bring in a single station. There were a few spots while tuning that the static changed but nothing that resembled a real signal. But to be honest I was somewhat expecting that because we have a metal roof. I went outside and tried again, and this time I was able to pull in a station or two on each shortwave band- though the majority of them weren't good enough quality to discern what the station was or even what language it was in.

I plan on tinkering with this more again later during different times of the day and night. If you are looking for a quality shortwave radio, this is not the product for you. If you are only willing to spend 8 or 9 dollars (and free shipping at that) then this product is better than having no shortwave radio at all.

I work for a small manufacturing business, which is located in a rural area of the Northeastern US. Our business utilizes several desk top computers, both for financial management and in the design and manufacturing of our products. As anyone who has used PC's can agree, the unexpected shut down of a computer (such as one caused by a power interruption) can result in lost data, requiring hours, if not days to reconstruct. The shut down may also be accompanied by power surges, caused by lightening strikes on the power line. This may result in permanent damage to the computers.

After suffering several power outages and related loss of data and damage to our computers, we began protecting ourselves with the APC Uninterruptible Power Supplies (UPS). Now, In the event of an unscheduled power outage, the UPS units immediately sense the loss of power and begin providing battery power to the protected PC's. If the power outage is long enough, and the UPS's software determines that the battery power will be exhausted within a predetermined time period, the PC's will be instructed by the UPS units to begin their shut down routine, so that the PC's may shut down safely, without loss of data. Interruptions of short duration may not even be apparent to the PC users because the PC's will continue to operate normally.

The price that you pay for this unit is small compared to the cost for equipment damage or recovering lost data.

I've had these for about three months now, so I'll go ahead and give them a review.

Sound Isolation:
This is one of the biggest positive traits of this headphone. I've been on the Koss PortaPro train for awhile now, and love them dearly. Unfortunately, they're not ideal for quiet environments as they are very "leaky" as they're an open design. These aren't. In fact, my music can't be heard at all, really, not even in a library, and I can't easily hear anyone else, especially the librarian who loves to scan about a hundred books at a time throughout the afternoon, each with an accompanying BEEP that resounds across the floor. A big plus.

Sound quality, with Bluetooth:
Like I've said, I've been a PortaPro fan for a number of years, so it was inevitable that I would compare the Runaway to them. To keep it brief, they do fall short. Quality through Bluetooth is "meh", though I didn't expect perfection going in since I'd read enough about how Bluetooth isn't meant for sound reproduction, blah, blah, blah. Bass is on the muddy side. Not bad or overwhelming, just lacking in detail. Imaging grows confused in portions of music with lots of detail. Cymbals in particular make these phones want to run away. See what I did there...

Sound quality, wired:
However, when these things are plugged in, many of the Runaway's shortcomings go away. These still don't have the airiness and treble that the PortaPro can sport. However, bass does start to come alive, and much of the lacking detail comes up to play, too. Overall, these are very fun, and for techno and other alt songs, I think I may actually prefer these, as these are not fatiguing to listen to.

Comfort:
This, along with noise isolation, makes up much of the rating on these. I wear glasses, let's get that out of the way. Many headphones are uncomfortable for me, as the clamping pressure of the headband and/or the pads exerted on my head become too much. These are not like those. I have been able to maintain 1 hr (or greater) listening sessions with these, which I have not been able to do except for the PortaPro's. For my head, the headband is nice, with enough padding to be comfortable, and enough pressure to make for a positive-feeling fit. The pads are nice and squishy and conform to my ears. They do make my ears sweat a little, but it is not overly bothersome as I do the majority of my listening indoors in an air-conditioned environment. The instances where I listened to them outside definitely made my ears warm, but it is currently late summer and very humid, so I don't think that will be a problem all year long.

Battery life:
I've only had to charge this once. Seriously. Uses very, very little power. However, don't trust the silky female voice that says in your ear that the battery is "high." That's a dirty, dirty lie. Had the headphones dying a couple minutes after this message. I'd say, charge it once a week or something, and don't worry.

Bluetooth signal:
Alas, this I feel is a bit of a weak point for what is otherwise a solid headphone. "Runaway" is a bit of a stretch. It is closer to "you can run around, but only within about 10 feet of your source." Any further, and I start to suffer from clipping. It's not bad, but it's not as nice of a range as some reviewers have reported. Take note, however, that range could always vary per the source. I've used a laptop, my tablet, and my smartphone, and range has been roughly the same for each. Maybe a little further for the laptop.
In addition, I have found that the source can have a HUGE impact on audio quality, at least over Bluetooth. I refuse to use my tablet as a source, it is that bad. I had considered returning these headphones when I first opened them up and listened to them on my tablet, and then later I decided to try my phone. Sound quality improved by leaps and bounds over my phone's connection. You really don't want to know what they sounded like on my tablet. As some others have noted, these headphones sometimes need to be re-paired to their source, or simply to have Bluetooth cycled on the source (on my phone, turning Bluetooth off, then back on again). I know when to do this when these things start clipping severely for no reason. Cycling the connection has, fortunately, solved this issue every time.

Conclusion:
A comfortable, isolating, and slightly-muddy-but-still-fun-sounding set of headphones, tempered by limited Bluetooth range, signal quality, and slightly underwhelming sound quality while wire-free. Let it be known that my three-star rating I consider to mean "solid", but for these things to merit four stars, Bluetooth connectivity would need to improve.

The point of this review is to talk about why I will never buy an Onkyo product again. Not because they don't sound or look good, it is just that the customer support is abysmal. 45 days after I got this receiver (not from Amazon unfortunately) it randomly would shut off. I called Onkyo and they denied it was a problem with the receiver, instead they said that it was a problem with my speakers Ohm rating and had me unplug everything from the receiver for a day and then plug everything back in and it will work again. It didn't work when I tried this. The second time I called in I told them that the Ohm rating was well within the bounds of what the receiver would handle. They then suggested that I could get the unit fixed under warranty and I went ahead with this process. They sent me an RMA number, etc. And then I was informed I would have to provide shipping for this unit.

The unit shipping would have cost $85 to ship from Colorado to their repair place in Michigan. I called them back up and said I wouldn't pay that amount and they sent me a pre-paid label to ship it out (so the shipping cost to me was $0, I just had to drop it off at FedEx). The unit arrived in their warehouse on July 20th, 2015.

I was wondering why no one contacted me to let me know they received it so I called the repair place in Michigan. They said they had sent out a letter to me asking for more information because they didn't have record of the RMA. Once I provided that, they said they would begin repair. I get a phone call a week later saying that they couldn't begin the repair without proof of purchase (which I don't have anymore because the store I bought it from has since closed).They said I would have to get a special authorization from Onkyo to get it repaired.

So after another phone call haggling with Onkyo to fix my unit that is barely out of the return period, they agree to fix it - with a clause: I would forfeit the rest of the warranty period (1.5+ years) to get it fixed just this once. After thinking it over I decide a working receiver outside warranty is better than a non-working receiver in-warranty. They authorized the repair.

I called the repair place in Michigan today again and they said it would be another month and a half before the parts would come in and after that they would ship it back. The part that broke was the processing board. The repair place said they have 7 other receivers with the same problem waiting on the same part from Onkyo.

I've learned my lesson - Never EVER buy an Onkyo product because of the horrible customer service.

I was pleasantly surprised and pleased by the Captain Bluetooth V3 speaker's audio quality and design. I have been mostly disappointed by little portable Bluetooth speakers. The Captain is bigger than most I've tried and sounds better., The bass is surprising good with the driver in the middle of the top gives

I find the unusual disk shape very attractive. The back has a mechanical on/off slide switch which I like though it is kind of "old school." The bottom has soft pads keeping vibration from carrying into a table top or surface it is resting on.

The Captain is Bluetooth V3 and not V4 so no multi-device pairing. Even with the older Bluetooth spec I was quite impressed with sound from my iPhone 6 or PC.

There is a noticeable delay when sending TV audio via Bluetooth from my Fire TV to the Captain. Being off by a bit gives that annoying effect where speech and video don't match. To be fair, I've never seen a Bluetooth speaker or headphone that got the lip sync exactly right or even really close.

But wait, the Captain has more:
1) A wired audio in via a 3.5mm plug sounds at least as good as the Bluetooth audio.
2) There is a built-in microphone and speakerphone function that works so-so with my iPhone 6
3) The FM Tuner brings in strong stations fairly well. The 3.5mm or USB cables appear to function as an antenna when plugged in.
4) There is a clock with alarm. This is pretty basic and works fine.
5) There id a micro SD card slot and USB for flash based media playback

What I like:
+ Bluetooth pairs quickly and easily
+ Audio quality exceeded my expectation by quite a bit, especially bass
+ There is a usable speakerphone function
+ FM is nice to have available even if I rarely would use it.
+ MP3 on flash media plays well and is convenient
+ It's good to have an alarm in case my phone
+ I have yet to run the battery out

What I don't like:
- While the Captain functions as a speakerphone, my iPhone 6 mic has better audio quality without the Captain
- FM Reception is limited to fairly strong stations
- No multi-pairing support: Bluetooth V3, not V4
- The top bass radiator depressed in the center of the top is just asking for a spilled drink

Conclusions:
While it has its share of weaknesses the Captain shines where it counts for me: audio quality. It is surprisingly good. Even as a sub-par speakerphone, limited FM and no multi-pairing don't bother me too much. I think this effective Bluetooth, analog and flash media player is worth 4 stars.

When I assess any device, I always consider a number of factors. In the case of this microphone, the primary one is how well it handles sound (of course). I compared its qualities to that of a much more expensive ($85.00), but similar mic that was also designed to pick up sound from many directions as well as do noise cancellation - that mic was also designed for talk use (Skype or other chat software). I found that this microphone had a lower pick up volume but was otherwise of a very similar quality. At a little over two feet from my mouth, this mic picked up at about half the volume of the pricier one. When it was near my mouth (sitting in front of me - about 6-8 inches), it was about the same. Note that I did a little research on this, and I discovered that Windows 7 and 8 both have issues with mics and volume, so this problem could have been specific to my PCs. However, since I didn't experience these issues with the other mic, I think it likely does pick up sound at a lower volume. If you're not speaking from far away, however, this should not be an issue. The noise cancellation was surprisingly good. It even filtered out a fan that was blowing directly at it from about five feet away. Note that this does not have a mute button or a power button so you'll need to control sound input from your software.

There are points which I absolutely love about this mic. One is the adorable old-fashioned design. If you want some personality on your desk, this is a great choice. Another is the extremely flexible tripod that allows you to position the mic in various ways. The only design element that didn't thrill me was the blue cable. It should have been black to match the tri-pod! However, they do score points for those who want to do a bit of karaoke on the computer since you can take the mic out of its stand and hold it in your hand for singing. Very few computer mics are designed to allow for this sort of use. It's a nice touch.

I had read that higher price doesn't necessarily mean much with digital antennas but that extra $20 was well worth it.

I first mounted the RCA antenna on a mast left on our roof after removing a DirectTV satelite. The antenna picked up most channels but the reception wasn't great on a few. I decided to try installing the antenna in the attic which was a little higher and because it didn't look like this antenna would survive a winter outside. The reception got a little better in the attic but also lost quite a few channels. I installed the Winegard last night in the same attic location and get a great picture on all channels.

With my beloved 5 year old Clip+ dying, I needed a new player. Thinking I'd get a little more for my money, I bought the Clip Sport instead of the Clip Jam and took off to Mexico.  First, The Good. - The sound quality is slightly better than the Clip+. Nice! - It can charge and play at the same time. Excellent!  Now, The Annoying. - Useless display screen. Can't see it in the sunlight (Not at all!). Can't change the garish colors (Who chose these? They're not just unfashionable. The color of the 'Music' screen is downright gross). When it does display an image, it looks horrible (Think 90s Gameboy). - Navigation buttons are flimsy and super-sensitive. When using it for yoga and having it clipped to my top, every time I stretch my arms it advances to the next song. - Reverses and fast-forwards in chunks instead of second-by-second. - Relatively big and heavy. It pulls on my top when I clip it to me. - When selecting an artist with multiple albums on the player, the first option is shuffle. When I select an album, then the first option is (again) shuffle. I could understand shuffle being the first option for a playlist, but having it as the top choice (twice) when you're looking for a specific song is exasperating.  Finally, The Worst. - When turned off and turned back on, the player doesn't keep your place. This isn't a big deal for music, but it's a huge deal when listening to multi-hour podcasts. It's up to you to remember where you were, and you'll have to fast-forward back to your previous place.  The Sport falls so short of the Clip+ that I've spent an embarrassing amount of time trying to figure out what on earth Sansa was thinking. Was it about price point? Did they use some focus group that didn't reflect their target audience? Did they ignore their own customers in an attempt to make something that would steal a few iPod Shuffle customers?  Ultimately, I wish I would have saved a few dollars and bought the Clip Jam. At least the screen would be easy to read.

Having used their components in the past, I was intrigued to see a midrange offering for a stand-alone, full-featured DAC from the folks at Meridian Audio.  I finally pulled the trigger, having read through discussions on forums and other sites which described its sound as "extremely musical".  This is the most precise characteristic of what you are getting with this DAC: a little gem which produces an amazingly smooth and pleasant palette, while maintaining the level of quality and detail expected of Meridian's heritage.  Driver installation is a breeze, and you could be enjoying this amazing sound in minutes.  Inside of this device is the same DAC circuitry found in a much more expensive headphone amplifier stack (Prime) - but with this device you can choose the right headamp for your headphones.  This DAC works amazingly well from just about any USB source, with no perceptible difference even from older PCs.  Adding a USB power conditioner / filter (iFi or Wyrd) does improve sound quality to the point where it can easily match that of Prime or other high end devices.  It may lack DSD support - but that's the choice made by its designer, and if you happen to have a few DSD titles, playback software can easily take care of the conversion to standard PCM in most cases.

After two weeks of use and charging (without power interruptions), the device still indicates zero minutes of runtime and has approximately 15 seconds of runtime after the power is disconnected (under a 110 watt load, the UPS manual claims an approximate 25 minute runtime at this wattage.) After three weeks the device won't allow the computer to fully boot up, as loading the UPS causes it immediately to flip to battery mode (when the mains power is still up and running without issue), and will quickly power off afterward. In short, my computer isn't usable with the UPS connected regardless of what the mains power is doing. So I've unhooked my UPS and will try to find another solution with either a new replacement battery, or an entirely new UPS (since this replacement batteries seem inadequate.)

Pros:
- Genuine APC equipment, in all packaging and appearance
- Recent manufacturing date on the packaging (< 1 year old)

Cons:
- Doesn't hold enough of a charge to boot my computer after 3 weeks of use

In summary: Would not buy again. Additional regret: Having to take the time to send this junk to the local lead acid battery disposal.

I found the 4 screws mentioned, down the outside of the rubber expansion chamber at the base, and loosened them which allowed the dark baseplate to come off. Having done that I could see that my black wire going to the speaker at the top of the expansion assembly had come loose up at the top at the speaker. But I wasn't able to reattach it because of the spring and distance with the assembly open.

Eventually I discovered I could pry the top cap carrying the speaker loose of the rubber expansion section, and that allowed me to re-solder the speaker wire (if indeed it was ever soldered). I was then able to reassemble it and restore it to function. How long it will continue to function is a guess. The two wires coming out of the base, red and black, that run up to the speaker are quite small and fragile and threaded up through the spring that pushes up the expansion chamber. It doesn't look likely to survive many expansion and compression cycles. YMMV.

This writer's review of the Winegard Flatwave FL5500A Indoor HDTV antenna will start off differently than other reviews as in the beginning I won't focus on the product, but rather, the "user" of this antenna. If you live in a home, you might want to use a Winegard "exterior/chimney mount" antenna for better results and point it in the proper direction of your broadcast towers. I live in a condominium and I don't have that option. Also, you may want to go on to websites like tvfool.com (and there are other websites!) and see where your broadcast towers are located to determine distance as well. Try to consider that things like buildings blocking reception and tall trees and, yes, even atmospheric conditions like wind and rain "can" effect this TV antenna's or other TV antennas' performance. The other product reviewers who indicate that a window mount is best are correct--when the antenna is mounted in the proper location. When I first did set up, I did try positioning this antenna in several locations on the best window exposure that I have available and I got fantastic results ("45" TV channels!), but when I lowered my 1" aluminum mini blinds most of the channels were lost! It was because the aluminum blinds blocked the broadcast signal from reaching the antenna. I found out that by replacing the above 1" aluminum blinds with 1" VINYL BLINDS that came close to matching the aluminum ones in appearance that this did the trick. I got back ALL 45 TV channels(!)--as if the blinds were in the full open position. Another tip a Winegard representative told me is "not" to incorporate a coaxial "extension" cable of more than 10 feet in length as this could also negatively effect the antenna's reception. 1. Pairing was as easy as Bluetooth pairing usually is. No problems.
2. Magnetized speakers keep the two speakers together when desired, on or off the base.
3. Small size and discreet lights. One half of these speakers fits in my hand, so they fit pretty much anywhere and almost disappear (unlike my small Bose, which is harder to hide). The front of each speaker has a thin, white, frosted light that's only noticeable in low-light situations. There's also a blue pin-sized light on the top of each speaker that's visible in any light. That said, it's not big or bright enough that I find it distracting. And no annoying flashing like some speakers.
4. Good sound. Together, the output is decent, although tinny. Splitting the speakers definitely adds to their room-filling ability and reduces the tinniness.
5. Came with all the cables you'll need. There's a charging cable that connects to the base, plus two micro USB cables that split to USB and aux outputs. This makes the speaker pretty flexible, since you can listen with either Bluetooth, headphone, or USB inputs.
6. Sound/power controls on both sides. This is actually a pretty handy feature. The volume, power, and bluetooth pairing buttons are duplicated on the top & bottom, in reverse order, so each speaker has a full set of buttons when split. Very nice for managing the music without having to hunt down one or the other speaker.
7. Rechargeable. This is a minor factor, since pretty much every other Bluetooth speaker I've run across is rechargeable, but it's still handy.

What I didn't like so much:
1. Sound is only "good." At this price, there are a LOT of better options for single speakers without the tinniness. For split sound, though, the sound improves a lot, making this speaker really only worth it if you plan to keep it in the split configuration.
2. Charging cradle. I realize the technical need for a single charging unit, but since I'll never use this speaker as one piece, the charging cradle is an annoying extra piece of equipment.
3. Despite the product description, the charging cradle isn't magnetized. The joined speakers do sit pretty well in it without the magnetization, but aren't as solidly seated as I expected.

These headphones are no joke. The people comparing them to Bose are actually being serious, as well. I generally use Bose Soundlink BT headphones for travel, and B&W P5's while I'm at home. While the wired P5's are obviously way better, the Bose Soundlink headset is very good, especially for wireless headsets. However, the price is out of the range of most peole.

Here comes the BOHM BT headset. A cheaper build for sure, utilizing faux leather (cheaper and rougher than Bose), milled aluminum (lightweight but prone to scratching and denting over time), annoying flickering LED's and poor button controls, the BOHM really isn't particularly impressive to look at. And it's not the most comfortable headset, the ear pads aren't super plush and will press gently (not uncomfortably mind you) against your ears. The noise isolation is there, but it's more noise muffling than anything else.

It's the sound that got me, and will get you. Clear mids. Clear highs. Fantastic lows. Lacks in bass (like all wireless headsets) but the soundstage is huge. I ran through a host of songs streamed via Spotify for almost an hour on my first run through. My ears didn't ache or feel fatigued (which they do with the Bose Soundlink, I will add). The sound was pleasant enough for me to really get sucked into the music.

Pairing was easy enough- follow the instructions and they'll pop up as BOHM's. You're paired and ready to go.

The downsides (and why I removed a star) is the cheap build quality (upshot: this is probably the cheapest headset you'll find with such sound quality), unintuitive controls, flashing signal LED's (for pairing or indicating it's on), but don't let this deter you. And, get the black set. The gold looks just silly.

Eton is known for producing quality emergency radios. First to produce shortwave radio (1986) and first to produce hand-crank emergency radio (2002). It also partners with Red Cross to produce these radios. As for this model FR1, it comes with many features that will be handy during emergency situations. Great for any family or even a college student who is away.

1. COMPACT. It measures 2 1/2" (w) x 5 1/4" (h) x 1 5/8" (d). It could be stored anywhere. In your family emergency kit or in a tool box.
2. STURDY. Being compact does not mean cheap. It is made of strong plastic. It will withstand casual bumps and bruises. BUT it is not shatterproof or waterproof. Best used in indoors or outside away from exposure to rain or snow.
3. GREAT FEATURES. This little thing has: [1] LED Flash Light, [2] Digital FM/AM/WB (Weather Band) channels, [3] DC Rechargeable micro USB port, [4] Hand-crank power, [5] USB connector for your smartphones, [6] Headphone jack and [7] Antenna.
4. NOAA (National Oceanic & Atmospheric Administration) Weather Band adjusts to your local weather station. The information is clear and up to the minute data. Great to have during power outages due to severe weather or natural disaster.
5. DIGITAL BANDS. FM/AM/WB are adjusted with digital bands. It is easier and accurate. You will receive clear sounds. All channels come through clearly.
6. HAND-CRANK. Initially I wasn't sure whether it will hold. The handle is thin (1/8") with a knob at the end. BUT I soon discovered that the plastic while thin, was very strong and well grooved into the radio for support. It was easy to turn, but it will make a high pitched noise. I was able to turn for 4 mins without breaking anything and it did charge the radio.

All in all, this is a great item for your emergency kit. Whether in your house, garage, glove box, or tool chest, this Eton FR1 is a must! Highly highly recommended!

Bottom line is I highly recommend this pair of MDR 570 for the current price

Lots of good reviews so I'll just add what may be newish: I'm using these mainly while riding a big mower on a golf course, pretty loud droning noise environment. With sealing ear buds only loud electric music was listenable, and then a lot of the detail was lost. With the ATs I can listen to, and enjoy, acoustic jazz and even appreciate the spaciousness of the sound. Sound is reasonably detailed too, and as others have noted these phones have a natural, balanced EQ. The sound of the mower is still perceptible, but now it is a distant soft humming that doesn't really intrude too much. Huge difference.

A few quibbles: if you want to also use these without the noise cancellation, the sound is much worse with the switch in the off position. If you mostly want a nice set of conventional phones, look elsewhere. They are bulky, sticking way out from the sides of your head. They barely extend far enough to cover my ears comfortably (comfort is fine, BTW) I have a big head, hat size 7 3/4, but not enormous. If my head were any larger, they wouldn't work for me. You may have to turn the noise canceling off and on a few times to get it dialed in - it seems the circuitry needs to sample the ambient noise and then produce the appropriate antidote, and this doesn't always work the first time.

Overall I am very pleased. A co-worker bought the $300 Bose, but I'm too cheap, and I don't regret my decision. I'm not an audiophile but I am a musician, and I like the sound of these.

I recently received my Orvibo WiFi Smart Socket S20 and was excited to put to use in my office setting, but was disappointed with some features. 1) Timers don't work: With my iPhone (IOS v8.4.1 - latest), I setup a Timer on the app so my desk lamp would come on at 8AM and shut off at 5PM every weekday. Programming this repeating timer was easy, but it didn't work for me. I arrived at my office after 8AM this morning to a dark lamp. I double-checked my time zone setting to make sure, and it was set correctly to my time zone.
2) Current device status doesn't work: On the app interface, the current status (on/off) of the S20 is supposed to be displayed. However, it appears as if the status indicator is actually showing the "commanded" status - in other words, what the app is telling the outlet to do - not what the outlet is actually doing. This is counter to the information provided by the manufacturer. This is an issue, because if you are remote and want to see if you accidentally left your space heater on back home, this won't help. In fact, it might get you into trouble if the heater was off and you inadvertently turn it on (thinking you were turning if off). This could cause a fire or other catastrophe, worst case.
Assuming the device status is communicated (2-way, as the box indicates) to the app, both of these defects could be corrected in software.
I implore Orvibo to fix these issues immediately, or lose market share to its competitors.

I bought this for my girlfriend (and another for me) because we wanted a Bluetooth speaker that sounded decent. Her Note 4 speaker was blown out and she likes listening to music so this was kind of the best solution. I bought this at Walmart for about $0.12 more than it cost on Amazon. However, the prices on this thing apparently change frequently so I have no idea how much more/less it is now.

Pros
1. Surprisingly good sound for a sub $30 speaker. That's of any speaker, be it computer speakers, headphones, whatever. For under $30, these sound fantastic. The bass isn't overpowering but you can definitely hear it. If you put it on a hard-surface table (ex: kitchen table), you can actually feel the vibration. Impressive. The sound is very clear and well balanced. It's obviously not as good as something you'd find for $100 or a good, $50 pair of headphones, but for its price, it's really, really good. Absurdly good for its price.
2. It feels well built. Solid building materials (a harder plastic with a metal speaker mesh). It has a heft about it that's probably mostly from the speaker inside. You feel like you're holding a $30 speaker.
3. I like the rubber ring on the bottom to prevent slipping. Nice little addition, especially on my slick, smooth computer table.
4. Works for music, podcasts, and videos. I've found that when paired with a smartphone or tablet, you can also use this for game sounds/music when the speaker just isn't cutting it. That was kinda cool.
5. Connected with no issues to my NVIDIA Shield Tablet, Note 4, iPad Air, and Nexus 5 (running the Android Marshmellow preview).
6. Line in jack in case I want to go hard-wired and it also comes with an aux cable for your line in which was pretty cool.
7. USB Charging cable lets you use a charging brick (like your smartphone charger) or your computer.

Cons
1. No volume controls which I didn't like. Whatever your phone volume is set to is what the speaker volume is set to. I would've liked to be able to control the volume on the speaker itself.
2. The pair light is obnoxiously bright. Maybe a softer light would've been nice.
3. The pair button is flush with the device. I have accidentally hit it on 3-4 occasions inside of a week just picking it up. Not a deal breaker, but a design flaw nevertheless.

Here's the bottom line, there were a few design quirks I didn't find particularly enjoyable (no volume controls). However, nothing was so inconvenient as to tarnish how much I enjoy this little speaker. It has a big, clear sound, good bass, and can easily fill a small room with sound loud enough to make people have to talk over it. Obviously you don't want to run it at max volume constantly or you'll blow the speaker but even at 75% volume this thing is pretty loud. I honestly was not expecting it to sound as good as it does. I'm used to the $15-$20 Bluetooth speakers that essentially sound like louder versions of the phone speakers = tinny and not "full". These aren't like audiophile quality, but it's certainly far more full and powerful than I anticipated.

I acknowledge that some people have had some quality assurance problems with theirs. I haven't had one yet and neither has my girlfriend but I will certainly update my review if one of us does. For now, I would recommend this to my friends and thus I would recommend it to pretty much anyone. It is surprisingly good and I wouldn't doubt it if these were the best in the "sub $30 range".

The unit does generate some heat.

Niles makes a WiFi Remote for this (nHR200), but for $830 bucks I'm quite happy using my cell phone thank you very much.

Individually the sounds are good, but it’s like they aren’t meshing together in perfect harmony. It’s almost like there’s an echo or the each earbud isn’t properly synced. It’s very hard to identify what is off, but something about the sound is off. I can also hear a very faint static or white noise all the time. It's more obvious in between songs but you can hear it during songs.

The Bluetooth range is lower than expected. On a fully charged battery I can make it to my living room before they lose connection. This is three rooms away. When the battery is lower if I walk more than about 2 yards away from my device the audio starts to cutout. At three yards away the audio is almost gone entirely. With other Bluetooth headphones I can walk around my entire apartment without losing signal at all.

Earbuds should generally be self explanatory regarding how to put them on. Previously I’d never understood why manufacture’s labeled the earbuds left and right. It was always blatantly obvious to me. These earbuds are hard to find the proper orientation. FSL’s Reflex Bluetooth Sports Earbuds aren’t labeled left and right. If you own these and need help figuring it out right had the inline microphone and volume control. It doesn’t help that the owner’s manual is poorly written. For instance there is a chart labeling each item on the earbuds but no key to identify the labels.

The cord of these earbuds is designed to go over your ear. But the loop on the cord is too big for my ears. This will at times cause the earbuds to fall out. Once I get them in right they feel better than any earbuds I’ve ever used. I typically don’t like earbuds. They are normally too big for my ears and the pressure is uncomfortable. As far as Bluetooth headphones go, these are pretty good. Prior to using these, my wife's most-used headphones were the Sennheiser HD 280 PRO Headphones, which have fantastic sound quality and amazing durability, but tragically have a cord that came between her and the total mobility she likes to have while listening to music from her phone.

These on the other hand, are an entirely different sort of beast.

These phones are lightweight, but well-built. They isolate sound decently, but not completely so you'll hear someone talking to you unless you have it cranked to the max, and even then you'll hear them yell (as opposed to a pair of over-ear Sennheisers that make it impossible to hear the outside world).

The sound quality is a bit hollow, but voice is very clear. If you're listening to pop music or phone calls, you won't have many complaints. Just don't expect the same sound quality you'd get from a similarly-priced set of audiophile corded headphones (bass is lacking, as you might expect). Overall, I'd say they are about 50-60 dollar headphone sound quality (better than even a top-notch pair of corded thirty dollar headphones). Bluetooth signal appears to be quite good and pairing is absolutely painless. Battery life is outstanding. I bought this rather than have an adapter hanging off my machine because I didn’t wan the extra leverage breaking the socket on the motherboard. I looked at many here and chose this one because it looked like it was made with good materials. Luckily I was right. The cable is machined well so it doesn’t wiggle like some cheap cables do when their tolerances are too high. The cord itself is very flexible. I learned that between cables of the same thickness, that a lower oxygen cable is more flexible, will last longer and of higher quality. Plus is also means you aren’t fighting with the cable to make it lay where you want it to.

It is also inexpensive: don’t fall for “gold” connectors and pay 3 times as much people. As long as the metal is conductive (non-corroded) and a solid connection is made (because of tight tolerances) a copper connection is just as good unless you live in a very humid/dirty area. This one just happened to have gold plating that means it won’t corrode, so it was a plus. But gold is not really essential for a quality cable. So, under ten was perfect for this 2m cable.

Usually, I prefer full headphones for all the regular reasons involving quality of sound and comfort. However, I love to keep a pair of ear buds with me for those times when full phones aren't my best option, or when I unexpectedly just need to get my jam on. You know how it is. You'll be working in the library and something will make you think of some great old school tune. No problem, pull out the buds from your pack.

Most buds stink. These, the Bose SoundTrue Ultra in-ear headphones, don't. Most buds deliver a tinny sound, as if too much music is being crammed down a tiny pike. That's largely due to the speakers in the earpiece and, to a lesser but still significant degree, the nature of the wiring used. This definitely includes the ones you pay $10.00 at the local CVS. I'd also include the ones which Apple supplies with their iPod. They get the job done, but only in the same way a taco bought at a street vendor tastes good in the moment. Compare it to a Prime Cut Porterhouse, and that taco doesn't look as good.

These aren't Prime Cut steaks, but they are better than fast food. Much better. They are ear buds and, as such, face the same engineering challenges all buds face. But they are very good. Bose developed an excellent product. They did not just slap their brand on to some disposable piece of junk, but onto a set you'll be careful to protect in the case they provide.

The bass comes through without overwhelming, and the high-end doesn't sound tinny at all.

Why only four and not five stars? The sound is worth five, given the context of these being ear buds. If you look at the pic, you'll see they've a rubber thing which is intended to stabilize the buds in the ear. That's a great idea but they aren't one-size-fits-all.

Also, the wire is sensitive and you can hear it vibrate if you aren't perfectly still. There is a clip to diminish this, but if your jam is especially good, you might catch yourself chair dancing, and that clip isn't up to the job.

In all, I'm happy and will use these.
