I've been very impressed with the Symphonized products I've purchased so far. The sound quality makes me want to listen to more music. These are no different. They are getting a four star rating because the mid range seems to get a bit more pronounced as you turn up the volume to "concert" levels. They sound good at middle and low volumes. The low frequencies are reproduced with the greatest of ease. Threw some sine waves through them to see how low they talk and discovered they start to roll off at 20hz and disappear after 16hz which is pretty incredible considering they are earbuds! They are pretty flat up to about 4khz and then do some weird dips and peaks. To my ear the midrange was a bit overly pronounced. I took one of the buds and put it directly on my iPhone microphone (not the most scientific but gave me an idea) and ran a spectrum analyzer to see if it was my imagination or not. This would explain the reviews that say that they are very clear. Especially in the vocal range. The boost adds a bit more attention to the top end static on a distorted guitar which is a little different as well as certain snare drums. Others have actually tugged at it without asking, not realizing that there's another cord that attaches to it. That's the only real drawback to these; aside from that, they're excellent headphones and I definitely adore them.

I purchased the competing [[ASIN:B00NNTVBEO Electrohome EAAC470 USB dual-charging alarm clock]] last Christmas for my wife, but it has a couple of critical design flaws that I hoped this iHome would correct. And it mostly does.

First, and perhaps her biggest annoyance, is that the Electrohome is super-lightweight. Which should be good for a travel alarm clock, but also means that any tug or nudge of a connected device causes it to easily slide off the dresser since it has absolutely no weight resistance. The iHome is only slightly heavier, but with better-designed grips on the bottom it does a much better job of resisting movement. This also means smacking the snooze button doesn't send it careening, although that was a clever way for the Electrohome to get my wife up in the mornings.

Second, the Electrohome has a blindlingly-bright blue display. Even on its lowest setting we usually end up flipping it face down to hide its omnipresent blue glow just so we can sleep. The iHome has a MUCH smaller display which does a reasonable job of dimming to a sleepable level. It supplements the smaller space with a large, front-facing speaker that offers a cleaner sound quality than the Electrohome.

Which brings me to the only downside of the iHome: its much-smaller screen. While most digital alarm clocks these days have gone for big, easy-to-read screens (the kind that prevent having to find my glasses first), the iHome screen is tiny my comparison. And since part of the screen is used for notifications and icons, the actual time-telling part is pretty small compared to most competitors. If you're like my wife and you go to sleep and stay that way, it won't matter to you. If you're like me and you wake up regularly and want to know the time, this could be more problematic.

The USB charging capability is not the fastest, but it's nice to be able to keep the phone on the nightstand without occupying another plug. The 3.5mm input jack worked perfectly with [[ASIN:B00OJPVNDK my HTC]] and [[ASIN:B00OC0USA6 her Fire Phone]].00OJPVNDK my HTC]] and [[ASIN:B00OC0USA6 her Fire Phone]].

When I was traveling abroad in Europe, pretty much every "cool-guy" boutique had Sonos system. The model that particularly stood out was the 5. Because of the high price point, I was heistant to invest in one. I thought about buying a SONOS system for a couple of months, and I finally bit the bullet and bought the lowest end 1. The reason was that I just wanted something that I can listen to in my kitchen/living room while I'm random stuff around the house (I have Audioengine A5+ for my computers – needed something casual).

I testdrove the 1, 3, and 5 all at my local bestbuy. I was totally indifferent about the sound quality and etc. I was completely wrong. The demo music was simply terrible. I was blown away when I played my HQ AACs and 320kbps mp3s. Despite the small size, it can totally fill a small apartment. One caveat I have is that the music is "engineered". I have monitoring headphones as well as speakers at home. Music doesn't really sound like the way it was intended. They rather sound somewhat artificial but made to sound pleasing (with exaggerated high's and low's - just like Beats but done in a tasteful way and without the bad connotation associated with Beats).

Setting up the system was very easy. If you can configure your home wifi, you'll be fine. The system is meant to be placed in a Mac OS X-based environment. The apps look and feel better on iOS and OS X.

The ability to stream music from the computer, iPhone, as well as Soundcloud (which is my go-to streaming source) keeps me entertained for hours.

Also, I'm probably one of the loneliest human beings. I have like no friends or family. It's cool to queue up songs as I approach my front door with the wifi turned on. I can listen to great music as soon as I walk into my house.

Anyway, $200 for the system is a bargain. I really wasn't expecting much but this thing is truly life-changing. Even if you are an audiophile, it is something to consider for versatility and most importantly, you are always in control of music wherever you are.

Up front, let me say that the sound on this puppy is truly amazing. Hook it up to good headphones or a reasonably high end stereo system and you'll hear detail in your music that you've never heard before. That being said, I'd only recommend this for early adopters.

The hardware in this system is sleek and smooth. The Fiio X5 reminds me of an early iPod classic, though heavier and built from titanium. Controls are sensitive, but the buttons and scroll wheel will not work if the screen saver has been activated. To skip a song or turn up the volume, you have to reactivate the screen first, an extra and sometimes frustrating step. The device comes with a rubberized case which is pleasing, but unfortunately does not allow for a good connection to your mini-USB cable. This results in errors in downloading files and frustration when you're trying to charge it. The only work around I've found is to completely remove the case when charging or loading files.

Storage is with micro-SD cards, which is actually very smart. Current cards have 128 gigs of storage and with two micro SD card slots, you can store a quarter of a terabyte of data. The first 256 gig card has just become available and I assume that Fiio will provide a system update to handle these.

The X5 is subpar in terms of display and UI. The display is small and uses a tiny font. For an old fart like me, reading the menus and album information is difficult. The album covers don't fare well on the small screen. That's not to say that it wouldn't be possible to code the display better, the power on and power off screens show what can be done. It's as if, the person that set up the display either has 20/05 vision or hasn't used an mp3 player before. The UI is complicated and requires digging down through the menus to get anything done.

I haven't created a playlist yet, mainly because the process as detailed in the docs (which you must download) appears to be a nightmare. Someday I'll get around to it, but not right now. Some smart person should create a user interface that you can put on your PC or Mac, so you can organize your files without having to deal with the clumsy device UI.

There's no provision for wi-fi or streaming, so all transfer of files has to be via the USB cable. On my Mac, that's most a drag and drop operation, but updating the OS is akin to the old task of updating a computer bios back in the day. You have to download the update file onto your computer, transfer it to a micro SD card, then transfer that file to the FIIOs and run it, the task isn't intuitive.

Getting music isn't as easy as just firing up iTunes and syncing. Hi Res files are only sold online from a few vendors, but alas not iTunes or Amazon. The best of the bunch is HDTracks, but be warned files are expensive. A typical album ranges from $17 to $25 dollars and the album size runs anywhere from 250 megs to several gigs. There seems to be a fair number of jazz and classical selections, but you will end up frustrated as many of your favorites are not yet available. You'll find the most obscure Beach Boys albums, but nothing by the Beatles. For gear heads, your other option is to rip files from an SACD disc or vinyl. If you're using this to listen to your el crummbo mp3 files, then you're wasting your money. Buy an iPod and be done with it. HDTracks has weekly sales of 10 to 20% off and it's easier on your pocketbook if you wait for them. Many of the other vendors are stock small labels, though Itrax and Acoustic Sounds look interesting.

In sum, if you're a early adopter or a gear head, and want to hear music as good as it gets, then spring for the Fiio. If mp3s are just fine or you're uncertain, wait. Paraphrasing Eton's response leaves you with, "Go screw yourself. If you don't want to do that, we'd be happy to screw you a second time".

On the whole these are pretty good headphones. Here's what I've found to be the Pros and Cons.
Pros:
- They are solidly built and easily adjustable to fit your head comfortably.
- The ear pads are ok and will probably soften a bit after I use them for a while.
- They come with a dual male 3.5mm jack cord. The cord itself is encased in a kind of woven material instead of the usual
black plastic so it feels like it's sturdier and will last longer. Also, one male end is straight and the other has a 90
degree jack. This may come in handy depending on what you're plugging into as you can reverse the cord from the device
to the headphones if you need to.
- Sound is pretty good. I'm not audiophile but I found the highs, mids, and lows to be well balanced.
- It has an inline mic.

Cons:
- The cord is pretty short, about 3 feet, so this can be pretty restrictive if you're connected to something stationary like
a PC.
- Passive sound suppression is not too good. I've been using these at work and they don't shut out the ambient sound as well as
I'd like.
- Length of wear is an issue right now. They're a little tight right now and I can only go about 1/2 hour before I have to take
them off for a while. This will likely improve over time as they get broken in.

Overall these are a good deal if you want some decent quality at a reasonable price.

I purchased this radio specifically for the hand crank feature to charge my LG phone and I-pod when camping or in an emergency situation. I tested the hand crank with both devices and both gave the indication that they were charging so I stopped, believing that that feature worked. A short time later I thought to actually see what sort of time frame it would take to fully charge my phone and i-pod just to have as reference so I hooked up my phone and began cranking. Again, the phone gave the visual indication that it was charging as I turned the crank and every 20 minutes or so, I would stop and unplug the phone and check the battery status and it would not change. I did this for an hour and a half total and the phone never increased it's charge. The same for the i-pod, It would give the visual indication in the display that it was charging but the battery status remained the same. I then plugged both my phone and i-pod in their chargers and they charged right up.  All of the other features on the radio worked as advertised. I emailed Electronix customer service and received a reply from two different rep's. One said my phone must be defective and the other confirmed by testing the USB output on the radio with an LG phone that it would not charge the phone. I arranged a return for refund and was sent instructions for return quickly but had to pay shipping. The refund was processed within 10 day's and I got a reply stating that upon inspection of the returned item, there were "scratches" and the unit appeared used so shipping charges would not be refunded to me. The unit was in excellent condition when I packaged it for return and I took extra care insulating the box with bubble wrap so that was another disappointment. In the end, I paid around $15 to test out a radio. If you are considering this radio for the hand crank USB output feature, test and confirm it will actually charge your devices when you receive the radio.

This charger is excellent: it charges up to 4 AA or AAA-sized batteries independently. It has various intelligent features to ensure charging stops a the right moment without overcharging. By default AA batteries get charged at 200mA (a safe but slow rate) but you can increase the current to 500 or 700mA for any or all of the batteries to charge them faster. The display can be set to show the charging current, total amount of charge supplied to the battery, battery voltage, or elapsed charging time for each battery.

It can be used as a plug-and-play charger: simply plug it into mains power, insert rechargeable batteries with the correct polarity, and come back in a few hours. The default options are safe and reasonable for all NiCd/NiMH batteries and you only need to adjust the charging current if you want to charge the batteries faster; the faster rates are also safe and reasonable. The display will indicate when each battery is full.

From a technical and feature standpoint it gets five stars, but some quirks with the user interface knocks one star off: the charging current in slot #1 sets the maximum limit for all other batteries. All the batteries charge independently with one exception: if the battery in slot #1 is charging at 700mA, batteries in slot 2/3/4 can charge at 200, 500, or 700mA. However, if the battery in #1 is charging at 500mA, batteries in other slots can charge at only 200 or 500mA. If #1 is set to 200mA, all batteries can only charge at 200mA.

After inserting a battery you're only given a few seconds to change the charging current from the default 200mA; once the current is set it's locked in for the duration of the charge or until the charger is unplugged -- I've found it easier to unplug the power adapter, insert the batteries, then plug it in and set the charging current for all of them.

The charging current selection for each slot is stored in volatile memory and is reset when a battery is removedfrom the slot or when the charger is unplugged. It would have been nice if it would save the last-used current selection so one doesn't need to push the buttons repeatedly for each battery when charging many batteries at higher currents.

I could argue that the Photive HYDRA is the best Bluetooth speaker for its price. Good sound quality and volume range, full water resistance, and looks are a few of the high points. There are few low points. If you are looking for a cheaper Bluetooth speaker that you can use outside and at home, this is it.

PROS
Price - I bought this during a promotion for $40. It was marked down from $60. I would be willing to pay the higher price for this.

Connection range - Keeping the connected device on one side of a house, the HYRDA stays connected on the other side (30-40 feet). I also took it down two floors and it still stayed connected as well. (I have an iPhone 6, results might differ per device)

Sound range – In my room a good volume level is about half the full volume range. At full volume, I can hear it from several rooms away and in a room of several people.

Design – About the size of a 16oz water bottle. It can rest on an angle. I like the way it looks.

Water resistance – The IP-66 rating is given as a result from testing and specific standards, so you can trust it. It does hold up against water with seemingly no damage. I tested this by first running the faucet over it for a minute, then holding it submerged under water for 2 minutes. I dried it off with a towel, opened the port cap and there was zero water inside. It’s still working.

CONS
Average bass – The bass isn’t terrible, but compared to Bluetooth speakers at a higher price point, it is lacking.

Pro: Holds Rated Weight Cons: Very difficult to mount, Design severely limits rotation to 35°–45° with wider speakers. Bottom Line: Would not recommend.  The mounts have several problems with larger speakers. With 11.5" wide speakers (which the product description lists as within design), the mounting arm can only be rotated 45° at most because the holding rails will hit the wall (see pics). I tried extending one as far as it will go and the one to be near the wall closer in, but I still only get 45° because the holding arms themselves are too short. In the both pictures you can see the mount is hitting the wall at about 45° when setup to mount 11.5" speakers. With the arm furtherest from the wall as far out as it will go, and with the speaker that have to be mounted a bit further back. So, the speaker touches the wall sooner as you rotate it. The result is he speaker can only swing about 35°.  The second problem being that the main arm itself doesn’t extend far enough out from the wall to rest the speakers center of gravity over the platform while mounting (again why the speakers can’t be rotated past a certain point). So, you need 2 people to mount large speakers that this thing claims to be made for: one to hold it, and one to drill the retaining screws into your cabinet from the bottom.  The fact that the retaining screw holes are on the bottom makes it very awkward to see and you have to work against gravity to make the screws tap. That’s where the next problem comes in: the wood screws are too dull and can’t tap anything made with real wood. My speaker cabinets are Walnut, so the screws wouldn’t tap them at all. Even after drilling a pilot hole the dull screws aren’t able to seat themselves because the speakers are pulling up (trying to fall forward) , and gravity is working against you.  There are other problems such as the pivot bolt (which you lose the ability to hold onto once it seated with the plastic turning sprocket) and nutrequire you to screw them in with more force (like 2 sets of drivers), and again you have to screw them in upward fighting gravity.  My other mounts for smaller speakers were a lot better designed with the arms standing further out & the securing screw holds on the side AND a safety chain that I was able to install them by myself. With these mounts, once you mount the wall plate to your studs, it all goes downhill from there. It has taken me twice as much time to attempt to mount one of these than it took to mount both of the other mounts.  If the arm was at least 12" out from the wall, vs. the ~8" it currently is, and the securing tap screw holes were on the side this would be much easier to mount. Also, fixing the vertical angle adjustment would also make aiming them down easier. But these mounts were never thought out nor tested at all for the tap screw and definitely without testing their maximum rated width. Avoid.

Full disclosure, I got this item at a discount specifically to review. That said I have reviewed it as though I paid full price for it.

I’ve been listening to Hi-Fi since the early 70s, having bought a Marantz receiver and Kenwood anti-resonance turn table early in high school using money methodically saved week after week from my paper route. I was an early adopter of CDs, picking up a unit in the first year they were available on the market.

As a music collector, I quickly found that my lack of library organizational motivation kept me from hearing much of my growing CD library. I had my favorites that sat in one pile, and the others stashed away in bookcases. It was a mess! The iPod was a godsend with respect to organizing the music and making it portable for my exercise routines, much better than the minidiscs that came before it. Unfortunately, the audio quality of the earliest iPod for Windows suffered. This was before iTunes, before AAC. The lousy MP3 encoder Apple bundled stripped the ambience, spaciousness, 3D structure, and nuances from the music. As Apple’s encoders have improved, I’ve ripped and re-ripped my library to keep up with the latest psychoacoustic model tweaking.

I’ve owned every iPod since the 2G 20Gb version, up through the 7G Classic. The absolute worse for sound was the iPod Photo, the 4G iPod, since it couldn’t drive headphones less than 50 ohms without substantial buzzing and distortion. The best was the 5.5G, with the Wolfson codec, though the noise floor was alarmingly high. (It wasn’t a black background, in today’s parlance.)

The iPod Classic 7G has it’s own problems--lack of ambience, spaciousness, 3D structure, and nuances from the music.

Fortunately, the iPhone 6+ is nearly perfect, except it doesn’t drive the bass of my Shure SE846s very well and its 128GB memory is not big enough for my library.

I was looking for the X5ii to provide the sound quality of the iPhone 6+, drive capability for my over-the-ear headphones (Sennheiser Momentum, AudioTechnica M50x), for my Shure SE846s, and my other array ofIEMs, plus more storage for my still growing 28000+ track library. I purchased two 128GB micro SD cards for the Fiio, giving me an additional 80GB or so of storage over the iPod Classic, so from that standpoint, I’ve reached my goal. But the sound quality is not equivalent to the iPhone 6+.

Fiio X5ii vs. iPod Classic 7G as heard with the Westone W3: The Fiio X5ii has a quieter noise floor than the Classic when the X5ii is set to either low gain or high gain. This is a cudo for the Fiio. Additionally, there is no hard drive whirr that the Classic produces when it’s buffering data from the hard drive. The X5ii is warmer than the Classic, with less high end extension. The bass on the X5ii is slightly stronger than the Classic. The Classic has slightly more detail and is somewhat less congested than the X5ii. Soundstage is roughly comparable, with the edge going to the Classic. Due to the lower noise floor, I’d give the X5ii the edge in sound quality compared to the Classic.

Fiio X5ii vs. iPhone 6+ as heard with the Westone W3: The noise floors are equally quiet and unnoticeable. But the iPhone 6+ takes the lead on detail, spaciousness, 3D surround. The X5ii is compressed towards the middle in comparison. The iPhone 6+ has no noticeable congestion—the finest details in the music get through. The primary and secondary echoes in a reverb are there in the iPhone 6+ while the secondary echo is missing from the X5ii. However, the iPhone 6+ doesn’t have the drive capability to push the over-the-ear headphones without an external amp. The X5ii can do it on its own.

Fiio X5ii vs. iPhone 6+ and Fiio Mont Blanc: I find the X5ii to be a better amp than the Fiio e12 Mont Blanc which has too high a noise floor for sensitive IEMs. The Mont Blanc would also compress the 3D sound field, even when fed from the iPhone 6+. As a result, it doesn’t get used much, except when I need to drive the over-the-ear headphones for quiet home theater listening. Of course, there is the e12a which is better suited for IEMs, but I bought the e12 one month before the e12a was introduced.

Massive Library Management: I didn’t buy the first X5 generation since it couldn’t handle more than about 5200 tracks. The X5ii did index my 28000 tracks. It took about 50 minutes. When finished, it was un-navigable since every click advances one song. This would be 28000 clicks to make it through the track list. The CD list is unmanageable as well. I broke the library into 8 folders, ABC, DEF, etc., split between the 2 micro SD cards. Now I can find the artist pretty easily and the albums under the artist. There is no album artwork to help you ID the album, just the album name. Artwork shows up when the track is playing. Note that you can start at the top of the track list and jump to the bottom by spinning the wheel "up." The volume buttons seem to perform forward and backward functions as well as volume when the display is off. Just push and hold to go either forward or backwards.

The operating system is basic. The EQ flattened the sound more than not having the EQ--pretty lousy. I’ve not fully tested the X5ii with the Shure SE846s, so will likely update this review later.

Summary: The X5ii gives more storage than the iPod 7G Classic. To my ears, the sound is roughly the same quality as the Classic. It doesn’t match the SQ of the iPhone 6+. How much difference is there? Way more than you would hear between a song ripped at 128kb/sec vs. 256kb/sec AAC. Why don’t I just use Spotify? Because Spotify somehow sacrifices the ambience and 3D soundstage even at the highest bit-rate settings even on the iPhone 6+. I always prefer the AAC 160kb/s VBR over the 320kb/s Spotify.

Post script: I spoke with a Burr-Brown chip designer during Apple’s switch from the Wolfson codec to the Cirrus Logic codec. He was surprised I could hear a 3D sound field difference. “You can hear things like that?” I think were his words. It would be nice if audiophile engineers who could hear the differences were designing the chips rather than electrical engineers who look at specs and circuit simulations.

I'm very glad that I was able to order this at a promotional discount in order to evaluate and provide my honest review.

First off, the setup experience was horrible on the PC. I came really close to returning this when attempting to connect to it via the PC. The remote refused to connect to the hub. At my wits end, I searched Google and to my surprise, you can actually perform the setup using the iPhone app - which was successful.

If you're having trouble and reading this, download and install the 'MyHarmony Application' for Windows. Launch it, but do not press anything other than ALT+F9 - perform the firmware update and reset procedure then proceed with the setup using the phone app if you have issues.

Since it's kind of unfair to the device to review it using a "what if" scenario, I gave it 5 stars (and avoided the "what if my mother had to set this up" scenario, and since she can't even use the cable remote properly - that scenario is bother unrealistic and again, unfair).

On to the remote itself:

Coming from a Harmony 1100, with wireless extender, this thing is night and day. I'll explain:

Convenience:
+ No more sticking RF extenders on IR ports on devices individually. The IR blaster has a very impressive range, and the hub itself is a blaster!
+ No more connecting both the extender AND the remote to the PC individually to perform updates.
+ No more tweaking, making notes and then performing said updates (the remote will tweak your settings, on the fly if something didn't setup correctly).

Performance:
+ No more lag using the buttons (which causes repeated key strokes or missing ones).
+ The new IR blasters are extremely responsive; keystrokes are registered immediately - no more repeated keystrokes either.
+ Remote can communicate 'natively' with my gaming consoles (PS3, PS4, Xbox One).
- Remote CAN'T communicate via WiFi to a Windows PC (yet?). Really big missed opportunity here since they already developed a iPhone app for remotely moving the mouse - why not integrate it here? Odd.

Usability:
+ Many more hard buttons (vs. the 1100), light and easy to use one handed.
+ Help menu doesn't just fix the remote's missing commands one time, it actually learns and adjusts the activity settings.
+ The Windows app is much more straight forward for configuring the remote and assigning buttons.
- The touch screen is nice, but the performance leaves a lot to be desired. Swiping and accidentally hitting menu items happen a lot for me. Though to their credit, the 'lock screen' is a nice touch to prevent this while you're just idle with the remote.

I haven't experienced a bug with the remote yet - I read that earlier FW had a lot of bugs, mine looks ok. This is definitely not a novice device to setup but the iPhone setup app is slick and is a huge step in the right direction. Just wished the Windows app worked just as well out the gate.

With such great core feature upgrades (software, key stroke performance, IR blaster performance and setup), I couldn't help but give this is 5 star even with the issues I had.

Unlike the original series of remotes and software, I didn't feel like I had to start from scratch every update or abandoned inside the setup if I got lost. Once that horrific pairing experience was done, the activity setup imported all of my activities and devices from my old Harmony device and running through the activities tweaked the plaguing issues I had with my Sony XBR850C TV.

So once you overcome pairing, the remote finally shines. Have a bit of patience, and this baby will pay off. Good luck!

The speakerphone feature of the Taco is far inferior to the speakerphone on my iPhone 5c, to the point that the Taco is not practically useable as a speakerphone. I tried calling 2 different people to test the Taco. Both could can barely hear me at 3ft/1m away from the Taco. At 9ft/3m away, all each could hear was a bit of noise. In contrast, when I switched to the iPhone's speakerphone on the same call, the other persons could hear me loud and clear as I walked around the room at more than 9ft/3m away. I tried the Taco at different volumes and with different positions, in case it's microphone was covered, but no improvement. I tested the Taco in a quiet home environment.

In an attempt to get around this problem I tried using the Taco with a wired connection in headphone mode. This allows the Taco to play the incoming voice over its speakers while using the microphone on the iPhone to pick up my voice. In terms of microphone volume, this works, but there is a very loud echo because the iPhone's microphone also picks up my voice coming through the Taco. As a result of this very loud echo, that headphone mode is unusable as a speakerphone.

Perhaps I got a bad one, or perhaps the design uses a low quality microphone without any noise and echo cancellation technology.

Since I bought this unit primarily to use as a speakerphone, I will be returning it.

As for music sound quality, it's pretty good and loud enough to fill a bedroom with sound. It does distort at the highest volume and is a bit boomy for my taste. If I wanted it only as I Bluetooth speaker, I would have kept it. Since I haven't tried other comparable Bluetooth speakers, I don't have an opinion about relative sound quality.

I also don't like the location of the charging port, which is on the bottom of the unit. When plugged into USB power, the unit does not sit flat but flops over on its side. If you plan to keep this unit plugged in, it willnot sit upright but will look funny and may roll around. While the unit can certainly operate on USB power, its physical design is intended to be run off of battery power and charged between uses, rather than to be plugged in on an ongoing basis, unless you don't mind it laying on its side.

So, two stars off for having an unusable speakerphone and one for poor power port position.

I love this receiver! It was a lot less expensive than the next 5.1 option and I couldn't imagine being much happier with a unit that cost $100 more. Except for built-in bluetooth (external add-ons are available) and maybe a second optical port, there's really nothing more I could want in a surround receiver. The USB input is great, I don't even have to hook up a phone or Mp3 player, I just bought a low-profile 32GB stick and it lives in the unit with my whole collection on it that I can access at any time. There is even on-screen info on the TV through HDMI and also on the receiver display screen for music and settings. The plethora of different presets and decoders is great, and I love that I have full control of all tone and individual speaker levels through the menus. Puts out plenty of power and sounds crystal clear. Could not be happier with performance. The easy setup mic is interesting, but I found that I would rather set the levels myself as it did some interesting things when I ran it. Two minor cons, but neither big enough to dent the 5 star rating I'm giving it. One- the unit is large. Like, standard stereo receiver large. I thought it would be smaller for some reason (cost?), but it is not any larger than your average receiver unit. Two- the receiver can be very picky about how it is wired in the back. I kept getting a "CHECK SP WIRES" message and an auto shutdown at around -20db for the first few days until I pulled out the unit and re-stripped and reinserted all the wiring VERY carefully. Now it works like a champ and will crank a lot louder than I need it to! Found a lot of online frustration with this issue and exactly what the cause is (speaker ohms, external wiring, bad speakers, etc.) and I am pretty confident this is where anyone having a problem should focus. Once all was up and running, I have nothing negative to say whatsoever. Would buy it all over again and will likely get another Yamaha unit if I ever have need to.

Would recommend plugging the VGA end into the monitor first, then turn on the laptop and monitor and plug in the HDMI in last so the computer can auto recognize the new hardware introduced.    Also read complaints that people loose sound. This is not true and there is an easy explanation and fix for why they experience this phenomenon. A computer instantly defaults to an HDMI output for sound since it assumes any thing plugged into the HDMI port will be the source of videos or sound-related media needs. Thus the computer defaults to the HDMI port for sound, and since a monitor by itself has no sound output, then folks perceive that they have lost sound.    So what is the fix? Go to the Sound dialog box (either right-click the sound option in the Taskbar tray (in lower-right corner) or access Sound dialog box from the Control panel. Once in the Sound dialog box do the following:    1. Click the Playback tab at the top of the dialog box.   2. Click the computer's Sound speakers in the list of options (to select this option).   3. Click the Default button to make this the default sound source option and click OK to exit the dialog box.  You're done and sound is restored. GREAT PRODUCT! Packaged well ... thanks for this easy solution to this type of situation needs.

At Walmart and Best Buy I tried a pair of wired Skullcandy Hesh 2.0 headphones and thought that the sound clarity was excellent. I compared this to other headphones available on display like Beats and Sony and felt that, surprisingly despite its bad rep amongst audiophiles, that the Skullcandy's were clearly the superior choice.

I scoured Amazon for a deal and found that there was a Bluetooth version of the Hesh and, quite hastily, decided on the spot to pay the extra to pick up a wireless version. They came in quickly, the packaging was immaculate, the build quality was sturdy and fairly comfortable when I happily tried them on (they did put pressure on the edges of my ears and make them sweat a little with an hours use, but with time I imagine the comfort would improve). Then I tried playing some music... and well, how to put it... the sound... just... sucked. Compared to the wired version I heard at the stores, the wireless version was far more hissy, had far less clarity/presence, and had a slightly lower volume. The difference felt pretty dramatic to me. I did some research and learned that this noticeable degredation of sound quality is a problem that plagues bluetooth headphones, which is why many audiophiles still go with wired (or use headphones built with apt-X encoding technology to get CD lossless quality, a technology which unfortunately neither these Skullcandy headphones nor my Sony smartphone supports).

Sadly Skullcandy's wired version had already spoilt me (go figure), and I simply couldn't stand the sound from these wireless versions. I even tried fixing it with equalizer apps on my phone to adjust the sound clarity to something more acceptable, but after a week of use my ears actually hurt from it.

I promptly returned these for a refund. I would have bought the regular wired Skullcandy's, but at this point I started to look at headphones as a long-term investment, so I begrudgingly did more research to learn ALL the available options, their upsides and downsides, etc. etc. I still recommend the wired Skullcandy Hesh 2's (they are good), but I ultimately purchased a pair of Sennheiser 2.0 Momentum's. They're more expensive (at a cost somewhat difficult to justify), but the sound quality is almost transformative in the clarity of the music, I'm quite literally hearing instruments I didn't even realize were in songs so it feels like I'm hearing all my music for the first time. It also has a folding form factor and style that better suited my tastes.

Again I would still recommend the wired Hesh headphones, but I wouldn't bother with their wireless offerings until they improve the sound quality, get apt-X or some other technology.

I've had these for less than a week (will update as I get more acquainted with them). I am an amateur music producer and sound engineer. I use similar (closed back) headphones to record, edit, mix, and master acoustic music. I also use noise cancelling BT headphones everyday also for media entertainment (phone and PC) and hearing protection at work. A lot of reviewers are comparing them to Bose BT/NC cans, so for reference, I will compare them to my trusty Sennheiser MM-550x BT cans with active NC (no longer in production, but around the same price range now).

Ratings on a scale of 1-10

Sound Quality:
Wired (no power): 9 - A little murky in the mid/high range (disappointed at first, but I am getting used to it), good, crisp bass response, not too boomy. Much louder than my 550x's. I do have hearing damage and ringing that can be exacerbated with certain frequencies (especially high range). These do exacerbate it a little under normal listening conditions, whereas my 550x's do not unless I am listening too long at high levels.
BT: 10 - The murky mid/highs are fixed with the onboard DSP. Using the highest quality sound setting (APT-X)(power on/hold vol+) these are as good or better than any other set of cans I've used. About equal to my 550x's.
Sound with NC activated (wired and BT): 10 - No noticeable change in audio quality, minimal hiss when audio is paused.

Active NC functionality: 8 - I like the auto detect which chooses best of 3 modes for different ambient frequencies. After all, you're not always on an airplane when you need NC. Side note: This active NC doesn't attenuate the muffled sound of your own voice when talking (or singing). My 550x's do completely attenuate that effect, but it comes at the cost of altering the audio quality such as cutting into your bass and elevating mid-highs. Overall, these won't mute out the world around you, but it helps. It would be great if they had a pass thru/pause buttonlike Sennheiser uses so you can talk to people without taking them off. Also, instead of ANC automatically turning on with the power, I wish it would remember the last setting before powering down and restore that instead.

Passive NC functionality: 7 - not bad, but not a great seal around the ear either. Not incredibly well sound insulated. Side note: the 550x's are excellent for that, but the sound of your own speaking or singing voice is equivalent to holding your ears shut. You have to use ANC to speak or sing. So the Sony's are a decent compromise.

Ease of pairing: 9 - had minimal trouble with Win 10

Ease of use/intuitivenes: 8 - takes some getting used to and I always accidentally bump the forward/back toggle. Volume up/down seems backwards to me.

Comfort: 9 - pads can get warm and sweaty around your ears. Top band presses on the top of your head after a while. But I can generally wear them all day. They are light and stay put.

Portability: 6 - It would be nice if the pads swiveled 180 degrees and folded up. Leaving the headphones to rest around your neck chokes you. Plus it only comes with a very thin sack for storage/carrying.

Power: 8 - Long lasting, but I wish it had a removable battery so you can use a spare and charge it on the side and use the cans while it's charging (either wired or using your second battery). Also, they only give you a very short USB cable with no wall adapter. When they say that you should use this cable and not others, listen to them, because many USB cables do not charge it. Furthermore, even with the stock USB cable, certain USB wall adapters don't charge it either. Not sure why. Good thing the charge lasts all day even ANC on which is way better than my 550x's can do on ANC.

BT Reception: 8 - Extends better than most when it's on the most stable sound quality setting (level 1), not so good on level 2 or 3. Sometimes it breaks up with my phone in my backpocket when on level 2 or 3.

Durability: 10 - so far so good, We'll see. Seems well constructed, but I am concerned about the the headband. If the guide inside the center head pad are plastic, then I am interested to see if it breaks after a while (as my 550x's have done twice).

Calling: 10 - works as advertised. People can hear you fine.

Misc: I like that the audio cable is 1/8" stereo on both ends (gives me an extra patch cord). I wish it was longer though.
It would be nice to have a voice command button as well (like my 550x's have).
The Sound quality selection is nebulous and took forever to figure out. There should be a better way to adjust that. Plus you have to look it up online or read reviews to even know it's there. But in a nutshell, Holding Vol+ and power on raises the quality to the next level up from what it was before (look for the blue lights blinking according to the quality level to confirm the change occurred). Holding Vol- and power on lowers it one increment from where it was before. All told there are 3 levels, but to get them set, you have to power off and power back on. It doesn't tell you what level you are on by default powering on. Using NFC on your phone to connect goes to level 2 by default, so I don't use that feature (kinda a waste cause I think it's cool).

Bottom line: These are good daily use cans with 10 times better sound quality than Beats and other gimmicky cans and for less than you'll spend on those gimmick cans. Features are on par with others in the same playing field. There are things that could be better, but I highly recommend them at this price range.

Well, after about two and a half months with the SC-1323-K I thought I would share my thoughts on it.

The first (of two) receivers shipped had a dead center channel. The MCACC setup figured that out before I did. Indeed the center channel was dead and did not even recognize a speaker was hooked up. This did give me a chance to talk to/evaluate Pioneer customer service, and they were a pleasure to deal with-seriously. Straightforward, led me through diagnostic steps, understood I had done troubleshooting already, and he even understood what "ohms" were. Went through a factory diag procedure, and the usual reset, and after ten minutes the agreement was.......center channel was dead. I did discover the nearest Pioneer service center was 120 miles away, which in TX is not considered a particularly long drive, but still. The return to Amazon was painless and a new receiver did arrive........ a working receiver arrived.

I still have a problem with Amazon shipping heavy electronic components, easily damaged components, like this via USPS. I specifically requested the replacement be sent via FedEx or even UPS, and I would cover addl shipping if required. It was still sent via USPS, oh well.

The new receiver worked as advertised. Most powerful receiver (amp) I have had since my old Kenwood M2A Basic. Lots of headroom, and I will leave it at that. As far as sound, very good, no glaring faults (criticism from an old fart still using Cerwin Vegas on his front two channels). It is a very "precise" receiver. I was listening to Yes 90215 on it after I got the receiver dialed in, and it was crisp, almost like listening through my Sennheisers, but with actual thump.

I got this radio to play around with along with my kids. I wanted one that was cheap enough that I wasn't going to worry about letting a 1st and 3rd grader mess with it, but one that worked well enough to no frustrate them because of lack of ability to catch stations, or difficulty to use. This seemed like a good radio to try for meeting that criteria.
First, let me start off by saying this is a very inexpensive radio. I gave under $20 for it, including delivery, and am taking price into my account in the review. For overall quality compared to other radios I have seen, it is probably 3 stars, at best, but considering that it really isn't that much worse than a $150 radio, I bumped it up to 4 stars.
First off, the build quality: Pretty decent for a $20 radio. All controls work properly, and with a reasonable degree of precision. The dials move smoothly, and the switches have a nice 'click' to them, so you know they are in position without being difficult to manipulate. The antenna is surprisingly good, it seems sturdy, telescopes smoothly, and swivels all around. It is recessed into a notch (kind of like a carpenter's rabbit) so that when folded, it does not stick out from the body of the radio, either to the top, or back. This limits the amount of bend/swivel it can achieve when trying to point it forward, above the face of the radio. I really don't consider this a negative, because you wouldn't want the antenna poking at your face whle you were looking at the dial anyway. If you need to orient the antenna a certain way to improve reception, just turn the whole radio, it isn't that big. The dial is fairly accurate to the stations, about on par with most low priced analog radios, meaning it is a close estimation, but not exact reading. There is a switch on the side for on/off, with a little red power indicator LED in front that lights up whenever the radio is on. Right next to that, is a green LED that indicates signal strength. When it lights up, the radio is receiving a signal, and the brighter it lights, the stronger the signal. This is nice for the kids, as they not only can hear when a station is coming in, but can use the light to get the strongest signal.
Tuning is typical old-school analog tuning, Buzz/hiss between stations, and even some buzz/hiss on weaker stations. I know Kaito makes a SW radio with digital tuning, or at least a digital filter to eliminate this, but I actually prefer this style for the kids, so they can learn to tune for the strongest signal. Also, there have been a few interesting stations we found, that had static, that may have not even registered through a filter. Tuning ability is actually pretty darn good for a $20 radio that catches so many bands. AM and FM reception is on par with my daughter's Kaito KA200, maybe even a little better on AM, but not equal to Sony's pocket AM/FM radio (which has the best reception of any pocket radio I have ever used, both AM and FM). Between myself, and my kids, we have this radio, a Kaito KA200 AM/FM, and a Sony AM/FM pocket radio. If you don't need the Shortwave capabilities, the KA200 has comparable performance, a much smaller size (about the size and thickness of a deck of cards) and lower price. The Sony is of comparable size and price (just a little smaller, just a couple $$ cheaper) but has truly superior tuning abilities in the AM and FM bands (no SW).
While I have limited experience with shortwave receivers, this one really isn't that far behind others I have used in its ability to tune in stations. They may not be quite as clear as a better radio, but they are there, and listenable. Just before bed last night, between 10:30 and 11 PM I tried the SW bands, and caught close to 50 stations while sitting on my sofa. Probably 20 were very clear, 15 were good, 10 were acceptable, and another 5 were static filled, but I was still able to tell what was being said. There were numerous other stations that I could find, but were so filled with noise, they were not worth listening to. I have a feeling if I tried even later, I could have gotten more, as I can only catch 10-15 stations during the daytime hours, with some variance depending on the time of day.
My biggest nit pick on the radio would be the band selection switch, or more specifically, the indicator for the switch. There are very tiny 'windows' that you look through to try to see a tiny red dot (that isn't all that bright) to see which band it is tuned to. It is not lit up that I can tell, and is a real bear to see in low light. The actual tuning needle and face is clear enough and easy to read, but is necessarily small. This radio is about the same overall size of the old-school transistor radios, the kind that take a 9V battery, but proportioned a little differently. It is not quite as tall, but a little wider. Next to the tuning needle/face, there is a small speaker that puts out way more sound than I ever expected. While not exactly room-filling, its output is impressive given its tiny size, both in sound volume and quality. Sound quality is also surprisingly good, considering everything is coming out one tiny speaker.
The volume dial as well as the tuning dial work smoothly, and work as they should, probably better than expected for a $20 SW radio. I really don't know how Kaito can fit 9 SW bands, along with AM and FM bands in a radio this small, and at this price point, that works as well as it does. The only compact radio I know for sure that has noticeably better tuning abilities is the one from Sony, and it is AM/FM only, really isn't any smaller, and only costs $2 or so less!
A few other nice touches would include:
Very good battery life, it takes 2 AA batteries, and I think one pair of new batteries would last all weekend.
The wrist strap, which you can use or easily remove.
The little protective pouch (admittedly not much to brag about, but keeps the dust off of it, and keeps the face from getting scratched).
The little 'kickstand' in the back, that lets you lean the radio back so that the speaker fires up and around, rather than just one direction.
This stand also makes it easier to see the tuning window when it is on a table or counter.
A pair of earbuds which were included with the radio. Nothing fancy, but they work.

I was wavering between 3 and 4 stars, as this really is an 'average' SW receiver, maybe even a bit below average, but when I factored in the price and small size, I think you'd be hard pressed to find a smaller radio that worked as good, especially at this price point. I have a feeling if I tried even later, I could have gotten more, as I can only catch 10-15 stations during the daytime hours, with some variance depending on the time of day.
My biggest nit pick on the radio would be the band selection switch, or more specifically, the indicator for the switch. There are very tiny 'windows' that you look through to try to see a tiny red dot (that isn't all that bright) to see which band it is tuned to. It is not lit up that I can tell, and is a real bear to see in low light. The actual tuning needle and face is clear enough and easy to read, but is necessarily small. This radio is about the same overall size of the old-school transistor radios, the kind that take a 9V battery, but proportioned a little differently. It is not quite as tall, but a little wider. Next to the tuning needle/face, there is a small speaker that puts out way more sound than I ever expected. While not exactly room-filling, its output is impressive given its tiny size, both in sound volume and quality. Sound quality is also surprisingly good, considering everything is coming out one tiny speaker.
The volume dial as well as the tuning dial work smoothly, and work as they should, probably better than expected for a $20 SW radio. I really don't know how Kaito can fit 9 SW bands, along with AM and FM bands in a radio this small, and at this price point, that works as well as it does. The only compact radio I know for sure that has noticeably better tuning abilities is the one from Sony, and it is AM/FM only, really isn't any smaller, and only costs $2 or so less!
A few other nice touches would include:
Very good battery life, it takes 2 AA batteries, and I think one pair of new batteries would last all weekend.
The wrist strap, which you can use or easily remove.
The little protective pouch (admittedly not much to brag about, but keeps the dust off of it, and keeps the face from getting scratched).
The little 'kickstand' in the back, that lets you lean the radio back so that the speaker fires up and around, rather than just one direction.
This stand also makes it easier to see the tuning window when it is on a table or counter.
A pair of earbuds which were included with the radio. Nothing fancy, but they work.

Okay, let me preface this review with the bottom line regarding these phones: they have unbelievable sound quality and PATHETIC build quality.

The first pair I received from Amazon, I looked so forward to opening them up and trying them out as I had spent the previous 6 months with an old pair of headphones that only produced sound from one bud. After opening the Sennheiser box, I was pleasantly surprised with how well it was packaged. However, once I got them out and plugged them in, ONLY ONE BUD WORKED!! At that point, I thought it was something wrong with my iPhone, not my headphones. However, I ruled that out after trying my friends' buds on my phone and both produced sound without issue. So I contacted Amazon and as anyone who has ever dealt with their customer service team can probably second, they were AMAZING. The guy offered to overnight me a new pair and create a free shipping label to send the defective pair back.

Woke up the next day, the box was waiting for me on my porch. I opened it up, plugged them in, and ahhhhhh....bliss. The sound quality on these buds is flat out amazing for $100. I am not rich enough to spend over $100 on a pair of buds, so all I can compare the sound to is other buds under the $100 max for me. Keeping this in mind, the Sennheiser's blew every other pair of buds I had ever purchased out of the water--really no competitors except for maybe my old Denon AH-C360's but even then the Sennheiser's were much better. So I enjoyed the hell out of these puppies for about a month when I noticed a hole in the rubber cable. It was a small hole, so I threw some electrical tape on it, and didn't think too much about it. However, then after another couple of weeks I get another hold right where the jack meets the cable; much bigger this time. Again I try to use electrical tape but it doesn't hold well because of the lip where the cable meets the jack. Now just a couple of days ago the left earbud went out.....AGAIN!!!!!

Overall, I gave the product two stars when it should only receive one for the simple fact that if you can't use a product what good is its performance. The only reason for this extra star is that these buds truly did blow my mind while I had them and while they worked. However, I have NEVER had a pair of buds last for less time than these--including the white Apple earbuds. So yeah, if you purchase this product, just make sure to do it through Amazon as they have been absolutely unbelievable in regards to their customer service. It's been three months since my original purchase, and they were still happy to issue me a full refund for the product.

I've had a GT40 for several years, since they first came out. I've solely used mine primarily as a DAC in conjunction with JRiver Media Center software, and recommend both heartily. The GT40 is one of the most satisfying and affordable components in my overall stereo system. Every other component cost $1,000 or more. Unlike other DACs I've tried, the output sounds nearly as good as original sources and the unit seems to be built like a tank. I've had no hiccups or failures of any kind. I assume that the other applications work as well, in fact I now remember using it successfully as a phono stage for vinyl conversion to WAV a couple of years ago.
UPDATE - 2/1/17 - I had my first issue with the GT40 tonight after several hours of listening via earphones with it (since my beloved 50 year-old 15" JBL speakers are being refurbished). I lost the right channel for no apparent reason, but if I pulled out the headphone plug part way, it would return. OK, it's just a displaced or dirty contact, I thought. I took the unit apart and to my dismay the receptacle is sealed, so I couldn't get to the contacts to "adjust" (translation - bend) and/or clean them as hoped. After putting it back together, I inserted and retracted the headphone plug aggressively several times, and voila -- I have both channels again. The next step is to treat the receptacle innards from the front with DeOxit. This turned out to be a minor glitch, so far, following years of flawless and frequent service. My previous 5-star rating stands. I'd give it 6 stars if I could!

Problem aside, the unit works as advertised, although I found the output signal a bit on the weak side, which, however, can be fixed by cranking up the volume.

SYMPTOM/PROBLEM
When I connected the Orei DA21x between my LG TV's optical digital output (set to PCM output as recommended by Orei), it seemed to work initially. However, the next day there was no signal out to the amp, even though I could see the laser beam in the digital optical cable from the TV. When I disconnected and reconnected the DC plug from the AC/DC converter (the only way to "reset" the device), it started working again. Thinking there was a flaw with the particular unit I received, I exchanged it for another unit with Amazon. Surprisingly, the new unit suffered from the exact same problem! (I wwitch off AC supply to all my electronics - including Orei - at night, and, upon power up next day, Orei doesn't work until a hard "reboot" by disconnecting and reconnecting the DC plug into the unit.) I figured the problem starts with me switching off the AC. As an experiment, I unplugged the AC plug of Orei's AC/DC converter, and sure enough, it stopped working when I reconnected the AC plug. I repeated this on both units. So, if the AC power to the unit is off, it seems to go into a weird state, and the only way to bring it out is to do a "reset" by disconnect/reconnecting the DC connector.

SOLUTION
To fix the problem, I have connected it to a non-switched AC power strip (i.e. one that I don't turn off at night). And now it seems to be working fine. However, since I travel, I will turn off AC to all the electronics in the house, including Orei. When I return, I suspect I'll have to "reset" Orei as described above. I've been testing various brands of high capacity 18650 lithium-ion batteries this past month with my new Foxnovo F2 charger. This charger gives values that are more consistent because it fully charges the battery then measures mAh during discharge down to a standardized cutoff voltage. I usually measure capacity at 0.5A discharge rate, and these Foxnovo batteries have about 3160mAh. An extrapolation to 0.2A discharge rate, which I believe is the standard for manufacturer ratings, gives a capacity of 3223mAh. On removing the Foxnovo label, I discovered that the batteries have Panasonic NCR18650BE cells inside, and these are rated at 3200mAh. Many of us have dealt with manufacturers that inflate battery ratings, and it is refreshing to find that Foxnovo is understating the actual capacity. Furthermore, these are a bargain since they provide 95% of the capacity of a 3400mAh battery at a substantial savings.

We recently dropped our cable service (because of constantly escalating and un-affordable prices), and were looking to go the route of streaming programming (Netflix, Hulu, etc.) supplemented with local HDTV broadcasts via an HDTV antenna hooked up to our 2 TVs.

Figuring then that we would need a more powerful rooftop-mounted antenna strong enough to get all of the main local HD channels we wanted, research into outdoor antennas brought us to the Antennas Direct Clearstream 2-V Long Range antenna, which after having been mounted in what was an optimum position (facing the mountain from which most of the signals are beamed) on our roof, after a channel scan, every single major network channel (plus about 60 more that we will never watch) came in crystal clear, and even better than they did via cable.
Love the antenna - is compact, easy to put together, and looks easy to mount. I say that because I hired a professional to install our antenna because I wanted them to use the pre-existing coax cable that was already wired (from a previous cable provider) in and under house, which required some professional know-how to connect to the new antenna.

My experience matches that given in the review by Moises R. Rosario. Belkin will not honor its connected equipment warranty. And I completely agree with his opinion on the quality of Belkin customer service. It's about the worst I've ever seen.

One difference in my experience compared to that of Moises is with the support number that was disconnected. When I called the number provided, multiple times over several days, I was never able to actually speak to anyone and was bounced out of the system after ~5 minutes on hold with a message saying they were closed and that I should call back during business hours. All of my calls were within their business hours.

Like Moises, I when through the online claim process, mailed my unit into Belkin and paid for shipping. After that I was not contacted by Belkin in any way until my unit was delivered back to me by UPS.

With the returned unit was a letter from the claims department that's nearly a letter-to-letter match to the letter that Moises has posted a picture of. My connected equipment warranty claim, like his, was denied because the Belkin unit had not been damaged by the voltage surge.

I'm now left with a surge suppressor that failed to protect my downstream equipment and out the cost of shipping the unit to Belkin. I'm definitely NOT putting the surge suppressor back in any of my systems.

The system using the Belkin surge suppressor was a SONOS wireless music player (ZP90) connected to a Audioengine N22 amplifier and a pair of in-ceiling speakers. The only electrical connection into the system was the power line via the Belkin unit. The damage was to the SONOS player, and it happened during a lightning strike to a large oak tree ~20 feet from my house. Unfortunately, the Verizon FIOS pole feeding my house is ~10 feet from the base of that tree and all of the FIOS boxes in my house and everything connected to them via an HDMI interface was blown out. The SONOS connected to the Belkin surge suppressor was the only piece of equipment in my house that failed that was not connected to a FIOS box. All of the other units (AV receivers, TVs) have been repaired by replacing their HDMI boards. Not required repair of their power supplies. Apparently my non-Belkin surge suppressors did their jobs.

Since receiving the suppressor back from Belkin, I've contacted Belkin to discuss the rejection of my claim only to be bounced from customer service to the warranty dept, to the claims department, to customer support (is that actually different than customer service), and was eventually given the number for tech support. It was the same number that I'd previously tried to call multiple times without being able to speak to anyone and being told to call back during business hour.

But, this time when I called tech support I actually got through and spoke to someone. I was completely surprised. The person I talked to confirmed that they did not open the unit for inspection, only examining the exterior and doing resistance checks through the inputs and outputs. This contradicts what's stated I the last paragraph of the claim rejection letter, where it says there was no arcing/burning seen inside the unit. The interior of the unit was not inspected.

I raised another point with Belkin tech support and later with Belkin customer support, which is about the voltage clamping spec of 300V. A surge under the voltage clamping spec will, by design, go straight through the surge suppressor. It's the voltage level at which the suppressor is supposed to start doing its job. Neither the tech support or customer service person that I spoke to know what that spec meant, nor could tell me whether the connected equipment warranty was valid if of up to 300V went straight through the suppressor and damaged connected equipment.

The connected equipment warranty is apparently valid only if the suppressor itself looks or perhapssmells like it is burned up.

Lesson learned - no more Belkin products - ever.

So to start off, being a previous QC15 owner, the QC25s are not overly better than the QC15s. I would say that the only reason to upgrade to the 25s might be the new design. However, for those who have never owned a QC15, you will love the QC25s.

In terms of sound quality, the QC25s sound very similar to the older QC15s but the bass and clarity is improved on the new QC25s. Everything sounds much tighter with better fidelity.

The effectiveness of noise cancellation seems the same to be quite honest.

Comfort is still phenomenal on the 25s. The QC15s were incredibly light and comfortable, and the tradition remains. The QC15 was one of the few headphones I could wear for long, long periods of time, and I'm glad that the QC25s continue to be insanely comfortable.

In terms of design, I much prefer the look of the new 25s. The 25s look much more modern and youthful, whereas the QC15s looked more executive and business-like.

Another great feature with the 25s is that they will still work without batteries. The noise cancellation won't work of course, but you won't be stuck with no audio. In addition to losing noise cancellation, you do also lose some fidelity in audio quality, it still sounds pretty decent.

Like the QC15s, the battery life on the 25s are still exceptional. I haven't done any extensive and scientific tests, but it can last quite a while.

Overall, the QC25s are great headphones. People criticize Bose for being overpriced, but they really aren't. The QC25s don't sound as good as some other $300 headphones, but they excel in many areas(sound, comfort, design, usability) unlike competing products that excel in only a few(sound only), making the QC25s a balanced and well rounded product, and that's what makes it worth $300.

First, I did receive this product free for the purpose of testing and review. While I realize that a review of a free product is something fundamentally different from a review of a product for which one has paid, I am hopeful that my impressions and observations will prove helpful to you in your decision making as I do take the review process seriously. If you have questions, feel free to post them in the comments section, and I'll do my best to answer based on my own use of the product.

What you're getting with this order:
(1) Pair Runner X9 bluetooth headphones
(1) Micro USB cord for charging
(3) Pair silicone ear pieces, S, M, L
(1) User's guide

What are these, and what are they supposed to do?:
These bluetooth headphones allow you to access your audio wirelessly via a bluetooth enabled device such as your phone. In addition, when connected to your phone via bluetooth, they allow you access to some of your phone's basic functions such as accepting, ending and rejecting a call. These feature an inline style control meaning the buttons are located on the cord and not on the ear. As their name implies, these are advertised as exercise headphones, usually meaning they are sweat resistant and have some kind of design to help keep them in the ear. These are currently being offered at the transition point between the budget price range and the mid-range price point (FYI, my personal scale of price points is budget= <$30; mid-range = >$30-$80; premium= .$80-$150; premium plus= $150-$200; deluxe=>$200).

Do they work?:
Yes. I'll break this down a bit more specifically for you:

Charging: These charge with a provided micro-USB cord.

Pairing: Pressing the power button puts the headphones into pairing mode and the headphones are discoverable on your device as "X9", once selected, they pair within 8-10 on the very first attempt and then automatically, within a couple of seconds on subsequent uses.

Appearance: If you're being honest, appearance matters and these have an attractive design. Done in a two tone color scheme, the cord is red and the housing black with metallic red accent. The cord is flat which helps with tangling and I think gives it a more modern look. The in line controls are located in a rectangular box on the cord. There is a slide on the cord which allows for adjustment of the cord for exercise. Appearance justifies a mid-range price point.

Build: This is a quality build. Materials and craftsmanship justify a mid-range price point. I've owned these for nearly 2 months and have had no issues with durability.

Sound: The most important quality is obviously sound and these do not disappoint. I was actually quite surprised by the quality in relation to the price here. These have a sound that would justify a price well into the mid-rage price point. A rich bass is reproduced that holds its quality even at max volumes. Mids are clear and crisp and the highs are excellent. No distortion at high volumes was noted. A quick test on audiocheck.net confirms some basics:

frequency response: 20Hz-20kHz (I have to recruit younger ears to hear the kHz)
Quality: No rattle or buzz when drivers were stressed through a variety of loud frequencies
Wiring: Left and right channels are correctly wired and polarity is preserved.

Phone functions: I so rarely talk on the phone that these functions are meaningless to me. The user's guide is very clear on how to access them, and I can confirm that they work. If you're a big phone user, these give more access than most in the price range (you can even toggle between two calls).

Running/sports: These definitely have a sweat resistant build. It is very nice running without a cord to the phone and if you've never used bluetooth to exercise before, you're going to be pleased. Because these have no ear hooks however,you will find yourself frequently pushing them back into your ear. This problem is eased by selecting the best fit from the 3 pairs of ear pieces provided, but regardless, you're likely to be adjusting these throughout your run.

I've noticed with the in-line style of controls on headphones that it causes extra pull on the right ear and these are no exception. You can alleviate this somewhat by adjusting the slider, but it doesn't completely solve the problem. One other thing about these (and really all) bluetooth headphones re: exercise is that while they appear to be designed to have the cord running behind your neck, they will catch and grab on your neck and pop out. I much prefer to have the cord hanging free at the front of my neck where I notice much less grabbing and catching.

Anything else of note?:
-As of the posting of this review, these are eligible for free shipping to members of Amazon Prime; that's always a check in the plus column for me.
-The back of the housing is magnetized which allows easy storage when not in the ears. They can be worn necklace style and stored with less risk of tangling.
-The ear pieces are angled into the ear which does at least help to hold the earpiece in during exercise.

Any negatives?:
-Fit will depend on your own ear canal and how one of the 3 provided sizes works for you, but you are very likely to require multiple adjustments during exercise. This is true of any headphone without ear hooks.
-In line controls are nice but will pull at the right ear during exercise.

Bottom line: When it comes to sound, these headphones impressed me, reproducing quality tones from bass to mid to highs. The appearance, build and sound all justify a price well into the mid-range and so the fact that these are being offered right at the intersection of budget and mid-range makes them well worth taking a look at. While they are sweat resistant and have in-line controls, it is difficult to keep earbuds in during exercise without hooks and so you should be prepared to adjust during runs, though how often will depend on individual anatomy. I really like these, from the design to the function and though I've only had them a couple of months, they have so far proven durable. When my Winegard amplified antenna died one day after only a few months of operation, the first thing I checked was to see if it was getting any power. The first thing I noticed was the pilot light on the injector itself was out and the wallwart PSU (Power Supply Unit) was extremely hot. I removed the PSU, let it cool down, then plugged it in and checked the output voltage. The PSU is rated at 18VDC yet I was getting 25VDC from it! Adding insult to injury, I noticed that the injector is rated for only 14VDC! What was Winegard thinking? Since others here had reported good luck from a 15VDC PSU, I \\"borrowed\\" one from an unused powered splitter I had knocking about and tried it. I was expecting that the amplifier and/or injector would be fried after getting hit with 25VDC but I was pleasantly surprised to find out everything was not only working again, I picked up two more channels.

I did order another 15VDC PSU to replace the one I \\"borrowed\\" but I also ordered another one of the PS-1403 just to get a spare injector in case the one I have now ever dies (I like this one better than the one others here recommended because it has a power pilot light and I wouldn't have redo my cabling if I ever needed to replace the one currently in use) but I tossed both the old and the new 18VDC PSUs rather take a chance with even the new one.

Over the years I've used several different banana plugs on upscale to high-end audio equipment. These are the best I've used. I just received my subwoofer so this is one of those reviews of a product that probably should "soak in" for a few months, but there's something that needs to be made clear immediately: this sub is NOT an amplifier. No matter how it's hooked up, an amplifier has to be in the circuit somewhere.

I was counting on connecting the line out from my phone (or whatever) to the "line in" connectors on the sub (and the sub to my bookshelf speakers), thereby shifting all amplification to the sub, both for the sub itself and for the bookshelf speakers. It doesn't work that way. The sub's "line in" RCA connectors are to be used only by home-theater amplifiers that have a subwoofer out connection. Lacking an amplifier with such a connection, a traditional amplifier has to be hooked up through the "speaker in" and "speaker out" terminals.

Either way, you need an amplifier.

With that said, I happen to have an amplifier that I'm fond of, so I used the "speaker in" "speaker out" terminals and the sub works just fine.

Best of all: Using the crossover frequency knob, I'm truly able to adjust the sound to eliminate the exaggerated boominess that's typically associated with powered subwoofers, yet still retain a confident bass presence. A simple subwoofer volume control (which this sub also has) just isn't enough for my liking.

Other pros: Nice cherry finish, more-than-ample power, and clean response all the way down to a sub-audible rumble -- the kind you feel rather than hear.

I've used subwoofers in the past, the kind that are a part of powered speakers for computers. This is heads-and-shoulders above that.

Full disclosure: I'm a happy purchaser of three pairs of R+ for various members of my family. Bluedio approached me with an offer of a free pair of ttheir new UFO series for a review. I am so happy they did, even though they have now spoiled me.

You see, I was an $80 headphone guy. The R+ was everything I could have wanted at the price range. They sound terrific, they are comfortable, they have wire or bluetooth, they connected to all my devices with no problems. How could they be better ?

Simple: They could be the UFO. It's hard to quantify, but the UFO's are even more comfortable. I work in an open office environment, and wear headphones several hours a day to block out sound. The R+ was acceptable. The UFO's are like they aren't even there. I've used headphones since the 70's, and I've never had a pair that I could forget I was wearing.

As a nice added touch, instead of just responding with beeps they speak out what mode they are in as you push buttons.There are other small improvements, like the hard case with a pouch for the cables.

The sound: I thought the R+ were fantastic, and there is nothing wrong with them. Until you hear the UFO's. They are clearer, I wish I could give some technical reason involving frequency response and signal/noise ratio -- but all I could do was switch back and forth over and over. They just sound crisper. I've played classic rock, 80s, metal, and classical through these. I used Bluetooth and cabled. In every test the sound was superior.

If your budget is around $100, you will be very happy with the R+. If you have $200 to spend on headphones, I can highly recommend the Bluedio UFO series.

While these headphones are marketed as intended for Samsung and Android, they work perfectly well with the current LG phones.

My daughter pulled up bass-rich electronica music and enjoyed an immersive listening experience, described as her hearing deep sounds she had not heard from the earbuds provided with her phone. While the headphones are not sound-cancelling--she is able to hear conversations conducted around her--she felt as if she were more centered in the music rather than having music in the background, as her old earbuds provide sound. She also describes a distinctive clarity in the music she has not heard from her phone before. She finds the fit comfortable to the point of forgetting that she is wearing headphones.

She is not likely to be using these headphones for her athletic activities, but she will definitely rely on them for a cozy listening experience, so I do not expect the wear-and-tear on the lines as described by other reviewers. Should such problems occur, I will update this review.

For now, however, there's one completely satisfied Bose user in our house. Recommended by her.

The mounting hardware that comes with the antenna works well, mounts the antenna firmly to the mast, and is easy to install.
