PROS:
Major sound upgrade for most TVs
Slim form factor/space saving
Can sit under a TV weighing 75 lbs or less
Simple set up
Bass volume control
Dialogue mode
Bluetooth connectivity
Multiple connection types (TOS link, RCA, coaxial)
Can sit under TV
Excellent bundled universal remote that is easy to set up

CONS:
Okay low volume sounds, but due to the form factor is not as effective as a larger, separate subwoofer
Minimal control of sound
No volume bar/graphic volume control
No equalizer function
Would be helpful to have a TV volume mute button on remote
Missing physical volume controls/on-off button on the device (all handled through remote)
More expensive than other options
No Wifi integration with other Bose sound systems or surround sound capabilities

OVERVIEW
The Bose Solo 15 Series II TV Sound System is an excellent way to upgrade the sound of your TV. This is an easy to use, all-in-one unit that will definitely add a lot of punch to your TV's home audio. The folks at Bose used their talents at miniaturization to create a unit that while still compact can really deliver great sound. That said, in order to keep the price point lower (for a Bose unit) some compromises were made here. This is not a unit for those who want the highest, audiophile sound quality, those who want true surround sound, or those who want maximum bass output. Moreover, it is designed as a stand alone unit: this is not a component system that you can buy to get in on the ground floor and expand later on. That said, I felt that it delivered big time for a slim unit that tucks easily under your TV.

WHATS IN THE BOX
The Solo 15 ships in a box that is not much bigger than the unit itself. Inside you will find the Solo 15 itself, a power cord, an optical digital audio cable (TOS link), an RCA analog stereo cable, a Solo 15 universal remote, and instruction manuals for the Solo 15 and a listing of codes to set up the remote. Kudos to Bose for minimalist and mostly environmental packing. The unit was wrapped in a thin foam sheet for protection but the rest of the package was cardboard and the device was set in two packing blocks that were made of pressed cardboard and totally biodegradable. No foam beans, no styrofoam blocks, or other miscellaneous stuff. It was simple to extract from the box and there wasn't a lot of packing material to dispose of. I wish every manufacturer would pack so efficiently.

The unit is basic black and lighter weight than you would expect. Construction is pristine and it has a nice, stylish curve to the front and that typical, minimalist Bose style. There are no physical buttons on the unit (including and on-off button) and all connectivity is on the back. Input ports include TOS link, dual RCA analog, and coaxial cable. There is a bass adjustment toggle to the left of the inputs. The power cord connects on the far right and to the left of it is a USB port. The USB port is only for upgrading the firmware and has no connectivity function whatsoever.

SET UP
Set up was fast and simple. I plugged in the Solo 15 power cord, connected the TOS link cable from my HDTV to the Solo 15, plopped the TV on top of the Solo 15 and everything was 100% functional. (If you have an older HDTV and don't have digital optical audio output, you can connect via the RCA or coaxial cable.) Of note, Bose states that the weight limit for setting the TV on top of the Solo 15 is 75 lbs. Additionally, they recommend that the base of the TV be no wider than 24 inches and no deeper than 12.25 inches. If your TV exceeds these specifications, the Solo 15 can be mounted on a shelf above or below your TV. After turning down your television's native sound to zero, you can set aside your HDTV's remote.

The Solo 15 universal remote was the easiest remote that I have ever set up. Every manufacturer has a code. My Verizon cable box, my Panasonic TV, my Samsung DVD player, and my Roku were all set up on the remote the very first time after typing in the code. Usually, I have had to fidget around with multiple codes and often had to search for device codes on most remotes. For this remote it was one code per device and it was set up in under 5 minutes. (Clearly, the more modern and mainstream your equipment is, the easier it is to set a remote up, but this was far simpler than others.)

THE SOUND
What you get with this unit is Bose's signature sound. The speakers have an incredible dynamic range for a unit of this size and the stereo separation is amazing for such a small unit. Treble and midrange sounds exit through the front of the unit and the two subwoofers are located in the back. You can control the overall volume and separately control the bass volume using the remote. In fact, you can tweak the default bass setting by turning the adjustment nob on the back of the unit to either increase or decrease the bass when you fire up the Solo 15. This is important if you are using a third party remote that may not allow adjustment of the bass as do the Bose remotes. You can also put the Bose into speaking mode, which brings makes dialogue extra crisp for news, interviews, and talk shows.

The sound is a major upgrade from my television sound, but there are some caveats here. First and foremost there are lovers and haters of the Bose sound. I still am blown away by the incredibly full sound that Bose engineers can get out of such a small system, but there are still limits to engineering wizardry. Given the size of the system, there is only so much bass and midrange sound that you can get from the Solo 15. I cannot stress how miraculous it seems that you can get the kind of sound you do from a system of this size, but it still can't compare to systems that have midrange speaker systems and a dedicated subwoofer. The main thing you will probably miss is that earth shattering bass, something that I think you can only get from a separate subwoofer.

Additionally, Bose is pretty enamored of their signature sound: the sound is amazing but there is no equalizer function so that you can personalize it. You really can't control anything other than the bass boost. Sound separation is amazing for such a small unit, but the stereo is still not as robust as a system where you can really separate the right and left channel speakers. Finally, this is not surround sound. There are not even options to connect other speakers to this system: this is a stand alone system with no options for wireless or even wired expansion.

Realize, though, that this is entry level Bose home theater. At the time of writing this review, the next system up, the Bose Cinemate 15, cost $200 more than this system. If you want a more surround sound type option, you'd have to spend another $100 and if you want a true audiophile experience from Bose, you'd need an extra $1,000 to get your foot in the door. So it's not as though the folks at Bose don't understand true audiophile sound. In order to give you great sound in a small form factor they needed to make some compromises.

MISCELLANEOUS FUNCTIONS
The Solo 15 has Bluetooth connectivity, so you can set up any Bluetooth capable device to stream through the unit. This works easily and smoothly.

I really enjoy using the Solo 15 universal remote. As above, I set it up in under five minutes and it works like a charm. The Bose remote works better than my Verizon remote to control my cable box and is better set up. Additionally, the remote works with my Roku and other streaming boxes.

Sadly, there is only backlighting on the source selection buttons. The only way to improve upon it, in my book, would be to add back lighting to all the keys. Moreover, there is not mute button or volume control foryour TV itself. In order to use the Bose speaker system you have to turn off your TV's audio, otherwise you get a strange echo effect. Simply having a mute button for the TV would make this a better option.

Still, I actually prefer using this remote to all the others in my house. (Note: the remote doesn't have motion control, so if you play games on your Roku that require this, you will need to use your native remote. Moreover, unlike my Roku remote, it is missing a headphone jack for private listening. These, of course, are non-standard, universal remote functions. But if you have a Roku, you will need to keep our Roku remote accessible to maintain these functionalities.)

SOME CAVEATS
Which leads us to the standard criticism of Bose, which is the price. Bose does charge a premium for their products. There are a number of similar systems that probably give you equivalent sound. This is where you need to actually go to a showroom and listen to the various choices before you buy. Two competitors that keep coming up are the ZVOX 555 Low Profile Single Cabinet Surround Sound and the Yamaha YAS-203 Sound Bar. The ZVOX system is far less stylish than the Bose, but will cut about $100 from the price. The Yamaha system is close in price to the Solo 15, but comes with a separate, wireless subwoofer. There are many others as well. What you need to do, however, is let your ears be the judge. When it is sound you are looking for you have to see with your ears. Realize, though, that none of these lower cost systems will get you the same sound and flexibility as $1500+ audiophile systems. High end, audiophile systems will give you better sound but aren't the real comparators for this system.

There are a couple of quirks with this system. The one that really puzzled me is that there is no volume bar or graphic volume control. The green LED in the center of the Bose blinks when you increase or decrease the volume. Oddly, when you adjust the bass, there are four blue-white LEDs that show you progression as to how high or low you have boosted the bass. I am unsure as to why they did not do the same for the overall volume control. My guess is that they were more concerned about keeping the system looking sparse, technological, and stylish. Moreover, that green LED is pretty bright and remains on while you are watching TV. It's not majorly distracting, but I would have preferred something that was off center or at least decreased in brightness once you set the volume.

Additionally, there are no physical controls (other than the bass adjustment on the back of the unit). You need the remote to operate the Solo 15 and there is no smartphone app that can be used to control it. In the same vein, it would have been nice if there was some way to connect to other systems in the house via WiFi.

The Solo 15 will give you a major upgrade to your TV's sound in a single compact and stylish unit. This is definitely a winner in my book. As with any audio system, sound quality is quite subjective. The only way for you to judge the sound quality is to try before you buy. So before you make a major purchase like this, I'd go to a showroom and take a listen to a number of systems. The major downsides from a purchasing perspective are that Bose does charge a premium for their products, the bass is less prominent than you will get from a system with a dedicated subwoofer, and the system is not expandable. These things aside, Bose again has packed major sound in a very small unit. I have enjoyed the boost in the audio quality of my TV viewing and in my small living room this passes for a theater-like experience. Recommended.. I'm going to open this by saying that while I have a background in music, I'm not an audiophile. I'm normally not terribly choosy, speaker-wise. I can tell the difference between something amazing and a pair of cheap earbuds, but I enjoy music enough that I'm happy to experience it either way.

The trouble comes when you start talking about things like television, where complex sound mixing, made for high end movie theater speakers, gets horribly garbled and distorted with cheap TV speakers, like the ones that my ancient flatscreen has. In most modern TV shows and movies, the explosions and gunshots and intense background music are too loud, while the dialogue is so inaudible that I'd started to wonder if I was losing my hearing. I was given a sample of this product to give an honest review. I've spent a good several hours using the audio recorder in different situations, and it's an overall great item, with just a few small flaws that hold it back from being a full five stars.

First of all, you'll notice when you get this that the packaging is top-notch. It comes in a very strong box and is well protected. Additionally, the recorder is charged right off the bat, so I was able to start using it right away. I was actually a bit surprised by the size of the recorder. I knew it was compact, but I had no idea *how* compact it was. It's extremely light and thin, making it easy to carry around with you, so that you can use it at a moment's notice. The recording ability it excellent. I have used this to dictate to myself in a car and while walking outside, to record meeting presentations, and as a dream journal, and every time, I managed to go back later and hear everything without issue. And because you can save in high-quality WAV formats (which works out fine thanks to an installed 8gb), it's easy to upload it to your computer and be compatible with audio editing software. On the whole, I would say that the quality you get, both from the physical device itself and your recordings is equivalent to recorders that cost $60-75.

Now, there's a couple issues I have with the recorder. First, while the recorder picks up sound very well, I don't feel the Dual-core Noise Reduction Mode works as well as it should, because I often seem to get quite a bit of background noise. (For example, while using it to record a presentation in a meeting, I could hear the speaker perfectly, but could also hear both the fans in the room and the clacking of keyboards. Still, I should emphasize that these did not drown out the actual voice.) Additionally, any pressing of buttons on the recorder will come through loud and clear, though that seems to be common to all recorders. Second, if you don't read the manual, you are done for, and even if you do read it, there are some non-intuitive elements that can be hard to remember (an example being that you have to hold Stop to actually stop a playback, else you just set up loop points). It's impressive what can be done with just a few buttons, but a couple more would probably have served the recorder better.

As far as accessories go, you get a micro USB cable, which allows for very easy charging and uploading of sound files. (You can also transfer songs from your computer onto the recorder, which works perfectly, but seems a bit superfluous.) You also get a pair of headphones, which aren't really any better than the standard kind you'll get from a MP3 player, but that you get them at all is a nice bonus.

Overall, it's probably the best voice recorder I've seen in a long time. I used to own a number of recorders in college, but over time, started using my phone to do that kind of work. When it comes to Bose, people either love or hate their products. Bose markets itself as a premium manufacturer of audio equipment that are sold at a premium price. Whether Bose products are truly "premium" is definitely up for debate. Most audiophiles tend to find the sound on Bose products to be artificial, misbalanced with too much focus on the bass and midrange, and have a poor acoustic response. Personally, I've never been the biggest fan of Bose products (speakers, home theater, and car audio), because you can get much better products for much less money. With that aside, when it comes to noise canceling technology, Bose is second to none. The Bose QC20 earphones take the technology from Bose's over the ear headphones and shrinks it down to work as in-ear earphones, and the results are amazing. Just flip the switch to power them on and ambient noise is instantly brought down to a reasonable level.  So do they work as well as the over the ear noise cancelling headphones? The answer is: almost. Over the ear noise cancelling headphones create a seal over the entire ear that helps to isolate ambient noise, and when powered on, active noise cancelation helps to cancel out further ambient noise. Earphones work much differently, as they rely on active electronic noise cancelation to reduce ambient noise and do not benefit from noise isolation because they do not seal and cup the ear. Since the QC20s rely more on electronic noise cancelation, you can hear an audible hissing sound when they are powered on (much like tape hiss) which simulates silence. After about 5 minutes or so, your ears will adjust, and you will likely not notice the hissing, but it is something to be aware of. Also, keep in mind that there is a little box at the end of the headphones near the audio jack. It's about the size of a pack of gum and weighs practically nothing, but it is a necessary evil due to the fact that it contains the lithium ion battery and noise cancelation circuitry. Itis somewhat annoying to have a dangling box from every device that you plug the QC20s into. I do wish that Bose had incorporated Bluetooth into that dangling box to give users the option to dangle or not dangle the box from their devices, but sadly, it was not incorporated this time around.  In reading most of the reviews on Amazon, there are a couple of major concerns that needs to be touched on that I have not read in any of the other reviews:  First of all, Bose recently released a redesign of the QC20 earphones, with an improved case, new design patterns (black with a blue stripe, or white with a blue stripe), and some very minor improvements. This would mean that the old QC20s (black with a grey stripe) will be out of warranty in less than a year. If you purchase Bose products from Amazon or any other retailer that is not a Bose store, BE AWARE that the one year manufacturer's warranty starts from the DATE OF MANUFACTURE and NOT from the date of purchase. This means, if you purchase the QC20s from Amazon, and they have been sitting on Amazon's shelves for 8 months, the manufacturer's warranty is only good for another 4 months after you receive them. Beyond this, the customer then has to pay $150 out of pocket for any replacements or repairs. Secondly, Bose decided to go with a non-replaceable lithium ion battery in the QC20 earphones. The problem with lithium ion batteries is that they will eventually degrade and will hold less of a charge the more that you use them. After several years of continuous use (or about 500 charges) they will eventually not be able to hold much of a charge and will only function when they are plugged in to a power source. It is important to understand that Bose QC20s will eventually need to be replaced when the battery gives out. My first pair of QC20s lasted about 7 months before they went from holding a 16 hour charge to a 6 hour charge. They were out of warranty in the 7 months that I had them (purchased in January, but the warranty expired in March, and Bose wouldn't replace or exchange them because I purchased them from a third party retailer and not from the Bose store; luckily, after much explanation, the manager at the Bose store understood my predicament and was kind enough to eventually replace them [your mileage may vary]).  Overall, the sound quality on the QC20 is above average when they are powered on. In terms of sound, the QC20s have that "Bose" tendency of sounding a bit overly enhanced, with the primary emphasis being placed on the midrange. Some may like this; some may not, but it's a very typical Bose sound. The noise cancelation is astounding when audio is playing through the earphones, as you can focus on what you are listening to, rather than what is going on around you. As someone who has a noise sensitivity, the Bose QC20s are an absolute godsend. They are much less cumbersome than over the ear headphones and do an amazing job at bringing ambient noise down to a reasonable level. So, is it worth the price? I definitely think so. The QC20s may be expensive, but they are currently the best noise canceling earphones on the market today. Aside from a few quirks, I highly recommend them, as I never leave home without them.

I purchased this radio to use for casual shortwave and AM listening. The Satellit is a compact radio (larger than the current Eton Traveler but smaller than my Grundig YB400PE) that offers standard FM, AM, LW and Shortwave bands along with an air (aviation) band. The Satellit also offers SSB. I chose the Satellit over the Tecsun PL880 primarily due to the fact that the Tecsun is dependent on an internal rechargeable battery which requires a USB connection for charging. In contrast, the Eton will run off readily available AA batteries and comes with an AC adapter. Additionally, the Eton will recharge NiMH AA batteries while plugged in ... this makes the radio more flexible, in my opinion.

Others have complained about the complexity of this radio and, like most modern multi-band radios, it is more involved than a simple AM/FM unit. However, I found the Eton's operation pretty straight forward especially if one consults the manual. My only two complaints about the features of the radio are that it lacks the capability of displaying a second time zone and the external antenna implementation is non-standard (more on that below).

Comparing this radio to the Grundig YB400PE, Eton Field, Eton Traveler III and the Grundig Traveler II, the Satellit is a solid portable performer. Sensitivity and selectivity are good and the sound is full and listenable if not quite as loud as either the YB400PE or the Field. The Satellit does a better job of rejecting strong AM bleed-over into the SW bands than the Traveler III. Additionally, the ability to select several bandwidth filters helps make weak signals more listenable.

To date I've only had the opportunity to use this radio with the built-in whip antenna and a clip-on 20' longer due to Eton's inexplicable decision to use a 3.5mm stereo plug for an external antenna vs. the standard 3.5mm mono. Radiojayallen.com details this in his review of the Satellit and includes a permanent remedy if you're not interested in warranty coverage. A less invasive solution requires a 3.5mm mono to stereo adapter (which is on order) if one wants to use a commonly available SW "spool antenna." The manual also indicates this jack can be used to feed the radio from a 50 or 75 ohm external antenna ... something I'll have to try once I get a PL259 to 3.5mm adapter.

I've been using this charger for about 9 months now, I guess, and feel like I originally got a bad one. I have no problems charging two smart phones and a tablet at once with this charger. It's not as fast as a high amperage single-port charger, but it still charges all three reasonably fast. I put my work phone on it at night, and when I leave to work during the day, it will often have two tablets charging on it at once. After the replacement came, I haven't had a problem with it charging anything in a reasonable amount of time. It charged my Galaxy S4 in a couple hours from a dead battery, which is all you can expect. I like the 5-port A LOT! It's handy to have so many available, and all in one spot rather than having a power strip and all those chargers plugged in!

I would recommend this charger, both for the price and the size of the unit. I purchased a handful of 10" USB cables from a local company to keep it nice and clean, and it has a 3' cord on it to give me some flexibility on where I put it. You could probably purchase a longer power cord for it, as it uses a standard connector to attach to the device (looks like the old stereo plug in cords... not sure how to better explain it!).

A comment on my old review said it was misleading because it is not UL listed, which after a little research I determined that it is not required to be UL Listed, but this one has had the testing done by another lab called SGS. I'm comfortable with that!

I've updated my review to five stars, because it does what it is supposed, pretty well. If I try to draw more than 8amps from it and it doesn't charge as fast, that's my own fault!

I love these types of chargers. I have used the [[ASIN:B00OT6YUIY USB Charger RAVPower 36W 4-Port USB Desktop Wall Charger Charging Station with iSmart Technology for iPhone iPad Samsung Galaxy Google Nexus Motorola HTC LG Nokia Lumia and More (Black)]] for a year or so now, and the only complaint is that I cannot charge more than two smart phones at a time. Granted, this isn't a common thing, but I have a personal phone, work phone, and my tablet that all need to charge at 2.0A or more each. Since it only had two 2.1A ports, I decided to look into a more capable charger, one that would ideally charge up to 4 devices and my iPod at the same time (the ipod can charge quickly on a 0.5A charger, so basically just need a port). The INAROCK charger seemed to fit the bill.

It has all the features I want: 5 ports, up to 2.4A per port, nice size and a decent look. I immediately put it on my bookcase when it arrived and connected my work phone on it. It seemed to work fine, so I didn't think much of it until a couple days later when I also connected my personal phone, and after a couple hours it had only charged from 17% to 35%. On my 1.8A charger the phone will charge in about an hour. "Maybe it has a bad port," I think to myself, so I switch to another one, and although I don't know how fast it was charging, the phone was charged when I went to bed about 4 hours later. The same thing happened with my tablet, except this time I connected it at 6am on my way to work, and it still wasn't charged when I got home 12 hours later. It had only charged approximately 30%, give or take. this time I just took it off and connected it to my Samsung charger for the tablet so that I didn't have to worry about it when I needed it later. The final straw, though, was today when I got home and my iPod - just your standard, no-frills basic iPod nano - which was on the charger for 24 hours, still wasn't charged all the way. I had no other devices connected, and it was on a port that had worked before.

I really like the idea of this charger, and I think it would work well for me, but it really hasn't been performing since I got it. As a matter of fact, I like it enough that I just requested an exchange to try another one, and I hope I get a good one. Every single other review on this item is positive, but I can't be the only one who had a problem. For right now, because it partially worked, I am giving 2 stars instead of only one. When I get the new one, I will test it out and see how it works. I don't have one of those fancy amperage/wattage usb testers, so I won't be able to go into that detail like others have, but I can tell you if it is charging at a reasonable rate, or not. If the new one works, I'll re-review it and raise my rating. I won't let a lemon ruin my opinion, since there appears to be few lemons being sent out for this item. This really does not do what users probably want it to do. If you intend to use this to strip analog audio from HDMI for use as an analog secondary zone signal (that's what I believe 99% of the applications for this are), you will be disappointed. It does not downmix to two-channel, so if you have a multi-channel source it will only grab the Left and Right channels. Since in a multichannel mix all the dialog is in the center channel, your secondary zone playback will be without the center channel signal - making it useless for this application unless you first change the digital source component to stereo (PCM) first. Which means you won't have multi-channel in your main system if you want usable stereo in your secondary zones for that source. Unfortunate.

There is an inherent design flaw that makes this unit subject to failure.  The folded tabs of the frame that hold the strap tightening mechanism pull on and stress the fold on the angle iron where it has been reduced to only about one inch in length.  The pulling forces on this short joint are designed to pull it open further and are at odds with the goal of a good tight fit around the chimney.  With my bare hands and only the short lever of the tightening mechanism I broke off one side and sent the whole unit careening down 20 feet to bounce off my air conditioner unit below.  Most disappointing!  Down but not defeated, I assessed the situation and established a field design change that eliminated the design flaw.  The flaw is on both sides of the unit so I purposefully removed the other holding tab on the opposite side of the one I broke by using a pair of Channellock pliers and a quick up and down tug again validating the weakness of the design.  Using my drill press I removed the swaged bolt from both of the tightening mechanisms and replaced it with a longer carriage bolt (about 3") that sticks out like a bicycle wheel axle on both sides.  An extra nut spun all the way up to the bolt head helps the top stick out adequately.  Then using a two pound hammer and an anvil I bent the tabs on either side of the gaps about half way down leaving enough room to slide the new bolt under both sides.  This new holding method allows the bolt to put pulling force on both sides of the frame as it is tightened, a much stronger proposition than the original design.  The bent tabs simply help to keep the tightening mechanism in place.  My field design change salvaged the day but this design as is earns only one star until corrected.  Buy with confidence if you feel you have the skills and tools to manage the field design change on your own.  Otherwise, please ensure that there are no people or animals below the installation site while tightening it down.  When the joint givessuddenly it is a dangerous situation.

Impressions
First and foremost, this is a very tiny speaker! (photos included) I was quite surprised when the box arrived. It is hard to tell the size from the marketing photos directly from Anker, so I expected it to be similar in size to the Jawbone Jambox (which I previously owned), but it is maybe about half that size. I love the inclusion of a carrying lanyard and a travel pouch. The travel bag has definitely come in handy already since I can just through the speaker in a bag without worrying about it getting messed up or scratched. It is 5v/0.5a so pretty much any MicroUSB charger you have will work… phone charger, laptop, battery pack (Anker!), etc.

Performance
Now to the important part… how does it perform? I believe that for what this device is trying to accomplish, it performed exceedingly well. I’m basing my opinion on price, size, sound quality. I’ll admit that when I first opened the box I had low expectations, based on the Jambox I previously owned… I simply didn’t think a smaller device could perform well. But, I was pleasantly surprised! Obviously a speaker this size will not vibrate the walls, but it actually has a well rounded sound (lows, mids and highs) and doesn’t rattle like some cheaply made bluetooth speakers I have heard in the past. The speakerphone (microphone is built in) functionality works quite well with clear output and the receiving end stated that they could hear me just fine, although I honestly probably will not use that feature much since most of my communication is via text. The auxiliary jack is a very nice addition and including a Micro SD slot is just wonderful! Using Micro SD cards can save your phone from draining when away from home (picnics, beach, hiking, etc). Battery life has been great so far, with playing a few hours at a time and charging every few days.

Build Quality
This speaker is solid aluminum, which means it is very strong but also not heavy. The finish is a regular aluminum polish instead of brushed aluminum, and I think it looks great! The speaker grill looks quite nice, in my opinion, and is protected by the small circular pattern in the aluminum housing, which I think is great for portability. The aluminum on/off switch is HUGE which makes the speaker extremely easy to turn on and off even in the dark (bed stand usage). And the rubberized buttons on the top feel well made and have a nice “click” to them (not squishy) when pressed. There are also two rubberized feet to keep the speaker from sliding on hard surfaces.

Comparisons
In comparison to a previously owned Jawbone Jambox (first version), I honestly think it performs every bit as good as that device for a fraction of the cost. I was much more impressed with the Anker speaker during first impressions than I was with the Jambox, for their given sizes. In comparison to a currently owned Bose Soundlink, the Anker speaker doesn’t quite hold up the the sound quality of the Bose (as expected), but the Bose is MUCH larger and 6x the cost.

Conclusion
As long as your expectations are realistic for a speaker of this size, this is absolutely the speaker to get. The price is phenomenal for a high quality bluetooth speaker. This speaker comes in around $45 at the time of this writing, which is by far the least expensive bluetooth speaker I have owned. The price vs performance of this speaker is by far the best of anything I have seen, from devices I own to friends various devices. I let a few friends listen to the Anker speaker and they couldn’t believe that it sounded as good as it does for it’s size. Although I like the sound quality of my Bose Soundlink speaker, it never leaves my home due to it’s size and poor battery life, which means it very rarely gets used. This Anker bluetooth speaker is now my preferred speaker for on the go. It is so small and portable that I just through it in my bag when I leave the house so it is always with me wherever I go!

First, I did receive this speaker free for testing and review. While I realize that a review of a free product is fundamentally different than a review of a product for which one has paid, I do believe that my impressions and observations can prove helpful to you in your decision making as I do take the review process seriously. If you have questions about the speaker, feel free to post them in the comments section and I'll do my best to answer based on my own experience with the product.

What you're getting with this order:
(1) Freeman X6 speaker/flashlight
(1) Charging cord
(1) 3.5mm Aux cord
(1) 2 piece handlebar mount
(1) Samsung 18650 Battery
(1) User's guide

What is this thing, and what's it supposed to do?:
This bluetooth speaker allows you to access your audio wirelessly via a bluetooth enabled device. In addition, when connected with your phone, it allows you access to some of the phone's simpler function such as accepting and rejecting a call. A 3.5mm Aux cord is provided and allows you wired access to audo via non-bluetooth devices as well. This speaker differs from most in that it is also an LED flashlight, and a remote for your phone's camera shutter.

Does it work?:
The short answer is yes. Let's take a look at its performance feature by feature for a little more detail:

Charging: The speaker charges via a provided cord. The flashlight button on the speaker's side flashes blue to indicate charging.

Pairing: Pressing the power button puts the speaker into pairing mode automatically and it becomes discoverable on your bluetooth device as "Trendwoo". Once selected it pairs within 5 seconds. The connection is solid up to about 30 when it will begin to cut out.

Sound: Normally, when a speaker is offered at the mid-range price point, I expect a significant difference from the sound usually encountered in the budget price range. However, I had tempered those expectations somewhat because this particular speaker has other functions that have bumped it up in price. I have to say though that the sound here is impressive, especially considering its small size. The mid range is incredibly crisp and for my ears it's the star of this show. The highs are reproduced quite impressively as well and even at max volumes these tones are solid with no distortion noted. The bass is surprisingly good at mid volumes but can deteriorate at the speaker's max volumes. I found that I needed to find the right mix of volume between the speaker and my phone to get the optimum bass and I think this level will be different for different devices. Overall, the sound here does justify the mid-range price point.

Design/Appearance:
This is an attractive speaker built in the shape of a flashlight that mounts easily to one's bike handlebars. It's got a 2 tone color scheme, the one I tested being done in black and grey. One end has the torch while the other has the speaker. The 5 buttons are located in a bar that is nearly flush with the body of the speaker and these light up when powered on. A very sharp looking unit.

Build: Build is solid and should prove heavy duty. I've owned it for nearly 2 months now, and have had no problems. If you are indeed planning to use it cycling I think you can feel confident that it'll hold up to bouncing and shaking quite well.

Shutter remote: There is a shutter remote button that allows you access to your camera's shutter when connected by bluetooth. I'm using the iPhone 6 Plus, and unfortunately was unable to get this function to work with the iPhone's camera.

Flashlight: Pressing the flashlight button cycles through a bright, dim, strobe and SOS modes. The light is LED and is bright but is not adjustable.

Anything else of note?:
-As of the posting of this review, the speaker is eligible for free shipping to members of Amazon Prime; that's always a check in the plus column for me.

Any negatives?:
-Shutter remote didn't work with the iPhone 6 Plus.
-While the light is bright, it isn't adjustable and may not be a wide enough beam for your cycling preferences.

Bottom line: This is a well built and attractive bluetooth speaker with multiple functions including an included handlebar mount, LED flashlight and shutter remote. I'm a bit of a headphone fanatic, and I've collected quite a few over the years. These Sennheiser OCX 686i are designed to be workout headphones, and as such, are designed for comfort, durability, and reliability while working out. They are not perfect, but by and large, these are some of the best headphones of this genre I have tested.

These are in-ear headphones, and those are not for everyone. My ears are shaped in such a way that most earbuds fall out pretty easily, and are therefore useless when doing anything but sitting there. I use in-ear headphones while traveling or moving about, as they provide great noise attenuation (though not active cancellation), comfort, and stability. These come with three sizes of ear buds to accommodate most ear canal sizes, and they provide a nice seal when inserted.

Microphonics are a common complaint with in-ear headphones; basically, it's the scratching/thumping noise you hear when you rub the cable on your clothes, or it hits something suddenly. Since it's a physical phenomenon (mechanical vibrations becoming electrical signals, like a mic), it can't be eliminated, but these headphones have a couple of tricks up their sleeves to diminish microphonics greatly: 1)they have a clip, allowing you to immobilize the cable and 2)the cables are ovoid, and made of lightweight plastic. The results is a marked improvement over standard audio cables.

The sound, as with all Sennheiser headphones, is terrific. It's balanced and shows good range, especially for small headphones. I personally hate headphones that skew towards bass, because the rest becomes a muddled mess, but these deliver a good kick without sacrificing mid-range and highs. The unit comes with a volume/action fob, allowing you to perform a host of operations, like fast forwarding and answering calls. It's not what I use headphones for, but it seems to work fine.

If you're in the market for comfortable, stable and quality workout headphones, you'd do well to consider these, they're not cheap, but they're worth it.y workout headphones, you'd do well to consider these, they're not cheap, but they're worth it.

This is different than the remote that comes with the Roku box in one important way: it relies on IR to communicate with the Roku, rather than RF.  Here's why that's important: IR is a lot like light, it can easily be blocked.  If your Roku is not in a position where the IR "light" can shine on it's little IR "window", it won't work.  In most cases, the IR "light" from an IR remote will reflect off things like walls and such and that reflected light will be bright enough to convey the information contained in that light -- but not so much with this Roku Replacement remote.  We found that it rarely works unless it is pointed right at the Roku and there is nothing blocking the beam.  An RF remote does not suffer from this limitation.  In fact, in many cases, the signal can even go through a wall [i.e. the Roku box can be controlled from another room].  Our original RF remote works far better than this replacement remote in most of the ways we use it.  Our Roku box sits just below our flat screen TV, which places it kind of low in the room.  A stack of books, someones head, a raised foot, a bunched up blanket at the foot of the bed, all have the potential of blocking the signal, making it necessary to strike silly poses to get the beam past whatever obstacle is in place.  This is never a problem with the original [RF] remote.  BUT, the MGO/Netflix/Amazon/etc buttons are fun and occasionally useful [what about Hulu and Vudo and...?].  Also, if there are Rokus in other rooms, then the fact that walls block the IR beam might be a boon -- preventing the remote from changing the channel on all the Rokus in the house [for instance].  This remote is lighter, sleeker and feels better in the hand.  Also, it has the "OK" button in the center of the arrow keys.  On our original remote, the OK button is below the arrow buttons -- drives me nuts!!!  In fact, this is the main reason I bought the thing!  But the fact that we, often, have to become contortionists to use it, means it's now collecting dust.  For those who say it doesn't work with their Roku 3 [or that it's "incompatible"]: I have a Roku 3 and it's fully compatible [though I haven't tried the Netflix/Amazon/MGo/etc buttons lately].  This negative experience might be due to the fact that it's an IR remote and not an RF remote.  If the little IR window, on the Roku box, is obscured in some way, the IR "light" from this remote will not be able to get to the Roku box.  The Roku box must be positioned such that it can "see" the beam that comes from the remote.  Also, the box must be close enough to the remote for it to work -- not sure what the range is, though.  In other words, the Roku box must be positioned with it's front facing towards all positions where the remote will be used, and it must have a clear "view" of that region.  Not sure what the maximum angle is between the front of the box and the remote, though, so experimentation may be required.

REVISED REVIEW -------------------------- I've dropped my review down to 4 stars. Why? Because I feel its deceptive and I wound up buying a "real" more traditional antenna that's in my attic (although will likely use the amplifier).  Here's the thing. If you have a whole bunch of "easy" (yellow and green in AntennaWeb) stations available, then yes, this will probably work connected to your window... or laid on the floor or probably anywhere, but not me. I was able to get ZERO stations (at least the major) ones for ANY window in my house. Downstairs, Upstairs, probably tried a dozen windows facing various ways. Nada. Even with the amplifier. The problem is that my core network stations (ABC, NBC, CBS, Fox) are in the Blue and Purple areas and the ONLY way to get stations is to have it POINTED.  POINTED, not just connected to the nearest wall or window. Yes, technically speaking, this does a decent job, but it requires you to have EXACT PLACEMENT. I spent probably 6 hours various days trying to get this to work and the only way I could finally get it to work was in my daughter's bedroom taped to her door with the door ajar in just the right angle with the wire going around to her cable jack. That's not a long term solution.  Here's what I suggest (and did). If you have a whole bunch of wires (like me) that you don't know what connects to where, then get this: "Jonard PT-300 Pocket Continuity Tester". It beeps when you have it connected to the matching wire. Makes it super easy to identify. Figure out where the junction is for your wires and figure out a strategy to have the antenna in your attic (if you don't want to mount it on the roof like I didn't) and in the farthest direction needed. So, my junction box and easier access were south, but I needed North, so I went up into the attic and found the farthest northern point. Next, I fed a wire from my unfinished playroom to there. I got this mid sized antenna ne "RCA Compact Outdoor Yagi HDTV Antenna" and connected it and then looked at my signal meter on my Tivo/TV until the signals were optimized. Surprisingly the direction didn't match exactly what I would've thought from AntennaWeb.   It's worth the effort. Now, instead of seeing wires, I'm using the wiring in my house and its all concealed. The antenna is in a stable position and there is no suction cups or shipping tape or whatever keeping it up.   This antenna might be appropriate for < 20 miles, but only as a LAST RESORT. If you do not have access to an Attic or crawl space or whatever, then, maybe, although people have even mounted antennas on porches and even under umbrellas.   Here is my original review:  ORIGINAL REVIEW --------------------------- First off, keep in mind something as you read these reviews. Every installation is different. Every one. Every house has different distances from the TV towers, has different altitudes, obstacles (hills, etc) and even in the same neighborhood, people place their TV in different locations meaning that someone that needs to pickup signals from the North might have their TV facing South (like us).  These are relatively simple devices, but placement matters a LOT.  My Zip: 30736 TV faces: South Purchased: 50 Mile Antenna with Amplifier  Lets step back. First off, I'm going to assume you're a cord cutter (or potential cord) cutter like me. This was/is my first "installation" and previously used Satellite TV service. Your first step needs to be to go to AntennaWeb.org. Really, do it now. Put it not only your Zip Code, but your address as well (the results CAN and DO change). This represents your situation. Some people will have a ton of signals within 5 miles and can connect almost anything (hanger or cheapest antenna available) and score 100+ channels with high signal rate. Others may not be able to use a Window Antenna and really need a gigantic, roof mounted, professionally installed antenna pointing in the exact direction and even then get only a fraction of the possible stations and not at a high signal rate. That's just the way things are.  For me, I have a the ability to pickup the major stations at about a range of 20-30 miles. As mentioned above, I bought the 50 mile antenna and used the amplifier as well (it might actually work better without the amplifier if you are closer and have lots of "Green" and even "Red" stations, but "Blue" and "Violet" will likely need it.  I started by placing it in the window and really didn't get much of anything at all. My TV luckily has a signal meter, so I used that and was getting Zero signal for just about anything. So, that should tell you about the reviews - many people in my situation would've posted a 1 star review right then and returned it.  HOWEVER, I did something that I didn't expect to work. I placed it on top of my entertainment center, FLAT, and pointed it towards the North (where the signals are) and lo and behold, started receiving signals. In fact, I spent a couple of hours turning it and it was amazing how much difference it made. Turn it an inch and get Zero, turn it and get 30, turn it again and get 45 (these are 0-100 scales). I'd have it pointed and go through channel scans and get anything from 2 stations (ABC/CBS) to a dozen to about 20 stations. Try it and experiment - you might be very surprised. The nice thing about doing it this way was that there wasn't a cable going across to the window and I didn't have to worry about seeing it in the window nor about falling off the window, it was just up and away on the entertainment system.  Next, I thought about it and came up with a great idea. I could use the wiring in my house to get it higher and facing North. So, I went outside and found the splitter and disconnected the wires to the splitter that sent them to the satellite and instead connected 2 of them together. Now I was able to connect the antenna to the upstairs connector and have that basicallyrun down and around and then connected to the wire that would connect to my TV. Awesome!  That's where I stand now and with the antenna sitting on a desk upstairs, I've gotten the best results of all and have gotten all of the major stations: ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox, plus CW and PBS (2 different stations), plus the various "sub" channels like a local weather station and other various shows and movies.  Right now, it's looking like I chose correctly as I don't want to install something outside, nor try to wire it up to the attic, so I like this transparent, thin antenna, although we'll see what the spouse thinks when seeing this antenna just sitting on a desk.  The neat thing is that the signals are BEAUTIFUL HD and now I have the option for things like Tivo or Tablo tostream them to all TVs (via Roku) in the house, plus iPad and even remotely as well as DVR shows which would be great to do.  In summary. Experiment. It's worth the effort to get a high quality antenna and signal as your options increase dramatically when you can access (and potentially DVR) the major networks.

These bluetooth headphones are just okay. I really wanted to love them. They are the earbud shape that I can wear; I can't wear the ones that are more like plugs that extend further into the ear. I must have small ears as the included attachments to ensure they stay in the ear don't fit for me, however I don't really need them as I typically use these when sitting at my desk. I move around my cubicle and down the hall a lot during the day, so I prefer bluetooth to twisting to grab something and have my phone fall because my earbuds are plugged into them.

Connecting my iPhone6 to the headphones was easy. The microphone/volume adjustment controls are fairly large, larger than they look in the picture and is pretty heavy. I've had many issues when people can't hear me clearly and some intermittent skipping when listening to streaming music with a solid wifi connection that doesn't skip/stop without the headphones, so I know it's the headphones and not the streaming connection. It took me a while to figure out that the volume toggles will only increase volume to your highest volume setting your phone is adjusted to, so if you'd like to use the volume controls completely, ensure your volume on your phone is increase to loudest. All the apps I use for streaming allow me to start playing sound with the middle pause/play button once the app is started on my phone, however with some apps I am not able to pause sound with that button and that is more important for me when people come to chat with me. That's irritating to have to ask the person to hold on while I have to mess with my phone to pause my audio book or whatever. The clip that is included to ensure the headphones don't fall off isn't too large, but it's very loose around the cord and unless I wrap the cord through it to keep it from freely moving down the cord, the cord will just slide through and I'll end up with one headphone all the way to the clip and the other dangling all the way down my front. I wear one headphone a lot, so this was an issue before I put a twist through the clip. By the way, these do have a pretty good range. I go down the hall to pick up items from the printer and can listen or answer calls about 25-30 feet away.

For now, I think this is my only option for bluetooth headphones of this shape, so they'll have to do. I'm hoping someone comes up with something better soon!

I test/review/buy lots of audio products. When one of those makes you sit up and take notice, you know you have something special.

I was not expecting a lot of the Ivery Cannon IV-8 earphones, but I was very wrong to assume. These are not only budget minded, but Audiophle approved.

*Price*
Easy on the wallet, but great for the ears. More on that later in the review.

*Packaging*
Unboxing is a pleasant experience. These come in a nice little wood box, where Cannons are snuggly fit in.

*Accessories*
Very standard here, includes: Three Different Sized Silicon Tips, A Shirt Clip and A Product Booklet.
Though, it would be nice if they came with a little portable bag or case.

*Build*
Quality materials from top to bottom. Function and form working together. More than adequate strain reliefs.
Cord is thick and tough. Little to no microphonics was noticed, but if there is an issue, that is where the shirt clip comes into play.

*Functions*
Has a microphone that works well and is very nicely designed. Callers hear me loud and clear.

*Fit*
The pictures do not convey just how small these little Cannons are. They are tiny and light. That also means that fit is easy as pie.
They are very light weight in the ears. They can be worn for long periods with minimal discomfort. With good ventilation, there is also no driver flex.

*Sound*
Lows - Bass tight, big and fun. Lower frequences are handled with ease, always in control.
These would be great earphones to get a basshead to transition to more of an audiophile sound signature.

Mids - Both male and female vocals shine through wonderfully. The heart of the IV-8, keeps the Lows and Highs
blended perfectly together.

Highs - Highs are clear and move up the range quit high, though they never sibilant or fatiguing.

Sound Signature - I hate to use the term "Musical", because that is what they are for, to produce music.
But they really do sound Musical. They are fun, energetic, controlled and clear throughout all bands.

Isolation - Sound blocking is on pair with may smaller IEM. Most should be able to product a good seal with the Cannons.

Noise - Little to no noise even at very low levels.

*Overall Thoughts*

For less that $20, the Ivery Cannon IV-8 is a no-brainer and very easy to recommend. They sound fantastic, regardless of price.
Easy to wear, easy to drive. An Easy earphone to love. Pick yourself up one and see for yourself.

Eventually I cleared everything out and started over, I began by putting a half-dozen folders of music, each identified by the artist, as a test into a single location. After sync, I found that a folder had been created in the player for each artist, each folder having one song (the first song of the folder) in it. All the other songs of all artists were collected in a system-created folder called "various artists". I could use the Windows explorer to move the 2nd and higher songs into the correct locations, where they did remain. Eventually I ended up loading the player using windows, without bothering with Media Go, organizing it the way I wanted it to be.

This soundbar is a great solution for those that want a plug and play solution to upgrading the poor sound quality that most TVs produce. This can be installed directly below the flatscreen and offers lots of flexibility to work around potential stud configurations. It comes with its own source switching and amplification, so provides an in-wall option to really simplify an installation and eliminate the need for a separate amplifier and separate speakers.

Pros:
- Easy to install - just cut out the wall board, install the bracket, install the speakers, and connect power and sources. I got this in the wall within 2 hours - measuring twice, leveling, mapping out studs, and cutting the wall board
- Significant Sound Quality Upgrade - The difference between the TV sound quality and this is night and day. Great for your typical room installation. While the sound quality does not approach what is possible with separates and custom speakers, this will work for most room installations whose requirements are different from a home theater. This is perfect for bedrooms and family rooms.
- Fast & Easy Amplification & Switching - The amplifier that bolts into the frame takes several inputs and will auto-switch them. This is great for the typical user. Really, other than the TV (Cable, Directv, Fios, etc.), the only other input that this can support is an optical or analog input in addition to the HDMI.
- Built In Remote Capabilities - This will learn your existing remote, so you can change volume and muting with an existing remote.
- No Hum - Due to the relatively simple implementation approach, this speaker is dead quiet with no hum or static.

Cons:
- The speakers hang below the cutout by several inches - so they hang on the frame. Would have been nice if they were symmetrical to assist with planning. They can be installed upside down if needed.
- A great feature is that this supports several inputs - HDMI, Optical, Stereo. To keep the front face uncluttered, these inputs are in the wall on the bottom of the built in amplifier. Would have been nice if the package included a wall plate to send those inputs into the wall. A single wall plate for the inputs would have worked. You will need to purchase separately.
- Sound Volume - This comes with a 30 watt amplifier which is perfect for normal and above average loundness. You will not get a movie theater experience.
- It would have been nice if the power was built into the frame or amplifier unit instead of requiring another hole in the wall, but it works. You need a cut out for the speaker and the power supply (behind the TV).

I'm not even sure how to start this review with just words. But if you don't want to read the rest of my review, here it is summed up - these are the BEST speakers you will ever own, hands down - so if you're not sure if it's worth the cost, don't you worry. I'm a HUGE audiophile. I critique even the highest end systems and can pick out flaws or things I don't like. Not crisp enough, too much bass, not enough treble, too much distortion at high levels, even when I've tweaked all the receiver/amp settings, etc. I can pick it all out. So when I bought my new house, it was time to step it up with the surround sound system. I did probably 15-20 hours of total research over the course of a month, reading hundreds of reviews on 10-20 different high end speaker systems. I compared multiple different Klipsch lines (Icon, Synergy, Reference, Reference Premiere), HK, Polk, Bose, etc. I went in biased because I’ve always wanted a Klipsch system, but I still gave all the others a true chance to earn my purchase. I looked into break downs on sound, performance, pros, cons, quality, build, longevity, size, style, look, etc. I had several different systems in my cart on multiple different sites (Amazon, NewEgg, Klipsch’s official site, Bose’s site) so I could compare price, see about sales or better prices, and make sure I configured the perfect system for me. This was going to be a very large purchase for me and based on how unbelievably important music and audio is to me, I was willing to spend money on the right system. So after all the research, I decided to open up my wallet and get a system from one of the world's leading speaker companies, Klipsch. I chose the Reference Premiere series, because unless you want to spend 30+k on a Klipsch Palladium system, your next best bet is spending 5k on a Reference Premier system.
Here is exactly what I bought (all are obviously Klipsch Reference Premiere):
(2) RP-280F Ebony Floorstanding Speakers
(1) RP-450C Ebony Center Speaker
(2) RP-250S Surround Speaker
(1) R-115SW Subwoofer
I hooked these all up to a Marantz SR7009 using Monster Cable speaker wire and a Monster Cable subwoofer cable. Keep in mind, you can't just get amazing speakers and expect them to sound amazing and perform at their high end levels if you're powering them with subpar receivers through subpar wires. You have to make sure you're feeding your speakers the highest quality power and quality that you can so they can do their job to the fullest extent. I'd highly recommend some of the higher end Marantz, Denon, or Onkyo receivers for this Reference Premiere set. If you are going to spend 4-5k on a speakers, and then skimp on the receiver, that won't make sense or do these justice at all. Plus with really cheap receivers, you risk damaging the speakers because they aren’t being provided the correct power, so they are essentially overworking themselves with less power and extra distortion.
It took me about a half an hour to hook this up correctly the way I wanted. I used all new wire, used a wire stripper to successfully and correctly strip the wires for optimal performance, installed the surround sound speakers, floor standing speakers, center speaker and hooked up the sub.

I've done a much more extensive review on the RP-280 floor speakers I bought as part of my Klipsch system purchase. However, it doesn't make sense for me to copy and paste it here because it was aimed more at the floor standing speakers. So I'll write a more condensed and "focused on these" one here.

Rear surround sound speakers are sometimes over looked, especially when buying a system where you purchase the speakers separately. "I don't care much about rear power, I'll just get cheaper ones for the back" or "They only provide a bit of sound from the rear, who cares" are sometimes things I've heard from friends or family. That is quite an incorrect way to thinking about it. It's almost like saying, I don't care if my back brakes work because my front ones work and are more important. If you're going to spend a fortune on front floor standing speakers and a subwoofer, why skimp on the "rear end" of the system? The speakers in the back do not have to produce the same amount of power or sound as the floor standing front ones do. But they need to be able to handle a lot of power if you're going to be blasting the system. Also, for audiophiles and movie buffs, you want a system that can really make you feel like you're there, 360 degrees around. These speakers will help you accomplish that and much more. Keep in mind, these are no small surround sound speakers. You're not buying a Bose system here with tiny cube speakers. These are heavy and meaty surround sound speakers for sure. They weigh a little over 13lbs a piece. I went with the 240's rather than the 250's due to the size of my room. It's a fairly small room and the 250's are meant for the largest rooms. Even the 240s are technically "too much" for a room the size I have them in, but I wanted Reference Premiere and these are the ones I liked most. Extremely easy to hang with a very sturdy bracket that is attached to the speaker. I bought some 27lb rated wall anchors and screws and used those. Twice the weight I needed, but why risk them falling off the wall.

They sound absolutely incredible. I have a nice Marantz receiver that is capable of creating some absolutely lifelike sound from my music and movies and these speakers come through in the clutch. When I play PS4, I'm hearing things in the game that I never heard before and they are coming from these rear surrounds. I'm very impressed with these and they are a powerhouse of a speaker. This speaker has a lot going for it. It sounds as good as or better than any speakers we have in our house, barring our home theater system. It takes inputs so many different ways: SDCard, Bluetooth, mini-jack, radio. The NFC is a great idea. It makes it a snap to make your mobile device (NFC enabled) pair itself with the unit automatically. It's one of the most useful things I've seen NFC do so far. It's small and light, and gives some good sound quality for its size, in my opinion.

There are a couple of shortcomings: 1) the beeps it makes when I turn it on, off, or switch inputs, is always way too loud, and doesn't seem to be affected by the volume control. 2) The volume setting doesn't seem to be remembered when you turn it off. Between these two, it becomes a little impractical to use this in our kids' room at bedtime, because it may end up waking them up. I'd like it better if it had an analog dial volume control.

The other thing is that it has so many input modes, it can be difficult to tell which one you've just changed to. It would be nice if it had an LED indicator showing which mode it is in. If you tend to use it in the same mode all the time, maybe this wouldn't be an issue.

I feel like those two additions could be expected in this price range, and would add value to the product. It'd be great if it had an LED display that let you navigate folders on your SD card, too, but I wouldn't expect that for this price.

This is a VERY good but not perfect home theater system. I was incredibly fortunate to be able to try out the system in exchange for an honest review.

The good:
- Clear directions
- Sound is very good for the size
- All speaker wires are included and are nicely color-coded
- Blu-ray player image is spectacular (as expected), also has 3D capability
- Blu-ray player capable of streaming all types of content
- Has audio inputs so you can play sound from your TV tuner, cable box, or external souces
- Looks great; speakers are small but in a nice piano-black finish, and the main unit is a combination unit (amp / Blu-ray player; no separate boxes or wires)
- Remote is fully-featured, easy to use, and even includes batteries

The not-so-good:
- Just cannot compete with large speakers; this system is fine for most users, but I am using it in a recording studio environment, and compared to my reference speaker setup it falls flat (but for a small living room, bedroom, apartment, etc, it will be just fine; infinitely better than built-in TV speakers)
- For streaming features, Blu-ray player requires a physical network connection (wireless adapter NOT included)
- The pre-wired speaker wire inside of the plastic stands easily slides out, and if it does that it is nearly impossible to re-thread the wire inside the stands (I even resorted to using a coat hanger, and still no luck; finally gave up after about 30 frustrating minutes)

In summary, for the retail price you are getting a nice system; the full surround speakers, subwoofer, Blu-ray player, amp, and speaker wires would quickly add up if purchased separately. For years I have been using an extension cord and 3 different wall chargers plugged in to the end of it next to my night stand. Finally I found a five port desktop charger. You've probably seen 5 port chargers before, there's dozens of them on Amazon, but what makes this one different is that it has a stand to put your phone in (not very useful to me because of my case) to save space on your desk and two AC outlets that are spread apart enough to fit 2 small adapters or 1 large adapter and one small cord. The outlets are very tight though, so you will need to put a hand on it to pull the plug out. I thought I was going to be disappointed in the USB charger, I don't like to have different amperage on different ports. I like them all to be the same. So when I got this and saw the 3 ports labeled 1 amp and 2 labeled 2.4 amps I wasn't happy. However, I recently bought a USB power meter to see how much power my iPad used (apparently the included apple lightning cable can't even give it 2.4 amps I had to use a better one). So here's how I test my chargers, I only do it when the iPad battery is low (below 30) because otherwise it won't take as much power. Then I play a YouTube video full screen at 1080p 60fps at full brightness. This is the most power the iPad can possibly use. I plugged in to the 1 amp port expecting to get .98 amps or like the other reviewer said 1.1 amps but I was getting 2.35. Amazing! I then moved it to the next port and got the same thing. Turns out the labels only represent the max output of the whole thing, not the individual ports, all the ports are the same.

Pros:
perfect travel charger (and everyday)
Long enough cord for my night stand
2 AC outlets
Phone stand to save space on desk
2.4 amp charging!

Cons:
Not UL listed/ certified ( but very high quality so that doesn't bother me)
Phone stand might be useless to people that don't have really thin phones or have cases.

I love sound systems and usually can pick out flaws or things I don't like. Not crisp enough, too much bass, not enough treble, too much distortion at high levels, even when I've tweaked all the receiver/amp settings, etc. So when I bought my new house, it was time to step it up with the surround sound system. I did probably 15-20 hours of total research over the course of a month, reading hundreds of reviews on 10-20 different high end speaker systems. I compared multiple different Klipsch lines (Icon, Synergy, Reference, Reference Premiere), HK, Polk, Bose, etc. I went in biased because I’ve always wanted a Klipsch system, but I still gave all the others a true chance to earn my purchase. I looked into break downs on sound, performance, pros, cons, quality, build, longevity, size, style, look, etc. I had several different systems in my cart on multiple different sites (Amazon, NewEgg, Klipsch’s official site, Bose’s site) so I could compare price, see about sales or better prices, and make sure I configured the perfect system for me. This was going to be a very large purchase for me and based on how unbelievably important music and audio is to me, I was willing to spend money on the right system. So after all the research, I decided to open up my wallet and get a system from one of the world's leading speaker companies, Klipsch. I chose the Reference Premiere series, because unless you want to spend 30+k on a Klipsch Palladium system, your next best bet is spending 5k on a Reference Premier system.

Here is exactly what I bought (all, except sub since there is not a Sub in the RP line) are obviously Klipsch Reference Premiere):
(2) RP-280F Ebony Floorstanding Speakers
(1) RP-450C Ebony Center Speaker
(2) RP-250S Surround Speaker
(1) R-115SW Subwoofer

I hooked these all up to a Marantz SR7009 using Monster Cable speaker wire and a Monster Cable subwoofer cable. Keep in mind, you can't just get amazing speakers and expect them to sound amazing and perform at their high end levels if you're powering them with subpar receivers through subpar wires. You have to make sure you're feeding your speakers the highest quality power and quality that you can so they can do their job to the fullest extent. I'd highly recommend some of the higher end Marantz, Denon, or Onkyo receivers for this Reference Premiere set. If you are going to spend 4-5k on a speakers, and then skimp on the receiver, that won't make sense or do these justice at all. Plus with really cheap receivers, you risk damaging the speakers because they aren’t being provided the correct power per channel, so they are essentially overworking themselves with less power and extra distortion.

It took me about a half an hour to hook this up correctly the way I wanted. I used all new wire, used a wire stripper to successfully and correctly strip the wires for optimal performance, installed the surround sound speakers, floor standing speakers, center speaker and hooked up the sub.

I decided to test out the system first by using an iPod just because it was quick and ready to go. Not bad, but obviously an iPod through an amp isn't going to give you the real performance you want. So I then went with a Blu-Ray concert DVD. Now I will be honest, I was a tiny bit disappointed during the first song or two that I played. It sounded good, but not as good as I expected for a system this cost that had this many amazing reviews all over the internet. But I had heard something about a "speaker break-in period". I'm still to this day not sure if it's a scientifically proven “thing”, but it seemed to be evident here. After about two songs playing at a moderate-high level (which I read is the best way to break them in), the speakers honestly just seemed to truly come alive. I was hearing music in a way that I had never heard it before in my entire life. I'm not kidding even in the slightest about this. I have a very high end system in my car, I have friends that have nice surround sound systems, I've been to some amazing concert venues in my life, but I truly, in 30 years of my life, had never heard my music quite like I did through this system. Since then, I've been using it sparingly due to time. But I did watch the movie The Town through this system as well on Blu-Ray. I swear to you that at times, it felt like I was on the streets with them because it was so clear and so precise. I’ve also never heard a movie quite like I have when using these speakers. I've never heard anything like it in my life.

So to conclude this review, I honestly couldn't recommend these speakers more. I’m just a HUGE music and audio fan and a system this impressive is very important to me which is why I was able to justify the cost. If you're thinking about buying one of their other lines of speakers (Icon, Synergy, etc), I would recommend you just spend the extra money on Reference Premier. I’m not saying the other lines are inferior, I’m not saying they aren’t great. But these sound AMAZING, look incredible, and are easily the best speakers you'll ever own. I couldn’t be more happy with my purchase and hopefully will have these for many years.

***UPDATE ABOUT A MONTH OR SO IN***
Incredible. I've made more time in my life to enjoy this system. I've now experienced the three big things you'd use this system for. Music, Movies, and TV. Music, it's unreal. As noted above, I haven't heard music sound this good, ever. Movies, it makes it sound as if you're there. The clarity is remarkable and the movie comes alive in front of your eyes and you believe you're there because of how real it sounds. TV also sounds awesome. Obviously the sound isn't going to match what you'd get from a Blu-Ray, but I've been very impressed with how well the crowd and games sound when watching sports and how clear things are when watching shows, etc.

Additionally, I've since added another sub for the back of the room. I went with the R112 SW 12" sub because two 15's would be too much for this room I have it setup in. There were 0 problems with the bass I was getting from the original 15, but I wanted a little extra punch and bass from the back, so I bought the R112 SW 12" with the added wireless kit. Some sellers on Amazon add the $120ish wireless kit for free. Definitely completed this system to be the best I'll ever own. Again, I didn't need the extra sub at all, but I wanted to go a bit overboard.

One note - just keep in mind how powerful this system really is. It legitimately shakes the house two floors up when not even being close to turned up all the way. I keep the subs at about 20-25% and depending on what I'm using the system for, anywhere from 25%-75% of what I know it's capable of (normal everyday TV, 25% volume and music/concert DVDs 75%). The device has been great. It clearly targets customers that are constantly on the move, an don't want to haul around something that is heavy and unwieldily.

Pros:
- The shape. The circular design of the C6 makes the little speaker unbelievably easy to pack, and to handle. It was unobtrusive on my Specialized mountain bike, fit well in my small school bag, and was great to hold in the hand. Other products such as the Jawbone JAMBOX may look nice, but are weird to have for someone that has an active life and is constantly mobile.
- Build materials. Honestly, I like the construction materials of the C6. The outside of the speaker is surrounded by a rubber material and is textured with holes to improve grip. The speaker grill is made of a metal that has withstood every drop onto dirt, gravel, and concrete. The remainder of the device is made a tough plastic that has a matte feel to it and is really great to hold with sweaty hands. The LEDs are well hid but still in sight with out being agitating in a dark room.
- Pretty loud. When I got and storm down a mountain biking trail there is enough noise that it makes it hard to hear. With the bike attachment, I was able to hear the device well with the volume at about 50%. At about 75% my friends behind me were able to hear the music as well clearly. Made for some great times.
- Decent sound quality. I like to consider myself an audiophile, (I am studying radio broadcast, I am a huge fan of Viper4Android, and I love my Sennheiser 439's and 650's to death...) and from what I expected of this speaker, I am impressed. The speaker utilizes a single driver for all ranges, but provides a great amount of coverage still.
- The attachments. This may be the selling point for many people because no other bluetooth speaker comes with so many ways to use it. I have tested all the attachments and I can say that they all work quite well. My absolute favorite is the bike attachment. It was a tight fit onmy Specialized Hard Trail, but it I got it on and it hasn't shifted, popped off, or dropped the speaker, and I have hit some HARD trails.
- The battery life. It is FANTASTIC. You just have to be carful that you turn off the device when not in use. Like all other bluetooth devices, if the connection is lost to paired item, such as a phone, then the speaker will continue to search for it endlessly. Thus major battery drain until certain death. When not searching for a device however, the speaker has battery that lasts me several days of pretty heavy use.

Mehs:
- The "Water-proofing". This device is NOT waterproof. Think of it as similar to the Samsung Galaxy S5. There is a definite "Accident-proof" feel to the device, but there is a HUGE difference between an IP65 (what this device actually has) rating and an IP67 (waterproof) rating. The IP65 rating says that this device can handle blasts of "water jets" for at least 15 minutes. An IP66 rating says that a device can handle blasts of "strong water jets" for at least 3 minute. A true waterproof device carries an IP67 rating and can handle immersion in up to 1 meter of water for at least 30 minutes. Therefore, this device is NOT waterproof. Sitting on the concrete next to the pool in the splash zone? Yes. In the pool with you? No. It is splash proof, and that works perfectly fine for my life. I hate swimming.
