First, I did receive this speaker free for the purpose of testing and review. I recognize that a review of a free product is fundamentally different than a review of a product for which one has paid, but I do take the review process seriously, and am hopeful that my impressions and observations will prove helpful to you in your decision making.. If you have questions, feel free to post them in the comments section and I'll do my best to answer based on my own experience with the product.

What you're getting with this order:
(1) Blade Speaker
(1) 1 Micro-USB cord
(1) 3.5mm Audio cord

What is this, and what's it supposed to do?:
This is a bluetooth speaker which enables you to access your audio wirelessly using a bluetooth enabled device. In addition, it can be used without bluetooth via a provided 3.5mm cord. While connected to your phone via bluetooth, it can perform some of the phone's functions such as accepting and ending a call. It is currently being offered at the mid range price point.

Does it work?:
Yes. I've tested this unit and have the following observations to share:

Build: The build on the Blade is solid. It's a basic design, a large, thin rectangle with an adjustable kickstand handle. The handle is composed of hard plastic, and is well attached. It rotates to your preferred position via a sort of cog wheel mechanism that holds each new position until you apply enough pressure to move it again. Buttons are located on top of the speaker and flush with the unit. A covered port on the speaker's back panel holds the Aux jack, the micro-USB port and a reset button. It also has a grille for bass enhancement. The entire front panel of the speaker is a colored metal grille (I reviewed the orange) of high quality. I've owned it nearly 2 months now and have had no problem with durability.

Appearance: The speaker has a two tone color scheme with black housing and a colored grille. I reviewed the orange and I really like the contrast provided. The Speaker is thin (hence the name) and this adds to its high tech feel. The handle is black with chrome colored hinge which is a nice touch. Overall a simple but modern looking design.

Charging: The speaker charges via a provided micro-USB cord. A red light indicates charging, and a blue light indicates a completed charge.

Pairing: When the power button is long pressed, the speaker powers on and automatically enters pairing mode. It is discoverable on your device as "Blade" and once selected pairs within 5 seconds. Connection is good up to around 30 feet.

Sound: In the mid-range price point, I expect a sound quality that differentiates a speaker from the budget price range. The Blade delivers a quality high, crisp treble and a respectable bass. When both the speaker and the device were at full volume the mids and highs retained their quality while the bass struggled just a little. Overall, I feel that the sound does indeed justify the Blade's mid-range price point.

Anything else of note?:
-As of the posting of this review the speaker is eligible for free shipping to members of Amazon Prime, and that's always a check in the plus column for me.

Any negatives?: Just that tiny bit of distortion when both the speaker and device are at max volume. There is plenty of volume to be had here, and so this combination really is unnecessary anyway.

Bottom line: This is an attractive bluetooth speaker with a unique design whose minimalist design ends up giving it a quite modern feel. The sound quality is good and justifies its price range. I really like the Blade, and am happy to recommend it to anyone looking for a quality speaker at the mid-range price point. It may satisfy some users who were planning to spend more. I payed $189 for the Klipsch KMC 3, which was by far the most expensive speaker in my lineup, also using a JBL Flip 2 ($72), a Vizio Soundbar 2.0 ($79), and a SoundBot ($47) among cheaper speakers averaging $20, which were moved around my room to have sound coming from all around. The Klipsch was the last speaker I ordered, and after receiving it I knew I had made a mistake... I shouldn't have ordered any of the other speakers, and should have had only the KMC 3, and maybe a KMC 1, to keep the surround sound feeling alive. This speaker adds quite a bit of depth to my sound, and ends up rattling whatever surface it rests on due to the impressive bass. When I have all speakers playing together, my room sounds amazing, but when I turn the KMC 3 off, the remaining sound feels almost thin. In the opposite action however (using only the Klipsch) my room continues to sound nice, and full of depth. Despite being marketed as portable, the speaker is quite large and is more of a bookshelf speaker in my opinion, but I could see myself loading it up in a backpack and bringing it to the beach for a booming sound. For my purposes, the size is a good thing, but if you are looking for a speaker that can be easily carried around, I would suggest something more like a Bose, or maybe the KMC 1, although I have no experience with it, so can only recommend it based on assumption. Overall, this speaker is great, and highly recommended, especially at the price of $189, although the $399 MSRP does not feel unreasonable to me either.

Put it as close to the output source as possible. and use a good quality cable.

This Kedsum is number 29 of the BlueTooth stereo speakers that I've tested and I have to say that in this price range it's a bit special. Here's why.

It's So Versatile

It has everything that you'd expect a BlueTooth speaker to have these days and it all works well. Volume and track skipping and call answering and the ability to 3.5mm hard wire to you devices and NFC also.

It also has a slot for your music on a micro SD card. It also has a carry handle, that you could remove if you prefer. It also has a tripod mount, which many might use for a handlebar mount, but I'll put it on a tripod outdoors just to put the speaker at ear level, I have more tripods than cameras.

It has FM! Don't tell anyone my secret, but I really don't like FM sound quality, but how convenient and it works great. When you turn it on it starts on BlueTooth, so hold down that button until you get FM. Then the call answer button will start it scanning until you have all the local stations. Now you can advance with the + button to find what you're looking for.

Finally, this is quite resistant to the elements. Don't go submerging it in water, but you can come pretty close, it's better than most outdoor speakers like this. It comes with a 2000mAh battery which is the highest current used in these small speakers, so this will play a long time. Oh,

And It Sounds

It's only fair that I first tell you that I listen to studio monitors more than anything else. But this sounds good for what it is, and I'll tell you why.

You've got a pair of 40mm speakers driven by a 3 watt per channel amp, just like almost all in this price range. This is housed in a very small, portable cabinet, so it seems that what they've done is to include passive radiators from the back to increase the sound pressure level of the lower frequencies.

So this isn't a large, loud and deep speaker, but they have made such efficient use of the space that it does have, that I'm very impressed with the sound. A while back, I tested a competitor's speaker that looks an awful lot like this one, but it was closed back. No passive radiator, and this model does sound better. But just so you know, the bass gets louder as the system gets louder and at low volume the bass is pretty weak, but this is just how passive radiators work.

The connection is BlueTooth 4.0 and works well with the three devices that I tested with. I don't see any mention of aptX, but I worry more about that in BlueTooth headphones, where critical listening is possible. I've tested it while watching internet TV and the sound stays aligned, and it's a good choice if you take your tablet with you into the bathtub.

I don't know all the different small, outdoor BlueTooth speakers, but when compared to the Solemo and Soundpal for instance, the Kedsum comes out on top.

The DBPOWER BX-100 is a surprisingly okay-sounding little speaker for such a small package, though its volume is limited. It's a substantial rectangle the size of pair of bars of soap end-to-end, with only a USB charging cable (annoyingly, a wall-plug AC adapter is omitted -- this limits its usefulness as a bedside or in-room clock radio) and a headphone connector. Switched on, it's easy to pair (giving its name as "BX-100") and works straightforwardly. You'll want to turn the volume up to maximum immediately, as that's the only way to get it to a listenable volume level (even then it's not very loud), and use your source device's volume adjustment from there. It provides sound of something like the quality of a tabletop FM radio -- not room-filling dance beats by any means, but perfectly pleasant as background listening even for most kinds of music, as well as podcasts and other talk content.  This won't really replace anyone's main stereo, or even their computer speakers or good headphones, but it's still a nice backup speaker for travel use, for hotel-room listening, or a small office desk or kitchen, that kind of thing. For that use, it's a nice pickup -- you'll just have to remember to keep it charged. For bedside use as a clock radio, I'd look for [[ASIN:B009NZ6SZE a different device]].  The manufacturer provided a sample for this review.

First the good:

- Lightweight.
- SD card slot.
- Standard USB data/charging.
- Build quality is fairly good.
- Battery life is ok.
- The price is definitely low (perhaps too low...)
- No vendor lock-in.

Now for the bad:

- The case is entirely open to the elements (look into the usb port: you can see out the headphone jack). Don't sweat!
- The controls can't be locked during playback. This is fine, if you don't move (if you do, you'll pause, stop, or skip the track)!
- Long *folder titles* scroll, but long *track names* do not. If your song or podcast titles all start the same way, you can't tell which is which.
- Folder navigation is insane. If you are in, say, a podcast directory, then click the back button ONCE, you return to the root of the file system!
- The UI is just plain ugly.

I see from reading other reviews that there's a new firmware version that includes a 'hold' option for the controls. Doesn't sound like the other negatives have been addressed.

If/when this unit dies--I sweat when running/riding, and the case is wide open, so I assume its lifetime will be short--I will *start* my search for a replacement by looking at units currently supporting Rockbox, made by anyone but Sandisk and go from there. This thing is junk.

My laptop is a nice PC, but the tiny speakers don't have much volume or clarity. I connected the RT419 Bluetooth transmitter to the headphone port, then paired it with a portable Bluetooth speaker I use with my tablet. Pairing was very quick, and the audio from the speaker was far superior to the laptop's sound. Granted, I could have hard-wired the speaker, but a wireless connection gave a lot more freedom to move the speaker, and it avoided having another cable cluttering up my desktop.

I also used the transmitter with an old Radio Shack portable radio that I keep next to my PC for listening to news and sports. I inserted the transmitter cable into the radio's headphone port, then paired the transmitter with the Bluetooth speaker. Again, pairing was very quick, and in a few seconds, I was listening to much better quality audio than with the radio's speakers.

A USB charging cable is included with the transmitter. Don't lose the cable, since it has a proprietary plug that plugs into a small port on the side of the transmitter. The transmitter can be recharged from a USB port of a computer or plugged into an AC charger.

They also include a nice set of 3.5MM input to RCA output if you wish to connect this to a large home stereo!

My verdict: This is a really handy little gadget with a number of uses both inside and outside the home. If you have an audio device that lacks Bluetooth capability, just connect the Bluetooth transmitter to the headphone port and pump the audio into a Bluetooth speaker for better sound and more portability.

As I’ve mentioned in my reviews before, I spent a fair number of years broadcasting “back in the days” of fairly amateur AM radio. That’s something to still be celebrated, especially in this age of the YouTube generation wherein everyone has their own show and web-based networks in development. As such, I like to think I know a thing or two about how something sounds, and while I probably couldn’t spend any time debating decibel issues with some of the more technically accomplished I still maintain what I prefer to call “an ear for quality.”

That said, I think this Desktop Microphone from iGearPro is pretty spiffy for what it is. The mike itself is USB-port enabled – a reasonable technological improvement over the old AUX-style posts that so many home computing systems come with. Granted, the quality is not going to be the kind of high-caliber input that gamers these days require in order to have a satisfactory gaming experience; but if you’re looking for a modestly-priced model that’ll be a step-up than what can included for free with your latest home PC then this one is an improvement.

Kudos to iGearPro as they’ve actually included a pretty nice tripod-style stand which the mike clips into. The bracket allows for the mike to be mildly adjusted to different directions; this way, you can set it up so as to avoid the potential ‘plosives’ when you speak (hard air blown out thru the oral cavity with P’s and D’s and B’s), meaning that you can easily diminish the cracking on the other end of your call or recording playback. I tend to think that – based on my learned ear – this would make good for crafting your web-based productions for those just starting out or even for budding auteurs looking to step up the quality just a notch.

Also, there’s something to be said for the ease and simplicity of plug and play technology, and iGearPro’s is no exception: just set this baby up on your desk and plug it into an available USB port and you’re good to go.

Highly recommended. It’s safe to say that this Desktop Microphone from iGearPro not only looks good but performs as expected in the variety of basic consumer tests I walked it through this weekend. Granted, it’s probably not going to produce the highest quality recordings imaginable – nothing would when you consider this price point – but it’s a far better mike than the cheapie low-end knock-offs which tend to come with desktop computer purchases these days. I previously had the Harmony One, which finally took a fall from which it couldn't recover. I rushed to replace it but found that it was no longer available. Shame. Oh well, this system fit the bill pretty well; not over-the-top but functional enough with some new perks.

I'm a huge fan of the hub concept, allowing for better interaction between the remote and the devices it's controlling. I have no idea how the system is more responsive than the Harmony One was, but it's most noticeable when doing things like pressing buttons repeatedly (like raising or lowering the volume). Dual function buttons (short- vs. long-press) really adds to the remote, although I swapped a few defaults to get them just right, at least for my usage.

The addition of being able to control the TV with a mobile device is maybe not quite as obvious at first. Sure, it's convenient, but the additional functionality you gain by being able to modify behaviors through the hub is very welcome. I'm talking specifically about features like the sleep timer (for an activity, not just a device) and some more advanced features previously unavailable like scheduling, etc. The ability to assign macros was another big win, although there's a shortage of buttons to assign these to outside the four colored buttons.

My only gripe, and the reason I didn't give a 5, is that the configuration of this unit is a bit restricted due to the lack of soft buttons. For instance, some of the buttons are reserved for smart home features. I see the value, but I'm not sure I'd reserve space on the remote for it. On the plus side, the reason I got this unit over the model that *does* have soft buttons is the placement of the FF, Play, Pause, RR cluster. Putting them at the top (soft button model) seems an ergonomic failure I didn't want to have to get used to.

I am extremely impressed with this purchase.  I agree with the reviewers who mentioned that the mount was heavy but I view that as a good thing.  Heavy, in this case, means its made of steel and of quality materials.  Remember, we are mounting a TV that needs to hang in mid air and at all different angles.... I'm not interested in doing that with something light and cheap feeling.  The installation was simple and I glanced through the directions and went to work.  I mounted mine in the garage directly to the cement block wall.  I did not use the supplied mounting hardware as I felt more comfortable and already had the correct size Tapcon's (Screws made for anchoring in concrete, block, brick, etc.). There are 7 locations on the wall mount bracket to give you plenty of options to make sure it does not go anywhere.  I was prepared for the fact that the screws that were supplied with the plate to attach to the back of the TV may not fit.  This was also the case with me as well.  I already purchased the correct size for the TV I was mounting.  Just read your TV manual and it will tell you what size mounting screws to use.  I was mounting a Vizio 32" and the screw size was M4 12mm.  The screws provided with the mount are huge so unless you are mounting a very large TV to this mount, the supplied screws may not fit your exact TV model.  It's hard for me to blame Mount Factory for this.....there is no standard size and I don't expect them to supply 4 of every possible screw size.  There are 2 features that really pushed this to the 5-Star rating for me.  As I mentioned, I mounted this in my garage so I was initially worried that this TV would grow legs and run out of my garage under someone's arms.  Well, it has 2 bolts and nuts that lock the TV in place to make sure it stays where you want it.  The other is the plastic covers that help hide the wires and keep them in place when you are extending and swiveling the TV.  This was a huge concern for me during ordering asI was wondering what would happen to the cable when you pull this off the wall 20" and then push it back.  I was expecting, kinking, twisting, etc. but they remain in place and best of all look very clean to me.  I would compare this to mounts that are way more expensive.  I am very happy with my purchase and know that this mount will outlast several TV's.  I highly recommend the purchase of this mount.

I bought the SoundPal Cube to replace my Scosche speaker I dropped one time too many. I literally agonized over this purchase. I compared more models than I care to remember trying to find a balance between price, positive reviews and my perceived quality. Overall, this really isn't a bad little speaker.

It is packaged in a simple, thin cardboard box, which isn't much larger than the speaker itself. Included are a very short Micro- to Standard-USB charging cable; an equally short male-to-male 3.5 mm cable to connect non-Bluetooth devices; and a two page instruction leaflet.

The speaker is simultaneously larger AND smaller than I expected. I really can't explain that. It just is. It's roughly 3" square. It's 2-3 times larger than my Scosche "bullet" speaker. The 3 control buttons on top are situated closer to the side with the full-range driver, which is also glossy black compared to the passive radiator on the opposite side. With the bigger driver plus a passive radiator I erroneously thought it would have more low end. Amazingly, my 1.5" inch diameter old Scosche had deeper bass and crisper highs.

That's not to say this speaker sounds bad. It's really pretty decent. At higher volume levels, sub-250 Hz frequencies *do* tend to distort. I recommend trying to keep the radiator about 2-3 inches from a solid surface, e.g. a wall or even a box of tissues. Strange as it sounds, this provides a bit of resistance to the radiator so lower frequencies don't distort as much. If you have an EQ on your source, you can tweak some pretty good sound from The Cube.

My chief complaint is the volume of the beeps when I first power up the speaker. They're LOUD!! You have no choice in the matter. I get at least one sarcastic comment from my wife or my mother-in-law every.single. time I turn the speaker on. Speaking of volume, the volume buttons have an extremely narrow range of control. Seems like 3 or 4 taps is the max and thespeaker emits a series of beeps that are louder than the source material.

The 3.5 mm Audio In port, the charging port and the power switch are jammed very close together on one side. So close in fact that attempting to charge the speaker while using the Audio In jack can cause the charging cable to fall out. The supplied charging cable is too short to use with anything but a USB port on a computer. I have been using a 1000 mA wall adapter from another device to charge the speaker with no problems. Well, one problem: None of my longer micro-USB cables seem to fit snugly into the port on the speaker. But I have the same issue with my Kindle so it's not a game-changer.

Bluetooth performance is actually good. It pairs up reasonably quickly. The signal remains clear up to about 20 feet indoors, through walls, etc. It's ridiculous to me to attempt to get farther away from the speaker than one could easily hear the sounds produced by it. However, some speakers claim distances up to 50 feet are possible. 15-20 feet is about as far as anyone needs, IMHO. This isn't a high-power home or car audio device!

Also, the product information claims this speaker has been updated to include voice control and SD card support. The model I received has neither. So if those are important features to you, keep looking because you may or may not receive what you were promised by the seller.

I have not tried receiving or making calls through The Cube. Just not my thing.

Other than those flaws, it's a decent enough BT speaker. Not great. Not awful. Just decent enough.

I bought this MP3 player to replace my last Sansa Clip, which was an older generation model. I primarily use these as running MP3 players, and I clip them to the collar of my shirt, and change songs, volume, etc. leaving it clipped to my shirt. There's a lot that I like about this model: good screen, intuitive controls, and the ability to set up a simple playlist on the device. When I hear a song that gets me pumped up mid-exercise, I add it to my GoList (this model is set up for 3 GoLists, which is nice). The biggest CON and the reason why I rated it 2 stars is that the clip seems to break after 2-3 months of use. It always breaks at the same spot (at the hinge), which is made of cheap plastic. I've owned about a dozen of these things, and I wind up throwing them out after a few months (probably why Sandisk continues to make such a flimsy clip). Well no more because I'm finally switching brands; if I'm going to have to replace it every 3-4 months, I'm better off buying a $10 clippable unit from Hong Kong. If they ever make these with aluminum clips, or a similar material, I might reconsider. Another major con: This thing is NOT sweat-resistant. On at least four runs that I can recall, the song or volume controls became stuck due to sweat exposure (not rain, just sweat).

PROS:
-Intuitive, easy controls
-Small, lightweight
-Nice playlist feature

CONS:
-Clip breaks quickly under regular use (which hasn't been fixed in the generations of these players)
-Not at all sweat or moisture-resistant

Overall, this player is too costly for them to maintain such a poor design.

This is a perfectly good product, with some impressively sturdy wires and connections, and great support.   I was at first dismayed that the leads appeared to be reversed and would not charge any of my batteries. However! After reversing the leads myself with a pair of pliers and some electrical tape (which got things working) I emailed the company to let them know they might have a serious issue with their product. They were very quick to respond and very helpful, explaining that like the large Tamiyas, mini-Tamiyas had the red (positive) wire connecting to the square lead, and the black to the circular lead.   This left me confused, as none of my mini-tamiya batteries had this setup. The answer, after some research on the internet, is that for some ungodly reason the airsoft industry decided to reverse the norm on SOME mini-tamiyas. This adapter is made for the standard setup, but my batteries (most of which are made for airsoft) all have the red wire connected to the CIRCULAR lead, and the black to the square.   In conclusion, this is a perfectly good product, with some impressively sturdy wires and connections, and great support. However, it will probably not work for your airsoft batteries, which will all come with stupidly reversed leads compared to every other industry that uses Tamiya connectors.

The four USB charging sockets worked as advertised, and I got close to 2A out of one of them (the tablet would not draw more), but there is a limit of about 4A across all four sockets. The product listing claims there is a surge suppressor and EMI filter, but the packaging and product themselves make no claims about this. The strip is not UL-listed but does have an ETL mark.

I was looking for a new pair of headphones, because I'd been having issues with my Sennheiser CX 5.00i. I'm glad I came across Flare Audio R2A because I love them!

First, these have excellent noise cancellation abilities. The "ear plug" style bud tips are genius - you squeeze the foam and let them expand once you put them in, so that they are fitting you exactly. They are extremely comfortable to wear and the foam tip does not come off easily and stays in my ears (a huge problem I had with my Senn's - I kept on losing the rubber tips as I took the headphones out of my ears or bag because they were very loosely attached).

The sound quality is top notch at a wide range of sound levels - great bass, vocals, articulate instrumentation, etc. The tone of the sound is also warm and balanced (relative to the Senn's but also on an absolute level). You feel like you're in a cocoon of sound and the listening experience is very pleasant.

One unusual design element is the metal Y splitter. Initially I wasn't a fan and considered removing it as I thought it would be a nuisance, but actually I've grown to like them a lot, as they give the earphones more weight/substance (so that they don't get lost in my bag). And moreover, I learned that the splitter is this way because the earphones are meant to be worn cable over ear. Indeed, although I enjoyed wearing them the other way, it is actually nice to have the weight of the metal splitter when wearing the earphones with cables over ear. I wear them in both styles as I walk long distances and on my commute, and I haven't found the splitter to be an issue. If that's not your thing though, there are ways to remove it (instructions can be easily found online).

The level of thoughtfulness and detail that makes the earphones really excellent is also evident in the whole purchase experience. For example, the minimalist, elegant design of the package impressed me. Once I opened thebox (which resembled a jewelry box), it was very intuitive and easy to set up the earphones with the memory foams. Delivery was seamless and I received a nice "welcome / intro" email from the seller with helpful tips on getting started with them.

All in all, I'm super happy with my new headphones and I'm looking forward to using them to listen to my favorite music!

I live in Los Angeles. When I first got the FL5500A, I was informed that the best place for it was next to a window. I placed it there and it located no local channels. I expected that because the only window in the room faces west and the transmitters are located in a northeastern direction. I then placed the antenna high on a south facing interior wall expecting similar results. Instead, it located 113 local channels. I checked the signal strength of these channels and most of them, while not being extremely strong, were still acceptable. I tried a few other locations in the room but that one produced the best results.

However, the next time I checked out the local channels, many of them that previously produced a decent signal now could not be reached at all. Subsequent tries were also hit and miss. Some channels were accessible while many were not. And not all channels reacted the same way every time I tried to look at them. I wanted something that would produce consistent access to my local channels and in that respect, the antenna failed.

I therefore came to the conclusion that if you're in the right place for it to work, this antenna could be excellent. However, if you're in a place where the antenna can't function properly, it will be very disappointing. Because it behaved in such an inconsistent basis, my only option was to return it.

If someone is looking for an effective indoor antenna, I would suggest that they try the FL5000A first. I think it's probably the best antenna of its kind available. If it doesn't work, Amazon will always take it back--minus small return shipping charges. If I could, I would have rated the FL5500A both five stars because of its great potential and one star because it may not work at all. I settled for a middle ground of three stars.

I've always been a music lover and had speaker system in my bathroom. I know as weird as it might sound I do. I listen to music in the morning. I use a pebble watch to control music on my iPhone plugged into the speakers. The reason to use the pebble watch is because it's waterproof and allows me to skip songs in the shower. I wanted to resolve the issue of having to wear the watch in the shower and be able to take phone calls. This speaker is exactly what I needed.

The TaoTronics TT-SK03 Shower Speaker came very well packaged, and everything included inside the box seems very high quality. In the box, you get the TaoTronics TT-SK03 speaker, a 5-Volt USB charging cable, and an instruction manual. The included instruction manual is well written and covers all the necessary information, including a useful FAQ. The TaoTronics TT-SK03 Shower Speaker should be able to connect to almost any Bluetooth-enabled device very quickly, and without any issues. We connected this speaker to our iPhone and iPad. And both of these devices found this speaker straight away, and connected to it instantly, without any issues. The suction cup on the back of the speaker is very strong and sturdy. So far our speaker has not fallen off our tiles, or slipped down the wall. The sound quality is brilliant on this little speaker. As the sound quality is well balanced, clear, with a very good bass and treble. It is able to handle a range of different songs. Also this speaker can go surprisingly loud, we were very pleased with how loud this speaker could actually go. It could easily fill an average sized bathroom full with music. On the front of the speaker, you will find all the buttons you need to control your speaker. Which means that you can leave your phone in a separate room, and can still control your music directly from the speaker. All the buttons of this speaker are very responsive. For example, if I press the next button, it goes to the next song almost immediately. The TaoTronics TT-SK03 Shower Speaker takes around two hours to fully charge. Then you should get up to 6 hours of playback depending on volume levels. With the volume set to medium, we got up to 5.5 hours of playback before needing to recharge this device again. The Bluetooth range is also superb. As you can move your Bluetooth-enable device up to 10 meters away from your speaker, and it should not lose connection. And best of all you can take hands-free calls, even whilst in the shower or bath. When you receive an incoming call, the speaker will automatically pause the music whilst you’re on the call. The call quality is crystal clear through the speaker. And other callers reported that they could hear my voice very clearly.

The TaoTronics TT-SK03 Shower Speaker is Bluetooth compatible, and has a very simple pairing process. Meaning you should be able to connect this speaker to almost any Bluetooth compatible device. Unfortunately Bluetooth is the only way you can connect to this speaker. So if your device does not have Bluetooth built in, then you will not be able to use this speaker. The TaoTronics TT-SK03 is a water resistant speaker, it’s not waterproof. So it can handle the odd splashes and steam whilst in the shower or bath. However it’s not going to be able to handle being submerged into the water. As mentioned earlier, the TaoTronics TT-SK03 Shower Speaker has a simple Bluetooth pairing process. Simply hold down the middle button (power button) for about 3 seconds until you hear a short tune. You will then notice a Blue LED light flashing rapidly, indicating that the device is in pairing mode. Then on your compatible Bluetooth device, go into your Bluetooth settings and search for the speaker. Once you select the TaoTronics Bluetooth speaker, they should automatically pair together in a matter of seconds. You will know whether your devices are paired together, as you will hear another tune and then the Blue LED light will stop flashing rapidly. It’s also worth noting that after you’ve paired this speaker with your Bluetooth-enabled device once. It will remember that device and automatically pair with it every time you turn the speaker on. The TaoTronics TT-SK03 Shower Speaker also has a built-in rechargeable battery. Which the manufacturers say can give you up to 5-6 hours of playback (depending on volume levels). Another brilliant feature included with this speaker is that you can take hands-free calls. As this speaker has a built in microphone. Which allows you to answer and end incoming calls. Just simply press the phone button on the front to answer calls whilst in the bath or shower. Like most TaoTronic products, you get a 12-month warranty included. Which gives you confidence in the product, and company you have purchased this device from.

I haven't played these speakers for more than 3 hours at low volume, so they may not be fully broke in yet, but so far, they sound fantastic!

I'm using these as my computer mains with a custom built sub underneath tuned to 30Hz. My mains amp isn't terribly fancy, but it does have a 5-band graphic EQ on each channel and was running a pair of Infinity Primus p363's previously that are now making their way down to my theater system, so my EQ was previously set for the p363's.

I swapped these p163's in place of my p363's earlier this morning and haven't even touched my EQ yet, which is +10dB at 100Hz (my sub is tuned super low, so the mains are taking care of my mid-bass) and +5dB at 10kHz - other than that, it's all flat. Right out of the box, they sounded fairly well, but they do seem to be breaking in very nicely and sound quite good given my crappy room acoustics (thinking about making some sound absorption panels). I can hear every cymbal hit and nuance music and am hearing instruments I never heard before in songs I'm quite familiar with. I even just heard a recording imperfection that I didn't know existed in a recording I've heard many many times before! This isn't really a true full-range speaker (-3dB is like 50-something Hz I think), so you will need a sub for the low stuff, but it does everything from mid-bass on very nicely. Money well spent and would certainly buy again! Heck, I'm even thinking of getting another set for my surrounds!

With a slight boost in treble (I do like my top end boosted a little for crisp-ness), the top end is nice and crisp, but not harsh or shrill - just nice and smooth. It sounds like the instruments are in the room with you! Very nicely done for a "cheap" speaker! Obviously, there are speaker out there that are "better", but you'll be paying several times the price and at that level, you really should be investing in proper room acoustics anyways.

I spent around 8 hours reviewing different power supplies my criteria was safe and affordable protection for a new
custom computer build.

I did not need nor want a power back up but something that would protect me from power surges from a near buy lighting strike
or simple everyday micro power fluctuations and this one rated very high it's specs for an affordable surge protection.

The other 2 models I almost chose were
1. Tripp Lite HT10DBS
2. APC P11VNT3 3020J 11-outlet

I actually bought choice #2 for my Dad for his cheaper computer he got earlier this year.

Pros.
When I was looking for myself for such an expensive rig I dug a little bit deeper on my search and what made this
one stand out over my other 2 choices that I narrowed down was the fact it has a LIFETIME warranty no hassle
replacement policy that other users have verified (means a lot when a company stands behind it's product)

2. Very high joules rating protection with a nice added bonus of a power filter to give consistent stable power.
3. It has Led lighting to indicate that your protection is still good and if it is grounded properly.
4. Unit can be used as a standard Surge protector or has an Eco setting that when a primary device such as a computer
plugged in to the master control when it is turned off so are all your printers speakers monitors Etc will have ALL their power cut off
so no vampire energy effects very nice feature that does it's job well on my stuff.

Cons.
1. The APC model is cheaper and has a better layout for plugins I like that design since normal cords went in the center
while bulky power supplies went above or below.

2. Ethernet protection is a Joke since it does not support today's higher internet speeds but at least if you have cable internet
like I do you can at least take advantage of the coaxial protection.

3. Wish you could rotate the transformer row plug in orientation since so many manufactures make them point to the side
instead of hanging down which unfortunately cover one or more of the plugs.
This can be remedied by purchasing a one foot extension here on Amazon (Monoprice 105296 1-Feet 16AWG Power Extension Cord)
cost is around 5$ per extension which I bought one wish I had gotten two of them. (The extension is very good high quality)

Overall this is a very good affordable surge protection from a reputable company that stands behind it's product and it's warranty
from the research that I did.

So for a good price without breaking the bank go with this unit.

If you have the money to throw around and don't mind taking up a bunch of Extra space I would go with
Monster Power Reference Center for around 300-400$ (I use this for my very high end entertainment Center)

The 3.5mm wire is completely intact, and the only indication of being a workhorse are the slight plastic finish erosion on the sides and small cracks on the sides of the ear pads. I should mention I am rough on my gear. Time to catch a flight? Throw it in the backpack or suitcase and wrestle the bag shut with no regards for their contents. Time to give them to a studio musician? Don't even bother handing it to them, just chuck it across the room and if they crash into the ground it's fine, they'll still work perfectly.

They sound as close to monitors as possible. The bass is clear though quieter than monitors. The treble is clear but not sharp. Want to mix loud? Crank up the volume. Your ears will break before these puppies.

I would not recommend mixing exclusively on these headphones (or any headphones), but they are a great reference point, and allow for general mixing. Overall I definitely recommend these - I have yet to find better headphones. $150 is a steal.

After changing the location of the antenna, FOX came in but no CBS. On the wall where the TV is located is another wall, a window is located in front of the TV. We moved the TV to where it was facing the wall and its back was to the window. The antenna was lying on the TV stand and at this point, it showed all channels. However, my friend does not want to move her TV.

She has another Samsung in the LR area. The TV's back is on the wall that is behind the wall in the BR where the other Samsung was located. In this case, the antenna would not show CBS, but showed the rest of the channels. There is a window near the wall but not get it close enough to where the antenna could be located. We moved it around the wall, but again no CBS channel. It seemed as though since the TVs were not located on an outside wall, the antenna would not pick up all the channels.

I took the antenna home and placed it on a Samsung that is located on an outside wall. All channels came in including CBS and FOX. I then took it to a BR with a Phillips TV that had a second wall near a bathroom. The antenna would not work until it was placed near the window in the BR. So, this antenna is sensitive. I'm keeping it because it does work, but depends on whether you can get a clear single or not. It is apparent if there is a double wall where the TV is located, this antenna will not pull in all channels.

What is being sold here (used) is not actually the original AG-790A which was sold prior to 2011, that got great reviews.

Looking through the air vents on top of the unit, you can see the main board is not an AG-790A board, but an AG-790E board. I was able to determine this because the schematics and main board layouts for both of these units are available on the internet. This unit built after 2010 is actually based on the AG-790E platform. The original AG-790A, apparently built between 2003 and 2010 was based on a Toshiba stereo chipset and had Fairchild Power Amplifier transistors (150W absolute maximum output). This post 2010 AG-790E like unit appears to be based on an obsolete stereo chipset made by a now defunct Chinese(?) company. The AG-790E Power Amplifier transistors are from Sanken and are rated at 130W maximum output, which when de-rated, would have to operate at a much lower RMS power.

The advertised specifications this product appear to be directly quoted from the 2003 Toshiba chipset data sheets.

Although this unit has some pretty nice features for the price, like switched AC outlets on the back, and a Loudness button, I found the performance of this post 2010 unit to be insipid. There is no way this thing is putting out 100 Watts per channel. The Bass output of this unit is lacking, and the Loudness control is imperceptible if there is any at all. The memory functions and multi function control knobs and buttons are frustrating to operate, although I could live with them. I can't live with the insipid performance, thus I will probably return the unit - the loudness button doesn't function anyways. I am just really dissatisfied with this thing.

Additional Note: I bought this unit used from Amazon. This is the second one of these units I bought from them, the first one I had to return because it was advertised as "Like New" and when it came, it was scratched, filthy and had damaged and missing parts. The second unit I received (the one being reviewed here) is actually in "Like New" condition, with all of the accessories.

After connecting the new unit up with our DirecTV Genie HDR, our AppleTV, and our Sony BluRay player, I ran the speaker calibration, and all seemed well. Unfortunately we soon discovered that about every 4th or 5th time we powered on our system to watch DirecTV, we would get no picture. Unfortunately, the new unit exhibited the same problem as the original, and in addition would also take several seconds to start playing audio whenever we skipped backwards in the show we were watching. Annoying, since the usual reason for skipping backwards was to try to catch a bit of dialog we had missed! Thinking again that surely HK didn't have a design problem, I spent several months experimenting with new cables, changing the order and timing of powering on components, etc., all to no avail. I explained to the new support person the history of my situation, and told him I was done with HK and wanted my money back. He asked if we had bought from HK directly. I said, no, from Amazon. Beautiful sound, far better than the price would suggest. Not sure how they do it, but I remember reading in the run up to Pono's release how some felt the sound felt almost liquid in its beauty. Hearing it now, I can well understand what they mean. Everything I throw at it sounds wonderful. It sounded great through regular earpieces. But what really made it bloom was getting balanced cables for my Sennheiser HD600's and listening through that. That gave the impression of a few more db in volume, but more than that. The music had more of a sense of 3 dimensions, if I'm not stretching too much. The soundstage was more defined and the separation of instruments improved. I bought the 24/192 of Every Picture Tells a Story last week from the Pono store and it was the best I've ever heard that, and I've heard a few remastered or otherwise enhanced versions. I could run through album after album and say the same. And of course it doesn't require that tracks be purchased from Pono - ALL my HD tracks up to 2x DSD sound great on it. As others have noted, navigation can be tricky because of the small size and sensitivity of the screen. I wish that were different, but one can't have everything, and it's not so bad that I would subtract a star.

So the device is an easy 5 stars. The store I'd have to put at 4 stars at most, though. The selection of 24 bit tracks is not what I expected. The way it was described before rollout made it seem ALL tracks would be HD. And there are many 24 bit albums. But the majority are 16 bit. Then Neil Young talked about that and made the point that he felt 16 bit WAS HD in comparison to MP3, and that MP3 was the real problem, not CD quality (16 bit). I probably heard what I wanted to hear to an extent, and I have found 24 bit albums in the Pono store that I don't see elsewhere, like Springsteen's The Rising. And 16 bit albums do indeed sound good through the Pono and I have bought a few 16 bit when no 24 bit version was available. And for that matter, MP3 sounds better through Pono.

And the Pono community and customer support are great.

All in all, an easy recommendation for those to whom sound quality matters.

These are great headphones! I have owned many, many headphones over the past few years (my wife would say far too many), and these are definitely in my top 5. There are three things I look for in a pair of headphones: 1) sound; 2) comfort; and 3) style.

1) Sound:
These headphones sound great, which is true of the entire V-Moda line-up of headphones (I also own the M-80's). They might have too much bass for so-called audiophiles, but I use them primarily with my xbox one controller, so they are perfect for videogames and movies. I don't spend too much time discussing sound because its highly subjective. They sound good and they have reviewed well.

2) Comfort:
With the stock ear pads, these headphones are of average comfort. They get somewhat warm, but they won't hurt your ears or head with prolonged use. The best feature of these headphones is that you can upgrade the stock ear pads with different colors and sizes. If you would prefer a much more comfortable fit, I strongly recommend that you pick up the XL ear pads for $20-25 in grey. The sound is a little better with the larger ear pads, but they become the most comfortable headphones I own at that point...more comfortable than the Parrot Zik wireless headphones (highly recommended), my Sony MDRXB950AP/H silver headphones (also highly recommended), and the V-Moda M-80's (not nearly as comfortable.

3) Design:
These headphones look really great...very futuristic with great materials. The white leather with grey trim and shiny metal accents creates a premium look that really stands out. The pictures don't do these headphones justice. They might stand out a little too much for those people who prefer a more-traditional black headphone look. You can change up the look with ear cup shields with different colors and finishes, but I actually really like the stock polished silver look.

One thing to note, the similar V-Moda M-80's I own had some frayingand unraveling of the headphone cord's fabric weave. I haven't had any problems yet with the LP's, and the cords can be replaced easily, but its something to keep in mind.

I've been looking for a nice Bluetooth speaker so I can listen to my tunes outside, either in the yard or in the campground. I think I just found it.

Initial charging took about an hour. It came pre-charged, but I wanted to "top it off" anyway. If you lose the included power cord, don't worry, you can just use the one from you cell phone, or any other microUSB cable. It is just the standard plug-in for today.
When you turn on the unit, it tells you "Power On". When you enter into pairing mode, it tells you "Pairing". When connected, it tells you "connected". And when you turn it off it says, you guessed it, "Power off". Pairing was a breeze to a Kyocera Hydro XTRM, LG Lucky, and my Dell laptop.
The controls are easy to use and intuitive. The instruction manual covers all of the functions very well.
Sound quality was very good for the price range. This isn't a Bose, but you aren't paying for one either. One trick when using this: try moving the speaker around a bit for the best sound, turning the 3D on and off. For example, when I put this in the bathroom, I found that putting it in the corner, facing out of course, it had the best sound. Just sitting out in the middle of the countertop left it sounding flat.
Call quality was a little bit "tinny" but I couldn't determine whether it was the caller or the speaker since even my phone made them sound tinny. Either way, the callers are easy to understand and they have no trouble hearing you clearly. For me, this works well for "family time". We can get everyone in the room and call the far off relatives, letting everyone in on the conversation. Definitely better than using the speakerphone option on my cell phone.

There is a lot to like about these Noontec ear buds. The overall fit and finish is excellent – these feel like they cost a good deal more than they do. The jack and cabling covering both feel sturdy and substantial. I like that the cables are flat. In addition to be tangle-free, I find flat cables to be much easier to deal with when using ear buds while exercising – the flat profile stays put much better than a round profile, even without using a clip (which is included). There’s also a slider to adjust the cable separation.

Also, simple things are done right, such as clearly marking L and R buds. Sounds like it would be easy to do that, but it is a feature that eludes a number of ear bud manufacturers. It also comes with a nice quality case and extra ear pads.

It also has a multi-function button with a mic if you want to do hands-free calling, skip, pause, etc. I don’t use that feature on ear buds, so I didn’t test it out. But I can say that the multifunction button also feels sturdy and substantial, and is easy to find on the cord.

But the main reason for getting them is the sound quality. In a word, it's excellent. I was not expecting it to be as good as it was given the price. Very clear and crisp throughout all ranges, with excellent separation. The bass is strong but not overwhelming. Granted, if you’re a fan of skull-crushing bass these probably will not be the best choice, but if you’re looking for clear, natural, balanced sound, these should be on your short list.

The in-ear comfort is also pretty good. It’s not as good as Brainwavz which, for my ear, remain the most comfortable of any in-ear buds I've used. I’d rate these as mostly comfortable – certainly comfortable enough for extended wearing without getting ear fatigue. I would like to see a thicker, more cushioned pad that has more give to it.

The small quibble with in-ear comfort brings my rating to 4.5 stars but I’ll round up to 5 due to the excellent build quality and clear, natural sound. These sound and feel like they should cost a lot more than they do, and are definitely worth considering if you’re looking for high-end performance at mid-range prices.

I think this item is a great idea. I don't bother much with wireless devices, but I do like my gadgets, so I have wires all over. These sleeves seemed like they would be a simple, attractive way to clear out the webbing of wires behind my computer and my entertainment system, so I ordered a set.

Unfortunately, when the items arrived and I started putting my cables in order, the threading on the first sleeve came undone and the zipper started pulling away from the sleeve. I thought maybe I had been too rough in bundling up the wires and trying to zip the sleeve closed (I hadn't), so I secured the broken end with a twist tie and moved on to the next sleeve, taking extra care not to put too much strain on the seam when I zipped it up. However, this one came loose as well. And so did the third one.

The fourth held. But finding three out of four sleeves defective was not acceptable.

I contacted the company and told them what happened. Like I said before, I really liked the idea of this product, and I didn't want to tarnish the highly positive reviews with a one star rating, unless it really deserved such. And I couldn't believe the product had received so many positive reviews if it literally came apart in one's hands.

I received a reply from Tech Vendor, and despite some mishaps with Amazon's messaging system not sending my replies, I had a pleasant experience with them. They did want photographic verification of the broken sleeves, which is certainly a reasonable request, so I provided it. Once they received and reviewed the photos, they offered to give me a replacement set. They went about this in a different manner than I would have - they asked me to purchase a new set from Amazon, and then they refunded me that purchase - but I'm not on their end of things and there may be factors that make handling the replacement in such a manner safer, beneficial, or financially worthwhile. It wasn't any trouble, and I'm sure they would have done it differently had I asked them to.

The replacement sleeves arrived in a couple days (Amazon Prime is great), and I was pleased to see they were all in fine condition. The seams were tight and did not break under the little stress test I performed on them. I was even a bit rougher with this set, pulling on the seams more than is reasonable just so I could write a thorough review, and they did not tear.

So this is a great idea, a great product, and a great company. I can definitely recommend doing business with them.

But my old Creative X-Fi buttons stopped working forcing me to search for a a replacement MP3 player that supported bookmarks for audio books. It turned the MP3 manufacturers just don't think that feature is necessary, but for me it kind of a deal breaker. That lead me to two options. Rockbox a Sansa Clip or the Conwon I9+.  So I bought the Cowon as a refurb; in part to lower the risk in case the I9+ did not meet my needs.  Then the battle began..  First it was the awkward and non-intuitive operating system. It was a couple of weeks before I finally felt comfortable of the operating system. It took some trial and error realize how the sub-menu's functioned when you hold the >/= for several seconds, to create bookmarks and retrieve bookmarks. For some reason I also struggled with the resume play function. I finally realized that you have to press >/= button twice. Knowing saved a lot of unnecessary bookmarking. (I seem to recall that you have to turn on the resume play feature first in the settings because it not enabled by default.)  So now all the operating system battles were resolved, I could just enjoy the player. From that I came to appreciate that in someways the design was simple and classically elegant in the Apple style.  The sound quality seemed very good, but I am no audiophile by any means. My one design annoyance is putting the sound control buttons on the opposite side from the menu button. It is way too easy to press the menu button accidentally while trying to change the sound level. To get around that problem I now hold the player between two finger of right hand while pressing the sound buttons with my left. That way the menu button cannot be touched.   Finally my second battle was with Audible, an Amazon owned company. After several weeks of hit and miss technical support, Audible announced does not support the Cowon I9+, only the I9. Because I have the (as it now turns out now unsupported) Cowon 9+, my entire library of about 80 Audible books cannot be used without purchasing another MP3 player on top of the Cowon, which I just bought recently from Amazon.  Very frustrating! For now I plan to suspend any further purchases from Audible until I can come up with alternative Plan B.  My suggestion is that someone contact Amazon immediately and add the non-compatible information to the Cowon 9+ device description. In fact, you should note Audible compatibility for all supported and unsupported devices to the Amazon website. At least that way, no one else will make the mistake that I just made.  I mean really, aren’t you the same company? Maybe it’s time to act like it so that consumer benefits.

One thing that surprised me about the unit is how small it is. It is basically the size of a postage stamp (remember those?). The only tricky thing about the Indigo unit (which oddly costs more in Indigo -- you would think that Black would be the optional color) is the fact that a single button controls all the functions. You need to have great hand-eye coordination to hold the button down for just the right amount of time (2 Seconds for ON/OFF, 5 Seconds for pairing mode, 10 Seconds for clearing all the existing pairings). This is not a fatal flaw and you just need to pay attention to the color and blinking pattern of the LED to let go of the button when it enters the right mode. I also found that the range is pretty limited. It works fine when you are watching TV, but if you walk to kitchen for a snack or to the bathroom, expect the signal to degrade and cut off at around 5 meters. The 30-meter range is pretty much a fantasy. It works fine for its intended purpose, but don't expect to be able to walk all over your house listening to the TV show.

Couple of pro tips:

1) When you are pairing your headphones with the Indigo, you must turn off the BT function on every other device in the general vicinity. The Indigo takes a while to connect and pair and if you have any other device that has BT turned in, it will jump in front ofthe Indigo and you will not be able to complete the process. I was having a terrible time until I realized that one of our IPADs was connecting to my hedphones before the Indigo had a chance to connect. One I turned off the BT on the IPAD, everything went smoothly.

2) Related to 1 above, be patient when connecting to the Indigo. It takes a bit longer than you are used to with other devices and getting impatient and pressing the button messes up the whole process and you have to start over.

3) Whenever possible, connect the Indigo to the cable box or other video/audio source rather than the TV. You will probably need one of these (http://www.amazon.com/3-5mm-Stereo-Female-Y-Cable-6-Inch/dp/B000I23TTE/ref=pd_bxgy_23_img_y), If you connect the Indigo to the TV, you will have to turn off the internal TV speakers to use the Indigo for its intended purpose. This works fine until another person in your household (who is less familiar with the TV settings -- you know who I am talking about) tries to use the TV during the day and you will inevitably get an annoyed call at work starting with \\"What did you with the TV again?\\" Connecting the Indigo to the audio source will let you just turn the TV volume down and control the volume using the headset controls. This may not always be possible, but if you can do it this way, you will not regret it.

Please note that I only used the TX mode and cannot comment on the RX mode. As a bonus, I noticed that when listening to a show on headphones improves the quality of the audio and the effects and makes the experience much more immersive.

I have used the previous version of [[ASIN:B002V8C3W2 eneloop AA-to-D Size Spacers/Adapters]]. One problem with the old version is that it uses the negative terminal of the AA cell directly as base. When used in my [[ASIN:B000IXAJVY MagLite ST3D016 3-D Cell LED Flashlight]], for example, the battery spring is too large to make proper contact with the AA cell.

The new D spacers in this product ([[ASIN:B00JHKSLRI Panasonic K-KJS1MCA2BA eneloop AA Pre-Charged Rechargeable Batteries with 2 "D" Spacers]]), however, have flat negative terminals like that found on real alkaline D cells. Therefore I can use them in my Maglite without problems. Using those D spacers also makes my Maglite a lot lighter, which is a good thing - as long as I don't need to use it as an impact weapon.

On the other hand, it is important to note that the energy stored in a real alkaline D cell is about 5-8 times greater than that in a eneloop AA cell. A typical alkaline D cell is rated for 18,000mAh when supplying a light load of 50mA. When used in a heavy-load appliance such as Maglite, the battery capacity drops to around 10,000mAh. Still, this is 5x higher than the capacity of a 2000mAh eneloop AA cell. Therefore I can expect just 4 hours of runtime from a set of three rechargeable AA cell, compared to over 20 hours from three alkaline D cells.

If longer runtime is important to you, consider D spacers that can accept two AA cells in each shell. Doing so effectively doubles the runtime. I have tested an inexpensive product and found it to work in my Maglite - after some modifications. See my review on [[ASIN:B0094DH1E2 AA to D Size Battery Adapter Case]] for details.

[Additional Note]
On the back of the eneloop spacer it says "Insert only a Panasonic rechargeable battery" and "Never insert a non-rechargeable battery" (in Red). The fact is, you can insert any brand of rechargeable AA cell into this spacer. You can even use non-rechargeable alkaline AA cell in case of emergency. I do not see any potential danger in doing so, although the battery life will be very poor.

I was supplied a sample for test and evaluation, and I promise that my review is fair and honest. From the moment I received the Anker A3143 Bluetooth Speaker I was impressed. The speaker looks and feels like a premium speaker. It is very solid in your hands and the glossy finish on the top is a nice touch. The bottom has a nice rubber that feels like it is going to last a long time. The rubber will keep the A3143 from sliding on a slippery surface but not collect every speck of dirt it comes across it. The buttons are very responsive and feel nice to the touch. The + and - buttons double as next/previous buttons and volume up/down buttons. To seek to the next/previous song simply tap the +/- button. To increase/decrease the volume hold the +/- button and the volume will start decreasing/increasing. Along with the +/- buttons there is also a play/pause button and a power button which is also used to pair the device. On the back of the A3143 there is a micro USB port for charging and an AUX port for connecting non-bluetooth devices. All of the cables you could possibly need are Included with the speaker (1 - micro USB cable and 1 - AUX cable).  Upon turning the speaker on for the first time I immediately knew it had amazing sound with plenty of base. The tone that plays when you power on the device makes it apparent it will be plenty powerful. Pairing the device with my Android phone was very easy. All you have to do is: Hold the power button on the speaker for about 6 seconds and the LED will flash blue. Then search for available Bluetooth devices on your mobile device and select the Anker A3143 . The speaker will play a sound notifying you it has paired. The sound quality is what you are all truly looking for and the A3143 does not disappoint. It is more than loud enough for the beach, pool, or even a small party in a good size room. My living area is open and approximately 20'x10' and its loud enough to easily fill the entire space and over power a group of peopletalking. I listen to all genres of music (rock, rap,hip-hop, pop, indie) and I couldn't be happier with the sound quality and the level of base it puts out. I've had a few speakers that didn't deliver with sound but I am as happy as can be that I finally found a speaker in the Anker A3143 Bluetooth Speaker that finally meets all of my needs.

I use this cable to connect my TV on one side of my bedroom to the speaker on my nightstand so I don't have to use headphones to hear what I'm watching. Like I said, this seems to be an inherent flaw with this type cable. But it's amazing to me that someone, somewhere, can't figure out a cost-effective solution. I'd like to imagine if I decided to pay 3- or 4-times this price I'd get a decent cable, but I'm a cheapskate. I'm just not going to pay that much for this type cable. The farthest flower bed she had to work on was about forty from the porch and the sound was clear and crisp with no interference. She then took the speaker and went around the back of the house, out of sight of the phone on the porch, and started to get some intermittent interference. I'm giving this 5 stars as an outdoor speaker but with the stipulation that it be kept in sight of the device it is paired with for the best performance.

I will be reviewing the VGA + 3.5mm Audio to HDMI Converter (model number ENK-VTH3020).

Picture Quality:
The picture quality is excellent. I used it on a full HD computer monitor and the picture was quite clear. It looked slightly fuzzy when closely compared to HDMI, but looked no less sharp than a VGA to VGA connection. Overall, I'm quite pleased with the picture quality.

Audio Quality:
The audio quality is very good. I tested it and it is stereo audio.

Lag:
I compared the lag when using this converter to using just an HDMI cable. There seemed to be only a very little bit of lag using the converter, so it should be fine for anyone except the most hardcore gamers.

Design:
The device is compact and good looking. On one side is the VGA video and 3.5mm audio input, and on the opposite side is the HDMI output. On the side to the left of the VGA side is the on/off switch, and opposite to that is the USB power port. You will need an available USB port to power this device, unless you buy a USB to AC adapter.

Value:
For the price, this device (plus the free HDMI cable that came with it) performs very well. I would definitely recommend it.

I bought the CNX since I needed a 1 stop solution DAC/ Streamer. Sadly I am very disappointed in the product although I had high hopes for it. The DAC section seemed ok, I believe it's a wolfson chip based DAC which is very standard nowadays, so sounds it just fine (although it will not support Hi Res DSD files, luckily for Cambridge that type of content is hard to come by still. My main issues were two. First off the controller app for iOS is terrible, it simply does not work, I tried to play songs to no avail, I could only add whole albums to the queue (?!) The provided remote does the trick and handles the library better but you would have to be sitting next to the unit to be able to read the little screen and who does that anyway? Additionally the streamer does not index your files so access is a little laggy, especially if you have a large collection like me. Finally it did not play well with my QNAP NAS, I could see the files on the Upnp server but no matter what I did they could not be played over the network, even though every other networked device at home accessed those files without a problem, I have a whole house multiple SONOS players setup and they connect to my NAS (along with every other computer and iPhone in the house) just fine. So as a pure streamer the CNX was a failure for me, other users may have more luck with another brand of NAS perhaps and once the iOS apps are improved it has the potential to be a good product, right now the streamer part of the CNX is sadly very mediocre. I will be returning the unit soon and maybe go for an Auralic Aries.

Just finished loading my 400th DVD, each in a cut-down paper sleeve, and the total result is a mess. The case itself is impossible to close perhaps due to the extra width added by the sleeves. The sleeve/DVD combo does work, fitting easily into the pockets but, obviously, the case itself doesn't have any wiggle room. Neither do the pocket pages - they seem, initially, to stack fine, lying easily on top of one another until you get to 10 or 15 pages and then the stack begins to start going oblique. My 50th page is angled at about 40 degrees. All of this might be due to the extra bulk of the sleeves but one flaw clearly isn't: after sliding the last DVD into it's slot, I picked the case up by the handle and immediately had the entire body of the page construction drop to the floor. 400 paper sleeves can't be that heavy.

Final point: each page is constructed of a nylon/fabric mesh as the interior side while the exterior is a U-shaped clear, flexible thin plastic, heat bonded pocket top. Looks fine until you take a close look at that nylon/fabric mesh. Stick a naked DVD in that pocket and watch the mesh scratch the hell out of it. It might be ok for half-a-dozen in-and-outs but the interior mesh is going to create a lot of wear. No way in hell I'd ever expose a naked DVD to it.

DVD storage is a bitch. Towers are fine for a small number of store bought packages but if you've got a ton of recorded-off-the-TV movies and stuff, well-protected in paper sleeves (jewel cases are too fragile and bulky and bugs can get inside), trying to find an easy way to store them while keeping them in order and not having them fly all over the place every time you're looking for or adding something is a major pain. Right now I'm thinking of something like an old-fashioned library card catalog, if anyone remembers those. Looks like I'll be going Arts and Crafts.

Back to the case: it might have worked fine with naked DVDs, except that those DVDs would be exposed to the excessive wear of the interior mesh. Not a well-thought-out product.

This splitter was intended to allow easier switching between two PC's connected to the same monitor (not both at the same time). The monitor has only a DVI-A combo (digitial and analog) input, no legacy VGA. One PC has DVI output, and other PC VGA output. Prior to trying this splitter, I'd been using a dedicated VGA to DVI-A cable on the latter PC, a straight DVI-I cable on the other, and manually switching the cables at the monitor's input.

This cable switching has gotten old, hence this splitter. However, when the splitter is in use, the PC with VGA output fails to recognize the monitor type, defaulting instead to "Generic Non-PnP Monitor". The practical effect is that the display driver reduces the screen resolution to a "safe" value well below the capability of the monitor. This particular resolution also distorts shapes on the screen, making it even less acceptable.

Admittedly, my application is not necessarily the original intended use case for this splitter-adapter (I imagine that it was to plug into a PC graphics card featuring DVI-A output, to permit either an analog or digital monitor to be connected). However, on the surface I can't see why my application shouldn't work. All other basic display functions do appear to work for the both the DVI and VGA connector. Hence the downgraded satisfaction rating.

I had an original pair of Pro4AA I bought new in the 70s that I gave to a friend when I moved. Later when looking to replace them and not being able to find any I bought a pair of Pro3AA Titanium. These seemed somewhat comparable in bass response to Pro4AA, are lighter and more comfortable but way too bright in the upper frequency range.  I found Koss had resurrected the Pro4AA so I bought those and was immediately disappointed. The similarity to the original is purely cosmetic; while a bit more comfortable than the original (they don't clamp on your head like a pair of vice grips) they don't sound anywhere near the same. Which brought me to the purchase of the Pro4AA Titanium... They are lighter and more comfortable to wear but sounded like crap: very hollow bass and lower midrange.  Quite accidently though I discovered if I pressed the earcups fairly firmly to my head they sounded remarkably like their original counterparts. After a bit of pondering it struck me- the difference was the liquid-filled ear cushions on the original 4AAs! The foam-filled cushions on the titanium are just too stiff and unpliable to conform around the ear and seal properly.  After brain-storming a bit I decided to 'ventilate' the cushions by perforating the backsides of them to let them be able to 'deflate'.  Bingo... not only did they feel more like the originals liquid ear cushions they now are sealing around my ears properly without pressing them  against my ears.  Problem solved.

First, I confess to a bit of hyperkinetic frame of mind when doing this review. I’ve been using a TV only its built-in audio for 3 years, and I know what I’ve been missing, as I have a nice JBL stereo system handling audio duties in the living room. It was a big improvement to deploy the Solo 15.

OVERALL
Smooth audio performance, though short of audiophile quality (not expected in this price range), handles an effective mix of signal types, including Bluetooth and YouTube streamed from smart devices. Especially good for well-recorded vocals streamed from uncompressed sources, but even good from higher quality MP3’s and even AAC.

TV + SMARTPHONE USES
The Bose Solo 15 was a welcome solution that was easy to set up and performed quite well across the audio sources that I tried. Keep in mind that this unit will not only handle TV audio duties, but you can use its Bluetooth source inputs to stream audio from a smartphone or tablet and listen to podcasts. For me, that makes it much more valuable than units lacking that feature. At the risk of belaboring the point, let me remind that includes streaming YouTube or MP4 files from your mobile devices -- in the event that you have an older TV that doesn’t have a YouTube hookup or a proxy for that feature, such as Google and Amazon offer.

Setup was easy. For the Dynex TV this was paired with, I used Coax audio (all required cable types are provided by Bose, albeit pretty short lengths, and includes the power cable; you might need an extension cord). There’s additional setup to unify your remote use so you don’t need to use both. In our case, we’re using an upgraded Tivo remote with an alpha keyboard in it, so we aren’t giving that up anytime soon.

For Bluetooth, select the icon on the Bose remote, and then pair the device. Fast and easy. There’s a “clear” devices button to undo it. (There is no visual cue for the Bluetooth setups. Bose offers an upgraded remote for separate purchase.)

PROS
Fast setup and separate remote
Smooth spectrum responsiveness
Sturdy enough to mount beneath Cable + Tivo tuner + hard drive boxes
Good for both classical and rock music (see my assessment below)
Especially crisp and pleasant for vocals
Loud enough for most uses

CONS

SPL follows its 75W rating
Reduced stereo separation vs. separate speakers
No tone controls
No separate subwoofer
A little latency before audio starts when changing channels
Not loud enough for an outdoor party

I'm not an audiophile. I just wanted something that was an upgrade from my tv speakers (Samsung PN60F8500). It's not a full sound system, but it is a significant upgrade over the tv internal speakers. The HDMI ARC capababilty is huge plus. I've had it over six months so I can say that it does not always turn on automatically when you turn on your tv even when using ARC (9 out of 10 times it does), but I use a macro on my logitech remote (a harmony 300) to turn them both on at the same time to get around this (there is still a 5 second delay or so). The distance b/w the subwoofer and the sound bar makes a difference in making a connection between the two.  As other reviewers have noted, 5-6 feet is optimal, otherwise it cuts out, it takes a little bit of time to find this optimal distance, but I've found a happy place now (it didn't take that much time). It does not support DTS which is a little more annoying than i expected (a lot of movies/shows support DTS but not Dolby), but it is clear that DTS is not supported. It shines when whatever you are playing supports Dolby Digital (I watched "We Were Soldiers Once" on Netflix which supported Dolby surround sound and it really shined). Stereo mode is still a significant upgrade over tv speakers. You can't turn the bass setting all the way up, the subwoofer will come in and out. I think I have the bass set at 0, treble at +4, sound at clear and surround sound turned on and have found that is perfect for me. For the price, I really am happy with it, but I am not an audiophile and I think you if are expecting a full surround sound audio experience then you will be disappointed, but if you really just want a very significant upgrade over your crappy flat-screen internal speakers at a good price, then you will be pleasantly surprised. As added information, I also have a Panasonic ST50 plasma tv which had better speakers and I am not moved enough to purchase this sound bar for that TV. The Panasonic's internal speakers are much better than the Samsung PN60F8500 (more than good enough for me). don't get me wrong, this sound bar would still be a good upgrade, but not enough for me. If I wanted to upgrade the speakers on that tv, then I would want a better sound bar to make enough of a difference (which would cost a lot more money).

Only caution is that the wall mount bracket is just 17" wide so it really is designed for maximum 16" on center stud spacing. If your studs are spaced 24" on center, either look for a mount with a wider wall bracket or plan on some construction work (e.g., to somehow span the existing studs). Also, It is best if the two studs you will be hitting are fairly well centered on where you you want your TV to actually sit. Our TV sits between two windows and we wanted it centered. The wall mount bracket ended up about 2" closer to one window than the other just because that is where the wall studs were. Our TV had the 400x400mm mounting pattern and the TV support rails are wide enough that we just shifted the TV about 2" off-center relative to the wall mount bracket and presto - TV is back to being centered between the windows.
