The BX-100 arrives in a sturdy and attractive box and includes a brief instructions sheet and both a micro-USB cable for charging and an audio cable for the line-in input. The speaker itself is an attractive design. I got the black with red accents design and like it very much. The finish is also a very good quality with a soft rubbery texture with a good feel and grip due to the non-slick surface (so you wont drop this when carrying it around). The design is angled slightly upwards which helps aim the speakers in your direction for casual, personal listening. All the inputs are on the back along with the power switch and the control buttons are on the top(and they are smooth and work well, while unobtrusive and not breaking the sleek design, much better than some I've tried.

You get audio input, a USB flash-drive port, a micro-SD (also known as TF) card port, and the micro-USB charging port. All work as expected and this nice, full complement of ports is a nice features missing from some BT speakers I've seen. I was able to play songs from USB drives and micro-SD cards without any issues, though you have little control of the order of play (common with these type speakers), just next-previous song, play/pause,volume, the basics. But nice to have none-the-less.

All my devices could connect via Bluetooth without problems and connection was fast and error free. Everything worked exactly as it should.

So...the most important thing for any speaker, BT or otherwise is sound quality. How does the BX-100 stack up? Well, in short, very well. The sound quality is up there with the best in this price range that I have heard, very balanced and with very good bass response for this size. It is much better than the average in this price range and I found the sound very pleasant. Vocals were crisp and clear, bass was good without being boomy, and mids and highs were sweet. Among the best I've heard, recently, for this low price. The loudness is more than enough for casual, personal listening. (You get two 3 watt speakers which is not the max you can find in this range, but plenty for this use and price.)

And we haven't even talked about the Alarm clock, yet, which can wake you to your favorite song (from a TF card or USB stick). Or the FM radio which worked well. (As I have more time with this unit, I will come back and update with anything significant that I discover.)

I had two players now, which gives some points of comparison.

I used this player and the "Diver (TM) Waterproof MP3 Player with LCD Display".

The Sony Walkman has the advantage of being in one piece, which means you don't have to plug anything to it when swimming. It is also light and compact. This has drawbacks too, though: first, it always gets entangled in everything that come in contact with it (my goggles, my swimming bag,...). Second, if you have small ears, the Sony will not fit well, and you spend about 1/4th of your time readjusting it. After 30 minutes, it starts aching, because the pressure on your ears becomes too strong. I also find it difficult to operate, since it has no LCD display.

The "Diver (TM)..." is more classic: you have a player, to which you connect your waterproof earphones. These have buds of different sizes, and there is one size that fits my (small) ears :). It fits my head much better, does not hurt, and is easier to operate. The main two issues I have with this one are (1) the first player I had did not work well, and I had to return it. Apparently, they fixed the problem: the company had great service: they returned the new model immediately, kept inquiring about whether the new one worked better, and offered to replace it again because of one quibble I had. The one I have now works great. (2) The player does not play mp4 files; only mp3 and wma (who's still using these???).

In both, the sound is OK, but not outstanding.

All in all, although it looks a bit old fashioned, I thus prefer by far the "Diver (TM)".

There is a lot to like about this Mp3 player:

1. 32GB of storage holds a lot of music and audio books.

2. The sound quality and volume control are excellent

3. Sleek appearance

My player is loaded with audio books that I listen to at the gym. I enjoy being read to more than listening to music when working out.

The only micro USB cable that works with the player is the one that comes with it, or one like it from a similar Mp3 player. It is both a data cable and a charging cable. The micro USB port on the player is purposely made a bit different than the micro USB port on phones and headphones, etc., so that you can't try to use a charging cable for another device and find that you can charge but can't load the player with books or music. Charging cables have 2 wires, data cables have 4.

Unfortunately, the battery life, at least on mine, is terrible. A full charge lasts no more than 1 hour.

To test the battery life for my review, I charged the player, turned it on and played an audio book. About 45 minutes later, it shut down because the battery was dead. I again charged the battery and played an audio book. This time it shut down in about 1 hour.

The earbuds that come with the player are too big for my ears, but I have others to use in their place and the User Guide is of only limited help, so expect some trial and error working it out. But those are nits.

The reason I am giving the player 3 stars is because I must charge it daily to have it ready for the next day's hour at the gym.

Probably like you, I've used several different HDMI cables over the years. The first pair that I ever got were two that I won in a contest - they sold for $75/each. No, these aren't going to work any better than any other HDMI cable rated for 3D, 4K, and ARC...and honestly, you'll probably never break a cheaper cable, either, unless you work at it. Trust me, I'm cheap - and I've bought my share of inexpensive HDMI cables. Probably more than my share. While they all work fine, none of them is anything but a utilitarian cable.

Now, that said, these aren't going to be the easiest to plug in. The metal connectors are longer than those on other HDMI cables that I own. Look/Feel:

Sound:

The bass can become a little too much beyond 50% volume and overall the sound gets slightly muffled as compared to the Symphony NRG that I have which does not have as much bass as this one does. It suffers from minor noise/distortion at higher volumes for standard Apple AIFF files or normal WAV files, but then again you won't listen to songs in such high volumes (or atleast you shouldn't). Overall the sound quality is above average and pleasing to the ears.

Comfort:
The earbuds are pretty comfortable and it comes with some additional ear pads in case you want to adjust to fit according to your needs. Options are limited though. The ear buds snug fit properly and has pretty good noise isolation.

Overall, this is pretty good if you are looking for a mid range earphone in a budget, if you are an audiophile who does not want abundance of bass in their headphones then look elsewhere.

We shall see.

I have had these headphones for about 9 months. I didn't want to review them until They had settled in and I was used to them. I have used several headphones in the past and currently own several. I have owned Grado SR325, Denon AH-D5000, PSB M4U-2, AKG K845, Audeze LCD2, and currently own Oppo PM2, AKG K712, B&W P3 and the HD800. The HD800 is my favorite headphone so far. It can be difficult to find the right amp for it. I have tried it with the Oppo HA-1 (balanced), Schiit Valhalla 2, and Marantz HA1. They were excellent with both but didn't really shine until I got my Luxman integrated amp. It is a pure class A amp and the headphone out uses it's speaker amp with a resistor in line to reduce the output. These headphones absolutely shine with this amp. They finally have deep, impactful bass. They were never really lacking in bass. The bass was beautifully detailed with great presence but didn't have the punch that it has now. I'm not sure what headphone amp would be similar to my Luxman but this is the ideal paring for me. Coincidentally my AKG and Oppo headphones do not sound as good with the Luxman as they do with my Oppo HA-1.
With the right amp pairing these headphones are absolutely amazing. They have an incredibly wide sound stage and "audio microscope" detail. They are the best "speaker replacement" headphone that I have found. No headphone is as good as a nice set of loudspeakers but these are as close as I have found. They will show any weakness in your system or the recording you are listening to. Beware, you will be looking for the best recorded/mastered versions of your favorite music and that can get expensive. They are also the most comfortable headphones that I have ever used. Most people don't think enough about comfort when they buy headphones but it is a huge consideration for me. If your headphones sound amazing but you can only listen to them for a half hour before they hurt the amazing sound quality does not really matter.

This amp is absolutely incredible! It is only rated for 20 watts into 8 ohms or 40 watts into 4 ohms but it must be very, very under rated by Luxman. I am listening to my Martin Logan Vistas right now and the volume knob is only a little over 1/4 of the way up in a large room and it is very loud. If your speakers are reasonably efficient this amp will drive them. The build quality is second to none. The fit and finish are incredible. The front panel feels like a finely crafted piece of machinery and looks like a work of art. It has a very retro look with large VU meters dominating the panel. The VU meters have a nice yellowish tint when the lights are on and can be turned off. The beveled glass over the meters fits perfectly and looks very high end. All the knobs are very heavy with a satisfying click when you move them into place. This amp exudes class and quality and to my taste is one of the best looking I have ever seen. This is a very full featured amp. It includes an excellent MM/MC Phono stage that sounds amazing with my VPI Traveler and Ortofon Rondo Red cart. It also includes a fantastic headphone amp. I have read that the headphone out uses the the speaker amp with its output attenuated. This amp drives my HD800 headphones better than any amp that I have ever used with them. It has a remote control included. It is aluminum and quite nice but the buttons are very small. The remote has the same retro look as the amp. There are a ton of features on the front panel. It has bass, treble, and loudness! Yes loudness. I have not seen this on an amp since the 80s but this is not your cheap 80s loudness control. This is a legit option to fill out the bottom end when you need to listen at low volume. It sounds good and works well. There is also a direct switch to bypass the signal processing controls. There is a subsonic filter as well that I have not tested. As beautiful and full featured as this amp is it would be a shame if the sound quality did not match. Not to worry, the sound quality is even better than the build quality. This amp drives my speakers with authority and control. It has replaced an Emotiva XPS-2 amp and XSP-2 preamp so my previous amplification was no slouch but this bests it in every way. I was afraid that by going from 500 wpc to 40 wpc I may loose some impact and dynamics. I could have not been more wrong. I hate trying to describe sound so I won't. I will just say that this amp sounds fantastic and puts a smile on my face when I use it. I really think that this will probably be the last amp I will ever need to buy.

This review is for the DBPOWER® Black NFC-Enabled Bluetooth 4.0 Music Audio Receiver.

The DBPOWER Bluetooth adapter (also available from other sellers like ESYNiC) is designed to add Bluetooth support to sound output devices that don't support it. For example, devices like speaker docks, speakers, sound systems, etc., even car sound systems. Connect the DBPOWER adapter to the line-in/aux input of the device, pair it with your audio playback device (mobile phone, for example) and stream audio. It doesn't contain a speaker itself - any audio is played back through the speakers of the device it's plugged in to.

For example: Mobile phone → (Bluetooth) → DBPOWER adapter → Sound system

The packaging includes:
• The DBPOWER adapter
• A 3.5mm male-to-male jack
• Mini USB charging cable
• Small instruction booklet
The adapter itself is small (about 5cm across) and it weighs only 68g. It is rechargeable and a Mini USB cable is provided for this purpose.

Pairing with the adapter for the first time is easy. Hold down the power button and it automatically enters pairing mode. It should then appear in the settings of the Bluetooth device you want to pair it with. Once paired, audio should play back over Bluetooth via the DBPOWER device through the connected sound output.

I had no problems pairing it with my iPhone 6 and sound quality through various connected playback devices (sound system, older iPod dock) was excellent. I even connected it to a pair of high-end headphones to see just how good the audio quality was - I was very impressed.

It has a built-in microphone so can also be used for hands-free calling, making it ideal for use in the car when connected to the aux-input of a car sound system. You do need to be sitting quite close to the adapter for the microphone to work well though - beyond about 5cm it becomes difficult for the other party on the call to hear you.

It does support NFC for easy pairing but unfortunately I haven't been able to use that as I don't have a device that supports it.

After reading reviews on the B&W T7, the Bose Soundlink III, the Braven 710 and Beats Pill, I decided to give them all a listen by purchasing one of each as graduation gifts for friends and family off to college this Fall. The Braven and Beats both cost around $170, and are packaged well with all the interconnects/power supplies needed. Both are quite compact and charge via USB, both have an aux input to plug into or daisy chain other units; and Braven has a USB out to top off phones or other USB devices, a nice feature.

Now about the Bose = $250, and the B&W = $350. I had read downer reviews on the T7 as compared to the Bose. This is clearly not the case, the T7 is worth every dollar more IF you like a good, full dynamic range from a portable bluetooth speaker. I agree with other reviews, the Bose had more bass, but it was overall a very muddy delivery. The T7's bass is good (placement helps as well), but the mids and highs from this rascal are hands down better than any other portable I've heard. Both are packaged well, (B&W packaging is always top notch) yet the Bose is a bit larger, maybe too large for me as compared to the other 3. Both B&W and Bose models charge from a 110V wall-wart power supply (not USB), both have an AUX in - but neither offer USB out for charging phones, etc. USB would be nice to make car charging easier, but run times per charge are certainly adequate on both.

Back to Braven and Beats, both good but I prefer the Braven's sound performance over Beats. A bit warmer and better lows, not as tinny as the Beats but I've heard worse than Beats for the same money. Both paired easily and had good run times, If you're looking for decent sound out of the home or a good gift, both are ok. If you're looking for a refined, crisp sound experience from a portable, buy the B&W T7. I'm keeping that one for myself.

A couple of caveats before I start.

I wrote this review for the Headfi forum and everything here is in reference to that forum. I was asked to post this here by another member and I gladly do so. These are great IEMs and what they offer for the price would be hard to match.

I did not buy this IEM from Amazon but from a kickstart purchaser who onsold them to me. I am very happy to recommend this product

Here is my review:

Time for a review of the R2As that I bought from a member on this forum. I currently own Sennheiser HD580s, Shure 840s, Griffin Woodtone (iem version) and the classic Senn IE80s.

It's the Senns I will be comparing with the Flares as they are in a similar price range.

I tried a variety of tips to get the best sound for each IEM and settled on one for each. In this case I used Spinfits on both. I suspect that there are even better alternatives for the Flares but they worked beautifully for the IE80s. The included Complys don't do it for me. I wonder what a good tip with a wider bore would sound like?

I used a variety of music including some bass specific tracks (e.g. Bassgasm by TPEB), Sledgehammer by Peter Gabriel for the sibilance and harshness test, Mountains O' Things by Tracy Chapman for a busy track with good bass, Phantoms Can't Hang by Deadmau5 for treble tonal accuracy, some Jackson Brown for male vocals, the Beaux Arts Trio Hummel and Schubert Piano trios for instrument separation, Ann Murray singing Schubert's Nacht und Traum for female vocals, and a variety of tracks for soundstage.

The Flares beat the IE80s hands down for bass in every department - tonal accuracy, depth, clarity, slam and that most important factor, PRaT, though the Senns perform well in the latter.

The midrange of the R2A is simply gorgeous. I suspect that this is because there is no bass bleed into this range. I thought that the Senns did well in this department until I compared the two and I'd have to say that some bass must escape into the midrange as it sounds somewhat dry and restricted.

While the treble is far more refined and liquid on the Flares I felt that the IE80s gave a bit more sheen and shimmer. However, the R2As appear to have a more realistic tone and this suits me fine. Violin string tone is very accurate.

Peter Gabriel's epic Sledgehammer suffers badly from sibilance and is also very shrill in places. Neither IEM totally tamed this though the Flares made a valiant effort. I think it takes a big pair of speakers to do this, like my Peerless. No headphone I've heard has done it.

Instrument separation is awesome with an almost three dimensional sense. It's interesting to listen to some tracks where, say, the violin stays firmly fixed in place and then another where they don't (like the vocalists in Immerseels Carmina Burana, who appear to wandering about the stage. I can assure you that they're not, this is just a poor piece of audio engineering.) I hadn't noticed it until I heard it through the Flares. The Sennheiser's instrumental separation is messy and somewhat blurred compared to the R2A. Soundstage is about the same for both.

One final thing I have never seen mentioned about about headphones is how they handle changes in dynamic range. The Flares do this brilliantly. Where a gentle crescendo/decrescendo is called for it happens so smoothly, with the R2As going from loud to very soft without losing any of the music. Maybe this is the clarity apsect, I don't know, but it sounds impressive.

One final word on power. I drove the Flares quite easily with my iPad Air without any amplfication from about 60% volume. However, on my PC I have my music streamed directly to a Fiio E7/E9 DAC/Amp combo. The dial on the E9 is set at about 9:00 am. The combo does make a difference but the R2As still sounded very good on my iPad.

So it's a hands down win for the R2Aover an IEM I still really like. The Senns are a very good IEM and well worthy of the praise they've garnered but the R2As are miles better. For the price these are just stunning. What is most impressive is the fact that they make music sound so wonderful and alive, so realistic. I am relistening to tracks I haven't heard for years to see what I've missed.

I am wondering what price I would have to pay to get a very noticable improvement over the R2As. I was going to get the IE800 but can it be that much better?

I hate to admit this, but the older I get, the less I hear in certain ranges--and for some reason, my Vizio TV seems to broadcast primarily in those ranges. Admittedly, the sound system in the TV is awful (though the picture is stellar for the price), but I find myself turning on the closed-captions way too often just to hear normal dialogue. What I didn't realize until I hooked up this Bose unit was how much other stuff I was missing--subtle background music (not soundtrack, but music playing on a car stereo in a blu ray, for example), doors closing, a babbling stream in the background, etc. I had been meaning to buy a sound bar for the TV, but I was never satisfied with the ones that I heard in places like Best Buy, so I'm glad that I waited and this came into my life.

I am using this unit in a 12 x 12 bedroom and while I live alone and could crank this if I wanted, it fills the room beautifully with very little push on the volume. In my den (16 x 20) I have is an old-fashioned (but pretty good quality) surround-sound system with seven speakers and a huge bass unit and it works great with the right dvd in the player, the sound will blow you away. Trouble is that it's not wireless and having to route wires everywhere and I'm constantly yanking them out by accident. The beauty of a sound system that sits under the TV is very obvious to me--though I still think a great satellite speaker system is superior in terms of enveloping sound.

The set up on this Bose unit is completely simple (as far as the main unit)--just a power cable and one optical cable. If you have someone to shove the box under the TV while you lift the TV itself, it takes seconds. I did it alone and it took some clever elbow work, but I was able to do it. The remote was a little more complex only because I have a cable box, TV, and a blu ray and it takes a while to coordinate all of those (the cable box was the worst, but that is the fault of a lousy sound menu in the box and has nothing to do with the Bose system).

OK, so the important thing: the sound. At first I thought the sound was too overwhelming for such a small room--it has a lot of power. But the separation that is achieved from the two side speakers is pretty impressive. Again, it's not the same as being in my den with speakers behind and beside you and mounted at different heights, but it is, ummm, like a trillion times better than the raw TV sound. The quality of the original matters, though I've fund the two best sources are well-produced blu rays and, interestingly, some of the videos that I've been watching from Amazon Prime (not all, just some). The precision and quality of the sound from the three front speakers is awesome and I have to admit that there is a good illusion of surround sound from the combination of the five speakers.

There is an open quality to the sound that, again, I'm a bit surprised at because the speakers are all in one box. I'm not a Bose addict of any sort. While I find some of their speakers are great and some are just a few notches above adequate, I've have at times heard better (and they are not always the most expensive, either). Overall though, Bose holds up to their own bragging pretty well. (As an example of an inexpensive speaker set that rocks, I have a $40 set of Creative [[ASIN:B00CDJJZV6 Creative A250 2.1 Multimedia Speaker System]] speakers on my computer that would impress anyone .) But this one-box unit is very high on my list of favorite speakers and unquestionably the best TV system for a bedroom (who wants wires hanging all over the place in a bedroom?). The mid and high ranges (the areas that I seem to be losing in my own hearing) are beautiful reproduced. The bass is more than sufficient and in a bedroom, I would never want more bass (the cats would never come into the room). I'd love to unplug this soon and test it in the den to see how it fills out a larger room, but for now I'm just loving watching movies and the evening news without having to turn on the captions. (By the way, I live about an hour north of Manhattan and so listen to the CBS flagship station on TV and they have the most superior TV sound I've ever heard.) I get nervous looking at that TV sitting on top of the box, but if the maker says it's good, I guess we have to trust them!

So do you LIKE throwing money down the drain? If so...you'll LOVE these 16340 batteries.

Let me explain something to you that NOBODY else will. The advancement in lithium battery technology has NOT reached the point where a 16340 rechargeable cell can accommodate 2000mAh. Therefore, RIGHT OFF THE BAT...these batteries are FAKE.

Top use-able capacity for a battery this size cannot extend beyond 800-900mAh MAX. The BEST 16340 batteries on the market cannot claim higher than 700-750mAh. What does this means in terms of available power? Well, to even assume that THESE are 700mAh would be assuming too much. If tested, you'll find out that they're about HALF what the normal capacity would be.

So...NOW what does it mean in terms of available power? Let's assume you're going to use 1 or even 2 of these in an LED flashlight. Given average flashlight output (using 1 - 16340) at 500 lumens... it'll last LESS than 30 minutes. So the only reason why you'd ever possibly NEED 10 of these, is in THIS case because you'll be charging 1 or more of them at a time... continuously!

Believe me when I say that for whatever device you might need them for, they'll be close to useless.

Talking dollars...even the best 16340 batteries (at 700mAh) can be bought online for about $4 each. That's pretty good. They'll last twice as long as these, and they won't be COMPLETELY useless within a few months...as these will be.

Look for Efest, Nitecore, or Eagletac.

Remember, that poor person living on the street is going to prosper about as much by buying them a bottle of liquor, as you will from using these awful batteries!

Bought 2 of these. One was for a 40" flat wall mount which was probably overkill but the second was for a 60" corner mount and the adjustability provided by the mount made the install really nice. Not knowing what angle I could achieve from a mount made the corner install very questionable which is why I chose this mount. The fact it can slide within the fixed wall plate provided the added ability to ensure I could bolt it to studs yet achieve the appropriate angle within the room. The long extension to the mount also facilitated the corner install. In addition the up/down tilt was also ample to provide a proper viewing angle. The mount feels nice and solid and swings the same if you need to get back behind.

Mounting was nice and simple which I achieved by myself. Once the wall plate and swing arm are in place on the wall you attach the mounting bracket to the tv. Then you partially thread the upper two mounting bolts into the tv mounting bracket which attach the bracket to the swing arm. The swing arm was configured nicely with 2 slots for screws to drop into which allow you to lift the tv into place and position it so these 2 bolts drop down into the slots. Having an assistant at this point is definitely handy to ensure the bolts drop into place. Once you have it positioned those 2 bolts will hold the tv on the mount while you get back in behind and secure the tv with 2 additional screws and tighten all 4.

One thing I thought was unnecessary and actually a little annoying was the ability of the tv to pivot laterally. In other words you can take one end of the tv and raise it or lower it to be parallel with the floor. I understand why this functionality is there but if you use a level when mounting the wall plate it seems unnecessary. So now any time you move the tv you need to ensure you level it afterwards. Just a small annoyance for what is otherwise a great mount.

I really love this little alarm clock! It has a very compact and efficient design and doesn't take up a lot of space. The absolute best feature is the dual usb charging capability. Now my wife and I can both charge our phones bedside and eliminate some of the cord clutter.

There are a number of features that I really appreciate. Operation of the clock is simple. It sets itself to the correct time out of the box and includes batteries for backup power out of the box too. The dual alarms can be set with a few button clicks, and they can either be turned off completely when they sound or silenced but left on for the next day (depending upon which button you push). When the alarm sounds, it starts off very quietly and slowly & gradually gets louder - no more jarring wake ups with this. The snooze bar is easily customizable for however many minutes you want to snooze. A nap feature allows one to easily set the alarm to sound after a set number of minutes - and it doesn't disrupt the dual alarm settings. The clock display has three brightness settings from very dim to very bright - perfect for light-sensitive sleepers like me and others who might prefer a very bold display. The settings buttons that are used often are easily accessible on top of the unit, while those you don't use much are wisely positioned out of the way on the back (daylight savings time adjuster, for example).

In some ways this clock feels "no frills" - it's very small, there is no radio, the design is unassuming. But what it does it does really well with a lot of thoughtful design features. If you want a swiss army knife alarm clock that tries to do everything, keep looking. If you want a dedicated alarm clock that's versatile, easy to use, packed with alarm-specific features, and provides two usb charging ports to boot this one is a no-brainer. Big thumbs up!

I now own 3 of these remotes for around my house, and used to own a Logitech 890 universal remote; so I'm very familiar with Harmony software and devices. This is a really fantastic universal remote system, especially if you have home automation devices like lights or blinds. This product consists of a small Wifi hub that sits in your entertainment center (like a more svelte Apple TV in shape/size) and a comfortable, all physical button remote combined with software best used via smartphone app (note this review applies to the app experience using iOS). So let's break down the major components/features:

Hub: The hub is a combination brain and IR blaster for the system. It receives commands via RF from the remote or through the cloud from the Harmony App or a 3rd party integration like IFTTT, then translates and sends those commands to your TV, cable box, blu-ray, game console, etc.. It can control those devices using traditional IR signals sent out from the hub itself and a small wired IR blaster accessory included in case you have an enclosed cabinet for your media devices and via Bluetooth for controlling some game consoles or connecting as a keyboard for AppleTV and other streaming devices. It can also connect to cloud services through its Wifi connection, which is primarily used to control home automation devices. The hub hardware could probably use an upgrade as some steps/changes in setup can take longer than I'd like, but I don't notice a lag in general use. The biggest drawback may be the 8 device limit, so larger entertainment systems might top out.

Remote: This might be the strongest Logitech remote in a while. It's very similar to the Smart Control remote, but adding the Home Control buttons towards the top made them shift the play/pause section down lower where your thumb naturally rests. With the shift toward DVR and streaming sources, it makes sense that users will want easy access to play/pause/ff/rewind. In fact, this shift is why I would recommend this remote over the Smart Control even for users without home automation devices to control. The buttons feel good on the hand, and the layout is just distinct enough to provide good location by feel, which is important because it doesn't have backlit buttons (to the detriment of WAF). No backlit keys does help prolong the battery life, which is rated for a year from a small CR style coin battery and can be easily replaced. You only get 3 activity keys, but each one can have a short and long press for a total of six activities triggered from the remote (you can have many more in the app).

App: The new app-based Harmony software works very well. The initial setup is easier than in the past and I didn't have to adjust any advanced settings to get devices to power up properly, which is a good thing because editing settings after setup can be a challenge. The settings menus aren't intuitive and it took me several adventures to find various options, particularly advanced settings that are common to traditional universal remotes like trigger lags and order. The app doubles as the configuration tool and an alternative remote. Fire it up and it logs into your hub (or the last one used if you have multiple) and shows you your activities. If an activity is already in progress, you'll get the power button on its left to turn it off or you can select it to bring up the controls for that activity. As cool as it sounds to control your tv from your phone and never lose your "remote" again, the novelty wears off quickly because the phone interface just isn't a good substitute for a physical remote. There's no tactile feedback or feel, so you have to look away from your tv and no longer get the visual confirmation of your button press. The app on a phone also shows very few controls per "page", so you have to swipe left/right often to find the right button(s). That doesn't mean the app isn't useful. For one, the app is the only placeto control individual devices separately from an activity, and it's where you need to go if an activity fails to turn all the right devices or change inputs (I have not had any issues with this so far). I also use the app occasionally to proactively start an activity in another room such as the basement before walking down (great for warming up a projector if you have one).

Home Control: The new part of the Harmony line is adding functionality for controlling Home Automation devices. Logitech generally works with the major players like Hue, Wemo, Nest, etc... and the Home Control remote adds 4 dedicated home control buttons as well as an up/down rocker for adjusting settings like dim level for the latest selected device. The dedicated buttons are great and despite a light bulb on two and an outlet on the other two, they can be assigned to pretty much any device. You can also add home control actions directly to activities, so Watch a Movie could include dimming lights and/or closing blinds if you have them to integrate. I make extensive use of these buttons through a connection to SmartThings. With the flexibility of SmartThings, you can make almost anything happen through those 4 home control features. Setup was easy and the app walks you through it; but in order to get the full power, you should be comfortable tinkering with settings and digging a little deeper.

Unfortunately, this is where Logitech could use the most work. The overall functionality is great, but it's very limited. You can't assign home control devices to other remote buttons and although you get short and long press options for all buttons, you can't assign two devices to a single home control button either. The functions a home control button has is determined by the type of home control device automatically. For instance, a light will turn on with a short press, off with a long press and the rocker will dim it up/down at a defined step (4% in my experience) that can't be changed. Opening this up to be configured by the user would allow for greater home automation integration and flexibility that might rival higher cost systems; features like having the lights dim up when pressing pause during a movie and returning down when pressing play again. I was able to emulate this via a home control button, but it was an arduous process and means I need to remember to pause via that home control button during a movie.

Overall, this is a great universal remote system that still needs some work on the software side for customization and flexibility. If you have a simple system and don't want to tinker, you'll find this easy to setup and use. The physical remote is in my opinion, one of the best physical remotes in terms of feel and button layout I've ever used (backlit buttons would probably put it over the top). The Home Control is an added bonus for users with systems in place, and it's the biggest WAF upgrade because my wife can turn off the lights or turn on the fan while lying in bed without digging out her phone.to control individual devices separately from an activity, and it's where you need to go if an activity fails to turn all the right devices or change inputs (I have not had any issues with this so far). About a year ago, I decided I needed a set of premium Bluetooth headphones, after going through numerous pairs of poor ones. I had been through so many pairs of such Bluetooth headphones which were under $100. Not only did they suffer from poor sound and performance, but they didn't last long before they malfunctioned or simply stopped working. I realized that I got what I paid for in all cases, and that I needed to upgrade. I was prepared to pay a lot of money, up to $500, as long as I knew what I was getting was great quality, but I was also open to the possibility that I might get a deal.

It was then that I ran across a set of headphones called "Bluedio R+ Legend" headphones on Amazon. These headphones were priced significantly lower than their direct competition, and that made me unsure whether this would be a wise investment, but the reviews seemed positive enough that I felt like I should take a chance. So I ordered a pair that was available at the time, a set of shiny sky blue Bludio R+ Legend for about $140. I received them in a few days, and was impressed with the look of them. But as good as these headphones looked, they sounded incredible. I had yet to run across any headphones that had better sound, and I was in bliss that I had found what I felt was a really good deal for such a higher performance product. Not only were they the best sounding headphones, almost everyone who saw me wearing them thought they looked great and and asked me where I had purchased them.

And then around eight months later, that joy was somewhat spoiled. The ear cushion of one end of the headphones came off and was hanging by a tiny piece. I glued the cushion back on and continued to use them, but eventually more damage occurred. I was worried that I had simply been careless with these headphones, and I decided to get another pair and be more careful. This time I ordered a pair of the darker black headphones as the light blue pair wasno longer in stock, and I was pleased that the price had gone down to less than $100 for this replacement pair. I was once again enjoying the amazing sound, and getting the same compliments.

And then, a short time later, as I was putting them on my generally oversized head, one end of the headphones snapped, leaving the ear piece hanging by a thread. This time, I was certain that I was not being careless. The item broke while in very careful use. It might sound crazy, but I decided to order a pair again. You see, I LOVED these headphones. I didn't want a new kind or to shop around again. I ordered a navy blue pair. And once again, they broke, this time while in my carry-on luggage while going on a plane trip. I decided I would buy one more pair, but only because I saw a cheaper used pair being sold on Amazon. After being so disappointed with the durability. I made a promise to myself that I would be VERY careful with this final replacement pair. I handled them with absolute kid gloves.

The reason I am relating this story in a review about a different set of headphones from Bludio is this: it's a testament to how much I liked the sound and look of these headphones that I was willing to buy four pairs in a period of two years instead of investing in a much more expensive brand like Monster, especially given that the total amount I spent on Bluedio R+ Legend had already eclipsed Monster's most expensive brands. You see, I was that convinced that I had found at the very least the best sounding headphones I had ever heard, and I was willing to just be REALLY careful with this final pair in order to enjoy that amazing sound.

A few weeks ago, I was asked to try out one of the newer brands that Bluedio had released, a successor to the R+ Legends, which is the brand I am reviewing today. I accepted the offer, and I am extremely glad I did. I didn't think it was possible for a pair of headphones to sound better than the R+ Legend, but these headphones do. It doesn't matter what I am listening to, it all comes across with amazing clarity and depth. I've found that even older monaural recordings sound almost like they are in stereo, and stereo recordings sound better than they have for me using any other device. It's quite the experience, and IMO no other pair of headphones tops this amazing sound.

Improving the basic sound of an already extremely impressive set of headphones would have been enough for me, but this pair of headphones didn't stop there. A new mode for sound has also been included with these headphones, called "3D DSP Sound Effect". This is an option that is exclusively available when connecting through Bluetooth, not through the wire. After going a few days with the basic great sound of the phones, I discovered this option in the manual, and turned it on while listening to some favorite songs from "The Smiths". Sound begins to come from many angles, and recorded performances begin to sound like live performances. I can't say that in these cases the sound difference is always an improvement. Sometimes a dramatic moment you've come to expect in a song is blunted in this mode. Sometimes the surrounding sound of the band overpowers the singer in this mode as well, when it doesn't in the standard listening mode. Despite these foibles, this is a pretty incredible mode offering and for the most part provides an improved listening experience. When reading up on this option, I found that some were reporting that movie sound in particular was greatly improved, and after having tested this, I can firmly state that this is indeed the case. I felt like I was watching each movie portion I experienced on my iPhone in a movie theater. Action movies are, of course, the ones to benefit most. Sound effects and voices come at you in ways that add incredible depth to the private movie-watching experience. This feature alone is worth the extra cost over other headphones.

Now to the thing I really love about these headphones: their construction quality, durability, comfort, and even usability all FAR eclipse the those of the R+ Legend headphones. These headphones are a little heavier than R+ Legend, but the difference is very slight for what we actually get here, and frankly the weight difference is there for a very good reason Unlike R+ Legend, most of the important parts of the headphones, particularly the frame, are made of metal, not plastic. Plastic is reserved for only items like the buttons. I could tell tell the difference immediately when I put the headphones on: no longer did I needed to be careful when fitting them onto my oversized noggin and over the ears. I could tell right away that there was little danger that the curse of a gargantuan cranium would endanger my new headphones. There is also, of course, significantly less danger that these headphones are going to be damaged in my hand luggage. Besides the fact that they are more durable in such situations, they also come with a nice hard case that will protect them when they find themselves in a cramped space. The R+ Legend phones only came with a velvet carrying pouch, good for carrying but not for protecting. This hard carrying case is a nice upgrade that will help me get the most life out of these headphones.

As for usability, there is definitely improvement there. I often found it difficult to find and use the buttons on the R+ Legend headphones, due to the fact that the spot to click on had to be located almost exactly, and even after pressing it, sometimes the action I was directing didn't actually occur. These new headphones solve that problem in two ways. First, there's no finger fishing that is required for finding the exact point in which to press. The button area on the right is now one big button, with pressing the center and the usual directions (up, down, right, left) being the only things you have to remember. Combined with the fact that these are not so easily pushed around or damaged, I find it significantly easier to use these headphones than the R+ Legend model. I have to admit that the passive aggression is still sometimes there. Button presses sometimes don't work and then having to be repeated to get the desire effect, but it happens far less often with these headphones than it did with the previous models. I also find, to my pleasant surprise, that these earphones don't hurt my ears nearly as much as the R+ Legend or any other pair of "on-the-ear" headphones I've owned. I can't really discern yet the reason why -- it looks like the same imitation leather I saw on the R+ Legend, but for some reason these don't have the same effect of bringing on an odd combination of pain and numbing. That's certainly a welcome change for me.

Are there any real downsides? Well yes. Despite everything else, I just liked the look of the R+ Legend headphones better than these. Those headphones had a sharper, shinier appearance, and were at least previously available in a lot of colors. I've seen them in sky blue, navy blue, red, black, silver, etc., and all of them were fantastic. These have a color selection of black and red, and neither look as spiffy as the corresponding colors of the R+ Legend. It's a shame that these are not available in the navy blue I've grown accustomed to. But let's get real here: the bottom-line is that these headphones are in every single other way an improvement over past offerings, and just to be very clear, I think they are the best performing headphones I've ever owned. I'm extremely glad I took the invitation to try them out. I'll go as far as saying I think the headphones are worth their original listing price, but at least here at Amazon, you'll pay well less than half that price to own a pair. Don't let these pass you by folks!

This is a very cool little amp. It does the job and then some. I opted for the 40 watt model, with "Tone" control since I tend to like my music a bit brighter than most, I need at least a Tone control if not separate Bass and Treble.

My model does NOT run noticeably "Hot", just normally warm. Note that you can't just SWITCH between between LINE IN and USB/MicroSD and Mini Plug input via the remote MODE button. This works on the display, but a media card seems to override all, and the mini jack on the front overrides the Line In jacks on the back, so you will have to manually choose one or the other. You can't, unfortunately, just connect everything and switch between them with the mode switch. At least you can't on my model.

The USB Drive or MicroSD seems to ONLY PLAY MP3 FILES. If you have M4A (iTunes Files) or other music files, you are going to have to convert them to mp3. There are various ONLINE sites where you can convert them for free, so if this is your goal, it's no big deal, it will just take some time to convert everything, unless you already have mp3. Then you are set. You can use the remote to skip, pause and play selections on your USB Drive or SD Card. There are also buttons on the amp to do this. The LED Display only shows track and input mode. No song information is displayed, so if you have 400 songs on a USB Drive, you'll only see track numbers, not song or album titles. However, for the price of this amp, it works well enough for me.

The fidelity of the unit is very good, there is no hum (as I usually hear on Pyle amps), and the 40 watt unit puts out a clean 10 - 20 watts per channel at 4 ohms before it starts to distort. If you only have 8 ohm speakers, you will probably get an honest 10 watts before it starts to distort. That's plenty of power for most people, unless you are going to have a dance party.

Overall, I'm satisfied. The major question, how LONG will it last? It's brand new, so I do not know. I can update this review if/when it fails, but for now, I'm satisfied. -1 star for not being able to use MODE on the remote to actually switch between input devices. Otherwise, all is well. Wow, am I happy with this speaker! I listened to several Bose, JBL, Harman Kardon (really shocked how disappointing that one was), UE and mini Boom, Altec Lansing, Soundfreaq ... you get the idea. Universally, it seemed to me that they were lacking in the high frequencies, which is really weird for small speakers (hasn't a tweeter in these things occurred to anybody?). Bass varies on all of them too, as does overall sound quality, and of course most don't even try to do stereo.

On the basis of several reviews I sprung for the DSB100 and am I ever glad I did. It has the finest full-range sound of any I've ever auditioned. In the past few minutes I've listened to Mannheim Steamroller (try "Door 4" from Fresh Aire 2 for a wonderful test of stereo separation, and "Classical Gas" from the Steamroller/Mason Williams collaboration for an overall sound), John Williams and the Boston Pops ("Imperial March" would be horrible without full-range sound), Dire Straits ("Fade to Black" sounds wonderful) and TransSiberian Orchestra ("Sparks" from Night Castle is a workout for any speaker). The amazing thing is that there really isn't a significant area of the frequency spectrum that is overemphasized ... well, maybe a little around the vocal upper-midrange, but really not offensive. I could wish for a little more of the really high frequencies (tweeters, Denon?) but unlike all the other speakers, those cymbals and guitar strings really do have a presence that only the highs can deliver. And the bass, while it'll never match a home system, is really stunningly good ... as in the electric bass from Dire Straits and TSO really does come through.

As for volume, it's loud enough for my wife to wish I'd dial it back inside ... haven't tried outside yet. It's definitely sufficient for my purposes though. No, it won't rattle windows like my home system, but be reasonable ... it hasn't got that much mass. At any reasonable volume, though, it's clean, distortion-free sound.

I haven't listened to the audiophile speakers that cost three and four times the price, so I can't say that they mightn't be better, but I can say without a reservation that in the sub-$200 range I have not auditioned another speaker that comes close. In addition, it's a very convenient small size that will fit easily in my carryon, and I had no trouble at all pairing it with my Motorola Droid Mini and my Samsung Galaxy Tab 3 8.0 (interestingly the sound is slightly better from the Galaxy than the Droid). Directly linked by a 1/8" cable makes a real difference with the Droid, but almost imperceptible difference with the Galaxy.

Oddly it comes with a USB cable but not a charger block, so you have to plug it into a PC or another USB charger. But this is a great speaker that will not disappoint anyone who wants genuine, quality sound.

So with most cells shipping with a protection circuit built in you really can't be sure what exactly you'll be getting. You might order some brand name you think you trust and if you pulled it apart you might find some cheap generic Chinese brand and get pitiful results out of it. Right now Panasonic makes some of the absolute best balanced 4.2V 18650s I've ever seen (not just in capacity, but overall performance) and when I'm recommending an 18650 to a family member who needs something they can just drop in and not worry about (I'm always afraid they'll run down an unprotected cell too far or manage to short it or even put it in backwards.) I suspect the seller is just installing these theirselves, but it seems every bit the usual professional job you'd expect from some rebranded cell. The difference is, with a rebranded cell, while you can research and research to try to figure out which one might actually contain a NCR18650 with likely a good margin of error for getting, say, a Samsung ICR, with this you can just look at it and you KNOW you're getting the NCR18650. The installer of the protection circuits is using a clear plastic to hold things in place and protect that circuit wire so you can tell just by looking at them what's inside without pulling anything apart. Now, I will say that the protection circuit did seem ever so slightly larger than the normal ones to me, but I didn't have a lot to compare with nor a caliper handy to test with, so I won't guarantee this. Still, I think some room for improvement in this area may be possible as I have seen extra slim circuits. Mind you, those slimmer circuits perhaps can't handle as much power. I'm not sure. The plastic is also a bit thick, so I think in these two ways there is some very small room for improvement. I'd like to give it a 4.8 star review. Given how few reviews there are I'm going to go ahead and round to five rather than down to 4 though I think the latter might be clearer.

BTW, of note here to any considering the Panasonic NCR18650 series: they design these to discharge down to 2.5V without damage rather than the usual ~2.9V. This is part of that extra capacity essentially along the same lines of the batteries that charge up to 4.35V instead of 4.2V except this has the disadvantage of the fact that very few things will discharge that far and still work. Most things stop working roughly around the 3.0V range, some even higher (~3.3V is probably fairly typical of circuits that need 3.3V to run.) However, if you look at Panasonic's charts for these batteries you'll note that the dropoff past that 3.0V is every bit as or even more sharp compared to the dropoff of a 4.35V battery down to 4.2V, so quite a lot of the really high capacity you see on these is actually still really in a usable voltage range. Since this only charges up to 4.2V, it's a bit safer in a lot of circuits and compatible with the largest range of chargers however. Thus while you may not have the advantage of that full advertised 3400mAh, you're still looking at an exceptionally safe and easy to use battery that will still produce a good capacity (it's hard to say for sure, but I'd say maybe 2800-2900mAh in a normal range.) This is just something to bear in mind with the NCR18650 series. This is why I call them "best balance" since they've found a middle ground to provide a high capacity without sacrificing compatibility due to a higher voltage. I'm planning to give these to family members to use with uncontrolled devices such as battery powered fans where the circuit could run a battery all the way down and ruin it easily and it may be possible they'll get that extra capacity out of them.

So far, these headphones are awesome for the price. While they are a little snug around my ears (I have medium to small sized ears), I have found that to be true of most "over the ear" headphones. However, these are much more comfortable than most that don't have plenty of room around the ears. This is because of the type of foam used in the ear cushions and on the headband, which is extremely soft and provides plenty of cushioning. The bluetooth works flawlessly and connects quickly. I have only used these for watching movies or listening to music on my laptop, so I cannot comment on the mic or its quality. The sound quality on these are very good for the price point. If you expect sound quality on par with $200+ headphones, you may be disappointed. However, they are much better than almost all sub $50 headphones I have tried, including wired ones. They also have plenty of volume. Some headphones suffer from being much too quiet even when you max out the volume slider. These are very loud at about half volume. The only issue to be aware of is that certain video players will have significant lag between the video and the audio. This is not an issue with the headphones, but rather with the video player. The biggest name out there with this issue is Netflix. Do a little research and you will find this to be a common problem with their video player and wireless headphones. Thankfully, Amazon Prime Video works flawlessly, and since most of the shows I watch are on both, this hasn't been too big of an issue for me. It is something to be aware of if you are a hardcore Netflix fan. Finally, the battery life is amazing on these. I have used these regularly for over two weeks and probably around 14+ hours and still have not had to recharge them! In summary, if you are looking for a great pair of bluetooth headphones for under $50, these would make an excellent choice. I went through a couple of pair before landing on these, but it was worth it to find such a great value.

UPDATE: A month or so after I posted this review, Netflix apparently fixed whatever the sync issue was. I have been watching Netflix ever since without any problem whatsoever. So I can wholeheartedly recommend these headphones to anyone looking for an inexpensive bluetooth option with great quality.

I bought this cable with the intention of phasing out the old, ugly composite (composite being one yellow wire for video) cable that I had been using with my PS2 since I got it. That old cable, mushy as the picture quality was, functioned just as you would imagine, no interference.

When used under exactly the same conditions as the original composite cable, this component cable had horrifying amounts of interference. After spending too much time troubleshooting I came to the realization that I had some cheap HDMI cables plugged into the TV that were causing the lion's share of the interference, but not ALL of it. Take a guess how I got rid of the rest.

Unplugging all the controllers. Barring the occasional flicker of a line across the screen, the last of the interference went away as soon as I unplugged all controllers from the console. I tested this with multiple controllers and the results were always the same.

I give this cable two stars rather than one because when I moved the PS2 to another room with less electrical devices in the general area, it worked flawlessly. If you have a big media center with lots of electronic stuff going on, this cable probably isn't for you.

For the record, the console I used this cable on was a PS2 fat. I was able to find a better-quality cable (for more money) that worked flawlessly under all the same conditions that this cable failed. When looking for quality PS2 component cables, keep in mind that component cables sold as PS3 cables will work on the PS2.

Hi,

This is my review of the product TT-SK05/ TaoTrinics Portable speaker: It is listed on Amazon as:

Bluetooth Speakers TaoTronics Wireless Speaker Portable Speaker (Bluetooth 4.0, High Fidelity Audio, Built-in Microphone, LED Light, A2DP Profiling, 6 Hours Playtime)-Black

I received this product last weekend and had time yesterday for a couple of hours to try it out for evaluation and review. I have also taken a series of photos and included it in my review if anyone is interested.

UNBOXING AND OBSERVATIONS:

The product comes in a reasonably packaged illustrated cardboard box. One of the confusing things about this box is that it’s the same one that’s used for both the black and white color speakers apparently. My box showed the black colored speaker and initially, I thought I got the wrong one, but when I opened the box lid, it was the correct white one that I ordered.

The front and top of the box has a photo of the Bluetooth speaker. The left side has the serial and model number. The backside has North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific e-mail support information.

I look at this illustration and if I was walking into a retail store, I’d actually pick this up to take a look at it. Unfortunately, there are no technical specs of the speaker around any sides of the box. I would recommend that this is stated, at least in summary, for the user to be aware of. As an internet company, it’s not a big deal, but if this company moved into retail space, this would be important.

Upon opening the top box lid, I found inside the white colored Bluetooth speaker wrapped in a plastic bag inside. When lifting that up, there’s a circular cutout cardboard that tucked the speaker into the box, and underneath that was the Micro USB cable and AUX cable included with the box.

The Micro USB cable is a standard type of cable for Bluetooth accessories such as the speakers. The AUX cable is used for plugging into a phone, tablet, laptop, or desktop that does not have Bluetooth support so that you can use the speaker with limited functionality while not needing any power from the speaker’s internal battery.

In looking all around at the Bluetooth speaker…

The top side has the speaker output with a ring around it that I later found out is to change colors to indicate pairing status and ON or OFF status. The front of the speakers has the Taotronics logo. The right side has a Mic hole. The backside has the ON/OFF sliding switch, DC 5V charging input port, Line IN for AUX cable, and a slider for the volume.

The bottom of the speaker has a pair of U shaped rubber stoppers to provide friction against a smooth surface so that the speaker can’t be slid around and knocked off of a table top easily. I tap against the side and it rocks around briefly but doesn’t really move that much.

In knocking it around, I found out that based on the shape of this speaker, it can lay rested on any of the sides all around it so that the speaker doesn’t necessary have to be stable and pointing up. It could be facing you. I liked that part of the design.

What I initially considered as a suggestion is that I like a multi-function button that has separate push buttons that have rubber padding, for the volume up, down, and play/pause functionality. In this case with this Taotronics speaker, it’s integrated together with a slider that rolls to the left or right, which is OK, but feels a little flimsy and feels like it can easily get mechanical failure or wear and tear over time. I’d rather have the push pads for buttons to control these functions. That’s my personal opinion.

I suggest all product owners read the user’s manual prior to operating this product so that they are aware of what you can and can’t do with this product.

Some notable information from the manual includes the following:

Specifications:

Bluetooth Version: 4.0
Bluetooth Profile: HFP, HSP, AVRCP, A2DP
Output Power: 3W
Frequency: 90Hz-20Khz
Input: DC 5V
Battery: 500 mAh Lithium Battery
Range: 33 feet (10m)
Working Time: 6 hours
Charging Time: 2 hours
Dimension: 2.48 x 2.48 x 2.95 inches
Weight: 5.94 oz

So in going through some of these specs with my perspective.

Bluetooth Version 4.0 is the latest Bluetooth next to 4.1 that is available in the market for Bluetooth accessories. I suggest all people find Bluetooth 4.0 products and not the 3.0 or lower. The 4.0 has better stability in terms of connectivity and performance, and better battery power management.

Output Power of 3W was something that I had to consider. It didn’t sound to the current level of power that I’ve been looking at for Bluetooth speakers, which is around 5W. But, at a current price of $10.99 whereas the others were selling for around $25, it was reasonable for the price. I’ll be taking close attention to how it feels by ear later on in the review. For now, my expectations were not too high.

I would’ve liked to see a higher battery capacity than 500mAh for this product. Perhaps up to 1000mAh or 2000 mAh with an increased price for that. 6 hours of playtime is good for a portable speaker of this price range. It may not last you the whole day, but if you use it off and on in the day, you’ll be good enough for about half of the day before you need to recharge the battery to full.

Fortunately, the specs state the charge time is about 2 hours, which isn’t too bad. That’s a good standard charge rate. I would like it to be down to 1 to 1.5 hours full charge time, but it may be a design or parts limitation. 2 hours is good enough to where you can charge this while heading out or having a bite to eat and watching TV or using your smartphone or tablet, then come back to see that it’s fully charged to use it again in the middle of the day.

The dimensions of this product make it very portable. I was looking at this and this could certainly fit into my jacket pockets. It might even fit into some of my pants pockets, but would cause a noticeable bulge out of the shape of my pants which would look unfriendly. But it is small and with it small, it can be stored in more possible locations for travel or placing onto crowded table top surfaces. I like the size.

The weight of it when lifted up with one hand is lightweight. I don’t see myself straining or tiring if I had to hold onto this with my hand for an extended period of time of more than 10 minutes.

In the User’s Manual, it talks about the LED indicator, which is the ring shape around the top of the speaker. It will turn red when charged, turn off when fully charged, flash green when in pairing mode, flash green for every 10 seconds when paired.

USAGE:

The evaluation of this product will be detailed, but before doing that, you have to pair the device to your phone or tablet. I had an iPhone 5s to test for the remainder of this review.

When turning on the power button on the back of the speaker, you’ll hear this brush of tones, followed by another tone. You’ll see the LED flash on the top of the speaker. By going to your Bluetooth Settings and letting it be in discover mode, it will find the product labeled as Taotronics TT-SK05.

Connecting to it will cause another set of tone noises from the speaker.

What I like about this Bluetooth speaker that my last two Bluetooth speakers of higher price failed to incorporate was support for the Bluetooth battery meter indicator on the smartphones like the iPhone. This Taotronics product has that, which is handy to monitor and gauge where along the 6 hour playback battery life it currently is in to plan to when charge theproduct.

It hurts the battery’s lifespan if you charge it too often from just minimal use. It’s recommended to try to fully drain or use until its low battery before charging it all the way to full.

After pairing, I tested the volume. The disappointment that I didn’t like about this product is that I found out it uses AVRCP 1.3 or older and I can tell because the volume on the speaker is separate and independent of the iPhone’s volume rocker meter. So to get the full volume, I’d have to crank up the speaker volume until it beeps, and also turn up my iPhone volume bar. The same is in the case of turning down the volume, although in my tests, you can slide the volume slider held down on the speaker and it will eventually mute the volume without needing to touch the iPhone.

For my test, I tried a few songs of both lyrical and instrumental and then bass.

First lyrical test of the sound quality was the song that I chose, which is:

Brandon Heath - The Light in Me

It’s a strong but calm lyrical song with mild instrumental accompaniment.

As I tested it out, I noticed that I had to crank the volume on my iPhone about 50% towards the max just to have the song heard fairly well. This was about 5-10 feet away. To get a good audible experience, I had to crank the volume to about 75% of the maximum volume on my iPhone. This was OK and expected for a 3W power output. But, I didn’t let it distract me too much. I placed the speaker in the center of my home on the first floor at the kitchen table and walked around with my paired iPhone. I walked end to end the full 30 feet of experience all around and the Bluetooth connection never broke or crackled in the semi open space that I walked around with my iPhone. I had minimal dry wood walls and exterior concrete walls that were in the way during some portions of the walk. But, this was impressive how the connection stayed good for that long of a tested semi open spaced environment.

At some points, I did crank the volume up to about 85% of the max to hear it loud and clear from near 30 feet away of semi open space. It didn’t hurt my iPhone, but this probably was draining the battery of the speaker more than tested. But, for a small product like this, I had to crank the volume high enough to have an enjoyable experience. And for me, I have normal hearing, but with these speakers, I did have to push my volume bar near max to hear it reasonably loud from about 20-30 feet away in a semi open space.

The lyrics in the song were clearly heard and I liked how the instrumentation and lyrics were heard well and distinctive with this speaker. Particularly the singing. I played through the whole 3 minutes of the song without issues.

My next test was the song by Nickelback - Figured You Out which has a combination of lyrics and instrumentals from a rock category.

I was able to hear the voice of the singer well. The instrumentation quality was second best. It was heard, but meshed together with the instruments to where it felt noisier than clear and distinctive. It was a good experience.

I tried Linkin Park – Lying From You, which has a lot of yelling and hard singing with instrumentation. The overall quality of how it sounded to my ears was OK. I could hear it well. It didn’t feel pounding to my ears. I heard some instruments loud and clear more than others in the song based on how it was projected through the speakers and the composition of the song. It still had a combined mesh of a noisy experience than distinctively hearing each instrument well.

My next song was a bass test. I went on YouTube and searched up “high quality bass”. I found a result that had over 1 million views and tested that song. I had the instrumentation playing while I heard the bass very well, but I had to crank up the volume to 80-90% near max inorder to hear it good. It was noticeable with the thumping sound coming from the speakers during the bass test, which was good for this size of portable speakers. You’ll hear the sort of loud thumbs at this volume range without needing to feel the power pressure of the bass reaching your ears. It was good for this size of a portable speaker. It met my expectations.

My next test for fun was testing out playing the 2015 best trailers video on YouTube just to test. What I found out was that depending on the audio combination of voice and sound effects, if I heard through the speakers, I could turn up the volume to about 75-80% and hear it well in a quiet background noise setting within 5 feet away, but any further than that, and it was muffled and hard to pick up to distinguish the dialogue that was being mentioned.

So from my tests, the speaker was good on clear lyrical singing in songs. With hard instruments playing, it was loud enough to hear, but felt meshed together with noise generated instead of distinctiveness. With bass, the bass was good as long as the volume was raised very high. The movie watching test with these speakers didn’t turn out as well, but I think it’s still better than not having a Bluetooth speaker and having to rely on your smartphone or tablet’s speaker.

The final test that I did was the talking and calling test. For this test, I used my landline speaker phone to call to my iPhone, and set the landline speaker volume up and in a different area of my house in which I had a sliding door close it from picking up my voice into the landline phone when I was talking into the Bluetooth speaker. So initially, I heard the incoming call from the landline phone to the Bluetooth speaker playing the projected music form my iPhone’s ringtone music. I was happy to say that I heard the ringtone well where it wasn’t too loud or too quiet. My previous experience with Bluetooth speakers was that it would play the ringtone music extremely loud and high to where it was harmful to the ears and ruined my experience. But here, everything was OK. I tested a few incoming calls and was able to take the call by pressing the multifunction button on the Bluetooth speaker. Same with hanging up, redialing, and rejecting a call. All of those required timing when to press into the play/pause multifunction button.

The great news about the calling test was that I found out this Microphone hole built into the Taotronics Bluetooth speaker is as good as my iPhone’s built in microphone in terms of frequency and range. I initially talked up close to the Bluetooth speaker and heard the audio echo through my landline speakerphone in the distance loud and clear. Then I started to distance myself from a couple of feet away to several feet away, and at one point, being an estimated 10 feet away from the Bluetooth speaker, and when I talked in a normal tone of voice, I could hear the echo through my landline phone most of the time. There were a few occasions where I had to repeat what I was saying to hear the echo come out word for word, but it was minimal. This mic on the Taotronics speaker is good in sensitivity, which works out well for group settings placing it in the center around them talking to someone.

One other thing to mention is the LED indicator. It’s a subtle green LED flashing light. It looks pretty cool. I was able to capture a photo of it in dim lighting. It makes the product look more stylish and modern. The light isn’t bright to where it would be distracting when trying to sleep.

IN SUMMARY:

PROS:

1) Small and portable enough to fit into most types of pants and jacket pockets
2) Green LED ring has a stylish and nice look in a dim light setting that makes the product look more modern
3) Good microphone sensitivity for picking up your voice during calls (tested up to 10 feet away)
4) Reasonable sounding bass when turning the volume up about 80-90% near max
5) The speaker can stand on its own or lay flat on either of its sides to face you with stability from rocking around
6) The ratio of playtime versus charge time is good
7) Connection testing with Bluetooth 4.0 on this product was good with semi open spacing of 30 feet all around the house

CONS:

1) It uses AVRCP 1.3 or older ,which requires the user to independently control two sets of volume, one on the speaker, and one on the phone or tablet
2) You have to raise the volume on your phone to about 75% to 85% to hear the music through this speaker fairly loud and clear from about 15+ feet away
3) Quality for movie or TV show content listening, particularly for action movies, isn’t as good as it could be.
4) Music where the instrumentations are playing with the singing sound too meshed together with noise rather than distinctively hearing them separately.

SUGGESTIONS:

1) Rather than a sliding dial to control the volume and play/pause, it may be preferable to have a model with a push button rubber padding for each multifunction
2) Provide a higher capacity battery into this product
3) Provide a travel pouch or bag to carry this speaker around and protect it from wetness and dirt or debris
4) Provide a lanyard extension from one part of the Bluetooth speaker to hook it onto the waist belt loop or travel bags
5) Increase the power output of this speaker to what is currently standard in the market for portable speakers in the low end of competitors, which is 5W. That way, the user does not need to raise the volume on their smartphone or tablet so high as I did with testing of at least 75% near max volume
6) Make an IPX5 or greater waterproof design for this type of product

USER SCENARIOS:

People who would use this product are those who:

1) Are looking for a cheap budget solution that is an improvement to the speaker quality of their smartphone or tablet
2) Cannot afford high end premium speakers
3) Want to have calling features with music listening experience combined
4) Have small group settings using this Bluetooth speaker, which allows a wide coverage of voice pickup to hear to the recipient of the call.
5) Like to have stylish affordable accessories added to their gadget list

Overall, this product proved to impress me than the initial expectations I had when reading the specs like the 3W power. Although I did have to crank up the volume very high to get a reasonably loud audible experience, the small portable speaker from Taotronics will be handy on small trips to provide entertainment for myself and a small group of people that is an inexpensive risk of loss or damage.

High priced 'boutique' HDMI cables are one of the biggest scams out there and paying more doesn't necessarily get you more. In fact, in the case of HDMI cables, hardly ever!
(go to your local 'red bullseye' store and see the outrageous prices for what should be a low priced item)

I have a medium to large sized setup with all my devices (Blu Ray, HD DVD, SACD , HD DVR and HDTV interconnected by HDMI cables. Bottom line for a good cable is simple. Either it works, or it doesn't. Well, that used to be the rule of thumb until 3D HDTV. Now it is important to have what is known as a 'High Speed" cable , one that can handle the higher data transmission rate of the 3D video signal.

These Amazon Basic cables fit the bill nicely. Plenty long enough for most any needs at 6ft and a pair of them at that for the price of less than one higher priced brand. I am impressed by the workmanship (albeit by machines I would think) of the actual connectors themselves and also the sturdy feeling, yet pliable cabling.

This is not to say that you can't have problems with HDMI cables and usually the problems are with the pins in the connectors themselves. Overuse of the cables (plugging and unplugging many times) can wear out the pins and keep the connectors from making an overall tight fit. My advice is to connect them the least possible times necessary to get your setup up and running. And that advice applies to pretty much any brand, not just lower priced cables.

Hey, cables are not sexy like a brand new Blu Ray Player or 3D HDTV but they are in integral part of your setup and you need them to be both functional, reliable and hopefully inexpensive. I truly believe these Amazon cables deliver on all three points and can totally recommend them for anyone needing high speed HDMI cabling.

As my review title states, I feel these Amazon Basics are as good as my slightly higher priced Mono Price cables which many AV web groups swear by.
