Bought these to replace my Bose outdoor speakers, which lasted a good 10 years. I prefer the sound of the Bose. I was influenced by the low price of these and their good reviews, but I will go back to Bose.

(free sample supplied for review purposes)  Consider my rating 4 1/2 stars.  The first thing I want to address is the charging problem some have and it has to do with one thing, it uses USB which requires it to be charged from a computer(trickle charge) and some outlet chargers. Some have mentioned that with this version and others they are only able to get about a half an hour to an hour worth of play time. If you charge it from a computer you will get 6 to 7 hours or more depending on what you are using it for.  I really like the dark red metallic color, it is not just cool looking it is also easy to spot when you set it down.  This unit has the 32 GB built in, there are other versions that have a micro SD card slot that come with a 16 GB SD card. So depending how much you want to do with it you will have to decide what is best for you but 32 GB internal storage is a lot and will be enough for most.  Let's start with the packaging and honestly this might be my biggest negative but really didn't effect my rating. It comes in a two part clear plastic case wrapped in glued on cellophane. Don't try to remove the cellophane, take a knife and slice along the sides where the two pieces of plastic come together, slice along the two long sides and the bottom short side, you will feel your knife slightly enter the slot along the sides. By leaving the top side connected you will have a flip open case.  The player itself fits my needs perfectly, mostly for walking and listening to music and audio books. I got over 4 hours of playing time using it for that and probably had more but decided to charge the player, I don't like to let the battery get to low. The player does so much more than play audio files, there are even 4 games included but watching video and playing games might not be the best things to use the player for because of the small screen size but you can, pictures and video quality were very good. You can also record what you are listening to on the radio to or use it as a voice recorder. The radio worked great and the reception was surprisingly good. My only real negative was the bass with the supplied ear buds was not very good even at the rock setting on the equalizer but I rarely get good bass out of ear buds, the bass was a lot better with an over the ear pair of headphones.  The player was very intuitive, I never did look at the instructions and only encountered a few minor bumps in the road that I eventually figured out. The interface has a quaint old school pixelated look but really was a non issue for me. For my needs it was perfect and is very highly recommended for those with similar needs to mine.

This is an initial review after using the unit for a week.

So far, the pros have vastly outweighed the cons. I am using it for perhaps an unconventional use, but it makes perfect sense. I am using it to control the automation on my hermit crab tank. Right now, the temperature management is handled through an Inkbird controller which is plugged into this strip, but in the future I intend to interface this strip with a probe unit so I can easily check temps over the internet.

Having 8 programmable outlets makes this unit far more cost effective than buying outlet timers. My hermit crab setup is a bit more complicated than most. It has recirculating pools with pumps on varying schedules, water filters, UV lamps, misting pumps, etc, so I'd be looking at $60-$100 in standard automation equipment anyway. Why not get something that allows for remote control for the same price? It's a no-brainer, really. This unit has so far performed perfectly in this capacity. I have had no problems with the GUI interface or command line.

Now for the one part that didn't work so well. The controller software has serious problems wanting to work with Java 8 present on your system if you're running Windows. If you have Java 8, you may need to uninstall, reinstall 7, install the controller, and then maybe you can install Java 8 again if you want. A minor setback, but I could see this being confounding to someone who isn't terribly tech-savvy (although I don't see non-savvy people being terribly interested in this anyway, so I'm not subtracting a star).

In the future I intend to write a few custom interfaces so I can do more advanced temperature control and feeders (for freeze-dried shrimp, and other things that don't easily spoil) but for now it's doing everything I need it to. I would recommend this to anyone looking to bring cost-effective automation to a terrarium / aquarium setup.

I have two points to make for the sake of full disclosure before actually writing a review of these headphones. First off, I received a free pair of the M6P headphones in exchange for an honest and unbiased review. I will do my best to deliver on my end of the bargain, with a review written for those wondering if they should spend their hard-earned money on the M6P. Secondly, I have never been an in-ear headphone person. I've used plenty of in-ear headphones in my day, but I have always preferred over-ear headsets as I find them to be, nine out of ten times, much more comfortable and high quality in their sound. That been said, I have been massively impressed by these headphones so far. Let's get to it then, shall we?

As with any headphones, primary concern for me is sound. How does the M6P fare in that regard? Surprisingly well. I have never owned a pair of in-ear headphones that has had such a good sound range as these do. Usually, this sort of headset is severely lacking in bass and lower-mid tones, but the M6P has a genuinely fantastic range. Of course, the bass isn't quite what you'd get with over-ear phones, but honestly, it sounds pretty great. A little adjustment to equalization settings is all it takes for it to sound the way I like. Highs, mids, and lows are all distinct and clear, with no one aspect overpowering the others. I've really enjoyed my time with the M6P so far. They also look pretty cool. I got the "clear" option, and it's got a nice clean science fiction look to it. I like it.

The M6P has several features that are worth noting as well. The last three or so inches of cords that go into the headphones themselves are made of a much stiffer material than the rest of the cord is. This "memory wire" is there is so you can mold them around your ear, making these headphones perfect to use while exercising or working. I have a physical job that allows me to listen to music while working, and these headphones have been incredibly nice for that. They rarely jostle or fall out. If you're looking for a good set of headphones for use while working out, these are ones I'd give serious consideration. The M6P also has an inline universal control that has a surprisingly large variety of uses for only having a single button, a volume slider, and a built-in microphone. The volume slider is incredibly nice as you don't have to fight to get your iPod/Mp3 player out of your pocket to adjust the volume. Same goes for the single button, which can be use for playing/pausing music and even skipping or restarting tracks depending on how you press it. The mic works pretty well for phone calls too. Overall, the inline universal control is a pretty convenient feature I rather appreciated. It's a pretty high-end feature that I've never had on any in-ear headphones before.

The M6P comes in an attractive little box with plenty of accessories in addition to the headphones themselves. There's a really small zip-up case that carries other things in addition to the headphones. There's a really nice folded up users manual that is very helpful in getting acquainted with the product and its various features. There's also a small zip-lock baggy with several different types of rubbery ear tips you can switch out if the default ear-tips don't suit your fancy. I really appreciated the extra ear-tips, as each of the six pairs pretty much guarantees that, no matter what your ears are shaped like, you will be able to enjoy these headphones comfortably. That's great. There's also a little clip that can be used to attach the phones into your shirt or whatever, which is a nice feature that helps keep the pressure off your ears if the cord gets tugged a bit. Overall, a nice package.

Truly, these are great headphones, but they're not without some quirks to consider. The memory wire, as great as it is for keeping the phones in your ears, makes it so the headphones take longer to put in than otherswould be. Once you put the earbuds in your ears, you'll want to make sure you won't need to take them out for a little while. I also found the memory wire a pain to struggle with right out of the box until they had broken in. The memory wire on the right-earbud on mine were particularly stubborn for a little while. Once broken in, however, the memory wire is very easy to make conform to your ears and wroks great. Finally, and this is admittedly a nitpicky gripe, I don't care for the plug-in jack myself. It is angled at 90', with an L-shape. I prefer straight plug-ins for headphones, but that's just my preference, and doesn't really take the quality of the phones down at all. None of these are issues that would keep me away from the M6P, mind you, but they are quirks to keep in mind.

All things considered, these are fantastic headphones. I've been supremely surprised by their high quality in comparison to all the other in-ear headphones I've owned. I have friends with high-end in-ear headsets that were twice the price (or higher) as these, but in my opinion, the M6P is much higher quality in terms of sound and has a much more robust feature set. These are a pretty awesome deal at $40! It appears you can get them for even cheaper than that on Amazon too, which astounds me. I'd definitely give these a hearty recommendation at this price. The hard part of the experience is getting the earbuds to fit comfortably and remain watertight throughout the swim. I had used the basic package of waterproof headphones for over two years. With some initial experimentation, I got them to work satisfactorily and enjoyed using them doing laps in the pool or out kayaking on the ocean. I was happy and a little surprised to have them last for as long as they did. They always seemed lightly constructed considering their intended use so I took great care in handling them.

When time came to replace the original set, I noticed that Swimbuds now offered a new, upgraded unit. Since it promised more rugged construction and a wider selection of earbuds to choose from (being able to achieve a comfortable, or at least tolerable, waterproof seal is essential otherwise the product is worthless) I took the chance and paid for the upgrade.

It was money well spent. The new kit comes with a much wider selection of earbuds. I immediately found a style that has worked perfectly for me from the very first swim. I routinely spend 45 minutes to an hour doing laps and never once have to stop and adjust my earbuds. I'm still hearing the music just as clearly in both ears when I exit the pool as when I entered. The earbuds I use now are so much more comfortable than what I was limited to using previously. And the sound quality if also much improved.

Forget the basic package. Pay for the upgrade. It's worth the expense.

Obviously you want to keep the base in a place where you won't lose it--ours is on top of the fridge. It would probably help to stick a post-it note on the back of the base to identify which button corresponds to which locator--something simple to do. The wallet finders should not be put in a wallet that you're likely to sit on--they won't survive that. Perfect for purses or wallets kept in front or coat pockets though. I've included a picture of both cases open so you can see how the one with CD booklets compares to all DVDs. They look the same when closed.

I've been a longtime Skullcandy user, and continue to use them as headphones of choice, but seeing the new Strum touting the "Best Fit Ever" tag, I figured I should give these a shot over the tried-and-true 50/50s and Titans. There's a little bit of regret, but in the end, these are pretty good headphones. I'm just glad I didn't pay $50 for them.

The build quality has gone down considerably and especially compared to Titan or 50/50 earbuds, and that was noticed right out of the box. The new plastic case is also not my favorite--I miss the old mesh ones, personally.

Sound wise, I was underwhelmed. The bass was okay, the mids were a little drowned out, and the highs were scrubby. It just sounds... cheap. The Mic2 setup also feels cheap (Also--really? A slider? On earbuds?) although it is nice to control my Droid Turbo without issue.

The best part--and the only part that sets these earbuds above anything I've tried on before, they are remarkably comfortable. They fit perfectly into my often too oddly shaped ears to be comfortable, but it feels like they're not even there. For that alone, they are worth a good looking-at. Nothing compares that I have tried, honestly.

All in all, the comfort is king here and what probably draws people to these anyways. If you don't mind not having top-notch sound, then by all means, these are the buds for you. Expect to feel a little cheated by the build quality of the buds EXCEPT for at the ear, where it counts anyway. Worth a look at, I just wish they sounded like the similarly priced Skullcandy earbuds.

This is a small portable speaker that has pretty decent sound quality. It sets up and pairs easily to all of my devices. Upon getting this speaker it came with a micro usb charging cable, instructions manual, the speak system, and a small bag to transport all of it in.

The speaker is set up to provide bluetooth and has an aux. jack so you can attach it directly. My phone, my nephews phone, and my tablet all located this speaker and paired to it in a few seconds of doing the search and pressing connect. The speaker stops functioning if you plug it in to charge as a safety feature for the speaker, like every other bluetooth speaker on the market.

When it comes to charging this speaker it is super easy. I was able to charge this speaker from my wall socket USB charger, my PC tower, my laptop, my car charger, and from my back up power bank. Bascially anywhere you can plug into a USB slot this thing can be charged from it. While it is charging there is a red light around the volume control dial that is red. Once the charge is completed that light goes off. The first charge took about 2 hours. Since that first inital charge it only takes about 30 minutes now to get a full charge. With a full charge the speaker lasts for about 7 1/2 hours.

The speaker provides a decent quality sound. It is a small speaker in an enclosed plastic housing. On the back of the unit are all of the main controls to the unit. There is an on/off switch for the power of the unit. There is an aux. jack in the back that is a 3.5mm and can be attached directly to your player. The last so is the micro USB charging slot. On the top of the unit is a round volume control button. With the volume control button I was able to take the speaker near max before I was able to notice any distortion. I was to 90% max volume on my tablet when the distortion started. For me that is more then good enough since I typically listen to my tablet at about 40% most of the time. The speaker system is also a full range set up. It does not have driving bass but it does offer the full range. The base of the speaker has some small rubber feet. This makes it where it does not make vibrating noise as you are playing it. It also makes it where it does not slide around.

If you are looking for a good bluetooth speaker I suggest checking this one out. It sets up easy and pairs easy. I can listen to it thoughout my entire house with the sound that it puts out and lasts for a decent amount of time. I've reviewed a lot of headphones. From Bluetooth, to gaming, to earbuds and so on. The 808 has some interesting features, but how do they stand up to the competition?

The 808 Performers are really targeting the DJ market. Things like the suspension system holding the speakers and the 90 degree cup swivel are designed to entice spin-wizards while the price tag is designed to make them an accessible purchase for even the casual listener.

Overall, I'm not all that impressed. Don't get me wrong, the clarity is there, the bass does bump and they're a solid set of cans all around. However, being marketed to audiophiles and DJs, I don't think the 808s are putting nails in the coffins of they're competition.

Sound quality is clear, but abrasive at higher levels. I've always felt that the mark of a great set of headphones is that as you increase the volume, it doesn't sound louder, it sounds clearer. I don't feel that the 808s deliver that clarity. While I do hear a more dynamic sound, additional instruments and effects, than when I'm listening to my apple earbuds - I get that on most over-ear sets that are half the price of the 808s.

The two "DJ" features are the swiveling cups and the suspended speakers. The swiveling cups is cool. It works well and seems to be well constructed. It's nice to be able to turn one of the cups up instead of needing to take the headset off or hold it to one ear. The suspended speakers is supposed to enhance the bass without distorting. I don't feel like it made any difference though.

All in all, it's a very solidly constructed set of headphones. The sound quality for the price leaves much to be desired, however.

Hi everyone. I'd like to start my review, explaining what exactly I was hoping for: a mid-range IEM for my subway commute, and gym use. This RHA model seemed to fit the bill. I originally had my eyes on the T10i, but finally had a listen... I thought bass was drastically over emphasized, and overall imaging to be poor for a $200 IEM. They weren't bad, but existed in a crowded price point. THEN the T20 was announced. They claimed to have controlled the bass, and gained clarity. I'd agree with that assessment, but am a bit let down.

Pros:
- Build quality and design is top notch, minus a point for not having removable cables (nearly all at this price tier has that feature)
- Cable noise wasn't noticeable, in fact, I couldn't hear myself stepping while walking on the sidewalk like I usually do with IEMs. Nice, RHA!
- Isolation is above average for a ported, dynamic driver

Cons:
- Sound was not to my liking... Bass was great - controlled, and I could tell the difference between a bass kick and bass guitar... RHA really nailed the bass frequencies. The mids seemed slightly recessed, but acceptable, and the highs were just meh overall, and a bit shrill at times.
- Non-removable cable.... come on RHA... most of your competition has added this feature in the past 5 years
- Would much rather have an L plug over the cool looking but impractical straight plug
- Don't understand the different tuning options... the neutral one that's on it is the only one I'd recommend, as the others sound artificial.

Overall I like these, but they certainly aren't worth my hard earned $240. I once bought a pair of IE80s here on amazon for 265 (currently 280) which I find to be much better sound wise. They also have removable cables, clearer mids and highs, much better soundstage. They do not however match the RHA isolation or build quality. If you want to spend less, the GR07 bass edition would be a much more cost effective alternative. Even if those died (they don't have the best build quality) you could buy them again, and end up at the cost of the RHA.

Just meh... RHA wants to sell these alongside the T10. I feel they refined the T10, and could easily discontinue those and just sell these for $200. They fix all the problems, while leaving little reason to purchase the T20.

**UPDATE**

The sound signature was unusually familiar to me, after the first day. I decided to compare them vs my other IEMs and have discovered a near exact match: The Brainswavs S1 which sell on Amazon for $50. They seem to have the exact same sound signature, but slightly less "clear." The RHA would be the better of the two, but costs 5x as much. Food for thought.

This is for the 60 mile version of the 1byOne Digital Attic/Outdoor HDTV Antenna.

All I can say is WOW! I live in a 1 story home surrounded by 2 story houses 33 miles from the broadcast antennas. Looking on the map, there are several two-story homes directly between my house and the broadcast antennas; one is right across the street. Plus there are two or three large three-story metal buildings within a mile also in the direct path. In other words, line-of-sight? Forget about it.

I had pretty much talked myself out of an attic install. I fully expecting to have to install an outdoor antenna raised high enough to reach over these obstructions. What a pain. However, at the last minute I decided to try this antenna instead. It looked simple, and I could always return it if it didn't work, right? So I went ahead and ordered it.

It arrived yesterday. Assembly was a snap. Installation in the hot attic in the middle of August was no fun, but was mainly uneventful. I mounted the antenna as high as I could inside the peak of the roof, pointed it in the general direction of the signal sources, hooked up the power unit, connected the signal feed to my TV using pre-existing wiring, switched on the TV, and did a scan. Every single OTA station from the distant antenna farm showed up!!! I'm not missing a single one. Most are UHF. One or two are down in the VHF-H band. They all came in clear with no pixelation. My TV doesn't have a signal strength meter so I can't tell you about that.

The only stations not coming in are a couple I wasn't interested in anyway, broadcast from a different location in a different direction. I consider this a no-loss.

Am I impressed? YES!!!

I have only just installed this antenna so I do not yet know how it will behave over time or how weather will affect it. I will post updates if anything noteworthy happens.

Update: December 2015. Despite my qualms regarding sound quality, I continued to use these headphones daily at work. They're gone for podcast audio. Every morning, I took them out of their bags, used them, then in the evening, carefully folded them up and placed the bag in my backpack, secured in a pocket. Hardly a tough travel regime. Over six months, the ear pad covers have come away, and I can't find s way to hook them back in place. See the attached photos for evidence of how these 'travel' headphones stand up to light travel. NOT recommended.  The key features of these headphones are in the name: premium, lightweight and travel, headphones, mic.  Premium: To some extent, yes. They are priced, at the time of writing, at $200. They have leather (or fake leather, I'm not sure) wrapped around the headband, they feel pretty solid, and the finish on the outside of each ear is obviously aiming for the Beats designer market. The cord is removable and therefore replaceable, which is a good feature to have. But the pads that make contact with the ears don't feel premium, cause sweating after a while, and have holes cut in them that look like they'll tear after a while. Philips were cheap though: the cord only has a mic and button, no volume controls. It must be too costly to get that iPhone/iPad certification. What's the point of being able to play/pause from the headphones, but not adjust volume without taking your phone out of your pocket?  Lightweight: Absolutely. They are light, they don't exert pressure on the ears during use, and they are barely noticeable in a bag. This does, however, make me wonder how 'premium' the electronics are when the set is this light.  Travel: They come with a bag and they fold up flat. When flat they are less than 2" deep and 2/3rds the size of a Moleskine notebook. the cord unplugs so you can wrap it up small. Very very good for travel.  Mic: Yes, I skipped 'headphones'. That comes next. As already stated, they have a Mic on the cord, with a button for play/pause. But without volume control, what's the point? If I'm moving from listening to music to taking a call, I need to increase the volume of the headset to take the call. On a phone, that means taking the phone out of my pocket. On a Mac, that means using the controls on the keyboard. In Windows, if there are no media keys, that means using the mouse to adjust the volume in the system tray. Due to this inconvenience, I didn't use the Mic when making calls, and can't report on it.  Now, onto the most important part: Headphones. If they sound good enough, all the other issues can be ignored. If they're average, the other factors could make/break the deal. If they're poor, nothing will make these cans worth the hefty $200 asking price.  Frankly, the sound is poor. Take a standard pair of $30 Apple earbuds that come free with an iPhone, and add more bass. That's pretty much it. If you are not offended by the earbud sound, this is an improvement, and you may like these. But it's not $200 worth of sound here.  I either own or have reviewed the following headphones: http://www.amazon.com/Sony-MDR7506-Professional-Diaphragm-Headphone/dp/B000AJIF4E/ http://www.amazon.com/Bose-TriPort-Headphones-Discontinued-Manufacturer/dp/B00009MK3T/ http://www.amazon.com/Bose-TriPort-Headphones-Discontinued-Manufacturer/dp/B00009MK3T/ http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00IUICOR6 http://www.amazon.com/Apple-MD827LL-A-EarPods-Remote/dp/B0097BEG1C/ and they make up my frame of reference. The cheapest are $30 and the most expensive list for $180. They are all fair competitors for the Philips under review.  These are ON-EAR headphones. Earphones/buds sit inside the ear canal. Around-ear phones have padding that wraps around the ear, blocking out external noise. These sit on the ear, without surrounding it. In ear phones can be uncomfortable, around ears may not fit well and cause the ears to sweat after a while. These should avoid both those pitfalls, but as I alreadystated, the pad materials made my ears sweat after a couple of hours' use. These also leak sound at low volume, unlike the around ears and in-ear models. Inconvenient in a quiet office.  But for me, the big issue is the sound. They are not much of a leap from the Apple earbuds (just better bass), are nowhere near as good as the $20 cheaper Bose (although that depends how much you like the 'Bose sound') and pale in comparison with the Sonys, which usually sell for around $80. If I just wanted to block out noise and have an ignorable soundtrack, I'd use the earbuds. If I want a light travel pair, the Bose fold down and have a removable cord, Mic and volume controls. IF I want decent listening quality, I'd take the Sony set. These don;t come close.  Others have said these sound great. I beg to differ. The recording engineer review was the most interesting, because the first thing I noticed with the cans was the lack of a coherent soundstage. 'What's a soundstage'? It's the illusion of a 3D layout of sound created by stereo speakers. IT makes you think the drummer and vocalist are in front of you, which the bass player's 2/3rds to the left of the stage and the guitarinst is 2/3rds to the right. It should be subtle enough to not be obvious, like the fake stereo of some 60's recordings (Like the Beatles stuff where the vocals come from the right and the drums from the left), but still, if you want, you should be able to work out where in the soundstage an instrument is.  The soundstage here is terrible. It's like turning two speakers to face each other, then standing between them. There's a very obvious gap in front of you, where no sounds come from. It's really weird, and the better the recording, the more obvious it is. Even mono recordings, which have no soundstage as such, have the same effect. However, it does depend on the type of music being played. Maybe that's why the sound engineer didn't have this issue. Listening to jazz was unbearable. Mono, which on headphones usually feels like it's just in the middle of your head, felt like the same music coming from two different rooms. Rock was pretty miserable - everybody was either far left or far right, or in the case of vocalists, both.  Where I had less issues was with hip hop and electronic music. Tech Nine's last album sounded great, but as with a lot of hip hop, there's no real stereo going on. Some of the simpler, pounding EDM sounded good too. But electronic music with intricate an soundstage was as poor as the other genres.  Maybe you think this isn;t a problem. It's sounds like I'm making a mountain out of a molehill. But I want my headphones to involve me in the music, certainly for $200. And this broken soundstage effect is so disconcerting, it's the aural equivalent of wearing an eyepatch: you'll get by, but things will never be 'right'. And for this price, there's no way the other useful features of these phones can make up for it.

Bottom end is also present but a bit muted, and if you're coming from consumer or processed headphones, you'll be "but where is the bass - my head ain't vibrating" - again, ACCURATE.

Anyhow, super-impressed with these headphones. They are big and bulky - not discrete. They are also not that great at keeping the sound in / isolation - I think my ATH-50's do better. I have a Dish DVR, An HDDVD player and a PS3. My Onkyo receiver, however, has just two optical inputs.  I've tried a couple non-powered optical splitters but the sound cuts in and out or just doesn't get through at all. I wanted something which would enable connection of both my HDDVD player and my PS3 optical sound outputs to one of the optical inputs of my receiver. My TV has plenty of HDMI inputs.  I have tested this unit with a full length movie on both devices and it worked flawlessly. There are a few minor annoyances which prevented me from giving it a 5 star rating:  Pros: Works as advertised with no signal loss! Passes DTS and Dolby Digital with no problems!  Cons: 1.Depending on your needs this could be a pro or a con but the unit seems smaller in your hands than it appears in the picture.  2.The remote is very small and would be easy to loose.  3.You must make sure you point the remote directly at the IR receiver bulb for operation. It works as long as your path is clear between your carefully placed receiver bulb and where you are sitting. There is a switch on the unit which toggles between inputs 1 and 2 and then to off but it is inconvenient IMHO. The remote offers a dedicated control for off or on as well as operation from across the room.  4.Lastly, and this is the biggest reason for taking a star off, this unit runs on USB power but there is no USB to wall outlet adapter included. There is a short cable included and that's it! I just happened to have an adapter from another device which I was not using and a power strip conveniently placed. You could use the USB connection from your TV or a computer and it would work fine so long as there is power at that source.  I know the "cons" seem to outweigh the "pros" but I felt the need to offer detail about the drawbacks so one is informed when choosing this item. This is a good product so far and the negatives do not effect how well this unit works. If those minor caveats do not deter you,I don't think you will be disappointed with this solution.

To start off this review I wanted to say that these headphones were surprisingly impressive. I have a wide varitey off headphones, a collection some may say. Headphones from skullcandy to top of the line sennhieser's. Out of all the headphones I have, these still impressed me. Not only do these sound good, but they are unique. Unique from the design to the changeble sound signatures.

Information- As some maybe unaware monster has an app called "Pure Monster Sound Experience". In this app if you have the monster DNA on ear or DNA pro you are able to customize the sound by selecting a genre preset. You are only able to do this when are listening to music from in their app. For an example if you are listening to classical simply go into app and turn on the classical option. Without using this app the sound already sounds good but while enabled different music genres sounds noticeably better. I was shocked by this and think it is great idea. The downside to this is the app is only avalible to iOS users free on the AppStore. But with or without the app these headphones still sound good.

Build Quality- The build quality on these headphones is the weakest aspect of these headphones. They are made up of mostly plastic with some metal and rubber parts here and there. While these headphones could with stand some minor impacts, if twisted or accidentally bent the wrong way these could possible crack. These also come with a velvet like carry pouch which is nice but wouldnt give the headphones much protection. While holding these I don't get that cheap feeling but like I said build quality could definitely be improved.

Comfort- These headphones have extremely soft and plush earpads but don't be fooled! They have a really strong clamping force and you will definatley start to feel something around an hour of wear. With that being said these have impressive noise isolation which does a good job of muffling out most background noise.

Design- In my opinion these headphones look great. The triangles over the earcups and headband offer a sleek and slim looking design. Plus the glossy finish and flashy colors make these things look even more awesome. Monster also includes a microfiber cleaning cloth to easily remove fingerprints on the headband and earcups. Most people because of Beats are under the impression if they look cool they sound absolutely horrific, but this is not the case, for these headphones do both.

Sound Quality- This is going to be the longest paragraph yet. And for a quick disclaimer this sound review will be assumed you are using the headphone without the app or any presets. I've been using these headphones for about 2 weeks now and have tested these headphones with all music genres. First of all these headphones are not specifically geared to rap or dance genres. Alright starting off with the bass it is a little over powered but doesn't distort the mids and highs. These headphones have a tight punchy bass with well constructed mids which sometimes makes the highs sound distant. Overall these headphones are pretty much well balanced. These headphones hit highs perfectly with clear sound when bass and mids aren't present. The sound was very detailed and I was able to pick up on all instruments playing in Genres like jazz and classical. Vocals seemed smooth and clear but sometimes sounded like they were hissy. The audio on these would start to disort as I hit about 85%. Acoustics also soundness pleasnt well listening to country.

Overall I enjoyed the sound of these very much. These are not bad sounding and somewhat comfortable as well. Definatley not as good as my sennhiesers but definatley gets the job done when it comes to sound quality and design. Thanks for reading, hope this helped you make a decision

[[VIDEOID:6eddfede054e4f701e98d3bf971e895b]]Charon UPS documentation claims a very impressive performance. To verify the numbers I started by testing Chafon performance with my laptop to see if it comes close to the documented performance.

Chafron documentation states that they expect a 13" laptop to run for 6 hours. I took out the battery from my laptop, set the power options to never go into sleep mode and not to shut down the screen and measured how long it can run after I charged Charon UPS to its full capacity. The laptop ran from 5:50 pm to 12:25 am, for a total of 6 hours 35 minutes. For the last 5 minutes the battery level was shown as 0% and blinking, so I had a warning that it was about to run out of juice. This is the best case power usage scenario as I was not running any programs on the laptop other than the idle mode of the operating system. If the computer was doing some more intense work the power consumption would be higher and the battery would last less time. Never the less my test confirmed the numbers stated in the documentation and this backup battery has an impressive performance.

Once I exhausted the battery in my laptop experiment, I timed how long it took to fully recharge the Chafon battery.

8:20am start - 3% full
9:30am - 56% full
12:30pm - 88% full
1:00pm - 100% full

It took 3 hour and 40 minutes to fully recharge the battery.

I like how Chafon clearly identifies how long the battery will last. They state that it produces 288 WH, which means it has capacity of 288 watts hours. To find out how long any devices will run on this battery you have to divide 288 watts by the amount of power a device draws. A watt is current multiplied by voltage. For example, if I measure my USB fan with a current monitor I get 0.40A and 5.05V which is 2.02 watts. This means this fan should run for approximately 144 hours (6 days) before this battery is exhausted.

The unique feature of Chafon UPS its portability. The Chafon box comes in a case with a handle, it weights 7 pounds and 1.2 oz, and its size is 11"L x 4.25"WS x 5.25"H.

Chafon has both AC and USB port. I found many uses for this large portable battery from using it as a back up when the power goes out at home to re-charging my Ghost drone (its battery requires an AC plug so my other battery chargers could not do it).

After purchasing several other SHARKK products, including their Bluetooth Keyboard of which I am a fan, SHARKK requested I evaluate and review their new Power Strip and USB Smart Charger (Model WP-SKPS42US). I think SHARKK was very timely with bringing this product to market now; I was already looking for one like this that didn't make my office look like a data center. Having already owned the Belkin 3-Outlet Mini Travel Swivel Charger Surge Protector with Dual USB Ports, (1 AMP / 5 Watt), I had come to appreciate the value of a strip that offers both AC outlets and USB ports.  Cosmetically, the Power Strip and USB Smart Charger is very appealing. The construction is of high quality silver/grey/white brushed metal and does not look cheaply made or poorly constructed in any way. If it wasn’t lightly printed SHARKK on the top of the strip, one could easily confuse it for an Apple product.  Some comments: • This power strip should will be appealing to users looking for a strip to be placed on a desk given its front-positioned USB ports. I does look cleaner to have the USB wires laying parallel to the desk than perpendicular and sprouting up from the power strip. However, for a floor based unit, in most cases it would be more appropriate to have the USB ports on the top of the unit. • The AC outlets are nicely spaced apart to allow four wall warts to plug in without issue. • Like many USB strips, it does offer 2.4 amps from two of the four USB ports. When testing the USB ports with a Portapow USB Power Monitor I saw good results: consistent voltage and high amperage. • I very much like the subdued color scheme and small fonts for the text and logo printed on it. You have to look very closely to notice the text.  Some critiques: • Like most power strips, the AC outlets on this one do not swivel or re-position. While the spacing of the AC outlets is wide and will accommodate four wall warts, those with horizontal AC adapters (especially ones that are polarized), will need to plan accordingly. However, SHARKK did a great job with the strip's contemporary look and feel, and a swivel outlet is often made of plastic and can look cheap and would detract from the minimalist look and feel of this unit. • The metal casing may eventually show signs of wear and tear as it absorbs bumps, nicks, and scratches. It would have been nice if it had a set of rubber or felt strips on the bottom to prevent it from touching the desk directly and possibly scratching. I stuck on two clear rubber risers I had previously purchased from a hardware store to accomplish this. The power strip is heavy enough so that it will not easily shuffle on a surface, say  from minor tugs on cables for example. • The power switch is on the back of the unit and barely noticeable, but it is very reminiscent of 1990s power strips with its orange plastic light and black plastic frame. It doesn’t compliment the contemporary look and feel of the rest of the power strip.  But, a man on a flying horse wouldn’t notice.  You won't either.  I had a power strip with 8 outlets ( 3 wide-spaced outlets / 5 tightly spaced outlets ) on my desk which had USB adapters. I am happily replacing it with the SHARKK Power Strip and USB Smart Charger.

I have three 7' monitors that require 12 volt DC power and 1.0 amps to run. I first thought these would run fine off of 9 volt AC adapters, but I found I was wrong about this. When I tried to use 9 volt adapters, I had bad blinking and bad 60 cycle line interference on the monitors. At first I thought this was due to a nearby AC and not the supply. Well, one of my monitor's on the 9 volt supplies went out and I had to replace it. This was when I found out that the monitor runs best between  12 to 24 volts and not 9 as I had been using. When I learned this, I pulled out a spare 12 volt adapter that ran at 1.5 amps as it matched pretty closely with what the monitor was needing. I thought I needed two more to switch all three over to the 12 volt set up and so order these two based on the responses from other buyers and the specs listed. Got them in yesterday, and started to install them only to find out that two of my monitors were already using 12 volt power supplies at the rated amps so I only needed one now. Put the spare up and proceeded to hook the other up. Since the monitor has no plug on it. that required me to splice the power leads together. (This adapter comes with a DC type power plug with the positive on the inner wire and the negative on the outer  wire of the plug.) The item I was going to use the adapter for had no plug or jack for the power, just the bare wire. Two handy things I did note: 1. The two inner wires for the adapter are color coded black and red. Red for positive and black for negative (ground) and that really helped when wiring this item up to the monitor leads!  2. This adapter comes with what seems to be a built in line filter on the cord. If so that would help with line interference. After installing the adapter to the monitor leads and making sure all taping up was done right, I plugged it in and powered up the little 7' monitor. Monitor came on without a problem when I pushed the power button on it. I noted the monitor's picture was stable and had lost all the 60 cycle line interference I was getting with the old power supply. Noted the supply didn't seem to run hot at all. It was slightly warm to the touch but not hot as the old one used to get. I've been running this adapter for 2 days now without the slightest problem. It even went thru a power glitch this AM with no problems. I noted when I measured the line output voltage on this adapter unloaded that it ran at 12.3 to 12.9 volts and stayed in this range for as long as I was measuring the voltage. Unit seems very stable. I'm very happy so far with this power supply for what I needed it for. I consider this a very good buy!

My wife's dad has Parkinson's, and often does not project his voice well. I bought this amplifier and a Bronstein LM15 lavalier/lapel mic to use with it (rather than using the headset mic that was included). So far, after a few days of use, the family has been very happy to be able to hear him again.  Here are some additional details, observations, caveats, etc…  I noticed that many of the voice amps on amazon seem identical, except for the brand name. (I would guess lots of them are manufactured by a single company in China.) The difference in cost probably has to do with the particular headset microphone included and the length of warranty offered (and of course, the amount of profit for the seller). I also noticed that the 12-watt models seem to get better reviews than some of the others. I ordered this Samyo version because it was cheaper than others that appeared identical, and I didn't plan to use the included headset mic (so I didn't care about its quality).  I didn't want my father-in-law to have to wear a headset when using the amplifier, so I looked for a decent, modest-priced lapel mic. The Bronstein LM15 seemed to get good reviews, so I ordered one with a standard 3.5mm stereo jack. I found it for thirty bucks plus shipping by doing an internet search. It's available with a variety of types of jacks/connectors, so make sure you don't order the wrong version. I don't know if the TRRS 3.5mm connector would work with this amp.  I noticed that the included headset mic had a mono 3.5mm connector while the LM15 had a stereo 3.5mm connector, so I also ordered a "Monoprice 107158 3.5mm Mono Plug to 3.5mm Stereo Jack Adaptor" (www.amazon.com/gp/product/B003DBTAZ4). I did that because I wasn't sure if half the output from the LM15 would be lost otherwise. I don't know whether the adaptor has any benefit, but fortunately it was pretty inexpensive.  Thus far, my father-in-law has always placed the amp on a table next to him, rather than wearing it on his waist or on a strap around his neck. When indoors with minimal background noise, the amp and mic have done a very nice job. However, they did not work well in an outdoor setting with noticeable background noise, e.g., vehicle traffic and a nearby gurgling river. Perhaps the headset would be a better choice when there is significant background noise. (That's speculation, since we haven't tried it.)

In the past I've owned both the Bose SoundTrue Headphones and the equivalent of the current Sennheiser HD 239 Headphones, so I can probably give a better comparison than most.

I'm a huge Sennheiser fan, and what I tell people is that while their $30.00 headphones routinely outperform headphones that cost triple that from other manufacturers, every dollar more you spend does indeed produce noticeably better sound if you buy Sennheiser.

Unlike their more expensive Sennheiser big brother, these are a leatherette, cheap-feeling yet very comfortable material for the earpieces. The sound is a bit tinny sounding at first, but after a few hours of break-in (not days, or weeks like the more expensive Sennheisers) the sound expands out nicely.

You won't get the deeper bass and fuller sound of a more expensive pair of headphones, but if you despise earbuds as I do and are at work or elsewhere where sound-isolation is a bad idea these phones are excellent.

Sound is cool, and optimized for pop-music. You have crystal clear vocals, but the instrumentation seems to drop away unless you increase the volume to a good level. Play these good and loud and your poor-quality mp3s of radio hits will shine.

I recommend these instead of the Bose SoundTrue model as they are one third the price and sound slightly better (the Bose set gave me a headache).

Recommended also to anyone just starting out with "real" headphones. Oh, and they are NOT pink. They are maroon in color.

I owned the [[ASIN:B0078GCLRY Panasonic SC-BTT190 Energy Star 5.1-Channel 1000-Watt Full HD 3D Blu-Ray Home Theater System (2013 Model)]], very similar spec wise. I remember when I hooked it up it sounded so flat. I am not one that wants my movies/music thumping the floor, but I do want to hear the bass. It took some tweaking with the settings and it was great. I had it for years and the reason I decided to upgrade was this system used the same network adapter as my other one. I already bought/owned the [[ASIN:B0087ND9WS Panasonic DMP-BD77, DMP-BD79, SC-BTT190 and SC-BTT195 Wireless Lan Adapter (DY-WL5)]]. In order to have the internet work on this system to use Pandora, Netflix, etc., you will need to purchase this separate.

Taking this out of the box seemed easy enough. It was very light weight. I was smiling thinking this was going to be a breeze since I already knew how to configure the settings. Three hours later, I had it set up. My old system did not have the standard speaker wires on both ends. They do into the back of the speaker, but not into the system. Instead, Panasonic clamps the speaker wire into a plastic casing that you have to plug into the back of the unit. I find that bothersome. It gets worse, more of the speaker wire to come later.

I already had the optical cable so plugging it in was a breeze. I noticed that the USB port for the network dongle was no longer in the back but it was now in the front. The unit is much bigger, wider and also in depth than the other system. Not sure why either, there is not much to it. Instead of having the USB adapter in the back and nicely out of view, you now have to plug it into the front of the unit where it sticks out. My daughter is almost five and knows not to touch it but if she were younger, I know her little hands would be pulling it out and playing with it. Why they changed that, I do not know. I tested each speaker as I plugged them in. They all worked. The do feel really cheap, not going to lie. But the other ones did too but I loved the sound. Here is what erks me the most. I was very happy with the back surround speakers. I loved that they stood high. As I built them I was so happy to have full surround sound again. I never placed the other ones behind the sofa and knew I was going to do so with these. The height was a dream, perfect for movies, my videos, you name it. I had visions in my head of what I would be watching. Not so fast. The speaker wire that comes with this system, they are all black and color coded as stated above. However, the back surround speakers have the shortest length! Again, you can’t just use speaker wire; they have the plastic casing over their wires at one end. Frustrated, I remembered the other system I had, the speaker wires were white and long, just what I needed. I have white wash floors and planned to run them under the house and up. They would blend perfectly. However, the plastic casing on the other system does not fit this one! I was so mad. The back surround speakers are sitting to the side of my TV right now and I am not happy about it. Why did they not put longer wires on the back speakers? I want to fire or talk to the person who designed this unit! That really bothers me. I am going to see if I can figure out the casing or call them to see if I can get longer wires. However, the wires are built into the back speakers. I can replace them but would have to tuck the existing wires away, does not make any sense.

When you start it up, it will take you through a brief set up. You will probably think you are done, not so fast. That is where you will be highly disappointed. The set up and default settings are terrible. Flat, very flat. What you need to do, mind you the remote is the sameas the other one I had but the set up on screen is different, follow these steps:
Hit the home key, hit the set up key, settings, down to audio. Once there, highlight and select ‘sound effects’. Equalizer is defaulted to Flat, change it to heavy. Subwoofer change to three, four is too heavy and it will shake too much. Just changing these settings will be a massive improvement. Of course, make sure you select the sound of your liking. A lot of people do not know you can change it though.

On my old system there was an audio button when you hit the home key. With this one, you hit home and there is no audio button. Instead, once home, you hit option, then select the audio you need. In my case, digital in. You will know you have the correct setting when you see it displayed on the front of the unit.

I have had no issues with any DVD’s freezing, they play fine for me. A lot of people mentioned a fan. I heard it when setting up the unit, but I do not hear it when I am watching TV. I sit about 20 feet or more back. I have noticed the movies on Netflix and Pandora load a lot faster. The other unit had a bit of a lag, not this one.

Again, without owning a previous unit, I would be upset. It took me time with my other unit to find out how to set it up. The short cable really is ridiculous and the fact that you can’t use standard speaker wire and have to use their wires, it annoys me.

However, I am very happy with the sound. It has the same watts as the other systems I owned, 1000 watts total, but it just sounds better. I really want to give this a 3 and a half but am going to bump it up to a four. Unpacking it is easy, setting it up is easy, tweaking it to your liking and the short back speaker wires are annoying. I didn't have much to lose when purchasing these earbuds. I couldn't find good OEM replacement earbuds that came with the Galaxy (and if I did they all went out on one side or got lost) and wanted something that was comfortable, sounded great and cheap. I'm pretty rough on earbuds since I commute everyday so I couldn't see myself spending more than $20 on a pair of cans. These turned out to be a welcome surprise for the money. Let's go to the breakdown:

Pros:
- Price. Under $20 which was the goal
- Fit. Takes some getting used to but I find the behind the ear wire more comfortable and stable than most other earbuds I've used. Plus the don't fall out of your ears as easily. The double flange on the earbud tips helps form a good seal in your ear canal. There is some noise isolation but don't expect it to be on par with $50+ earphones.
- Sound. I listen to a lot of bass heavy music (funk, hiphop, dnb) so I always check for a certain frequency response in the low end. These have good bass. Boomy but not overwhelming and muddy. Treble and Mids compliment each other. Again, super-audiophiles will probably nitpick the frequency response but I found them just right without having to adjust my phone's eq too much.
- Jack is at 90 degree angle, which lessens the chance of it damaging the port.
Cons:
- Feel of the cord is a bit stiff and plasticky. The wire behind the ear is a nice touch and I hope it will last but the rest of the cord feels like it will potentially get brittle and break.
- Remote controls didn't work with my phone but I think it's a firmware issue as I've not been able to get any to work.
- When pushing one of the headphones in, it made a crinkly sound. Didn't effect listening but it lowered the quality on these a bit. You get what you pay for and they are decent regardless.

Hi,

This is my review of the product listed as:

EasyAcc DP100 Ultra-Portable Bluetooth 4.0 Speaker with Microphone and Aux function, 25 Hour Playback Time, Black

I received this product last week and have been using it for a couple of hours today for a detailed review. I have also included a set of photos in case anyone is interested.

UNBOXING AND OBSERVATIONS:

I had mixed feelings about the unboxing experience.

The good news is that this product box is covered by hard plastic wrap that you have to tear off along the edges when you first get it. That protects the box from dust and minor scratches to the box. I liked that.

The bad news that I didn’t like is that the product box has a somewhat inconvenient way of tearing the lid off and revealing the contents and the cables inside. First, when I removed the product cover sleeve from the cardboard box, there wasn’t a quick standard way of opening up the lid. There’s actually a trial of precut outlines that you have to tear off on your own to form your own opening and closing lid. On my first try, I got half of it off correctly, but the other half tore the wrong way and it left the boxing damaged. That made me realize that this box will not be reusable for storage as compared to my other product boxes. Next, to reveal the Micro USB and AUX cable inside with the User Manual, the user is instructed by an embedded note on the box that you have to pull upwards from a hole, which requires some effort to remove before revealing the contents underneath it. My User’s Manual was bent like an arch and rolled up when I removed that layering of the cardboard, which I didn’t like. I like my brand new User Manuals to be printed flat to the boxing or tucked so that it doesn’t wrinkle. I suggest EasyAcc to improve its design on the product packaging boxes and how it’s designed to store contents within it.

When I removed everything out, here’s how it looked:

- The Bluetooth speaker was already inside a travel pouch tied up that had been tightly squeezed into the box. That speaker was wrapped and covered in a transparent bag.
- The AUX and Micro USB cables were packaged together in a transparent bag that you had to tear off and remove. That was nice packaging to provide some minimal protection
- The User Manual was available by itself and arched

The AUX cables are silver plated connectors, which is what my photos show. I would’ve like seeing gold plated connectors since those are better quality and I suggest EasyAcc upgrade to those since they are quite popular for technology geeks.

The Micro USB cable is pretty standard for a wireless accessory used to charge. That’s good to know because you won’t have to worry about buying any other type of unique or standard cable for this product, such as a custom made cable or the Mini USB cables, which are not common for these types of Bluetooth or wireless accessories.

Before doing anything with the Bluetooth Speaker, I felt it was important to read the User’s Manual prior to operation so that you know how to use the speaker in and out. I suggest readers to do the same if they purchase this product.

Some notable information in the User Manual worth mentioning are:

Technical Specs:

Charging Time: 3-4 hours
Playback time: 15-20 hours
Talk time: 8-10 hours
Standby time: 300 hours
Effective operating distance: 10 m
Capacity of built-in lithium battery: 2200mAh
Maximum power output: 4W
Frequency response: 100Hz-20kHz
Materials: Metal + ABS

In looking at these specs:

I think 3-4 hours charge time is reasonable for a product that lasts 15-20 hours. For a product that lasts that long, you could use it nonstop from the time you wake up until you go to sleep and then charge it overnight for beyond 3-4 hours and have it ready by the next morning to rinse and repeat the pattern. They didn’t specify, but I’m assuming the charge time for 3-4 hours is for those who use a wall charger or charging station to charge their Bluetooth speaker. I would not recommend charging this product with a USB port on the laptop or computer because that will result in a slower charge time. Unless an emergency and no wall outlet options are available, then I would avoid it.

Playtime of 15-20 hours is impressive. For my review, I used the product for about 2 hours to write up and talk about it because I didn’t have time to delay talking about it after trying it out for a week. I think that you’ll peak at the 20 hours if you leave the volume within 70% or lower of the total output power. Also, it depends on what type of music you’re playing if it requires a lot of energy and effort from the speakers. But either way, even at 15 hours, this is impressive. I like how long it lasts because it could be used as a weekend trip without charge. I could go somewhere for the weekend, charge it Friday night, and then leave Saturday morning to casually use it on Saturday and Sunday afternoons and night, and if I’m casually using it, it will last me before I head home on Sunday to charge and have it ready by Monday.

Talk time of 8-10 hours is good. I will be later testing the microphone sensitivity and quality of this speaker. But being able to talk for that long through your speakers is also impressive because I can imagine it would be fun to be around a group of people like friends and family and have this speaker in the center table to have a group call to a certain special individual.

Bluetooth of any version is meant to handle up to 33 feet of tested reach from the source of the Bluetooth device in an open space. I will be testing that later, but my expectations is that Bluetooth 4.0 technology should make the connection from a far distance much more stable and handle minimal dry wood walls along the way.

The battery of 2200mAh is really good, which then dictates the length of usage, play, and talk time. Prior to this model, I had seen other Bluetooth speakers in this price range that only have batteries in the 3 digit range.

The material being ABS and Metal is an interesting combination. Most accessories of Bluetooth products and wireless products in general are ABS, which are heat resistant to the outside from contact with people holding or touching the product. It can also handle impact from low level drops well.

In looking at the Bluetooth speaker, my thoughts was that this product has some reasonable weight to it. The weight isn’t on the user manual, but even though I could hold and grip it with one hand, it’s not something that I can hold onto for long hours without issues. Because of this, what would’ve been nice to have for this product is if there was a hook extension to link a lanyard to this to hook it to your waistline belt loop or a backpack zipper to have it hang by you so that you don’t have to carry it when walking around. I provide that as a suggestion.

The speaker measures 2 and ½ by 2 and ½ by 3 and 13/16th inches

There is a metal ring around the top of it that gives it some sort of a shiny glary design to it. The top has the play/pause button, a plus button that indicates volume up and skip forward, and a minus button that indicates volume down and skip backward. The buttons are very easy to press into. They’re quite flexible and responsive to gentle touch when pressed into the engraving area of the button symbols. They make a small click sound when pressed for the mechanical response. On the top of the speaker is also a mic hole and a small led indicator display.

Around the sides of the speaker is the speaker itself. IT looks as though to provide over 180 degrees of coverage, which looksinteresting as I have not had or seen a Bluetooth speaker that has a rounded speaker coverage.

At the bottom is the EasyAcc logo and certifications. It also mentions the model: EasyAcc-DP100 and the website.

What’s nice is that at the bottom is a ring of rubber stopper that is about 7/16th of an inch thick all around to provide grip to the surface you put it on and doesn’t let it slide as easily without a lot of resistance to keep it still. Tapping along either side will make it rock around and stay neutrally grounded. I’m holding around the speaker and trying to move it up and down, and there’s a lot of weighted pressure and resistance thanks to the rubber stopper at the bottom.

Towards the backside of where the speaker stops circular coverage is the DC IN for charging the speaker with the provided Micro USB cable, the ON and OFF slider switch, and the AUX input for plugging in the cable to listen without battery use.

USAGE:

When turning on the product for the first time, I heard some beeps and the LED indicator was flashing white to indicate it is ready to pair. I had with me an iPhone 5s to test so I went to my Bluetooth settings and found the EasyAcc-DP100 listed to pair. Once paired, I heard another beep, and then the LED indicator started to turn ON and OFF more slowly. That means that it’s been paired.

Now for the audio music quality test.

For this test, I used a few apps:

- An AOL Radio App
- An Amazon Music App
- YouTube

I played several songs, but the first one was a lyrical test.

I played: BRANDON HEATH LYRICS - The Light In Me

That song is mostly lyrical with mild composition of instruments. While the song was playing, I varied the volume and walked around.

I had placed the speaker at the center of my first floor house where the kitchen table was and walked around end to end of my house while the volume was about halfway.

The nice feature of this Bluetooth speaker is that it uses an undocumented AVRCP 1.4 and newer model, which allows me to directly control the volume of the speaker and the iPhone volume together into one. So I can turn the volume up and have it move both devices up, or vice versa with down. Other older models of competing products have 1.3 or older versions, which require me to control two separate independent volumes, which can be a pain.

I was able to walk around end to end of my house and hear the song very well and clear lyrically. The Bluetooth connection rarely made a choppy audio output. When it did, it was because I was walking by a microwave or stove top which caused interference. In an open space, it passed the 30 feet test with clarity of the music.

The lyrics sounded very clear and well heard at a halfway volume setting. I never needed to go past two or three ticks past the halfway marker when I was about 20 feet away because it was pretty loud already. I think with my open doors and windows, the neighbors in my backyard probably were able to hear the music. It was pleasant music though.

The next test was a rock alternative song. I chose Linkin Park - Lying From You because it had a lot of yelling and alternated tones of instrumentals and lyrical singing.

With this test, I found that the music was heard OK. If I listen carefully, the instrumentations could be heard a little distinctively when playing together in sync. However, the overall experience sounded a little meshed together of the singing and instrumentation, which sounded more noise generated than clear distinctive individual recognition the instrumentation and singing. But, it was an OK experience. For a $30 sales price product, it passes this test well for its price range.

One of the things that I was disappointed in that I didn’t like was that even though the speaker appears to have a design of over 180 audio output coverage semi around, I paid attention to the music while I was listening and walking around as well as being up close holding the speaker, and what I found out was that the speaker projects most of its outputted sound from the front side. But from the left and right sides and back, it’s very faded and you can’t tell that the same level of power is being produced from those sides as compared to the front. I walked 20 feet along the front side and it was different than walking 20 feet from the backside. It’s very noticeable. But, even though this product doesn’t provide the all-around consistent output along its sides like how it appears, it’s still a good powerful speaker.

The next test was a bass test. I went on YouTube and played DJ Snake, Lil Jon - Turn Down for What. It seems that most rap songs produce a lot of bass.

The bass quality that I heard from this song was evident. I could hear the bass more noticeably pounding a little more than a gentle feel when I cranked up the volume to about two thirds of the way towards maximum. At the halfway point of the volume, I could hear the bass, but it was weak. You’d have to crank up the volume higher to hear the bass while the rest of the song’s instruments and lyrics are being sung. I think for this Bluetooth speaker from EasyAcc, the bass is better than other models in this price range that I’ve tested and tried. But, I would suggest on making improvements on it to give a better enriched experience with the bass pressure.

Next up was the calling feature using the MIC test on the Bluetooth speaker.

For this test, I first did a few things between my iPhone 5s and my landline phone that has speakerphone on it to call each other.

One of the things that I finally noticed at this point of the evaluation is that this Bluetooth speaker model does not offer a battery meter indicator on my iPhone. Some products offer that and it is a benefit because it allows the user to periodically check on the power left remaining before a full charge needs to take place to predict and plan. For a product like this that offers 15-20 hours playback, that’s a long time to gauge when the battery is getting ready to get lower to fully charge the product. Charging a product too often with minimal usage really causes wear and tear on the battery lifespan. I learned about that, so that’s why I suggest EasyAcc to design future models with this feature for Android and iOS.

I first tried to call to the iPhone from my landline phone. I had an unexpected surprise that hurt the review of this product. For some reason, this Bluetooth speaker not only projects the ringtone music of your iPhone, which is OK, but it blasts it out so loud, that I was about 15-20 feet away, and it startled and shocked me when my ringtone was heard through the Bluetooth speakers. Imagine you’re playing a calm setting song next to you or a casual song next to you and all of a sudden, you hear like a pitch high loud music from your ringtone of an incoming call. It’s worse than a wake up morning alarm clock or horn being blown. I didn’t like this about this Bluetooth speaker. This is what upset me and ruined what was a good positive experience up to this point in the evaluation. I tested a few times and each time, the speakers blasted loud as if I had maxed volume on the speaker of my ringtone playing. It didn’t matter if my volume was only 3-4 ticks on the iPhone volume meter. It just blasted it. But oddly, after the 6th or 7th time, I switched around apps while listening to music and had an incoming call and the ringtone music through the speakers dropped incredibly low by itself and stayed that way for the rest of my evaluation.

Defective product or just a strange design? I’m not too sure. But I’d rather take a lower calmer ringtone music projected through the speakers thanbeing blasted out to where it hurts my ears like how it initially acted.

I suggest that EasyAcc retest this speaker model for incoming calls while playing music from music apps to detect this issue and fix it with future models.

The good thing is that with this Bluetooth speaker’s feature, when you hang up on a call, it automatically resumes where you last left off on the song. I like that and it’s a common feature standard across many Bluetooth speakers.

What I really liked about this calling test was that the microphone was very sensitive to picking up my voice, almost better than my iPhone’s built in microphones in terms of range and coverage. I had my landline speaker phone on my desk in my living room area and closed the door to hear it from the other side of the room. I talked into the mic of the Bluetooth speaker up close inches away. I heard my voice feedback reasonably good with no muffle. Then I continued to about a foot away, then a couple of feet away, then freely walking around the table while talking without leaning into the speaker while it was at the center of the table and my voice could be echoed through the landline speakerphone just fine. I went as far as about 10 feet away towards my sink and talked out in my normal tone of voice and I still heard my voice echo back. Of course, this was tested when everything around me was quiet, but based on this test, it shows the microphone on this Bluetooth speaker is impressive and is as good of a feature as the battery life on this speaker.

IN SUMMARY:

PROS:

1) The product comes with a travel pouch can be used to tie up and travel around with you looped onto handles and zippers
2) Very good microphone sensitivity for picking up voices while walking distantly away (up to 10 feet tested)
3) 15-20 hour playback time under a full charge means that this product will take care of your music loving ears for more than a whole day
4) Simple player control designs on the top of the speaker
5) Rubber stoppers at the bottom to give friction enabled stability and prevent it from slipping or sliding around off the table

CONS:

1) Noticeable weight to it with one hand that means that it is not designed to hold onto for a long time without fatigue
2) Inconvenient packaging design of the boxing and storage of the contents inside the box. It made my included travel pouch damaged with scratches and hard to undo crease lines
3) Music and audio output does not project 180 degrees all around like how it looks and appears to be designed to do
4) Inconsistently extremely loud to extremely quiet projection of the ringtone music of my iPhone while an incoming call was occurring which ruined my overall experience and startled me with frustrations and concern over my hearing

SUGGESTIONS:

1) Improve the design of the opening of the box and interior boxing compartments to hold the contents
2) Provide gold plated connectors for AUX cable
3) Provide an extension of this Bluetooth speaker to allow a lanyard to link to it for looping it to a zipper, bag, or waist belt loop
4) Improve the bass quality to be more powerful without needing to crank up the volume of the overall sound playing experience
5) Include a Bluetooth battery level meter indicator for iPhone and Android devices to show what the battery level status is and when it is low and needs recharging

USER SCENARIOS:

This product would be useful for those who:

1) Like to listen to music
2) Are going on a road trip
3) Are spending time outdoors or camping adventures
4) Want to have group calls with individuals
5) Can’t afford more premium high end portable speakers
6) Need something convenient to carry with them that is stronger in audio quality than their smartphone or tablet volume

Overall, I liked most of the features of this Bluetooth speaker, including the microphone quality for calling and talking from a distance and still have it able to pick up my voice well. Music tests passed well, but I encourage further improvement to the bass quality. Major downside that was disappointing was being shocked and startled to how suddenly high my volume jolted to the music of my ringtone playing through the Bluetooth speakers when there was an incoming call.

But for $30, this is a good deal. I expect EasyAcc will make improvements to this model and line of Bluetooth speakers

A cheap pair of headphones that posses high quality sound, with good soundstage.

COMFORT, 5/10: Occasionally they do feel a bit uncomfortable, but generally discomfort can be easily alleviated with a five to ten minute break. Most of the discomfort stems from the stiff and uncompromising faux-leather cups, take care that they actually don't rest on your upper ears or you'll regret it. The headphones do little to allow a comfortable experience, but it's not painfully uncomfortable; they're average.

DURABILITY, 7/10: Thick and hardy cable, also a tad long for casual listening but that's always welcomed by me. I would feel more comfortable if the cable was detachable/replaceable but for the price of $30, you can easily replace the headphones with one of the same pair or a different pair of headphones. Faux-leather and plastic brace feel sturdy, and well constructed.

SOUND, 7.5/10: Excessive, almost piercing highs; subdued mids; subtle and pronounced lows. Out of the box, with no equalization it has overly sibilant highs, this might help you pick out details from music and but after a while, your listening experience can be exhausting. With equalization, you can make the cans adopt a more warm feel instead of the overly harsh brightness it comes with.

Due to the semi-open nature of the headphones, they do not isolate themselves well in loud environments; meaning that it's very easy for others to hear what you're listening to, and you can easily hear what's around you. But this isn't exactly a bad thing, as a semi-open soundstage allows for a rather wide soundstage that is very wide, and there's not a lot of headphones that can provide a soundstage of this caliber. Because of this, it's not unusual to see these pair of headphones to be commonly recommended by gamers, especially those on a budget.

FEATURES: No frills. Standard phone connector is a 3.5mm Stereo Adapter. Comes with a 1/4 inch adapter and a carry-bag. 8 Foot Cable, which may seem a bit overkill for casual listening, but I welcome this.Foot Cable, which may seem a bit overkill for casual listening, but I welcome this.

The kit has a great number of parts for the dollar. However, I had quite a time getting the arduino board to talk to my computer, which runs Win 8.1. The problem you may run into has to do with installing arduino drivers for the serial port. Unless they are "signed", Windows wants nothing to do with them, and the board isn't recognized when you plug it in. All I found in the device manager was "Unrecognized Device".

So, what to do? The summary is: (a) install IDE software, (b) be sure "secure boot" has been disabled in your BIOS, (c) disable driver signature enforcement in the advanced startup options, and (d) install the arduino.inf driver supplied by the IDE once you've booted without signature enforcement. Then you can run the IDE software, and pick the correct serial port.

A more detailed set of instructions can be found by googling: forum arduino rejoyce "missing digital signature for driver" [go to post #42, to get step (a)] and then go to post #13 to get steps (b) - (d)]. Yes, spell the google search exactly as I have noted. Even with these steps, it took me a couple of tries to unplug the board, and plug it in while the IDE was running. But it finally started working. Also, you may wish to donate to the young man that produced the IDE for step (a). I had another well-known IDE in place, and could NOT get it to work, even with all the steps I've recommended. I had to use the arduino.inf from IDE developed by the forum user "eried", marked "Download (2013-05-24)" [you will find this linked in post #42, listed above]. The other IDE (called MPIDE) simply didn't work until I used the driver from "eried". So kudos to him!
