This review is for an Electrohome "SelfSet Clock Radio" model EAAC601, manufactured in June, 2015. Some of the earlier reviews posted must be for another model of clock radio because some of the criticisms mentioned do not apply to this model. As others have suggested, one should keep the instruction manual because while most of the buttons' functions are intuitive, some buttons have more than function depending whether it is briefly pushed or pushed-and-held (for 3 sec.) or used in conjunction with another button. This model is compact with a footprint of about 3.5 by 5.5" and 4.5" high. Clock screen brightness can be set to high, low or off by repeated pressing of a button. We use the low setting and the clock, which is within 1.5' of my face, does not disturb me. Changing the clock light intensity setting does not change the projected time brightness, which is a red image about 1' by 0.5' on an 8.5' ceiling. The projected clock image is composed of red bars, while the clock screen uses light blue/white dots on a medium dark blue background. We have no trouble reading the clock or projected time (without glasses) in a dark room. The clock radio arrived with a CR2032 button battery installed and functional, so when it is plugged in, the clock radio comes on with the correct time for the Eastern time zone ("Time Zone 2 is the default"). The clock can be easily adjusted for time zone and for optional daylight savings time. This is NOT an atomic clock even though the instruction book says it is "equipped with "auto time set"". They mean that the clock comes set because of the internal battery, which holds time and radio information during a black out or when the clock is unplugged. I do not tested to determine if a set alarm would function during a blackout. The screen and projected time are not visible when unplugged. This clock is clearly manufactured for the Canadian market because time zones and daylight savings time are mentioned for provinces, but it is no problem adjusting for US locations. This clock radio operates on 110-120V AV only, not 220V or battery. The radio's sound is reasonable for a speaker this size and is clear and static free. Because we are in a tight valley in the Blue Ridge Mountains and the walls are 1.75' solid concrete, radio reception in the house is poor. Even with a high quality radio, usually we get 1 local AM station and no FM stations, so I cannot address on the radio's sensitivity. Dialing is done by either an "up" or "down" button. The radio has 20 presets, 10 AM and 10 FM, indication that it has a digital tune (not analog tuned by a rotary knob as some reviews state. In dialing one sees the stations' id. numbers, but once set, the station id. does not appear on the screen. This may be a problem for some people because one is less likely to know what station is playing until the station identifies itself.
So far (having used it only 3 days) we are completely pleased with this clock radio and recommend it highly.

I requested the Bose TV sound system hoping it would be an improvement over the cheaper Polk Audio soundbar we got a few years ago. Unfotunately, the sound isn't nearly as good on the Bose system.

We did back to back tests with tv sound, the soundbar, and the Bose system while watching music videos and a television show. The Bose system is definitely a huge improvement over the television's built-in speakers, but it doesn't come close to matching our Polk Audio soundbar. It's not surprising that our Polk Audio soundbar, which has a dedicated subwoofer would out-perform the Bose Solo system on bass, but even in the mids and highs and better on the Polk Audio system. The highs especially sound a bit tinny on the Bose system, and voices sound just a little less full on the Bose system than they are on our Polk Audio soundbar.

Comparing the Bose Solo system, which is designed to rest under a television to a soundbar that can't do that is a bit unfair. If you need a television sound system that can rest under the television so that it won't take up any extra space, the Bose Solo system is a huge improvement over standard television sound. But if you have the flexibility for another speaker configuration, there are definitely better options for your money.

We get around 60 channels and the reception is very good.  The only things I will add is if you buy steel pole from a big box home improvement store, make sure you use 8 gauge grounding wire.  I used a coated ground wire as I had to run a portion of it across my metal roof and wanted the added protection.  I used a 10" pole and sanded the bottom and sprayed a rubber sealant on the bottom to put my mind at ease.  I unfolded the antenna while I was on the roof and then ran the  ground wire, the coaxial cable, then attached the antenna to the pole, oriented it (using TVfool signal locater) and then secured it to the chimney, connected the coax through the attic and boom job done.    Side notes it was 114 heat index and on the metal roof felt a lot hotter.    I get channels from San Antonio 25 miles away and Austin 40 miles away and we live in hill country with lots of oaks. UPDATE 9/5/2015: After about a month of working with technical support, it was determined that in order for DLNA and Spotify Connect to work in conjunction with eachother on my unit, I needed to factory reset, install an intermediate firmware update  (this was emailed to me/not available on the site or discussed in the manual), and THEN install the Spotify Firmware update. After following the above steps, everything began working spectacularly. I'd once again recommend this product, but shaved a star off my initial rating because I believe many people would give up on the L16 before finding this kind of solution.  UPDATE 8/31/2015: The Spotify Connect firmware upgrade has left this device incapable of connecting to DLNA. My choices are to do a factory reset and lose Spotify Connect, or live without DLNA and lose a substantial amount of audio quality. I have been working with JBL customer support for over a month to no avail. Consider me truly disappointed. My recommendation is withdrawn.  Unfortunately I cannot return this device despite their false advertisement.  Let me first say that my true "audiophile" setup exists in a different room from where I placed the Authentics L16. I purchased this as a way to easily play high quality music in my living room. I've been very impressed with its performance, and often wind down after work using it to play jazz or folk, both of which it handles very well. The difference in sound quality between bluetooth and DLNA is surprising. I've often entertained guests with it - all of whom have left envious of the clarity and life it breathes into music. Is this a true audiophile product? No. Does it produce exceptional clarity and bass when compared against the wireless competetion? Absolutely. This product is excellent for its intended purpose and great way to start out your quest for hi-fi audio. I will say that the quality of the media you play through it has a substantial effect on the quality of the sound - I usually stick to 320kbps, V0, or FLAC. Setting up wireless/DLNA was actually rather difficult through the app, so I wound up downloading the manual and connected it through the steps provided within. All in all, though, a great living room companion.  Edit: If your wireless router doesn't broadcast across the 2.4ghz range, this product is not for you. It is designed to recognize 2.4ghz rather than 5. Dual band routers should be OK so long as they discriminate against the two frequency bands, but if you're stuck at 5 you may have a few more years left of waiting (none of the DLNA speakers I tried supported 5).

Audiophile speaking. In this review I'll reference two other sets of over-ear headphones that I own, and why I think either of them is a better choice than the 808 Performers.

Pros of the 808:
-Deep bass
-Cool design choices. The speakers are held in their plastic retainers with cord, which is meant to look like the bump-isolating rig you put a microphone in. It looks cool, although I'm not sure how durable it would be.

Cons of the 808:
-Basically everything else.
-The build feels pretty plasticky and doesn't seem very durable, despite all the attention paid to cool-looking details. Edit: I noticed the description says steel construction, and went back and was only able to tell there was metal in the headband because the air conditioning was on and the metal had gotten cold. For some reason the finish and paint put on the headband was made to resemble cheap plastic? I'm confused as to why anyone would do this. If the headband felt more like metal, I might have had a better first impression, not that this would make much difference because top-of-the-line headphones are all plastic with no issues.
-The sound is so bass-heavy that it obscures and mutes everything else. It's like listening to a set of bass-heavy headphones when you've got light hearing damage. Honestly after listening to these for a while I had a very faint ringing in my ears, probably from the exaggerated bass.

Versus the Sony MDRZX100 ZX:
The sound quality in the 808s is surprisingly worse than the ZX, and the ZX costs around a quarter of the price. The ZX doesn't obscure the rest of the audio range like the 808s do, while still delivering okay bass. If you want cheap headphones that sound good, I highly recommend the ZX.

Versus the Audio-Technica ATH-M40x:
No comparison. The M40x costs only a bit more than the 808s, yet have a completely superior sound profile. To be fair the M40x is more of a "studio" headphone, meaning it has a very balanced sound profile- you will only hear the bass the same way that it is recorded, not enhanced like the 808s. The earcups even feel cooler on my head, the M40 is just made better.

Head-to-head: I kept going to the 808 throughout a head-to-head on a few types of audio. The 808s were consistently bassy, but sounded muffled or maybe even like the audio was lower quality. The fit on the 808s continues to bug me, it seems like the right ear never quite wants to hold on correctly. The budget-bin Sony ZX headphones were crisp and clear for all types of audio, delivering better overall sound with a bit less bass. The Audio Technica M40x headphones are better than the ZX across the board, and in another league compared to the 808s. Back-to-back in terms of only sound quality, with 10 being professional-quality studio headphones, I'd rate the 808s a 4/10, the ZX a 6/10, and the M40x a 9/10.

There are much better headphones in this price range, and I'd argue there are even better headphones in the bargain bin. Still, good reception on FM, AM/MW and shortwave, just more background hiss than better radios. Lots of hand capacitance, to be expected in a small, cheap radio like this.  Antenna joint and battery cover look thin, flimsy and cheap and are sure to get quickly damaged by any rough use. Wrist strap is too small to fit a hand through! I would NEVER get AAA radios.  Tuning knob is stiff and jumpy, making it all too easy to skip over stations when scanning around, and difficult to fine-tune on the station you want.  Dial isn't very accurate, and so small it wouldn't help a lot if it was. I really prefer digital displays (still with analog tuning). NO clock/alarm option, in case you were expecting one.  Good-enough choice for an emergency radio. Has the extended US frequencies  (1610-1710kHz) for the AM/MW band which cheap imports often ignore/omit. So I've been on the hunt for some quality earphones that I can use while working out. And by working out I mean long winded workouts on a daily basis. Not the casual here and there workouts that most average reviewers practice.

With that said, I came across a few websites during my search that had these earphones at the top of the list so needless to say I went ahead and purchased them in hopes that I would be a happy customer.

I must note that prior to going on the hunt, I had been using the Monster Livestrong ISport Earphones, which, although not perfect, were far superior to these. But in the end I lost them during a trip recently. They are now discontinued so I am now left to find something new.

So onto the review.

Package was decent enough but nothing special. Earphones come with various sizes of ear inserts that attach to the actual earphones themselves so finding a good fit shouldn't be a problem.

The wiring is a bit flimsy and where it attaches to the actual earphone is somewhat fragile. Although it didn't happen to me in my handful of usages, I can see how over time (not very long at that) the wire could fail from the earphone and either break or lose connection. Most earbuds I've had have a relatively rigid wire at the point where they actually connect to the earphone.

When I put them into my ears It almost felt as if they weren't in all the way. The outer rubber ring is supposedly supposed to secure the earphone to your ear by pushing up against that little bridge of cartilage that runs along the outside of the inner ear. To me, it didn't feel like it was big enough to be pushing up against my outer ear. But during my run during an actual run it miraculously stayed in little to no adjustment required during the entire 3 miles that I ran. And it also felt pretty non existent as others reviews have stated. So in terms of comfort, I definitely give it props as it not only stays put during rigorous activites but it also almost feels like it's not there.

Sound quality was nothing to rave about but was probably about average given it's size and isolation style. However, while running, the wires did bounce quite a bit and the resulting noise from that managed to obstruct the music. I was able to somewhat resolve that issue by using the wire clip to attach to my shirt. Ambient noise is pretty apparent as well. These earphones aren't meant to block out surrounding noise so if that's what you want then you're out of luck. That or you just max out the volume to hopefully drown out any other noise.

The biggest issue I had with these is that the inline remote wiring was extremely faulty. I may have gotten a defective pair but I need to share my experience nonetheless. On my first run with these I used my newer Ipod Nano. As I started running I immediately noticed that the songs kept on skipping randomly. At first I thought maybe I had the nano set to shuffle when shaken but that was not the case. It kept on doing so until I finally clipped the wire to my shirt to lessen the bouncing of the wires. That helped somewhat but every so often it would still skip spontaneously.

Second run, I decide to use a different older model of nano thinking that it might be an issue with the player and not the headphones. This time around it was worse. Skipping, volume changing, pausing, unpausing...it was basically all over the place. On top of that, the right earphone was going in and out.

In summary, I think the design is great for the purpose (running, working out, etc.) however, the audio and functionality are totally non existent. Even if the wiring on my unit was defective I can only see that a working unit would eventually go bad based on the flimsy wiring alone. I'm no audiophile as well but I just thought that the sound was subpar for headphone at that pricepoint.

Anyhow, I don't recommend these headphones as there were easily more negatives than positives.

I was sent this wireless speaker for my honest and unbiased opinion.

On receiving the package, I was most surprised about its size and on unpacking it I was very doubtful about its intended use. Was Anker out of their mind or have they started making children's toys?

Well, mama always said, "The proof of the pudding is in the eating". So I whip out my phone, quickly set up a bluetooth connection which was a breeze, and crank up the volume. Hmmmm...tiny speakers - impressive sound.

But one can not really judge without a benchmark so I decide to pit it against the Jabra Soulmate (First Generation). The JS is a beefy wireless speaker and I was surprised to see and hear this tiny Anker hold its own up against it. No doubt that they are not in the same league but with a few twiks, the Anker may even surpass the JS.

The Anker produces more of a treble filled sound, and holds up well at high volumes with no noticeable distortion. Though not being a party host, it will fill your medium sized UK room with excellent sounding music of all types - Classic, Jazz, Rock, Afro, Rap, Heavy Metal, R'n'B; you name it. The range was great too. With the speaker with me in the bathroom behind closed doors and the streaming tablet more than 10 feet away, there was no distortions or break in connection.

Charging to full capacity took about 2 hrs, and I had about 4 hrs of music at maximum voice. I loved that it came with a lanyard (the black link rope in mine was a bit rough for wear), a protective bag. The speaker has rubber non slip tabs underneath which helped dampen any vibrations from the speaker and also gave it adequate clearance.

Honestly, I'm truly impressed though it needs a few improvements such as a indicator for when one has reached maximum volume when pushing volume up bottom, say a beep or tone. Playing music via 3.5mm cable and SD card was effortless. They take priority over Bluetooth. One can only appreciate what I am trying to say by listening to one.

It is an excellent travel companion and will be going with me on my next holiday. I recommend it to everyone especially music lovers and Audiophiles.

It has been a few months of amazing listening pleasure with my AKG-K550s so I here offer my thoughts in gratitude for the many others who came before me, and therefore helped guide me to these gems. As is tradition for these reviews: My listening arrangement is a FireStone “Cute Beyond” headphone amplifier powered by two UB1280 scooter batteries. It was formerly powered by their accompanying “Supplier,” but I could still hear more AC-Ripple and RF-Noise than I wanted. My hearing is such, and has been professionally tested as such, that I can quite readily hear content at -110dB. Using batteries eliminates the AC-Ripple because no AC electricity is involved; and by placing my amplifier between the batteries their size and lead-acid content essentially eliminates RF-Noise. At even modestly unreasonable listening levels this arrangement is essentially silent. My own biology – my heart beating, my breathing, etc. – is much louder than the amplified music. Mostly I source my music from a Cowon D2 (from the old days when Cowon rocked), but occasionally from my Lenovo T530i laptop. My prior headphone experience was my eight year relationship with my Sennheiser HD-280 Pro headphones.

As is also tradition for these reviews: My criteria for a headphone upgrade was 1) warm, yet well-articulated sound reproduction, 2) large round ear-cups, 3) light weight, 4) modest head grip, and 4) a straight cord. Anyone who has used the Senn-280s knows that they are the opposite of these criteria – bright, oval, heavy, and tight with a coiled cord. However, I still really like my Senns for casual listening, it was simply “time to grow up” if I could afford it. It was just over 30-years ago that I purchased my first audiophile room speakers – Allison CD9s. It was their “warm, yet well-articulated sound reproduction” that I wanted to approach or improve upon with new headphones.

I Internet-reviewed and specification-compared about adozen headphones narrowing for serious consideration four cans: the Shure SRH-1540s, the AKG-K550s, the new-model Sennheiser Momentums (which reviewers claimed to actually be over-the-ear similar to my 280s in size), and the Beyerdynamic DT-770s (in their original high impedance version).

I noted in the specifications for the K550s that their Total Harmonic Distortion was about 1/5th of the distortion of my HD-280s and similarly in the -100dB range. Since I can hear quite well in that range, but apparently many people cannot, I was anticipating an extraordinary clarity of sound. I read many reviews that opined that the K550s were somewhat “flat” or “neutral” sounding which was exactly what I was seeking both because I prefer to listen that way, and it is easier to add sonic character than to correct for poor performance. Many reviews noted an “extended bass,” due largely to their 60mm diaphragms, which was also clear and neutral. Finally, there is an extensive “benchmark” review out there that claims that the K550s have a “sweet spot” where the sound-field significantly opens and richens.

In my humble few hundred hours of listening I agree with all that I just shared, including the presence of that somewhat elusive “sweet spot.” My only difference of opinion would be that I do NOT find the “sweet spot” significant in anyway. I take no time to “find it” because the sound “outside it” is wonderful. The slight increase in sonic richness and sound-stage was notable when I first experienced it, but nothing worth chasing-it-about when I can simply lay-down, get comfortable, and enjoy the best sound I have heard in 35-years.

The first piece that I listened to was “Mount Saint Helens Symphony” by Alan Hovhaness which “blew me away” with its newly-heard textures and bass. Next was his short piece “Elibris, Dawn God of Urardu” and I found myself crying. The next day was “Orion” byPhilip Glass in which the full tapestry of composition was finally revealed to me. A few days later I switched genres with “Book of Secrets” by Loreena McKennit and found myself in a freshly renewed relationship with her three later albums (and still appreciating her first two). Onto “Days of Future Passed” by the Moody Blues to be yet again astonished at the intricacy of their classical/rock blend. I then surfed some contemporary jazz with Norah Jones, some vintage jazz with Mile Davis, some southern jazz by Wynton Marsalis, and came around again to two of my favorite folk/popular albums each by Amy Fradon and Leslie Ritter. Each and all were more intimately satisfying than ever before. I took a quick swim through “Babel” by Mumford and Sons, a quick spin with the a capella wonderfulness of The Pentatonix, and finished off with some Fever Ray. I would end my experimentation with “From Me Flows What You Call Time” by Toru Takemitsu which would find me crying again. My AKG-K550s are HERE TO STAY, and don’t ask to borrow them!

One niggle: Dear AKG, if you’re going to send us a “straight cord” how about NOT wrapping it so tightly that the bends may never come out. In doing so it becomes a “zig-zag cord” when the box is so graciously spacious that a gentle wrap is totally doable.

Finally, I earlier noted “if I could afford it.” When I finished my reviews I had decided that only the AKG-K550s and the Shure-1450s were clearly desirable upgrade potentials. I could replace my satisfying Sennheiser HD-280s for a mere $80 so my final questions were: Could the K550s provide 4x greater benefit, could the 1450s provide 6x more benefit, and how was I going to cope with denying myself an upgrade since I could not afford either of them? On my final “price check,” to end and document my research, the K550s were on sale for $190 and free shipping. Could they provide 2.5x greater benefit? At that price-point theywere worth trying. As we know THEY ARE MINE now, and don’t ask to borrow them. But I am not so sure about the 4x or 6x greater benefits at normal street price; especially when one cannot know what they are missing.

1. The power lead indicators on the circuit board are backward. If you hook the power in as shown on the board, you'll burn the board. The way to tell if you have the power hooked up correctly is to BRIEFLY touch the power leads to the connectors and see if the blue LED lights. If it does, you're good. If it doesn't... reverse the leads. Friend of mine across country reports the same issue on his. He thought it was defective until I suggested he reverse the leads... then his worked fine. That little glitch can cause board destruction-- and drops 2 stars.
2. The volume pot could easily have been made on/off as well. Instead if you want an on/off switch you will need to install it separately, between the power connector and line. I would like to see them upgrade the board with an on/off volume pot. Is easy.

I have had a pair of Sennheiser HD590s since highschool. Lord did I love those things. These days they look rather ratty and are slightly blown out in the left ear, but they were a fantastic workhorse for over a decade. Heck, they got me through obtaining a bachelors in music! But that's the past and these days I am software engineer earning his second degree at ASU. As such, I got to order a MacBook with a nice student discount, and with it came...a Beats Solo2 Wireless.

I instantly fell in love with the cordless cans life. It even had a microphone builtin! No more uncomfortable setups for gaming or business VoIP! Except...on-the-ear just outright hurt after 30mins and the sound frankly sucked. They advertise hard hitting bass, and that is exactly what it is. The only genres that made me raise an eyebrow was rap and hip hop - two of my least listened to genres. They even managed to screw up other, supposedly, bass heavy genres such as psytrance. I had grown up on the "flat" sound of Sennheiser and ended up resenting the EQ decisions that the Beats was making for me. But did I desperately want to keep the cord cut.

So out I went. All I wanted was my HD590s, but wireless. Sennheiser had done me SO well for over a decade that I was instantly drawn to this headset. It seemed like exactly what I desired. Well, that's what I told myself anyways. These are really are meant to be competitors to the Beats. That is, worn in public with a bass emphasis. The result is the earpads are small and tight to avoid leaking and there is a slight EQ bias towards bass (not nearly as much as the Beats, I don't think Sennheiser had the heart to so completely butcher its core sound). Unfortunately I had no intention of wearing these in public, I needed a domestic headset. That means I was dealing with the discomfort of tight earpads and a less than desirable sound profile in exchange for bluetooth at home...all at the tune of $300.

To me that was just too much compromise for $300. So I returned these and bought a pair of [[ASIN:B0042A8CW2 Sennheiser HD 598 Over-Ear Headphones]]. These are a true replacement for my HD590s and are fantastic for my purposes. I am keeping the Beats for mobility and VoIP, but the HD598s are for day-to-day use.

So, I believe that these are far better than the Beats Solo2 Wireless, but they simply were not what I was looking for, plus I already had the heavily discounted Beats. If you are in the market for a direct Beats competitor I would definitely give these a look as they do better across genres than the Beats do.

We all have rusty old speakers that we love to keep and no throw them away. Be it your college dorm speakers or those speakers in your garage or attic where you listened to hard rock songs. You just are unable to let them go. But with the advent of bluetooth speakers and world going wireless, those speakers feel dated.
You can achieve a middle ground here by "converting” the existing wired speakers to bluetooth ones. This little nifty box is a NFC Bluetooth Audio Receiver which will enable bluetooth connection to you old / wired speakers.

This is what you get...
NFC Bluetooth Audio Receiver
MicroUSB Cable
Wall Charger
RCA Cable
3.5mm Audio cable

The way it converts your old and wired speakers to bluetooth is that you connect the speaker’s 3.5mm Aux In / Audio In or RCA In to the Aux Output of this bluetooth audio receiver. Remember that this is an audio receiver so you will now be connecting your phone or tablet or any audio device with bluetooth by connecting it over bluetooth. The audio receiver shows up as “GT BT-Receiver 15” on your phone / tablet. Once you have paired the audio receiver to your phone, you can transmit music / audio from your phone to this receiver. Now since the receiver is connected to your speakers, you can hear the music using your existing speakers but this time over bluetooth.
In the front of the receiver, there is a blue light which lights up when the receiver is either in pairing mode or connected to a device. The top of the audio receiver is glossy and looks very polished and sophisticated. This bluetooth receiver needs just 500mA current so this means you can even use a power bank to use this outside your home where wall charger won’t be available.

The device as also can be paired using NFC (just remember, NFC is used only for pairing, audio is still transmitted using bluetooth). Only some phones support NFC so you need to check your phone’s specifications. I willstrongly suggest keeping this bluetooth audio receiver in the direct line of sight to your transmitting device for the most efficient audio reception.

Use in Car ->
Yeah this is one awesome use of this bluetooth receiver if your car does not have inbuilt bluetooth but has AUX In. This way you can have bluetooth in your car. Just use the MicroUSB Cable and 3.5mm audio cable and connect the aux out to car’s aux in and for charging purpose, use a USB car charger and you are set. Don’t buy those cheap bluetooth china receivers. Buy some good quality ones like this.

Google Cardboard's original design did not fit my IPD and so I'm glad I found a headset that actually accommodated me. I use this with my LG G4 (leather back), and it's a very... very tight fit. When I load it in, I actually have to press in on the entering side of the phone to get it flush with the plastic (due to the phone's slight curve), and at that point I can slide it in no problem.

In all, highly recommended for movie/video watching, not recommended for vr gaming. Surprisingly comfortable.

FULL DISCLOSURE: I received this product for free so that I could review it.

I like the look of the clock; it is fairly compact (so it could be taken on a trip), and it runs silently (no \\"ticking\\" like the actual old mechanical clocks). The alarm dial is accurate to about 5 minutes (+/-) of the time you set, which is OK, although most folks are used to exact wake up times these days.

The only thing I didn't care for is the alarm. It has an electronic \\"beeep, beeep, beeep\\" sound that is not very loud - the two big bells on top are not used. The alarm basically sounds like a small travel alarm clock. This is fine if that is enough for your sleeping pattern, but unexpected because it LOOKS like the sound is going to rock your wake up.

I almost gave this three stars, but I actually do really like the clock. if the bells on top had worked it would be a five star product.

Summary: It works well and is compact. I like it overall, but wish it had a louder alarm. Recommended for light sleepers.

This alarm clock/radio is great! It's quite small, has two alarms which can be set to radio, buzzer or random "calming" sounds (put in quotes simply because they're just not my thing). Some people were complaining about the complexity of setting an alarm. That is false. Are there a lot of steps? Yes. It's only because there are a lot of options to go through. Plus, if you actually read the manual - it's riveting - it tells you that if you want to set the alarm without going through all the steps (like if you just wanted to change the time of the alarm), you hold the sleep/enter button and it will set the alarm without making you go through every single option. It will just keep whatever options you set the first time.

I have only used the radio as a wake-up so far. I love that it gradually gets louder until it reaches the volume you set. However, and this is why I took away a star, if you hit sleep, the alarm will come back on right at the set volume, rather than slowly crescendoing until it gets there. I am a happy user of the Bose SoundSport in-ear headphones. But I will say right up front that I have not in the past been a fan of in ear headphones, especially ear-buds like the ones supplied with phones and MP3 players and so forth. For one thing, I am, evidently, part of the minority of human beings on Earth who do not have the ideal ear lobe, as imagined by earphone designers, on which to hang or insert the typical ear-bud earphone. They will just not stay in, no matter what. And, in my experience, 99% of ear-buds earphones that I have ever tried had, for me, terrible sound.

Not so with these Bose SoundSport in-ear headphones. The sound is fantastic, with solid mid tones and lower frequencies. Very natural sounding. And, best of all, they will stay in my ear. This is partly due to the depth to which these earphones are inserted, but also in part to the "brackets" that use the inner lobe to brace the bud in place. Bose makes a big deal about promoting the various surface treatments that make the earphones comfortable and also keep them in place. Although it remains to be seen how well that aspect holds up over time the earphones are in the early going very comfortable and also stay in place. It was possible to hear what was going on in the real world while listening to music at a reasonable volume, important for those who listen to music while working or working out unless the real world absolutely demands their attention. All in all I would rate these highly and, although a bit pricey, as are all Bose branded items, they are not over priced for the quality on offer. RECOMMENDED.

I switch sides a lot when lying down, and with the too short cord I had to take my tablet with me to the other side. With a longer cord, this wouldn't be necessary, and when using the extension I had plenty of slack to move around as I pleased.

Overall, I'm happy with these headphones. Every pair of budget (to me 'budget' is $15 or less, which these headphones fall into at the time of review) earbuds and headphones I've owned have had some issue, either minor or major. The too short cord to me is a minor issue, and the many pros of these headphones outweigh the few cons.

Anker supplied me this product for testing and evalution purposes and I promise that my review is honest and fair.

As always with Anker the packaging is minimalist but more than ample to house and protect everything inside.
Contents of the box contained the speaker, a 3.5mm audio cable, mini USB cable, inctructions and a neat little bag for the speaker.

To fully charge the speaker doesnt take too long ,during which an led glows red above the power lead to give a visual indication of charge status. Although depending on use I've gotten an average of between 6-8 hours of use out of it (Really does depend how loud you like your music!). This is while having it constantly connected via bluetooth to my phone.

The speaker itself has a really nice look to it, almost classic in design but still looking very fresh and modern. 2 little rubber feet give it something stand on and stops it sliding around. The device is very well made and feels solid and is really nice to handle.

On top are three buttons, 1 for play/pause, and the two volume/skip buttons. On the left is the Auxiliary 3.5mm audio jack, mini USB charge port and surprisingly a memory card slot! A great idea as it means you dont need to connect to a phone etc to play your tunes! Just play them direct from the card! On the right is the on/off button.

Connection via bluetooth was really simple and easy and done in a matter of seconds.

The speakers in it are surprisingly powerful, with music being clear, well audible and with great bass from such a small speaker. It's certainly a lot louder than it looks when turned up to full volume. More than enough power to upset the neighbours!

Overall an amazing speaker with the added benefit of the memory card slot. It looks great and doesnt look out of place anywhere you decide to place it. Would highly recommend it, so much so I will be selling my JBL speaker!

I recently received a Satechi Aluminum 4-Outlet Power Strip ( model ST-ALPS ) for a product review.

The power strip has 4 regular (3-prong) AC power ports and 4 USB power ports. The power cord itself is 3-prong (grounded I assume) and thick. The power strip has a power switch that also seems to be the reset in case there is a surge.

I really liked the design of the product - it would look great on any desk. It has two mounting holes on the back, so you can mount it against the back of your desk or a wall - whatever works best if you rather not have it sitting on the desk or don’t have the space.

The USB ports are rated to handle 2.4A each port, with a max of 6A across the device. To test this, I connected two devices ( tablet and smartphone ) with USB meters and two fixed loads that were about 2A each. The total was just under 6A, and the unit was able to handle it.

Bottom line: Overall this is a solid power strip, that would work great in any situation where you need AC plugs and USB ports.

I've been slowly getting to appreciate over-ear headphones more - maybe it's to block out the sound of my screaming kids (and/or wife).  Anyway, these Philips SHL3060's (I refuse to say "DJ Style") are a welcome addition to my over-ear headphone collection and they've done a pretty decent job thus far at providing me a little sanctuary amidst the chaos (as long as I keep my eyes closed).  Pricepoint-wise I noticed these Philips seem to be all over the map - I've seen them as low as $25 and as high as $44 depending on the retail outlet, the color, and timing (note:  Target currently has them for $25).  My assumption is these are headphones in the $25 pricepoint range thus somewhat comparable to a very good value-priced headphone Sony MDRZX100/110 (~$20).  To my layman ears the sound is pretty comparable to my Sony's which is good - crisp sounds, decent bass.  Comfort-wise these Philips are slightly less comfortable than my Sony because the Philips rattle around more due to the extra "fold flat" joint.  The extra fold-flat joint is both a blessing and a curse.  It's a blessing when you need headphones that fold extra compact if you don't have much space in your bag - I think you do pay the price for this option though because the headphones rattle around a bit more because of this extra folding joint - my preference would be to do without the extra fold so I have the extra rigidity.  So to summarize in a nutshell - these are a competent offering in the $25 pricepoint range - they are pretty comfortable although they could use a bit more rigidity, the sound quality doesn't dazzle me but is good for this pricepoint, they are fairly attractive (I have the black color though my first choice would be the white), they do a pretty good job of blocking out outside sound such as screaming wives & kids.  Overall 4-STAR rating for me in consideration of price/value at $25 (3 stars if you pay $40+).

This a fantastic screen for the money, and now I know why it is so frequently recommended by A/V review sites over competitor products that cost at least two times more. Out of four people, I was the only one who noticed it and was bothered by it (if you haven't guessed, I'm the overly picky everything must be perfect type of person), one other person noticed and didn't care, and the rest didn't know what I was talking about. I'm a big fan of portable bluetooth speakers. I take them camping, to the beach, picnics, parks... pretty much everywhere. I own a Jambox, a Big Jambox, and a Bose Soundlink Color, so this review will be in comparison to those products.''

SOUND QUALITY: I think that quality of sound is the single most important aspect of a bluetooth speaker. Listening to music is pretty much the main reason any of us get these. What impressed me most about the Anker bluetooth speaker was its sound quality. The low price point made me a little hesitant that the quality simply wouldn't be there, but I was wrong. It sounds GREAT! The mids and highs are both distinct and clear, and have a rich and clean tone. The lows, however, do lack a little bit. That's not to say they don't sound great, but if you're looking for some deeper bass, I think you'd be better served with a jambox (especially the Big). The mids and highs, which are impressive, aren't quite as good as the Bose Soundlink, but they are perfectly adequate for most listeners. And frankly, if you're a huge audiophile who needs perfect lows, mids and highs, you probably aren't buying a bluetooth speaker to begin with.

PORTABILITY: The second most important quality for a portable bluetooth speaker! The product has a nice weight to it. It's not too heavy so as to make toting it a pain, but it has a solid build quality to it. It comes with a bag that will really only prevent scratches. Jamboxes have nice little sleeves that have some cushioning, whereas my Bose Soundlink didn't come with anything. In terms of size, it's a little larger than a regular sized jambox, much smaller than the big, and about the same overall size (much different shape) than the bose soundlink. As other reviewers have already pointed it works right out of the box almost. (except for Win, Power, More/Info buttons). I do not use WMC, I've bought it for KODI in Win7. Most buttons work without any tinkering. However there's no button for context menu (c) so you'll have to find a work around. Without going into any register key fuss I opt to install MCERemote add-on and mapped more/info button for the task.

Since in my particular set up I don't need WMC I also wanted to use green Win button for starting KODI. (Out of box it starts WMC) One can easily set it by right clicking KODI shortcut and from properties assigning it a short cut key. Then map those key to green button with MCERemote.

The last small glitch is arranging an exit button. You can simply find the keymaps file in KODI (C:\Program Files (x86)\XBMC\system\keymaps for Win7) and copy it to %appdata%\Roaming\XBMC\userdata\keymaps. Then edit the file for producing a Quit shortcut key. For example ctrl+s is the default shortcut for taking screenshots. Replace it like that:
change <s mod="ctrl">Screenshot</s>
to this line:

Ease of Use:
Unboxed, changed and connected to my iPhone 6 and iPad Mini without an issue. It really doesn’t get an easier. The speaker also allows for hardwiring via a 3.5mm jack which is a nice feature not available on all Bluetooth speakers. The jack allows for playback from devices such as an MP3 player or other such devices.

Build (Size and Weight):
The unit is solidly built, when you open you’ll notice a little weight, which I’m assuming comes from the unit’s battery. To be honest I prefer speakers that have a little weight to them, feel they have a tendency to produce a less tinny sound. Size, it’s has about the same diameter as a 12oz soda can and about two thirds as tall.

Battery Life:
Battery life is excellent, with audio play lasting for 10+ hours on a full charge (the unit still had change left).

Sound Quality:
The unit has good sound quality. The sound easily fills a room due to sound being directed out on three sides of the speaker. The speaker also performs well outside, easily able to hear from 50 feet away. I would say the bass is not heavy, but then again this is not a high end unit.

Range:
I was able to move about 30 feet away from the unit without any interference, but walls and other objects between you and the speaker do decrease the distance relatively quickly. This is stated in the documentation. I did experience some drops in connections, but couldn’t recreate them enough to say there’s an issue.

Con:
The skip and volume buttons are the same button. So to skip forward you give the button a quick tap, to turn up the volume you hold the button. On move then one occasion I skipped to the next song when just trying to turn up the volume.

Included:
EasyAcc DP100 Bluetooth Speaker
Micro USB Charging Cable
3.5 mm AUX Cable
Cloth Bag
(Last 2 items are nice extras.)

Overall:
The true test for me is would I recommend this unit to a friend, and the answer is yes. At this price point this unit provides good sounds and features found only in higher end units. This unit is worth the money.

This is an excellent set of Sports headphones that sounds great and stays put when you're getting your workout in. The headphones use a dual magnet, dynamic moving coil micro speaker to deliver a frequency response of 10HZ to 19kHz making them more than adequate for listening outside of the gym as well. While these headphones work with any device they are truly made for the Apple line of products (iPhone, iPad, iPod) as the control box gives you control over the volume, skip tracks and even take calls.

►► SOUND QUALITY ◄◄

The sound across the board is excellent from the low-end through the mid-range and high-end. They are not as open and airy as my Ultimate Ears TripleFi 10's, a set that listed for $399 retail, but they don't feel muted at all when listening to them.

Testing through a variety of music genres it would seem that these are tuned for the louder, upbeat music that you'd listen to while working out which makes sense since these are Sports headphones. With that said if I would have no problem listening to acoustic music through these as they product a nicely balanced, clean sound that is better than a lot of wired headsets I've tried. They are way better than the headphones included with my iPhone.

►► COMFORT ◄◄

For me comfort is just as important as sound quality because if your in-ear monitors aren't comfortable you won't want to wear them for extended periods of time. This set does a couple things right in the comfort arena with the design of the oval earbuds and the over the ear wire design that keeps the headphones in place and makes them feel as close to weightless as you can get.

I was a bit skeptical of the oval design of the earbuds as I am very used to the circular design and have been very happy with the Comply tips that I normally use. With that said the oval design here truly does seem to make a difference in the comfort of these tips as the included tips are more comfortable than most, if not all, of the standard tips I've had included in a set of headphones.

►► CONTROLS ◄◄

There is a small control box attached to the clip that you can use to keep the cord in place. The control box is very similar to those on other sets of headphones I have tested and it worked pretty much as expected except for the way you move up and down in the track list.

The top button on the control box is used to raise the volume on your device.

The bottom button on the control box is used to lower the volume on your device.

The center button is the most versatile as a quick click will play or pause your music or answer a call if the phone is ringing. A double tap of the center button will move to the next track in your track listing and a triple tap of the center button will move to the previous track. Pressing and holding the center button for a second will initiate Siri. While I am used to the volume buttons normally doubling up as the previous / next track control once I was used to this system it was a breeze to use.

►► PHONE CALLS ◄◄

The headset does a nice job with calls due to the fact that the microphone is nice and clear so there is no worries about taking a call while wearing these headphones.

►► CONCLUSION ◄◄

Overall this is an excellent set of Sports headphones that are both comfortable and sound great. They stay firmly in place and seem to be built to handle whatever wear and tear you will throw at them while working out. I love having full control over my iPhone with the included control. For me this is about as close to perfect as you can come with a Sports set of headphones. Highly recommended.

I don't have a lot of desk real estate and I wanted something that pumps out a punchy deep sound when I'm playing really action packed games, watching movies and listening to my music (mostly EDM). The Leviathan was a fantastic option. I am a member of the cult of Razer and I trust their products and this is why. It just works beautifully.

The soundbar gives you a host of options for connection. You can use NFC to pair your phone through bluetooth just by tapping your phone on it. The SDPIF connection in the back lets you use 5.1 fiber optic sound from your PC, Mac or gaming console and really does resonate a clear wide sound field. It's not true 5.1 so it won't beat a real surround sound system, but when racing in Forza Horizon 2 I could hear cars coming up behind me with clarity. There is also a traditional headphone style input which is very nice for quick on the fly plug ins.

The only gripes I have are that the connector for the subwoofer is a little goofy. It doesn't seem as strong of a connection as it could be... maybe a bit flimsy. But these things don't move so once you get it in place it'll be fine. The other little problem I have are the attachable feet. Two sets come with the bar to let you raise and angle the bar how you want it. But try removing them and the glue holding the feet to the plug portion pops right off. I had to re-glue them in place.

The last option is that there's no pass through. I would have really liked if I could have run my sound into the sound bar and then to headphones. Right now I have a SPDIF splitter for my fiber optic signal. One goes to the soundbar the other goes to my Astro Mix Amp for my headphones. It's not a very elegant solution and I hate the extra cables. Maybe the Leviathan Pro can include something like that, and maybe it'll even have some of Razer's Chroma lighting accents which would be nice.

The question is should you spend your money on this or save $10 and get something cheaper, maybe spend $20 more and get something better? I’m using the Bose to simply compare the speakers to. Hear me out before you call foul, I know I’m comparing $20-$40 speakers to a $250 one. The goal isn’t to beat the Bose Sounddock, it’s to see which of these budget speakers can get you the closest to the sound dock for less money.

The purpose of these speakers is portability. You want to take you music or podcasts with you. They need to be easy to move, sound nice, and look good. No one wants to buy an ugly speaker. Being portable means having a battery. So which one should you spend your money on?

The Urge Basics seems bring the fewest features to the table. Both the Onyx and the SplashEtech have NFC. The SplashEtech as you can judge by the name is water resistant.

I have an iPhone 6 that’ll I’ll be using to test these, so I won’t be using the NFC. If that’s what you’re after the Urge Basics isn’t the one for you.

The sound qualitycoming from these,
The SplashEtech has very nice sound, clear sound with mild bass. It’s not very loud though.
It has one 3 watt speaker and it does well.

The Urge Basics is working with two 3 watt speakers and it’s quite a bit louder than the SplashEtech but it does sound underwhelming near full volume. This is because it lacks the bass it needs when you turn it up.

The Onyx has two 5 watt speakers and it shows. It’s louder than the other two and it pumps the most bass by far. I love the sound coming from this thing.

The battery life claims around 14 hours and it seems true. It charges using MicroUSB.

Of the three of them, if you’re looking for a small desk speaker any one will do. If you want a shower speaker only the SplashEtech is going to last, if you want a speaker to fill the room with music there’s only one choice. The Onyx Cube wins out.

Now the Bose comparison. They seem to be the gold standard that most people compare speakers to here. If you’re looking for true Bose quality it can be found in other speakers but you won’t find it at this price range. It’s not just the name. To get higher quality speakers and components you need to spend more. Don’t be fooled by other reviews thinking you’re getting a $200 speaker for $30. It’s the same as comparing a Honda Civic to a Corvette. Sure they can both go fast, but one does it a lot smoother and better than the other.

With that being said don’t assume these speakers are trash, they’re far from it. They’re worth every penny and then some. I highly recommend the Onyx Cube for anyone looking at Speakers in this price range. I was offered a discount on this speaker in exchange for my review.

I always compare any new headphones to the Sony MD 7506 because they are the standard that any sub $200 headphones should be measured against, and they frequently sell for $80 or so ($79 today). There's a reason that you find them in literally every recording studio in the world, and that's because they reproduce the mix accurately while being comfortable and inexpensive. I'd love to find something else to buy with $80, because the Sony's are a little, well, ugly, and I'd like something with a replaceable cord. Sadly, these aren't the cans I'm looking for.

These aren't even close in terms of sound quality, comfort, or build quality BUT they do have some innovative features that may be more important to you like:
1. The ability to adjust the angle of the headphones 90 degrees forward and back relative to the head band. It's a gimmick as far as I can tell, but it's well executed with ball and hole detents for nice-feeling adjustment.
2. Near-zero noggin top padding. It's a nice, flat area of thin, open-cell foam rubber. Super cheap to make though, so that's good for someone.
3. Extra bass. If you think that the world's recording engineers consistently scrimp on the bass line and take too much sizzle out of the high hat while putting in too much midrange, these will undo those mistakes.
4. They don't LOOK like the Sony's. These have modern flat black rat rod styling and a cool looking bungee-type suspension system, along with fabric-covered cordage for your inner hipster.

I purchased this product right when it was just released—before it was even in stock on Amazon.  While I'm obviously very happy with the SRSX88, I’m writing a detailed review so I can share with you some of the key opinions that I would have liked to have heard when I was weighing my options:  - First, Sony SRSX88 is plenty loud.  I bought it primarily to bring out onto my screened porch so I can enjoy some music when I’m out there.  The speaker has plenty of power to fill this outdoor space from 10 feet away, even when set to well below max volume.  It’s power capability is overqualified for relaxed listening outdoors, and I think it would even have plenty of power to use during a small deck party without distortion.  I tested the speaker inside too, and it easily fills a 20’x13’ room with sound.  This wall powered unit is in a totally different league than the portable Bluetooth speaker systems I’ve heard before (e.g. Jawbone or Monster Clarity).  - The bass response is outstanding for such a tiny package, and it is comparable to the bass you’d get from very good mid-range bookshelf speakers connected to a standalone amplifier.  The whole unit vibrates to the touch, so you get the sense that the whole system is working hard to give you solid bass.  I can HEAR all of the bass in virtually any song, which is a real pleasure.  For example, the bass vocals in Bastille’s “Pompeii” sound rich and full, as are the bass lines and percussion of rock songs like “Only Happy When it Rains” (by Garbage).  Even dance and rap like “I Cry” (Flo Rida) and “The Real Slim Shady” (Eminem) are reproduced with a solid bass punch.  Only in songs where you expect to FEEL the bass (e.g. Michael Jackson’s “Billie Jean”) was there any sign that I was not listening to a home stereo system with a subwoofer.  In other words, this unit far exceeded my expectations for bass response.  - The full-range musical detail of these speakers is high.  It’s easyto pick out the character of individual instruments in lush, complex compositions like Steely Dan’s “My Old School.”  The specs listed on Amazon say this unit has a max of 10% harmonic distortion, which sounds like a lot (it’s about two orders of magnitude worse than my hi-fi system’s).  My experience, however, is that my music sounds as good or better than I expected on the SRSX88.  Whatever sound processing Sony might be using to get big sound from a compact, all-in-one unit, it’s working very well, even if it may not technically qualify as “high fidelity.”  - The materials and build quality of the unit are outstanding.  The glossy, piano black plastic and brushed metal finishes are attractive, sleek and modern.  The unit has a reassuring, heavy weight to it.  Since the SRSX88 does not have a battery for on-the-go use, I presume all that heft is from the amplifier and speakers.  Nice.  - Connecting the SRSX88 to an iPhone was nearly effortless via Bluetooth and only slightly more complicated via Wi-Fi, which required the free Song Pal app.  When placed on my porch, the Bluetooth connection between my iPhone and the SRSX88 started to get unreliable if I went inside.  The connection via Wi-Fi was far more robust.  - Not surprisingly, stereo separation is unimpressive due to the fact that the system is an all-in-one unit.  It would be very interesting (but too expensive for me) to purchase a second SRSX88 to connect via Wi-Fi / Song Pal and see how much better it would sound with one SRSX88 placed in each corner of my room.  Alas…  - One of the only disappointments was that in order to connect to the SRSX88 via the more robust Wi-Fi method, I had to use the Song Pal app.  This app is problematic to me for two reasons.  First, it replaces Apple’s user interface for accessing my music library with its own interface (when using the SRSX88 only).  The app’s interface has navigational quirks that for me made browsing my music more cumbersome.  Second, in order to use the app and Wi-Fi connectivity to play your own existing music library on the SRSX88, you have to agree to privacy policies from Sony and about four other companies (including Google).  Every person’s preferences regarding interface and privacy details are different, but I suspect that some people accustomed to Apple may share my displeasure with this situation.  Longer term, I may just use the SRSX88’s Bluetooth connection and Apple’s standard Music interface.  In a comparison with Wi-Fi, I perceived only a slight decrease in musical detail using Bluetooth, if any, so long as my iPhone stayed near the unit.  The last comment I will make is about value.  When I purchased this speaker, I felt like I was buying a really expensive powered Bluetooth speaker that I hoped would do the job out on my porch, a location where I couldn’t easily connect a permanent sound system.  But once I heard how great it sounds (power, bass, etc.), I now see the SRSX88 as a good value in a totally different frame of reference.  To me it sounds as good as a pair of good, mid-range bookshelf speakers connected to an amp.  Throw in simple Bluetooth connectivity with my iPhone, and I’ve got a very convenient way to bring the full sound of a bookshelf stereo system out onto my porch for less than the price of a complete bookshelf system.

I rarely rate products and of that subset i rarely give any product a 5 star, but these QC25's deserve it.

I am a huge headphone guy, i've probably spent over 10000 dollars on headphones in my life (i'm only 30), i have dacs, i have amps, i've had tons and tons of pairs. I'm not a "super audiophile must have flat response or it sucks" guy. I'm a guy who goes to work at a desk for 9 hours a day, goes home to play computer games at night and then goes to bed.

I was a big fan of the q15's, i had 2 pairs, including a limited edition pair, but i had a few issues with them. The QC25's have solved all but one of these problems. Let me explain.

The QC15's and QC25's have noise canceling that can sometimes be over whelming, if you're in a very windy environment, or in a super loud construction zone, the way the cancellation works, it actually can hurt my ears. The QC15's had no ability to use the headphones with the active noise cancellation (ANC) turned off. That was beef one. The second was the cable on the QC15's was so long, obnoxiously long. So long. Like long. And finally the QC15's did not have bluetooth wireless capabilities.

So, as we know the QC25's do not have bluetooth either, but because of the other issues being resolved, i'm looking over this, and solving this problem by getting a small battery powered bluetooth adapter, many can be found on amazon for under 30 dollars. This is not a perfect solution but it works.

In other words, the qc25's do allow you use them when they're off, granted at a degradation of sound quality, but honestly its not so insanely crappy sounding with it off that if your head is just a little pressed from the ANC or you just want to listen to talk radio or something, i find this is an excellent feature, that and if your battery dies you can still listen to your entertainment.

The cable is MUCH better, out goes the huge clunky headphone side which is replaced by athin connector, as well as a much more reasonable length. Its a huge improvement over the QC15s.

The ANC is so amazing, at the office, its like i have my own office in a sea of cubicals, at home my window AC unit that has to run 24/7, disappears. Literally, its gone. And they're so comfortable. I can wear them for hours and hours without pain or pressure points, and i wear glasses, so this is a hard task to achieve.

If you're looking for ANC headphones that are comfortable sound good, ANC can be disabled while still using them, just get these. Get them. I love them, i really do, and i paid full price. I just love them. Thank you Bose.

EDIT 8/21/2015:
+++++++++++++
A few minutes after posting my original review on Amazon, I received a phone call from the company discussing the issues I raised (when you sign up to their service they ask for your Amazon order #, so I guess that's how they were able to track me). So first of all, I give their customer's service 5 stars. They care very much about their customers' experience and I find this very refreshing.

The person who called me explained to me the inaccuracy issue: Turns our that on battery operated GPS there will always be "ghosting" (meaning, the location shown could be off by several feet) but ONLY when the GPS is stationary, in order to conserve battery life. And indeed, when I checked the accuracy when the car was moving, the GPS was right on. And indeed the battery lasts much more that the 5 days I originally had, it actually depends on how much you're driving. My MasTrack GPS that I compared this one to is connected to the car, so it's always powered, that's why I don't have the ghosting effect on it.
So if accuracy is very important to you, keep in mind that with battery operated GPS, when the GPS is not moving the location may be off (from my experience it was off by up to about 150 feet). I've decided that for me it's not going to be a deal breaker.

As per lack of app, I learned that they do have an android app, but are still testing their ios one. I am looking forward to the app, as it is much needed. I saved their mobile webpage on my iphone's home screen, but that's no replacement.

Once they have a working ios app and have better instructions (it's surprising that they have such a great feature - SOS button - and they don't mention it at all, I found out about it by reading some reviews on Amazon), I could definitely give them 5 stars. Their stellar customer service already deserves the 5 stars!.

I ordered the DA21 to convert digital audio from our LG HDTV television, which has no analog audio output, only an SPDIF connection. While the DA21 converted  the digital audio signals from Direct TV satellite, it delivered only a motor-boat type of noise when our LG set was tuned to local HDTV signals arriving via an indoor antenna. It turns out that local HDTV is broadcast using a different audio protocol (I believe it is a Dolby format) than the digital audio that arrives via cable and satellite which is, I believe, PCM format. Unfortunately, this difference is rarely mentioned in the ads for digital-to-analog audio converters, and people wanting to shed cable/satellite in favor of local HDTV using an indoor antenna are, like me, disappointed to hear noise instead of usable analog audio unless the converter can process the digital audio format broadcast by local HDTV stations. So I assign 4 stars instead of 5 because of the lack of full information about this confusing situation.

Since the release of the AKR03 (Roxanne), there are now "better" earphones available in the same product line, the Laylas. The Roxannes are generally considered to have a more musical signature while the Laylas have a more neutral signature. The Laylas are also considered to be better because of the larger soundstage. However, both have the adjustable bass feature and both have twelve drivers. The Layla also costs considerably more than the Roxanne ($2500).

Regardless of which one you pick, and I have heard both, these are MASSIVE in-ear headphones...probably the largest universals that you can buy currently. Other than the weight itself, fit can certainly be an issue. Among the vast collection of headphones I have tried, the Roxanne/Laylas are among the hardest to reliably get a good fit with. I would personally suggest using Comply tips or Spinfit tips to get a better fit (I personally use Spinfits). The fit is CRUCIAL to the sound. Not being able to get a good fit will usually lead to a fuzzy, veiled sound.

You will also need to have a good source and/or a good DAC/Amp combo. Right out of the iPhone, needless to say, the Roxanne/Laylas sound terrible...probably the worst of the high end headphones. At the very least, you'll probably need something like the Aurender Flow to complement your iPhone or use the AK240 as a source. I personally use the AK240 as a source connected by optical line to my Chord Hugo. This pairing is quite excellent for both headphones.

Before you choose to buy Roxanne or the more expensive Layla, you definitely need to try them out. The difficult fit is definitely something you need to try before you buy. In addition, the signature sound of both headphones can be a bit difficult to accept at first if you come from a "typical" HiFi product, most of which emphasize bass or treble to unnatural levels. Preferably, get a listen of a Roxanne or Layla that has been burned in (supposedly, I don't hugely believe in burn-in as such) because apparently they sound a lot better that way.

I've been talking about the Roxanne and Layla as one unit up until this point because they share a lot of the same technology. Realistically, most people will get this Roxanne over the Layla, as the Layla is much more expensive and offers a more analytical sound rather than the fun sound of the Roxanne. If you really want a neutral headphone in the Roxanne price range, I'd suggest the SE846 if you want a neutral IEM for a cheaper cost. The Layla is definitely nice, but I'm not 100% convinced it's $2500 worth of nice.

In summary, the Roxanne and Layla are both great headphones, and if you are serious about getting one or the other, then it is worth taking the time investment to do some research and perhaps find a way to try them out before they become a huge money investment. I personally think both headphones are great, but you should definitely get a sense of their fit, the sound signature, and the differences between the two before you decide to make the decision to buy.

My husband called the other day while we were coming back from the park on the cart and I just had a normal conversation with him using this speaker. He never even knew I was using it actually. • Power bank and battery life: The 15 hour life on this is pretty legit. I have marveled at how much longer it lasts than my other speakers. I love that I can just plug into this for a little extra juice.

Then if I want to charge my phone with the power bank feature of this, I have to bring my own micro USB cord. What a wacky design. Why not just use a standard USB-Micro USB cord? I bought this mini amp to play mp3 files through a pair of speakers on my deck, accompanied by an interior pair so you don't lose the music when coming inside. For that purpose it does very well, although with a few shortcomings I will note later. I apparently received a newer version of the unit since it no longer has FM Car Radio printed on the back and the included power supply is12V, 5A with a smaller form factor than pictured.

First off, you need to understand this is basically a 12V car radio repackaged as a mini-amplifier for playing mp3 files and FM radio, two things it does very well, just don't expect it to deliver more than what the typical car radio can produce. So where does it fall short? Most notably the display is old school red LEDs and very limited. >> and << buttons are used to step through mp3 files. A remote control is supplied so you can access files by number, which is a big help; however, only file number is displayed, not file information. By default, file numbers are assigned in the order you save your mp3 files, whether you organize them in folders or not. There is no playlist capability, which forced me to actually think about how to organize my mp3 files, rather than rely on playlists to do it for me. For that purpose I simply picked up a 10 pack of 4Gb SDHC cards (the cheapest option) and organized my mp3 collection across them, keeping track of the storage order on each card so I would know the number for each mp3 file. It actually works great, with each card basically serving the role of a playlist - I just plug in the card for the collection I want and it starts playing. I don't know if adding ID3 tags to the files will allow you to effectively re-order them or not, since I haven't tried it. There is also a USB input for mp3 files I haven't tried, so I don't know what happens if you have both a USB and an SDHC card plugged in at the same time. In contrast, using FM is easy since scanning is built in and station numbers are displayed. There are 20 presets if you want to set it up for multiple stations; otherwise, it simply brings up the last station you listened to. FM reception is excellent, even with the dinky "antenna" supplied (a length of cable with an RCA plug).

What else? Documentation is in English; however is so scant you will have to figure stuff out for yourself or see what other users have figured out via things like these reviews. The unit does have auxiliary jacks, but I'm not using them for any purpose so can't say what will and won't work in them. There is no mic jack, so if that's a feature you need, you should consider the Pyle unit that is somewhat similar to this one.

The only real shortcoming for my purposes is the lack of independent volume controls for each speaker pair to allow listening to either or both. Other than that, I'm very happy with the unit and how well it performs.

Armin van Buuren exploded onto the electronic music scenes around 2000, and he is currently one of the world's top DJs. I was very excited to try the Philips A5Pro DJ Headphones that bear his name. Not surprisingly, these are amazing headphones that provide the sound, comfort, and features that I want when I'm mixing.

The single most important feature for headphones is the sound quality. The 50mm 3500mW drivers deliver stunning power and crispness. That clarity of sound makes a huge difference when listening for the spaces between the beats. These are not really bass-heavy headphones (though the lows are crystal clear without reverberation or bottoming out). I was very happy with how these headphones performed in my home studio.

While I rarely get to spin in public, these headphones are loaded with features that make the next DJ gig that much better. The thick earpieces and soft cushions dampen external noise extraordinarily well. The cushions are replaceable when the originals wear out (moreover, replacement pads come in a variety of sizes). The earpieces are considerably better built than most headphones, and they have a heft what reflects this quality. The headband is cushioned which helps make these headphones exceptionally comfortable even after wearing them for extended amounts of time.

Finally there are a few amenities that make these 5-star headphones. The coiled extra long cord can attach to either earpiece which is a small but very nice feature. The headphones are collapsible with reinforced aluminum hardware. That means I can pack them and unpack them without worrying about wearing them out prematurely. A little travel bag is included to store the headphones cleanly and securely.

These headphones are perfect for anyone that works closely with music. Professional and would-be professional DJs will be happy with the many features designed around public performance. These headphones have become the only ones I use when I am working with music..

When I ordered this item from Amazon Vine in early August 2015, I did so "blind," as it were; Amazon at that time featured no product page on this item to describe the specifics. The product link from the Vine listing to offering the product page was then nonexistent.

And so it remained as of this writing on August 12, and so it would appear, until mid September 2015. In all that time, Amazon offered no product of this specific name available at all. A search on Amazon for this item, Bose Solo 15 Series II TV Sound System, came up blank. In fact, a search of the entire internet for this specific item comes up blank.

Needless to say, Amazon listed no product dimensions on the Vine offering page, and no useful details, either.

All of that background should explain this somewhat unconventional report on a product that I did receive, granted, free, in exchange for an honest review.

Here's the description Amazon Vine provided:

"The Bose Solo 15 Series II TV sound system is a one-piece speaker that delivers dramatically better sound than your TV.

"Advanced Bose technologies make each word and detail sound clear at any volume, and create an experience that's wider than the screen. The system also produces impressive bass that adds impact to your shows. And when you want even more clarity, dialogue mode makes every word easier to hear without having to adjust the volume from scene to scene.

"Setup is easy, with just one connection to your TV. The system fits under most TVs up to 50 inches yet is still small enough to place on an open shelf.

"It features Bluetooth connectivity, so you can stream music wirelessly, and includes a universal remote."

That's all I had to go on, so I took a flyer. Alas, the thing proved much too large for our purposes.

The only thing Amazon listed that sounded close to this item was, I assumed, version I, i.e. the original Bose® Solo 15 TV Sound System, although it includes no Roman numeral in its name, And that sounded like it might be workable, at least.

I also assumed, from the photo on Vine page offering the item, that it was much smaller than it in fact is. Alas, it is quite large, as another reviewer I can see as of Setepmeber 24, has also commented. But until very recently there were no reviews visible, since there was no product page.

I had hoped to use this with a 24-inch TV that we use as a computer monitor, and also as our digital TV, but the system is far too large for a computer desk, measuring roughly 28 inches wide. But this thing is not "small enough to place on an open shelf." It is much deeper than all the shelves in our house, about 17 inches deep.

So, Bose, I recommend that you get your product page straight before offering this item to anyone else, and that you also provide some useful information, that is, dimensions, weight, etc. etc.

I don't mind that I can't use the item, as I did not pay for it. I give a completely neutral review, as I also cannot test it. Well, this is an interesting item. I wanted to run "Zone2" for my backporch, and "Zone3" for my garage, and so far I haven't seen a good option other than the Lepai 2020A+, which is what I'm running right now. Those are great amps, but it doesn't look very good mounted on the wall, versus an in-wall unit.

This unit have no reviews, but there's MCM in-wall amplifier that has decent reviews. That unit however does not have an "On/Off" switch, so this is a superior product with more feature and lower price. I took a plunge and bought one to try it out.

I tested it using a pair of Polk Atrium Outdoor speakers wired up using 16GA wires. I tested first using the Lepai 2020A+, and it's nice and loud at 1/2 level of the volume knob. At 3/4, it's too loud for the 20x20 room I was testing in, if this was outdoor, it would probably be too much.
On the Pyle PWA15BT, using the stereo connection, at 1/2 it is also the same loudness as the Lepai, but at 3/4 or full volume, it's slightly less loud. Definitely wont be using it pass 1/2 volume much, but it is definitely not as powerful as the Lepai, but for the price and the convenience, it's good enough. On Bluetooth, the volume is much less, and I pretty much have to have it at full volume to get the same result as 1/2 of the stereo connection. The sound quality is good overall, not crisp, but good enough. It's only for outdoor and garage, so I'm not going to be watching movie quality sound through it, just internet streaming music. I didn't have a MIC to test, but I'm going to assume it's just a stereo to mono adapter and uses the same connection as the stereo. I did not test the USB charging either, I hope it's more than 500mA of power output.

The build quality left a little to be desire. Some of the wires are hot glued over, and the soldering job look like it was done very quickly and with poor quality control. But that's to be expected with the price. Overall, I likeit, and will get a few more to get overall house music system going.
