This review is, except for the following initial paragraph, a verbatim repeat of the review I posted for BOSE's SoundTrue Ultra In-Ear headphones. In 500 posted reviews, I have never done this before and shall now explain:

These SoundSport in-ear headphones from BOSE are somewhat different in design than the SoundTrue set - owing to the additional attention to keeping them safe from water and sweat exposure while exercising. Differences are noted in the shape of the ear-insert pieces. After several hours spent listening to each, I found that what I had to say about the SoundTrue set is all equally applicable to this SoundSport set. Thus, a repeat of the review of those is entirely accurate and honest here. As follows:

BOSE has a reputation for making fine quality sound devices - and this set of SoundSport Ultra in-ear headphones contributes to sustaining that well-earned reputation. While BOSE has made and continues to offer some truly 'high-end' (read "quite expensive") speakers and headsets of different kinds, these in-ear headphones are priced in what is regarded as medium-priced. To summarize what I am about to say: These headphones are genuinely outstanding in terms of comfort and sound delivery.

Once one adapts to the style of earphones using the curved ear stabilizers, these earphones are as comfortable as having something sitting on and in your ear can be expected to be. While some aficionados insist on over-the-ear insulated headphones for premium listening, these headphones offer up a more than reasonable challenge to that presumption.

What they will not do is improve on poor quality digital recordings - I do not believe that any listening device can really offer that; but, with high-quality digital material, the sound delivered is honestly astounding - as good as the finest over-the-ear headphones made by BOSE or anyone else.

The spectrum of sound is faithfully reproduced. The highs are crisp and not at all thin or tinny; the bass is deep but not overpowering and clear - and the midrange comes through as nicely as it might in a professional studio or insulated listening room with high-quality speakers. I really don't understand the details of how BOSE accomplishes this, but they do!

The case is a circular one that helps keep the cords from getting tangled.

The overall experience is one of excellence.
Yes, you can be 'earphones' for $5., but these headphones are a fine example of the notion that sometimes, you get what you pay for - and, once in a while, you actually get something more.

First, grab hold of the side of the padded part of one of the two ear cups. Gently pull left, right, up or down (not towards/away from yourself) so that eventually the leather lip that holds the pads to the base comes loose. Do this all the way around until the pad comes off, and then do the same to the other side. You should notice a small piece of foam in the center of the base of the headphones (not the pad) that is glued on. Pinch the center of this and rip away at it until there is no foam left. This Bose SoundSport in-ear headphone appears to be an updated version in a new charcoal color. It looks the same as the previous version but without the Apple remote and mic. It comes with 3-pairs of StayHear tips (S/M/L), a shirt clip and a circular zipper case with a carabiner attachment. An extension cable found in the previous version is no longer included.

The Bose SoundSport headphone sounds really good. It has a good balance between the bass and treble. The lows are fairly deep while the highs are crispy clear. Vocals are clean and clear as well. It's good for a wide genre of music. It's not a bass heavy headphone though. If you like EDM, Hip hop and R&B, you may find it too weak. On the other hand, I enjoy jazz, classic rock and classical, and this headphone doesn't disappoint.

The SoundSport is perfect for running or gym use. The StayHear tip does a pretty good job of keeping the headphone in the ear even during very active workouts. I tend to perspire a lot and this headphone has good water resistance. Another nice thing about the StayHear tip is that it doesn't completely isolate the outside sound. I like to be able to hear my surroundings during a workout for safety reasons and this headphone allows me to do so. Many in-ear headphones on the market plug into the ear directly and isolate the outside sound just too much for me.

The headphone has a straight plug, which could be an issue for some people who like to keep their phone or music player in the pocket. It doesn't bother me since it does have a good strain relief for the cable. The cable seems flexible and yet durable. It is relatively tangle free.

Overall, this is a great headphone for general sport use. It stays in the ear and doesn't completely block out the outside sound. It also has good water resistance. More importantly, it sounds great and allows me to immerse myself in my favorite music during workout. I really like it a lot.

Coming from a pair of Sennheiser HD 429s, I am surprised to say that I am pleased with Monster's NTune headphones. I expected the headphones to sound a lot like Beats By Dre; muddy, overwhelming bass with no mids or treble. To my surprise, I was completely wrong. While these headphones certainly deliver a lot of head rattling bass, the mids and trebles aren't lost. To my surprise, music was very clear with just the right amount of bass to deliver a nice thump but not too much bass to completely drown out everything else like Beats. Also, these headphones can get loud. REALLY LOUD. But do note that once they are turned up a fair bit there will be some noticeable distortion and once turned up all the way the music is incredibly distorted. The on-ear style isn't the most comfortable but is decent for short listening sessions. If you wear glasses with your headphones, prepare for a lot of discomfort with these headphones. Listening to music, especially while eating, with these headphones on will make your ears sore after about ten minutes. While these headphones are one of the more comfy on-ear headphones, they still are uncomfortable for me. The rubber top cushion when moved would pull my hair with it which wasn't so pleasant. On a better note, these headphones look great. They come in many different colors and look premium. They also feel premium to with the leather ear pads and quality plastics used throughout. I would recommend these headphones to anyone who wants a lot of punchy bass without drowning out the rest of the music and anyone who wants good looking headphones without paying a lot of money.
Pros: Clear sound, powerful bass, great looks
Cons: Uncomfortable after long periods of time

This is a very capable speaker. I bought it after my Sol Republic Punk died within 4 months. However I did not keep this because even with the $100 price difference, the JBL Charge 2+ so much better it was worth it. You can read my review of the JBL Charge 2+ on that detail page (I also compared to the UE Boom).

Obviously the Oontz is not in the league of either the JBL or the Boom, but it is a very capable speaker for the price. You can crank up to full blast without feeling like the thing is going to fall apart (I didn't notice much distortion, but I'm not an audiophile.). I like that you can pause/play from the speaker, but would have liked it better if you could skip tracks too (which the Punk could do, as well as the Charge 2+). One reviewer mentioned that the connection could sometimes would cut in and out depending on which you powered on first (the speaker vs the device), and I noticed the same thing on my unit, which wasn't acceptable to me.

Battery life IS superb. It's also very light (substantially lighter than the Boom and JBL). Materials don't feel lush, but it doesn't feel like complete crap either. The Oontz is loud, but not really really loud - as others mentioned, it wouldn't be anything but background noise for a backyard bbq. I was blown away by how good these headphones sound for the price. These seriously sound amazing. The comfort level for these 'phones is very good too. After wearing a few minutes I'll forget I even have them on, and I'm talking hours later.

...But the noise cancelling. Oh dear God.

First, it isn't very good at actually cancelling noise. It slightly dampens the sound around you, but if you were to let someone use these without knowing they are noise cancelling, nobody would even notice a difference over any other over the ear close-backed headphones.

Second, when the noise cancelling is on, the headphones will pick up electronic noise from EVERYTHING anywhere near it. If you use these with anything that is plugged into a power supply, well you can say hello to Mr. Loud Buzzing. If you place this thing near a lamp, if you place it near a computer screen, if you place it near a television, or really if you place it near anything that has a wire going to a wall outlet, you will be in a world of noise.

Last of all, the noise cancelling feature causes an ambient buzz all the time for no reason whatsoever.

The great thing about these headphones though? You can use them with the noise cancelling turned off. So that fixes all the above problems, well that is unless you care about noise cancelling. If that's the case, stay far away.

So final verdict: Great sounding, comfortable, well build headphones, with ridiculously bad "noise cancelling".

[[VIDEOID:5e079dfe033513c82f1f90f66e96b806]] I work with a lot of Bluetooth speakers and I have developed an ear for speakers that are good and ones that are not so good. A good speaker is well-made, has great sound and has good operational range in terms of distance from the music source - for starters. This speaker is a good one and it works very well - I like it.

This is an unusual looking speaker, about the size and shape of a cucumber and quite a bit heavier than expected. It is encased in a heavy rubberized sleeve and should hold up against some abuse and repel water. It is listed as waterproof, but I would hesitate to deliberately submerge it.

I tested the operation range and it maintained a solid, unbroken connection at over 30' from the source. There was no skipping, no cut-outs or any other types of glitches as I got farther away from the source. I really cannot ask much more of this speaker - the average speaker I have tried has had a range of around 20', the best being over 50' and the worst being less than 5', so this one is better than average in that regard.

Eton's Traveler III is a nice portable (almost pocket) radio that offers many features (AM, FM, SW, RDS) but is hampered by poor ergonomics and some over-sensitivity.  The Traveler is compact and, despite its light weight, seems well-constructed. Its display is very readable and the backlight can be adjusted. One glaring omission is a direct entry keypad, an oversight that becomes annoying due to the Traveler's small and quirky buttons. This may not impact AM and FM users but it makes roaming the shortwave bands a painful exercise. The tiny buttons used to select bands require a very firm and deliberate push and getting the radio into scan mode is difficult. One can adjust the tuning speed of the tuning knob but the knob is too small to make manual tuning over the shortwave bands practical. The radio lacks any provision for an external antenna and that's probably a good thing for most users; the radio exhibits a surprising amount of over-sensitivity to AM/MW interference on the shortwave bands. Bleed-over from strong local AM stations is present (although faint) at times using the built-in whip but becomes overwhelming if a modest longwire (15') is attached to the antenna. On the plus side the RDS works well and the radio has good sound for its size.

Music teacher life pro tip: wrap the ends of all instrument/ microphone and yes 3.5mm audio cables with electrical tape. The ends are usually the weakest part of the cable which means it is the first part to break. Wrap the ends in order to strengthen the point where the cable meets the end piece and your cable will last way longer. I recommend this cable because: it has gold ends (better connection means better sound quality), it is short (more audio signal is lost the longer the cable is. I recommend 3 ft. There is a big difference between 3 ft and 10 ft. 20 feet is way too long. After 10 feet the sound quality suffers at a more rapid rate. It has extra metal on the ends so that you can put it in an iPhone or other smartphone without taking off or modifying your case. That turned into a big deal for me after a while. Having read the reviews here (even the screaming one a bit lower down by the brave poster "Anonymous"), I thought I'd add my 2 cents to the discussion. I've had a variety of DAPs over the past 3-4 years (Colorfly C3, iBasso DX50, Fiio X5, Fiio X1, iPhones from 3-6, and several iPods). I now have two Ponos. The Pono is superior to all of the aforementioned DAPs and smartphones in terms of sound quality. True, the Apple products have longer battery life, and are easier to load using iTunes. But if you are looking for sound quality, you'd have to go to players costing 4X more than the Pono to achieve even a small bit of superior sound.

The Pono functions is much the same way as the rest, in this case using a touchscreen and three buttons. You can load music on it using the Pono computer app (a derivation of JRiver's app) or simply side load by plugging in your Pono to your computer using a USB cord and dragging the music files onto the internal Pono HD or the supplied 64gb MicroSDCard (I use a Mac, and this works perfectly). I have found that the Pono app is a bit unwieldy, with a steep learning curve, so have simply used the same method I used with my other non-Apple DAPs and used drag and drop. So, there is no need to use the Pono app to load music unless you want to use it. The same goes for the Pono music site. Yes, you can buy music there, but you can also simply use the music you already have. Out of 300+ albums on each of my Ponos, I have probably purchased five from the Pono site. So you don't have to use the Pono site to buy music. You can buy from other sites, you can rip your CDs, or you can simply transfer whatever music you already have on your computer.

Yes, Neil Young suggests buying hi-res music to get the most out of the Pono. I have lots of hi-res music on mine, but I also have lots of 16/44 CD rip on mine as well. You don't have to buy hi-res music to enjoy the Pono. Yes, hi-res sounds great on the Pono.So does CD-rip quality.

What the Pono does is present music with clarity and detail. Ayre, the high-end audio company which is responsible for much of the engineering of the Pono, did a marvelous job of creating a device that is able to present a full-bodied musical environment at a price point far below top-end players that do the same. If you are a casual listener of music, then stick with a smartphone or iPod. If you think you might like to hear your music presented in a better way, then try a Pono.

Is it yellow, and looks like a Toblerone bar? Yes. Is Neil Young involved with it? Yes. Is it a great player, if you like music and want to really hear it in all of its glory? Yes. Is it worth the price? Yes.

If you want to read more about the Pono, check out the two Pono threads on Head-Fi.org.

This was my winner after casually testing out 2 other speakers: The Oontz Angle Plus and UE Boom.

I initially got the Oontz Angle Plus after my Sol Republic Punk died (you can check out my review of that product there). For $35 the Oontz was capable, but not as loud as I would like. I wanted a speaker for three things: working out in the garage, in my office when I write, and for the beach. Therefore I was also looking for a splashproof speaker.

The UE Boom cost 5x the Angle Plus on sale. The Boom has nice aesthetics, and is quite loud. I didn't think it was worth the difference in price, but my husband said I could not keep the Oontz after he listened to the Boom. Obviously the Oontz is not in the same league (but it is a very serviceable speaker), but my husband didn't like the wimpy sound compared to the Boom. We found the JBL Charge 2+ on Warehouse Deals, so we threw that into the mix to test.

Compared to the Boom, the JBL Charge 2+ is not as loud...I say about two clicks less. Depending on the song, my husband tested about 8 db less on the Charge. A few songs, there was no audible difference, nor measurable difference in the casual db tester. However where the JBL wins is definitely the bass. The UE Boom sounded like it was screaming at you vs the full, sexy, resonating sound of the JBL. Bass is relative though...neither speaker will rumble your baseboards. But comparatively, the UE Boom had no bass to speak of next to the JBL.

The JBL on my kitchen scale weighed about 3oz more than the Boom, and it is wider so it's a little bulky for my smaller hands. The Boom also just looks cooler, compared to the giant candy colored beer can look the JBL has going. But I really like several things on the JBL better in additional to the quality of sound:

- The battery indicator - the 5 dots gives you a nice idea of battery level
- The volume buttons to me were easier to push than the Boom, however I like that it's easier to tell in the Boom when you hit max vol (I keep just pressing on the JBL until I think I've gotten there)
- The ability to skip, pause, and play from the speaker. I leave my tablet in the house as it doesn't pick up wireless well in the garage. I put the JBL in my elliptical's cup holder and can skip tracks by pressing the phone button twice quickly. (pressing once pauses, pressing it once again plays.) All you can do on the Boom is adjust volume from the speaker itself. Even the Oontz allowed at least pause/play from the speaker.

I have used the JBL in the shower, no problem, and it was actually too loud for a backyard party at full strength. Battery life tested was close to the 11-12 hours, but for at least 6 hours, I was playing at full blast, so that's pretty good. I have not yet used the actual charging feature, and while I don't think I'll be using it any time soon, it's nice to have the option. Same goes for the social mode. The Boom also has NFC, but honestly I don't find the 2 extra steps for bluetooth pairing that difficult and don't miss it on the JBL.

Ultimately, it depends what you are looking for. But for the $30 price difference I was judging between the Boom and the JBL, the JBL was the clear winner.

This radio is underrated. I was always a fan of the HR 2510, but never got around to getting one when I was into CB radio about 15 years ago. I just got back into it about 6 months ago and have been continuing to upgrade my mobile setup. I had been using a super modulated Cobra 25 LTD classic, but wanted uppers and lowers and also SSB. This radio caught my eye with it's small size and slick look. I couldn't fine much online about except people in the UK using it on sideband and FM. Something told me this radio was a killer on AM too. I went to a few forums and they all said to leave it alone and don't touch anything inside. Well I didn't listen and when I got it the first thing I did was clip the white wire inside to expand the channels. Before doing this I put it on the meter and monitored the audio. It was low and the radio had very little swing. I turned the modulation up, turned down the AMANL, lowered the low end carrier to 1 watt and the high end to 10. I also turned the FM modulation up a bit. The sound on the air is loud and clear after some adjustments inside. I'm talking modulation that is more like a Galaxy, but with that crisp, smooth ham radio sound. After the adjustments it has some swing, but this is not a swinging radio. This means if you run an amp you may have to run your dead key a littler higher to get your max wattage. Hopefully someone will post some swing mods for this radio, but honestly it doesn't really need it.  The echo is junk. On 1 it has way too much echo. The high cut, ANL and NB help a lot for receive noise, but the receive while sensitive can be noisy when driving in areas with a lot of static. SSB works well. People when properly tuned sound clear and on pitch. The transmit is on frequency. The radio on the right side can run a little hot. The microphone is really small and the mic cord is pretty short, but it sounds good on air. FM sounds pretty good after turning up the modulation, but nothing amazing. Lots on menu options

With that said this speaker produces more than enough bass to make listening to it over a variety of different musical styles quite pleasing.

If you are looking for the best bass response from this device indoors placing it closer to a wall or even better a corner of a room will give you the best bass.

I like the fact that the speaker is angled up as mid-range and high-end are directional sounds so you can place this down on a table or desk and get great sound since the speakers are aimed up at you.

►► VOLUME ◄◄

This little speaker truly puts out a ton of volume. I tested the volume capacity with a decibel tester positioned about 1 foot away from the unit and got a maximum volume of 101 decibels. To put that number in perspective 90 to 95 decibels is the level at which sustained exposure may result in hearing loss.

►► CONTROLS ◄◄

I really like that the controls here are easily labeled. You can easily see which button is which. On the unit you can pause and start music, take a call, make the volume higher or lower and move forward and back in your track list. The volume of the speaker and the volume of your device are synced so changing the volume on your phone or the device do the exact same thing.

The only thing I don't like is that to control the volume you have to press and hold the buttons down since it shares the control with the previous / next track capability. It can be hard to release at just the right point to get the volume you want but that is a small issue and nothing that would change my opinion of this speaker.

►► PAIRING ◄◄

The Bluetooth pairing worked quickly and easily with my iPhone 6. When you power up the speaker it will go into pairing mode if it cannot find a device to which is way previously paired. While this unit has NFC pairing available my iPhone 6 does not support it so I was unable to test that out. Those with Android based phones that have NFC should be able to pair simply by touching their phone to the speaker.

►► POWERING ◄◄

The speaker runs off an internal rechargeable battery that is recharged via USB. You can use the speaker while it is charging so adding a power bank to the mix will guarantee you non-stop music all day long. As it is the unit will last around 6 hours of music listening on a full charge.

►► CONCLUSION ◄◄

This is a well made and nice sounding speaker that delivers a lot of sound from a small package. It is the perfect little speaker to take with on the go or use around the house. Recommended.

The batteries are SigmasTek that I just received.  I am not sure how the brand will stack up, but they are about half the cost of a genuine RBC7.  Keep in mind this listing/product has had various sellers over the years.  The current seller is BatterySharks.com and you can buy these $3 cheaper on their site (not sure if it ships as fast though, I have Prime).  It's a simple process to setup the batteries...place them so the connectors are in the middle (one positive will be next to the other's negative).  Pop the terminal covers off your original battery (held on by 4 pieces of double-sided foam tape).  If you have double-sided foam tape that can be used to tie the batteries together, but you have be accurate...and easier method is to hook up the fusible link and then simply run a piece of packing tap across to top width-wise and then a couple pieces around the sides and bottom....make a 3" tape flap at the fuse end so you can pull the battery out next time.  Connect the power leads (make sure positive and negative are correct)...pop the two terminal covers back on and as you have it about ready to slide in connect the plug inside the UPS to the new battery....pop it in and you are back in business after a couple screws and putting the cover back on.  With Smart UPS 1500's and IBM 2130R5X/UPS1500TLV's these can be done without turning off the UPS and without having to power down any connected devices (hot-swapable).  Even with my genuine RBC7, I am lucky to get 2 years out of a battery set as I am coastal and the power flucuates constantly turning the day.  If I get more than a year out of these, I am still ahead.  They come in a sealed factory box as well, some vendors ship used batteries that are almost impossible to tell from new (other than getting much less life) or batteries that have been sitting on a shelf for a year+ which also will have shorter lives.

First off, I'm a fanatic with reviewing and dissecting a product before I buy it. I was looking for a Bluetooth in ear headset to replace my Plantronics Go Beats 2 which wouldn't stay in my ear no matter how I retrofitted them. My first step was to look at the top 10 at toptenreviews.com and then look at the reviews on Amazon. The former would capture initial performance and the latter would capture longer term use and reliability. From a design standpoint, I liked the Denon AH, Blueant Pump, Plantronics Backbeat and Beats Powerbeats 2. What I soon learned is that every single pair has some type of issue. The Denon has pairing issues over time, the Plantronics Backbeat have horrible bass response (I got a pair of these and soon discovered this and the frequency range indicates this), the Beats Powerbeats 2 have a tendency to break at the ear stem and the Blueant Pump have ear buds that tend to come off.

I decided on the Blueant Pumps and have not been disappointed after 3 months of use. To overcome the buds coming off, I super glued them to the post. The other issues I found with them is it can be difficult to orient them to go in your ears; in other words you have to untwist the cable to get them in the right position to insert them in the correct ear. This is minor and gets easier over time. The other minor issue was I experienced some intermittent squeaking while running with them which I attributed to the ear bud sliding once getting coated with sweat. This tends to go away if you dry the moisture out of the inside and outside of the bud. This has happened only a few times and not within the last month.

On the positive side; the sound is great, the volume is sufficient, the battery life is superb and they are very easy to pair and operate. I have not used them for a phone call yet so I can't comment on that feature. The price is awesome for what you get and this is an example of not needing to buy the most expensive item to get the best product.

1- sound quality and volume is just ok. It sounds fine but by no means hi-fi quality. There are two small speakers on one side and two passive resonators on the other that look like speakers but only resonate the internal noise outwards. For me I use this at the beach and when at a setting like that it simply cannot compete with the background noise of the waves. You can hear this if at full volume and within about 8 - 10 feet. Beyond that and you cannot hear it. That may sound misleading because you can hear it fine inside a quiet room or perhaps at a quiet park but for a weather resistant, rugged speaker I imagine others may also use it at the beach or near a stream so keep this in mind.

2 - Bluetooth is older technology with no range. The range I get out of this is about the same as the sound travel at the beach - maybe 5-10 feet. If your phone is in your pocket and you walk away slightly the music stops. It will reconnect if you get back close so I just leave the phone in a pocket of a chair or beach bag. Pros: -Reasonably priced -Bluetooth connectivity!  The number one reason I purchased this MP3 player. -Good sound quality -Excellent battery life -No special transfer program or drivers required to send files to internal storage- use Windows File Explorer -Small & lightweight -Color display screen supports album artwork -Physical on/off switch -Several preset EQ settings  Cons: -Confusing counter intuitive sometimes erratic menu system- many reviewers complain about the same issue -Uses old style FAT chronological ordering system for song playing order -No user adjustable 5 or 7 band EQ- only preset EQ choices (rock, classical, etc..) -To change volume while playing a song- you have to hold the center button for several seconds, wait a few seconds, then the player enters "easy mode" then you can change the volume or skip to the next or previous track. If you want to do anything else while still in "easy mode" then you have to hold the center button again for several seconds to enter "normal mode" where you have access to the settings, etc.. that's a lot of work just to change the volume.  Thoughts: Biggest con is the confusing, counter intuitive and sometimes erratic (sometimes it does things differently even with the same button press sequences) menu/navigation system. It's not too bad if you use headphones exclusively, but once you add a Bluetooth device and possibly a second Bluetooth device it's really confusing to disconnect the previous device then pair to a new device then get back to your music and EQ settings.  Other issue is the old style FAT chronological ordering system for song playing order- first songs dragged to the music folders get played first no matter if you put 01, 02, 03, etc... in front of the file name. This isn't really too much of a problem because it's easy to work around if you know that the player works this way. Simply drag the contents of your album over to the player one file at a time (vs. select-all then dragging/transferring all at once) in the order you want the songs played.  If the developers re-wrote the firmware to make a simple and user friendly menu/navigation system like the old Sansa Fuse and made the Bluetooth pairing system easier to use this inexpensive MP3 player would easily get five stars!

The good news is that once set up everything did work more or less. Registering devices is like installing devices in Windows 95, you just keep trying until it finally works (pretty much every device gave me "This device is missing system requirements" errors, but then passed on the second or third try). I can access DVR recordings from home or outside of home including while connected solely to a cell network (AT&T LTE in my case). Now the not so good.

I'm not sure why we need this device in the first place. The older DirecTV2pc application did just fine streaming directly from the DVR and didn't require you to spend another $100 on a box that takes up another port on your router, runs hot enough to cook an egg on, consumers large amounts of power 24/7 and provides lesser picture and sound quality than the app.

The picture quality is pretty bad. DirecTV quality is not great to begin with, watching regular HD programming on anything 65" or larger looks blurry and pixelated, but this takes the cake. Even on a 10" tablet the image looks very soft/smudged and fast motion produces severe tiling in the image. The audio also sounds sub-par. If you're used to the kind of quality you get with Netflix streaming you're going to be very disappointed with this.

There is also a limit of five devices that can be registered with the box. Note that of those devices only ONE can actually be streaming at a time. So if my wife is watching a show already on her PC the other four users/devices are out of luck. Even worse in order to upload anything to your device for offline use you have to encode it first, about 20mins of encoding time for each hour of play time, and while the unit is encoding a program it can't stream to even one device, everyone is shut out at that point.

All in all quite a backwards step from the DirecTV2PC program. If Netflix are ever able to add live TV and local channels to their line-up DirecTV wil become one of the most spectacular nose-dives in history. It is just so much more complicated, needs so much more hardware and so much more expensive to use DirecTV and the quality is now nowhere near what you can get on Netflix or even Amazon prime (and that's just talking HD 1080p).

And then there's the actual recordings. Not really anything to do with GenieGO 2 but how is it that DirecTV can think they're so brilliant at coming up with the idea of recording programs that they patented it (so what exactly were we doing with VCRs all those years?), yet their algorithm is still as dumb the dumbest VCR in that it works off clock on the wall time - rather than the true start/end times. You'd think that the company broadcasting the programs would actually know when the programs start and finish. I'm so sick of missing the final sprint of a Tour De France stage because the recording stopped before the end of the program. Or playing a recording of a of a Formula One race only to catch the end of previous show where they're telling you the finishing order of the drivers and congratulating the winner.

Comparison of 4 Amazon Stereo Headphones:
I grew up using partial over the ear but this style is difficult to find these days. I use the headphones when exercising, during yard work, or fix-up projects around the house. I wear an extra large male hat size.
My favorite is the Maxell SL-3, hp-200. I like the way they feel as they are the most comfortable of the group. The sound is well balanced throughout the frequency range. The over the ear component aligns with the middle of each earpiece so the angle feels good. One potential drawback is that the cord is a straight plug connector as opposed to the firm rubber right angle plugs that are more common. I remember having many of these straight connectors that eventually went bad at the connection.

My second favorite is the Sonxtronic XDR-8000. These have ends that go into the ear. They are comfortable. These are lacking in the base and low frequency range and require a higher volume setting to achieve the same sound as the padded Maxell and Panasonic headphones reviewed. The sound is a bit “tinny”. I am keeping these because while they don’t sound the best, they don’t have the foam pads and thus will hold up much better for those times when I am sweating heavily.

My third favorite is the Panasonic RP=HT21. These headphones have the overall best sound and have a very full stereophonic sound. They have the best bass and low frequency sound. They have a very good 90 degree connector plug. The cord is a great length. The problem is that they are narrow and sized for a person with a smaller, narrower head than mine. Furthermore, the over the head portion attaches to the earpiece at its front section. This design causes the earpiece to flare away from the back of the ear and the sound suffers. If you hold the earpieces to your ears with your hands the sound improves significantly. In addition, this design results in a pinching effect that is very uncomfortable. If the headpiece connected to the mid point of the earpiece I believe the problems would be solved and this would jump to the #1 favorite position. At the price I am willing to keep them and see if they become more comfortable with time, but I am very doubtful.

Totally unacceptable is the Sony MDR-A17G. Although they say Sony on the item, I doubt they are really made by Sony. The earpiece quality is terrible and had extra plastic that scratches the ear. The overall quality looks very cheap. The sound is terrible, with a very tinny sound and no bass. These will be returned.
The overall clarity was marginal, surprised to see the Sennheiser brand on a pair of so-so headphones.

Before buying I read the previous reviews and yet did not know what to expect from a 25$ earphone (I got it at 16$ reduced price). When I first tried it with a Samsung tablet and an iPhone I was immediately charmed by the full and clear but never sharp sound of this equipment. Bass is not 'deep bass' as claimed by other manufacturers, but full, warm and exact. Voices are crisp, and the high range is accentuated but not sharp or hard-sounding. I am a friend of natural-sounding music equipment, and this ear-phone is pretty close to a characteristic of a studio monitor. A minus for the performance with very complex sounds, such as big orchestra or e.g. some Pink Floyd performances, when the resolution is limited and the single instruments/sources are not easy to distinguish anymore. However, I still have to try it on my headphone amplifier with a good CD source, as the compressed music source is not ideal to reproduce complex sounds, too.

Wearing comfort is great, the fit (with the medium sized plugs) is perfect and gives an amazingly good noise isolation. The cables are tangle-free as far as can be expected. The downside is the sensitivity to structure-borne noise, transmitted through the cable into the phone. Listening during activity can therefore be disturbed by such scratching noises.

The look is pleasant (I have the red cable edition with dark wood), soothingly different to the regular plastic toy style. The apparent build quality is very good, the wood is even in color and shape, the connections are smooth and clean.

Conclusion: This earphone is maximum sound and comfort for the buck, 5+ stars for the overall rating. Sound rating alone (price-independent) would be around 4 stars.

My son and I have been using these Panasonic in-ear headphones for several years, at least.  Great sound value, remarkably good for the price.. If you like a nice balance across the sonic range from bass to treble, these ear buds are good.  They're definitely not for bass lovers. They're also not audiophile headphones. That being said, these 'phones are good for situations where high sound quality is not the primary goal, like when you're out running errands and need some background music but you also want to hear some of the external noise so you can be aware of your surroundings.  Be sure to check which ear bud tips provide the best seal.  It makes all the difference for sound quality. But don't expect good noise isolation, since the ear buds and tips don't seem designed for that.  Also, the wires are thin, and they'll most likely fail at the connection to one or the other ear bud, or to the jack.  My son doesn't take the best care of his ear buds, so he goes through several of these a year (now you know why I like the price).  I'm careful with mine, so I'm currently on my second set in two or three years.

First off, I notice this is called the Series II. The two main differences I can see from the Series I are fairly significant. Firstly, there is Bluetooth capability -- this is a very welcome addition. Secondly, there is a \\"bass\\" setting on the remote now. From what I've read, Series I required turning a knob at the back of the soundbar itself, and that's not always convenient. There may be other enhancements/improvements I'm not yet aware of. At the time of writing this review (mid August), the Series II does not look like it's publicly available. It's not even mentioned on the Bose website. If somehow you're reading this and are about to pull the trigger on a Series I, perhaps hold off a bit!

Now onto the review:

As someone who has never bought into the whole Bose marketing machine, I was hugely skeptical about this unit. I already have a decent Sony AV receiver which offers reasonable quality sound with HDMI ARC, plenty of different audio pre-sets, and a number of other options.

This Bose is more bare bones. No HDMI, just optical/coaxial connectivity only. But it does come with a pretty nice universal remote, and while at first I considered this inessential, it has actually turned into a decent freebie, and my family approves of just having a single remote controlling all our TV viewing these days instead of many.

However, simplicity is good sometimes, as this was a breeze to set up. Optical instead of HDMI isn't as bad as I expected: the Bose still comes on automatically when you switch on the TV (there's a setting to enable/disable this), and the Bose remote paired fine with my TV, cable box, DVD player, and even Roku, while the cable box and TV remotes paired nicely with the Bose so I can control volume from any remote.

And here's the thing, despite reading terrible things about Bose and their over-priced components, I'm going to say something that will probably make most audiophiles scoff at me: the Bose Solo 15 Series II is good. It's clear, it's loud enough, it really does a nice job of enhancing my TV viewing. There's enough bass, sufficient middle, and bright highs with a soundscape that fills the room well and sounds wider/fuller than my current system.

Even the cheapest soundbar is likely to be a step up from the in-built speakers on most current TVs (except, perhaps, some of the more expensive models), and Bose has created something here that is great at enhancing your general TV viewing, unless you're looking for theater-quality sound. It still lacks a little dynamism and sparkle, but both dialog and music are perfectly serviceable and clear.

Sure, I might not be getting the flexibility of the Sony system, nor the multitude of settings and different audio options, but the Bose just works, and I think that's why I like it: I very rarely need to tweak and fiddle like I do with my current Sony receiver. It's not as temperamental either: HDMI ARC, for all its advantages, can sometimes be a bit hit and miss (the Sony receiver occasionally gets turned off when changing sources -- probably a fault with my Samsung TV, but a notable irritation -- and it doesn't always play friendly with the Samsung so-called \\"Smart Remote\\").

The Bose doesn't have the same booming bass response or loudness, but it's more consistent, and less `muddy.' For some sources, I found the Sony receiver a little more sibilant, with less warmth, so a lot depends on the quality of the audio track on what you are watching, e.g. it's a bit more picky. The Bose copes with all kinds of music, audio, TV, movies, sports. It may lack a display, HDMI, and other useful stuff, but believe it or not, I'm sticking with it, because for everyday use, it's just ideal -- and I think that's the key. If I had a dedicated theater room, no way, but I'm talking about a TV that we watch kid's TV on in the morning, then a bit of baseball in the evening, perhaps a movie at the weekend, some Netflix via Roku, maybe some music via Chromecast, or even (yes, really) an old-school DVD. The Bose keeps up with the variety better than the Sony receiver, and that's why I like it.

And that universal remote -- I'm digging it. It's probably not as feature-happy as the Harmonys and Logitechs out there, but for free, it does exactly what I need.

Am I converted to the Bose cause? Perhaps not -- this is a Vine review so I was fortunate enough to get the product for free. I'm doubtful I would have purchased it myself, but I'm glad I got to try it because despite the Bose marketing hype, I can see why their stuff is successful -- it just kinda works, and it reminds me a bit of how Apple do things. It's probably not going to satisfy an audiophile (I can hear the folks on AVForums laughing at me already), and it's a little overpriced (I'm sure there are as-good items out there for less), but the Bose Solo 15 Series II is much better than I expected, especially for everyday use, and the bonus of having Bluetooth makes it a keeper for me.

I'm very happy with the sound quality coming out of these speakers. They emit a very premium sound and are they are undoubtedly the best pair of speaker's I've ever owned. I appreciate that they have a wide and clear field of sound and they are not nearly as uni-directional as my outgoing set of speakers. Basically, each channel does not have to be aimed directly at your ear for a great listening experience.  The size of these speakers is a bit large for my space as they are hooked up to the computer in my office and sit on either side of my monitor. I knew when I purchased them that space could be an issue so I have no one to blame but myself. The depth of the speakers is almost comical. If you don't have a flexible space in terms of placement, it would be worth your while to look for something a touch smaller.  Bass response is clean and sounds wonderful. I expected a little more thump given the massive cabinet size, but with 6.5" woofers, I don't think it is realistic to expect much more. If it is chest-thumping bass you crave, a component woofer will be a required pairing.  The real question when it comes to writing a review is this: Would I buy these speakers again? Certainly I would think long and hard about the size of these speakers and whether or not I have the real-estate for them. If slightly smaller speaker could sound this good, then I'd do that in a heartbeat! But, until I find those speakers, I'm going to jam out to my Polk 220B's. Even given their dominating footprint on my desk, the sound they produce is just way too good.

Since the legs aren't directly connected to each other, sliding the TV sideways feels a bit weird as the legs turn a bit. But even so, it still feels solid and I have no worries of it falling over.

The only con is the style of it. While it doesn't look offensive, it certainly isn't going to match the sleek style of most TV stands for modern TVs. It's a minor con for me as I don't really notice the stand, but I can see it being a bit of an eyesore in some living rooms, especially if you're mounting a sleek $2k TV.

But as a replacement stand on a budget, it succeeds at its purpose. Highly recommended!

What makes these a little bit special is the sheer ease with which they reach down into the deep bass and up into the highest highs--as they should when using two dynamic drivers on each side. Besides the bass being very powerful, it is also well-textured and clear, and the highs have a sense of delicate detail too--you usually don't get both at the same time. But the problem lies in between. The midrange isn't very clean and in fact can be a little harsh. If you check the graphs for these at InnerFidelity.com, you'll see that there's a strong peak at 2 kHz. On my Fiio X7, I EQ the 2 kHz range down about 3-4 decibels, and also EQ the rest of the treble range down just a decibel or two. Because of the excellent extension in both the highs and the lows, these provide grand, large-scale sound, but they're not the best for voices or acoustic instruments since the midrange isn't good enough. Still, for some kinds of electronic or orchestral music they can be impressive. Also they need quite a bit of power to run well. I use the "high" gain setting on my X7, and even sometimes use the AM2 amp module, which has more power.  KEF's unusual system of fitting these into your ears works fine for me, even though it is slightly awkward and a tiny bit uncomfortable over long periods. But from the other reviews here and elsewhere on the Web, it obviously doesn't work for everyone. And over long listening sessions, I become aware that these really aren't the cleanest sounding IEMS, and their sound can become a little fatiguing as a result.

This is perfect! It has everything I could want, and many features it never occurred to me to want. The alarm starts very quietly and then gets louder, so if you wake up quickly you don't have to suffer the onslaught of a loud noise. The display is very easily dimmable, which I so appreciate because I hate bright alarm clocks in the bedroom. There is a "nap" feature, where with the touch of a button you can take a nap of set lengths from just a few minutes to an hour and half. You can change the length of the snooze alarm. The charging docks, backup battery, easy-to-operate alarm setting, and manual backup time set (for if/when the auto-set feature fails, like it's failed on my last 6 auto-set clocks). If only the auto-set feature lasts as long as the rest of the clock, it will be truly the most wonderful clock ever. Time will tell. (Get it?)

The one thing I can point to as a possible problem has to do with the charging cord. I've never seen an alarm clock that doesn't have the power cord permanently attached to the clock, so there is a possibility that an over-zealous snoozer could yank the clock out of its power charge cable. Also, the end of the cord is not an ordinary 2 or 3 prong plug, but has a large transformer attached, that would need to be plugged into the bottom of the 2 outlets or you'd lose the outlet underneath the transformer. In my bedroom, the outlets next to the bed (where I would plug in an alarm clock) are half wired to the wall switch, (so you could turn out a bedside light at the wall), and it's no good to plug an alarm clock into the wall-switch outlet. Luckily, in my case the wall-switch outlets are the top outlet of the 2, but if they were on the bottom, I'd lose that plug since I'd be forced to plug the alarm in the top outlet and it extends down far enough to cover the other plug. So if that might apply to your situation, caveat emptor.

I grew up using partial over the ear but this style is difficult to find these days. I use the headphones when exercising, during yard work, or fix-up projects around the house. I wear an extra large male hat size.
My favorite is the Maxell SL-3, hp-200. I like the way they feel as they are the most comfortable of the group. The sound is well balanced throughout the frequency range. The over the ear component aligns with the middle of each earpiece so the angle feels good. One potential drawback is that the cord is a straight plug connector as opposed to the firm rubber right angle plugs that are more common. I remember having many of these straight connectors that eventually went bad at the connection.

My second favorite is the Sonxtronic XDR-8000. These have ends that go into the ear. They are comfortable. These are lacking in the base and low frequency range and require a higher volume setting to achieve the same sound as the padded Maxell and Panasonic headphones reviewed. The sound is a bit “tinny”. I am keeping these because while they don’t sound the best, they don’t have the foam pads and thus will hold up much better for those times when I am sweating heavily.

My third favorite is the Panasonic RP=HT21. These headphones have the overall best sound and have a very full stereophonic sound. They have the best bass and low frequency sound. They have a very good 90 degree connector plug. The cord is a great length. The problem is that they are narrow and sized for a person with a smaller, narrower head than mine. Furthermore, the over the head portion attaches to the earpiece at its front section. This design causes the earpiece to flare away from the back of the ear and the sound suffers. As with all audio reviews, I am going to break this into the following categories: build quality (1 point), design (2 points), comfort (2 points), and sound (5 points). An extra point can be earned for a really unique or intuitive feature, or for sound so good it gave me uncontrollable goosebumps.

I had the pleasure of auditioning these at a major retailer that had them on display. Of course, this is not the best way to audition anything that is emitting sound, but I was so impressed that I decided to purchase them and try them out at home. These are marketed as luxury audiophile-grade portable headphones, and I applaud Bowers & Wilkins for getting it dead on the nose. These truly are portable and will play at a deafening volume when played on my iPhone 5S and my Mac.

After a couple of days listening to it on my iPhone and Mac, I decided I needed to see how well these scaled. I plugged them into a Questyle Q192 DAC and amp, and I auditioned them for hours side-by-side with a pair of HiFiMan HE-500. These two headphones could not be any different: one is closed back (P7) whereas the other open. One uses traditional speaker drivers (P7) whereas the other uses planar magnetic (aka orthodynamic). One is portable while the other takes quite a bit of juice to drive and cannot be played on portable products. They really are apples and airplanes.

BUILD QUALITY: 1/1 point

They're wonderfully built. They feel very sturdy both when held and on your head. I appreciate that they came with two cables: one that has a straight connector with no microphone, and one that's an L-connector with a microphone. They're easily changeable: simply pull off the left ear cup (they're magnetic) and unplug the cable. Voila! All-in-all, I think you'd be hard-pressed to find ANY headphone constructed more carefully and with better materials than these. Bowers & Wilkins are legendary for design and craftsmanship, and these may just be their Magnum Opus (aside from The Nautilus, of course).

DESIGN: 3/2 points (+1 point for the WOW factor)

Just look at them. They're absolutely gorgeous. The retro style, luxury materials, and brand make these the best looking headphones I've ever seen. The lambskin leather, while certainly opulent, transform these headphones into a luxury status symbol. They're so nice, I'm afraid to wear them in public for fear that I'll be mistaken for a wealthy businessman from New York. I feel as if I should wear them to Bruce Wayne's fancy dinner parties. Plus, they come with a carrying case made out of quilted lambskin leather. I mean...c'mon, can life get any better than quilted lambskin leather?

COMFORT: 1.5/2 points

It's really hard for me to deduct half a point for comfort as they've been nothing but perfectly comfortable since I've put them on. I've worn them for hours at a time, and I've had nary a whiff of fatigue. However, I know for a fact that these will cause your ears to become pretty moist if you wear them in very warm environments. Normally, I wouldn't deduct any points for this, but given that these are marketed as portable, it's something to take consideration of. Additionally, these do come out of the box pretty stiff and may put more pressure on your head than you'd like for the first day or so, but they will adapt to your head pretty quickly. For those of you with large ears, you may find the cups to be too small and they may sit on parts of your ear. I don't have this problem. All-in-all, these are very, very comfortable.

SOUND: 4.5/5 points

Ah, finally: the single most important part of this review. How in the world do they sound? In a word, resplendent. If you've ever heard B&W speakers, they sound remarkably like that. The "B&W Sound", as it's called, isn't for everyone. Some call it "too warm" and "colored". If I were to give it adjectives, I'd use the following: "rich", "inviting", and "luscious". Bowers and Wilkins have done a phenomenal job combining a warm, rich sound with detailed and discerning qualities. The bass is fantastic: tight, strong, without bloom or muddiness. The mids are, in true B&W fashion, very pleasant. Treble is surprisingly fantastic for a dynamic driver style. While it may not be a "flat" pair of headphones, the "B&W Sound" makes almost everything sound better.

As I alluded to above, I had the opportunity to listen to these side-by-side a pair of HiFiMan HE-500s. Let me tell you, that was a treat. I was able to come up with the following conclusion: the HiFiMans are, by most measures, a superior headphone: better clarity, better treble, a substantially wider soundstage, more detail, etc; however, it lacked the mid-bass and bass that the P7s have. Additionally, many of the Top 40 songs that are out sound extremely cold on the HiFiMans. They discriminate heavily on source quality (aka "recording quality"), and a poor recording will come through like a knife on a chalk board. While the P7s still benefit from great source material, they do a much better job at glossing over poor mixing and compressed dynamics. Most songs sound absolutely stunning on the P7s whereas many songs sound quite terrible on the HiFiMans. With that being said, the HiFiMans will outpace the P7s every single time with songs that are not bass heavy and are recorded well. They're just simply in a different league. They're truly "reference" quality.

For example, Wild Winds by The Honey Trees sound almost haunting on the HiFiMans: the airiness of the vocals will penetrate your soul and fill you with goosebumps. The harmony will make you wonder if you've transcended into another dimension. The soundstage is so broad, you'll wonder if you're in a wide-open field. With the P7s, you get amazing sound and quality, but you aren't enveloped with soundstage like you are with the HiFiMans. The experience is good, but it isn't soul-piercing like the HiFiMans.

However, Wagon Wheel by Darius Rucker flipped the results on its head. On the HiFiMans, the sound was almost hollow. Darius's sultry baritone vocals sounded almost metallic. The kick drum wasn't very strong, and the bass guitar didn't have great presence. On the P7, it was exactly the opposite: the rich tones absolutely amplified the song into another country. It had me tapping my foot so loud I thought I was going to wake up the dead. I didn't have the detail that the HiFiMans gave, but that wasn't the point of the song, and thar be the rub: a lot of music wasn't mixed/recorded to be analyzed like a science experiment, and the HiFiMans are some of the best scientists you'll ever see.

Don't get me wrong: the HE-500s are better in almost every way when you look at it objectively; however, if you like listening to modern music and you're on the move, The P7s will absolutely delight you. They're almost perfect. Almost.

OVERALL: 10/10 points

Can you get better sounding headphones for the price? Sure. Can you get better sounding headphones that are portable with these looks and build quality? If you do, please let me know, because I can't find them. At any price.

These headphones could potentially be great, but there are some caveats buyers should be aware of. First off, the MSRP on these is a whopping $250, and these are often listed at around $200. At this price range, I'm not so sure if these headphones are worth it as there is a lot of competition there. However, I managed to snag these at a very nice price of $125, and I believe AKG puts these on sale relatively regularly so be sure the price is right before buying.  I have never owned or heard the previous versions of these headphones (the k550 or k551), but from what I've read these sound similar and are more or less an updated version with some spikes in the midranged fixed. However, there is one huge problem with these: the seal. Without a proper seal (these are closed headphones after all), the k553s will sound terrible. They're designed for very large heads and have little clamping force. It may be necessary to bend the headband for a better fit. Fortunately for me, these fit rather well (probably thanks to my weird combination of my thin head+thick hair) after some adjustment and the seal problem was solved. They are also quite comfortable and can easily be worn for hours and hours without any issues.  They isolate quite well and very little sound is leaked. The sound of these is very neutral with a slight bias towards the bright (not much though). You aren't going to get thumping, rumbling bass with these, but you will instead get clean, accurate bass that is better for critical listening. Despite these not being perfectly neutral, for the price of $125, it's really hard to complain. The mids and treble are quite accurate to me and it's overall and enjoyable experience to listen to my wide range of music with these cans. All in all, these are a good option to consider while on the hunt for that perfect set of headphones. Highly recommended for those seeking that clean, neutral sound while on a budget.

I grew up using partial over the ear but this style is difficult to find these days. I use the headphones when exercising, during yard work, or fix-up projects around the house. I wear an extra large male hat size.

The over the ear component aligns with the middle of each earpiece so the angle feels good. One potential drawback is that the cord is a straight plug connector as opposed to the firm rubber right angle plugs that are more common. I remember having many of these straight connectors that eventually went bad at the connection.

My second favorite is the Sonxtronic XDR-8000. These have ends that go into the ear. They are comfortable. These are lacking in the bass and low frequency range and require a higher volume setting to achieve the same sound as the padded Maxell and Panasonic headphones reviewed. The sound is a bit “tinny”. I am keeping these because while they don’t sound the best, they don’t have the foam pads and thus will hold up much better for those times when I am sweating heavily.

My third favorite is the Panasonic RP=HT21. These headphones have the overall best sound and have a very full stereophonic sound. They have the best bass and low frequency sound. They have a very good 90 degree connector plug. The cord is a great length. The problem is that they are narrow and sized for a person with a smaller, narrower head than mine. Furthermore, the over the head portion attaches to the earpiece at its front section. This design causes the earpiece to flare away from the back of the ear and the sound suffers. If you hold the earpieces to your ears with your hands the sound improves significantly. In addition, this design results in a pinching effect that is very uncomfortable. If the headpiece connected to the mid point of theearpiece I believe the problems would be solved and this would jump to the #1 favorite position. At the price I am willing to keep them and see if they become more comfortable with time, but I am very doubtful.

I purchased this speaker to use in my basement/garage for parties. It is easy to move between rooms and can be plugged into via an AUX cord or connected to via Bluetooth.

Sound:
-Good solid sound up to a certain level. The speaker will definitely fill a room and be loud to the point of pain without any sound distortion. Outdoors and in larger spaces, when the speaker is turned up to a high level the sound can distort and the music will ultimately sound horrible. But for an indoor space with as many as 30-40 people the speaker is plenty loud with very good sound.

Battery:
-Unreal, this battery can go on and on and on. I have gone days without charging it and the indicator light will still show a full charge.

AM/FM Channels:
-Work perfectly, haven't had to use them too much, but the signal is strong even in my basement.

Bluetooth functionality:
-The bluetooth on this speaker is ok. It will connect to a phone pretty much right out of the box but if your phone disconnects and another one connects it can be a challenge to get the speaker to recognize your phone again without tinkering around with the unit.

ISSUES:
-The speaker sound gets badly distorted about 70% of the time if the phone is placed on top of or touching the speaker. This happens both on AUX and on Bluetooth settings. Also, the sound will often distort if there is a phone plugged into the charging port while music is being played.

-Overall a pretty good, loud speaker with some technical and high level sound shortcomings.

12/7/2015 Update:  And it's dead.  I managed to get about 100 or so uses out of it before it stopped working for about 30 seconds at a time and powering off without warning.  If you think of it as a disposable blue tooth speaker, it's not so bad I guess.  If you're looking for someone that is actually probably waterproof/resistant, and that is going to last more than a few months, I recommend spending a bit more money.  Pros:  Loud enough to hear any sort of audio over your shower.  Easy to pair with your blue tooth device.  Cons:  Not quite shower compatible/water resistant.  So for an $8 or so item this is a pretty sweet purchase.  It's loud and doesn't distort sound too badly at it's max audio level.  I would not recommend sticking it in your shower or anywhere where it could possibly experience a regular amount of contact with water.  Within two days the tiny, improperly sized rubber plug that is supposed to cover up the AC/power slot had fallen off.  And even before that, the plug did not fit the power port properly.  Simply transporting the speaker from one room to my shower resulted in the plug coming loose and leaving the hole that you attach the power cord to exposed to water.  (LATE EDIT:  I discovered the apparent cause of said rubber plug functioning improperly.  When the speaker is at louder volumes, the air pressure from its sound waves are forced out of it's power charger port.  Also--Be sure to turn the speaker off or at the very least hook it to it's charger.  Otherwise you will be woken up at 4 AM to the voice of a strange woman telling you to charge it, which has given me nightmares ever since.  With that being said, you can simply just place the speaker right outside of your shower and avoid any possible issues.  It's loud and clear sounding enough to serve it's purpose.

I've updated by review from three stars to five and DEFINITELY recommend purchasing this product! (A bunch of my friends loved the speaker so much that they bought one for themselves--and you should, too!)  I bought this speaker for the full purpose of taking it on a float trip this last weekend (Saturday, August 9th). Upon receiving the speaker and testing it out at home, it worked really well--the sound was nice, the Bluetooth range was pretty good, and everything seemed pretty perfect for the trip. Other people brought speakers with them, so I knew that I would only use mine on the actual river--so I charged it fully and didn't turn it on until I was on the raft.  Well, the speaker worked really well for about 3-4 hours or so. I had it tied to a dry sac that I had and bungied it onto the top of a cooler (which was also bungied to the raft), ensuring that I wouldn't lose the speaker and that it wouldn't get very wet (aside from the potential mist of water here and there from the oars). About 3-4 hours in, the volume on the speaker suddenly dropped to the lowest setting and refused to turn back up. I ensured that the volume on the MP3 player was fully turned up, the Bluetooth connection was good, and tried pressing/holding the volume on the Omaker speaker itself--but nothing changed. You could still faintly hear music if you pressed it up against your ear, but that's about it. I tried breaking/reconnecting the Bluetooth connection and rebooting all of the devices involved as well to no avail. With five+ more hours left on the river, I was pretty disappointed.  When we got back to camp, I put the speaker in my car and decided not to mess with it until I got home. Yesterday (August 10th) I paired everything once again to see if the issue still occurs, and it most certainly does. Nothing happens when you press/hold the volume buttons whatsoever, and the speaker simply shuts off once you press/hold the power button OFF (it's supposed to give a bit of an "Off" jingle). The only button/functionality that seems to be working properly is the jingle that occurs once you press/hold the power button to turn it ON.  With that said, I was only able to use this speaker successfully for about three or four hours--which really stinks. I loved this speaker once it worked, which is why I'm giving it a two star rating--but my rating would skyrocket if the little guy would work again like it's supposed to.

Seems that kids and headphones are an interesting blend.... some fit and work well and others not so much. In this case, these Philips headphones are a nice physical fit for my daughters (one is nearly 11 and the other 9) and seem to hold up to a mild amount of abuse.

The styling is nice and the overall design is excellent. These are the types with 'yolk' wiring (the lines split delivering sound to the right and left ears) as opposed to a single line to one ear then splitting that line over the top of the headset. I tend to think that the yolk style is more apt to damage or breakage due to the potential for splitting or getting hung up on something.

As far as sound quality is concerned I believe that there is a mix here: Excellent quality music gives a good sound quality through the headphones. Marginal quality music results in pretty terrible sound quality (tinny and hollow). Make no mistake, these are not intended to be studio quality headphones so make sure that you understand that prior to purchasing.

For the large majority of music my kids listen to, the quality of the stream is excellent therefore the sound quality is pretty good. Of course, the actual music they listen to is terrible but that's another story.. ;)

These headphones do have a built-in volume limit however I do think that the volume can be turned up louder than I would have guessed. I do not have any method to measure this but, to me, seems like it is allowed to go louder than I would have first thought. Thankfully my kids don't listen to things too loudly so all is OK there, for us.

As far as gaming, YouTube and other audio streams of wildly differing qualities these headphones are just fine. Even great to wear on long car rides, etc. where comfort is king.

Overall these are good headphones; noise limiting, great style and decent audio quality.

I bought my first Diver mp3 player this past spring. I am a runner and I was tired of shelling out cash for mp3 players that died when I ran in the rain or really hot days as sweat has ruined many players too.

The good: I have used this player in the rain with no issues. I like how I can attach it to my shorts with the clip. It is very easy to operate while running. It is very easy to load and unload songs using my computer. The sound quality meets my needs equally on par with my various ipods and Samsung Galaxy S5. This little sucker is very close to being a home run for all of my needs as a runner, but 2 significant flaws hold it back from being great.

The bad: The head phone jack. Like I said I am a runner. So I prefer to wear headphones that do not block out all outside noise. Thus the swimming headphones that are meant to plug your ears with the in-ear rubber to avoid water penetration (and thus all outside sounds) are not good for me. And the sound quality of the provided headphones are lacking. So when I plug in my higher end yurbuds that allow ambient sounds (to avoid getting hit by a car), the sound quality is much better. But wait! This mp3 player is not user friendly to other headphones! I have to insert the headphones into the jack about 95% of the way to get great sound in both ears. If I insert the whole way, the sounds quality is muffled and goes in & out. Damn it! It will not work for running with normal headphones (I tried 4-5 different pairs with no luck. The jack prong on the headphones provided is slightly shorter in length. So the standard length prong you will find on just about all headphones besides the ones that come with this player are almost useless. Yes, you can sit at a desk and enjoy the sound with it plugged in 95% into the jack. But while running this is not possible. Yet I did find some little extension cord from JBL in my huge box of various audio and computer cords that I slightly modified to seat into the player to provide optimum sound and then plugged my yurbuds into the extension. It worked great for 300+ miles of running. So I ordered another player. And disclaimer: I was sent another for free if I would write a review. Since then my extension cord has become faulty. So I can only use the headphones provided which I do not feel comfortable using while running because they block out all sound.

So all in all, they are now paperweights for me and I am back to my search for a runner-friendly, waterproof mp3 player. Such a shame that they do not use a standard headphone jack or it would be 95% perfect player. The only other improvement would be to have a shuffle option instead of playing the songs in order as they are loaded as the only option.

Comparison of 4 Amazon Stereo Headphones:
I grew up using partial over the ear but this style is difficult to find these days. I use the headphones when exercising, during yard work, or fix-up projects around the house. I wear an extra large male hat size.
My favorite is the Maxell SL-3, hp-200. I like the way they feel as they are the most comfortable of the group. The sound is well balanced throughout the frequency range. The over the ear component aligns with the middle of each earpiece so the angle feels good. One potential drawback is that the cord is a straight plug connector as opposed to the firm rubber right angle plugs that are more common. I remember having many of these straight connectors that eventually went bad at the connection.

My second favorite is the Sonxtronic XDR-8000. These have ends that go into the ear. They are comfortable. These are lacking in the base and low frequency range and require a higher volume setting to achieve the same sound as the padded Maxell and Panasonic headphones reviewed. The sound is a bit “tinny”. I am keeping these because while they don’t sound the best, they don’t have the foam pads and thus will hold up much better for those times when I am sweating heavily.

My third favorite is the Panasonic RP=HT21. These headphones have the overall best sound and have a very full stereophonic sound. They have the best bass and low frequency sound. They have a very good 90 degree connector plug. The cord is a great length. The problem is that they are narrow and sized for a person with a smaller, narrower head than mine. Furthermore, the over the head portion attaches to the earpiece at its front section. This design causes the earpiece to flare away from the back of the ear and the sound suffers. If you hold the earpieces to your ears with your hands the sound improves significantly. In addition, this design results in a pinching effect that is very uncomfortable. If the headpiece connected to the mid point of the earpiece I believe the problems would be solved and this would jump to the #1 favorite position. At the price I am willing to keep them and see if they become more comfortable with time, but I am very doubtful.

Totally unacceptable is the Sony MDR-A17G. Although they say Sony on the item, I doubt they are really made by Sony. The earpiece quality is terrible and had extra plastic that scratches the ear. The overall quality looks very cheap. The sound is terrible, with a very tinny sound and no bass. These will be returned.

So there's good and bad here. First, really the main gripe: the overhead projection is too small -- it projects about 12" letters onto the ceiling, whereas the previous one I had (a Timex model) had letters almost twice as big -- bigger is much easier to read without glasses on. Since the big benefit of the overhead projector is so that I can find the time in the dark without fumbling for glasses, this little detail was a big deal.

Aside from that, there are lots of little quirks that aren't that great. The three available backlight-brightness levels are "no backlight", "a little too bright", and "way too bright". Setting the alarms is VERY complicated -- even if you've used many an alarm clock in the past, you will find this one to be more complex than you expect. It's not a big deal to do once in a while but if you need to set different alarms throughout the week you will find this very tedious. Finally, the numbers themselves aren't very elegant. The way they're made up of gigantic "pixels" instead of 7-segment lines makes it a little uglier IMO.

On the good side, this clock has been optimized for a specific use-case, and it does that very well: if you have a certain time you want to wake up each day (on weekdays -- and possibly a second time for weekends), you can set this up and forget about it. You can even set different radio stations for each alarm, and different volumes, too. So you can have the "sleep" function play one station at loud volume, and the alarms play a different station at softer volume, or whatever. So this alarm takes your radio preferences very seriously and has a surprising depth to how you can set it up.

The clock's miscellaneous functions seem... kind of bizarre. Like I'm not sure when you would need an indoor-only thermometer display. But I presume someone somewhere would find that function very helpful. (And BTW, you can change the overhead projection to display the temperature instead of the time. Again... no idea why you'd do that. But if you need that, I doubt there's any other clock that would fit your need!)

I've been using a Sansa View media player for years, but when mine started dying (especially when it couldn't copy playlists anymore), I started looking for something new. I've heard lots of complaints from iPod users, usually because of iTunes, and so I wanted something different and I finally chose the FiiO X1 because it seemed to be the best for its price, and for what I wanted.
It is a nice machine- it plays smoothly and the sound quality is very good (depending of course, on the quality of the files- it makes you want to re-evaluate some of your file choices) and it has the nice perk of being able to make playlists on the device itself, which my Sansa View never could. It also has a nice feel to it, a good weight, the wheel actually moves, and the buttons are sturdy- no accidental skips here. The only things I miss are things I had on my Sansa: firstly, there is no clock on the device, so it can't work as a timepiece; secondly, playlists on shuffle will never stop unless you have a "sleep" setting on; thirdly, music is all you can do, so no radio, no pictures, and no videos like the Sansa; and finally, the device doesn't come with a wall charger, only a computer charger, which it says is not ideal (it takes several hours.) However, you can buy a wall charger, it's just an extra step...
So, overall, FiiO X1 is what is says on the tin- it plays music, and excellently. I am pleased with it, and it does its job well. I guess I just miss a few amenities...

The battery life is very good (rated at 15 hours) while the range of 33 feet or 10 metres (through clear space) is fairly average. Connectivity with my laptop running Windows 8.1 was instant and consistent. Kindle, ditto. The pricing is very competitive, in fact, considering the sound quality, performance and excellent manufacture, I would consider this a really good choice. I would happily recommend this speaker to a friend.
