I have historically never bothered to run a UPS, but I've been having minor power flickers in my house lately, a couple times a week that would reset my computer much to my annoyance (I run my desktop 24/7). I thought I should get a slightly bigger UPS since I have a custom built budget gaming rig, but I did some quick finger math and decided this one would work "for now". The device came with about a 95% charge if I remember correctly. I plugged in my computer and one monitor to the battery side and let it charge up to 100%, then gave it an extra hour or so. It claimed something like 150 minutes of runtime in the APC monitor program so I decided it needed a calibration. I set it all up for a worst case scenario simulation -- I used MSI Kombustor to load up the CPU and GPU and then pulled the plug. I wasn't 100% sure I'd picked one with enough wattage but it didn't flinch. It did however tell me I had 1 minute before shutdown (set to shutdown when 5 minutes remained). So I quickly set the computer back to idle and the runtime jumped back up to 7 minutes.

I let it run to shutdown and everything worked just as it should. However one of the safety features caught me off guard. Forgive me for not looking up the specifics right now, but basically wait a couple minutes after power is restored if you drain the unit until it shuts down. If my memory serves, the safety feature will shut down the battery for 2 minutes (or maybe one?) after power is restored after a full drain then cycle the power. So being "that guy" who doesn't like to read directions, when it died I plugged it back up and hit the power button on my computer... It booted most of the way up then there was some beeping (from the UPS) as it cycled the power and my computer reset, and about the time it got back to the BIOS screen it cycled the power again with some more beeping. The more you know.

It can't possibly be good to fully discharge a battery in 7 minutes or less, but this thing functioned flawlessly and could be a life saver. It didn't even heat up that I could tell. After my "calibration", the monitor program now says I should have 15 minutes at idle, which is probably pretty close to accurate and more than I should ever need. The next day after I hooked it up the power dropped out for a couple seconds during a storm, the UPS kicked on just like it should, and reported the problem to me in the monitor program. Now I'm just wondering why I didn't buy one of these sooner! Note that this thing takes forever to charge itself (think 12+ hours from 20% which was the magical 5 minute cut off on my system), probably to avoid unnecessary lead-acid battery related risks on your carpeted floor, but that shouldn't be an issue unless you're having constant power problems.

Just a note for anyone who (like me) sat around scratching their heads about which UPS will do what you need, maybe this will help... I already told you the estimated runtimes I got, here's a rundown of the power consumers on my rig:
CPU - AMD FX-4350 @ 4.2ghz
GPU - MSI NVIDIA GTX-760 Gaming
Storage - 2x WD Red HDDs, 1x Samsung 840 EVO SSD
Monitor - Asus 23.5" 1080p

Update 10/16/2016: This unit is still doing its job without a complaint. The PowerChute program tells me that the unit has switched on twice for "blackouts" totaling 9 seconds and twice for "electrical noise" totaling 24 seconds, in the past 24 weeks. It doesn't seem to register extremely short-lived problems (a second or so), I say that because on a couple occasions I've seen the house lights flicker and heard the unit rapidly click on and off with no report. No big deal. Also the Estimated Battery Time has gone back up to 145 minutes, I haven't bothered to recalibrate because I never really look at it anyway and I know what it'll do. Perfect small size internet radio receiver. Note the word receiver - there is no speaker. The headphone jack is as you would expect, and like any receiver the RCA outputs are pre-amp line out type (no volume control on radio) and need to go into a powered speaker system with an independent volume control or into a full blown AV receiver. The Grace unit was easy to set up - plug it in and follow the instructions. It did require a software update before Sirius-XM would work, and the Sirius-XM username and password need to be 10 characters or less - I simply changed my account to match up.10 presets on the remote (programmed into my Logitech universal), access to my Pandora, Rhapsody, and Sirius accounts. All is working well.

For Wi-Fi security, despite it stating it only works with WEP or WPA, it connected to my WPA2-PSK wireless network just fine. If you have a hidden SSID, you will need to manually provide it in the network setup as the radio won't by itself connect to a wireless system with a hidden SSID. Wi-Fi is 2.4 GHz only - sort of a bummer because of how noisy that band is, but radio audio has such a low throughput requirement and is buffered that it really has been no problem. I do note that when the microwave oven was on, the audio did become distorted - that's no fault of the radio, but rather that Microwave ovens and 802.11 2.4 GHz are in the same frequency range. I am moving to a wired adapter as soon as one is available (see below).

The only negatives are very minor - the menu for entering usernames / passwords is clunky and has no delete key capability - so if you make a mistake, you have to start over. Fortunately you only need enter each service once. The second issue is that the only USB-Ethernet adapter that will work is the Grace sourced model - and they are out of stock everywhere as of the date of this review. Except for those two rather minor issues I would have rated it a 5.

Let's start off by saying this isn't some fake review, though I did not purchase this sub brand new I bought a single 12 with no box in like new shape for 40 bucks off a friend of mine. I ended up building a custom built 2.1 cubic ft (after displacement) ported box tuned to 33 hz, which is right in kicker specs.

Over all build quality is not too bad, it's what you would expect from lower end kicker. For some reason the magnet is screwed into the basket from the back, if you unscrew the screws the magnet will come loose... lol weird design. The cone seems a bit lighter in design from the older comp models, and the surround isn't stitched to the cone anymore. The terminals absolutely REQUIRE the female spade terminal connectors in order to wire up the speaker, which in my opinion is stupid... a simple cheap spring terminal would've sufficed but they make it so you NEED the female spade terminal.

Now onto the sound quality, for the most part the still sound like the same old loud, boomy, muddy kicker sound.. it's improved just a tad, but over all its still not all that great. I have the kicker spec'd ported box, and the correct amount of power going to it, so it's not like I threw it in an atrend box and called it a day. Bc the cone is a bit lighter and the suspension of the sub is not as stiff it did improve a bit in sound quality, but it's no game changer. For the most part it's the same old kicker just a newer look, the only thing I will give it is that it does get pretty loud, for one 12 in a custom box it does get decently loud, but like anything kicker, they need a huge box to get there... two 12's requires right around 4 cubes all together, which is a huge box just for 12's. But if you're on a budget and looking for something that's cheap and sounds half decent I would stay away from anything kicker, though they do get loud they just pump out loud muddy bass and wouldn't recommend them for any SQ design. Their is plenty other brands out there with lower end model subs that cost the same as this, and would blow this sub out of the water, look at brands like sundown, soundqubed, RE audio, Dayton audio, Skar audio, alpine and phoenix gold just to name a few. The Good:
* The sound quality out of these suckers is amazing. * The ear pressure from these headphones is really high, probably to make the isolation as strong as it is. It's well distributed, but these get uncomfortable after a few hours.

I really wanted to like the Sony SRS77 speaker. the speaker has lots of great features (Bluetooth, NFC, and Airplay), it is very attractive, PLUS it has loads of power to help belt out your music. Unfortunately, the sound performance does not match the specs. I know a few others have graded it highly, but for me.... not so much.

In my tests I compared it to the Harmon Onyx and the Fluance Fi50 (both of which are less expensive) and both speakers sounded much better than the Sony SRS77 (although neither of those speakers are considered *portable* with built in batteries). In fact, the difference was so great I began to wonder if I got a bad copy of the Sony.

Notes -

Sound Performance - Surprisingly shallow - it does not have much pop on the low end nor does it feature a strong high end. Music with strong bass notes will fall noticeably flat (like Meghan Trainor's "All about the Bass"). I find that music seems to be pushed into the mid-tones.

Sound Volume - Again, surprising low for a 40 watt speaker. The Sony is loud enough to fill a medium sized room, and even, the area around a swimming pool, but it will never be considered thumping. However, with its emphasis on the mid-tones if it were much louder the sound would not be pleasant.

Battery - I am not sure of the life, but it does seem to have a beefy Li ion battery in it... this is definitely worth a few browny points since the SRS77 is truly hand portable (although you may want to forget about taking it in your suitcase). Personally, I prefer the Creative Sounds Roar, in every way possible (and it is half the price).

Connectivity - should be a plus since the speaker connects via bluetooth, NFC, and over your wifi network using AirPlay. I had some issues connecting via bluetooth after I updated the speaker. In fact, I had to manually reset the speaker and wipe out the update before it would work again. In theory (and practice) you can connect your computer and a multitude of other devices.

Expand ability - the Sony SRS 77 can be expanded and used in conjunction with other speakers around your home. This feature doesn't excite me... and I did not try to expand the set-up.

App- I am not sure why some of the speaker manufacturers try to entice us to use their (often) clunky apps? I downloaded this one... and I guess it is ok... but honestly, do you really need much more than the music app on your iphone ... is there really a need for a 3rd party app?

Final verdict. I like some of the connectivity features, but I have a hard time getting past that the Creative Sounds Roar is half the price, sounds better, and much more portable.... the Sony might be a little louder, but not much. Also compared to stationary units like the Fluance fi50 and the Harmon Kardan Onyx there really isn't a comparison.

I purchased this speaker because I was looking for something that was both portable and durable. I also wanted good sound quality, but most of all, the unit needed to be waterproof and able to stand up to the rigors of cycling and kayaking. I do a lot of cycling (road biking mostly) and Kayaking down rivers. For our more leisurely rides, the group likes to have some music added in. Bluetooth is the go-to technology for this, since wires can be a real nuisance in situations like this where the wires may get wet, or tangled up in the bike otherwise.

That being said, I've been very happy with the Geega waterproof speaker.

FORM FACTOR
Nice and small, this form factor is pleasing both for functionality and for design. The cube design makes it very easy to strap onto the rear rack of my road bike, and the lanyard attachment makes it incredibly easy to secure to the kayak.

WATERPROOF
Better yet, if it does happen to fall off the kayak - Who cares? The unit is waterproof and I can attest to this as it *has* fallen in the water and I have also used it on the rack in my shower. It has been splashed, rained on, and fully submerged. No issues yet!

VOLUME
The sound quality is decent, especially being so small and bluetooth. It's also quite loud. I usually have it on max volume when cycling due to wind and traffic noise, but I don't need to use nearly full volume when using in the shower or kayaking at a slower pace. These clip on headphones sound quite stunning for the price.

Pros:
They sound great for how small and light they are and are certainly good sounding for the price.
The clips on them work well for running and exercise, but there are a few problems with them.
They're comfortable for at least an hour because of the light weight and reasonable clamping strength, but might get slightly uncomfortable after multiple hours.

Cons:
Clips will lose their strength over time and will eventually developed a click with clipping them if you extend them even slightly too much.
Foam develops wear fairly quickly and can be a bit scratchy.
Noticeable sound leakage.

Overall:
These sound good, and are acceptably comfortable. If you're at least somewhat gentle with them and don't mind the sound leakage I would recommend these to you.
